In Samuel’s time, Israel faced external threats and internal discord, and the judges only provided a fleeting sense of security. Israel wanted a king. The book of 1 Samuel records Israel’s transition from a federation of tribes to a centralized kingdom. Saul, Israel’s first king, did not remain faithful to God. But then God chose David as king, and God’s plan to save Israel—and the world—began to unfold.

Setting

Moses had predicted that the people of Israel would ask for a king to reign over them (Deu 17.14–20). God spelled out the requirements for a king (Deu 17.15) but also warned of the evils commonly associated with human kings. A king would want many horses, numerous wives, and large sums of gold and silver (Deu 17.16–17). To mitigate these tendencies, God instructed that each king of Israel must study God’s law (Deu 17.18–20).

Throughout the days of the judges, Israel’s tribes lacked unity (see Jdg 17.1–21). By Samuel’s time, Israel was looking for a king to unite the nation and protect it from internal and external threats.

Gideon, who judged Israel about one hundred years before the time of Samuel, had acted a lot like a king. Gideon rejected the invitation to inaugurate a hereditary dynasty (Jdg 8.22–23), but he began to act like a king: He accumulated gold and used it to build a religious idol (Jdg 8.24–27), he took many wives (Jdg 8.30), and he even named one of his sons Abimelech, which means “my father is king” (Jdg 8.31). Gideon acted like the kind of king God wanted Israel never to have. A monarchy would give an imperfect human even more control than the judges exercised. 1 Samuel records the trouble that surrounded Israel’s first king, Saul, and begins to outline God’s unfolding plan to establish an eternal kingship through the line of David.

Summary

In 1Sa 1.1–7, Samuel emerges as a judge and prophet of God. Samuel was born to a devout woman named Hannah, who had previously been barren (1Sa 1.1–23). As a young child, Samuel, a Levite, (1Ch 6.33–34) became an apprentice in the Tabernacle under the supervision of Eli the priest (1Sa 1.24–1Sa 3.18). Likely trained to be a Tabernacle assistant, Samuel instead became a prophet with a growing reputation (1Sa 3.19–1Sa 4.1a). Evidently, he was not yet prominent in Israel’s national life when the Philistines harassed the Israelites and captured the Ark of the Covenant (1Sa 4.1–1Sa 7.2), as he is absent from that narrative. In chapter 1Sa 7.1–17, Samuel reappears, calling Israel to repentance; and acting as a judge, he drove out the Philistine oppressors.

Samuel’s leadership as Levite, prophet, and judge spanned all spheres of public life. Yet his sons did not prove worthy of carrying on in his place (1Sa 8.1–3), so Israel asked Samuel to appoint a king to lead them, just like the other nations. Samuel was outspoken in his opposition (1Sa 8.10–21), yet the Lord instructed Samuel to anoint Saul as king (chs 1Sa 9.1–10). In his farewell address, Samuel reminded the Israelites of God’s power and care for them (ch 1Sa 12.1–25). He wanted them to realize their sin in asking for a king rather than trusting in the Lord.

Initially, Saul was a good king. He defeated the neighboring Ammonites and saved the city of Jabesh-gilead from doom (ch 1Sa 11.1–15). But Saul soon proved, by his disobedience to God, that he was unworthy to be Israel’s king (chs 1Sa 13.1–23, 1Sa 15.1–35). By contrast, Saul’s noble son Jonathan seemed to be an ideal successor (1Sa 14.1–52). But Jonathan would not succeed Saul, because God had different plans (chs 1Sa 16.1–31). God instructed Samuel to anoint David secretly as Saul’s successor while Saul was still king (1Sa 16.1–13).

Saul’s relationship with David was good at first, thanks in part to David’s musical gifts (1Sa 16.14–23). However, David’s success with Goliath (1Sa 17.1–58) made Saul jealous (1Sa 18.6–16), and Saul tried to eliminate the threat David posed to his kingship. He brought David into his family by marriage to provide greater opportunities to kill him (1Sa 18.17–29). He attacked David directly (1Sa 19.1–10) and executed anybody who harbored David (chs 1Sa 21.1–22). Yet all of Saul’s attempts to eliminate David proved unsuccessful.

Both Saul and Jonathan died in battle against the Philistines (1Sa 31.1–6). This paved the way for David to begin his reign, though not without further difficulties (see 2Sa 1.1–1Sa 5.5).

Authorship

The title “Samuel” comes from the important role Samuel played in Israel’s transition to a monarchy, not from the book’s authorship. Samuel could have written parts of 1 Samuel, but he could not have written any part of 2 Samuel, as his death is recorded in 1Sa 25.1. The final editor of 1 Samuel is never identified.

Composition

The books of 1–2 Samuel were originally one book. The translators of the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) divided it into two books, 1–2 Kingdoms. Later Hebrew tradition also divided the book but retained the name Samuel, as do most English versions.

Some scholars contend that 1–2 Samuel (along with 1–2 Kings, also one book originally) were created from a variety of sources during or after the Babylonian Exile (586–538 BC). Multiple sources were doubtless used in 1–2 Samuel—for example, Samuel, Nathan, and Gad all chronicled events from the life of David (1Ch 29.29). The inspired author of 1–2 Samuel would have made use of such information. However, the book also could have been near its final form during or shortly after the reign of Solomon (971–931 BC).

Shortly after Judah’s exile to Babylon, 1–2 Samuel was incorporated into the larger body of material that also includes Joshua, Judges, and 1–2 Kings. This section of Scripture traces Israel’s sacred history, beginning with blessing (conquering the land) and ending with judgment (losing the land). It explains to an audience in exile how their grave misfortune came about.

Manuscripts

The text of 1–2 Samuel that is found in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, 200s BC) is different in many places from the Hebrew (Masoretic) text (around AD 1000). The Hebrew texts of Samuel in the Dead Sea Scrolls (around 250–50 BC) found at Qumran agree in some places with the Septuagint, in other places with the Masoretic Text. In still other places the Dead Sea texts have their own readings. Readers will encounter notes such as “Hebrew lacks . . . ” or “Greek reads . . . ” more frequently in 1–2 Samuel than in other Old Testament books. However, few of these textual variants significantly alter the meaning.

Meaning and Message

The emphasis on kingship in 1 Samuel first appears in Hannah’s prayer (see 1Sa 2.10). The idea that Israel would have a king was as old as God’s promise to Abraham and Sarah (Gen 17.6, Gen 17.16). God neither mandated nor forbade a monarchy but only spelled out the excesses from which Israel’s kings must abstain (see Deu 17.14–20).

During the period of the judges, Israel changed dramatically for the worse—both spiritually and nationally. This steady disintegration reaches a horrible climax in Jdg 17.1–21. The book of Judges hints that, to help correct this decline, Israel needed a king. Israel’s greatest threat was not the Philistines or any other predatory neighbor but Israel itself and its breaking of the covenant. Israel needed a king to guard the covenant, which the pre-monarchical order had put at risk.

If the king’s responsibility was to administer the covenant (Deu 17.18–20), the prophet’s duty was to interpret its stipulations. For this reason, the prophet Samuel protected his divinely authorized claim over kings with a holy zeal. Not only did Samuel anoint Israel’s first two kings (1Sa 10.1; 1Sa 16.13), but he was also compelled to censure the king when he stepped outside of covenantal boundaries (1Sa 13.8–15; 1Sa 15.10–33).

Saul did not have the character or integrity needed to lead Israel into a successful, God-honoring monarchy. Saul was not fated to fall, as though he had no control over his decisions. In fact, God wanted him to be a good king and made every provision for that to happen (such as changing his heart and giving him his Spirit). But God does not force righteousness, holiness, or obedience. His grace is persuasive but not coercive.

Despite the deep disappointments of the era of the judges and the early monarchy, God’s sovereign control over Israel’s history is demonstrated in several ways: (1) A once-barren woman gave birth to Samuel, God’s agent for the transition to monarchy (ch 1Sa 1.1–28); (2) a devastating Philistine victory became a Philistine defeat without human participation (chs 1Sa 4.1–6); (3) the king whom the people demanded became God’s anointed (chs 1Sa 8.1–10); (4) this king was rejected by God for his unfaithfulness (chs 1Sa 13.1–23, 1Sa 15.1–35); and (5) the eighth son of an obscure family, a man after God’s own heart, was chosen as the future king of Israel (ch 1Sa 16.1–23).

Unlike Saul’s rule, David’s kingship over Israel lasted, and one of his descendants later became the sovereign King of the whole world. Jesus is the final heir to David’s throne (Joh 7.42; Rev 5.5; Rev 11.15). He perpetuates his ancestor’s virtues but never exhibits his flaws. Jesus is the world’s perfect and eternal Shepherd and King.

Elkanah was a Levite (1Ch 6.22–27). After the conquest of the Promised Land, the Levites were given towns in the territories of the other Israelite tribes, including Ephraim (Jos 21.20). • Elkanah’s hometown was Ramah (1Sa 2.11). This location should not be confused with the Ramah in the tribal area of Benjamin (see Jos 18.25; Jdg 19.13; Mat 2.18). • The region of Zuph was named after one of Elkanah’s ancestors, a Levite of the clan of Kohath (1Ch 6.35). Saul first met Samuel in Zuph while searching for his father’s donkeys (1Sa 9.5). • Elkanah’s lengthy genealogy suggests he was socially prominent.
Hardly an instance exists in Scripture where a man’s simultaneous marriage to two wives did not produce serious friction (1Sa 1.6–7; Gen 16.1–16; Gen 21.1–34; Gen 29.1–35).

Elkanah made this trip each year; the law required that people attend three annual festivals (Exo 23.14–17). • According to God’s law, Israelites were to sacrifice at God’s chosen sanctuary (Deu 12.1–28). From the days of Joshua (Jos 18.1) through Samuel’s era, God’s sanctuary—the Tabernacle—was at Shiloh, a town in Ephraim some 8.5 miles north of Bethel en route to Shechem. King David eventually moved it to Jerusalem (2Sa 6.1–23). • the LORD of Heaven’s Armies: Throughout the Hebrew Old Testament, God is often referred to as Yahweh Tseba’oth or ’Elohim Tseba’oth. Traditionally, these titles have been translated “LORD of hosts” and “God of hosts.” The term “hosts” (Hebrew tseba’oth, traditionally “sabaoth”) usually means “armies.” It can refer to human armies, such as the armies of Israel (e.g., 1Sa 17.45), or foreign armies sent to fulfill the Lord’s purposes (e.g., Isa 9.11–13). However, most often it refers to God’s angelic armies sent from heaven to do his bidding and wage war on earth (e.g., 2Ki 6.17). This designation anticipates God’s role as a mighty warrior in the episode involving the Ark of the Covenant and the Philistines (1Sa 4.1–6).
sacrifice . . . portions of the meat: Certain sacrifices involved sharing part of the sacrificial animal in a communal meal (see Lev 7.11–34).
the Tabernacle: Also called “the Temple of the LORD” in 1Sa 1.9. These designations reflect that the Tabernacle, a portable structure, served as the central sanctuary at Shiloh.
the Tabernacle: Literally the Temple of the LORD. Solomon’s Temple had not yet been constructed, so the word Temple here means the Lord’s sanctuary.
Theme: Vows to God

Hannah’s vow was a promise to give the child back to the Lord as a Nazirite (see Num 6.1–21). Hannah might have hoped that her child would be another Samson (cp. Jdg 13.1–25), a deliverer of God’s people.
Some people might have used the feast times at Shiloh as an occasion to get drunk rather than to worship. Eli mistakenly assumed Hannah was another drunken reveler (cp. Act 2.13–15).

wicked woman (Hebrew a daughter of Belial): An expression used to describe a worthless person. Belial (“worthlessness”) is later used as a name for Satan (2Co 6.15). In Hebrew, a son of or daughter of a quality is a person who exemplifies that quality.

A blessing was more than mere wishful thinking. It was often God’s means of conferring a real benefit (see, e.g., Gen 27.1–40; Gen 28.1–4; Gen 32.22–32; Gen 48.1–1Sa 49.28). Because this blessing from God’s high priest provided assurance that Hannah’s prayer would be answered, she was no longer sad.
Profile: Samuel
until the boy is weaned: Hannah would have nursed Samuel two to four years.
Elkanah could have overridden Hannah’s promise (Num 30.12–14), but instead he affirmed and supported it.

Hannah’s Prayer of Praise celebrates Samuel’s dedication to the Lord’s service by rejoicing in God’s uniqueness (1Sa 2.1–2), his ability to reverse fortunes (1Sa 2.3–9), and his ability to strengthen his chosen king (1Sa 2.10). Like Mary’s Song of Praise (Luk 1.46–55), Hannah’s prayer emphasizes God bringing down the rich and powerful and exalting the poor and the downtrodden (1Sa 2.7–8; Luk 1.52–53). David’s prayer in 2Sa 22.1–51 is another beautiful proclamation of God’s saving power as it relates to his chosen king (1Sa 2.10). The rich, unrighteous rulers of the land (Eli, Saul, Herod) will be brought down, while the leaders who fulfill God’s purposes (Samuel, David, Jesus) will be exalted.

made me strong: Literally has exalted my horn; cp. 1Sa 2.10. The horn of a powerful animal, such as an ox or bull, was a symbol of strength that was held high in triumph after defeating an enemy (cp. 1Ki 22.11).

no one besides you: David responded similarly after receiving God’s promises concerning his kingship (2Sa 7.22). • Rock (cp. 2Sa 22.2–3, 2Sa 22.32): God provides stability and security for those who trust in him.
proud and haughty: Peninnah typified this attitude (see 1Sa 1.6–7). Hannah, by contrast, was humbly dependent on God.
Hannah celebrated God’s sovereign ability to radically reverse human circumstances.
those who were starving are now full: Cp. 1Sa 1.7, 1Sa 1.18. • The phrase seven children poetically means that the childless woman would be blessed with a house full of children (cp. 1Sa 2.21).

all the earth is the LORD’s: God, the creator and ruler of all things, is able to change circumstances (1Sa 2.4–8), protect the faithful (1Sa 2.9), judge the wicked, and empower his anointed king (1Sa 2.10).

The king was to fulfill the descriptions of 1Sa 2.4–9 by using his God-given power to care for the oppressed, the hungry, and the barren (see Psa 72.1–4, Psa 72.12–14; Pro 31.8–9). • he increases the strength: See study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 2.1. • anointed one (Hebrew mashiakh): This climax to Hannah’s prayer is prophetic both of Israel’s anointed kings and of God’s supreme Anointed King—the Messiah, Jesus Christ (see 1Sa 12.3–5; 1Sa 24.6, 1Sa 24.10; Psa 132.17; Dan 9.25–26).
Profile: Eli

scoundrels (Hebrew sons of Belial): See study note on 1Sa 1.16. • had no respect for (literally did not know) the LORD: Although they were priests among God’s people, they did not acknowledge God or seek to abide by his will (cp. Jer 2.8).
The priests were supposed to receive their portion of the meat only after it had been boiled (see Num 6.19). Eli’s sons disregarded God’s instructions (1Sa 2.13–14, 1Sa 2.17).
God’s law stipulated that the sacrificial animal’s fat was the Lord’s portion and had to be burned on the altar first (Lev 3.3–17).

The clause Samuel . . . served the LORD describes the ritual service of Levites and priests (see, e.g., Num 3.4; Num 8.19, Num 8.24; Deu 18.7). Like Eli’s sons, Samuel was a Levite (see study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 1.1). But unlike Eli’s sons, he lived up to his calling. • He wore a linen garment like that of a priest, as did the priests who ministered in the sanctuary (see study note on 1Sa 22.18).
Eli would bless: Blessing was one of the functions of a priest (Num 6.23–27; Deu 10.8; 1Ch 23.13). See study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 1.17–18.
Eli’s weak attempts to change his sons’ behavior (cp. 1Sa 2.29) indicate that he had raised them without discipline (1Sa 3.13).
seducing . . . women: Eli’s sons had probably been influenced by Canaanite religious practices, which included sex as part of the ritual. • who assisted at the entrance: See Exo 38.8.

God (or the judges; Hebrew ’elohim): The Hebrew verb translated mediate is plural here, and when ’elohim means “God,” it often appears with a singular verb. In addition, some ancient translations render ’elohim as “judges” here. If that is the correct translation, then the judges would mediate for the guilty party in a common human court. However, many Hebrew scholars believe that ’elohim should never be translated “judges.” If this is the case, in what sense could God mediate for the guilty party? Possibly Eli considered the court verdict to come directly from God. God might work through his revealed law or other circumstances to either acquit or convict an individual charged with wrongdoing. Or Eli might have been referring to the sacrificial system. • The sexual immorality (1Sa 2.22) and gluttony (1Sa 2.12–17) of Eli’s sons were sins against the LORD because they were corrupting Israel’s worship of him. No one can intercede for sinners who rebel so completely against God’s will (cp. Mat 12.31). • Eli’s sons did not listen to their father because the Lord had already begun to punish them by hardening their hearts (cp. Exo 4.21; Exo 7.3; Exo 8.15–32; Exo 10.27; Exo 11.10).
As children, both Samuel and Jesus possessed extraordinary qualities (1Sa 2.21; see also Luk 2.40, Luk 2.52). Samuel was one of Christ’s forerunners.
Man of God is another name for a prophet (1Sa 9.6; 1Ki 13.1; 2Ki 1.9).
By failing to stop his sons’ wickedness, Eli showed contempt for God’s sacrifices and offerings. Eli benefited from his sons’ activities, and God held Eli responsible for letting them continue.

that your branch of the tribe of Levi would always be my priests: See Exo 29.9; Num 25.13. God would honor another of Aaron’s descendants (see study note on 1Sa 2.35) and despise Eli’s family, removing them from the priesthood (1Sa 2.31–35).
live out their days: In the Old Testament, a short life often expresses God’s disfavor, while long life represents God’s blessing (cp. Gen 15.15; 1Ki 3.14; Psa 91.16).
a faithful priest: Zadok and his descendants later replaced Eli’s family in the priesthood (1Ki 2.26–27, 1Ki 2.35).

messages . . . were very rare . . . visions were quite uncommon: God was not disclosing his will through prophets or priests, so the period was spiritually dark. However, that darkness was about to end when God communicated with Samuel (1Sa 3.2–1Sa 4.1).
Eli was almost blind, both physically and spiritually (1Sa 3.1).

The priests were responsible for keeping the lamp of God burning through the night (Exo 27.20–21; Exo 30.7–8). • That Samuel was sleeping . . . near the Ark symbolizes his nearness to God’s presence and purpose, in contrast to Eli and his sons.

Samuel did not yet know the LORD: He lacked direct experience of the Lord. In contrast, Eli’s sons did not know the Lord (see study note on 1Sa 2.12) in that they were morally and spiritually deficient.
Eli realized: Despite his many shortcomings, Eli was not completely without spiritual insight.

The doubling of the name calls attention to the seriousness of the moment (cp. Gen 22.11; Exo 3.4; Mat 27.46; Luk 22.31; Act 9.4). • Samuel omits “LORD” (see 1Sa 3.9) from his response either out of reverence for the name or because of a lingering uncertainty about who was speaking.
The phrase a shocking thing conveys the magnitude and severity of God’s judgment. God’s actions would also be of national significance for Israel (cp. 2Ki 21.12; Jer 19.3).
my threats: See 1Sa 2.27–36.
his sons are blaspheming God: They were expressing contempt for God through their actions. • hasn’t disciplined them: Eli rebuked his sons (1Sa 2.23–25), but he did not restrain them.

Neither blood sacrifices nor offerings would be acceptable on behalf of Eli and his sons. The offerings of Lev 4.1–5 were for sins committed inadvertently or unintentionally, whereas the sins of Eli and his sons were deliberate and rebellious.
Samuel was afraid to tell Eli of God’s plans for him and his family either because he respected Eli’s position or he feared for his own safety.
proved to be reliable: Samuel was an authentic prophet (1Sa 3.20; see Deu 18.21–22).

The whole nation, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, acknowledged that Samuel was God’s prophet. • confirmed as a prophet: The reliability of Samuel’s message (1Sa 3.19) made it evident that God was speaking through him.
The LORD continued to appear: God reopened the lines of communication with Israel through Samuel (cp. 1Sa 3.1). • Shiloh: See study note on 1Sa 1.3.
The crisis surrounding the Ark of the Covenant demonstrated Israel’s need for Samuel’s leadership and fulfilled prophecies about Eli and his sons (1Sa 3.11–14).

the Philistines: See “The Philistines” Profile. • The exact location of Ebenezer is unknown. It was probably just east of Aphek (see also 1Sa 7.12 and corresponding study note 1Sa 7.12). • Aphek was west of Shiloh, well inland and well north of Philistine territory. By camping there, the Philistines might have been trying to seize more Israelite territory.
Theme: The Ark of the Covenant

The Israelites were often defeated in war because of the sin of one individual or the entire nation (Jos 7.1–26). In this defeat, no one inquired whether sin was the cause; apparently no one had even asked the Lord whether they should engage the Philistines in the first place (cp. 1Ch 14.13–16). Instead, the Israelites treated the Ark, the most sacred symbol of the Lord’s presence, as a charm to ward off misfortune. Carrying the Ark into battle was not necessarily wrong (cp. Jos 6.2–21), but neither would this act ensure God’s blessing and victory.

LORD of Heaven’s Armies: See study note on 1Sa 1.3. • enthroned between the cherubim: A representation of God’s glorious presence hovered over the Ark in the Most Holy Place (God’s “throne room”). • The involvement of Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, foreshadows the disaster that ensued (see 1Sa 3.11–14).
Like the Israelites, the Philistines regarded the Ark as a powerful talisman (see 1Sa 4.2–3) and believed that its presence in battle would mean sure disaster for them.

the same gods who destroyed the Egyptians: The Philistines, who worshiped many gods, knew of the Lord’s power. Yet they knew nothing of his nature as the one true God. • destroyed . . . with plagues: The Lord later showed his power against the Philistines similarly (see 1Sa 5.6–1Sa 6.6).
30,000 was more than seven times as many as haddied previously without the Ark (1Sa 4.2). The Israelites learned the hard way that the Ark was not a talisman to ward off misfortune.

That the Ark . . . was captured was devastating to the Israelites (1Sa 4.12–22). • The deaths of Hophni and Phinehas fulfilled the Lord’s word to Eli (1Sa 2.34). Although they are the only casualties named, they were not the only Israelites who had sinned (see 1Sa 7.3–6).
had torn his clothes and put dust on his head: This description indicates grief and loss (e.g., Jos 7.6; 2Sa 1.2; 2Sa 15.32; Job 2.12).
blind: See 1Sa 3.2 and corresponding study note 1Sa 3.2.

Eli fell backward: Either he was startled or he had a heart attack when he heard the message. Eli’s fatal fall symbolizes his family’s fall from the priesthood and the end of the abomination that his sons began (1Sa 2.12–17). • Israel’s judge: Priesthood and judgeship were not incompatible (cp. Exo 18.13–26; Deu 17.8–13). Samuel replaced Eli as Israel’s judge and provided leadership that Eli had failed to provide (see 1Sa 7.12–17). • The phrase for forty years incorporates Eli’s career into the conceptual and temporal framework of the book of Judges (cp. Jdg 3.11; Jdg 5.31; Jdg 8.28; Jdg 13.1).

The name Ichabod contains the Hebrew word kabod (glory; see Exo 24.15–17). A similar word is used to describe Eli in 1Sa 4.18 (Hebrew kabed, “heavy”). The disappearance of the Ark parallels the demise of Eli’s house. Although the Israelites experienced a stunning loss of divine glory and protection (cp. Eze 8.1–10; Luk 19.41–44; Luk 21.20–24), God’s glorious presence would subsequently return to his people (1Sa 6.1–21; cp. Eze 43.1–8).
Ebenezer: See study note on 1Sa 4.1b 1Sa 4.1. • Ashdod, one of the five important Philistine cities (see 1Sa 6.17), was located along the same major trade highway (the Great Trunk Road) as Aphek.
Theme: Canaanite Religion

Dagon was one of the Philistines’ gods (see Jdg 16.23–24). The name could be related to the Hebrew dag (“fish”), an appropriate name for a god of seafaring people. More likely, it reflects the Hebrew dagan (“grain”), suggesting a fertility or agriculture god.
his head and hands had broken off: A symbol of God’s supremacy over the idol (1Sa 5.7; see also 1Sa 17.51).

step on its threshold: While the Philistines might have believed that Dagon’s amputations resulted from their failure to honor the god properly, the true failure was in worshiping an idol rather than honoring the one true God (Isa 44.6–20).

tumors: The Hebrew term can mean simply “swellings.” A possible alternative translation is “hemorrhoids.” They were possibly the fatal buboes of bubonic plague, which attack the lower body, especially the rectal area. Rats are known carriers of the plague.

rulers (or overlords): Each of the five major Philistine cities had its own ruler (1Sa 6.16–18). • Move it: Despite the obvious danger, the Philistines relished their captured trophy enough to relocate it rather than return it. • Gath, one of the five major Philistine cities, was nearby.
God often used great panic to incapacitate and overwhelm Israel’s enemies (1Sa 14.15, 1Sa 14.20; Deu 7.23; Eze 22.5; Amo 3.9).
Ekron, another of the five major Philistine cities (see 1Sa 6.17), was just five miles north of Gath.
priests and diviners: Divination was a part of Philistine religion (cp. 1Sa 28.7; Deu 18.10–14).

It is unlikely the Philistines were aware of Israelite worship regulations. A Philistine guilt offering would have been a payment to the deity in an attempt to avert his wrath (contrast the notion of atonement from Lev 16.1–34).
rats: See study note on 1Sa 5.6.
The Philistines had thought they could overcome the Lord by fighting harder (1Sa 4.9). They had defeated the Israelites, but they now realized that they could not defeat Israel’s God.
shut their calves away: If the cows went against their maternal nature and left their calves to take the Ark to Israel, it would prove that the plague was from Israel’s God (1Sa 6.9).
Beth-shemesh was the closest Israelite town to Ekron (1Sa 5.10).
Harvesting wheat was usually done in May or June.
This burnt offering could have been for forgiveness of sin (see 1Sa 7.9–10; Lev 1.3–17), but it was more likely a freewill expression of love or thanksgiving (see Lev 22.18–22).
Providentially, the Ark had arrived in Beth-shemesh (1Sa 6.13), which was a Levite city (Jos 21.13–16). The men of the tribe of Levi who lived there could safely move the Ark (see Num 4.15).

guilt offering: See study note on 1Sa 6.3. • Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron: These five major Philistine cities were located on or near the Great Trunk Road. This major ancient trade route connected Egypt with Mesopotamia via the coastal plain of Canaan. Each city was governed by a king-like ruler (1Sa 6.16).

seventy men: Beth-shemesh was a small village. • because they looked into the Ark: Physical contact with the Ark was prohibited (Num 4.15; 2Sa 6.6–8), as was looking inside it (Num 4.20). Those who were killed lacked reverence for God’s holiness.

Who is able to stand? Even God’s people were not immune to his wrath when his holiness was violated. • Where can we send the Ark? When faced with God’s holiness, the Israelites echoed the distress of the pagan Philistines (1Sa 6.2).
Kiriath-jearim was nearby, about ten miles northeast of Beth-shemesh.

The men of Kiriath-jearim who transported the Ark and Eleazar were probably Levites (see 1Sa 6.15; Num 1.47–51). • in charge of it: The same verb describes the Levites’ duty of guarding the Tabernacle (Num 1.53; Num 3.7).
Twenty years covers the time until Samuel assembled the people at Mizpah (1Sa 7.5–6). David later brought the Ark to Jerusalem (2Sa 6.1–19).
The change in the people’s standing with God, not the presence of the Ark (see 1Sa 4.3–11), led Israel to victory against the Philistines.

People cannot expect God’s blessing unless they get rid of what is contrary to his will (see Gen 35.2; Jos 24.14). • Ashtoreth was the Canaanite goddess of fertility associated with Baal (1Sa 7.4). Worship of Canaanite deities was an ongoing problem throughout Israel’s history. The people started worshiping idols during the twenty-year period mentioned in 1Sa 7.2, or perhaps they had done so ever since the days of the judges (1Sa 8.8; Jdg 6.25; cp. Amo 5.25–26). Israel’s devastating defeat by the Philistines was due not only to the sins of Eli’s two sons but to several generations of unfaithfulness to God.

Mizpah was an administrative center and rallying point for the nation (see 1Sa 7.16; 1Sa 10.17; Jdg 20.1). • I will pray . . . for you: Eli’s question in 1Sa 2.25 is answered here; Samuel was the intercessor Israel needed.

drew water . . . poured it out: This type of ceremony is not mentioned elsewhere in the Old Testament. • At times Israelites went without food to express grief or to seek the Lord’s favor (2Sa 1.12; 2Sa 12.22–23; 1Ki 21.27; Ezr 8.21–23; Neh 9.1; Est 4.3, Est 4.16; Joe 2.12; cp. Luk 2.37; Act 13.2–3; Act 14.23). • To have Samuel as Israel’s judge was refreshing compared to Eli’s failed leadership (see 1Sa 4.18 and corresponding study note 1Sa 4.18) and the leadership of some other judges (e.g., Gideon, Jdg 8.22–27; Jephthah, Jdg 11.30–1Sa 12.7; and Samson, Jdg 13.1–1Sa 16.21).
The whole burnt offering was probably for forgiveness of sin (see Lev 1.1–4). • The LORD answered with a forceful thunderclap (1Sa 7.10).
voice of thunder: See 1Sa 2.10. God often used similar tactics to throw Israel’s enemies into confusion and defeat them (e.g., Exo 14.24; Exo 23.27; Jos 10.10; Jdg 4.15).

Ebenezer: The location of this stone memorial is unknown. The Philistines had defeated Israel and captured the Ark at a place with the same name (1Sa 4.1; 1Sa 5.1). Samuel erected this memorial to commemorate God’s help in turning the tide against the Philistine attacks.
The Philistines were quiet for some time—until Saul became king (see 1Sa 13.5). • God’s powerful hand, not Samuel’s giftedness, was the key factor in Israel’s deliverance from the Philistines.

The Amorites had inhabited Canaan and the region east of the Jordan before Israel’s conquest of the Promised Land (see Gen 15.16; Deu 3.8; Jos 2.10). Some Amorites remained in the area after the conquest (see 2Sa 21.2).
judge for the rest of his life: Once Saul became king (ch 1Sa 10.1–27), Samuel’s role was more judicial than military.

Bethel and Mizpah were places of national assembly in the judges era (Jdg 20.1, Jdg 20.18, Jdg 20.26; Jdg 21.1–2). Bethel’s significance went back to the days of Abraham (Gen 12.8; Gen 13.3–4; Gen 28.10–22; Gen 35.1–15). • Gilgal, located near Jericho, had been a sacred place since Joshua’s day (Jos 4.19–24; Jos 5.2–10). From this circuit, Samuel influenced “all the people of Israel” (1Sa 10.17).
Ramah was Samuel’s hometown (see 1Sa 1.1).

During Israel’s transition to a monarchy, neither God (1Sa 8.7–9) nor Samuel (1Sa 12.1–25) was pleased by the people’s demand for a king. Saul, the first king (chs 1Sa 9.1–11), failed in his role (chs 1Sa 13.1–31) and fulfilled Samuel’s warnings (see 1Sa 8.10–18; cp. 1Sa 16.1–13).
Theme: Monarchy
Samuel’s two oldest sons functioned as judges in Beersheba, fifty miles south of their father’s home.
they were not like their father: They were more like Eli’s two sons (1Sa 2.12–17). Their corruption was a primary reason the era of the judges ended.

you are now old, and your sons are not like you: Judges tended to be local leaders; kings, as national leaders, were more capable of uniting a whole nation in times of crisis (1Sa 8.20). However, a spiritual problem underlay the request for a king (1Sa 8.7–8). • Other nations, such as Egypt and Sumer, had monarchies for almost 2,000 years before Samuel’s time.
Samuel was displeased: He probably felt personally rejected (1Sa 8.7).

Do everything they say: God rarely instructed a prophet to heed the voice of the errant populace. The will of the people and the will of God would converge in King David (see 2Sa 7.8–17). • they are rejecting me: Their rejection of judgeship was a deeper rejection of God’s rule and sovereignty (see also 1Sa 12.1–17).

followed other gods: The people’s request for a king was tantamount to idolatry. Israel’s monarchy was a divine concession rather than a divine gift. Kingship or any other human institution becomes idolatrous when it replaces trust in God.
These verses list the disadvantages of kingship. Each sentence begins with something the king would take. A king would be a confiscator, not just a protector.
While the people wanted a king to judge them, Samuel warned that the king would reign over them. They wanted a leader but received a ruler.
The king would take people as well as possessions.

A tenth of the harvest was already required as a sacred donation to support God’s Temple and servants (Deu 12.6, Deu 12.17–18; Deu 14.22–29; Deu 26.12–15). The king would demand an additional tenth, a burdensome amount given the uncertainties of agriculture.
you will be his slaves: By demanding a king, the people whose ancestors had once been slaves in Egypt were risking a new enslavement (cp. 1Ki 12.1–20).
The people would beg for relief as their ancestors had done in Egypt under another punishing and exacting ruler (see Exo 3.7).

God had set Israel apart from the nations (Lev 20.26; Num 23.9). By insisting on a king and desiring to be like the nations, they were rejecting God’s plan (see 1Sa 8.5–7; cp. Deu 17.14). • judge us and lead us into battle: Kings performed three basic functions: (1) waging offensive and defensive war, (2) administering law, and (3) ensuring economic well-being.
repeated to the LORD: The role of a prophet included bringing the people’s case before God (cp. Num 27.5).
give them a king: See study note on 1Sa 8.7; cp. Rom 1.24–26.

Saul’s rise to power involved a threefold sequence: (1) his secret anointing by Samuel (1Sa 9.1–1Sa 10.16), (2) his selection by lot (1Sa 10.17–27), and (3) his victory over the Ammonites (1Sa 11.1–15). See also study note on 1Sa 13.1–1Sa 16.13.
influential man named Kish: Saul came from a wealthy family.
Profile: Saul
Saul’s mere appearance—most handsome . . . taller than anyone else—inspired loyalty among the people (see 1Sa 10.23; cp. 1Sa 16.12; 2Sa 14.25–26).
Zuph, which was probably located in Ephraim, was Samuel’s home region (1Sa 1.1). God’s providence led Saul there.
The phrase man of God was used to describe a prophet (1Sa 2.27; also Deu 33.1; Jos 14.6; 1Ki 13.1–32).

anything to offer him: Evidently, it was customary to take a gift when one sought the help of a prophet (cp. 1Ki 14.2–3; 2Ki 5.5, 2Ki 5.15; 2Ki 8.8). Some false prophets demanded gifts in return for their services (Mic 3.11). Saul’s concern might reflect the spiritual ignorance of thinking that advice from a prophet of God could be purchased (Act 8.20).

Leaders of a community would normally convene for business at the town gates (cp. Rut 4.1–2). • take part in a public sacrifice: Samuel is one of very few individuals in whom prophetic and priestly ministries unite (also Moses, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Jesus). • place of worship (literally high place): An open-air altar or platform on a hill near the city gate. High places easily became sites for pagan idolatry (see Num 33.52; 1Ki 15.14; 1Ki 22.43; 2Ki 12.3; 2Ki 14.4; 2Ki 15.4, 2Ki 15.35).

to eat: Part of a sacrifice made during worship was burned on the altar, while the remainder was eaten in a ceremonial feast by the guests (see also 1Sa 1.4). • to bless the food: As a Levite, Samuel’s priestly role included offering blessings (see Deu 10.8; Deu 21.5).

God’s directive to anoint him (by pouring olive oil on the head) marked Saul’s elevation in status and consecration for a special purpose (see Exo 30.22–33; Lev 8.12; 1Ki 19.16; Isa 45.1). • He will rescue them: As they had requested (1Sa 8.20; cp. Jdg 13.5). David eventually subdued the Philistines (2Sa 5.17–25; 2Sa 8.1; 2Sa 21.15, 2Sa 21.18–22). • for I have . . . heard their cry (cp. Exo 3.7–9): The Philistines were again threatening to conquer Israel and demand homage from them as vassals.

the smallest tribe: Saul tried to downplay Benjamin’s prominence, but they were powerful warriors (Jdg 20.14–31; cp. study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 10.17). What better tribe to lead in battle? • least important of all the families: Cp. 1Sa 9.1.
A typical house had a flat roof that was used for a variety of purposes, such as sleeping in warm weather (see Deu 22.8; 2Ki 4.10).

Samuel later repeated this process by anointing David with olive oil (1Sa 16.13). • The people of Israel did not belong to the king but to the Lord. The king was to act as manager rather than owner (cp. 1Sa 8.10–18).
These three “signs” were to convince a reluctant Saul (1Sa 9.21) that he had in fact been chosen to be king.
Rachel’s tomb at Zelzah: See Gen 35.16–20; the precise location is unknown.
oak of Tabor: This location, somewhere in Benjamin, is not to be confused with the village of the same name in Zebulun (1Ch 6.77). • Bethel: See study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 7.16.

Gibeah of God, Saul’s hometown (1Sa 10.26), had been a lawless city (Jdg 19.1–21). Nowhere else is it described as being “of God.” This description might point to God’s ownership of the town despite the occupation of the Philistines. • band: Prophets often lived in groups (e.g., 2Ki 2.3). • harp . . . lyre: Ancient prophets sometimes used musical instruments to stimulate and accompany prophesying (e.g., 2Ki 3.15).
prophesy: Cp. 2Sa 23.2; Act 2.29–31. • different person: Saul would become a spiritual and charismatic national leader (cp. 1Sa 16.14).
for God is with you: God’s presence empowered Saul to carry out his responsibilities.
Gilgal: See study note on 1Sa 7.16. • wait for seven days: Saul apparently fulfilled this instruction in 1Sa 11.14–15 (cp. 1Sa 13.8).
a new heart: God gave Saul courage and strength, helping him overcome his hesitancy and enabling him to be king (1Sa 10.6).

the Spirit of God came powerfully upon Saul: See “The Spirit’s Presence” Theme Note; see also 1Sa 11.6; Jdg 14.6, Jdg 14.19; Jdg 15.14; cp. Act 2.17–18, Act 2.39). • When Saul . . . began to prophesy, it was a clear sign that he had been chosen to lead Israel (see also 1Sa 19.18–23).

Those who knew Saul might have known him to be nonreligious and thus an unlikely candidate for prophet. Their surprise might indicate disappointment at receiving a prophet instead of a king (cp. Joh 6.14–15).

“Can anyone become a prophet, no matter who his father is?” Unlike priests and kings, prophets never inherited their office. Possibly the people were asking why Saul, whose well-to-do father was well known, would associate himself with a group of people who had no pedigree.
Perhaps Saul didn’t tell his uncle because he had lingering uncertainty about what had transpired.
An earlier generation had gathered at Mizpah to decimate the tribe of Benjamin (Jdg 20.1–4), making the city an ironic place to inaugurate a man of Benjamin as king.
rescued you . . . from all of the nations: Israel did not need a human king to rescue them; they needed God, but they had rejected him (1Sa 10.19).
rejected your God: See also 1Sa 8.7. Israel was rejecting God’s ability to protect and save them. • Clans are subdivisions of tribes.
chosen by lot: Cp. Lev 16.8; Jos 18.6; 1Ch 26.12–16; Act 1.26.

rights and duties of a king: See Deu 17.14–20. • He wrote them: Cp. Exo 24.4; Jos 24.26. • Samuel placed the document before the LORD—presumably in the Tabernacle. This position showed that God would honor those who lived by the covenant and punish those who violated it.
Saul proved his capacity for leadership by tolerating opposition and rescuing the town of Jabesh-gilead.
whose hearts God had touched: God gave people confidence in Saul’s ability to lead (cp. 1Sa 10.9).

These men were scoundrels (cp. 1Sa 2.12) because they scorned God’s chosen king. • Gifts were given to show homage (Gen 32.13, Gen 32.18, Gen 32.20), political friendship (2Ki 20.12), or submission (Jdg 3.15, Jdg 3.17). • ignored them: Saul’s self-restraint while being insulted was a sign of maturity. In contrast, Pro 16.14 speaks of a king’s potentially explosive rage when somebody crosses him. See also 1Sa 11.12–13. • [Nahash . . . Jabesh-gilead]: See NLT note. Whether this paragraph was part of the original text is uncertain, but it provides historical context for 1Sa 11.1–15 (e.g., 1Sa 11.2).
Saul’s kingship was confirmed through a military victory, the very reason the people wanted a king (1Sa 8.20).

Ammon (see Gen 19.38), located on the east side of the Jordan, represented a threat to Israel similar to the Philistines to the southwest (see also Jdg 10.6–1Sa 11.33). • Make a treaty with us: Cp. Jos 9.1–27; 2Sa 10.19.

gouge out the right eye: Mutilation of captured soldiers was a common practice in the ancient Near East. These disfigured soldiers would have lost all depth perception, seriously curtailing their potential for fighting in a revolt.
Nahash agreed to grant a reprieve of seven days, reflecting his arrogant confidence of victory and his desire to humiliate Israel as much as possible.
Not to participate would indicate rejection of the leadership of both Saul as king and Samuel as prophet.
Bezek was about fourteen miles west of Jabesh-gilead. • The narrator’s use of the terms Israel and Judah anticipates the later division of the kingdom (1Ki 12.1–33).
No one will be executed: This was a time for rejoicing, not revenge.

renew the kingdom: “Renew” indicates that someone or something had deteriorated or had been damaged (cp. Psa 51.10). Whatever effect the scoundrels (1Sa 10.27; 1Sa 11.12) might have had in undermining the people’s confidence was now rectified by Saul’s victory over the Ammonites.

The solemn ceremony before the LORD acknowledged Saul’s sovereignty as king while affirming that the Lord was Israel’s true King. • Peace offerings were common on historic occasions that inaugurated important institutions (see Exo 24.5; Lev 9.4, Lev 9.18, Lev 9.22; 1Ki 8.63–64).
The reaffirmation of Saul’s kingship at Gilgal (1Sa 11.12–15) was the final step in his installation as king. The event was a fitting occasion for Samuel’s farewell address as leader of Israel.

God’s anointed one was Saul (see 1Sa 9.16). • Whose ox or donkey: Cp. Num 16.15. • have I stolen? In contrast to the behavior of kings (1Sa 8.11–16). • Have I ever taken a bribe and perverted justice? No, but Samuel’s sons did (1Sa 8.3).

my hands are clean: Samuel’s life and leadership before Israel had been above reproach (cp. 1Co 9.1–14; 2Co 7.2; 2Co 11.7–9; 1Th 2.1–12). Saul, David, and Solomon—kings rather than prophetic judges—would not be able to make this claim.
In 1Sa 12.1–5, Samuel put himself on trial and was found innocent. In 1Sa 12.6–25, he put the nation on trial and found it guilty.
Moses and Aaron were not self-made leaders but were appointed by God as leaders.

handed them over: See Jdg 3.8; Jdg 4.1–3. • the king of Moab: See Jdg 3.12. Not all of Israel’s enemies in the era of the judges are listed (e.g., the Ammonites and Midianites). This list is representative to emphasize the highs and lows of that era.

Then they cried to the LORD: Sometimes only suffering turns people’s hearts toward God. During the period of the judges, Israel repeatedly went through cycles of sin, oppression, repentance, and rescue. • Baal and Ashtoreth: When people turn away from God, they inevitably turn to idols (see 1Sa 7.3; Jdg 2.13; Jdg 10.6). • An attitude such as if you will rescue us turns worship into a debased bargain, in which God must perform some action to a person’s liking. God deserves obedience and worship because he is God, not because of favors he can perform.
As in 1Sa 12.9, this list of leaders is representative. • Bedan: Greek and Syriac versions read Barak (see Jdg 4.6–24; Jdg 5.1, Jdg 5.12, Jdg 5.15). The identity of this judge remains uncertain.
you were afraid of Nahash: Israel’s trouble with Nahash apparently preceded 1Sa 11.1–11 (cp. 1Sa 8.5, 1Sa 8.20; 1Sa 10.27).
Even though the Israelites’ request amounted to a rejection of God as king, the LORD . . . granted it (see study notes on 1Sa 8.7 and 1Sa 8.8).

To show that even under a monarchy Israel must still keep its covenant with the Lord—who was always to be their true king—Samuel echoed language from the Sinai covenant (e.g., Exo 19.5–6; Lev 26.1–46; Deu 30.11–20).
Worship is meaningless if it does not result in obedience.

The wheat harvest occurred in late spring or early summer, when little or no rain fell in Israel. Thunder and rain would thus demonstrate God’s power as a sign of the people’s wickedness in asking for a king.
terrified: Cp. Exo 19.16.

The people asked Samuel to intercede for them (see also 1Sa 7.8) rather than praying themselves probably because they were out of fellowship with God (note the use of your God rather than “our God”). • added to our sins: The sins included idol worship (1Sa 12.21; see study note on 1Sa 8.8).
worthless . . . totally useless: Israel was slow to learn this lesson (e.g., Isa 40.18–26; Isa 44.9–20).

because that would dishonor his great name: God will never contradict his own character and detract from his glory (see also Isa 37.35; Isa 43.25; Isa 48.9–11). Therefore, he always keeps his covenant promises, even if his people do not. • his very own people: Israel is God’s treasured possession (see Exo 19.5; Deu 9.25–29). He will never abandon them (see Rom 11.1–5, Rom 11.25–32).

I will continue to teach you: Samuel was both intercessor and educator. • Although this address marked the end of Samuel’s political leadership, he continued his spiritual ministry for some time (e.g., 1Sa 19.24).

swept away: David later used this same Hebrew verb for Saul’s death (1Sa 26.10, “die . . . in battle”) and for his own possible death at Saul’s hands (1Sa 27.1, “get me”). The warning would remain in force throughout Israel’s history as a monarchy.

Saul’s fall from power involved a threefold sequence, as had his rise to power (see study note on 1Sa 9.1–1Sa 11.15): (1) He offered the sacrifices himself and did not wait for Samuel (1Sa 13.1–14); (2) he made a rash oath that put Jonathan’s life in danger (1Sa 14.1–46); and (3) he failed to obey God by eliminating the Amalekites and their belongings (1Sa 15.1–35).

For the kings of Israel and Judah, Scripture normally records the age of ascension and the length of reign (e.g., 2Sa 5.4–5; 1Ki 14.21). • thirty years old: The number represents a plausible age for Saul’s ascension. The Hebrew text and most Greek manuscripts omit the number , making it difficult to know the original wording. • reigned for forty-two years: See NLT textual note. Most scholars agree that something has fallen out of the original manuscript, most likely due to a copyist’s error. The majority of English translations have forty-two based on the approximate number in Act 13.21.

Earlier, Saul had employed 330,000 troops to fight against a much less formidable foe (1Sa 11.8). The selection here of 3,000 special troops probably does not reflect overconfidence (cp. Jos 7.3–4). Rather, Saul likely recognized the need for a smaller, highly trained, elite militia to deal with the troublesome Philistines (see 1Sa 14.52). • Micmash was located in Benjamin about two miles northwest of Saul’s home in Gibeah.
Profile: Jonathan

Geba was located between Jonathan’s forces at Gibeah and Saul’s forces at Micmash. A deep gorge separated Geba and Micmash (see 1Sa 13.23; 1Sa 14.5). • The ram’s horn (Hebrew shofar) was used to raise a signal—e.g., to muster an army (Jdg 3.27). For other uses, see Lev 25.9; 2Sa 6.15; 2Sa 15.10; 2Sa 18.16; 2Sa 20.1; Hos 5.8; Joe 2.15. • Non-Israelites often used the term Hebrews disdainfully (see 1Sa 14.11; 1Sa 29.3; see also Gen 39.14; Gen 43.32). Saul might have used it to strike a nerve and arouse the people’s pride in their identity.

Saul had destroyed: The commander in chief often got credit for what his soldiers accomplished. • Saul’s kingship had been reaffirmed at Gilgal (1Sa 11.15). Now the Lord would reject his kingship there because of his disobedience (1Sa 13.7–14).

The Israelites were massively outnumbered, hence their fearful responses. • The Philistine army’s 3,000 chariots and 6,000 charioteers indicate Israel’s underdog status. Nowhere in 1 Samuel is Israel said to have had any chariots (see study note on 1Sa 13.19–22).
The land of Gad and Gilead ran the length of Transjordan (the region just east of the Jordan River).
seven days . . . as Samuel had instructed: This instruction most likely was not the instruction in 1Sa 10.8 but an unrecorded instruction on a separate occasion (see study note on 1Sa 10.8).

the burnt offering and the peace offerings: These general-purpose offerings (see Exo 24.5; Exo 32.6; Num 10.10; Num 15.8; Deu 27.6–7) were always offered on a solemn occasion filled with either danger or joy. Typically, only priests were to offer these sacrifices (but see study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 13.13).
meet and welcome: Saul seemed unaware he had done anything wrong.
What is this you have done? Samuel’s question was a rebuke, not a request for information (cp. Gen 3.13).

asked for the LORD’s help: The purpose of the burnt offering was to entreat God to grant victory in battle. Samuel himself had offered a similar sacrifice, which did lead to victory in battle (see 1Sa 7.7–11). But Samuel, unlike Saul, served in a priestly role.

the command the LORD . . . gave you: Other kings offered sacrifices without censure (David, 2Sa 6.13, 2Sa 6.17–18; Solomon, 1Ki 3.15; 1Ki 8.64; Ahaz, 2Ki 16.12–13), as did judges (Gideon, Jdg 6.26), illustrating that on occasion non-priests could conduct sacrifices in a way that pleased the Lord. However, Samuel, God’s prophet, had given Saul the order to wait (see study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 13.8).
a man after his own heart: This prophecy pertains to David (see also Act 13.22) rather than to Saul’s son Jonathan. The rejection of Saul was also the rejection of his family dynasty.
only 600 were left: Most of the 3,000 troops (1Sa 13.2) had abandoned Saul (1Sa 13.6–7).

Armies would send out raiding parties to plunder and sow panic among the enemy. These raiders embarked north (Ophrah), west (Beth-horon), and east (Zeboim), but not south, where Israelite strength was consolidated and where the terrain did not allow easy movement of forces (see study note on 1Sa 13.23).

no blacksmiths: The Philistines kept the Israelites unarmed by gaining a monopoly on the iron necessary to make weapons. Iron technology had not existed long in Canaan; it might have developed in the Aegean area, and metalworking skills were possibly introduced into Canaan through seafaring peoples, including the Philistines.
The pass at Micmash was a strategic passage through the canyon that separated Micmash from Geba, Gibeah, and other towns to the south.

Saul’s behavior in this chapter further justifies his dismissal as king (1Sa 13.8–14; see also ch 1Sa 15.1–35). Saul was alienated from both Samuel and his heroic son Jonathan. 1Sa 14.1–52 anticipates the significant role that Jonathan played in the transition from Saul’s kingship to David’s.
Jonathan again fought in his father’s battles (see also 1Sa 13.2–4; ch 1Sa 31.1–13).

armor bearer: See study note on 1Sa 16.21. • Jonathan did not tell his father because he knew that Saul would not grant permission for the dangerous plan. But he also knew that Saul wanted no one—not even his own son—to upstage him.
camped: Saul’s inactivity contrasts with Jonathan’s initiative (see also 1Sa 22.6).

Ahijah the priest was an adviser who could give Saul divine guidance through the ephod (1Sa 14.18–19; see also 1Sa 2.18 and corresponding study note 1Sa 2.18; 1Sa 23.9–10). • son of Eli: Saul, the rejected king (1Sa 13.13–14), kept in his company a priest from the rejected priesthood (1Sa 2.27–36). • Ichabod: See 1Sa 4.21.
The Philistines had already secured this area (1Sa 13.23), so Jonathan and his armor bearer had to move carefully.

pagans (literally uncircumcised): A disdainful term for enemies of Israel (see also 1Sa 17.36; 1Sa 31.4). • Perhaps: Jonathan had no guarantee of survival, but he was certain that God could grant them victory despite the odds. Victory was in God’s hands; Jonathan offered himself as an instrument God could use. • many warriors or only a few: Jonathan knew what Gideon had learned many years earlier (see Jdg 7.2–8).
Hebrews: See study note on 1Sa 13.3. • crawling out of their holes: See 1Sa 13.6.

panic broke out: This parallel with the Gideon story depicts Jonathan as a judge-like figure (cp. Jdg 7.19–22). God had not anointed or expressly gifted Jonathan to be leader, yet God used him to rescue his people. • raiding parties: See study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 13.17–18.

Bring . . . Israelites: See NLT textual note; the Greek text is likely original. The Ark remained at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years (1Sa 7.2), and it was never used for getting information about the future, as the ephod was (see study note on 1Sa 2.18).

Previously, a large group of Israelites had gone into hiding out of fear (1Sa 13.6–7). Others might have joined the Philistine army. However, the statement that they revolted when the opportunity arose suggests they might have been taken as prisoners of war and forced into the Philistines’ service.

It was God, not Saul, who saved Israel; Jonathan was just a willing instrument in the Lord’s hands. • Beth-aven was due west of Micmash (see 1Sa 13.5). The Israelites forced the Philistines to retreat all the way to Aijalon that day (see 1Sa 14.31).

With his oath, Saul forced abstinence from food on men who were already hungry and exhausted from battle. This oath was probably a pagan-like attempt to manipulate God into giving them a favorable result (cp. notes on Exod Exo 23.26; Exo 25.22; Exo 32.4). • That Saul said my enemies rather than “our enemies” reflects his self-centered pride.

made trouble: Joshua had used this verb in speaking with Achan (Jos 7.25), and Jephthah had used it with his innocent daughter (Jdg 11.35). Saul’s foolish oath limited Israel’s victory (1Sa 14.30) and put his son’s life at risk (see also Jos 6.18; 1Ch 2.7).
Aijalon: If the Philistines fled along the likely route through Beth-horon, then the Israelites kept up the pursuit for close to twenty miles.

The men were famished, so they ate meat without draining the blood. This act violated God’s law (see Lev 17.10–14) and thus constituted sinning against the LORD. To prevent more sin, Saul used a large rock as a field altar so that the animals’ blood could be properly drained. The incident would never have occurred had it not been for Saul’s foolish oath.
first of the altars: This altar is the only one mentioned. David later built an altar that would become the site of God’s Temple (2Sa 24.18–25).
God made no reply: Neither the “no” lot nor the “yes” lot of the Urim and Thummim appeared.

Casting sacred lots involved the Urim and Thummim (Exo 28.30; Lev 8.8), which David also used when soliciting God’s guidance (1Sa 23.2; 1Sa 30.8; 2Sa 2.1). The Urim and Thummim were two small objects (perhaps flat stones, sticks, or arrows) that may have been cast like dice. They would provide a positive answer, a neutral response, or a negative answer.
The people, aware of God’s blessing on the real hero of the day, were wiser than their king.
In contrast to the folly described in 1Sa 14.1–46, these verses summarize Saul’s military successes. A similar summary of achievements ends the description of each king’s reign in 1 Samuel—2 Kings.

secured his grasp: Samuel had used this verb repeatedly when speaking about what a king would do: “He will take . . . take . . . take” (1Sa 8.10–18). • Moab, Ammon, Edom, . . . Zobah: David confronted these same foes during his reign and expanded Israel’s territory in the process (see 2Sa 8.1–14).

conquered the Amalekites: See 1Sa 15.1–35. The Amalekites, a nomadic group in the south, periodically raided and pillaged Israel (see Exo 17.8–16; Num 14.45; Jdg 3.13; Jdg 6.3, Jdg 6.33; Jdg 7.12; Jdg 10.12).
Profile: The Amalekites
This information about Saul’s family, placed here rather than at the end of his reign, hints that his reign was essentially over and he would not be succeeded by one of his sons.

Saul’s sons included: Another of Saul’s sons was named Abinadab (1Sa 31.2). • Ishbosheth means “man of shame” (see study note on 2 Sam 2Sa 2.8). He was also called Esh-baal (“man of Baal”). He served briefly as a rival king over the northern tribes during David’s early years (2Sa 2.8–11).
Profile: Michal
Ahinoam is mentioned only here in Saul’s story. In 1Sa 25.43, David marries a woman also called Ahinoam (who might or might not have been the same person; cp. 2Sa 12.8).

Saul had easily defeated the Ammonites (1Sa 11.11) but was having much less success with the Philistines, given their well-organized fighting machine and their monopoly on iron and bronze (1Sa 13.19–22). • he drafted him: Samuel had warned earlier that the king would take people as well as possessions (1Sa 8.11).
After Saul failed to obey God and completely destroy the Amalekites, God rejected him in even stronger terms than before (cp. 1Sa 13.8–14).
Theme: Complete Destruction

LORD of Heaven’s Armies: See study note on 1Sa 1.3. • to settle accounts: In Moses’ time, the nation of Amalek had inhabited southern Judah and the Negev area south of Judah. As Israel traveled to Canaan, the Amalekites preyed on the sick and the weak and those traveling at the rear. They were the first people to attack Israel after the exodus from Egypt, for which God had promised to judge them (Exo 17.8–16; Deu 25.17–19).
completely destroy: See “Complete Dedication” Theme Note.
Telaim: Possibly Telem (Jos 15.24).
The unnamed town in the valley was located somewhere near a Negev wadi, a streambed or riverbed that fills with water only when rain falls.
The Kenites were nomadic metalworkers and descendants of Moses’ father-in-law (Jdg 1.16). • you showed kindness: See Exo 18.1–27; Num 10.29–32.
The area where the Amalekites lived stretched from Havilah in northern Sinai to Shur near the eastern border of Egypt.
Agag was probably the descendant of an earlier king by the same name (see Num 24.7; cp. Est 3.1).

Saul and his men directly disobeyed the Lord’s command to “completely destroy” the Amalekites (1Sa 15.3). Though the entire army participated in the disobedience of God’s command, Saul alone was responsible as their leader.
Theme: God’s Change of Mind
Carmel was a town near Hebron in southern Judah. • Saul commemorated his own accomplishments by erecting a monument to himself. In reality, he had earned shame (1Sa 15.16–19). • Gilgal: See 1Sa 13.4.

I have carried out the LORD’s command! Cp. 1Sa 15.3. Saul apparently thought his actions were justified (1Sa 15.15; cp. Lev 22.19). Samuel, however, cut through Saul’s pretense (1Sa 15.17–19) and carried out God’s command himself (1Sa 15.32–33).
Saul blamed the army even though he was the commander. Certainly, his real motivation was not spiritual (1Sa 15.9).
As the anointed . . . king of Israel, Saul bore the responsibility for disobeying God, which neither false humility nor making excuses could diminish.
my troops: Saul persisted in blaming others (see 1Sa 15.15). • Gilgal was a religious center. Saul tried to use religion to justify disobedience to God.
What is more pleasing: God values obedience much more than ritual (see also Psa 40.6; Hos 6.6; Mat 12.7). • the fat of rams: The choicest parts of the animal were offered to God.
Rebellion . . . and stubbornness, sins of the heart, are as bad as the sinful practices of idolatrous pagans. • Scripture condemns witchcraft (see study note on Deut Deu 18.10).
Saul finally confessed his sin. But it was too little, too late—and still accompanied by excuses.

I was afraid of the people: Saul continued to blame others (see 1Sa 15.15, 1Sa 15.21). • what they demanded: There is no hint of such pressure in the chapter. Saul’s confession appears dishonest (cp. David, 2Sa 12.13; Psa 51.1–19).
Saul soon discovered who this someone else was (1Sa 18.8–9; cp. ch 1Sa 16.1–23).
nor will he change his mind: Samuel spoke prophetically of God’s commitment to make David king and to preserve his dynasty. God had rejected Saul, but he would never reject David (see 2Sa 7.8–17).
honor me before the elders: To help Saul save face.

The verb phrase mourned constantly is usually used for grieving over someone’s death. Although Saul was still living, his royalty was coming to an end. Samuel might have been grieving out of personal attachment to Saul, a sense of failure, or concern that Israel’s condition would be worse. • the LORD was sorry: See “God’s Change of Mind” Theme Note.

David was Saul’s replacement. There are striking similarities between the two: Samuel anointed both. Neither was pursuing the position. Both were unlikely candidates (Saul was from the smallest tribe; David was the youngest son). Both were impressive in appearance (1Sa 9.2; 1Sa 16.12). And the Spirit came mightily on each when he was anointed king (1Sa 10.10; 1Sa 11.6; 1Sa 16.13). The key difference was that David was “a man after [God’s] own heart” (1Sa 13.14; cp. 1Sa 16.7), while Saul was not.

mourned long enough: See study note on 1Sa 15.35. • Bethlehem was about five miles south of Jerusalem. It was later known as the City of David (Luk 2.11) and the birthplace of Jesus. • Jesse was the grandson of Boaz and Ruth (Rut 4.22). • I have selected: This Hebrew verb implies that God had seen one of [Jesse’s] sons and based his choice on what he saw. God, the eternal king, knows better than the people of Israel how to choose a good king to serve the nation, and he provided a replacement for Saul who would lead Israel well.

say that you have come to make a sacrifice: God sometimes leads his servants into dangerous situations. He protects his own—sometimes by miracle, sometimes by strategy (cp. Exo 3.18–22). In Samuel’s role as a priestly judge, he would not have raised any suspicions by offering a sacrifice (see 1Sa 10.8).
the elders . . . came trembling: News of Samuel’s rebuke of Saul and execution of Agag had likely reached Bethlehem.

Purify yourselves: Self-purification included bathing and abstaining from sexual intercourse (see Exo 19.10–15; cp. Gen 35.2–4). • The sacrifice likely took place the following morning (see Num 11.18; Jos 3.5; Jos 7.13–14). • Samuel performed the purification rite for Jesse and his sons to make sure they were ready for the sacrifice and for the anointing of the new king (cp. Exo 19.10; Jos 3.5).

his appearance or height: Like Saul, Eliab, Jesse’s oldest son, had an impressive outward appearance (cp. 1Sa 9.2). Also like Saul, he was rejected (cp. 1Sa 15.23). God had another man in mind to anoint as king. • the LORD looks at the heart: God can give a new heart (1Sa 10.9), touch hearts (1Sa 10.26), and peer into the deep motivations of the heart (Psa 139.1). God sees what people cannot see—a person’s true character. Eliab’s character comes out in 1Sa 17.28.
Profile: David

The Spirit of the LORD came . . . upon David, as was consistently evident (e.g., 1Sa 16.23; 1Sa 17.48–54; 1Sa 18.5, 1Sa 18.12–16). The Spirit of the Lord had also come upon Saul (1Sa 10.10) but had left him because of disobedience (1Sa 16.14). • Ramah: Samuel’s hometown (1Sa 1.1).
Theme: The Spirit’s Presence
Saul’s kingship continued its downward spiral after God’s Spirit departed from him. His reign ended in shame and defeat (ch 1Sa 31.1–13).

Spirit . . . left Saul: In contrast with David’s receiving the Spirit (see “The Spirit’s Presence” Theme Note). • The LORD sent a tormenting spirit as a consequence of Saul’s disobedience (see also 1Sa 18.10; 1Sa 19.9; cp. Jdg 9.23; Rom 1.28–29).
harp: The instrument was probably a lyre (as in 1Sa 10.5). • the LORD is with him: People recognized that God’s Spirit was upon David (1Sa 16.13).

Although at first Saul loved David very much, this love soon turned to intense jealousy and hatred (see 1Sa 18.8–14). • An armor bearer in ancient Israel served as the personal attendant of a warrior chieftain (see 1Sa 14.1–15; 1Sa 31.4–6; Jdg 9.54; 2Sa 18.15).
David’s father, Jesse (1Sa 16.18), arranged for David to continue serving Saul while still fulfilling his shepherding duties at home (see 1Sa 17.14–15).

Saul would feel better: David was more than a handsome lad gifted in music; he was the anointed king. Here David illustrated what a king should be: one who brings relief. Later, David composed dozens of psalms that have brought comfort and relief through the ages. • the tormenting spirit would go away: Even those who are disobedient and rejected can receive relief and comfort through the Lord’s servant.

The Philistines presented an ongoing threat throughout Saul’s reign (see 1Sa 14.47–52). • Socoh in Judah was fourteen miles west of Bethlehem toward Philistine territory. • Azekah was a few miles northwest of Socoh (the precise location of Ephes-dammim is unknown). The Philistines were encroaching on Israelite territory.
The valley of Elah was a fertile area that ran east–west, fifteen miles southwest of Bethlehem.

champion: In ancient times, rival forces would sometimes agree to let selected individuals from each side decide a conflict. This reduced casualties and other costs. The same kind of combat is reflected in 2Sa 2.12–17. • Gath was one of five Philistine cities with a reputation for having giants as citizens (2Sa 21.15–22).
Although Goliath was a fully armored warrior of terrifying size, he did not have God—a far mightier warrior—on his side (1Sa 17.45–47).
Ephrathite: Ephrath is a name for Bethlehem (Gen 35.19; 1Ch 4.4).

went back and forth: David apparently served as a musician and armor bearer in Saul’s court (see 1Sa 16.19–23) while maintaining his duties at home. The intermittent nature of David’s service might explain why Saul was unfamiliar with David during the encounter with Goliath (see 1Sa 17.55–58).

What will a man get: Cp. 1Sa 18.17–27. David’s interest in a reward was overshadowed by his determination to silence Goliath’s defiance of God (1Sa 17.45–47). • pagan: Literally uncircumcised. See study note on 1Sa 14.6.
Eliab . . . was angry, perhaps resentful that David, rather than he, was anointed to be king (1Sa 16.6–13).
I’ll go fight him! David’s courage stands in contrast to Saul’s fear (1Sa 17.11).

A stream flowed through the valley of Elah (1Sa 17.2). • A sling was a leather pouch attached to two leather thongs. When the sling containing a stone was whirled rapidly, one of the thongs could be released, sending the stone toward its target. David probably became deadly accurate with a sling as a shepherd, but the sling was used by warriors as well (Jdg 20.16).

ruddy-faced: The same Hebrew word is translated “dark” (1Sa 16.12) and “very red” (Gen 25.25). Here, it emphasizes David’s youthfulness and inexperience. • boy: Saul had expressed similar disbelief (1Sa 17.33). As a champion, Goliath expected to be met by an Israelite warrior of similar rank.

a dog: A metaphor for a compliant, bowing servant (cp. 2Sa 9.8). • a stick: David had concealed his sling, and Goliath could see only his staff. • by the names of his gods: Since Goliath appealed to his gods, David’s victory over Goliath would also symbolize God’s victory over Dagon, the chief god of the Philistines (1Sa 5.2, 1Sa 5.5).
A corpse left to scavengers such as birds and wild animals was grievously cursed (cp. Deu 21.23; Deu 28.26).
the LORD of Heaven’s Armies: See study note on 1Sa 1.3. Despite the Philistines’ apparent military advantage, David knew that Israel had the supreme advantage in the one true God.
Goliath’s forehead remained exposed beneath his enormous helmet. • stumbled and fell face down: The stone only incapacitated Goliath; David killed him by decapitating him (1Sa 17.51).
The Israelites chased the Philistines to Gath, some six miles to the west. • Ekron was a Philistine city five miles north of Gath. • Shaaraim was a city of Judah near Azekah (1Sa 17.1).
Unless expressly prohibited (e.g., 1Sa 15.3; Jos 6.18), victory in battle allowed for the taking of war spoils (Deu 2.35; Jos 8.2).

Jerusalem became an Israelite city later, when David captured it from the Jebusites (2Sa 5.6–7). Jerusalem was probably the final destination of Goliath’s head, after David had become king. But David might have taken it to Jerusalem earlier to intimidate the non-Israelite occupants.

In light of 1Sa 16.14–23, it is surprising that neither Saul nor Abner knew who David was. It is possible that the events of ch 1Sa 17.1–58 happened either before or long after David’s tenure of intermittent service mentioned in ch 1Sa 16.1–23 (Saul probably served as king for forty-two years, 1Sa 13.1).

David and Jonathan had much in common: both were young and capable, were military heroes, had a robust faith in God, and had a claim to the throne of Israel. It is a testimony to Jonathan’s true character that he recognized and supported God’s choice of David to be the next king of Israel (see 1Sa 18.3–4; 1Sa 20.12–17). • Jonathan loved David: See 1Sa 20.17; 2Sa 1.26. Others in this chapter are also said to love David: all Israel and Judah (1Sa 18.16), Saul’s daughter Michal (1Sa 18.20), and Saul’s servants (1Sa 18.22). Some modern interpreters see a homosexual relationship between David and Jonathan, but the text implies nothing other than a deep and loyal friendship.
David had previously served Saul part-time (see 1Sa 17.15 and corresponding study note 1Sa 17.15); now Saul kept David with him full-time.

Out of his love for David and recognition that God had chosen David to be Israel’s next king (see 1Sa 20.13–17, 1Sa 20.30–31; 1Sa 23.17), Jonathan made a solemn pact of friendship with David. By giving David items that symbolized his official status as the king’s son and crown prince, Jonathan symbolically gave David his right of succession to the throne.
Theme: Hostile Authority: David’s Response

thousands . . . ten thousands: This dramatic increase in number between two lines of Hebrew poetry was a way of intensifying the statement (cp. Deu 32.30; Psa 91.7). Because of his great military victories, David was beginning to eclipse Saul (1Sa 18.16, 1Sa 18.30; 1Sa 21.11).
Saul came to view David as a threat rather than an ally and would do anything to get rid of him.
In his jealousy and fear, Saul would have been happier with one dead David than with thousands of dead Philistines (1Sa 18.7).
the LORD . . . had turned away from Saul as king as punishment for his disobedience. Saul’s kingship would fail, and David’s would succeed (1Sa 18.14).
Saul offered his older daughter, Merab, to David. But it was an insincere gesture.
Saul had promised his daughter to anyone who could slay Goliath (1Sa 17.25; cp. Jos 15.16; Jdg 1.12), but he tacked on additional risks for David (see also 1Sa 18.21, 1Sa 18.25).
Who am I, and what is my family: An expression of humility (see also 2Sa 7.18; cp. Exo 3.11). David’s family could not afford the bride price to marry the king’s daughter (1Sa 18.23–25).
So: Or But. Either David declined the offer, or Saul reneged.
really likes you: The same Hebrew word describes Jonathan’s love for David (1Sa 18.3; 1Sa 19.1–2, “strong affection”). Here, it was completely untrue.
The future son-in-law would give the bride price as a gift to his bride’s father (see Gen 34.12; Exo 22.16–17).
even more afraid: Saul’s fear was unfounded. Although he made himself David’s enemy, David consistently honored Saul as king (see chs 1Sa 24.1–22, 1Sa 26.1–25).
Jonathan addressed his father as the king out of reverence.
vowed: Violating a vow is a serious offense against God (see Num 30.2; Deu 23.21–23; cp. Ecc 5.4–5). But Saul soon disregarded his promise and again sought to kill David (1Sa 19.9–24).
hurled his spear: See also 1Sa 18.11; 1Sa 20.33.
See Psa 59.1.

an idol: Hebrew teraphim, which were household idols (see Gen 31.30; Jdg 17.5; 2Ki 23.24). The presence of an idol in the home of David and Michal might show the pervasive influence of pagan idol worship among the Israelites; perhaps the idol belonged to Michal. Apparently David did not object to its presence. (Cp. Rachel’s theft of her father’s household idols in Gen 31.19.) • Siblings Jonathan (1Sa 19.1–7) and Michal (1Sa 19.11–18) saved David from their father and undermined their father’s plans to eliminate him. Members of Saul’s royal family played a significant role in David’s rise, though David did not usurp Saul’s throne.
Ramah: Samuel’s hometown (1Sa 1.1). • Naioth was a tiny village not far from the other Ramah in Benjamin.
Prophets often assembled in groups under a single leader (see 2Ki 2.15; 2Ki 4.38; 2Ki 6.1–7). • The Spirit of God came upon Saul’s men to allow David to escape (1Sa 20.1).
other troops . . . a third time: Each time Saul sent troops, David’s would-be captors were captured by the Spirit. Prophesying diverted them from pursuing David.

When Saul tore off his clothes and lay naked, he unwittingly acted out his true spiritual condition of having been stripped of the kingship (1Sa 13.14; 1Sa 15.10–11, 1Sa 15.23; see “Prophetic Sign Acts” Theme Note). • Is even Saul a prophet? In 1Sa 10.9–13, Saul was rising as God’s chosen king; here, he is descending under the weight of God’s rejection.
Jonathan was naive about his father’s intentions. David’s willingness to swear . . . by the LORD showed how convinced he was about Saul’s intentions.

new moon festival: The ancient Hebrews followed a lunar calendar, and the new moon marked the start of a new month. Every month was begun with a special sacrifice (Num 28.11–15), which became a monthly festival.
Israelite families might designate one of the new moon festivals as an opportunity for an annual family sacrifice (see, e.g., 1Sa 1.3).
Loyalty (Hebrew khesed) denotes faithfulness between covenant partners. • a solemn pact: See 1Sa 18.3; 1Sa 20.16.

may the LORD strike me: Jonathan invoked a curse upon himself to reassure David that he would keep his promise. • as he used to be with my father: Jonathan recognized that David had received the blessing from God that his father had once had. The divine favor that had brought Saul into royal office (1Sa 9.14–1Sa 10.1) would bring David into royal office as Saul’s replacement. Jonathan accepted this even though he was the natural successor to Saul.

faithful love: Hebrew khesed (see study note on 1Sa 20.8). Jonathan was reminding David to keep his commitment to him when he became king. It was reasonable for Jonathan to be concerned that David might kill any descendant of Saul who could make a rival claim to his throne. Saul later made a similar request of David (1Sa 24.21).
treat my family: David later treated Jonathan’s son, Mephibosheth, as one of his own sons (2Sa 9.1–13).

Jonathan’s ruse would allow David to get the message even if there could be no face-to-face meeting; the boy’s presence would allay suspicion and provide Jonathan an alibi for going to the field. As it happened, no one but the boy accompanied Jonathan to the field, so when the boy left, David was able to speak with Jonathan face to face (1Sa 20.40–42).
Abner was Saul’s cousin and served as commander of Saul’s army (1Sa 14.50; 1Sa 17.55). His importance is indicated by his position beside the king at this festival.

A number of circumstances could render a person ceremonially unclean and thus unfit for attending a sacred festival (see Lev 7.20–21). Often, an unclean person was required to be excluded from such functions only until the evening of the same day (Lev 15.1–33). This explains why Saul became suspicious after David did not arrive the next day. • Saul referred to David as the son of Jesse (also in 1Sa 20.31; 1Sa 22.7), a description that functioned as David’s surname.
get away: This verb also describes David’s earlier escape from Saul (1Sa 19.10–12, 1Sa 19.17–18).

You stupid son of a whore! This epithet was as strong and insulting in Hebrew as it is in English. • shaming yourself: Saul was interested in the legacy of his own dynasty. He viewed David’s actions as ultimately directed against Jonathan, the hereditary successor. To Saul, Jonathan was stupidly hurting and shaming himself by supporting David.

hurled his spear at Jonathan: See also 1Sa 18.11; 1Sa 19.10. • at last Jonathan realized: Jonathan had been reluctant to believe the truth about his own father (1Sa 20.2–3), but he could no longer deny it.

David bowed: Jonathan had the higher social rank, so David’s homage was fitting. • Both of them were in tears: For the first time, the record of the emotion between these two men shows mutuality (see 1Sa 18.1, 1Sa 18.3–4; 1Sa 20.17).
sworn loyalty to each other in the LORD’s name: See 1Sa 18.3; 1Sa 20.15–17; 1Sa 23.16–18.

Nob was just north of Jerusalem, in the southern part of the territory of Benjamin. • Ahimelech the priest was a descendant of the condemned family of Eli (1Sa 14.3; 1Sa 22.9). • The elders of Bethlehem had also trembled when Samuel unexpectedly came to their city to anoint David as Saul’s replacement (1Sa 16.4). On both occasions, a prominent individual who had strained relations with Saul showed up unannounced. Both Ahimelech and the Bethlehem elders were concerned about being suspected of supporting an enemy of the king, which could result in death. In this case, what was feared came about (see 1Sa 22.9–19).
The king has sent me: David lied to conceal his outlaw status and to dispel Ahimelech’s worries.

Only priests were permitted to partake of holy bread (see Exo 25.22–30; Lev 24.5–9), and only within the sacred precincts. • slept with any women: The consecrated bread was to be eaten only by the ritually pure, so the priest verified that David’s men were free from ritual impurity caused by sexual activity (see Lev 15.16–18). Typically, such bread would not be available for consumption by laity. The priest made an exception in this case probably because he sensed the men’s physical needs and he believed they were on a royal mission.

gave him the holy bread: Jesus referred to this incident to teach that meeting people’s physical needs takes precedence over rigid adherence to sacred institutions (see Mat 12.1–8; Mar 2.23–28; Luk 6.1–5). • The Bread of the Presence consisted of twelve loaves (possibly one representing each tribe) that were laid out on a table in the Holy Place. They were replaced every Sabbath (see Exo 25.30; Lev 24.5–9).
having been detained before the LORD: Ahimelech sought guidance from God on others’ behalf (1Sa 22.15), so it is possible that Doeg was awaiting a response to an inquiry.

The sword of Goliath, which David used to decapitate the giant (1Sa 17.51), had been taken as war spoils, as had Goliath’s head (1Sa 17.54). • The ephod mentioned here might not have been the priestly garment of the same name; some passages give the impression that an ephod could also be a statue (Jdg 8.27; Jdg 18.17).
