Gath, a major Philistine city and the hometown of Goliath, was a clever but dangerous place for David to seek refuge from Saul.
the king of the land: David’s reputation as a mighty warrior even greater than King Saul (see 1Sa 18.7) had grown to the point where foreigners began referring to him as Israel’s king.

The lengthy title of Psa 34.1–22 refers to this incident but names the Philistine king Abimelech rather than Achish. “Abimelech” might have been the common title for Philistine kings (in Hebrew it means “my father the king”). The name Abimelech also appears in Gen 20.2; Gen 26.1.
Saul’s character becomes evident here. Unable to exact revenge on David himself, Saul slaughtered those he believed to be guilty of giving aid and comfort to David.

Adullam was some sixteen miles southwest of Jerusalem, near Philistine territory. • Had David’s brothers and all his other relatives stayed in Bethlehem, they would have been vulnerable to Saul’s revenge.

in trouble . . . in debt . . . discontented: By attracting such down-and-out people to himself, David foreshadowed Jesus, who would attract to himself the hurting, the burdened, and the outcast (Mat 11.25–30).

Mizpeh in Moab lay east of the Dead Sea and the Jordan River—not an easy trip from Adullam, especially if the 400 men (1Sa 22.2) accompanied David. • David’s parents stayed in Moab: Jesse’s grandmother was Ruth, a Moabite (Rut 4.13–22).
The prophet Gad was David’s special adviser (2Sa 24.11). God was no longer communicating with Saul but was guiding David.

men of Benjamin: Saul was suspicious of his own tribesmen, believing that David had bought their loyalty. Worse, Saul did not even trust his own son, convinced that he had joined the supposed conspiracy.
David had deceived Ahimelech into thinking he was on a mission for Saul (1Sa 21.1–9), so Saul’s accusations of conspiracy were baseless.
your son-in-law: David had married Saul’s daughter (1Sa 18.17–29).

Doeg the Edomite . . . killed them: As a non-Israelite, Doeg had no concern for the sanctity of God-anointed priests. He knew he was executing innocent men. This evil foreigner partially fulfilled the prophecy about the condemned priestly line of Eli (1Sa 2.27–34; see 1Ki 2.27). • still wearing their priestly garments: This incident illustrates how mad Saul had become. Not even those holding a sacred office were safe.

Saul had been unwilling to carry out God’s orders to destroy completely the Amalekites and their possessions (1Sa 15.3, 1Sa 15.9). Yet now, in his rage, he did not hesitate to decimate the priests’ families and their possessions (see Pro 14.29; Pro 16.14; Pro 27.4).
Abiathar became an adviser to David, providing guidance from the Lord through the ephod (1Sa 23.2–12; 2Sa 15.24–36). Later, he conspired with Adonijah against David and Solomon (1Ki 1.1–2).
Profile: Abiathar

Thanks to informants (1Sa 23.7, 1Sa 23.13), Saul was able to stay on David’s trail. David also had informants, allowing him to keep one step ahead of Saul (1Sa 23.1, 1Sa 23.9, 1Sa 23.15, 1Sa 23.25). David’s chief advantage was access to divine guidance and resources (1Sa 23.2, 1Sa 23.4, 1Sa 23.12), which Saul lacked.
Keilah was near Adullam (1Sa 22.1) at the western edge of Judah, not far from the Philistine border (see Jos 15.44; Neh 3.17–18).
David asked the LORD either directly in prayer or by using the ephod (see 1Sa 23.6, 1Sa 23.9; 2Sa 2.1; 2Sa 5.23–24). God’s answers were a sign of his blessing and protection (cp. 1Sa 28.6).

the ephod: Saul had slain eighty-five priests who were wearing their ephods (1Sa 22.18; see study note on 1Sa 2.18), but the priest who escaped had the high priest’s ephod, which contained the Urim and Thummim.
God has handed him over to me: To the contrary, see 1Sa 23.14.
The strongholds of the wilderness were not man-made structures but natural rock formations that provided refuge. • Ziph was approximately ten miles southeast of Keilah (1Sa 23.1).
Jonathan . . . encouraged David because he knew that God had chosen David to be king.

You are going to be the king. . . I will be next to you (literally second to you): Jonathan recognized God’s selection of David and renounced any personal ambition to the throne. Jonathan never occupied an official position in David’s court but was killed in battle along with his father (1Sa 31.2).
their solemn pact: See 1Sa 18.3–4; 1Sa 20.12–17. • Jonathan returned home: This was probably the last time David and Jonathan saw each other.

Hakilah was a hill in the wilderness region of Ziph (1Sa 23.14). • The term Jeshimon is sometimes translated as “wasteland” rather than as a place name. It refers here to a specific wasteland located north of the Dead Sea, on both banks of the Jordan River (see Num 21.20).

Both Keilah (1Sa 23.12) and Ziph (1Sa 23.14; Psa 54.1) were located in Judah, but neither one provided sanctuary for David, a native of Judah. David’s ascension to power was not the result of his own tribe’s loyalty but because of the will of God.

Maon was about three miles directly south of the wilderness of Ziph (1Sa 23.14), approximately ten miles south of Hebron. • The Arabah Valley is a deep rift stretching from above the Sea of Galilee down both sides of the Jordan River to the Dead Sea.
the Rock of Escape: It was not uncommon for a place name to commemorate thankfulness to God (e.g., Gen 22.14; Gen 28.19; Gen 32.30). The exact rock formation that received this name is unknown.

David traveled eastward from the area of Ziph (1Sa 23.14) and took refuge in the strongholds of En-gedi. These rocky highlands were located on the western shore of the Dead Sea. There was an oasis in this region, making it an ideal place to find water and food.
3,000 elite troops: David’s force was outnumbered five to one (1Sa 23.13).

David’s men believed, as Saul did, that if the circumstances seem right, the LORD is telling you through those circumstances what to do (cp. 1Sa 23.7). • Perhaps David was able to cut off a piece of the hem of Saul’s robe without being apprehended because Saul had taken off the robe and laid it aside, or perhaps he fell asleep in the cave.
David’s conscience began bothering him because he had dishonored God’s anointed king.

The LORD’s anointed one was not to be violated (1Sa 26.9, 1Sa 26.11, 1Sa 26.16, 1Sa 26.23; 2Sa 1.14, 2Sa 1.16; 2Sa 19.21). David would not harm Saul even though God had anointed him to be the next king (1Sa 16.13).
my father: Saul was, in fact, David’s father-in-law (1Sa 18.27). David was demonstrating his respect for the king and recalling a day when their relationship had been much friendlier.

May the LORD judge: There was no human authority to adjudicate between Saul and David (cp. Gen 16.5; Gen 31.53; Exo 5.21; Jdg 11.27). • Perhaps the LORD will punish you: David rested in God’s will rather than trying to force God’s hand.
The proverb vindicates David and indicts Saul. David refrained from evil deeds, such as killing Saul. Saul, however, repeatedly tried to kill David.
I realize that you are surely going to be king: This was Saul’s first open admission of the truth (cp. 1Sa 23.17).

Saul returned home, and this may have been David’s last personal encounter with him.

refused to answer: Earlier, Saul had consulted the Lord by sacred lots with mixed results (1Sa 14.36–42). God’s refusal to speak was a sign of his judgment (1Sa 14.37; Lam 2.9; Eze 7.26; Amo 8.11–12; Mic 3.6–7).

God has left me: The same Hebrew term is used in 1Sa 16.14 and Jdg 16.20. • won’t reply by prophets or dreams: Cp. 1Sa 28.6.

you refused: Samuel’s message to Saul had not changed (cp. 1Sa 15.19).
here with me: In Sheol, the abode of the dead (cp. 1Sa 2.6, “the grave”; see also Num 16.30–33; Job 17.1–16; Psa 49.11; Rev 1.18).

This meal the medium shared with Saul recalls the fine meal Samuel had shared with Saul (1Sa 9.22–24) before he anointed Saul as king. David was spared by divine providence from actually fighting against his own people.
Aphek was the site of an earlier confrontation between Israel and the Philistines (1Sa 4.1). • Jezreel was about forty miles northeast of Aphek.

servant of King Saul: To Achish, David was a valued defector. Yet David had been deceiving Achish the whole time (see 1Sa 27.1–12).
handing our heads over: The commanders’ fears were justified (cp. 1Sa 17.51; 1Sa 18.27).
This jingle referred to slain Philistines (1Sa 18.7). It is remarkable that David could find refuge in their midst.
by the LORD: Achish used the unique name of Israel’s God to prove his own sincerity. • a trustworthy ally: This assertion was not completely true, though Achish did not realize it (1Sa 27.8–12).
Ziklag: See study note on 1Sa 27.6. • Perhaps the Amalekites were retaliating for David’s raids against them (1Sa 27.8).

Ahinoam: See study note on 1Sa 25.43. • Abigail: See 1Sa 25.3–42.

in great danger: Saul had used the same expression about himself: When “in deep trouble” (1Sa 28.15), Saul turned to necromancy, with disastrous results. David, by contrast, found strength and success in the LORD his God.
the ephod: See study notes on 1Sa 2.18; 1Sa 23.6.
Unlike Saul (1Sa 28.6), David inquired of the Lord successfully (see 1Sa 23.9–12; 2Sa 2.1; 2Sa 5.19, 2Sa 5.23).
Besor was a large brook in Philistine territory that emptied into the Mediterranean southwest of Gaza.

too exhausted: David’s men had traveled for three days (1Sa 30.1) and were now in hot pursuit of the Amalekites without having rested. David did not upbraid them or drive them on mercilessly. See 1Sa 30.23–25.

because I was sick: Only healthy and vigorous slaves were valuable to the Amalekites; the rest were expendable.
The land of Caleb was in the wilderness of Judah, south of Hebron (see Jos 14.6–15).
The total number of Amalekite raiders must have been quite large if 400 young men escaped.
David generously divided the spoils among those who participated in the battle and those who were too exhausted to take part.
greeted them joyfully: David did not reprimand them for not participating in the battle.
tell them to be gone: This heartless group wanted to drive away the nonparticipants with no reward.
what the LORD has given: Some of David’s men ascribed success to their own military prowess; David attributed victory to God and gave him the glory.
share and share alike: Cp. Num 31.25–47, where Moses divided the plunder of war between those who fought and the rest of the people.
elders of Judah . . . his friends: David extended his generosity to influential people throughout his own tribal area, possibly to secure their support for him as king.
The places mentioned here were all in southern Judah. David eventually emerged from this territory as king (see 2Sa 2.1–4).
From Hebron, David reigned as king over Judah for 7½ years (2Sa 2.1–7; 2Sa 5.5).
While David was in the south successfully fighting the Amalekites (ch 1Sa 30.1–31), Saul was in the north unsuccessfully fighting the Philistines.

The Israelites fled southeast from the Jezreel Valley (1Sa 29.1) to higher and hillier ground. With their chariots, the Philistines had the advantage in the more level valley. • Mount Gilboa is southwest of the Sea of Galilee, far from the territory of the Philistines.
Jonathan . . . Malkishua: See 1Sa 14.49. This is the first mention of Saul’s son Abinadab (cp. 1Ch 8.33; 1Ch 9.39).

David had once held the position of armor bearer (1Sa 16.21). • kill me: This is one of many parallels between the death of Abimelech in the time of the judges (Jdg 9.1–57) and Saul, Israel’s first national king (cp. Jdg 9.54).
The victorious army would strip the dead to search for anything valuable (such as clothing, weapons, or jewelry) on the corpses.

In the ancient world, the death of an enemy king was good news, for it meant that the enemy’s god had been defeated. However, little did the Philistines know that their victory would be short-lived and hollow. David, the Lord’s true anointed king, would soon come to power and pay back the Philistines mightily. Far from defeating Israel’s God, the Philistines were simply fulfilling his purpose.

the Ashtoreths: See 1Sa 7.3. • fastened his body: This practice further degraded the executed person by depriving him of proper burial. It also served as a deterrent to other potential enemies (see also Gen 40.19; Deu 21.21–22; Jos 10.26; Est 9.6–14). • Beth-shan was a short distance east of Mount Gilboa.

The people of Jabesh-gilead were returning the favor Saul had done for them when he saved them from the Ammonites and their king Nahash (1Sa 11.1–13). Jabesh-gilead was about twelve miles southeast of Beth-shan and across the Jordan River.
burned the bodies: Cremation was rare. It is possible the bodies were burned because decomposition had already set in.

bones . . . Jabesh: This was not the final resting place of Saul’s remains (see 2Sa 21.12–14). • The ending of 1 Samuel brings Israel’s history back to the situation at the end of Judges, when “Israel had no king.” Once again, the Philistines were in control. David had God’s anointing but no crown. He had wives but no sons. His affiliation with the hated Philistines might jeopardize his standing among his own people. David’s future path would be challenging, but God was clearly with him.

The Second Book of Samuel

Purpose

To describe the reign of David and to demonstrate God’s commitment to David’s line

Author

Unknown

Date

Records events that occurred around 1011–971 BC

Setting

Following Saul’s death, David sought to establish his throne over all Israel and to expand Israelite territory

David’s ascension to power over all the tribes of Israel was lined with violence, politics, and intrigue. David was far from a perfect king—he committed adultery, then committed murder to cover it up, and chaos ensued in his family and the nation. Yet God was eternally committed to David and his descendants. He protected David during the many challenges to his authority and mercifully forgave and restored him when he sinned.

Setting

While Saul was still reigning, Samuel anointed David as Israel’s next king (1Sa 16.1–13), but it was several years before David assumed the throne. Throughout most of this period, David was the object of Saul’s jealousy and wrath. Saul tried many times to kill David, but David never reciprocated when he had the chance. Instead, David trusted in the Lord’s plan and timing.

David’s reign brought significant changes to Israel, both internally and externally. Internally, the nation began to develop a new awareness of itself as a unified nation. During Saul’s reign and the early part of David’s reign, the nation was not completely unified, and the twelve tribes still primarily found their identity at the tribal level rather than as a nation. By the end of David’s reign, a sense of national unity was in place that set the stage for the glory days of King Solomon.

Externally, Israel’s position in relation to its neighbors improved significantly during David’s reign. Most notably, the constant threat posed by the Philistines, so obvious in the book of Judges and throughout Saul’s reign, largely vanished as the result of David’s skillful leadership (see, e.g., 2Sa 5.17–25; 2Sa 21.15–22; 2Sa 23.9–17). David’s reign brought peace and stability to Israel’s borders.

Summary

For 7½ years after the deaths of Saul and Jonathan (2Sa 1.1–27), David reigned as king of Judah only. For two years of that time, Saul’s only surviving son, Ishbosheth, was king of the northern tribes, and this led to a murderous civil war. David became progressively stronger while Ishbosheth became weaker. In the end, Ishbosheth and his top commander, Abner, were assassinated against David’s wishes (2Sa 3.22–2Sa 4.12). Following Ishbosheth’s death, the leaders of the northern tribes pledged their loyalty to David. David immediately relocated his capital from Hebron to the more centrally located Jerusalem, driving out its Jebusite inhabitants (2Sa 5.6–16).

Jerusalem was more than David’s political capital. By bringing the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem, David made it Israel’s spiritual capital as well (2Sa 6.1–15). Shortly thereafter, God made an eternal covenant with David and his descendants (2Sa 7.1–29). In these early years, David enjoyed success on every side (2Sa 8.1–18; 2Sa 10.1–19) and fulfilled his vow to treat the descendants of Saul and Jonathan kindly (2Sa 9.1–13).

Then David made the worst mistake of his life: He brought Bathsheba, who was another man’s wife, to his house for sexual intimacy (2Sa 11.1–5). She became pregnant, and David arranged for her husband’s murder (2Sa 11.6–27). God was angry with David’s actions and chastised him (2Sa 12.1–12). Although David repented and experienced God’s forgiveness, the child conceived in the affair died (2Sa 12.13–23). Yet David remained God’s chosen king (2Sa 12.24–31).

From this point forward, problems compounded for David. Amnon, one of David’s sons, raped his half sister Tamar, and her brother Absalom avenged the act (2Sa 13.1–39). Later, Absalom tried to overthrow and replace David, but he was killed in the coup (2Sa 14.1–2Sa 19.43). Sheba, a Benjamite, also led a revolt against David but was defeated and executed (2Sa 20.1–26).

As king, David twice acted to allay God’s wrath against the nation (2Sa 21.1–22; 2Sa 24.1–25). In the second instance, David built an altar in Jerusalem (2Sa 24.18–25) on what became the site of the Temple (see 1Ch 21.18–2Sa 22.1). Sandwiched between these two episodes are passages that celebrate God’s power working through David and descriptions of the loyalty and heroism of David’s special warriors (2Sa 22.1–2Sa 23.39).

Authorship

The same anonymous author who wrote 1 Samuel probably also wrote 2 Samuel (see 1 Samuel Book Introduction, “Authorship”).

Historical Issues

Evidence for David. For a long time, David’s name had not been discovered in any document from antiquity outside of the Bible. This led some critical scholars to claim that David and his story were fictitious. However, in 1993, archaeologists working at Tell Dan in northern Israel found an inscription in Aramaic about Hazael, king of Syria (around 842–800 BC), who was celebrating a military victory over Israel and Judah. The inscription reads, “I put Jeho . . . , son of . . . ruler of Israel, and . . .iahu, son of . . .g of the house of David to death” (ellipses represent portions of the text illegible in the inscription). This inscription provides evidence of David’s existence and acknowledgment that he founded a dynasty in Judah.

Violence. To a greater degree than any other biblical book, 2 Samuel tells of murders and executions, most notably those involving David’s political rivals and their supporters (Saul and Jonathan, 2Sa 1.1–15; Abner, 2Sa 3.30; Ishbosheth, 2Sa 4.6–8; Absalom, 2Sa 18.14–15; other male descendants of Saul, 2Sa 21.8–9; Amasa, 2Sa 20.10; Sheba, 2Sa 20.21–22). However, the narrator is careful to show that David was not responsible for these murders. Contrary to the claims of some (see 2Sa 16.5–8), David could not be accused of murderous political ambition. David was guilty of murder only in the case of Uriah. Without question, this was a horrible sin, but it was devoid of political motive.

David had no involvement in the many murders surrounding his rise to power. He was not a usurper who violently eliminated the previous royal family. In fact, he genuinely lamented the deaths of Saul and Jonathan and ordered the executions of those who killed Saul and Ishbosheth (2Sa 1.1–16; 2Sa 4.12). David had deep respect for Saul as the Lord’s anointed king. Although David was aware that God had anointed him to replace Saul, he refused to take the matter into his own hands.

Meaning and Message

The book of 2 Samuel reports how God brought the private anointing of David as king (1Sa 16.1–13) to public fruition. Moreover, God made a covenant with David to solidify his commitment to David’s dynasty.

God’s covenant with David bears significant similarities to the covenant with Abraham. Both include promises of great fame (Gen 12.2; 2Sa 7.9) and of rest from their enemies (Gen 15.18–21; 2Sa 7.10). Both are binding forever (Gen 13.15; 2Sa 7.16), and much of the land God promised to Abraham and his descendants (Gen 15.18) was acquired through David’s expansion of his empire (2Sa 5.17–25; 2Sa 8.1–14; 2Sa 10.1–9).

God’s commitment to David was crucial to David’s successes—despite civil war, revolts, the murderous ambition of some loyal subjects, and his personal failures. His shortcomings—particularly his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah—could lead one to wonder whether David would become like Saul, rejected by God and replaced by another. God certainly did punish David when he sinned (2Sa 12.1–2Sa 20.26; 2Sa 24.1–25). Yet God remained committed to David and to his dynasty (2Sa 7.14–16). God’s commitment, rather than David’s merit, explains his success.

Kingship was central in God’s plan for his people and his creation. God’s commitment to David points beyond David and his immediate descendants to a distant son, Jesus Christ. The New Testament both begins (Mat 1.1) and ends (Rev 22.16) by focusing on Jesus, the Eternal King, as the descendant of David.

The forty years of Saul’s reign came to a painful end. The Philistines inflicted a crushing blow on Saul’s people, killing his sons and dismembering Saul’s body after his suicide (1Sa 31.1–13). On the heels of these tragedies, David’s career as leader came into focus.

An unnamed Amalekite sought out David, claiming to have killed Saul. This was a lie, as Saul had committed suicide (1Sa 31.4–6). The Amalekite might have hoped that David would reward him for making it possible for David to assume the throne. Instead, David ordered him killed for harming the Lord’s anointed.
David returned from his victory: Just prior to this encounter, David and his men had killed many Amalekites because of what they had done to David’s city and family (see 1Sa 30.1–31).

What happened? David was not aware of what had happened to Saul—he had no part in Saul’s death. • Saul and . . . Jonathan are also dead: Two other sons of Saul, Abinadab and Malkishua, were killed as well (1Sa 31.2). The Amalekite was either unaware of their deaths or he mentioned only the son who would stand in the way of David’s uncontested path to Israel’s throne.
The Amalekite man’s second lie is, I happened to be on Mount Gilboa. Instead, he had probably scoured the area after the battle, looking for victims whose valuables he could take.
Then he begged me: This is the Amalekite’s third lie; instead, Saul was probably already dead (cp. 1Sa 31.4–6).

The Amalekite apparently got to Saul’s corpse before the Philistines did, for they would not have left royal items such as his crown and his armband on his body. • Israel’s king wore a crown (Hebrew nezer, “consecration”) as a sign of his consecration to God and status as the Lord’s anointed (2Sa 1.14).
Where are you from? David’s asking again (2Sa 1.8) likely reflects the depth of his grief.

The Amalekite expected a reward for killing David’s rival but was instead condemned for killing the LORD’s anointed. David himself had twice refused the opportunity to kill Saul (see 1Sa 24.5–7; 1Sa 26.9–11).

The extrabiblical Book of Jashar is no longer available. It was probably an Israelite epic poem or an anthology of poetry that covered, at minimum, Joshua’s conquest of Canaan (see Jos 10.13) and the ascension of David.
Your pride and joy: David’s description focused more on Saul’s royal position than on his personal characteristics.

Gath and Ashkelon were major Philistine cities. Announcing the news of Saul’s death to the Philistines would give this hated foe the opportunity to gloat and glorify their false god, Dagon, while mocking Israel’s God, Yahweh. • daughters of the Philistines: In ancient war culture, young women sometimes celebrated victories in song (cp. Exo 15.20–21; 1Sa 18.7).

Saul and Jonathan died in the mountains of Gilboa (1Sa 31.1). • let there be no dew or rain: David was invoking a curse on the place of their death. In a Canaanite text from the 1300s BC, a father invokes a very similar curse on the place of his son’s death. • The shield of Saul symbolizes his military exploits as king. It would no longer be anointed with oil for the same reason that Saul was no longer the anointed king, because of his death.
the blood of their enemies: Saul and Jonathan were known as military heroes (see 1Sa 11.1–11; 1Sa 14.1–23, 1Sa 14.47–48), though neither to the degree that David was (1Sa 18.7; 1Sa 21.11).

beloved and gracious . . . together in life and in death: Although the relationship between Saul and Jonathan was strained, especially due to Saul’s treatment of David (see 1Sa 20.30–33), Jonathan nevertheless fought and died alongside his father while defending Israel against the Philistine menace.

deeper than the love of women: Jonathan’s loyalty and friendship to David involved personal risk and sacrifice. This commitment was unmatched in David’s experience, including the love of his wives. The phrase in no way implies a homosexual relationship. Jonathan’s love for David is highlighted three times in 1 Samuel (1Sa 18.1, 1Sa 18.3; 1Sa 20.17).

After Saul died, those loyal to David (the tribe of Judah) clashed with those loyal to Saul’s son Ishbosheth (the remaining tribes of Israel). The Philistines, who at this time were essentially overlords of all Palestine west of the Jordan River, likely favored and encouraged this division because it made it easier for them to divide and conquer.

David asked the LORD (cp. 2Sa 5.23–24; Jdg 1.1–2; Jdg 20.18; 1Sa 10.22) by consulting the Urim and Thummim (see Exo 28.30; Lev 8.8; Deu 33.8; 1Sa 14.41) administered by Abiathar, David’s priest (1Sa 23.1–12; 1Sa 30.7–8). David acted when God directed, not before. • Hebron was nineteen miles southwest of Jerusalem. Abraham had lived in this area for a time and eventually purchased a nearby cave for a family burial plot (Gen 23.1–20). The people of the area were sympathetic toward David (see 1Sa 30.26–31).
Ahinoam: See study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 25.43. David’s other wife, Saul’s daughter Michal, had been given to another man after David fled from Saul (1Sa 25.44). • Abigail: See 1Sa 25.1–44.

Once established in Hebron, David made good faith gestures to those still loyal to Saul, such as the men of Jabesh-gilead. However, because they were loyal to . . . Saul and his dynasty, they rejected David as king (2Sa 2.8–11). David was also in league with Nahash, king of the Ammonites (see 2Sa 10.2; 2Sa 17.27–29), who had caused havoc in Jabesh-gilead (1Sa 11.1–15).
David’s anointing by the people of Judah provided the legal basis of his kingship, just as it had for Saul (1Sa 11.15). He had been anointed by the prophet Samuel years earlier (1Sa 16.13).

Abner: See study note on 1 Sam 1Sa 20.25. • Mahanaim was located east of the Jordan River, deep in the highlands of Gilead near a plentiful source of fresh water. Saul and his family had close ties to Gilead (1Sa 11.1–11; 1Sa 31.11–13). Locating east of the Jordan made Ishbosheth’s regime less susceptible to attack by David’s forces. This same area was later King David’s temporary refuge after Absalom’s coup (2Sa 17.24, 2Sa 17.27). • Ishbosheth means “man of shame.” His original name, Esh-baal, means “man of Baal.” The name Baal (“lord, master, possessor”) was associated with a pagan Canaanite deity (e.g., see Num 25.3), so it is likely that Ishbosheth’s name was later changed because of that association.
Profile: Abner

Gilead was the easternmost district of the northern kingdom, Jezreel the northernmost, and Benjamin the southernmost, with Ephraim in the middle. It is unclear which area was the land of the Ashurites. All the rest of Israel refers to the tribes that Ishbosheth ruled over rather than to the geographical area of his kingdom.
Ishbosheth . . . ruled from Mahanaim for two years at some point during David’s 7½-year reign from Hebron. Apparently a gap of five years occurred in which the northern tribes were without a king.
A protracted civil war ensued between Judah (led by David) and the northern tribes (led by Saul’s dynasty). These events set the stage for Abner’s murder (2Sa 3.22–39).
Gibeon, about five miles northwest of Jerusalem, was a key city in Benjamin.
The pool of Gibeon extends down some 80 feet to the water table. Archaeologists estimate that the original diggers had to remove about 3,000 tons of limestone to create it.

a few of our warriors: In the ancient world, enemy armies would sometimes choose individuals or small groups to fight each other as representative gladiators—a custom often referred to as champion warfare (see also 1Sa 17.1–58). • fight hand to hand: The Hebrew term usually includes a component of play. A contest of champions might have been seen as a type of high-stakes game. In this instance, it settled nothing; the fighting expanded into a much wider confrontation with heavier casualties (2Sa 2.17–32).
The casualty count of this fierce battle is noted in 2Sa 2.30–31.
Zeruiah was David’s sister (1Ch 2.15–16), so Joab, Abishai, and Asahel were his nephews.

Go fight someone else! . . . Get away from here! Abner’s words reflect respect between peers trained for the same career, as well as a sense of fair play. The youthful Asahel would have been no match for the more experienced Abner. Abner also knew that if he killed Asahel, the conflict with David would escalate and David’s forces would seek revenge (see 2Sa 3.22–39).
they set out after Abner: See 2Sa 3.27. • Ammah (“conduit”) and Giah (“gushing”) suggest that there was an aqueduct system connected to the pool at Gibeon (2Sa 2.12–13).
bitterness is the only result: Realizing that such wars go on generation after generation, Abner wisely negotiated a truce.
The ram’s horn signaled the beginning and end of combat (see also 2Sa 18.16; Jos 6.15–16). For other uses of the ram’s horn, see study note on 2 Sam 2Sa 6.15.
Abner was wise to put as much distance as possible between his troops and Joab’s forces, recognizing that their desire for blood vengeance could overpower the truce.
The 360 who died were all from the tribe of Benjamin, Saul’s tribe, under the leadership of one of Saul’s relatives. This defeat was a direct blow to Saul’s dynasty (cp. 2Sa 3.1).

The house of David increased, while Saul’s house dwindled. The crucial occasion came when Abner, the real political power in Saul’s camp, switched allegiance to David, taking a considerable number of his northern kinsmen with him.
a long war: This civil war likely continued for most of the seven-plus years that David ruled from Hebron. The truce called by Joab and Abner (2Sa 2.26–28) was short-lived.

One way David “became stronger and stronger” (2Sa 3.1) was by taking more wives and having a son through each. Three of David’s Hebron-born sons died violent deaths, two during David’s reign (Amnon, Absalom), and one shortly after his death (Adonijah).

Geshur was a small Canaanite kingdom in upper Transjordan (the area east of the Jordan) near the Sea of Galilee. Marrying into neighboring royal families created political alliances and secured David’s position against the northern tribes. Solomon also followed this practice (1Ki 3.1; 1Ki 11.1).

accused Abner of sleeping with one of [Saul’s] concubines: It is unclear whether Abner actually did so. Taking a king’s wife or concubine was often part of a usurper’s attempt to replace the king (see 2Sa 12.8; 2Sa 16.21; 1Ki 2.17–25). • Rizpah: See also 2Sa 21.8–14.
some Judean dog: Cp. 1Sa 17.43. • by not handing you over to David: Abner had control over the life and death of Saul’s son.
help David get what the LORD has promised him! Abner was aware that God had chosen David to be king over all Israel (see also 2Sa 3.18).
and give it to David: Cp. 1Sa 28.17. • I will establish the throne of David: Whether an ally or enemy, Abner was a powerful man. Here he speaks like God (see 2Sa 7.13).
didn’t dare say another word: Ishbosheth’s silence speaks loudly of his weakness as a ruler. Abner, who had installed him as king (2Sa 2.8–9), was the real power behind Ishbosheth’s reign.
In the proposed solemn pact (or covenant), Abner recognized that David would be king, while perhaps he hoped to be second-in-command.

Saul had given his daughter Michal to David as his wife (1Sa 18.20–27). However, when Michal saved David’s life from her father (1Sa 19.11–17), Saul terminated the marriage and gave Michal to another man, Palti (1Sa 25.44). For David to get her back now would further cement his claim to Saul’s kingdom (cp. 1Ki 2.13–25).
the lives of 100 Philistines: Saul had hoped that David would be killed in his attempt to secure the bride-price (see 1Sa 18.17–27).

Ishbosheth took: Although Abner made the deal with David (2Sa 3.12–13), it was Ishbosheth who gave Michal to David. This transaction illustrates Ishbosheth’s weakness as a king and his fear of Abner (2Sa 3.11).
In spite of Palti’s anguished weeping, he was powerless to stop what was happening (cp. Jdg 18.1–26). • Bahurim was probably a center of support for Saul’s clan just east of Jerusalem (cp. 2Sa 16.5).
Apparently, there had been growing momentum among the elders of Israel in the north to accept David as king, though the text has made no mention of it to this point.
See also 2Sa 3.9. By bringing relief from the Philistines, David would accomplish what Saul had failed to do (1Sa 9.16).

Because Saul was from their tribe, the men of Benjamin no doubt viewed David, from Judah, as a usurper of Saul’s throne. However, Abner was well-respected in Saul’s regime and so was able to elicit support for David even among Saul’s own tribe.

The narrator emphasized that David sent Abner safely on his way as a friend and an ally (restated in 2Sa 3.22–23). David was at peace with Abner and was not involved in the renowned military leader’s murder (cp. 2Sa 3.28–29). • Despite the murder of Abner (2Sa 3.27), the northern tribes eventually did make a covenant with David to make him their king, just as Abner had promised (2Sa 5.1–3).
The precise location of the well of Sirah is unknown; presumably it was not far from Hebron. • David knew nothing about it: See study note on 2Sa 3.21.

as if to speak with him privately: Joab accused Abner of deception (2Sa 3.25), but he used deception himself to lure Abner to his death. • in revenge: Joab was motivated by the practice of blood vengeance, avenging the death of a kinsman by killing the killer.

David made it clear that he had nothing to do with Abner’s death, labeling it as a crime. David knew that because his second-in-command had killed Abner, rumors would circulate among those loyal to Saul’s dynasty that David had ordered the killing. • I vow by the LORD: David called on the Lord to hold him accountable if he were lying.

leprosy: While leprosy is a possible translation, the Hebrew here probably refers to a broader range of skin inflammations, not only Hansen’s disease. • who walks on crutches: This curse effectively alienated Joab from David, and from this point on they had only a professional relationship. David’s deathbed order to Solomon to get rid of Joab (1Ki 2.5–6) and Solomon’s exoneration of David in Abner’s death (1Ki 2.31–33) indicate that David’s mourning over Abner was genuine.

David himself walked: David’s public presence in the mourning procession, his open weeping at the gravesite (2Sa 3.32), and his dramatic fast (2Sa 3.35) made evident to the public that he had not ordered Abner’s killing (2Sa 3.37).

Burying Abner in Hebron, David’s capital city at the time, rather than at some northern site reinforced Abner’s shift of support from Saul to David. Presumably it encouraged others from the northern tribes to follow Abner’s example.
as fools die: Abner was deceived by Joab, an enemy who posed as a friend (see 2Sa 3.27).
a wicked plot: Normal warfare could not defeat Abner, a seasoned warrior. Only treachery could.
begged him to eat: See also 2Sa 12.17.
See study note on 2Sa 3.31.
too strong for me to control: Just as Ishbosheth could not control Abner, David could not control Joab. However, David had faith that the LORD would repay Joab for murdering Abner.
all Israel became paralyzed with fear: Abner’s true power was evident in Ishbosheth’s reaction to his death (cp. Jos 2.9–11; Jos 5.1). Ishbosheth’s timidity bred the same among his followers.

Beeroth was located in Benjamin near Gibeon. Probably because of Saul’s persecution of the non-Israelite residents in that region (see 2Sa 21.1–9), the citizens of Beeroth had fled to Gittaim, the location of which is unknown.

This parenthetical statement shows that, with the death of Ishbosheth (2Sa 4.5–7), Saul’s dynasty was unable to continue—the only other heir was a young child who was crippled (see also 2Sa 9.1–13). • Mephibosheth is a nickname meaning “from the mouth of shame,” possibly referring to his physical condition. No crippled animal could ever be offered to God, and no disabled priest was allowed to stand before God with the people’s offerings (Lev 21.19). Likewise, Mephibosheth’s condition probably disqualified him from the crown. His name change from Merib-baal (see 1Ch 9.40) also removed association with Baal (see study note on 2 Sam 2Sa 2.8).
Recab and Baanah believed they would gain David’s favor by committing this treacherous act.

your enemy Saul: As far as we know, David never referred to Saul as an enemy. • the LORD has given . . . revenge: Wrongdoers often presume upon God’s favor to justify political ambition. However, David would not reward treachery.
Someone once told me: Cp. 2Sa 1.1–16.

cut off their hands and feet: Displaying the dismembered bodies of Ishbosheth’s killers shamed them by denying them proper burial (cp. 1Sa 31.8–13); it was also a public testimony of David’s innocence in Ishbosheth’s death.

After the murder of Abner and Ishbosheth, the elders of the northern tribes accepted David as their king. David thus obtained an extended empire (2Sa 5.1–5), a new capital city (2Sa 5.6–10), a new palace (2Sa 5.11), a new family (2Sa 5.13–16), and renewed confidence (2Sa 5.17–25).
your own flesh and blood: Years of civil war had set brother against brother, resulting in much bloodshed (see 2Sa 3.1).

you were the one: In the ancient world, a covenant relationship (a suzerain-vassal treaty) was sometimes formed between subjects (the vassals) and a ruler (the suzerain) because of past aid, often rescue from enemies (see Jdg 8.22, Gideon; Jdg 11.8–11, Jephthah; 1Sa 11.1–15, Saul). This type of relationship is the background for the covenant concept in Scripture: God was Israel’s covenant Lord because he had freed them from Egypt (cp. Exo 19.4; Exo 20.1–2). • the LORD told you: Israel was already aware of God’s selection of David (cp. 2Sa 3.9). • shepherd of my people Israel: This phrase is quoted in Mat 2.6 when King Herod asks the leading priests about the prophecies concerning the Messiah.

King David made a covenant that demanded the people’s loyalty, yet allowed them to maintain a sense of tribal privilege and individual dignity. It served as a constitution, containing stipulations obligating both the king and the people. • they anointed him king: While David had already been anointed by Samuel (1Sa 16.13), this public ceremony demonstrated the people’s acceptance of David as king.
Hebron: See study note on 2Sa 2.1.
David acquired a new capital city, Jerusalem, for the newly extended kingdom.

The Jebusites resided in Jerusalem prior to its conquest by David (see Exo 34.11; Deu 7.1–6; Deu 20.17; Jos 15.63; Jdg 1.21). Nothing is known of them outside the Bible. In archaeological discoveries from Mari in Syria, a similar name (Yabasi) appears as both a clan name and a geographic location. • Even the blind and lame: The Jebusites had a false notion of invincibility. Another possible translation is you won’t enter here unless you can get rid of the blind and lame, implying that David’s capture of Jerusalem was as likely as achieving a miraculous cure for blindness and lameness.
Theme: Jerusalem

the fortress of Zion: At this time Jerusalem was probably a small site of nine to twelve square acres. The Jebusites’ arrogance, and the fact that the city had not been conquered previously, suggests that it was well fortified.

How David conquered Jerusalem is debated. Possibly he used a water tunnel as a conduit for his troops to enter the city, but not all interpreters agree. Another possibility is that David and his men conquered Jerusalem with the more traditional siege works and by scaling the walls. The term translated water tunnel occurs only here and in Psa 42.7 (“raging seas”); the statement might be metaphorical, referring to the ferocity of the attack. • The blind and the lame may not enter the house: House could refer either to the Temple, which had not yet been built, or to David’s palace. The proverb may explain why Mephibosheth, Saul’s descendant, was barred from the throne (see study note on 2 Sam 2Sa 4.4). • David also promised that those who undertook the siege of Jerusalem would become the commanders of his army (see 1Ch 11.6).

made the fortress his home: Jerusalem was a practical place from which David could effectively administer the extended kingdom. It was a centrally located neutral city on the border between Judah and the northern territories, and its natural fortifications and water tunnel were useful in case of siege. • the supporting terraces: See study note on 1 Kgs 1Ki 9.15.
the LORD . . . was with him: While David was a skilled and charismatic leader, his growing success was ultimately due to God’s blessing.

Hiram of Tyre: Although the meeting of these two neighboring kings is reported just after Jerusalem’s conquest, it probably happened much later. Hiram remained on the throne in Tyre at least until Solomon’s twenty-fourth year, and one ancient source notes that he had a reign of thirty-four years. Another tradition implies that Hiram became king of Tyre just eight years before Solomon became king of Israel. The same king performed a similar act for Solomon (1Ki 5.1–18). The report of Hiram’s support is perhaps given here because it ties in with the theme of David’s confirmation and establishment as Israel’s king (2Sa 5.12).
David realized that his reign as king over Israel was for the sake of God’s people Israel, not just for his personal benefit or enrichment.
The expansion of David’s family reflected his growing success and power as Israel’s king. Solomon was David’s most important Jerusalem-born son (see 2Sa 12.24–25).

For the first time as king, David engaged the Philistines in battle. • David’s life has been portrayed thus far in 2 Samuel with a repeated pattern: He was crowned king in Hebron (2Sa 2.4), won a battle (2Sa 2.12–17), became stronger (2Sa 3.1), and started a large family (2Sa 3.2–5). Now he was crowned in Jerusalem (2Sa 5.3), became stronger (2Sa 5.10), expanded his family (2Sa 5.13–14), and won a battle (2Sa 5.17–25). This parallel structure draws attention to both of David’s coronations with signs of divine blessing and prosperity.
The valley of Rephaim is located between Bethlehem and Jerusalem (cp. 2Sa 23.13–14).

Baal-perazim: David used the term Baal to honor the Lord for the victory he gave Israel. The title means “the lord of earthquakes/openings,” and was evidently an acceptable title for Yahweh until the Canaanite worship of Baal became an overwhelming problem in Israel. Every time David engaged in combat with the Philistines in 2 Samuel (2Sa 5.17–25; 2Sa 8.1; 2Sa 21.15–22; 2Sa 23.13–17), he won without losing a single soldier. How different from Saul, for whom victory over the Philistines was impossible!

David . . . confiscated them: David’s confiscation of the Philistines’ idols was payback for their capture of the Ark during Eli’s time (1Sa 4.1–11). David burned the idols rather than carrying them off as trophies (1Ch 14.12).
David again asked the LORD (2Sa 5.19), but this time God gave a much more detailed answer. Unlike the frontal assault of 2Sa 5.20, God instructed David to circle around behind the enemy.
Gibeon: David cleared the Philistines from the central hill country of Israel between Gibeon in the east (in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem) to Gezer in the west.

Except for the brief reference in 1Sa 14.18 (see note), the Ark of the Covenant has not been mentioned since 1Sa 7.1–2, when the Philistines returned the captured Ark to Beth-shemesh and then to Kiriath-jearim, where it was placed in Abinadab’s home. The Ark’s virtual absence during Saul’s forty-year reign highlights that Saul, in his spiritual insensitivity, did not seek the Lord (see 1Ch 10.13–14; 1Ch 13.3). David brought the Ark into Jerusalem, effectively acknowledging and enthroning (see 2Sa 6.2) Yahweh as the true king over Israel in the new capital.
Theme: Celebration
is enthroned between the cherubim: See also 1Sa 4.4; 2Ki 19.15; Psa 80.1; Psa 99.1.

According to God’s instructions (Exo 25.14; Exo 37.5; Num 4.6), the Ark was to be carried by Levites of the clan of Kohath, holding two poles slipped through four rings at the corners of the Ark. God’s instructions were ignored in this instance. • Uzzah and Ahio: In 1Sa 7.1, Eleazar, another son of Abinadab, was put in charge of the Ark.
The musical instruments were played by Levites (1Ch 16.4–6).

steadied the Ark: Although Uzzah meant well and acted instinctively, he violated the Ark by touching it (cp. Exo 19.12–13; Num 4.15). He suffered the same penalty as the people from Beth-shemesh (1Sa 6.19). David later had the Levites carry the Ark into Jerusalem in accordance with God’s will (see 1Ch 15.2, 1Ch 15.13–15).

David was angry . . . the LORD’s anger: Cp. Gen 4.5; 1Sa 15.11; Jon 4.1; Luk 15.27–28. • Perez-uzzah: The first part of this name appears in 2Sa 5.20 (Baal-perazim) as the place where God burst through the Philistine ranks.
David was . . . afraid: Similarly, Moses trembled at the display of divine wrath (Deu 9.19) and at the dramatic display of God’s fiery presence (see Heb 12.21).

Obed-edom was a Levite (1Ch 15.18, 1Ch 15.21; 1Ch 16.38; 1Ch 26.4, 1Ch 26.8, 1Ch 26.15; 2Ch 25.24) who lived either in the Philistine city of Gath or in an Israelite town of a similar name (e.g., Gath-rimmon, a city given to the Levites, Jos 21.25).

God blessed Obed-edom with health, prosperity, and family. God’s presence, which is a curse to the ungodly (1Sa 5.1–12), is a blessing to his people. Obed-edom must have taken care to preserve the Ark’s sanctity.
David reasoned that if God blessed Obed-edom simply for storing the Ark, God would surely bless David for placing the Ark in a dwelling specifically built for it in the capital city.
David offered this sacrifice of praise to God immediately, just six steps into the journey.

priestly garment: This word (Hebrew ’epod, “ephod”) is associated with an Akkadian word, epattu, meaning “a costly garment.” Richly ornamented with gold, this garment was used for robing statues of gods. Because priests and (sometimes) kings were considered sacred persons, they traditionally used garments of this type (see 1Sa 2.18, 1Sa 2.28; 1Sa 14.3; 1Sa 22.18; 1Sa 23.6, 1Sa 23.9).

In 2Sa 15.10, rams’ horns announce the crowning of a new king; in 2Sa 20.1, they proclaim rebellion. Here they celebrate placing the Ark in its own tent (see study note on 2Sa 6.17), which in effect installed Yahweh’s throne in Jerusalem.

Michal is identified as the daughter of Saul three times (2Sa 6.16, 2Sa 6.20, 2Sa 6.23). The use of her father’s name underscores the ambiguity of David’s relationship to her. Was she more David’s wife or Saul’s daughter? Had David reunited with her (2Sa 3.13) because he loved her or because she was politically useful to him? • Michal might have been filled with contempt for any of the following reasons: (1) She thought David’s behavior was too sexually suggestive in front of a young female audience; (2) she was jealous over the glory David was receiving while she sat at home, a neglected wife; (3) she resented David’s indifference to her for many years, his taking of other wives, and her being torn away from her second husband Palti (2Sa 3.16–17); or (4) she felt sorrow for her late father and David’s success at the expense of Saul’s dynasty (see study note on 2Sa 6.21).

While the special tent for the Ark was not as opulent as the tent used during the wilderness wandering, this tent was a return to the wilderness tradition suspended two generations earlier at the destruction of Shiloh (Psa 78.60–61). David’s special tent was the very last Tabernacle; Solomon, David’s successor, built a permanent Temple for the Lord. Because this occasion was joyous, not penitential, the sacrifice included burnt offerings and peace offerings but not sin or guilt offerings.

blessed the people: Although blessing was typically the express function of priests, kings also offered blessings at significant national occasions (Solomon, 1Ki 8.14, 1Ki 8.55; 2Ch 6.3; Hezekiah, 2Ch 31.8).
David’s gifts of food to every Israelite anticipated other royal gifts they would receive under his reign.
David’s response to Michal might hint at the real reason for her indignation—that she resented David’s success in light of the tragic decline of her father’s family.
David would not restrain his enthusiasm in celebrating before the Lord. In fact, he would exceed the enthusiasm he had shown thus far.

Michal was the only one of David’s many wives who did not bear him at least one child. Either God was punishing her (cp. Gen 20.17–18) for her disdainful attitude toward David’s exuberant praise, or David and Michal’s relationship had become so strained that they never again shared the marriage bed. Because Michal remained childless, yet another aspect of Saul’s dynasty was cut off. This occasion is Michal’s last appearance in the text.
David was not satisfied merely building a tent for the Ark (2Sa 6.17). He wanted to build a house for God.
If God had only a tent while David had a palace, it might create the impression that David was the real king rather than God. Thus, David intended to build a temple for God.
from all . . . enemies: See Deu 12.9–10; 1Ki 5.4; 1Ki 8.56. David’s rest was temporary because shortly he was at war again (see 2Sa 8.1–18).

Nathan is recorded in David’s life on three occasions: (1) here with a promise for David; (2) in 2Sa 12.1–15 with a parable of judgment against David; (3) in 1Ki 1.11–27 with a plan for installing Solomon as David’s successor. • A cedar palace would have been made of stone with cedar paneling inside.

Go ahead and do whatever you have in mind: Nathan’s counsel to David was Nathan’s own idea. As it turned out, God disqualified David from building the Temple (see 1Ch 22.8). Even true prophets are fallible when speaking on their own initiative rather than from God’s revelation.
Theme: God’s Covenant with David
Are you the one? God wanted someone to build him a house, but David wasn’t the right person.

never lived in a house: Prior to the building of the Temple in one fixed location, God’s dwelling was the Tabernacle, a mobile, tentlike structure. The text here uses language of human experience to describe a truth about God (see study notes on Exod Exo 29.18; Deut Deu 8.2). Although God is omnipresent, he chose the Tabernacle and Temple as his “dwelling place” in ancient Israel (see study note on 2 Chr 2Ch 2.5–6; cp. Act 17.24).

I have never once complained . . . never asked: While it was a less impressive structure than the Temple, the Tabernacle honored God because he had ordained its use for that period of Israel’s history.
Instead of David’s building God a house, God promised to build David a house, a permanent dynasty of kings from David’s descendants.

tending sheep: Kings in the ancient Near East were often called shepherds (see 1Ki 22.17; Isa 44.28; Eze 34.2; Eze 37.24; Nah 3.18; Zec 10.3). David, who had been a shepherd, called the Lord his shepherd (Psa 23.1).

I have been with you: Through his guidance and protection, God was actively involved in shaping David’s entire life. • I will make your name . . . famous: God made this promise only to Abraham and David. (see Gen 12.2).

never be disturbed: Through David and his heirs, a lasting peace would engulf the land, in contrast with the intermittent and temporary periods of peace during the days of the judges, when one predatory nation after another shattered Israel’s well-being. God’s promise of rest from all your enemies was first mentioned by Joshua (Jos 1.13, Jos 1.15; Jos 22.4), and later realized in the ministry of some of the judges (Jdg 3.11, Jdg 3.30; Jdg 5.31; Jdg 8.28).

he will make a house for you: God wanted to do infinitely more for David than David could conceive of doing for God. While David was primarily interested in projects such as building a temple, God was interested in bringing blessing to his people through one righteous dynasty of kings.

one of your descendants . . . will build a house . . . for my name: David’s son Solomon would build the Temple; David’s personal involvement in military conflict and bloodshed disqualified him from building God’s Temple (1Ch 22.8–9).

I will be his father, and he will be my son: Kings in David’s line would enjoy a special covenant relationship with God, as the whole nation of Israel did (cp. Exo 6.7; Lev 26.12). Jesus later became the ultimate fulfillment of this prophecy (see Heb 1.5). Paul quotes this phrase in 2Co 6.18 and applies it to all believers. • If he sins, I will correct and discipline him: God would steer David’s offspring, the future kings of Israel, back onto the right track whenever they sinned. Cp. the experience of Jesus, who never sinned, yet endured God’s discipline (see Heb 4.15; Heb 5.8; Heb 12.1–11).

for all time . . . forever: God’s promises do not negate human responsibility and accountability (2Sa 7.14). Wrongdoing requires a just response from God. However, no wayward son of David could move God to withdraw his promise to preserve David’s dynasty. Although the dynasty disappeared for hundreds of years, David’s house and kingdom were renewed in Jesus Christ, the sinless descendant of David who reigns forever.
David responded prayerfully to God’s promise of a dynasty, repeatedly acknowledging God’s true kingship as Sovereign LORD.
David’s question, “Who am I?” was an expression of genuine humility (cp. Exo 4.11).
God’s plan to give David a lasting dynasty stretched well beyond his lifetime. The promise is fulfilled forever in the eternal reign of Christ (Rev 11.15).
You know what your servant is really like: God made his promises to David with full knowledge that David had both strengths and weaknesses.

God’s will, rather than David’s personal ambition, enabled David to accomplish great things. • you have done: David spoke of what God promised to do for his heirs over the generations as an already-accomplished fact, showing his unshakable belief in God’s faithfulness.
There is no one like you: David affirms God’s uniqueness (see also 2Sa 22.32; Deu 4.39; 1Sa 2.2).
Israel was set apart from every other nation by the uniqueness of its God and by the relationship the people had with him.

David praised God for his goodness in redeeming and establishing the nation of Israel (2Sa 7.23–24), not just David and his royal line (2Sa 7.18–21). His prayer is corporate rather than just personal.
Confirm it: David was not asking God for a sign (as Gideon had done, Jdg 6.17). Rather, David was saying, “God, may it be so.”

Although God had promised to make David’s name great (2Sa 7.9), David was concerned that God’s name be honored. David knew that if God were not the focus of the people’s praise, then David’s dynasty would count for nothing.
The expansion of David’s empire through military victories (2Sa 8.1–14) and the establishment of his royal bureaucracy (2Sa 8.15–18) fulfilled God’s promise of a famous name (2Sa 7.9; cp. 2Sa 8.13).

Moab was on the east side of the Dead Sea. Earlier, the people of Moab had provided David’s parents with refuge during Saul’s reign (1Sa 22.3–4); David’s great-grandmother, Ruth, was from Moab. For whatever reason, no such fraternal relationship existed any longer. • two groups to be executed for every one group to be spared: This is the only time in 2 Samuel that David executed captives taken in battle (see Num 21.29; Num 24.17; Deu 2.9).

Hadadezer reappears in 2Sa 10.16 as David’s foe. He was either the direct son of Rehob and his successor or the reigning king of a dynasty established by a king named Rehob, whose kingdom was near the northern city of Dan (see Jdg 18.28; cp. Num 13.21). • Zobah was north and east of David’s kingdom. • It is possible that David, not Hadadezer (literally he), marched out to strengthen his control. • the Euphrates River: Literally the river; 1Ch 18.3 specifically identifies the Euphrates. Cp. 2Sa 10.16.
David would have crippled . . . horses to prevent their reuse by the enemy and because kings in Israel were not to accumulate horses (Deu 17.16).

Hadadezer’s neighbors, Arameans from Damascus, were of no help to him in repelling David. They would later be more successful against Solomon (1Ki 11.23–25) but less successful in their attack of Samaria during the days of King Ahab of Israel (1Ki 20.1–43).

David established army garrisons in Aram but not in Moab (2Sa 8.2), which suggests that Aram was a more formidable force and that David needed a military presence there to maintain control. • the LORD made David victorious: Cp. 2Sa 8.14. God was the real source of David’s growth and power.

gold shields: See also 2Ki 11.10. • brought . . . to Jerusalem: In conformity with God’s stipulations for a good king (Deu 17.17), David dedicated these valuable items to God (see 2Sa 8.11) rather than hoarding them for his own wealth and splendor.
Hamath was northwest of Hadadezer’s Zobah.

his son: King Toi dispatched the crown prince rather than another entourage on this mission because he considered it vital to stay properly connected with David. • Joram: The prefix Jo- is an abbreviated form of Yahweh; Joram means “Yahweh is exalted.” In 1Ch 18.10 the prince’s name is Hadoram, which means “Hadad [a Canaanite god] is exalted.” It is possible that Toi changed the prince’s name for diplomatic reasons, to make it more agreeable to David.

Captured war booty and diplomatic exchanges went into God’s treasury rather than the king’s treasury. Voluntary gifts (2Sa 8.11) and plunder exacted from defeated foes (2Sa 8.11–12) also were dedicated . . . to the LORD.

These two verses highlight three of David’s war policies: (1) inflict heavy damage on the enemy (18,000 casualties); (2) reduce them to vassalage (they became David’s subjects); (3) place army garrisons in the conquered territory to maintain control over them. • Edomites: This name is very similar to Arameans in old Hebrew script. Edomites is more likely, however, because the Valley of Salt (the Dead Sea area) was adjacent to Edomite, not Aramean, territory.

David’s bureaucracy included (1) military officials (Joab); (2) a court historian (Jehoshaphat); (3) priests (Zadok and Ahimelech); (4) a scribe or court secretary (Seraiah); and (5) a security officer (Benaiah, who became a commander under Solomon; see also 1Ki 2.25–46).
Profile: Zadok

the king’s bodyguard: Hebrew the Kerethites and Pelethites. Both peoples were probably foreigners, especially the Kerethites, who might have come from the island of Crete (see also 1Sa 30.14; Eze 25.16). These groups might have been Philistine mercenaries. • David’s sons served as priestly leaders: David was from Judah and was not a Levite. Alongside the traditional priesthood, David might have inaugurated a religious class specifically tied to his dynasty, probably to serve the royal court (see also study note on 2 Sam 2Sa 20.26).

David showed mercy to Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s crippled son. The incident is sandwiched between David’s victories in battle (2Sa 8.1–18, 2Sa 8.10), indicating that David also had concern for individuals and a compassionate heart.

show kindness: The Hebrew word (khesed) speaks of covenant loyalty and faithfulness. The word frequently describes God’s commitment to his people, but it can also describe the devotion and loyalty between any two persons. David’s use of the word here echoes the language of the covenant of friendship between himself and Jonathan (1Sa 20.12–17). • for Jonathan’s sake: Mephibosheth was Saul’s only remaining descendant and the only son of Jonathan.
Mephibosheth was crippled in both feet from a childhood accident (see 2Sa 4.4).

Lo-debar was a small town in northern Transjordan (the area east of the Jordan), close to Mahanaim, the capital city of Mephibosheth’s late uncle, Ishbosheth. The town was also near Jabesh-gilead, where Saul first made a name for himself (1Sa 11.1–13). • Makir son of Ammiel, Mephibosheth’s host, later supported David during Absalom’s revolt (2Sa 17.27).
As Saul had once sent for David (1Sa 16.19), now David sent for Mephibosheth. However, Saul sent for someone to minister to him, whereas David sent for someone to whom he could minister.
Given Mephibosheth’s physical limitations, bowing low to the ground must have been very difficult.
David had confiscated all the property that had belonged to . . . Saul.
a dead dog like me: Mephibosheth knew that anyone with a possible claim to the throne might be killed as a threat.

Both Ziba and Mephibosheth (2Sa 9.6) used the phrase “I am your servant” when presenting themselves before King David. By referring to himself as David’s servant, Ziba showed that he was no longer loyal to Saul’s dynasty. The sincerity of both later came into question (2Sa 16.1–4; 2Sa 19.17–30).
crippled in both feet: See 2Sa 4.4.

Following the interlude of ch 2Sa 9.1–13, the narrative returns to David’s military feats. The Ammonites were likely the dominant political power in Transjordan (the area east of the Jordan) during Saul’s reign and the early years of David’s reign.
The king of Ammon insulted David’s ambassadors, which led to two battles between Israel and Ammon (2Sa 10.6–2Sa 12.31).

Some time after this: King Hadadezer appears in 2Sa 10.1–19 as David’s active and capable foe (2Sa 10.16), yet in 2Sa 8.1–18 David had defeated him (2Sa 8.3) and plundered his city (2Sa 8.7, 2Sa 8.12). Either Hadadezer was still alive, had regrouped, and revolted in 2Sa 10.1–19; or possibly 2Sa 10.1–19 unpacks the events of 2Sa 8.1–18 as a prelude to 2Sa 11.1–27.
In both chs 2Sa 9.1–13 and 2Sa 10.1–19, David wanted to show loyalty (khesed; also in 2Sa 9.1, 2Sa 9.3).

Shaving half of each man’s beard was intended to maximize the humiliation and ridicule. • cut off their robes: The humiliating display of genitalia or the buttocks was associated with military defeat and exile (Isa 20.1–6).

The city of Jericho had not yet been formally reconstructed (see 1Ki 16.34), but the site was located adjacent to the largest and most plentiful spring in the land, so people continued to dwell in the area. Anyone traveling from Ammon to Jerusalem would pass right by it. It was a place of seclusion from the men’s humiliation.

Aramean foot soldiers: See 2Sa 8.5–6. • Beth-rehob and Zobah: See 2Sa 8.3, 2Sa 8.12. • the land of Tob (literally the man of Tob) possibly refers to a vassal king and region under Hadadezer’s sovereignty.
The Israelites had a double battle: against the Ammonites in front of their fortifications at the entrance of the city gate and against the Aramean army in the open fields.
Be courageous! Often the priest or another leader offered prebattle exhortations (cp. Num 31.6; Deu 20.2; Jdg 4.14; 1Sa 4.4; 1Sa 14.3; 1Sa 23.9).
Hadadezer: See study note on 2Sa 10.1. • Helam is unknown. • Apparently David had extended his empire as far north as the Euphrates River (see also study note on 2Sa 8.3).

David’s affair with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah show that David was capable of great failure and cast a dark shadow over David’s life and career. These failures came during a time of great military success against the Ammonites (2Sa 10.1–2Sa 11.1; 2Sa 12.26–31).

In the spring of the year, the land began to dry out after the heavy winter rains. Kings avoided war during the rainy season. • David stayed behind either because he was irresponsible in carrying out his royal duties or because he trusted Joab to efficiently handle the Ammonite problem (cp. 2Sa 10.7). This is the first mention of a leader of Israel staying off the battlefield in a time of war.

walking on the roof: The roofs of houses were flat and were regularly used for a variety of purposes, such as drying and storing produce (Jos 2.6), strolling and socializing, and sleeping in warm weather. • Bathsheba was taking a bath in plain view of the roof of the king’s palace, but perhaps she assumed everyone would be inside, seeking refuge from the heat or having a midday rest.
Profile: Bathsheba

Bathsheba means “daughter of seven” or “daughter of oath.” Her father Eliam was the son of Ahithophel (see 2Sa 23.34), an adviser sought by David and then by Absalom (2Sa 15.12; 2Sa 16.23). Much to David’s chagrin (2Sa 15.31), Ahithophel later shifted his allegiance from David to Absalom (2Sa 17.1–4, 2Sa 17.14) and advised Absalom to sleep with David’s concubines on a rooftop, in open view (2Sa 16.20–22). • Uriah is a Hebrew name (meaning “Yahweh [is] my light”); either he was a foreign mercenary, a convert to Israelite religion, or an Israelite of Hittite heritage. Uriah might also have been a member of the non-Israelite aristocracy in Jerusalem that predated David’s conquest of the city. He was one of the Thirty—David’s mightiest warriors (2Sa 23.39).

It is not clear whether Bathsheba came to David’s palace voluntarily. That no protestations are recorded (cp. 2Sa 13.12–13) and that she married David, bore him another child, and persuaded him to designate their child as heir (1Ki 1.11–21) suggest that she might have been a willing partner. However, Bathsheba mourned for her husband (2Sa 11.26–27), and only David was condemned for this act (2Sa 11.27), so she might have been violated against her will. • The phrase after having her menstrual period (see Lev 15.19–24) is included to show that the child Bathsheba conceived could not possibly have been Uriah’s.

and relax: David assumed that Uriah would have sex with Bathsheba while on this weekend pass. Then everyone except Bathsheba would assume that the child was Uriah’s, conceived on this night. • a gift: David might not have even cared whether the husband and wife were intimate. Uriah’s return to his house would stifle any rumors as to how and when Bathsheba became pregnant.

in tents (Hebrew, sukkoth, the name behind Sukkot, “the Festival of Shelters,” Deu 16.13–17): These were temporary structures made of branches and foliage used by soldiers in the field, herdsmen protecting their cattle, or grape harvesters in the vineyard. • wine and dine and sleep with my wife? Uriah was willing to wine and dine with David (2Sa 11.13), so it was not sharing the table with Bathsheba that Uriah wished to avoid but sharing the marriage bed. The Israelites considered the war camp a holy place because God was present to fight for his people. Thus, soldiers on duty avoided anything that caused impurity, such as sexual intercourse (Lev 15.18; see also 1Sa 21.5–6).
Uriah was not the only casualty: David sacrificed several other Israelite soldiers while attempting to hide his sin.
Wasn’t Abimelech . . . killed . . . by a woman: Cp. Jdg 9.54.
The sword devours this one today and that one tomorrow! David’s callous attitude toward the unnecessary deaths he caused is chilling.
Chapter 12 expands on the last phrase of 2Sa 11.27.

The LORD sent Nathan to David at least nine months after his adulterous sin. • This story is a rare Old Testament instance of a parable (see also Jdg 9.8–15). Such stories can be effective for communicating truth. • David was rich in the royal treasures he possessed, the number of wives he had, and all the promises of God for his future. Uriah by contrast was poor: he had one wife, one home, and no lineage.
like a baby daughter: Nathan’s comparison of this lamb to a daughter (Hebrew bath) strikes a parallel with Bathsheba’s name (see study note on 2Sa 11.3).
he took the poor man’s lamb: Samuel had previously warned that a king would take what was not his (1Sa 8.11–17).

The rich man of the parable did not deserve to die according to the law; instead, he must repay four lambs (cp. Exo 22.1). Intriguingly, David would later lose four of his sons (Bathsheba’s first child, 2Sa 12.18; Amnon, 2Sa 13.29; Absalom, 2Sa 18.14–15; Adonijah, 1Ki 2.25).

You are that man! David did deserve to die for his crime (Lev 20.10). • I anointed . . . I gave . . . I would have given you: David’s sin not only violated God’s commandments against murder, adultery, and coveting (Exo 20.1–17) but also amounted to a brazen disregard for all that the Lord had graciously given him.

His wives were probably the concubines of Saul’s harem (cp. 2Sa 3.7). The phrase could refer to Saul’s wife Ahinoam, although David probably married a different woman with the same name (cp. 1Sa 14.50; 1Sa 25.43).

from this time on (literally forever): Contrast God’s gracious “forever” promises of 2Sa 7.13–29. • The reminder of what David had done with the sword (2Sa 12.9) and what role the sword would play in his family recalls David’s cavalier response to Joab’s report of the deaths of Uriah and other innocent Israelites (2Sa 11.25).
I will cause your own household to rebel against you: Absalom’s revolt against David (chs 2Sa 14.1–19) fulfilled this promise.

Nevertheless . . . your child will die: At times, God transfers punishment of fathers to their descendants (Exo 20.5; Exo 34.7; Num 14.18; Deu 5.9; Jer 32.18). Although David repented and was forgiven (2Sa 12.13), it did not cancel all retribution; it delayed it until a later generation (cp. 1Ki 21.27–29).
The series of actions described here show David resuming normal life activities. That he did so this soon after his son’s death amazed his advisers (2Sa 12.21).
David grieved before his son’s death, hoping to ward off punishment.
Can I bring him back again? I will go to him one day: The irreversibility of his son’s death forced David to face his own mortality. But he also showed his confidence in the afterlife.

Even after Uriah’s death, Bathsheba was still called Uriah’s wife (2Sa 12.9; see also Mat 1.6). Only here is she called David’s wife. • Solomon: Pronounced Shelomoh in Hebrew, it probably means “his peace,” from the Hebrew shalom. It might mean “his replacement”; cp. Shelemiah (Jer 36.14, “Yahweh has provided compensation”) and Shelumiel (Num 1.6, “God [is] my compensation”); both contain the root shelem (“replacement, compensation”).
Jedidiah means “loved by Yahweh.” This God-given second name for Solomon, mentioned only here, guaranteed his future, as it expressed God’s special love for him.
David’s battle with the Ammonites, begun in ch 2Sa 10.1–19, ended in success.

David removed the crown: David had, in effect, become the Ammonites’ king. • a vast amount of plunder: Instructions against taking such booty during a conquest (Deu 7.25–26) show how dangerous David’s actions were. Such wealth might seduce the king’s heart away from God.

He also made slaves of the people of Rabbah and forced them to labor with: Enslaving defeated peoples was in accord with Deu 20.11. Solomon later did the same with the Canaanites (1Ki 9.20–22; see also Jdg 1.30, Jdg 1.33). The alternate reading might indicate torture inflicted on the defeated Ammonites (cp. 1Ch 20.3).

Absalom had a beautiful sister: Tamar was Absalom’s full sister but Amnon’s half sister (see 2Sa 3.2–3). Absalom would later avenge Tamar as her nearest relative (2Sa 13.23–29; cp. Gen 34.1–31; Num 35.19).
Profile: Absalom

obsessed . . . ill: As the story reveals, Amnon’s “love” (2Sa 13.4) for Tamar was a sickly erotic obsession. • She was a virgin: Amnon’s fixation deepened because Tamar was sexually untouched. • thought he could never have her: The law prohibited marriage between brother and sister (Lev 18.9, Lev 18.11; Lev 20.17; Deu 27.22). But Amnon did not want to marry Tamar; he only wanted to have sex with her.
crafty (literally wise): Jonadab’s “wisdom” was akin to the serpent’s shrewdness (Gen 3.1). • In the context of a royal court, the Hebrew term for friend is closer to “counselor” or “adviser.”
morning after morning: Amnon’s obsession was all-consuming and ongoing.

wicked things: The Hebrew word nebalah (“outrage,” “deplorable act”) often describes sexual crimes such as rape and adultery (Gen 34.7; Deu 22.21; Jdg 20.6, Jdg 20.10; Jer 29.23) that the perpetrator must pay for with his life. • in Israel: The addition of this phrase either indicates indignation that the crime happened among Israelites or characterizes the act as a violation of Israelite standards of sexual morality.
he will let you marry me: Tamar said this to gain time; Amnon knew that the law prohibited marriage between half siblings (see study note on 2Sa 13.2), and he refused to back off.
since he was stronger: Tamar resisted as much as she could.
That Amnon’s feelings for Tamar so quickly turned to hate shows that his so-called “love” for her (2Sa 13.4) was really only selfish lust.
worse than what you’ve already done: A virgin who had been raped became unmarriageable (2Sa 13.20; see Deu 22.28–29).
a long, beautiful robe: The same phrase is used to describe Joseph’s robe in Gen 37.3.

Tamar tore her robe to symbolize the violation of her virginity and honor and to mourn the death of her future (2Sa 13.16). • Ashes represented death; sitting amid ashes or putting ashes on one’s head were signs of mourning (Est 4.1–3; Job 42.6; Dan 9.3; Jon 3.6).

keep quiet for now . . . Don’t you worry about it: Absalom’s words of comfort seem hollow in light of her disgrace and mourning; this toned-down response hid Absalom’s rage (2Sa 13.22) from the already distraught Tamar. • as a desolate woman: See study note on 2Sa 13.16.

King David . . . was very angry: But he apparently never punished Amnon—as in the Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek version, which add that it was because he loved Amnon. Another possibility is that as an adulterer himself (see 2Sa 11.1–2Sa 12.24), David considered himself in no position to punish his son’s sexual sin. A third possibility is that David thought this was God’s “eye for an eye” punishment for his own sexual indiscretion.

Baal-hazor should not be confused with the famous fortified city of Hazor located north of the Sea of Galilee. The generally accepted location of Baal-hazor is Jebel el-Asur, some fifteen miles north of Jerusalem. • a feast: Sheep shearing was a time for sharing bounty and blessing with others (see 1Sa 25.2–8).
David tore his robe, as Tamar had done after being violated (2Sa 13.19)—a sign of great distress or remorse (see also Gen 37.34).
Absalom, now a fugitive, sought refuge among his mother’s family.
fled to his grandfather: See 2Sa 3.3. • Geshur was in Aram, northeast of Israel’s territory (see 2Sa 15.8; Jos 13.13).

And King David: Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek version read And the spirit of the king. • longed to be reunited with his son Absalom: David’s grief over Amnon’s death was evidently alleviated; any desire David might have had to execute Absalom had dissipated.
The woman with a reputation for great wisdom was summoned to carry out a delicate mission in the royal court (cp. 2Sa 20.16).
If you are criticized: If David allowed a murder to go unavenged, he would be liable for not carrying out justice and would likely draw criticism.

As surely as the LORD lives: When the woman pressed David for a greater commitment of protection, David responded with this solemn oath (cp. 2Sa 4.9; 2Sa 12.5; 2Sa 15.21; 1Sa 20.3; 1Sa 28.10; 1Sa 29.6).

for the people of God: The woman argued that David was harming everyone in his kingdom by leaving Absalom in exile, perhaps because alienation in the royal family would be reproduced in the larger society or because David’s obsession with Absalom would distract him from attending to more important matters (2Sa 14.16).
God . . . devises ways: The woman encouraged David to be reconciled with Absalom as God does with his people. God did not remain estranged from David when he sinned; he forgave the repentant king.

The woman again addressed her specific situation. The king’s concern for Absalom (see 2Sa 13.39 and corresponding note 2Sa 13.39) was keeping him from attending to matters of justice among his people. • cut us off: If her only remaining son were killed, the woman’s family would lose ownership of its ancestral property (cp. Num 27.1–11).

you are like an angel of God: This flattering expression is not used for anyone else in the Bible but appears four times to describe David (see also 2Sa 14.20; 2Sa 19.27; 1Sa 29.9). The woman was expressing confidence that David would act with God-given wisdom and justice.
as wise as an angel of God: This wise woman (2Sa 14.2) knew it was good policy to flatter a king rather than risk insulting him.
bring back . . . Absalom: It seems that David was not yet interested in full reconciliation with his son (2Sa 14.24).
Geshur: See 2Sa 13.37–38.
cut his hair only once a year: Absalom’s hair, an aspect of his attractiveness, ended up being a deadly snare for him (see 2Sa 18.9–15).
Absalom’s three sons apparently died before he did (see 2Sa 18.18). • Absalom named his daughter Tamar after his sister, and she too was very beautiful (2Sa 13.1).
Joab persuaded David to welcome Absalom back (2Sa 14.21–22) but then backed off from assisting Absalom further; perhaps Joab wanted to avoid aiding a would-be usurper (2Sa 15.1–12).

Absalom bowed low, assuming a posture of respect and deference to the king’s majesty (see also 2Sa 14.4, 2Sa 14.22). • and the king kissed him: The lack of conversation, hugging (cp. Luk 15.20), or weeping (cp. Gen 33.4; Gen 45.2, Gen 45.14) suggests that this was a formal meeting rather than an affectionate reunion.

Absalom revolted against David eleven years after Amnon violated Tamar (cp. 2Sa 13.23, 2Sa 13.38; 2Sa 14.28; 2Sa 15.7), approximately the twenty-fifth year of David’s thirty-three-year reign in Jerusalem.

a chariot and horses, and . . . fifty bodyguards: These three items, distinct signs of kingship, were also the first items that Samuel said the king would take from the people (1Sa 8.11). Another of David’s sons, Adonijah, collected the same items when he coveted the throne (1Ki 1.5).
To bow before . . . Absalom was, in effect, to honor him as king (see 2Sa 14.33).
stole the hearts: Absalom’s accessibility and false pretense of care for the people gained their loyalty.

After four years: Hebrew reads forty years, which would put Absalom’s uprising in David’s last year as king and create many chronological difficulties with events that happened afterward (also see study note on 2Sa 15.1–19). The Greek and Syriac reading is much more likely. • fulfill a vow: Unlike the freewill offering of devotion and gratitude that a worshiper promised to God, this type of offering was to fulfill a promise to God (see Gen 28.20–22; Jdg 11.30–31; 1Sa 1.11). Absalom was probably lying (cp. 1Sa 20.28–29).

Geshur in Aram: After killing Amnon, Absalom had sought refuge in the homeland of his mother (also see study notes on 2Sa 13.34–39, 37 2Sa 13.37). • The perfect place for Absalom to turn his grassroots popularity into a full-fledged revolt against David was in Hebron, David’s first capital.

Ahithophel was Bathsheba’s grandfather (cp. 2Sa 11.3; 2Sa 23.34); years later, he might still have been angry over what David did to his granddaughter. • Giloh was located in the region of Hebron (Jos 15.51, Jos 15.54).
