Possibly David left ten of his concubines behind because he believed his exile would be short-lived. See 2Sa 16.21–22.

600 men from Gath: This alliance went back to David’s relationship with the Philistines in Saul’s day (1Sa 21.10–15; 1Sa 27.1–12; 1Sa 29.1–11). • the king’s bodyguard: See study note on 2 Sam 2Sa 8.18.

Ittai, a Philistine from Gath, was associated with Gibeah in Benjamin (2Sa 23.29; 1Ch 11.31); the Philistines had established a garrison in Gibeah at the beginning of Saul’s career (1Sa 10.5; 1Sa 13.3). • David was stepping aside for King Absalom, who had successfully swayed the loyalty of Israel.
The Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem, separated the City of David from the Mount of Olives.
Zadok was one of two priests who served David (2Sa 8.17). He later anointed Solomon (1Ki 1.39) and became the high priest after Abiathar was deposed (1Ki 2.26–27).

take the Ark of God back: People fleeing invasion normally took their idols to avoid having the items fall into an enemy’s hands. The capture of a god could be interpreted by rebel elements to mean that the gods had abandoned the ruling dynasty. However, the Ark was not a mere idol or talisman (cp. 1Sa 4.3–11; 1Sa 5.6–2Sa 6.9). It was the central object in the sanctuary and represented the presence of the Lord, the God of Israel (see Exo 40.34–35). David intentionally permitted the Ark to fall into Absalom’s hands, trusting God’s grace and promises (2Sa 15.26; see 2Sa 7.8–16) whether or not the Ark was with him.
Ahimaaz and Jonathan supported David during Absalom’s coup d’etat by serving as his secret messengers (see 2Sa 15.36; 2Sa 17.17–22).
let Ahithophel give . . . foolish advice: David also sent a double-agent, Hushai, to confound Ahithophel’s advice (2Sa 15.32–37; 2Sa 17.1–14).

At this point in Israel’s history, people worshiped God at multiple altars across the land. The Tabernacle as it had existed from the time of Joshua and Samuel was gone and the Temple was yet to be built. • An Arkite was possibly a non-Israelite from the region south of Bethel (Jos 16.2).
While David was confident that God’s providence was at work behind the scenes, he also took strategic action to further his own cause.
Ziba: See study note on 2Sa 9.11; see also 2Sa 9.1–13; 2Sa 19.24–30. • As Saul’s grandson (2Sa 16.3), Mephibosheth was a potential rival for the throne.
Ziba was lying to David for his own gain; Mephibosheth later set the record straight (2Sa 19.24–30).

Bahurim was in the territory of Benjamin east of the Mount of Olives on the way to the Jordan River. It is likely that many people from Benjamin, Saul’s tribe, harbored lingering resentment against David’s rule. In the case of Shimei, his loyalty to Saul was even stronger because he was from the same clan in the tribe of Benjamin.
Shimei cursed David, holding him responsible for the violent death of Saul and his clan.
The LORD is paying you back: Shimei interpreted Absalom’s rebellion as the Lord’s retribution. However, David was innocent (see study notes on 2Sa 1.4, 2Sa 1.15–16 2Sa 1.15–16).

Abishai was David’s nephew (1Ch 2.13–16) and evidently a member of his personal guard. He believed that no one should talk this way to the king and live to tell about it (cp. 2Sa 19.21). David was slower to judge (cp. 1Ki 2.8–9).
Profile: Abishai
If the LORD has told him to curse me: David felt it might have been punishment for past sins. • David was—contrary to Shimei’s charges—reducing the violence that surrounded him.
even more reason: David understood why a supporter of Saul might hate him.

Long live the king! Hushai’s words were deliberately ambiguous. He was in fact an agent of the true king—David was truly “the man . . . chosen by the LORD” (2Sa 16.18). Hushai avoided using the king’s name, leading Absalom to believe that Hushai was loyal to him rather than to David.

why shouldn’t I serve you? (literally and second, to whom will I do service? Not before his son?): The ambiguous language continues. Hushai phrased his profession of loyalty as a question rather than as a commitment. His intent, lost on Absalom, was to serve David while fooling Absalom into thinking that he had changed sides. Similarly, just as I was your father’s adviser, now I will be your adviser! is literally, as I served before your father, so I will [serve your father] before you.
Go and sleep with your father’s concubines: A usurper took a predecessor’s harem to assert or strengthen his claim to the throne (see 2Sa 3.7). Absalom’s action was in violation of Deu 22.30.

Absalom intended to show the people that he had assumed the throne with its royal prerogatives. His shameful act echoed David’s adultery with Bathsheba, which also began on that roof (2Sa 11.2–4); the episode fulfilled Nathan’s prophecy (2Sa 12.11–12).
from the mouth of God: Cp. 2Sa 17.14.

Ahithophel proposed a quick surprise strike against David with a small force (12,000 men, 2Sa 17.1), which would give David no time to organize and fight back. Then David’s double-agent Hushai suggested taking more time to mobilize the entire army of Israel (2Sa 17.11). This plan would supposedly give them an insurmountable numerical advantage and prevent David from engaging in guerilla tactics. Because the Lord was working against Absalom, he rejected Ahithophel’s good strategy and accepted Hushai’s bad advice (2Sa 17.14; cp. 1Ki 12.1–15).
as a bride . . . you seek: The Hebrew text has the loyalty of all the people depend on the death of David. The Greek version pictures a young wife who returns to her husband after a short quarrel.
The nationwide military conscription from . . . Dan to Beersheba (the northern and southern limits of Israel) was intended to produce an overwhelmingly superior fighting force.

Ahithophel’s strategy was actually better. However, Hushai had the psychological and rhetorical advantage as well as the Lord’s purpose, so he won Absalom’s favor. • the LORD had determined to defeat: Despite early advances, Absalom’s power grab was doomed from the start.
Jonathan and Ahimaaz: See 2Sa 15.27, 2Sa 15.36. • The location of En-rogel is uncertain, but it cannot have been too far east of Jerusalem.

Bahurim was the home of Shimei, the pro-Saul Benjaminite (2Sa 16.5; 2Sa 19.16). Shimei’s cursing of David at Bahurim reflected David’s decline, while the escape of Ahimaaz and Jonathan pictured the hope of David’s resurgence.
hanged himself: Ahithophel foresaw David’s victory and Absalom’s undoing, and he preferred to die by his own hand rather than by David’s.
Mahanaim, once the capital city of Ishbosheth and Abner (2Sa 2.8, 2Sa 2.12, 2Sa 2.29), became David’s base of operations.

According to 1Ch 2.15–16, Abigail and Zeruiah were David’s sisters. But since Abigail is called the daughter of Nahash, she and Zeruiah were apparently David’s half sisters (Nahash was probably their father; his widow would then have married Jesse and given birth to David and his brothers).

Shobi was probably the brother of Hanun, who had humiliated David’s messengers after the death of Nahash (ch 2Sa 10.1–19; see study note on 2Sa 10.1–5). • Makir was Mephibosheth’s host before David summoned him (2Sa 9.4–5). • Barzillai of Gilead was probably not the same as Barzillai from Meholah (2Sa 21.8).
Profile: Joab
You are worth 10,000 of us: Although David’s men flattered him, their insistence that he stay behind might actually suggest David’s advancing frailty (see 2Sa 21.15–17).
Joab violated David’s order to deal gently with young Absalom (2Sa 18.11–15). This was the second time Joab killed someone against David’s wishes (see 2Sa 3.22–37).
The forest of Ephraim was an area east of the Jordan settled by the tribe of Ephraim.
more men died because of the forest: The topographical conditions of the forest apparently took away the numerical advantage of Absalom’s forces.

Absalom, who took such pride in his hair, died because of it. He who had built “a monument to himself” (2Sa 18.18) was then thrown into a pit after his death (2Sa 18.17) and denied the dignity of a proper burial. These ironies highlight the difference between Absalom’s aspirations and his destiny.
Perhaps a hero’s belt was a sword belt that decorated a soldier for bravery and courage in battle (cp. 1Sa 18.4).

plunged them into Absalom’s heart: Earlier, Joab had played the role of reconciler between David and Absalom (ch 2Sa 14.1–33). It is possible Joab believed that allowing Absalom to live would only invite ongoing trouble for David and for himself. (Absalom had appointed Amasa, Joab’s first cousin, to fill Joab’s position as commander of Israel’s army; see 2Sa 17.25.)
surrounded . . . and killed him: Perhaps Joab had his armor bearers finish the job so that he could make the case to David that he himself had not killed Absalom.
all Israel fled to their homes: Absalom’s supporters (2Sa 17.11) knew their lives were in danger (cp. 2Sa 19.8). They had backed a usurper whose coup d’etat had been thwarted.

I have no son: See study note on 2Sa 14.27. In the absence of a lineage, Absalom hoped a monument would preserve his name and memory. • to this day: The narrator was probably writing during Solomon’s reign; the monument’s location is now unknown.
Zadok: See study note on 2Sa 15.24.

a man from Ethiopia: Joab thought it would be better to send a foreigner to tell the king of Absalom’s death. If David overreacted, the loss of a foreigner was not as critical as the loss of a priest’s son.
If he is alone, he has news: A solitary runner was usually a courier.

Everything is all right! (Hebrew shalom): David then asked, “Is it shalom with the young Ab-shalom?” (What about young Absalom? . . . Is he all right?). Even though Absalom was David’s rival, he was also David’s son. David was more concerned about his son’s fate than the well-being of his fighting servants (2Sa 19.5–6).
David was not afraid to show his emotions openly, whether engulfed by rapturous joy (2Sa 6.14–19) or crushed by sadness. His feelings for Absalom were real, not theatrical.
These verses provide the only recorded instance of Joab openly rebuking the king (cp. 2Sa 24.3).

The argument among the tribes of Israel (possibly referring only to the northern tribes) resulted in the consensus that they should ask David to come back, perhaps instead of going back to the semiautonomy of the era of the judges (cp. 2Sa 20.1).
When David realized that the northern tribes would welcome him (2Sa 19.9–10), he sent emissaries to goad Judah, his own tribesmen, into welcoming him as well. See also study note on 2Sa 19.41–43.
commander . . . in his place: Amasa’s appointment would be short-lived (2Sa 20.7–10).

On his return to Jerusalem, David showed mercy to Shimei, the pro-Saul northerner who had cursed David when he fled from Jerusalem (see 2Sa 16.5–14), but Shimei’s action did not go unpunished (1Ki 2.8, 1Ki 2.36–46).
Gilgal was an important city in the days of Samuel and Saul (see study note on 2Sa 19.40; 1Sa 7.16; 1Sa 11.15).

I know how much I sinned: Shimei’s repentance might have been genuine, or he might simply have been backpedaling in a desperate attempt to save his life. David’s concern for Absalom’s safety had shown that David was not a self-promoting, bloodthirsty throne-stealer, as Shimei had thought; and Absalom had not replaced him (2Sa 16.8), as Shimei had charged. • in all Israel (literally in all the house of Joseph): Just as Jacob’s name could stand for all Israel (e.g., Num 24.19; Isa 10.20), Joseph’s name could stand for all the northern tribes (e.g., see study notes on Amos Amo 5.6; Zech Zec 10.6).

Cp. 2Sa 16.9–12. • Abishai: See study note on 2Sa 16.9. • you sons of Zeruiah: See study notes on 2Sa 2.18; 2Sa 17.25. While it was Abishai who consistently wanted to kill those hostile to David (cp. 2Sa 16.9; 1Sa 26.8), David also expressed his frustration with Joab, Abishai’s brother (see 2Sa 3.28–29, 2Sa 3.39; 2Sa 19.13; 1Ki 2.5–6).
David’s oath of protection was not binding on David’s heir, Solomon, who later ordered Shimei’s execution for far less serious crimes (1Ki 2.36–46).

Mephibosheth’s inattention to grooming throughout David’s absence from Jerusalem was an act of mourning that proved his loyalty to David. If Mephibosheth had designs on the throne (2Sa 16.3), he would not have retained such an unkempt appearance.

like an angel of God: See study note on 2Sa 14.17. • I could expect only death . . . What more can I ask? If Mephibosheth had wanted to betray David, it would have been a profound show of ingratitude for all that David had done for him.
Mephibosheth’s disinterest in claiming even half of his property showed conclusively that his happiness over David’s return was genuine.
Because he was very old and frail, Barzillai declined David’s invitation to the royal court in Jerusalem as reward for his assistance. David took Barzillai’s son Kimham instead (see also 1Ki 2.7).
Gilead was part of Manasseh’s territory on the east side of the Jordan (Jos 17.5).
kissed him: This was a genuine and affectionate kiss, in contrast with David’s cold kiss for Absalom (2Sa 14.33) and Absalom’s calculating one for the people (2Sa 15.5).

Gilgal, a natural stop along David’s westward route, was also a politically significant location: It was where the people had proclaimed Saul king (1Sa 11.15) and Samuel later announced the end of Saul’s reign (1Sa 13.13–15). David’s kingship now had a new beginning at Gilgal.

This dispute, prompted by David’s favoring his own tribe of Judah, reflects the roots of the division that eventually split Judah and Israel into separate nations (1Ki 11.31; 1Ki 12.16, 1Ki 12.20). • Weren’t we the first: See 2Sa 19.11–12.

Down with the dynasty of David! By the same rallying cry, the northern Israelites later dissociated themselves from Solomon (1Ki 12.16). Sheba’s failed revolt foreshadowed the ultimate failure of the northern kingdom, which was founded on a similar revolt by Jeroboam (1Ki 12.1–33).
The fate of the ten concubines (2Sa 15.16) whom Absalom had publicly violated (2Sa 16.21–22) was like Michal’s (see 2Sa 6.23 and corresponding note 2Sa 6.23).
The king had installed Amasa in Joab’s place as commander of the armies (2Sa 19.13–14). David apparently expected from Amasa the same efficiency and effectiveness as Joab had provided.
the king’s bodyguard: See study note on 2Sa 8.18.
to kiss him: This affectionate greeting was not always genuine (cp. 2Sa 14.33).

Amasa . . . died: For the second time, Joab killed a commander of the opposing army by treachery (the first was Abner, 2Sa 3.26–27). Twice, David tried to merge feuding parties by absorbing the military leader of the opposing side (see 2Sa 3.6–13; 2Sa 17.25; 2Sa 19.13); twice Joab scuttled David’s plans by treacherously murdering the rival commander (see also 2Sa 3.22–30).
Abel-beth-maacah was in the northernmost region of Israelite territory, four miles west of the city of Dan.
A siege ramp was often an earthen ramp built up against the wall, a well-known tactic for breaching a walled city’s defenses (see also 2Ki 25.1; Jer 52.4).
wise woman: Cp. 2Sa 14.2.

The woman told a saying to convince Joab not to slaughter an entire city, especially such a noble city as Abel (a shortened form of Abel-beth-maacah, 2Sa 20.15), just to capture one criminal. • an important town in Israel (literally a town that is a mother in Israel): It was common to refer to outlying villages around a larger city as its “daughters.”

This list of David’s leaders and the similar list in 2Sa 8.15–18 bracket chs 2Sa 9.1–20 in David’s life. Even after the major crises described in these 12 chapters, David’s monarchy did not fall apart; he still had an intact administration.

In 2Sa 8.16, Joab was called “commander of the army,” but here he is commander of the army of Israel. David’s wider control of Israel was established when the northern secessionist movements were defeated.

Adoniram: The addition of the officer in charge of forced labor (not mentioned in 2Sa 8.15–18; see also 1Ki 4.6) shows that David had now gained sufficient control of Israel to require the payment of taxes and to conscript labor throughout the kingdom (cp. 1Sa 8.11–17).
In contrast to David’s personal priest (see 2Sa 8.18; 2Sa 20.26 and corresponding notes 2Sa 8.18), Zadok and Abiathar presided over public worship.
David’s personal priest was probably not a Levite but rather a special class of religious servant appointed for his royal court (see study note on 2Sa 8.18)

The final chapters of 2 Samuel are a coda, a concluding section that summarizes the important themes from the preceding material. These chapters are thematic, not chronological, and not all the events described here happened at the end of David’s reign (e.g., 2Sa 22.1). The materials are arranged according to a common Hebrew literary device, a chiasm (mirror-image): A: Saul’s sin against the Gibeonites and its collective punishment (2Sa 21.1–14); B: David’s heroes and their exploits (2Sa 21.15–22); C: David’s Psalm (2Sa 22.1–51); C′: David’s Psalm (2Sa 23.1–7); B′: David’s heroes and their exploits (2Sa 23.8–39); A′: David’s sin against the census taboo and its collective punishment (2Sa 24.1–25). A chiasm highlights the central section—here David’s hymns, which focus not on David but on David’s God.

asked the LORD: The Hebrew verb is the same as that used when David “begged” for the life of Bathsheba’s child (2Sa 12.16). On these two occasions, “seeking” was in the desperation of a moment of crisis. However, most often in the Old Testament, “seeking God” refers not to a specific prayer of petition but to the dynamics of daily devotion and obedience to God (e.g., Psa 40.16; Psa 105.4; Pro 28.5). • Saul and his family are guilty: The famine resulted from violating an oath taken before the Lord (Jos 9.19–20). • murdering the Gibeonites: This incident is not elsewhere recorded. Illicit bloodshed had polluted the land, making it sterile and unfruitful (cp. Gen 4.10–12; Num 35.30–34).

Though the Amorites were a specific people group (Gen 10.16), here it is a general term for the pre-Israelite inhabitants of Canaan. • When properly directed, zeal is commendable (e.g., Num 25.11; 1Ki 19.10). Saul’s misdirected zeal, however, involved blatant disregard for Israel’s covenant with the Gibeonites.
Saul’s actions had caused the Gibeonites to curse Israel (cp. Rom 2.24); once David had made amends, the Gibeonites would bless the LORD’s people again.

seven of Saul’s sons: Although the law codes of other ancient Near Eastern nations sometimes permitted members of a family to be punished for crimes a guilty individual had committed, Deu 24.16 prohibited such punishment among the Israelites. This penalty was God’s prerogative alone (Deu 5.9). The few instances in the Bible when offspring were punished were not regular criminal cases. Rather, they involved offenses against God, such as violation of the kherem (the taboo on goods in wars of total destruction ordered by God; Jos 7.24–25) or of national oaths (as here). • at Gibeon, on the mountain of the LORD: This probably refers to the high place at Gibeon that Solomon later visited (1Ki 3.3–4; 2Ch 1.3). If the Hebrew reading is correct (see NLT note), the Gibeonites were sarcastically referring to Saul as “the chosen of the LORD.”
the oath: See 1Sa 20.14–15. In contrast to Saul, David was honoring his oath while dealing with the deadly fallout of Saul’s violation of an oath.

Armoni and Mephibosheth were Saul’s only two remaining sons. • Saul’s daughter Merab: See NLT note; the NLT follows the Greek here because Michal remained childless (2Sa 6.22–23). Also, Merab was married to Adriel (1Sa 18.19), whereas Michal’s other husband was Palti (2Sa 3.15). • Barzillai from Meholah (cp. 1Sa 18.19) should not be confused with Barzillai of Gilead (2Sa 19.31).
The beginning of the barley harvest was in April. • Before the LORD means “before the Lord’s altar” (see study note on 2Sa 21.6).

Because the Gibeonites were not Israelites (2Sa 21.2), they had no law such as the Israelite one in Deu 21.22–23 requiring the quick and proper burial of a criminal. Rizpah was intent that her sons not be further shamed after their death.
Rizpah’s action shamed David into likewise honoring the dead of Saul’s family.
The precise location of Zela is unknown. • the famine: See 2Sa 21.1–2.
The extended account of battles with the Philistines highlights some notable accomplishments of David’s mighty warriors (see also 2Sa 23.8–39).
The description of David as weak and exhausted helps shift the focus from his ability and accomplishments to God as the source of his success (ch 2Sa 22.1–51).
a descendant of the giants: Cp. Gen 14.5; Deu 2.10–11, Deu 2.20–21; Deu 3.11.

Abishai was an accomplished warrior and fiercely loyal to David, whom he heroically rescued (see “Abishai” Profile). • the light of Israel? Cp. 2Sa 18.3. Both passages reflect the glowing adoration that David’s men had for him.
The location of Gob is uncertain.

Some traditions identify Elhanan as David, principally because Elhanan was also from Bethlehem and because David killed Goliath (1Sa 17.48–51). But it is more likely that the words brother of were omitted from the Masoretic Text by scribal error.

Although this prayer of thanksgiving (also recorded in Psa 18.1–50) is placed near the end of David’s story, David probably offered it to God much earlier in his life. This prayer and Hannah’s (1Sa 2.1–10) together enclose the book of Samuel with an inclusio (literary bookends). Hannah was saved from barrenness; David was saved from his enemies. The placement of this hymn also provides a parallel to Moses. The stories of both Moses and David end with a song or hymn giving lavish praise to God (see also Deu 31.30–2Sa 32.43). Both highlight God as a “Rock” (Deu 32.4, Deu 32.15, Deu 32.18, Deu 32.30, Deu 32.31; 2Sa 22.2, 2Sa 22.3, 2Sa 22.32, 2Sa 22.47). Both are followed by second and shorter poetic pieces—Moses’ final blessing to the Israelite tribes (Deu 33.1–29), and David’s last words (2Sa 23.1–7).

Hannah had said, “there is no Rock like our God” (1Sa 2.2), while David said, the LORD is my rock, which recalls God’s rescue of David from Saul at the Rock of Escape (1Sa 23.28). The Hebrew word translated “rock” in 2Sa 22.3 (different from 2Sa 22.2) refers in 1Sa 24.2 to “the rocks of the wild goats,” where Saul suspected that David was hiding. • fortress: The same word referred to David’s physical “stronghold” (1Sa 22.4), where David and his men sought refuge from Saul.
The phrase the power that saves me (literally the horn that has saved me) is similar to Hannah’s “the LORD has made me strong!,” (literally the LORD has exalted my horn, 1Sa 2.1).
Although his sanctuary sometimes refers to the Tabernacle or Temple, here it refers to God’s heavenly dwelling; neither the Tabernacle nor the Temple were in existence at this time.

David vividly expands on how God heard him (2Sa 22.7). David describes God’s rescue as a theophany (manifestation of God’s presence; see study notes on Exod Exo 19.16–25; Deut Deu 1.33) that recalls God’s manifestation at Sinai (Exo 19.16–20; cp. Jdg 5.4–5).
The LORD thundered from heaven: Cp. 1Sa 2.10.
David’s divine rescue and success were related to his own obedient walk with God. God honors those who order their lives in a way that pleases him (see also Lev 26.1–13; Deu 28.1–14; Psa 1.1–6).

David composed these words much earlier (2Sa 22.1), before his sin with Bathsheba. Still, his claim to being blameless should not be construed as a claim to perfection. David was simply noting that he had kept the covenant and followed its law.
David glorifies God for rescue in the past and for his promises to David’s house for coming generations (see 2Sa 7.8–16).
David probably encountered deerduring his many days of hiding out in hilly terrain and caves (1Sa 19.11–2Sa 27.12).

David’s military accomplishments before he became king were impressive (see 1Sa 17.12–58; 1Sa 18.17–30; 1Sa 23.1–5; 1Sa 30.1–31). Yet rather than exalting himself, David glorified God and gave him the credit.
This passage comes from the end of David’s career and reflects on his experience as king, even as ch 2Sa 22.1–51 reflects on his experience before becoming king.

David’s last words were not necessarily the last words he actually spoke (see 1Ki 1.16, 1Ki 1.29–30, 1Ki 1.33–35; 1Ki 2.1–9) but his final public expression of worship to God as king (cp. 1Sa 12.1–25). • David . . . speaks: The language indicates that he was about to utter an oracle, a revelation from God (2Sa 23.2). • the sweet psalmist of Israel: For other references to David as musician and poet, see 1Ch 23.5; 2Ch 29.26, 2Ch 29.27; Neh 12.36; Amo 6.5.
The Spirit of the LORD speaks through me: David spoke of God, and in the process, God spoke through David.

my family . . . everlasting covenant: David is referring to the prophecy Nathan made about David and his descendants (2Sa 7.12–16). Jesus is the everlasting king who is the “descendant of David” (Mat 1.1).

This section is a listing of David’s elite warriors by name, the most prominent of whom are listed with a notable accomplishment. These warriors were some of the “iron tools” that God used to “chop down” the godless (2Sa 23.7). • The list divides into the Three and the Thirty. Some Hebrew scholars have suggested that the Thirty be translated as “Officers.” If that is correct, then it is possible that the Three was originally a term for a specific military office.
to collect the plunder: Cp. 1Sa 30.9–10, 1Sa 30.21–25.
The cave of Adullam was a place of refuge for David from Saul (see 1Sa 22.1). • The valley of Rephaim was located between Bethlehem and Jerusalem (see 2Sa 5.17–25).

remarked longingly: This Hebrew verb elsewhere carries the idea of excessive desire (see Num 11.4, “began to crave”; Psa 106.14, “desires ran wild”). It is unclear whether David’s craving for water was excessive, but it certainly led to dangerous exploits. • well by the gate: David had memories from his younger days of growing up in Bethlehem. The location of the well is unknown.

This water . . . these men: When David poured the hard-won water on the ground, it did not signal ingratitude. Rather, he regarded the water as equivalent to the warriors’ blood; it represented life that only God was worthy to receive (Lev 17.10–13; Deu 12.23–24).

Here are examples of the prowess of Abishai and Benaiah. Elsewhere, Abishai was intensely combative toward David’s enemies, especially Saul (1Sa 26.6–9) and Saul’s kinsman Shimei (2Sa 16.9–11). Abishai had saved David’s life during one of the Philistine wars (2Sa 21.16–17). • Benaiah appeared first as the commander of the mercenaries who served as David’s bodyguard, independent of the regular army (2Sa 8.18; 2Sa 20.23). He was also the leader of a 24,000-man division of the regular army that served the king in the third month of every year (1Ch 27.5–6). He played a major role in Solomon’s ascension to the throne (1Ki 1.32–49) and became the commander of Solomon’s army, as Joab was for David.

Asahel, David’s nephew, was killed by Abner during the war between David and Ishbosheth (2Sa 2.18–32). Asahel’s inclusion here suggests that parts of these lists go back to the beginning of David’s career. • Elhanan son of Dodo should not be confused with Elhanan son of Jair (2Sa 21.19; 1Ch 20.5).

The very last name mentioned is Uriah the Hittite. There is an earlier reference to his father-in-law, Eliam, father of Bathsheba (2Sa 23.34; see 2Sa 11.3). By contrast, the Chronicler, who never mentioned David’s sins against Bathsheba and Uriah, placed Uriah’s name inconspicuously in the middle of the list of David’s mighty men (1Ch 11.10–47). This author not only described the sins (2Sa 11.1–27) but puts emphasis on Uriah’s name by placing it at the end of this list. Uriah was no ordinary conscript but a loyal member of David’s elite guard, which makes David’s treachery against him all the worse. • There were thirty-seven in all: Only thirty-six names are mentioned, assuming that “Shammah . . . from Harar” (2Sa 23.11) is different from “Shammah from Harod” (2Sa 23.25), and that “Benaiah son of Jehoiada” (2Sa 23.20) is different from “Benaiah from Pirathon” (2Sa 23.30). Perhaps the thirty-seventh warrior was Joab, who is mentioned only peripherally (2Sa 23.18, 2Sa 23.37) and is absent from the list of names. Many commentators say that he is excluded because he was David’s chief military leader and did not need to be included. The omission could also represent David’s long and troubled association with Joab, who was eventually executed when Solomon carried out David’s deathbed command (1Ki 2.5–6, 1Ki 2.28–34).

The reason God’s anger . . . burned against Israel is unknown (but see Deu 4.25; Deu 6.14–15; Deu 29.22–28; Deu 31.16–18). • Caused . . . to harm reflects a Hebrew verb (suth) used elsewhere in the sense of enticing or inciting someone to do wrong (1Sa 26.19, “stirred you up against me”). Census-taking was usually unpopular with citizens, who resented it as an intrusion into their private affairs. They regarded it as a prelude to taxation or forced military service (see study note on 2 Sam 2Sa 24.9). If David was motivated by pride or was preparing for an illegitimate war (as 2Sa 24.9 might suggest), this might explain why it was a sin for him (2Sa 24.10).
Theme: God or Satan?
Dan and Beersheba were the traditional northern and southern boundaries of Israel. This phrase meant the entire land of Israel.
why . . . do you want to do this? Joab either realized that such a move would be unpopular among the people, or he believed that it was wrong before God.

The phrase capable warriors shows that the census focused largely on those fit for military service. The total for Judah here might be rounded up from the total in 1Ch 21.5; the different number for Israel in 1Ch 21.5 (1,100,000) might come from combining a regular standing army of 300,000 (elsewhere unrecorded) with the 800,000 discovered through the census.

I have sinned: See study note on 2Sa 24.1. David believed his sin was the cause of the plague and that the removal of his sin would make things right (see also 2Sa 24.17). It is clear, however, that Israel rather than David was the true object of God’s wrath (2Sa 24.1).

Gad . . . David’s seer appears only here and in 1Sa 22.5. Seer is an early name for a prophet (1Sa 9.9, 1Sa 9.19). Unlike pagan magicians or sorcerers, biblical seers had divinely inspired visions (see also 2Ki 17.13; Isa 29.10; Isa 30.9–10; Amo 7.12; Mic 3.7) and functioned as God’s messengers.

David had already experienced the first two options—fleeing from Saul and Absalom, and famine because Saul had murdered the Gibeonites (2Sa 21.1). While three days of severe plague sounded less traumatic, 70,000 people perished (2Sa 24.15).

the LORD relented: God might stop his judgment when a third party intercedes for the intended target (Exo 32.12–14), when the sinful person repents (Jer 18.8), or simply because he decides to do so. • the death angel: Cp. Exo 12.23. • A threshing floor was an unwalled space where harvested grain was threshed and winnowed to separate the kernels from the chaff. Gideon encountered God at a threshing floor (Jdg 6.37). Araunah’s threshing floor later became the site of the Temple (1Ch 21.18–2Sa 22.1; 2Ch 3.1). • Araunah the Jebusite: Even though David had taken Jerusalem from the Jebusites (2Sa 5.6–9), he had not eliminated them or driven them away.

I am the one who has sinned: David’s earlier confession of sin was limited to his circumstances (“forgive my guilt,” 2Sa 24.10); now he prayed for those he considered innocent (but see 2Sa 24.1) and offered to die in their place. • as sheep: David was the shepherd of Israel (see study note on 2Sa 7.8).
so that he will stop the plague: David did not know that God had already announced the end of the plague to the angel (2Sa 24.16).
David performed priestly functions when he built an altar, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and prayed for his people; in response, the LORD answered his prayer (cp. 2Sa 21.14).

The First Book of Kings

Purpose

To outline the glory of Solomon’s reign, the division of the kingdom, and the degradation of Israel

Author

Unknown

Date

Records events that occurred around 973–853 BC

Setting

Begins at the high point of the Israelite monarchy (Solomon’s reign) and ends with a divided kingdom and a low point in the Israelite monarchy (Ahab’s reign)

Solomon’s kingdom was the pinnacle of Israel’s glory. “King Solomon became richer and wiser than any other king on earth” (1Ki 10.23). The Queen of Sheba confirmed the glory of Solomon’s kingdom, saying, “Everything I heard in my country about your achievements and wisdom is true! I didn’t believe what was said until I arrived here and saw it with my own eyes” (1Ki 10.6–7). First Kings celebrates the splendor of Solomon’s kingdom. But Solomon’s reign also illustrates the dangers of spiritual infidelity, and 1 Kings warns about the results of preoccupation with luxury, fame, self, and security. It is a timeless warning to us all.

Setting

At the height of his power, Solomon administered a kingdom that stretched “from the Euphrates River in the north to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt in the south” (1Ki 4.21). Solomon’s power and wealth brought him in contact with many surrounding nations—especially the important maritime city-state of Tyre and the age-old empire of Egypt.

The mid-900s BC was an ideal time for Solomon’s kingdom to expand, for the traditional political powers of the area were in decline. The strong Hittite kingdom to the north had broken up into a number of small states. In Mesopotamia, years of struggle with the Arameans and the Hittites had weakened Assyria, which remained weak until the accession of Ashur-dan II (934–912 BC). In the south, Egypt’s presence in Canaan had weakened during the 21st dynasty (1069–945 BC). Egypt would not make an effective military comeback until the rule of the 22nd dynasty pharaoh Shoshenq I (Shishak, 945–924 BC).

Unfortunately, Solomon’s foreign diplomacy involved marriages with the daughters of foreign kings. This was a common way to cement alliances in the ancient Near East, but it was spiritually disastrous, for “in Solomon’s old age, they turned his heart to worship other gods instead of being completely faithful to the LORD his God” (1Ki 11.4).

Tensions that had been smoldering between the northern and southern Hebrew tribes surfaced with Solomon’s death in 931 BC. The resulting schism restructured the kingdom into Israel (the northern ten tribes) and Judah (the remaining two southern tribes). Israel and Judah skirmished repeatedly during the era of the first two northern dynasties and the reigns of Judah’s first three kings (931~874 BC). The hostility subsided when King Ahab of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah found a common cause against the Arameans (chs 1Ki 20.1–43, 1Ki 22.1–53).

The Hebrew kingdoms of Israel and Judah were increasingly entangled by the expansionist ambitions of their neighbors. They were invaded by Shoshenq I of Egypt in 926 BC, and throughout the 800s BC they faced the constant menace of the Arameans and the rising power of Assyria. During the reigns of the Assyrian kings Ashurnasirpal II (883–859 BC) and Shalmaneser III (858–824 BC), Assyrian troops moved steadily westward to the Mediterranean Sea. At the famous Battle of Qarqar (853 BC), a coalition of western allies, including Israel’s King Ahab, withstood the Assyrian king Shalmaneser and temporarily sidetracked Assyria’s advance.

During this time, the two Hebrew kingdoms struggled spiritually. Israel stopped worshiping the Lord at Solomon’s Temple, and Jeroboam I, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel (931–910 BC), instituted apostate religious practices that led the northern kingdom astray (see 2Ki 17.21–23). Judah’s first two kings, Rehoboam and Abijah, lapsed spiritually, while the subsequent two kings, Asa and Jehoshaphat, maintained greater, though not perfect, spiritual fidelity (1Ki 15.11; 1Ki 22.43).

Summary

Beginning with King David’s last days, 1 Kings describes the establishment of Solomon’s glorious empire (971–931 BC) and the events that subsequently divided the kingdom in two (the kingdom of Israel in the north and the kingdom of Judah in the south). The book then traces the varying fortunes of the two kingdoms to about 853 BC, into the reign of Ahaziah in Israel (853–852 BC).

The first eleven chapters center on King Solomon, recounting both his fabulous reign and his later spiritual compromise. Solomon’s story begins and ends in controversy. Solomon was David’s chosen successor, but his older brother Adonijah attempted to seize the throne (1Ki 1.1–1Ki 2.46). Solomon triumphed over Adonijah’s rival claim, then used his God-given wisdom to reorganize the government and make it more efficient. He facilitated the kingdom’s commercial expansion on land and sea and undertook extensive building projects, including the marvelous Temple and the palace complex. Toward the end of his reign, however, Solomon’s spiritual decline (1Ki 11.1–13) and oppressive administrative measures (e.g., 1Ki 5.13–18) incited political adversaries both inside and outside the country (1Ki 11.14–40).

God appeared three times to Solomon, giving us a glimpse of his personal spiritual journey. The first time, early in Solomon’s reign, God granted his request for wisdom to rule the kingdom (1Ki 3.5–15), which resulted in great prosperity and honor (1Ki 3.16–1Ki 8.66). After Solomon finished building the Temple and palace, God visited him a second time to remind him that his continued success would depend on spiritual fidelity (1Ki 9.1–9). However, Solomon’s great fame (1Ki 9.10–1Ki 10.29) led him into foreign alliances, cemented by customary marriages with the daughters of foreign kings. Solomon’s resulting spiritual compromise eventually led him so far as to sponsor the worship of pagan deities (1Ki 11.1–8). God visited Solomon a third and final time; this time he rebuked Solomon for his failure to honor the covenant. Solomon’s unfaithfulness would ultimately cause the kingdom’s division after his death (1Ki 11.9–13).

The second section of the book (1Ki 12.1–1Ki 16.26) demonstrates that God’s judgment came quickly after Solomon’s death. At the beginning of the reign of King Rehoboam, the northern tribes requested relief from forced labor and heavy taxation. Rehoboam rebuffed their request and antagonized them, so the northern tribes rebelled and established the kingdom of Israel in the north, with Jeroboam I as king. Rehoboam remained on the throne of Judah, now a separate kingdom, in the south (1Ki 12.1–24). During the following era, Israel’s first two dynasties (Jeroboam I to Tibni) spiritually degraded the northern kingdom, while the kings of Judah degraded the southern kingdom. Political instability marked the northern kingdom, with royal assassinations, contests for power, and the establishment of Israel’s notorious third dynasty, founded by King Omri, who was one of the most powerful and evil kings of Israel (1Ki 16.25–26).

The final section of 1 Kings is primarily devoted to the reign of Omri’s son Ahab (1Ki 16.29–1Ki 22.40). Israel had begun worshiping the Canaanite storm-god Baal, so the Lord commissioned Elijah to confront Ahab and to demonstrate the Lord’s power, showing that he alone is God (1Ki 17.1–1Ki 18.46). Elijah then fled from the wrath of Queen Jezebel, but God reclaimed and recommissioned him, with Elisha as his successor (1Ki 19.1–21).

On the political front, King Ahab faced repeated challenges from the Aramean king Ben-hadad, against whom Ahab fought three campaigns (1Ki 20.1–25, 1Ki 20.26–43; 1Ki 22.1–40), the last of which cost Ahab his life. Between the second and third campaigns, Ahab, aided by his ruthless wife Jezebel, murdered an innocent man named Naboth and confiscated his property (1Ki 21.1–29).

God’s prophets figured prominently in the events of Ahab’s reign. In Ahab’s first two campaigns against the Arameans, an unnamed prophet first counseled the king (1Ki 20.22) and then rebuked him (1Ki 20.35–43). The prophet Elijah later censured Ahab’s seizure of Naboth’s vineyard (1Ki 21.1–29). Then, before Ahab’s third battle against the Arameans, the prophet Micaiah warned of Ahab’s impending death (1Ki 22.5–28).

The book of 1 Kings closes with a brief word concerning the character and reign of Judah’s King Jehoshaphat (1Ki 22.41–50) and introduces Ahab’s successor, Ahaziah (1Ki 22.51–53), whose story begins 2 Kings.

Authorship and Composition

The books of 1–2 Kings reflect the coherent perspective of a single unknown author, whom Jewish tradition identifies as Jeremiah (Baba Batra 15a). The author witnessed firsthand the fall of Jerusalem and was well acquainted with sources that enabled him to compose a rich history of Solomon’s reign and the divided monarchy. Available to the author were official archives of the palace and Temple and records kept in various prophetic centers. He skillfully weaved these sources into a unified presentation, displaying a central concern regarding his people’s repeated failure to honor their covenant relationship with God.

It is uncertain whether the author was still alive and wrote the final appendix concerning Jehoiachin’s release (561 BC; 2Ki 25.27–30; cp. Jer 52.31–34). If not, these verses were appended by someone well acquainted with 1–2 Kings and of a kindred spirit with the primary author.

The books of 1–2 Kings cover essentially the same time period as 2 Chronicles. Accordingly, there are numerous parallel passages with similar wording. But the authors had different purposes in writing, and these differences can be highlighted by comparing the various parallel passages.

Date

Because 2 Kings records the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC (2Ki 24.18–1Ki 25.21), the composition of 1–2 Kings must have been completed afterward.

The dating of the reigns of various kings and the chronological arrangement of 1–2 Kings remain somewhat problematic, but the general dating of the period seems clear. The basic period for 1 Kings stretches from around 973 BC (including approximately the last two years of David’s reign in Jerusalem, 2Sa 5.4–5) to around 853 BC, during the reigns of Jehoshaphat of Judah (872–848 BC) and Ahaziah of Israel (853–852 BC). Second Kings picks up where 1 Kings left off (originally, 1–2 Kings was one book). The final appendix to 2 Kings (2Ki 25.27–30) was written shortly after the death of Nebuchadnezzar II in 562 BC.

Chronology

The dates for the reigns of the kings of Israel and Judah are determined by comparing biblical data with information from other sources from the period, including historical annals and records of astronomical phenomena. The data frequently highlights the practice of co-regency, whereby a reigning king designated his son as both heir apparent and co-ruler. This practice was common in both Israel and Judah. Hence, the dating of the various kings is not necessarily sequential, but contains a certain extent of overlap. While ascertaining precise dates across the monarchical period is complex, the remarkable harmony between the records of Assyria, Babylon, Aram, Egypt, and Israel highlights the historical reliability of the biblical records.

Meaning and Message

The primary concern of 1 Kings is Israel’s spiritual condition: How well did Israel’s rulers and people keep God’s covenants? God’s special covenant with David had conditions for blessing Israel’s king and his kingdom (2Sa 7.12–16; Psa 89.20–37). God’s three appearances to Solomon highlight the potential for a successful and meaningful spiritual life, as well as the tragic consequences of spiritual infidelity and relying upon expediency. Each succeeding king is evaluated by his faithfulness to God—by his success or failure in keeping God’s covenants.

The book of 1 Kings emphasizes the role of God’s prophets in advising, admonishing, and warning the kings. While particular attention is devoted to Elijah’s ministry (1Ki 17.1–1Ki 19.21; 1Ki 21.1–29), God also works through other prophets to claim his people’s loyalty.

The spiritual odysseys of Israel’s kings and prophets challenge all of God’s people to faithful devotion and service. Israel’s frequent preference for what is tangible and expedient reminds us to “keep away from anything that might take God’s place in [our] hearts”(1Jo 5.21). Like the prophets of old, God’s servants today are to proclaim the necessity of worshiping God alone.

The book of 1 Kings opens by emphasizing the continuity of the Lord’s covenant with David (see 2Sa 7.11–16). Solomon was the legitimate and divinely chosen heir to what God had granted his father David. The challenges to Solomon’s succession to the throne (1Ki 1.1–1Ki 2.46) foreshadowed challenges to his kingship at the end of his reign (1Ki 11.1–43) and the continuing struggles between Israel and Judah thereafter.

At seventy years of age (2Sa 5.4–5), David was feeble, perhaps because of years of warfare and stress. He needed a young person to impart warmth, a medical remedy also described in Josephus’s Antiquities and by the Greek physician Galen. David’s diminishing powers encouraged Adonijah’s attempts to take the throne.

Adonijah was David’s fourth son. Because his older brothers, Amnon, Daniel, and Absalom, were all dead, Adonijah assumed he would succeed his father. Yet, in keeping with ancient Near Eastern custom, Solomon—the son of David’s favored wife, Bathsheba—was to succeed him as king. David had already communicated this fact to Solomon (1Ki 1.13, 1Ki 1.17; 1Ch 22.6–10). Adonijah’s self-seeking nature, likely encouraged by his father’s lax discipline, surfaced in his declaration, “I will make myself king.”
Joab, David’s military commander, and Abiathar, the high priest, gave Adonijah powerful military and religious backing in his pursuit of the throne.

Solomon also had influential friends supporting his right to become king. Zadok was in the priestly line of Eleazar, Benaiah commanded David’s bodyguard and his thirty mighty men (2Sa 23.20–23), Shimei was one of Solomon’s district governors (1Ki 4.18), and Nathan was David’s trusted prophet. Rei is unknown beyond this verse.

En-rogel (modern Bir Ayyub, “Job’s well”) lay south of Jerusalem at the intersection of the Kidron and Hinnom valleys. Earlier, it harbored David’s two informants, Jonathan and Ahimaaz, during Absalom’s rebellion (see 2Sa 17.17).
Profile: Solomon

Bathsheba was Solomon’s mother and David’s favored wife. Their affair led to the death of Bathsheba’s husband, Uriah the Hittite (see 2Sa 11.1–27). • Nathan, the prophet who revealed God’s covenant with David (2Sa 7.1–17) and announced God’s love for Solomon at his birth (2Sa 12.24–25), confirmed God’s selection of Solomon to succeed David as king (see 1Ch 28.4–7). Although Nathan had sharply rebuked David for his affair with Bathsheba and his murder of Uriah (2Sa 12.1–15), the king respected the prophet. • Adonijah certainly observed Nathan’s close association with Bathsheba and Solomon. All three could expect to be killed if Adonijah’s plot to seize the throne succeeded (see 1Ki 15.29; 1Ki 16.11).
David reassured Bathsheba that Solomon would be the next king by repeating his earlier vow in God’s name (see 1Ki 1.17).
David affirmed his pledge by ordering a public display of support by the priestly, prophetic, and military representatives, Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah.

Riding the king’s own mule was a sign of prestige. In an ancient text from Mari, King Zimri-Lim was advised that royal protocol would be served by his riding in a donkey cart. David’s sons rode mules (2Sa 13.29; 2Sa 18.9). Similarly Zechariah predicts that Israel’s king will come “riding on a donkey’s colt” (Zec 9.9), a prophecy fulfilled by Jesus (Mat 21.4–7; Joh 12.14–15). With Solomon mounted on David’s royal mule, the people would know that Solomon’s anointing as king had David’s blessing. • The Gihon Spring, just outside Jerusalem’s eastern slopes, was the city’s major water source. In this common gathering place, Solomon’s anointing would be well known, yet not visible to Adonijah’s supporters at En-rogel.

Solomon’s anointing followed established protocol in being administered by a prophet (see 1Sa 16.1–13). • Priests also played significant roles in royal matters, and the populace would welcome Zadok’s blessing. David later confirmed Solomon’s kingship in a public ceremony (1Ch 29.22).

sit on my throne: Due to David’s age and infirmities, Solomon officiated publicly for about two years before his father died. Co-regency provided for orderly royal succession and became commonplace during Israel’s divided monarchy. It was also practiced in Egypt. • The Hebrew term for ruler, used for various leadership positions, can have theological significance; the king was seen as both a spiritual and administrative leader of God’s people (see Deu 31.10–11; 1Ch 28.4–6; Psa 89.3–4; Isa 55.3–4).
The king’s bodyguard were foreign mercenaries from Crete; they served David throughout his reign (2Sa 8.18; 2Sa 15.18; 2Sa 20.7).
The priest . . . anointed Solomon with olive oil. This act, a widely accepted Near Eastern practice, gave the ceremony divine sanction.
Those attending Adonijah’s banquet at En-rogel could not see the celebration, but it was so joyously noisy that they could hear it.
Solomon was proclaimed as king and warmly welcomed by the people. Adonijah and his followers panicked and fled, aborting the attempted coup.

Fearing for his life, Adonijah sought refuge at the horns (projections at the corners) of the altar (Exo 27.2), hoping for mercy according to biblical precedent (cp. Exo 21.12–14). However, such protection was provided only for unintentional homicide, so Adonijah’s treason could only be forgiven by the king. Solomon treated him graciously on the condition that he remain loyal. Appearances aside, Adonijah was still looking for ways to usurp the kingship and was later killed as a troublemaker (1Ki 2.13–25).
David gave his final charge to Solomon in two sections: personal advice for spiritual living (1Ki 2.2–4) and instructions about people David had dealt with (1Ki 2.5–9).
Theme: God’s Covenant with Israel’s Kings

David’s advice to Solomon combined the spiritual and ethical standards of Deuteronomy, the standards of the covenant through Moses (see Lev 18.4–5; Deu 5.33; Deu 6.4–5; Deu 8.6; Deu 10.12), and the promises of the covenant with David (2Sa 7.12–16, 2Sa 7.25). If Solomon would keep God’s standards of righteousness, the promises would be transmitted to his heir, who in turn could claim God’s blessings and convey them to subsequent generations (Psa 89.3–4, Psa 89.20, Psa 89.24, Psa 89.27–37). • The preeminent heir of David, the Messiah, would embody true righteousness (Isa 11.1–5), receive the full benefits of the covenant (Jer 33.14–16), and enact a new covenant with the people of Israel and Judah (Jer 31.31–34; Eze 34.24–31; Eze 37.24–28). The New Testament reveals Jesus as that son of David who has come (Mat 1.1; Rom 1.1–4); he will come again to fulfill Old Testament prophecies and bless all people (Luk 1.67–79; Gal 3.26–29; Rev 3.21).

Take courage and be a man: God and Moses had given this same charge to Joshua at the time of the conquest (Deu 31.6–7; Jos 1.6–7, Jos 1.9). Joshua and Hezekiah gave this admonition to Israelite forces when facing enemies (Jos 1.16–18; Jos 10.24–28; 2Ch 32.7). David had learned the value of godly courage (Psa 27.13–14; Psa 31.23–24). When Paul urged Christians to be courageous (literally be men) and strong (1Co 16.13), he used the same words as the Greek Old Testament uses for the charges by Moses, Joshua, Hezekiah, and the Lord. An interesting parallel is found in the account of Bishop Polycarp’s martyrdom. As he was led into the stadium facing execution, Polycarp heard a voice from heaven saying, “Be strong, Polycarp, be a man!” (Martyrdom of Polycarp 1Ki 9.1).

Joab had supported David’s bid for kingship but had become too ambitious. He had murdered former military rivals Abner (2Sa 3.22–30) and Amasa (2Sa 20.10), as well as David’s son Absalom (2Sa 18.1–18). A party to David’s murder of Uriah the Hittite (2Sa 11.14–27), Joab had grown very powerful (2Sa 20.23), and his backing of Adonijah posed a serious threat to Solomon.
Barzillai unwaveringly supported David during his trouble with Absalom, while Shimei openly opposed David (2Sa 16.5–13; 2Sa 19.6–23).
at your table: As he had done for Mephibosheth (2Sa 9.6–13), David provided for Barzillai and his family. This privilege assured their continued loyalty.
Mahanaim was David’s refuge during Absalom’s rebellion (2Sa 17.24). The Egyptian pharaoh, Shishak, invaded it during Rehoboam’s reign (see 1Ki 14.25).

David died peacefully after a forty-year reign, knowing that the kingdom was firmly established in Solomon, his designated heir. Various locations have been proposed for David’s tomb, but none has been confirmed (cp. Act 2.29). Royal tombs were used at least until Hezekiah’s days (2Ki 20.21).
Adonijah contradicted his supposed peaceful intentions when he declared, the kingdom was rightfully mine.

let me marry Abishag: Possessing the king’s concubine was a mark of royal legitimacy. When David became king, he was given Saul’s wives (2Sa 12.7–8). The rebellious Absalom claimed David’s concubines (2Sa 16.20–22).
Solomon understood the intentions behind Adonijah’s small request. Adonijah’s desire to marry Abishag could have launched a claim to the throne, whether or not she was officially in David’s harem.
Because Adonijah violated his terms of submission to Solomon (1Ki 1.52–53), the king ordered Benaiah (see 1Ki 1.8, 1Ki 1.26, 1Ki 1.38) to execute him.
Solomon presumed that Adonijah’s chief supporters, Abiathar and Joab, remained involved in Adonijah’s schemes, so Solomon dealt with them as well.

Abiathar had treasonously supported Adonijah (1Ki 1.7, 1Ki 1.25). But he was deposed rather than killed because he had carried the Ark (2Sa 15.24, 2Sa 15.29, 2Sa 15.35), had supported David, and had shared all his hardships. Abiathar’s removal from the priesthood fulfilled the Lord’s word about the house of Eli in Ithamar’s line (1Sa 2.30–35). Zadok’s appointment (1Ki 4.2) returned the high priesthood to Eleazar’s line as it had been before Eli (Num 20.22–28; Num 25.11–13; 2Sa 8.17; 1Ch 6.1–8, 1Ch 6.50–53; Ezr 7.2–5) and as it continued throughout the divided monarchy (2Ch 31.10; Eze 43.19).

Following Adonijah’s example (1Ki 1.50), Joab hoped to find mercy by grasping the horns of the altar according to the provisions of the law of Moses (Exo 21.12–14; Num 35.22–25; Deu 19.4–5). But because Joab was a murderer, he could not claim clemency (see 2Sa 3.27; 2Sa 18.14; 2Sa 20.10).
The confinement of Shimei prevented him from reaching his kinsmen in Benjamin to stir up trouble for the king.

Shimei’s journey to Gath, ostensibly to recover his runaway slaves, violated his agreement. Technically, he did not cross the Kidron Valley in going to Gath, but the penalty was understood by both parties to apply to Shimei’s going anywhere else. Because Shimei violated his oath to the LORD (1Ki 2.43) and because of his past hostilities toward David (2Sa 16.5–13; 2Sa 19.16–23), Solomon instructed Benaiah to execute him.

As was common in the ancient Near East, Solomon sealed a political alliance with the king of Egypt by marrying one of his daughters. The bestowal of an Egyptian princess and the city of Gezer to Solomon as a wedding present (1Ki 9.16) demonstrated the Egyptians’ high regard for him. The pharaoh was probably Siamun, of Egypt’s weakened 21st dynasty. The alliance was mutually beneficial: Pharaoh gained access to trade routes through Israel, while Solomon increased security on his southern border. Apparently, Solomon had previously married the Ammonite Naamah (see 1Ki 11.42–43 with 1Ki 14.21). • City of David: This section of Jerusalem was the old Jebusite city in the southern portion of the eastern ridge. When Solomon extended his building activities northward, he built a special palace for Pharaoh’s daughter (1Ki 7.8; 1Ki 9.24; 2Ch 8.11).

The Ark of the Covenant sat in David’s tent in Jerusalem before the Temple was built, and the people . . . sacrificed their offerings at local places of worship (see study note on 1Ki 8.1). However, this detracted from unified worship at a central sanctuary (1Ki 12.1–24) and increased the danger of mixing with Canaanite religious practices. Israel’s worship at such places was forbidden (Deu 12.1–14).

God’s gift of wisdom to Solomon is narrated as a chiasm (a symmetrical arrangement in which sections A and B are mirrored by sections B’ and A’), drawing the focus in on Solomon’s transaction with the Lord: A: While he sacrificed at Gibeon . . . the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream (1Ki 3.4–5). B: Solomon prayed for wisdom to govern his people equitably and efficiently (1Ki 3.6–9). B’: The Lord favorably answered his request and granted additional blessings (1Ki 3.10–14). A’: Solomon awoke from the dream and offered additional sacrifices to the Lord (1Ki 3.15).

The city of Gibeon lay six miles northwest of Jerusalem. Its altar, the most important of these [local] places of worship (literally the great high place), accommodated sacrifices of royal proportions. Gibeon was also the site of the Tabernacle (1Ch 16.39–40; 1Ch 21.29; 2Ch 1.2–6).
Theme: Solomon’s Wisdom
The Hebrew word translated faithful love (khesed) expresses God’s gracious treatment and loving kindness toward humanity (Psa 118.1–2), especially to his covenant nation Israel (Deu 7.9, Deu 7.12).

The Hebrew term translated little child was often used of someone who lacked experience in his profession (“assistant,” 1Ki 19.21). Solomon humbly recognized his inexperience and his need for an understanding heart. If he desired to govern the people well and render proper decisions, he knew that he needed God’s help.

God was pleased with Solomon’s unselfish request and granted him a wise and understanding heart. These incomparable qualities are demonstrated in the next section (1Ki 3.16–28) and as Solomon sets up his administration (ch 1Ki 4.1–34), business dealings, building activities, international relations, and worship practices (chs 1Ki 5.1–10).
Solomon’s sacrifice after the dream completes the narrative.
Solomon’s judgment concerning the real mother of the living baby illustrates his wisdom in cases of civil jurisprudence. Chapters 1Ki 4.1–10 illustrate his wisdom in all areas of his rule.

prostitutes: While the law condemned prostitution (Lev 19.29; Deu 23.18), it still existed in ancient Israel. Though these women were of the most despised class of women in Israelite society, Solomon demonstrated his kindness and availability to all people by dealing justice to them as mothers, not as prostitutes.
Kings often claimed special wisdom and the ability to make just decisions. As God promised, Solomon’s wisdom was greater than that of other wise men (1Ki 4.29–34; 1Ki 10.6–9, 1Ki 10.23–24).
Because Zadok was now quite old, his grandson (see 1Ch 6.8–9) Azariah succeeded him as high priest.

The court secretaries were state officials and Solomon’s private secretaries. Shisha, the father of Elihoreph and Ahijah, had served David in this capacity (2Sa 8.17; 2Sa 20.25; 1Ch 18.16). • The royal historian functioned as chief of protocol for palace affairs and ceremonies. As in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, such officials often represented the king in important negotiations (see 2Ki 18.18; 2Ch 34.8).
Benaiah . . . Zadok and Abiathar: All three men had also held special posts in David’s administration. Though deposed as high priest (1Ki 2.26–27), Abiathar still functioned as a priest.
Two sons of Nathan also served in Solomon’s inner circle. Azariah supervised the twelve district governors, while Zabud . . . was a trusted adviser, a post held by Hushai under David (2Sa 15.37).

Ahishar functioned as manager of the palace property, an office that became powerful under Uzziah’s son Jotham (2Ki 15.5). Later, this position was held by Eliakim, one of Hezekiah’s representatives, who met with emissaries from King Sennacherib of Assyria during negotiations concerning the siege of Jerusalem (2Ki 18.18). • Adoniram was head of the corvée (the system of forced labor). Samuel had warned about this loathsome institution (1Sa 8.12–17), and the leaders of Israel later complained about it to Solomon’s son Rehoboam (1Ki 12.4).

The twelve district governors probably handled lesser administrative duties, such as securing revenue and providing food for the king’s household. Solomon’s twelve districts did not exactly coincide with the old tribal allotments.

God’s promise to Abraham (Gen 15.18–21; Gen 17.8; Gen 22.17) finds historical fulfillment in his blessing of Solomon. The surrounding lands conquered by David and Solomon (2Ch 8.3) remained loyal to Solomon. They sent tribute money . . . and continued to serve him throughout his long reign.
Solomon’s court was enormous and splendid, as indicated by its daily food requirements.
each family had its own home and garden: Solomon’s subjects lived under ideal conditions that foreshadowed the coming messianic era (Mic 4.4), enjoying widespread prosperity and tranquility.

4,000 stalls: The number 4,000 reflects the parallel text in 2Ch 9.25, a suitable number for Solomon’s 1,400 chariots (1Ki 10.26; 2Ch 1.14). • 12,000 horses: The Hebrew can be translated as “horsemen” (Exo 15.19–21) or “horses” (Joe 2.4). To be prepared for battles, Solomon built towns to accommodate his forces (1Ki 9.19).
wise men of the East: Babylon was well-known for wise men. Yet Solomon’s God-given wisdom (1Ki 3.9, 1Ki 3.12, 1Ki 3.28; Pro 1.7; Ecc 12.13) exceeded them all (1Ki 4.34).

Ethan and Heman were among the musicians appointed by David (see 1Ch 6.33–47; 1Ch 15.16–19; Psa 88.1–18, Psa 89.1–52). • The sons of Mahol were Temple singers, so Heman, Calcol, and Darda may have participated in the worship services (see 1Ch 15.17, 1Ch 15.19–22).

proverbs . . . songs: Solomon wrote much of the book of Proverbs and composed Psa 72.1–20 and Psa 127.1–5. His knowledge of plants and animals reflected his careful observation of nature (see Pro 6.6–8). Solomon’s wisdom and literary prowess (see Mat 12.42) are reflected in the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes. No wonder many, including kings (1Ki 10.1–9), sought the wisdom of Solomon.

King Hiram of Tyre had . . . been a loyal friend of David (2Sa 5.11–12). This might mean that the two shared a covenantal relationship (a treaty). Hiram was a valuable ally and commercial partner (1Ki 5.7–11, 1Ki 5.18; 1Ki 9.11, 1Ki 9.26–28; 1Ki 10.22). His name is a shortened form of Ahiram, a name seen elsewhere in Phoenician inscriptions.

Solomon responded to Hiram by sending word through Hiram’s ambassadors that he intended to build a Temple to honor the name of the LORD, following his father David’s desire and provisions for its construction (2Sa 7.1–3; 1Ch 17.1–15; 1Ch 22.14–19; 1Ch 28.9–12).

gave him victory over all his enemies (literally put them under the soles of his feet): Ancient Near Eastern inscriptions and paintings often depict victorious kings with their feet upon the necks of vanquished foes or with enemies subdued at their feet.
Theme: Pure Worship

Unlike David, Solomon enjoyed peace [literally rest] on every side. Solomon’s name (Hebrew shlomoh) may be a variation of the word for “peace” (Hebrew shalom). • The name of the LORD signifies God’s self-revealed character and reputation. The Hebrew term translated the name was sometimes used in oral reading of Scripture so the reader could avoid uttering the personal name of God (the tetragrammaton—YHWH). The New Testament applies the term “the name” to Jesus (Act 5.41; 3Jo 1.7).

please command: The main thrust of Solomon’s message was his request for cedars from Lebanon, indicating Hiram’s wide commercial influence. Ancient Near Eastern literature often cites the use of Lebanese cedars in building and furnishing temples and palaces. • Sidonians was a general name for Phoenicians; Sidon was more ancient than Tyre.

Hiram’s reply to Solomon confirmed and perpetuated the cordial relations that he had with David. The venture was mutually beneficial. Solomon received needed construction materials for the Temple; in return, he supplied necessities for Hiram’s household (1Ki 5.9–10) and paid Hiram’s workers (1Ki 5.6). The passage illustrates the Phoenicians’ skillful commercial enterprises and Solomon’s immense wealth, and it again emphasizes Solomon’s God-given wisdom. The largely commercial venture led to a formal alliance of peace (1Ki 5.12).

Praise the LORD: Hiram did not acknowledge Israel’s God as his own but, following ancient Near Eastern protocol, he politely recognized Solomon’s God (see 1Ki 10.9; 2Ki 18.22–25; Ezr 1.2–4; Ezr 6.12; Dan 2.47; Dan 3.29; Dan 6.26–27).
This passage describes Solomon’s work force and the division of labor. Forced labor was a common practice in the ancient Near East (see study note on 1Ki 4.6).

Aliens with permanent residency in Israel comprised the bulk of Solomon’s labor force. Native Israelites were apparently temporary supervisors for Solomon’s building projects (1Ki 9.22–23; 1Ki 11.28).

3,600 foremen: In 2 Chronicles (2Ch 2.2, 2Ch 2.17–18; 2Ch 8.10) the foremen total 3,600 non-Israelite and 250 Israelite chief supervisors. The numbers in the Hebrew text of 1Ki 5.16 and 1Ki 9.23 are 3,300 foremen and 550 chief supervisors. It is possible that 250 of the chief supervisors were Israelites, with 300 non-Israelites holding the same rank.

Large blocks of high-quality stone were probably cut to size (see 1Ki 7.10) in a quarry near Jerusalem (1Ki 6.7). The need to handle these massive stones is probably what led Solomon to institute forced labor. The craftsmen included men from . . . Gebal (Byblos), a port known for exporting timber, according to ancient Egyptian inscriptions.

The building of the Temple and palace complex and the celebration of the Temple dedication are central to the 1 Kings account of Solomon’s era. The Temple, erected to glorify God, was Israel’s most important building, so the writer of 1 Kings carefully recorded details of its construction.

Solomon’s fourth year was about 967 BC. Treating the number 480 as representing calendar years yields a date of about 1446 BC for Israel’s exodus from Egypt. Those who view the number as symbolic (12 generations times 40 years each) suggest that the Exodus occurred at a later date, around 1270 BC (see Exodus Book Introduction, “The Date of the Exodus”).

Like the Tabernacle before it, the Temple (literally house) was the place where God met with his people. David had stored up materials to be used in its construction (1Ch 22.2–4, 1Ch 22.14) and had drawn up plans for the Temple and given them to Solomon (1Ch 28.11–12). The Temple’s floor plan resembled that of the Tabernacle but doubled its length and width and increased its height (cp. Exo 26.3, Exo 26.15–30; Exo 36.26–34).
Unlike the Tabernacle, the Temple had an east entry room (or porch) and two freestanding pillars before the entrance (1Ki 7.15–22).

The LORD had an encouraging message for Solomon. Because God appeared to Solomon before (1Ki 3.5) and after (1Ki 9.2) this event, this message probably came to him by a prophet. The words reminded the king of God’s prior promise (1Ki 3.14): If Solomon remained faithful to God, the Temple that he was building would become an eternal dwelling place for God.

The focus shifts to the Temple interior. While the Temple site is not mentioned here, the Chronicler located it at the former threshing floor of Araunah (1Ch 21.18–25; 2Ch 3.1). This site is traditionally thought to be the location of Mount Moriah (Gen 22.2). Solomon’s Temple was in the northeastern corner of Jerusalem (now called the “old city”) in the area now associated with the Dome of the Rock.

paneled with wood: The interior walls were paneled with cedar from floor to ceiling so that no exterior stones could be seen. The effect was exquisitely beautiful, reflecting painstaking care and great expense.

Following the pattern of the Tabernacle, the inner sanctuary, which was overlaid . . . inside with solid gold, was separated from the main room of the Temple by a curtain (2Ch 3.14) and gold chains. Like the Most Holy Place in the Tabernacle, the inner sanctuary was a perfect cube. It housed the Ark of the LORD’s Covenant that symbolized God’s presence. The place of atonement was atop the Ark (Exo 25.17); the high priest annually made propitiation for the Israelites by sprinkling the sacrificial blood of the atonement on it (Lev 16.1–19). • The altar that belonged to the Most Holy Place stood in the main room. The priests burned incense there daily (Exo 30.34–38; Exo 37.25–29). The altar was made of cedar and covered with gold. • Like the inner sanctuary, the main room was also completely overlaid with gold, which reminded the priests that Almighty God was present. The main room also housed ten golden lampstands, ten tables (2Ch 4.7–8), and other furnishings (1Ki 7.48–50).

In the inner sanctuary were two cherubim (see study note on 1 Chr 1Ch 28.18) made of olive wood and overlaid . . . with gold. Standing like sentries facing the door (2Ch 3.13), their combined wingspan reached from wall to wall. Along with the two smaller cherubim facing each other atop the Ark (Exo 25.17–21), they symbolized the awesome presence of the Most Holy God.

The inner courtyard surrounding the Temple was restricted to the priests (2Ch 4.9) and contained the bronze altar (2Ch 4.1), the bronze Sea (1Ki 7.23–26; 2Ch 4.2–5), and ten carts that could hold ten basins of water for purification (1Ki 7.27–40; 2Ch 4.6).
midautumn, in the month of Bul: The year was 960 BC.

Before describing the Temple’s furnishings, the writer mentions the construction of Solomon’s palace complex. The multiple buildings within this complex took nearly twice as long to build (thirteen years) as the Temple (seven years, 1Ki 6.38). The entire building project took twenty years (1Ki 9.10). Although construction details are brief, archaeological discovery of two of Solomon’s buildings provides an idea of how this palace might have looked. Despite its grandeur, Solomon’s palace is not the author’s focus; his interest is in the Temple, God’s dwelling place.

The Palace of the Forest of Lebanon was named for the abundant use of cedar in its construction. It would house 300 gold shields (1Ki 10.16–17) and possibly served as both treasury and armory (see 1Ki 12.25–28; Isa 22.8). The Egyptian pharaoh Shishak later carried away the shields as booty (1Ki 14.27).

The Hall of Pillars was apparently a colonnaded entry to the Hall of Justice, where Solomon sat to hear legal matters (see also 1Ki 10.18–20). Similar throne rooms have been found in Syria and Mesopotamia. • Solomon erected separate living quarters for Pharaoh’s daughter (see 1Ki 3.1; 1Ki 9.24; 2Ch 8.11).

As with the Temple, the stones for Solomon’s palace complex were high-quality stone, cut . . . and trimmed to exact specifications. Similar stonework has been found at Megiddo. Cedar beams between the courses of the wall provided better protection against earthquakes.
The great courtyard that encircled the Temple and palace complex provided a gathering place for the people (see Jer 7.1–2; Jer 36.10).

Huram: Like his father, he was a master craftsman in bronze and other materials (2Ch 2.12–14). His skillful metal work is detailed in the following verses (1Ki 7.15–50). • skillful and talented (literally filled with wisdom and understanding and knowledge): The Israelites placed great emphasis on practical skills and considered them a form of wisdom (Pro 22.29).
The two bronze pillars were probably free-standing since the narrator describes them here rather than in the earlier discussion of the Temple structure (1Ki 6.3–6).

The giant bronze basin called the Sea replaced the smaller bronze washbasin used in the Tabernacle service (see Exo 30.17–21). The Sea was cast as one solid piece, excluding the twelve bronze oxen on which it sat. The oxen were placed so that three faced each direction, perhaps to remind priests that they served God on behalf of all twelve tribes of Israel. Ahaz later replaced the oxen with a stone base (2Ki 16.17). The priests used the Sea, like the bronze washbasin before it, for ceremonial washing (2Ch 4.6) as they prepared to minister before God (see Exo 30.17–21). The apparent discrepancy in the volume of water it could hold (see 2Ch 4.5) is probably due to standards of measurement that varied according to place and time.
The ten bronze water carts each held a basin for rinsing burnt offerings (2Ch 4.6). Five stood on either side of the Temple. Because they had wheels, they could be moved as needed.
Huram had great skill in casting items of varying size and complexity. He also made the bronze altar for the inner court that was used for burnt offerings (2Ch 4.1).

between Succoth and Zarethan: This area east of the Jordan River (see Jos 3.16; Jdg 8.4–5) was known for metallurgy. Abundant clay for molds, wood for fuel, and a prevailing north wind facilitated the casting process.

The gold altar replaced the altar for burning incense used in the Tabernacle (Exo 30.1–10). The one table and one lampstand used in the Tabernacle (Exo 25.23–40) were replaced by ten such sets in the Temple. Although the author lists a single gold table for the Bread of the Presence, the Chronicler reports ten tables, five on each side of the Temple’s main room (cp. 2Ch 4.8), along with ten lampstands of solid gold. The bread represented God’s provision for his people, and the lampstand characterized God as the source of life and truth. Both symbols pointed to Christ, the bread of life (Joh 6.35) and the light of the world (Joh 8.12).

The writer emphasizes Solomon’s abundant use of gold in furnishing the Temple. David and the people had collected an enormous amount of gold to be used for the Temple (1Ch 29.1–9), and Solomon also amassed gold annually (1Ki 10.14), so he had a ready supply (see 1Ki 10.21).

Solomon’s building activities climaxed with the Ark’s move to the newly erected Temple. The king offered both prayer (1Ki 8.22–53) and words of praise and blessing (1Ki 8.56–61) to dedicate the Temple for the Lord’s service. After the dedication, the assembled gathering enjoyed the great Festival of Shelters. The focus of the account is on Solomon praising God and blessing the people (1Ki 8.12–61).

The Ark was being kept in a tent in the City of David (2Sa 6.3–17; 1Ch 13.7–14; 1Ch 15.1–1Ki 16.43). Solomon had gone there earlier to sacrifice after the Lord appeared to him in a dream in Gibeon (1Ki 3.4–15).

Although the Temple was completed in the eighth month (1Ki 6.38), Solomon apparently delayed the dedication until the following year so it could take place at the annual Festival of Shelters, which is held in early autumn in the month of Ethanim. This schedule allowed time to prepare for the spectacular celebration and gave the occasion double significance. As prescribed in the law, Solomon and the people expressed their gratitude to God for the completed harvest season. They also celebrated the fulfillment of Moses’ song of deliverance, which promised that God would one day settle his people in the Promised Land and make his dwelling there (Exo 15.17; Deu 12.10–14). Solomon’s dedicatory prayer and blessing may indicate that he was consciously leading his people in covenantal renewal, as prescribed in Deu 31.10–13, in the seventh month of the seventh year of his reign.
The priests and Levites brought up the Ark of the LORD as prescribed in the law (Exo 25.14–15; Num 4.5–8; cp. 2Sa 6.1–15).
The incalculable sacrifices by the Israelites marked both the joy and the solemnity of this occasion.
In accordance with the law (Exo 25.15), the carrying poles were required to stay with the Ark.

The focus on the two stone tablets that Moses placed in the Ark (cp. 1Ki 8.21; see Exo 25.21; Deu 31.26) suggests that Solomon had in mind both a renewal of the Mosaic covenant and the Temple dedication.

As the priests came out of the Holy Place, they were greeted with music praising the Lord (2Ch 5.11–14). Previously, the glorious presence of the LORD had filled the Tabernacle (Exo 40.34–35). Now it filled the Temple to show that God was again dwelling among his people. Ezekiel recorded its later departure from the Temple (Eze 10.18–19), to return at a blessed future time (Eze 43.1–5). In the New Testament, John wrote that God dwells among his people through his son, Jesus Christ (Joh 1.14). Paul affirmed that Christ now dwells in each believer (Col 1.27) as a foretaste of a future when “God’s home is . . . among his people” (Rev 21.3).

Solomon began with prayer (1Ki 8.12–13), then blessed the people while praising God for fulfilling his promises (1Ki 8.14–21). As in many praise psalms, Solomon elevated God, subordinated himself, and testified to God’s great goodness.

thick cloud of darkness: Solomon recognized the cloud filling the inner sanctuary as a manifestation of God’s presence, but he also understood that God could not be contained in a man-made Temple (see 1Ki 8.27). Solomon fulfilled his commission to build the Temple (1Ki 8.19; 1Ch 28.10), believing the promises that God would dwell in the sanctuary (see Exo 15.17).
Solomon’s blessing was expressed as praise to God, who had kept his covenant promises and blessed his people (see 2Sa 7.12–16; cp. 2Ch 6.1–11).

Like Solomon’s preceding prayer, his prayer of dedication for the Temple praised God and blessed the people. He emphasized God’s covenant faithfulness and his own role in building the Temple and prayed for God’s continued response to their prayers (1Ki 8.22–30). Solomon then made seven distinct petitions to God (1Ki 8.31–53) and concluded with a blessing (1Ki 8.54–61).

As Solomon prayed, he lifted his hands toward heaven and knelt before the Lord on a platform erected in clear view of the congregation (1Ki 8.54; 2Ch 6.13). Jesus condemned hypocritical individuals who displayed religiosity without true, heartfelt belief (Mat 6.5–8). But Solomon’s public piety was genuine, leading his people in worship and encouraging them to live in full dependence upon God. The nation that knows and obeys the Lord, and whose leaders rule in righteousness, is particularly blessed (2Ch 7.14; Psa 33.12; Psa 45.6–7; Psa 144.15; Pro 29.2; Isa 11.1–5).

Solomon’s prayer affirmed God’s incomparable nature and the fulfillment of his promises to David. Solomon also prayed that God would keep his promise that David’s descendants . . . will always sit on the throne.
Solomon asked God to hear the prayers of his people from the Temple. He then addressed specific instances in which they would need God’s answers.
Theme: God’s Faithfulness to His People

Solomon asked that God render the proper decision and carry out justice in court cases when the litigant’s innocence could not be determined due to a lack of witnesses (cp. Exo 22.7–12). Perhaps Solomon realized that later officials would not have the special wisdom God had given him (1Ki 3.12; e.g., 1Ki 3.16–27).

Solomon asked concerning future situations when the people of Israel sinned and God allowed the enemy to defeat them (see Lev 26.14–17; Deu 28.15, Deu 28.25–26, Deu 28.45, Deu 28.49; Jos 7.1–26) and then the people genuinely repented. Solomon asked that God honor his covenant and forgive them (Lev 26.39–42).
Theme: The Land

Solomon prayed about drought brought on by the people’s sin (Lev 26.19; Deu 28.23–24). Solomon prayed that if the people confessed and truly repented, God would forgive them and restore fertility to the land so that the people would learn to live righteously before God.
