lots were cast . . . (the lots were called purim): Throwing the purim was like throwing dice. The Hebrews used lots from time to time to understand God’s will (Lev 16.8–10; Neh 10.34). Persian astrologers used purim in the first month of the year to determine which days that year would bring good fortune.

who keep themselves separate: Jews intermarried within tight-knit communities and resisted integration into the larger culture. • Their laws are different: They had a unique set of laws (eating and religious customs) and were to be separate from the sinful customs of the people around them (Lev 14.42–45; Lev 15.31; Lev 19.2, Lev 19.26–37). • they refuse to obey the laws of the king: This accusation, which is false in general, probably refers to Mordecai’s refusal to bow to Haman. • So it is not in the king’s interest to let them live: Haman played on the king’s fears and interests as Memucan had done in Est 1.16. Intolerance toward any particular group of people ran against the general Persian tendency to be respectful of other people’s cultural and religious differences.

Haman tipped his hand by offering to bribe the king with a large sum of silver, which should have made the king suspicious of Haman’s motives. The value of the proposed gift is so astronomical that Haman may have been exaggerating to show his intended generosity.

The king agreed with no inquiry. The king is presented as someone very irresponsible and easily manipulated. By removing his signet ring, the king gave up his control over official policies; by giving it to Haman, he signified that Haman had complete authority to seal the decree. • the enemy of the Jews: The narrator’s new title for Haman is an ominous note regarding his power to persecute the Jews (see also Est 8.1; Est 9.10, Est 9.24). • The money and the people are both yours: It may appear that the king did not want the bribe, but Est 4.7 suggests that Haman did give the money. The king was following a customary protocol to make the bribe and his greed less obvious (cp. Gen 23.10–16). For the sake of public appearance the king pretended not to be interested in the money, but in reality he was.

So on April 17: Haman’s choice of the day before the Jewish Passover began (see Exo 12.6) was probably calculated to terrorize and demoralize the Jews. But as he did at the Exodus, God would deliver the Jews miraculously from a tyrant who was trying to destroy them.

The phrase killed, slaughtered, and annihilated is repeated with ironic effect in Est 8.11 and Est 9.5. • on March 7 of the next year: Haman’s “lucky day” that was chosen by casting lots (Est 3.7) was eleven months after the decree, by God’s providence, giving time to overcome the decree. • The property of the Jews would be given to those who killed them: Haman ingeniously bribed the would-be executioners.

This decree carried the full weight of Xerxes’ royal authority. • The foolish king and wicked Haman celebrated this occasion, but the people of the fortress of Susa were perplexed, bewildered, and confused at such a ruthless and unjust decree.
Mordecai’s dramatic response showed extreme grief and mourning (see 2Sa 1.11; Ezr 9.1–15; Jon 3.5–9).
no one was allowed: The king did not want to hear all the sorry stories of misfortune and people pleading for mercy.

great mourning among the Jews: In these reports of lamenting, God’s name is not mentioned, but the lamenting and fasting implies crying out in prayer for God to intervene and save his people (Exo 2.23–25; Ezr 9.5–15; Dan 9.1–19).

A copy of the decree with the king’s seal would prove to Esther the seriousness of the situation. • to beg for mercy: Mordecai gave Esther no reasons to present to the king, only an appeal to the king’s mercy and Esther’s influence on him on behalf of her own people.

anyone who appears . . . without being invited is doomed to die: Access to the king was strictly controlled by his guards to prevent unwanted guests from wasting the king’s time with petty requests. Since these were the official rules of the court, the danger to Esther’s life was enormous. Apparently she ruled out requesting an audience with the king through a messenger, possibly because she would have to tell the messenger why she wanted to talk to the king. • has not called for me to come to him for thirty days: Esther had no guarantee of the king’s favorable response.

Don’t think . . . you will escape: Mordecai did not back down and did not excuse her because of the danger, and he reminded her that it would be more dangerous for her to say nothing to the king. • deliverance and relief for the Jews will arise from some other place: Mordecai knew God’s promises and realized that God would not allow his chosen people to be annihilated (see Gen 12.3; Gen 22.18; Gen 28.14; Isa 60.1–5). • perhaps you were made queen for just such a time as this: Esther’s rise to power at this precise time was not just a lucky chance of fate—her position as Xerxes’ favored wife and queen was a role that God had given her to influence history for the Jewish people.

fast for me: Esther was convinced, but she wanted as many Jews as possible to pray that God would intervene to save her life. • Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day: A total fast without any food or water often lasted only one day (Lev 16.29–31; Jdg 20.26). The three-day length was consistent with the seriousness of the situation and the absolute need for God’s intervention. • though it is against the law, I will go in to see the king: In spite of the danger, she determined that she must act for the sake of her people. • If I must die, I must die: She, like Mordecai, was a person of character who would do what was right in spite of personal danger.
he welcomed her and held out the gold scepter to her: She was not killed for entering the king’s presence without an invitation (Est 4.11, Est 4.16).

I will give it to you, even if it is half the kingdom! This conventional idiom meant the king would be generous toward her request. The king did not want anything to prevent Esther from speaking the full truth.
If it please the king: Esther showed proper deference (cp. Est 1.12).

please come . . . tomorrow: It was a customary protocol not to appear anxious about asking for a favor or negotiating an agreement. The delay provided opportunity for Xerxes to discover Mordecai’s act of loyalty, which led to the foiling of Haman’s plot (see Est 6.1–14).
This brief interlude emphasizes the depth of Haman’s hatred for Mordecai.
Mordecai’s fasting had ended and he was back at the gate operating in his official capacity. Not standing up or trembling was an even stronger refusal to show Haman honor (cp. Est 3.2–6).

A sharpened pole was a common device of execution (see also Est 2.23; Gen 40.19, Gen 40.22; Jos 8.29). • Seventy-five feet is unusually high, but Haman wanted to make an example out of Mordecai, with everyone viewing his dead body. The number might be a hyperbole for effect—fifty cubits is an obviously round number—or it might reflect a stake placed high atop the city wall for public viewing.
the king had trouble sleeping: God was working to protect Esther and Mordecai. • the book of the history of his reign: Ancient kings kept royal annals of their reigns.
Providentially, the king’s servant happened to open the royal annals to the page describing how Mordecai had exposed the plot (Est 2.21–23).
What reward or recognition did we ever give Mordecai? The Persian kings were known for generosity to their supporters, so the king was probably surprised that nothing had been done.

Just as the king was pondering what to do to honor Mordecai, Haman arrived to seek Mordecai’s death. With great irony, the narrator recounts the king’s consulting with him about how to reward Mordecai.

Haman delighted in public acclaim and recognition. He wanted to be honored as the king, to wear kingly attire, and to ride the king’s horse; in other words, he wanted to be king for a day. • Haman thought another one of the king’s most noble officials would honor him through the streets of Susa. Instead, Haman himself would fill that role for Mordecai (Est 6.10).
do just as you have said for Mordecai the Jew: With utter shock at this complete reversal, Haman could do nothing but obey the king’s command, right down to the last detail.

Since Mordecai—this man who has humiliated you—is of Jewish birth, you will never succeed in your plans: Haman’s wife and friends could see that this was more than just a series of coincidences. The text does not explain why Zeresh and the advisers felt that the fact of Mordecai’s Jewish heritage would necessarily mean that Haman’s plans would not succeed.

my life and the lives of my people: The statement that someone wanted to kill the queen and her family must have surprised and shocked the king. • my people and I have been sold: Esther carefully referred to the huge price Haman had paid the king to approve the decree (Est 3.8–11). She also used the exact terminology of Haman’s decree when she said that its purpose was to kill, slaughter, and annihilate (cp. Est 3.13). • If we had merely been sold as slaves, I could remain quiet: Esther humbly justifies her request as due to the severity of the attack on her and her people.

Who would do such a thing? The king could hardly believe what he was hearing and could not imagine someone trying to do this atrocious thing. He asks for no details about Esther’s accusations, assuming they were all true (cp. Est 3.10).

Esther finally identified this wicked Haman as the enemy. • Haman grew pale with fright: With this surprising and aggressive accusation by the queen and the evident rage of the king, Haman’s doom suddenly became apparent.

he fell on the couch where Queen Esther was reclining: A major mistake, for no one should touch the queen, much less be on the same couch with her. • Will he even assault the queen . . . before my very eyes? This exaggerated rhetorical question implicates Haman with the worst possible motives.

He intended to use it to impale Mordecai: Harbona, one of the king’s seven eunuchs (Est 1.10), was apparently no friend of Haman and was already aware of Haman’s plot. • impale Haman on it! This great reversal of fortunes demonstrates the guiding hand of God. Regarding impalement, see study note on Est 2.23.
Just as Haman had promised the wealth of the Jews to those who would kill them (Est 3.13), Xerxes gave the property of Haman, the enemy of the Jews, to Queen Esther.
The signet ring that Haman had used to seal the decree to destroy the Jewish people (Est 3.10) was now given to the Jewish person he had most wanted to destroy.

Esther probably expected the king to reverse Haman’s decree right after he was killed, but that did not happen. This time she was much more insistent on raising the issue of Haman’s plot against her people.
Esther was asking for the unusual favor of reversing a law signed with the king’s seal. • the orders of Haman: Esther diplomatically avoided suggesting any responsibility on the king’s part.

According to Persian law, whatever has already been written . . . can never be revoked (see Est 1.19; Dan 6.8, Dan 6.12; cp. Psa 148.6). However, a new decree with the king’s royal seal could give different or competing directions.
on June 25: The details of writing and sending the new decree purposely match the account of sending out the original decree in Est 3.12.

The king’s decree did not permit the Jewish people to start a war but to defend themselves and plunder the property of those who attacked them (reversing the decree in Est 3.13). • The phrase kill, slaughter, and annihilate is an ironic repetition of the words in Haman’s original edict (Est 3.13; see also Est 9.5).
March 7 of the next year: This date was nearly a year after Haman’s original decree was published (Est 3.12).

The Hebrew word translated to take revenge could also mean to establish justice. In situations where civil government could not exercise authority over all the parties involved in a conflict, this law would allow people who were attacked to establish justice by redressing wrongs committed against them.

Just as the city of Susa had been in great confusion after Haman’s original decree (Est 3.15), now there was great rejoicing by all—they understood the injustice of the original decree and the justice of the new one.
many . . . became Jews themselves: That is, they became proselytes of Judaism.
on March 7: When that fateful day arrived, there were many enemies of the Jews who wanted to carry out Haman’s wishes.
Theme: Purim
People saw that Mordecai was the man in charge, so they knew it would not be wise to oppose him.

They killed and annihilated their enemies: It was not an attack on defenseless people or a ruthless uncontrolled killing spree, but a victorious self-defense against their attackers. The phrase used here repeats the terminology of Haman’s original decree (Est 3.12).
Although most people in the fortress of Susa itself supported Mordecai, the Jews killed 500 men, a mini-revolt that probably consisted of killing Haman’s relatives and close supporters.
They also killed . . . the ten sons of Haman: Now everything that Haman had boasted about (Est 5.11) was gone, even his ten sons.

But they did not take any plunder: Although taking plunder from those who attacked was permitted (Est 8.11), the Jews did not want anything to do with the defiled wealth of Haman’s sons. Many years earlier, Abram had refused his portion of the plunder from the king of Sodom (Gen 14.21–23).

If the king had been disturbed by the high numbers, he would not have allowed another day of fighting (Est 9.14–15). It seems more likely that the king was astonished that there were so many people who followed Haman and opposed the new regime directed by Mordecai. He was thinking of the political stability of the empire.
Possibly Esther knew that some of the people in Susa who had attacked Jews on the first day had gotten away and would be planning additional attacks to avenge the death of Haman.
So the king agreed, and the decree was announced in Susa: It was not in the king’s interest for there to be warring parties within the palace plotting to kill one another.
Once again, the Jews took the high moral ground and took no plunder from their enemies, though it was legally permitted (Est 8.11; Est 9.10).

75,000 seems like quite a large number. The Old Greek translation has 15,000 and the Targum has 10,107 men. The Hebrew word translated thousands can also indicate an extended family or lineage, so it is possible that 75 extended families were killed.

they rested, celebrating their victory with a day of feasting and gladness: God is not mentioned, but surely they thanked God on this day for their rescue. This was the beginning of a new festival, later called Purim (Est 9.19–32).

The annual festival and holiday of Purim celebrates God’s blessing of peace from their enemies (see Deu 25.19; Jos 21.44; 1Sa 7.11–14). The narrator reports that the festival was celebrated to this day. Now, more than 2,400 years later, it is still celebrated annually by Jewish people. • The exchange of gifts of food demonstrated the unity of the people and their care for one another and helped them to spread an atmosphere of joy for everyone celebrating the festival.
These verses summarize the events leading to the Festival of Purim.
This paragraph justifies Purim as an approved Jewish festival even though Moses did not authorize it along with other festival days.
The letter that Queen Esther . . . wrote provided further official endorsement to Mordecai’s proposal (Est 9.20–23).
King Xerxes imposed a tribute: Persian taxes on the provinces were heavy. This burden supported the Persian government’s free spending.

The Book of the History of the Kings of Media and Persia was the Persian royal annals. While many ancient Persian records have survived, this reference to the greatness of Mordecai has not been found in any records excavated thus far.

Mordecai the Jew did not brag about himself as Haman did (Est 5.11–12), but this righteous man who continually looked out for the good of others was rewarded with a high government position (prime minister) and the high esteem of his people (He was very great among the Jews).

The Book of Job

Purpose

To offer reflection on the issue of human suffering, primarily by questioning the oft-held connection between moral goodness and prosperity

Author

Unknown

Date

Unknown

Setting

The patriarchal period, possibly in the land of Edom

When suffering comes to us, we often ask why. People sometimes say it’s because the sufferer did something wrong. The book of Job examines the suffering of one man who suffered precisely because he was blameless. Job’s friends supposed that he was guilty of some unknown sin. They tried to persuade him to repent, but Job knew he hadn’t sinned, so he questioned God. Finally, God appeared, but he did not give Job the answers he sought. Instead, God confronted Job, changed his perspective, and blessed him.

Setting

The book of Job unfolds early in the patriarchal age, before Israel became a nation. Job’s wealth, like Abraham’s, was in livestock and slaves (Job 1.3; Job 42.12; see Gen 12.16; Gen 32.5). He was his family’s priest, as was a common practice before the law of Moses (Job 1.5; Job 42.8; see Gen 4.4; Gen 8.20; Gen 12.7–8; Gen 13.18; Gen 15.9–10; Gen 26.25; Gen 33.20; Gen 35.1–6; Gen 46.1). During Job’s time, the Sabeans and Chaldeans were nomadic raiders (Job 1.15, Job 1.17), not important political and economic powers as in the late monarchical period (cp. Isa 45.14; Joe 3.8). The money used by Job and his relatives was called the kesitah, which was used during the patriarchal age (Job 42.11; see Gen 33.19; Jos 24.32). Only those who lived before the flood (Gen 1.1–6) and the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob) matched or exceeded Job’s longevity (Job 42.16; see Gen 5.3–32; Gen 25.7; Gen 35.28; Gen 47.28; Gen 50.26). With Job, we return to the beginning of history, when mortals first struggled to know God and understand the world.

Summary

The prose introduction to the book of Job (Job 1.1–2) provides the heavenly perspective on Job’s suffering and sets the context for the human dialogue that forms most of the work. Job was a righteous man whom God allowed Satan to test. In the heavenly courtroom, Satan argued that if God removed his blessings from Job, he would “surely curse you to your face” (Job 1.11). Instead, Job responded, “Praise the name of the LORD!” (Job 1.21), and, “Should we accept only good things from the hand of God and never anything bad?” (Job 2.10). God’s praise for Job was vindicated.

The reader then leaves the court of heaven and enters the council of humans as three of Job’s friends come to sympathize with him. Their silent, seven-day vigil is apparently a genuine attempt to console Job (Job 2.11–13). However, when Job breaks his silence with a bitter complaint (Job 3.1–26), his counselors begin to criticize and condemn him. In three rounds of debate (Job 4.1–27), their rhetoric varies from innuendo to blatant accusation. Job’s friends argue a tight theological case: Since God is righteous, he rewards each person according to what that person has done; therefore, Job’s suffering must be the just punishment for some evil he has committed. Job responds to each of their speeches by insisting that he is innocent and that his suffering is undeserved and unfair.

After the three rounds of dialogue between Job and his friends, a poetic interlude praises God as the sole source of wisdom (ch Job 28.1–28). When Job then makes his final statement about both his misery and his righteousness (chs Job 29.1–31), his three friends give up on him (Job 32.1). Elihu, a new voice, then renews the human struggle to explain Job’s suffering (chs Job 32.1–37). Finally, God arrives to challenge Job (chs Job 38.1–41). Instead of hearing Job’s case, God demands answers and poses questions that demonstrate his own power and sovereignty. Job responds with repentance and acknowledges that he does not have the right to question God (Job 42.1–6).

In the final prose section (Job 42.7–17), God reaffirms Job’s righteousness and faithfulness, pronounces judgment on Job’s friends, and pours out tremendous blessings on Job.

Job as History

The heavenly setting of the book’s opening and the manifestation of the supernatural at its closing tempt the modern reader to cast the book of Job as a fictional parable. The poetic dialogues also suggest that it is something more than just a dry historical record. But history can be described in flights of poetry just as well as in detailed narrative (cp. Exo 14.21–31; Exo 15.1–12; Psa 78.1–72; Psa 105.1–45). The biblical record elsewhere suggests that the account of Job is historical. Both Ezekiel and James referred to Job as an example of righteousness and endurance (Eze 14.14, Eze 14.20; Jam 5.11).

Author and Date of Composition

The authorship and composition of Job is a riddle. Although the story has a patriarchal setting (around 2000 BC), the date of its composition appears to be much later. Commentators have suggested dates that range from the era of Israel’s wilderness wanderings (Exodus—Numbers) to the era following the return from exile (Ezra—Nehemiah). The final composition of Job probably took place during the monarchy (1–2 Kings), when other wisdom materials such as Pro 1.1–Job 31.31 and Ecc 1.1–Job 12.14 were being accumulated.

Even if we accept that Job was a historical character, we still do not know who the author was, where he lived, or what level of society he came from. The author appears to have been a sage who was skilled in the use of proverbs (e.g., Job 4.2; Job 6.5–6), rhetorical questions (e.g., Job 21.29), and the art of eloquence. He also knew about plant and animal life, foreign culture, and antiquity, including the patriarchal period.

The book cannot be dated with certainty by reference to (1) events or people mentioned or implied in the book (the earliest reference to Job is during the Exile, Eze 14.14, Eze 14.20); (2) theological ideas in the book that point to distinct dates; or (3) its textual relationship to other material in the Old Testament (e.g., cp. Job 3.3–10; Jer 20.14–18). Job may even have been edited over a period of time by a number of different people.

Literary Characteristics

Ancient Parallels to Job. The book of Job has several parallels in ancient Near Eastern literature (The following list of parallels is based on James B. Pritchard, ed., Ancient Near Eastern Texts Relating to the Old Testament , 3rd ed. [Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1969]):

• The Canaanite “Legend of King Keret” tells of a king who loses his family in a series of natural disasters; his god El restores his family.

• The Egyptian document “Dispute over Suicide” (2000s BC) tells of a man who considers suicide and hopes that someone will take up his case with the heavenly council. (Job wishes he had never been born, but he never considers suicide.)

• Also from Egypt, “Protests of the Eloquent Peasant” (2200s BC) tells the story of a robbery victim who is not treated justly and appeals to local authorities. At first he is polite, but as he keeps presenting his case, his language becomes increasingly strident.

• From Babylonia, the story “I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom” tells of a pious man of high rank who is struck with illness and mocked by friends. Unlike Job, this man believes that he has committed some accidental sin, perhaps something that he never thought was wrong. Rather than maintain his innocence, he acknowledges his guilt and begs for mercy. After a series of exorcisms that bring healing, his god restores his fortunes. In gratitude, he concludes with a long hymn of praise to his god.

• Also from Babylonia, the “Babylonian Theodicy” follows the same dialogue form that the book of Job uses: The sufferer complains, and his friends respond with rebukes. The arguments on both sides are remarkably similar to those in Job. Yet we also see key differences: (1) The “Babylonian Theodicy” is polytheistic, whereas Job is monotheistic; (2) its sufferer threatens to abandon his faith and give up obedience, even as he ends with a petition to his god and goddess. Job remains committed to the Lord throughout (e.g., Job 13.15–16).

Relationship to Israel’s Wisdom Literature. The book of Job has the flavor of other works of Old Testament wisdom literature. Job’s friends follow lines of thought spelled out in Deuteronomy, Chronicles, and Proverbs. They argue that wisdom and righteousness lead to life and prosperity, while folly and wickedness lead to death and failure. Job joins the author of Ecclesiastes in questioning the simplistic, universal application of this doctrine.

Meaning and Message

The book of Job does not explain suffering. That is not its purpose. But it does demonstrate that suffering is not necessarily God’s retribution for sin. Job does not get an answer as to why bad things happen to good people, and neither do we.

The central conflict of the book is between the integrity of the Creator and the integrity of a man. Heaven and earth appear to be at odds. It is too easy simply to line up with Job’s three friends in denying Job’s innocence, as we can appeal to various New Testament passages that deny that any human is righteous (e.g., Rom 3.10, Rom 3.23; Luk 18.19). Job’s righteousness is genuine and thorough, though his obsession with his own rectitude sometimes borders on self-righteousness. He grows so adamant in defending his integrity that he seems ready to defy God. Job’s three friends set out a view of God that is more orthodox, at least on the surface. These counselors are more than weak, imaginary straw men; they accurately develop most of the biblical ways of explaining suffering. But their presumptuous applications go sour. They insist on a quid pro quo view of retribution, in which all the good and evil that people experience is directly related to what they have earned or deserved.

The book works within the basic commitments of Old Testament Israel’s faith. Job and all of the other speakers take seriously the covenantal ideas of blessing and cursing (Lev 26.1–46; Deu 28.1–68) and of sowing and reaping in this life (Psa 34.11–22; see also Gal 6.7; 1Pe 3.10). They don’t even consider solutions to the problem of why God permits the righteous to suffer (theodicy) from outside the scope of biblical revelation (e.g., metaphysical dualism, polytheistic tensions, or materialistic naturalism). Instead, the book’s speakers explore only biblical answers. They explain the meaning of suffering as (1) punishment for sin (e.g., Job 4.7–9); (2) the inevitable lot of mortals, who tend toward sin (e.g., Job 15.14–16); (3) God’s discipline (e.g., Job 5.17–18; Job 33.15–28; Job 36.8–15; see Pro 3.11; Heb 12.2–13); (4) part of God’s mysterious plan (e.g., Job 11.7–8; Job 37.19, Job 37.23); or (5) a test imposed on earth to satisfy a heavenly dispute (e.g., Job 1.6–12).

Since life “under the sun” (see Ecclesiastes) is an arena too small to provide answers to all the great questions, the writer looks to the courts of heaven for a divine dimension to what takes place on earth. But the answer is not disclosed even there. Why did God entertain Satan’s challenge in the first place?

In the end, the book of Job shows God defending Job’s innocence and rejecting easy explanations of suffering. God also rejects Job’s demands for an explanation. Since Job could not possibly understand the whole universe, he should not demand an explanation of how his suffering fits into that order. The world cannot be explained in terms that humans can fully understand.

The book of Job thus offers a complex picture of God. He could have rejected Satan’s suggestion, having nothing to prove; yet he chose to allow the test, ultimately demonstrating his power and bringing defeat to Satan through the human Job. God never explains to Job what is happening behind the scenes. Instead, God challenges Job’s right to question the integrity of divine justice (Job 40.8).

The way to live through calamities is not just to keep a stiff upper lip but to bow reverently before God and trust his sovereign goodness. In a day of calamity, humans can respond to God by worshiping him and acknowledging the wisdom and justice of his ways, regardless of how harsh the pain or dark the confusion. God’s holy purposes for human suffering are sometimes hidden. In the end, Job draws closer to God through his suffering: “I had only heard about you before, but now I have seen you with my own eyes” (Job 42.5).

The opening phrase, There once was a man, can introduce either a parable (2Sa 12.1) or history (1Sa 25.2). • Job is also mentioned in Eze 14.14, Eze 14.20 and Jam 5.11. • Uz is east of the Jordan, either in Edom to the south (Gen 36.28; 1Ch 1.42; Jer 25.19–20; Lam 4.21) or in Aram to the north (Gen 10.23; Gen 22.21; 1Ch 1.17, 1Ch 1.42). Job was not an Israelite—he lived before the nation was born and outside its later territory. • Job was morally blameless—a man of complete integrity (Job 1.8; Job 2.3; see Psa 25.21; Psa 37.37; Pro 2.7; Pro 20.11; Pro 29.10). He did not claim to be perfect or sinless (Job 6.24; Job 7.21; see also Ecc 7.20; Rom 3.23; 1Jo 1.8), but he was righteous; his suffering did not result from guilt. He feared God (see Psa 111.10; Pro 1.7; Pro 9.10; 2Co 7.1) and did not appeal to any of the ancient Near Eastern gods (Job 9.8; Job 23.13; Job 31.26–28).

Job was prosperous in sons, daughters, livestock, and servants (cp. Gen 30.43; Deu 7.13; Psa 107.38). • Numbers such as seven and three (and 7,000 and 3,000) indicate the completeness of the blessing Job experienced (see Job 42.13; see also Psa 127.3–5; Psa 128.3). • the richest person in that entire area: The figures that catalogue Job’s wealth might not be exact, but they are realistic for a wealthy man of that time (cp. Nabal’s wealth, 1Sa 25.2).

Ritual washing and changing garments were common ways for individuals to purify themselves before offering a sacrifice (Gen 35.2; Exo 19.10, Exo 19.14). • The common time for conscientious piety was early in the morning (see Gen 22.3; Psa 5.3; Mar 1.35). • cursed: The Hebrew term barak (literally blessed) is used here as a euphemism for cursing (cp. Job 1.11; Job 2.5, Job 2.9; 1Ki 21.10, 1Ki 21.13; Psa 10.3). Job was concerned that his children might have committed this capital crime (Lev 24.10–16; 1Ki 21.9–13; cp. Job 1.11; Job 2.5, Job 2.9). Job understood that sinful attitudes in people’s hearts constitute sin (Jer 17.9–10; Mar 7.21–23).
God and Satan agree to a test that would bring about Job’s troubles and confirm his integrity (Job 1.20–21; Job 2.10). None of the book’s characters ever learn of this heavenly council.

The members of the heavenly court are heavenly beings; they may be either holy angels or rebellious demons (Gen 6.2, Gen 6.4). They join God in his deliberations, including at creation (Gen 1.26) and in his rule over creation (Job 1.6; Gen 3.22; Gen 2.1; 1Ki 22.19–22; Psa 82.1; Psa 89.5, Psa 89.7–8; Dan 3.13, Dan 3.17, Dan 3.23, Dan 3.25; Dan 7.9–14). • The account remains unclear as to whether Satan usually came with other members of the heavenly court to make a report or whether he was intruding as Job’s adversary. • Where have you come from? The question was God’s sovereign demand for a report from a subordinate (see Gen 3.9). • Satan was not patrolling to implement God’s judgments (cp. 1Ch 21.1–14; 2Ki 19.35 // Isa 37.36; Eze 1.5–9) but to oppose God’s purposes (2Ti 2.26; 1Pe 5.8).
Profile: Satan
my servant: This title was used for the patriarchs (Gen 26.24; Exo 32.13), the prophets (2Ki 17.13; Jer 7.25; Zec 1.6), and David (e.g., 2Sa 7.1–29; Psa 18.1; Psa 36.1).

Job has good reason (Hebrew khinnam; see study note on Job 2.3) to fear God: The wisdom tradition links piety with prosperity. Satan went a step further by suggesting that Job’s piety was contingent upon his affluence.
wall of protection: See 1Sa 25.16; Psa 5.12; Psa 34.7; Zec 2.5; cp. Isa 5.5.

reach out . . . test him . . . Do whatever you want: Satan was God’s agent; the hand he put forth was the Lord’s as well as Satan’s, for here they acted against everything Job possessed and later against Job himself (Job 2.5–6). • Job later cursed the day of his birth (Job 3.1, Job 3.8), but he did not curse God (Job 31.30), even when his distraught wife urged him to do so (Job 2.9). • God allowed Satan to test Job to prove that Satan’s cynicism was incorrect (1Co 10.11; see Jam 1.13; cp. Luk 22.31–32; Joh 19.11).

These attacks destroyed the blessings enumerated in Job 1.2–3; Job was left alone with the four ominous messengers who came to report and a wife who offered misguided counsel. • The repetition of while he was still speaking emphasizes the relentlessness of the attacks (see Jer 51.31). The repetition of I am the only one who escaped to tell you emphasizes the total obliteration of Job’s resources.

The Sabeans were marauding bandit tribes from the desert (cp. Jdg 6.3). By the 700s BC, the southern Sabeans would become a national power that traded in gold, precious stones, perfume, and slaves (Psa 72.10; Isa 43.3; Isa 45.14; Isa 60.6; Jer 6.20).
The fire of God . . . from heaven (Job 20.26) might have been lightning (Lev 10.2; 1Ki 18.38; 2Ki 1.10–14), wildfire (Num 11.1–3), or volcanic activity (Gen 19.24).
That the wind . . . hit the house on all sides suggests that Job and his children were settled farmers living in houses rather than nomads living in tents.

Job tore his robe and shaved his head; both were common Near East rituals that demonstrated grief. These actions sometimes substituted for self-mutilation as a physical response to shock, horror, or bad news (Job 2.12; Gen 37.29, Gen 37.34; Jdg 11.35; Jer 16.6; Eze 7.18; Amo 8.10). • He fell to the ground, not to wail in despair, but to worship in hope (1Pe 5.6).
This scene is an exact repetition of the scene presented in Job 1.6–8.
The phrase without cause (Hebrew khinnam) is a wordplay on Satan’s question in Job 1.9.
take away his health (literally strike his flesh and bones): Bones were thought to be the seat of health.
spare (literally guard/watch over): God ironically made Satan responsible for guarding Job’s life (cp. Job 10.13–14; Job 13.27; Job 33.11).
This term for terrible boils was used for any inflamed, running sores (Exo 9.10; Lev 13.18–20; Deu 28.27, Deu 28.35).

Job might have scraped his skin to relieve itching; the Greek Old Testament says that it was “to scrape away the pus.” • The ashes might refer to a place where lepers were quarantined, but Job was probably demonstrating his grief and dismay (Job 30.19; Gen 18.27; 2Sa 13.19; Isa 58.5; Jon 3.6).

Job’s wife first summarized the essence of Job’s temptation by echoing God’s words (Job 2.3); Job was trying to maintain his integrity. In her frustration and anguish, however, she then counseled Job to curse God and thus unknowingly fulfill Satan’s prediction (Job 1.11; Job 2.5).

Job’s acceptance of bad as well as good things from God’s hand demonstrates his righteousness and faith (cp. Job 1.21; 2Sa 12.16–20; Luk 22.42). • By saying nothing wrong, Job controlled his tongue (Pro 13.3; Pro 21.23; see Jam 3.2).

It might have taken several months for Job’s friends (see study note on Job 6.14–27) to hear of his afflictions (see Job 7.3). • The text implies that Job’s friends were Edomites, a people who were famous for their wisdom (Jer 49.7; Oba 1.8). • Eliphaz the Temanite was probably a descendant of Esau’s grandson Teman (Gen 36.10–11, Gen 36.15); his land was located in Edom (Eze 25.13; Amo 1.11–12). • The Bil- element in Bildad would remind Hebrew readers of names like Bilhan, a descendant of Esau (Gen 36.27; 1Ch 1.42). The -dad element would remind them of names like Bedad, father of the Edomite king Hadad (Gen 36.35; 1Ch 1.46). • Shuhite: No place named Shuah is known, but Abraham’s son Shuah was sent to “a land in the east” (Gen 25.1, Gen 25.6; 1Ch 1.32). • The Greek Old Testament lists Zophar instead of Zepho as one of Esau’s grandsons (Gen 36.11, Gen 36.15; 1Ch 1.36). A Naamathite might reside in a town named Naamah, but no such location is known. Two Old Testament women are named Naamah, but neither is a likely ancestor of Zophar (Gen 4.22; 1Ki 14.21).

they scarcely recognized him: This expression indicates the extreme suffering Job had experienced (cp. Isa 52.14; Isa 53.3). • Job’s friends mourned by wailing loudly, just as they would have done for a dead man. • Throwing dust sometimes expressed anger or disdain (see 2Sa 16.13; Act 22.23), but here it signaled mourning (see Jos 7.6; 1Sa 4.12; Neh 9.1; Lam 2.10).

Job’s friends sat on the ground to identify with Job’s suffering (see Job 2.8). • The standard period for mourning the death of a notable person or for acknowledging other disastrous news was seven days and nights (Gen 50.10; 1Sa 31.13; see also Eze 3.14–15).
Job’s outburst did not mean that his integrity had cracked under the strain (Job 42.7–8; Jam 5.11). Elijah and Jeremiah, both godly men, used the same hyperbolic language (1Ki 19.4; Jer 20.14–18).

Job spoke and thus put at risk his refusal to sin with his mouth (Job 1.21; Job 2.10). • Job cursed the day of his birth in great detail. However, his words sound more like pitiful complaints. Job didn’t curse God as his creator, but he lamented the conditions of his existence.
Theme: Complaints
Job longed for the sinister darkness of the underworld (Exo 10.22; Pro 4.19; Joe 2.2) and the gloom of death (Job 10.21–22; Job 38.17) to claim the day of his birth.
The expression experts at cursing refers to professional cursers such as Balaam (Num 22.1–24).
Venus and Mercury, the morning stars, herald the dawn (Job 38.7).
shut my mother’s womb: Closing or opening the womb sometimes refers to conception (Gen 16.2; Gen 20.18; Gen 29.31; Gen 30.22; 1Sa 1.5–6), but here it refers to birth (see also Job 38.8).

Job’s language turns from curse to lamentation. Job alternates between repugnance for life and a romance with death. Seven times, Job laments his situation by asking why (Job 3.11, Job 3.12, Job 3.16, Job 3.20, Job 3.23; see Psa 10.1; Psa 22.1; Jer 20.18; Lam 5.20).
The dead were thought to continue their identities and social status after death. Perhaps Job wanted the world’s kings and prime ministers to acknowledge his own princely status (Job 1.3).
rich in gold, whose palaces were filled with silver: This might refer to treasure-filled tombs, but it more likely refers to the futile hoarding of wealth that ends in death (as in Job 3.14).

Job equated light with life (Job 33.30; see Joh 1.4; Joh 8.12). • Bitter might mean “short-tempered” (Jdg 18.25), “enraged” (2Sa 17.8), “anguish” (Job 7.11), “distress” (Pro 31.6), or “discontented” (1Sa 1.10; 1Sa 22.2).
People in misery long for death with the desperation of those who dig for hidden treasure.

This section begins three rounds of speeches by each of Job’s three comforters, each with a response from Job (Job 4.1–Job 27.23). In this first round, Job’s friends exhort him to seek God so that he can again enjoy prosperity.

Eliphaz the Temanite (see study note on Job 2.11) was the most prominent and probably the oldest of Job’s friends; his speeches are longer and more ornate than the others. • who could keep from speaking out? Eliphaz mimicked the urgency of a prophetic revelation (Job 4.12–16; see Jer 20.9; Amo 3.8).
People . . . who were weak were depressed and suffered from low morale (Isa 13.7; Isa 35.3; Eze 7.17).
Job probably counted his children among the innocent dead (Job 1.5), and even Eliphaz must have known that innocent blood is sometimes shed (cp. Deu 19.10; Pro 6.17; Jer 7.6).
Theme: Material Reward

The harvest metaphor illustrates the scriptural principle that behavior merits judgment (Pro 22.8; Hos 8.7; Rom 2.9–11; Gal 6.7–8). The New Testament describes the final judgment as a harvest (Mat 13.39). Jesus rejected simplistic attempts to analyze people’s lives by this principle (Luk 13.4; Joh 9.1–3).
They vanish in a blast of his anger: Eliphaz understood the wind of Job 1.19 as divine judgment (cp. Isa 40.7; Hos 13.15).
Eliphaz posed as a prophet, implying that God spoke to him in secret (Num 12.6); later God did speak to him, but not to affirm his counsel (Job 42.7).
Eliphaz probably referred to the God-induced sleep associated with prophetic vision (Job 33.15; Gen 15.12; Num 12.6; Isa 29.10).

Fear is common in God’s presence (Gen 15.12; Dan 8.17–18; Dan 10.8–10), but God tells his people not to be afraid (Gen 15.1; Gen 26.24; Isa 40.9; Isa 44.8). • Eliphaz’s bones trembled like those of a prophet with terrible news to deliver (Jer 23.9; Hab 3.16).
A spirit (or wind) swept past my face: Wind is a physical display of God’s powerful presence (Job 38.1; Nah 1.3; Act 2.2; cp. 1Ki 19.11).

As the characters in the book repeatedly acknowledge, no one is truly innocent or pure (see Job 9.2; Job 15.14; Job 25.4; Job 35.7) because all are depraved (Psa 14.3; Psa 53.3; Rom 3.10–11). Eliphaz used these terms to mean that human beings are sinful creatures and God is the sinless Creator. Job and God used them to mean that Job had faithfully carried out the duties inherent in his relationship with God. Job and Eliphaz never agreed on the meaning of these terms. Later, God said that Eliphaz had spoken inaccurately (Job 42.7).
The concept that God does not trust his own angels and that he charged his messengers with foolishness is otherwise unknown (but see Gen 6.1–4).
A tent was a common symbol for mortal life (Isa 38.12; 2Co 5.1; cp. Ecc 12.6).

The angels (literally the holy ones), probably a reference back to Job 4.18, are called “holy ones” because of their proximity to God, not because they were morally perfect (Job 15.15; Dan 4.14; Dan 8.13; Zec 14.5).
The court (literally the gate) was the site of legal and commercial deliberations in which Job had participated (Job 29.7; see Deu 21.19–21; Rut 4.1–11).

To go to God meant lodging a formal appeal with God for assistance, counsel, or vindication, sometimes by way of repentance (Amo 5.4, Amo 5.6) and possibly through a prophetic oracle (Gen 25.22; 1Sa 9.9; 1Ki 22.8). • Job wanted to present his case to God (Job 13.3, Job 13.15, Job 13.18; Job 23.3–8), and later he attempted to do so (Job 29.1–Job 31.40).
Eliphaz’s doxology praised God as the wonder-working Creator and Sustainer of the universe (Job 5.9–10) and as the righteous Judge who brings down the powerful and lifts up the poor (Job 5.11–16).
Job’s region depended upon rain rather than irrigation (see Job 36.27–28).
God traps the wise in the cleverness of their words (Pro 12.13). Paul alluded to this verse in his rejection of worldly wisdom (1Co 1.19).
the discipline of the Almighty: See Deu 8.5; Pro 3.11–12; Rev 3.19.

six disasters . . . even in the seventh: This wisdom formula reflects a sense of completeness (cp. Pro 30.15–31). • This list reflects Mosaic covenant blessings and curses (Lev 26.1–46; Deu 28.1–68). Eliphaz thought that people in right relationship with God would be free from famine (Job 5.20, Job 5.22; see Lev 26.4–5, Lev 26.10; Deu 28.4–6, Deu 28.8, Deu 28.11–12), war (i.e., death, Job 5.20) and the destruction it causes (Job 5.21, Job 5.22; see Lev 26.6–8; Deu 28.7, Deu 28.48), and slander. They will even be at peace with wild animals (Job 5.23; see Lev 26.6) and the stones of the field. This peace might indicate fertile rather than stony fields (2Ki 3.19, 2Ki 3.25; Mat 13.5), or it might symbolize wider harmony with the natural world (see Psa 91.11–12).
nothing will be missing: See Deu 28.11–12; cp. Job 1.6–19.
descendants . . . as plentiful as grass: See Gen 22.17; Lev 26.9; Deu 28.4, Deu 28.11–12.

Job’s response attacks his counselors (ch Job 6.1–30) and challenges God (ch Job 7.1–21). He excuses his passionate words by referencing the depths of his misery (Job 6.2–3; Job 7.11). Job says that Eliphaz has failed to offer comfort or sympathy as a friend, having chosen instead to haggle over stale theological precepts.

In the Old Testament, arrows are associated with supernatural peril, pestilence, and destructive ills (Job 7.20; Job 16.12–13; Deu 32.23–24, Deu 32.42; Psa 7.12–13; Psa 38.2; Psa 64.7; Psa 91.5–6; Lam 2.4; Lam 3.12–13; Eze 5.16).
the tasteless white of an egg? Job’s riddle-like complaint probably refers both to Eliphaz’s weak counsel and the detestable situation God had allowed him to endure.
At one time, both Moses and Elijah wished that God would kill them (Num 11.15; 1Ki 19.4).

Job and his friends might have been bound by a covenant of loyalty and faithfulness (Hebrew khesed; see Gen 21.23; Exo 15.13; 1Ch 16.34) that made them like brothers (Job 6.14–15), protectors (Job 6.21–23), and trusted friends (Job 6.27). If this was the case, Job was accusing his friends of violating their covenant with him.

The city of Tema in the northern Arabian desert was at the junction of roads from Damascus to Mecca and from the Persian Gulf to Aqaba (Isa 21.14; Jer 25.23). It might have been named after one of Ishmael’s descendants (Gen 25.15). It was not the same as Teman, Eliphaz’s home in Edom. • Sheba, located in southwest Arabia, was a market city for precious commodities (Psa 72.10, Psa 72.15; Isa 60.6; Jer 6.20; Eze 27.22–23; Eze 38.13).
even send an orphan into slavery: Job, the former protector of orphans (Job 31.17, Job 31.21), used a proverbial example of his counselors’ hard-heartedness toward the defenseless (see Job 17.5).
Don’t I know the difference between right and wrong? (literally Can’t my palate discern malice?): Job might have been echoing his earlier comment about a tasteless, revolting diet (Job 6.6–7).
Human life has been a struggle since the Fall (Gen 3.17; Gen 5.29; Ecc 1.2, Ecc 1.13–14; Ecc 2.11, Ecc 2.17; Rom 8.20–22).
A worker was to be paid at the end of each day (Lev 19.13; Deu 24.15), though this did not always happen (Jer 22.13; Mal 3.5; Jam 5.4).

Job’s trial might already have gone on for months. • The Hebrew term (‘amal) that runs throughout Job is translated as “misery/miserable” (Job 3.20; Job 11.16; Job 16.2; Job 20.22) or as “trouble” (Job 3.10; Job 4.8; Job 5.6, Job 5.7; Job 15.35).
Job’s reference to maggots signified mortality (Job 25.6) and the rampant corruption of Sheol (Job 17.14; Job 21.26; Job 24.20; see Isa 14.11).
Job cried out to God, complaining that life was too brief (Job 7.6–10). This complaint contrasts ironically with his earlier desire that God end it all (Job 6.9).

Those who call upon God to remember are typically seeking covenant mercy (Psa 35.6; Psa 106.4). • Job’s declaration that life is but a breath (Hebrew ruakh) meant either that he was one breath away from death or that his life was like a passing wind (Psa 39.9, Psa 39.11).
You see me now, but not for long: The Greek Old Testament omitted this verse to avoid the implication that God would be unable to see Job in Sheol (see study note on Job 7.9).

die (literally go down to Sheol): This is the first explicit mention of Sheol in Job. It is described as a place of rest from earthly pressures and distinctions (Job 3.13–19) and as a dark dwelling place (Job 10.21–22; Job 17.13) deep in the earth (Job 11.8) that is covered in dust (Job 17.16). It is the destiny of all the living (Job 30.23) from which no one can return (Job 10.21; see Gen 37.25; 2Sa 12.12).
I cannot keep from speaking: Job echoed Eliphaz’s inability to refrain from words (Job 4.2).

The sea monster (Hebrew yam) and dragon (Hebrew tannin) represent chaotic opposition to God’s orderly creation. In Canaanite mythology, Yam was the primordial sea god and Tannin was a sea monster (Jer 51.34) or a mythological deity of chaos (Psa 74.13–14). This kind of chaos is also represented in Job as Leviathan (Job 3.8; Isa 27.1) or Rahab (Job 9.13; Job 26.12; Isa 51.9). The Lord is sovereign over the sea and all that it represents (Job 26.12; Job 38.8–11; Psa 89.9–10; Jer 5.22).
Job’s sickbed dreams and visions echoed those of Eliphaz (Job 4.12–16).
for my few remaining days: Literally for my days are a vapor (Hebrew hebel); see “All Is “Vapor”” Theme Note.

that you should make so much of us: Cp. Psa 8.4–5, which treats the same thoughts positively. • examine (Hebrew paqad): In Psa 8.4, the same term means “to honor or care for”; Job used the term ironically, meaning “to be pestered” (cp. “attacked,” Isa 26.14).

Won’t you leave me alone (literally How long will you not look away from me): Job sought the opposite of the watchful care that faithful people usually seek (Num 6.25; Psa 27.9; Psa 69.17; Psa 80.3, Psa 80.7, Psa 80.19; Lam 1.9). • to swallow: This is equivalent to “a chance to catch my breath.”

watcher of all humanity: Rather than praising God for his goodness expressed in watchfulness (Deu 32.10; Psa 25.21; Pro 24.12), Job blamed God for hostile surveillance, which actually characterizes Satan’s activity (Job 1.7). • Why is from the language of lament (see study note on Job 3.11–24). • your target: See Job 6.4; Lam 3.12.

Like Eliphaz, Bildad the Shuhite (see study note on Job 2.11) believed that Job’s sufferings were God’s retribution (Job 8.3–6, Job 8.13; cp. Job 4.7–8; Job 5.2–3). This counselor revered the wisdom of the past (Job 8.8–10; cp. Job 4.7) and addressed Job with a mixture of instruction (Job 8.3–6, Job 8.8–10; cp. Job 4.12–21; Job 5.9–16) and encouragement (Job 8.5–7, Job 8.20–22; cp. Job 4.6; Job 5.19–26). His point was that Job should quit blustering. He advised Job to repent and allow God’s justice to bring about restoration (Job 8.1–7).
How long? Bildad’s question might be an ironic parody of Job’s question in Job 7.19.

According to Bildad, God does not twist justice, so the death of Job’s children proved that they had sinned against God. Bildad divided people into the blameless (Hebrew tam, Job 8.20; see Job 1.1) and the secretly wicked (Hebrew khanep, Job 8.13). He believed that they could be differentiated by watching what God did to them.
you will end with much: Bildad’s words were more true than he realized (Job 42.12; cp. Job 5.19–26).
Bildad made the case for traditional wisdom by appealing to ancient tradition and history (Deu 4.32; Jer 18.13).
born but yesterday and know nothing: Bildad suggested that Job’s generation was either born too late to be acquainted with ancient wisdom or was too young to have accumulated it.
Papyrus reeds grow as high as ten to fifteen feet.
To forget God does not mean to have a lapse of memory but to act as if God did not exist (see Psa 10.4; Psa 14.1; Zep 1.12) or cannot see (see Job 22.13–17; Psa 94.7).
In this parable, a plant with roots that grow down through a pile of stones gains stability by becoming entwined with the rocks.

Job responded to Bildad by describing God’s cosmic and judicial power. His speech sounds like a complicated legal case, with a summons and response (Job 9.3, Job 9.14–16, Job 9.19, Job 9.32), the possibility of self-incrimination (Job 9.20), an arbiter (Job 9.33–34), an accusatory question (Job 9.12), a legal sentence (Job 9.22), and a declaration of guilt (Job 9.28–30).
If someone wanted to take God to court: Job later expressed the wish to meet God in court (Job 13.3, Job 13.15, Job 13.23; Job 23.4).
When God moves the mountains and when the foundations of the earth tremble, it is a sign of his presence as lawgiver (Exo 19.18), judge (Jer 4.24), or rescuer (Psa 18.7; Isa 13.13; Isa 29.6).
The Bear (also at Job 38.32) is commonly identified as Arcturus but might also refer to the constellations of Ursa Minor or Leo. • The Pleiades is a group of seven stars (Job 38.31; Amo 5.8).

monsters of the sea (literally the helpers of Rahab): Job personified demonic powers as creatures like this mythical sea monster that represents chaos in ancient literature (Job 26.12; Psa 89.11; Isa 51.9).
with a storm: Perhaps the words translated “with a storm” (bis’arah) are a double entendre with besa‘arah (“for a hair”; i.e., “for the littlest thing”), which would parallel without cause.
Job was indeed innocent (Job 1.1, Job 1.7; Job 2.3), and he maintained this claim throughout the debate (Job 23.11–12; Job 27.5; Job 31.1–40).
The word you makes it clear that this is a prayer, although the phrase O God is not explicit in the Hebrew.
wash myself: Job spoke of cleansing himself with the strongest soap to represent ridding himself of all sin (Job 1.5; cp. Psa 26.6; Mat 27.24).

The muddy ditch (literally pit) can refer to the place of the dead (Job 17.14; Job 33.18), so it might allude to the defilement of death. • The filthy clothing of guilt contrasts with the clean clothes of acquittal (Zec 3.3–5; see Isa 61.10; Isa 64.6; Rev 19.8).
A mediator would not judge God and man but would work to bring them together (see Job 16.19–21).
Theme: The Righteous Suffer

A succession of images describes God’s role in creating Job. • You formed me with your hands . . . made me from dust: This was how a potter made a vessel (Isa 45.9; Jer 18.1–12). Although the potter has incontestable sovereignty over the clay (Isa 45.9; Jer 18.5–12; Rom 9.20–25), Job was questioning God. • back to dust: This common motif in Job represents the temporary nature of life (Job 4.19; Job 7.9–10, Job 7.21; Job 14.1–2, Job 14.10; see Gen 3.19). • You guided my conception and formed me in the womb: The Hebrew terminology (literally You poured me out like milk and curdled me like cheese) evokes graphic images of a newborn baby still covered with the creamy substance called vernix.
Earlier, Job had painted a fairly pleasant picture of Sheol (Job 3.13–19); now he describes it as a land of darkness and utter gloom (see also Job 7.9–10; Job 14.7–22).
Zophar the Naamathite (see study note on Job 2.11), the most severe of Job’s three friends, dealt only with the issue of sin.

this torrent of words: Verbosity is characteristic of fools (Pro 10.8, Job 10.14) and sinners (Pro 10.19), but Job was innocent. • mock God: Zophar viewed Job’s words about God’s justice as sinfully sarcastic (Job 10.2–7, Job 10.13–15).
My beliefs are pure: Job was not defining doctrine but defending his own integrity.
punishing you . . . less than you deserve: Zophar believed that calamity indicated divine retribution for sins (cp. Job 34.36).
No one can discover everything about the Almighty (literally find out the limits of the Almighty), who is beyond the limits of the heavens, underworld, land, and sea (Job 11.8–9).

Zophar laid out three conditions for restoration (Job 11.15): (1) prepare your heart, in an inward act that is not just a ritual; (2) lift up your hands, a symbolic gesture of prayer, appeal (Exo 9.29; Pro 1.24; Isa 1.15), or surrender; (3) leave all iniquity, not by sacrifice and remorse, but by quitting the sin (cp. Heb 11.6; Jam 4.8; Jam 5.16).
In his longest speech thus far, Job addresses not only Zophar’s remarks but the entire first round of speeches.
A switch from you (plural in Job 12.2–3) to you (singular here) probably indicates that Job is directing his comments to Zophar.

ask the animals . . . birds . . . earth . . . fish: Job believed that the reason for his misery was obvious and that even nature would understand it (Pro 6.6). Later, God directed Job’s attention to the animal kingdom to convince Job that he did not understand (Job 38.1–40).

from the hand of the LORD: This is the only place in the dialogues (chs Job 3.1–27; Job 29.1–37) that the Hebrew Yahweh (“the LORD”) is used. For Job, the dispute was not about who caused his misery but why it happened.
the mouth distinguishes between foods: See Job 6.6–7.
Wisdom belongs to the aged: Job’s friends defended this opinion (Job 8.8–10; Job 15.10; Job 32.6–9), but Job questioned it (Job 12.20).

stripped of good judgment: The NLT adds “of good judgment” for clarity. In this image, God metaphorically strips leaders of their abilities. It could also refer to being stripped of the symbols of office or to becoming naked captives (Job 12.18–19).
Theme: Counsel from Others

When God removes the royal robe of kings, he takes away the symbols of their authority (cp. Job 19.9). It could also be translated as “God loosens the bonds of kings,” referring to the bondage they have imposed on others.
The priests are figuratively stripped of status (the NLT adds “of status” for clarity) or are actually stripped of priestly robes; they might even be naked captives (Job 12.18).
pours disgrace upon princes: Cp. Psa 107.40. • disarms (literally looses the belt of): The strong are no longer girded for battle.

uncovers mysteries (literally uncovers the deeps): This phrase might allude to Zophar’s words that God’s knowledge is “deeper than the underworld” (Job 11.8). • darkness . . . deepest gloom: The Old Testament often describes God as dwelling in darkness (1Ki 8.12; 2Ch 6.1) and as manifesting himself through darkness (2Sa 22.10, 2Sa 22.12; Psa 18.9, Psa 18.11), as when he gave the law at Sinai (Deu 4.11; Deu 5.22–23) or when he comes in judgment (Zep 1.15).
Cp. Dan 2.21. • strips kings of understanding: See Job 12.18; cp. Dan 4.23, Dan 4.32–33. • He . . . leaves them wandering in a pathless wasteland like the princes in Psa 107.40 (see Job 12.21).
Perhaps foolish counsel made the kings stagger like drunkards (Job 12.17; see Isa 19.14); it resulted from “drinking” God’s wrath (Psa 75.8; Jer 25.15–27).
Job appealed to experience, as his comforters had done (Job 3.12–17; Job 5.2).
defending God with lies: False witnesses were forbidden even if speaking on God’s behalf (Exo 20.16).
Ashes are worthless (cp. Isa 44.20).
Job had contemplated finding an arbiter to remove God’s heavy hand (Job 9.33–34). Eliphaz had urged Job to accept God’s chastening (Job 5.17).

Job wanted God to summon him, and then Job would answer in his own defense; or Job would speak to God, and then God would reply to substantiate the charges against Job. Since God did not take the first option, Job initiated the second one (Job 13.23). Eventually, God did summon Job (Job 38.1–3; Job 40.1–2), and Job was unable to reply (Job 40.3–5).

God can turn away in wrath (Deu 31.18; Isa 54.8; Jer 33.5) or refuse to show friendship (Psa 30.7; Psa 69.17; Psa 102.2). • Job, perhaps playing on his own name (’iyyob), denied that he was God’s enemy (’oyeb).

In the Old Testament, dry straw is a common image for what can be blown away (“chaff,” Psa 83.13; Isa 40.24; Jer 13.24) or burned (Exo 15.7; Isa 47.14; Mal 4.1; see also “dry grass,” Isa 5.24; Isa 33.11), or for what is weak (Job 41.20–21) and trifling (Isa 41.2).
The flower is an image of life’s brevity (Psa 90.5–6; Psa 103.15–16; Isa 40.6–7). • A shadow passes swiftly (1Ch 29.15; Psa 102.11).
keep an eye on: Job lamented God’s relentless surveillance (Job 7.8, Job 7.17–20; Job 10.6, Job 10.14; Job 13.27).

do not rise again: Job himself did not have even the minimal evidence of resurrection found in the Old Testament (2Ki 13.21; Isa 26.19; Dan 12.2; cp. Job 19.25). • Job was not focusing on the end of the universe when the heavens will be no more (Psa 102.25–26; Isa 34.4; Isa 51.6; Heb 1.10–12) but on the eternity of the heavens (Psa 148.6; cp. Psa 72.5, Psa 72.7, Psa 72.17; Psa 89.29, Psa 89.37). His phrase refers to the permanency of death.
Since the grave is a permanent abode (Job 14.10–12, see Job 3.13–19; Job 7.6–10; Job 10.20–22), Job could not even fulfill his request from Job 13.20–21 by hiding temporarily in the grave.
guard my steps: Here, Job refers to God’s providential care (Job 10.12) rather than to his surveillance (Job 13.27; Job 14.3).
If sins are sealed in a pouch they do not await a time of reckoning (Deu 32.34–35; Hos 13.12)—they are hidden forever. Job was requesting acquittal.

Job no longer saw Sheol as a haven (Job 3.17–19; Job 14.13–17). The Old Testament usually depicts the dead as being without feeling (Psa 88.12; Ecc 9.5; cp. Isa 50.11; Isa 66.24); the doctrine that the dead suffer painfully is clearer in the New Testament (Luk 16.23, Luk 16.28; Rev 14.11).
In this second round of speeches, Job’s friends focus on the fate of the wicked and imply that Job’s condition shows he has sinned.

You are nothing but a windbag (literally You fill your belly with the east wind): Since the east wind was hot, it might represent heated (Exo 14.21; Hos 13.15; Jon 4.8) or violent (Job 27.21; Jer 18.17) speech.
Your own mouth condemns you: Job feared that this would happen (Job 9.20; see Mat 26.65).
When the Lord himself later issued a similar challenge, Job found it convicting (Job 38.1–11).
The book’s readers know about God’s secret council (Job 1.6–12; Job 2.1–6; see 1Ki 22.19–20; Psa 89.5–7), but Job and his company did not.
Aged, gray-haired men claim a monopoly on wisdom (Job 8.8–10; Job 12.20; see Job 12.2).
What has weakened your vision (literally Why do your eyes blink): This sentence might be a metaphor for unbelief, or it could indicate winking like a schemer or blinking in disbelief.
Can any mortal be pure? Eliphaz repeated himself (Job 4.17–19) and Job (Job 7.17; Job 14.4). • anyone born of a woman: Both “mortal” and “born of woman” imply weakness.
The heavens, traditionally associated with purity (Exo 24.10), were not absolutely pure; they had been defiled, perhaps by rebellious angels (Job 1.6–7).
before any foreigners arrived: Eliphaz’s contempt for foreign ideas is ironic because wisdom literature has a more international flavor than is characteristic of other Old Testament writings.

The wicked also suffer everything that happened to Job (see Job 1.16–19)—attacks by marauders (Job 15.21), loss of possessions (Job 15.29), crumbled houses (Job 15.28), and fire (Job 15.30, Job 15.34).

Although Eliphaz generalized the terror that the wicked experience, Job had undergone similar experiences (Job 3.25; Job 6.4; Job 9.34; Job 13.11, Job 13.21; Job 23.15; Job 27.20; Job 30.15). Bildad (Job 18.11, Job 18.14) and Zophar (Job 20.25) spoke of more terror to come. • The Sabeans and Chaldeans were examples of the destroyer (Job 1.13–17), but this could refer to any destructive agent (Job 1.18–19). Destroyers might be agents of Satan (1Co 10.10; Rev 9.11) or divine agents that punish wickedness (Exo 12.23; 2Sa 24.16; 2Ch 32.21; Act 12.23; Heb 11.28). Eliphaz meant the latter.
for fear they will be murdered (literally he is marked for the sword): The wicked might be killed by murder or by the sword of God’s wrath.

They wander around, saying, “Where can I find bread?”: Like the wicked (Job 15.20), Job either experienced hunger (see Job 15.27) or (following the Greek Old Testament) had been “appointed to be food for a vulture,” which would parallel “marked for the sword” (Job 15.22).
Job had complained earlier that God was treating him like a formidable foe (Job 7.19–21; Job 13.24).

The burning sun (literally The flame) might be the scorching sun or a flame of judgment from God (Job 15.34, see Num 16.31–35; Psa 106.17–18; Eze 20.47). • The breath of God might be a desert wind or a more direct theophany (a manifestation of God’s presence) that caused the burning of Job 15.34.
The flame of judgment (Job 15.30) will burn the unjust gain of the godless.
Job might have wanted to shake his head in mockery or in horror (2Ki 19.21; Psa 22.7; Psa 109.25; Isa 37.22; Jer 18.16; Lam 2.15; Mat 27.39).
Job’s family here means his extended household, including his servants (Job 1.15–19).

jeer and laugh at me: Job was the subject of mockery (cp. Psa 35.21; Isa 57.4; Lam 2.16; Lam 3.46). • To slap the cheek was less an act of violence (Psa 3.7; Mic 5.1) than an insult (1Ki 22.24; Isa 50.6; Lam 3.30; Mat 26.67).
took me by the neck: This might refer to a wild animal with its prey (see Job 16.9), but it is more likely a military image that signaled defeat (Gen 49.8; Psa 18.40).
pierce me: Literally pierce my kidneys. • my blood: Literally my gall. The picture is of wounds to vital organs.

Again and again he smashes against me: Job pictures himself as a fortress that God is besieging. Job saw God as a warrior (cp. Exo 15.3; Psa 24.8) who did not defend him or offer him salvation (Jer 20.11; Zep 3.17) but attacked him as though he were dangerous (Job 6.12; see Isa 42.13).

Since Job insisted on his innocence, his wearing burlap (literally I sewed on burlap) was a sign of mourning, not penitence. Perhaps it was attached to indicate that he would never remove it because he could never be consoled (Gen 37.34–35). • My pride lies in the dust (literally I have buried my horn in the dust): A horn symbolized dignity and power (1Sa 2.1; Psa 75.4–5; Psa 89.17, Psa 89.24; Psa 92.10; Psa 112.9; Psa 148.14); cutting it off inflicted degrading humiliation (Psa 75.10; Jer 48.25; Zec 1.12).

done no wrong (or done no violence; Hebrew lo’-khamas): If violence is the meaning, Job was possibly denying that he was a formidable warrior who should be attacked (Job 16.12–14; see also Isa 59.6; Jon 3.8). • Contrary to Eliphaz’s charge (Job 15.4–5) and Bildad’s assumption (Job 8.6), Job’s prayer was pure because he was innocent (Gen 20.5; Isa 59.3).
Job expected his suffering to prove fatal (Job 7.7, Job 7.21; Job 10.20–22); he pleaded with God to reveal his innocence even if he died first.
Job’s blood would cry out that he had been innocent and that he had suffered undeservedly (cp. Gen 4.10–11; Isa 26.21; Eze 24.7–8).

my witness is in heaven: Job wished for a benevolent third party who would mediate between him and God (see Job 9.32–35). Job wanted an advocate from heaven (Job 16.19; cp. Zec 3.1) who would eventually stand on the earth (Job 19.25; cp. 1Sa 24.15; Joh 14.16, Joh 14.26; Joh 15.26; Joh 16.7; 1Jo 2.1).
My spirit is crushed: This can refer to a properly contrite attitude (Psa 51.17), but more often it connotes an unbearably sad heart (Pro 18.14).

surrounded by mockers: Laments typically describe mockery as the response of the wicked to the distress of the righteous (Psa 22.7; Psa 69.10–12; Psa 89.50–52). In wisdom literature, mockery is directed against the right behavior (Pro 1.22; Pro 9.7).

defend my innocence, O God (literally please keep my pledge with yourself): A pledge (Hebrew ‘erabon) can be a deposit guaranteeing payment (Gen 38.17–20; Exo 22.26–27; Deu 24.10–14; see Pro 20.16; Pro 27.13), so this might suggest atonement. It might also be another reference to Job’s desire for an advocate to plead his case (see study note on Job Job 16.19–21).
To spit in someone’s face was even more insulting than a slap (Job 16.10) because spit made the person unclean (Num 12.14).
Some scholars view these verses as being out of place, but perhaps Job was ironically quoting his opponents’ words.
Job gave up on his comforters (Job 6.15–21; Job 13.4–5; Job 16.2–3; cp. Job 12.2) and believed he would die a hopeless death.
to the grave (Hebrew to Sheol): The realm of the dead was visualized as a house (Job 30.23; Psa 49.11; Ecc 12.5).
my father . . . mother . . . sister: This bitter parody of a family reunion in a graveyard shows how Job envisioned his impending death.
the grave (literally the bars of Sheol): Sheol—the abode of the dead—was seen as having a barred gate, allowing no escape.
How long before you stop talking? Bildad addressed Job in the plural, perhaps meaning “people like you.”
The light of the wicked will be snuffed out could be a metaphor for a life of confused darkness (Pro 4.19); more likely, it indicates an early death (Pro 13.9; Pro 24.20).
The stride that is shortened is the opposite of walking and running in the blessed life (Pro 4.12).
A series of hunting devices illustrates the biblical principle of retribution (see study note on Job 34.11).
Bildad applies the biblical principle of retribution (Job 18.8–10) to Job, as do Eliphaz (Job 15.21–23) and Zophar (Job 20.25).
death devours: Isaiah later reversed the figure and saw the Lord as swallowing up death (Isa 25.8; see 1Co 15.54).
The image of burning sulfur recalls the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19.24) and suggests the fate of all the wicked (Psa 11.6; Rev 19.20; Rev 21.8).
Being forgotten by those who come later is a familiar curse against the wicked (see Job 18.19; Psa 34.16; Psa 109.13; Pro 10.7).
This curse of childlessness (see Job 18.16; Psa 109.13; Isa 14.21–22) and Bildad’s earlier cruelty (Job 8.4) show that he regarded Job’s condition as the just reward for his wickedness (Job 1.18–19).
in the west . . . in the east: These phrases might refer to people from times past and times to come or to people from various places.
Bildad kept implying that Job had rejected God (Job 15.4, Job 15.13, Job 15.25).
The number ten did not represent a specific count but an indefinite large number (e.g., Gen 31.7; Lev 26.26; Num 14.22; Dan 1.20).

Job was convinced that justice had been delayed (Job 19.7) and that God had wronged him (Job 19.8–12). Later, Elihu (Job 34.12) and God himself (Job 40.2) disagreed. • capturing me in his net: Job might have been responding to Bildad’s accusation (Job 18.8–10).
Help! (literally Violence!): Cp. Jer 20.8; Hab 1.2–3. • no one answers: See Psa 22.2; Lam 3.8; Hab 1.2–3.
blocked my way: See Job 3.23; Job 13.27; Psa 88.8; Lam 3.7, Lam 3.9.
stripped me of my honor: See Job 12.17–19; Job 29.7–14, Job 29.20.
my own family: Job might have been referring to his tribal line, his parents, his own children, or his siblings.
Those I loved have turned against me: See Job 2.11; also Job 6.14–15, Job 6.21–23, Job 6.27; cp. Psa 41.9; Psa 55.12–14, Psa 55.20.
escaped death by the skin of my teeth: This is an idiom for a narrow escape; the Hebrew could also mean that Job was reduced to a skeleton with a toothy skull.
The hand of God had struck Job through the permission he gave to Satan (Job 1.11; Job 2.5).
persecute (literally pursue): Job complained that God had tracked him like a hunter (Job 10.16) or a warrior (Job 16.13).
Job wanted his words . . . inscribed on a monument, not in a book; Job desired a permanent record of his claim to innocence in response to Bildad’s assertion that he would be forgotten (Job 18.17).

Job’s faith in a Redeemer could find fulfillment only in Christ; the same was true of his request for an advocate (Job 9.33) and a witness in heaven (Job 16.19). The term “Redeemer” (Hebrew go’el) comes from both criminal and civil law. An individual could redeem or avenge wrongful bloodshed (Num 35.12–18) or redeem lost property, perhaps by buying back a slave or marrying the heir’s widow (Lev 25.25, Lev 25.47–49; Lev 27.11–13; Rut 3.13). The Old Testament knew the Lord as redeemer (Exo 6.6; Psa 19.14; Psa 103.4; Pro 23.10–11; Isa 43.1 [“ransomed”]; Isa 54.5); New Testament believers know the Redeemer as the Lord Jesus Christ (Eph 1.7, Eph 1.14; Heb 9.12; 1Pe 1.18). Job wanted his Redeemer to declare his innocence (see Job 1.1 and corresponding study note Job 1.1).
Theme: The Afterlife
Job had faith that he would be vindicated even if death came first.

I will see him for myself: The thought is the same as the psalmist’s in “when I awake” (Psa 17.15). For Job, this hope could only be fulfilled in seeing God at the end of time (Mat 5.8; 1Co 13.12; 1Jo 3.2; Rev 1.7) in transformed flesh (1Co 15.43–53; Phi 3.21).

Given the biblical principles against bearing false witness (Job 13.7–11; see Mat 7.1–2; Jam 4.11–12), Job warned his friends that they should fear God’s judgment. They did eventually face his judgment, but they also received mercy (Job 42.7–8).
thrown away like their own dung: Cp. 1Ki 14.9–11; 2Ki 9.36–37; Psa 83.10; Jer 8.1–2.
Because stolen riches are ill-gotten, they provide no lasting benefit (Job 20.18–21).
poisonous venom . . . cobras . . . viper: In the end, the wicked are no longer deadly to others (Mat 3.7; Rom 3.13) but only to themselves (Pro 23.29–35).
The streams of olive oil and rivers of milk and honey signify superabundant blessing (Exo 5.19; Deu 27.3; Joe 3.18).
Like the grave or death (Pro 27.20; Pro 30.15–16), the wicked are always greedy and never satisfied (Ecc 5.19; Isa 57.20–21; Hab 2.5).
The wicked cannot escape trouble (cp. Isa 24.17–18; Jer 15.2–3; Amo 5.19; Amo 9.1–2). When they try to escape one threat, they fall victim to another.

terrors of death: Although the words “of death” are not in the Hebrew, they are implied because the arrowhead glistens with blood (literally with gall), indicating a deadly hit on a vital organ (Job 6.4; Job 16.13; Psa 7.12).
Images such as deepest darkness and wildfire are often associated with God’s presence (Deu 4.11; Deu 5.22–23; Heb 12.18) and especially with his judgment (Exo 9.23–24; Exo 10.21–29).
heavens . . . will testify: Cp. Deu 4.26; Deu 30.19; Deu 31.28.

Job’s friends insisted that they were delivering God’s own message of comfort (Job 15.11), but Job found no comfort in their words (Job 16.2), so he asked for the consolation of their attentive silence (see Job 13.5).

When I think about what I am saying: Job was dismayed by his horrible task of complaining against God (Job 13.3, Job 13.15–16, Job 13.22; Job 23.1–5) and discussing his terrors (Job 6.4; Job 27.20; Job 30.15). • My body trembles: This reaction resembles that of Habakkuk (Hab 1.5; Hab 3.16), Ezekiel (Eze 3.14), and Daniel (Dan 8.27; Dan 10.8–9).

In spite of assertions by Eliphaz (Job 5.4), Bildad (Job 18.19), and Zophar (Job 20.10), Job noted that the wicked enjoy children and grandchildren, which should be the reward of the righteous (Pro 17.6) but was apparently not going to be his own reward (Job 1.18–19; but see Job 42.13–16).
light of the wicked never seems to be extinguished: Job countered Bildad (Job 18.5–6, Job 18.18) and standard wisdom (Pro 13.9; Pro 20.20; Job 24.20; see God’s remarks, Job 38.15).

you say: Job was quoting and rebutting his friends’ arguments. • God will punish their children: These were the words of Eliphaz (Job 5.4) and Zophar (Job 20.10), but Job thought God should punish the ones who sin (see Eze 18.19–20).

The rhetorical answer is that no one can teach a lesson to God (Isa 40.13–14; Isa 45.9; Rom 11.34; 1Co 2.16). • The most powerful might refer to angels or demons (1Co 6.3; 2Pe 2.4; Jud 1.6; Rev 20.1–3) or, more likely, to the powerful on earth (Job 34.17–19).
vigorous and fit (literally the marrow of his bones [is] moist): Bones were thought to be the seat of health.
in bitter poverty: Job repeatedly complained about the apparent futility of existence (Job 3.20; Job 7.11; Job 9.18; Job 10.1).
eaten by the same maggots: Cp. Job 17.14; Isa 14.11; see Job 19.26.
houses have vanished because of their sins: Job was echoing Bildad (Job 8.22), Eliphaz (Job 15.34), and Zophar (Job 20.26).
the earth gives sweet repose: Job viewed death as a relief (Job 3.17–18).
They told lies about Job (Job 13.4) and about God (Job 42.7).
In this third round of speeches, Job’s friends explicitly accuse Job of being among the wicked and sharing their fate.

Eliphaz did not understand that God would gain pleasure from Job’s righteousness (Job 1.8; Job 2.3), as he does from every righteous person (1Ch 29.17; Psa 147.10–11; Pro 11.1, Pro 11.20; Pro 12.22). God would also gain glory from Job’s steadfast faith, which emphasized the lie behind Satan’s challenge (Job 1.9–12; Job 2.4–6). • Job steadfastly claimed that he was perfect (Job 23.10–12), as did God himself (Job 1.1, Job 1.8; Job 2.3).

Demanding clothing as security for lent money was forbidden by the law and condemned by the prophets (Exo 22.26–27; Deu 24.10–13; Eze 18.7–8; Amo 2.8). In contrast, Job had provided clothing for the poor (Job 31.19–20).

The Old Testament gives Israel the responsibility of caring for widows and orphans (Deu 10.18; Deu 14.29) and repeatedly condemns their neglect as the worst of social evils (Exo 22.22–24; Deu 27.19). Job agreed that it was wicked (Job 24.3, Job 24.21) but claimed that he was innocent (Job 29.12–13; Job 31.16–18, Job 31.21).
That’s why: Job had not claimed that God can’t see, but others have (Psa 10.11; Psa 73.11; Psa 94.7).
I will have nothing to do with that kind of thinking: Eliphaz threw Job’s words back at him (Job 21.16).

The righteous will be happy to see the wicked destroyed: They will be glad to see justice done and injustices avenged (see also Psa 58.10–11; Rev 19.1–4). Eliphaz’s sentiment neglected God’s desire that sinful people repent (see Eze 33.11).

The term instructions (Hebrew torah, “law,” Deu 17.11), used in Job only here, frequently refers to the Pentateuch (Genesis—Deuteronomy). • Listen . . . store: See Deu 4.1–2; Deu 6.6–9; Psa 119.11; Pro 2.1–9. Job had done this (Job 23.12).
return to the Almighty: Bildad (Job 8.5–6) and Zophar (Job 11.13–14) had already misapplied this biblical principle (Isa 55.6–7; Hos 14.1–2; Zec 1.3; Act 26.20), and now Eliphaz also misapplies it.

precious gold (literally Ophir): Ophir was probably located in southern Arabia (see 1Ki 9.28; 1Ki 22.48). The gold of Ophir was the standard in fine gold (Isa 13.12); queens wore it at weddings (Psa 45.9).
God promises to be his people’s treasure (Psa 16.5; Isa 33.6; Mat 19.21; Mar 10.21); although they possess nothing, they will be rich (2Co 6.10; Jam 2.5).

Ironically, Job will pray, God will hear, and Eliphaz will reap the benefits (Job 42.8). • you will fulfill your vows: Vows were often stimulated by repentance and forgiveness (Hos 14.2; Jon 1.16; Jon 2.9) and when seeking divine intervention (Jdg 11.29–40; 1Sa 1.1–28). Vows are binding (Num 30.2; Deu 23.23; Psa 22.25; Psa 61.5, Psa 61.8; Psa 116.14, Psa 116.18; Ecc 5.4–5).

This difficult text probably conveys the effectiveness of a righteous man’s prayer. The principle (Psa 34.15, Psa 34.17; Psa 145.18; Pro 15.8, Job 15.29; Jam 5.16) is illustrated throughout Scripture (see, e.g., Gen 18.23–32; Gen 19.29; Gen 20.7, Gen 20.17; Gen 32.28; Exo 9.28–32; Exo 17.11; Exo 32.10–14; Rom 5.19).
Job dropped the doubt he had expressed earlier (Job 9.14–20, Job 9.32) and here expressed confidence that he could successfully present his complaint.

present my arguments: Job wanted to make his case with God (Job 13.3, Job 13.18, Job 13.22; Job 16.21; Job 31.35); Abraham pled directly with God regarding Sodom (Gen 18.25–32), and Moses did the same for Israel (Exo 32.12–13; Num 14.13–19).

Earlier, Job had believed that God was too strong for him to summon (Job 9.19), so he had requested an arbiter (Job 9.33–34) and asked God not to terrify him (Job 13.21). Here he expressed more hope that God would grant him a fair hearing. • acquitted: Job did not want to be pardoned as a guilty man but to be declared innocent (Job 13.18; see Psa 17.2–3; Psa 26.1–3).

tests me: Job did not want the kind of chastising that would cleanse him like a refiner’s fire (Pro 17.3; Zec 13.9; Mal 3.2–3). He wanted an examination that would prove that he had been as pure as gold and did not need to amend his life (Job 22.23).
No one can change God’s mind (Job 9.12–13; Job 11.10; Job 12.14; Job 34.29; Num 23.19–20; Jam 1.17).

terrified in his presence: See Psa 77.3; Psa 88.16; Psa 119.120. • Job had complained earlier of being plunged into darkness (Job 19.8); Eliphaz (Job 15.22; Job 22.1) and Bildad (Job 18.6, Job 18.18) ascribed this fate to the wicked.

bring . . . to judgment (literally set times): The times for God’s judgment are set (Ecc 3.17; Ecc 8.6; Dan 2.21; Luk 21.22–24), but they are not known to us (Act 1.7). They will be revealed at the proper moment (1Th 5.1–28; 1Ti 6.15).
This inventory of criminal behaviors focuses first on crimes against the weak (Job 24.2–12) and then on the criminals themselves (Job 24.13–17).
The law, wisdom literature, and prophecy all condemned the moving of boundary markers (Deu 19.14; Deu 27.17; Pro 22.28; Pro 23.10; see study note on Hos Hos 5.10).
The law did not allow seizing necessary belongings as security or collateral for a loan (Job 22.6–9; Deu 24.6, Deu 24.10–13, Deu 24.17–21).
