glean in the vineyards of the wicked: Job was depicting the desperate condition of the poor. If their fields had been stolen like Naboth’s vineyard (Job 24.2; see 1Ki 21.1–29), the poor would harvest for the thieving owners what should have been their own crops; instead of owning the whole crop, they would get just the leftover pickings for themselves. Perhaps the point is that the poor were forced to glean from the fields of wicked people who left no gleanings (Lev 19.10; Lev 23.22), instead of being able to glean from the righteous, who leave something for the poor (Lev 19.9–10; Lev 23.22; Rut 2.1–23).
Unjust lenders sometimes left debtors without clothing or covering, which they had seized as collateral on loans (Job 22.6; Exo 22.26–27; Deu 24.11–13; Amo 2.8).
widow’s child . . . security for a loan: See 2Ki 4.1; Neh 5.1–5; Mat 18.25.

without being allowed to taste it: These words, which are not in the original text, are implied by the parallel with starving and suffer from thirst. • To force workers to tread in the winepress as they suffer from thirst violates the principle of letting workers enjoy some of the produce they are harvesting (see Deu 25.4; cp. 2Ti 2.6).

ignores their moaning: It appeared to Job that contrary to God’s own character (Exo 2.23–24; Psa 12.5), God neither relieved the plight of the wronged (Job 24.2–12) nor hindered the wicked from harming their victims (Job 24.13–17).

These sentiments appear to oppose Job’s observations, so some scholars suggest that they were the words of Bildad or Zophar. However, Job might have been pronouncing curses on the wicked, sarcastically quoting his friends’ views, or saying that the fate of the wicked presented by Eliphaz (Job 5.2–7; Job 15.17–25), Bildad (Job 8.8–19; Job 18.5–21), and Zophar (Job 20.4–29) also overtakes the righteous (Job 21.23–26).

Eliphaz had said that it is nearly impossible to be innocent or pure (Job 4.17–19; Job 15.14–16), and then only after suffering (Job 22.21–23). Bildad claimed that only the totally blameless could hope to be pure (Job 8.20).

Job’s friends had not helped him (Job 12.2; Job 16.4). Bildad’s denial that acquittal was possible hit Job’s most sensitive nerve (Job 10.1–7; Job 13.3, Job 13.13–19; Job 16.18–21; Job 19.23–27; Job 23.2–7).
Eliphaz (Job 4.15), Zophar (Job 20.3), and Elihu (Job 32.18; Job 33.4) all claimed to be prompted by the proper spirit (see Jer 29.8–9; 1Co 12.10; 1Jo 4.1).
The underworld (Hebrew Sheol), the abode of all the dead, is located beneath the waters of the sea. • The place of destruction (Hebrew Abaddon) existed specifically for the wicked.

The Hebrew tsapon (“north,” Gen 13.14) sometimes refers to the northern mountain of the Canaanite gods (the Canaanite equivalent of Olympus); here the NLT understands it to refer to the sky, stretched out over empty space (see Gen 1.6–8; Psa 104.2–3; Isa 40.22–23).
created the horizon: See Gen 1.6–10; Psa 104.6–9; Pro 8.29.

Mountains at the edge of the horizon might be the foundations (or “pillars,” Jdg 16.25–26) of heaven or the earth (Job 9.6). They were thought to reach from below the waters of the sea (Jon 2.6) and up to the clouds to support the vaults of heaven.

the sea grew calm (cp. Exo 14.21; Mar 4.39): Or the sea was stirred up (cp. Isa 51.15; Jer 31.35). In either interpretation, God performed a miracle on behalf of his people. • crushed the great sea monster: God’s dominance over the sea demythologized popular beliefs about the sea’s divinity. See also Psa 74.13–14; Psa 89.9–10; Isa 27.1; Isa 51.9–10.

His Spirit (or wind): God’s authority clears the skies after a storm (Job 26.12). • The gliding serpent corresponds to Yam and Rahab (see study note on Job 7.12); it provides background for the image of Satan as a dragon (Isa 27.1; also Psa 74.13–14; see Gen 3.15; Rom 16.20; Rev 12.9; Rev 20.2).
Job continued speaking, no longer responding to the three friends but returning to the themes of his opening statement (Job 3.1–26).

The Bible permits a vow by the living God (Rut 3.13; 1Sa 20.21; 1Sa 25.26; 1Ki 17.1; 1Ki 18.15; Jer 4.2), although sometimes it is done foolishly or falsely (1Sa 14.39, 1Sa 14.45; Jer 5.2). • Elihu later criticized Job for saying that God had taken away his rights (Job 34.5). • embittered . . . soul (Job 7.11; Job 10.1; Job 21.25): Cp. Naomi (Rut 1.20–21) and the widow from Shunem after the loss of her son (2Ki 4.27).
Theme: Job’s Innocence
Job considered it profane and reprehensible to concede that his friends were right. Condemning the innocent, as they were doing to him, was an abomination (Exo 23.7; Pro 6.16–19; Pro 17.15).
Some interpreters see a new speech here and ascribe it to Zophar because otherwise Zophar has no speech in this cycle.

This section is a self-contained speech. No speaker is listed, so it could be a continuation of the preceding words. However, some consider this a poetic interlude by the author of Job that sums up the argument to this point, emphasizes the failure of human wisdom, and lays the foundation for the Lord’s speeches.
Miners melted rock by burning a fire in a mine for days or even weeks to melt out the ore. Some alternated fire with cold water to split the rocks.
Wisdom does not originate among the living. God is the source of true wisdom (Job 28.23–28).
The metals, gemstones, and glass listed here were precious in the ancient world, but the speaker says that wisdom is much more precious than wealth.
When God looks throughout the whole earth (Job 28.23), he sees his own wisdom expressed in his creation. God later showcased his wisdom for Job when he took him on a cosmic tour (chs Job 38.1–41).
fear of the Lord (Hebrew, ’adonay): In Job, this name for God appears only here, which might be one argument for understanding ch Job 28.1–28 as the narrator’s own poem.

Job contrasts his former happiness, honor, and wealth (ch Job 29.1–25) with his loss of social dignity and divine friendship (ch Job 30.1–31). He concludes his speech with wide-ranging oaths of innocence (ch Job 31.1–40).

Although elsewhere Job uses the Hebrew shamar to describe what he perceived as God’s oppressive surveillance (Job 10.14; Job 13.27; Job 14.16), here it refers to God’s kindly care (“watch(es) over,” Psa 121.3–8).
The city gate was a town’s administrative center (see Rut 4.1–2, Rut 4.11).
Job described his righteousness in royal terms. A robe is a common biblical image for righteousness (Psa 132.9; Isa 59.17; Isa 61.10; Rom 13.14; Rev 19.8).
Job actively searched out and assisted strangers who needed help.

after a long, good life (literally after I have counted my days like sand): Job thought the length of his years would signify God’s blessing, like the great number of Abraham’s offspring (Gen 15.5; Gen 32.12) or the abundance of Joseph’s supplies in Egypt (Gen 41.49).
In the past, Job had comforted those who mourned (Job 4.3–4). This verse is a prophetic mandate closely associated with the work of the Messiah (Isa 40.1; Isa 61.1–3; Luk 4.18–19; cp. 2Co 1.3–4).

In the past, the most honorable members of society spoke well of Job (Job 29.11); now, the least honorable mocked him (Job 30.1) and spit in his face (Job 30.10). Cp. Psa 35.15; Psa 69.12; Mar 14.65; Mar 15.17–20.

live in frightening ravines, in caves and among the rocks: The wretched life of Job’s mockers resembled Israel’s situation under Midianite oppression (Jdg 6.2), David’s life as he fled from Saul (1Sa 22.1–2), and Elijah’s life as he awaited the Lord’s instruction (1Ki 17.3–8).
They taunt me! See also Job 17.6; cp. Psa 69.12; Lam 3.14, Lam 3.63.
won’t come near me: See also Job 19.13–15; cp. Psa 88.8; Pro 19.7; Mat 26.56. • To spit in someone’s face was to display revulsion or contempt (Deu 25.9; Isa 50.6; Mat 26.67; Mat 27.30; Mar 14.65).

The series of images presented here is drawn from a military advance against a fortified city. Job had already used this image for God’s attack on him (Job 19.10–12). • The word translated traps might refer to siege ramps raised against a city’s walls.
terror: See also Job 6.4; Job 7.14; cp. Psa 88.15.

God grabs . . . the collar of my coat: The Hebrew in this verse is difficult to translate; it could mean that Job feels like he is in a chokehold and is about to be thrown into the mud (cp. Job 30.19).
dust and ashes: Earlier, Job was sitting “among the ashes” in anguish (Job 2.8); later, he would “sit in dust and ashes to show . . . repentance” (Job 42.6).
you don’t answer: This was Job’s frequent complaint (Job 9.16; Job 19.7; Job 23.2–9; Job 31.35), which God soon answered (Job 38.1).
Job felt tossed into the whirlwind and blown about like worthless straw or chaff (Job 9.17; Job 21.18; Job 27.21; Psa 1.4; Isa 17.13).
Before his testing began, Job had been respected in the public square (Job 29.7–10, Job 29.21–25); he helped others who were in need (Job 29.11–17).

I am considered: Job might have been expressing what he thought of himself, how others viewed him, or both. • By claiming that he was a brother to jackals and a companion to owls, Job might have been describing himself as in the throes of lament (Mic 1.8). Jackals were associated with desolation or ruin (see Psa 63.10; Isa 13.22; Isa 34.13; Isa 35.7; Jer 9.11; Jer 10.22; Jer 49.33; Jer 51.37; Lam 5.18; Eze 13.4; Mal 1.3).
The skin of a person who lived in comfortable circumstances was protected from the sun and wind; dark skin indicated physical and social decline (Lam 4.8; Lam 5.10).

Job called down curses on himself if he were guilty of the accusations made against him. Except for his mention of idolatry (Job 31.26–27), Job addressed his fidelity to God in terms of the second half of the Ten Commandments, summarized by the command to “love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev 19.18; Rom 13.9).

Job’s covenant with his eyes included a self-cursing oath (cp. Mat 5.28–29). Perhaps lust of the eyes was at the head of Job’s list because the eye is the first instrument of sin (Gen 3.6). • To look with lust at a young woman violates the spirit of the seventh (Deu 5.18, see Mat 5.27–28), and potentially the tenth (Deu 5.21), commandment.

If Job had lied to anyone as part of a business deal, it would violate the eighth commandment (Deu 5.19); if it occurred in court, it would violate the ninth (Deu 5.20). This sin would merit fiery judgment (Rev 21.8). • If Job lusted for what his eyes had seen, he would violate the tenth commandment (Deu 5.21). • then let someone else eat: This was a self-curse.

Whether she seduced him or he waited for her (Job 24.15–16), if Job lusted for his neighbor’s wife he would break the seventh (Deu 5.18, Mat 5.27–28) and tenth (Deu 5.21) commandments. • serve: Literally grind for. This might refer to servitude (Exo 11.5) or to sexual intercourse.
The Hebrew term zimmah (shameful sin) is associated with sexual crimes such as incest (“wicked act,” Lev 18.17), gang-rape (“terrible . . . crime,” Jdg 20.6), and prostitution (Eze 23.49).
The association of fire with hell or the grave is rare in the Old Testament (cp. Deu 32.22).

unfair to . . . servants: This might refer to violations of the fourth commandment (Deu 5.12–15). • God created both me and my servants: Job extended the implications of being created in God’s image to the poor (Pro 14.31; Pro 22.2) and even to slaves.
knowing the judges would take my side: Job was respected and regarded as a member of the elite class (Job 29.7–10).
If an arm was used in sinful action (Job 31.21), having it torn from its socket would be a fitting punishment and better than facing God’s judgment (cp. Mat 5.28–30).

Have I put my trust in . . . my gold: Job left the consequence of this oath unstated because the if-then pattern was now established (Job 31.5–23). He rejected Eliphaz’s implied judgment (Job 22.24–25; see Psa 52.7; Psa 62.10; 1Ti 6.10, 1Ti 6.17).
gloated about my wealth: See Deu 8.17–18; cp. Isa 10.12–14; Dan 4.28–30; Hos 12.8.
Like adultery (cp. Job 31.1, Job 31.9–12), worshiping the sun and moon was a capital crime. Both were sins of the eye that enticed the heart, and both types of sin were tried before judges.
Have I looked at the sun . . . or the moon: This oath denies violation (cp. Jer 8.2; Jer 44.17; Eze 8.16; Act 7.43) of the first commandment (Deu 5.7; see Deu 4.19; Deu 17.2–7).
secretly enticed in my heart: See Job 31.9. • throw kisses at them in worship: Cp. 1Ki 19.18; Hos 13.2.
In Israel, the judges (see Job 31.11) were to punish idol worship by execution (Deu 17.2–7). • Denying the God of heaven violated the first commandment (Deu 5.7).

rejoiced when disaster struck my enemies: See Pro 24.17–18; cp. 2Sa 16.5–8. • Cursing anyone violated the spirit of the sixth commandment (Deu 5.17; see Mat 5.21–22). • It was against God’s will to ask for revenge (Mat 5.43–44; Rom 12.14; Jam 3.6–10; 1Pe 3.9).
never turned away a stranger: The Old Testament values hospitality (Gen 18.1–13; Gen 19.2–3; Jdg 19.20–21), and the New Testament commands it (Mat 25.35; Rom 12.13; 1Ti 3.2; Heb 13.2; 1Pe 4.9).
sign my name: Job wanted to make the proceedings official (Job 19.23–24).
face the accusation proudly (literally carry it on my shoulder; cp. Exo 28.12; Isa 22.22): He would take full responsibility for his actions.
A prince who had been wrongly accused had the right to come before his king to make an appeal.
The land was the chief witness to crimes committed upon it (Job 20.27; see Gen 4.10; cp. Jam 5.4).
let thistles grow: Job’s curse on himself echoed God’s primal curse on Adam (Gen 3.17–18; cp. Isa 7.25; Zep 2.9).

Having completed three cycles of speeches between Job and his three friends, we now hear from a new voice. Elihu has not been previously introduced, but he is a young man who has listened to everything the others have said.
Job’s three friends (see Job 2.11) failed to comfort him (Job 6.14–30; Job 13.4; Job 16.2; Job 19.21; Job 42.10).

the Buzite: Buz had connections with Aram (Gen 22.21) and Arabia (Jer 25.23), as did Uz (Job 1.1). • Elihu repeatedly stated that he was angry; he probably regarded his anger as righteous zeal (Psa 69.9).
Elihu’s deference to elders followed a well-known principle (see also Job 12.12; Job 15.10; Lev 19.32; 1Ti 5.1; 1Pe 5.5).

The spirit within people might not be the prophetic Spirit that Elihu later appeals to (Job 33.14–15), as Eliphaz had done (Job 4.12–17; cp. Job 32.18–20). This spirit might simply exist by virtue of creation (Job 33.4; Gen 2.7; Act 17.25).

As translated, the phrase you sit there . . . you are silent is addressed to Job’s friends. An alternate translation is they sit there . . . they are silent, in which case Elihu is speaking to Job about his friends.

The length of Elihu’s speech (Job 32.1–Job 37.24) demonstrates that he truly was full of pent-up words. • Elihu probably thought the spirit (Hebrew ruakh) within him was prophetic urgency (Job 32.8, Job 32.19–20; Psa 39.3), but the reader might find him full of wind (Hebrew ruakh; see study note on Job Job 15.2–3). • Like Zophar, Elihu must speak to find relief (cp. Job 20.2).
Listen: Elihu begged to be heard (Job 33.1; Job 34.2, Job 34.16), which is what Job had also sought (Job 13.6).
By inviting Job to make his case, Elihu acted as though he were God, or at least the arbiter that Job had been seeking (Job 9.32–35).

you don’t need to be afraid of me (literally my terror shall not make you afraid): God’s terrors (Job 6.4; Job 7.14; Job 9.34; Job 13.21; Job 23.15) had been thrown in Job’s face by Eliphaz (Job 15.21, Job 15.24; Job 22.10), Bildad (Job 18.11, Job 18.14), and Zophar (Job 20.25). • Elihu promised not to come down hard on Job, but later he broke his word (Job 34.7–9, Job 34.33–37).
You said: Job claimed to be pure and without sin, using various terms (Job 9.21; Job 10.6–7; Job 11.4; Job 13.23–24; Job 15.14–16; Job 16.17; Job 31.1–40).
Job frequently complained about God’s surveillance (Job 7.20; Job 10.14; Job 13.27); he wanted relief from having his every move scrutinized (Job 14.16; Job 29.2).
Job’s central complaint was that God does not respond (Job 9.16; Job 19.7; Job 23.2–7).
He speaks in dreams: See, e.g., Gen 15.12; Gen 20.3; Gen 31.24; Gen 40.1–Job 41.36; Dan 2.1–45; Joe 2.28; Act 16.9–10.
from crossing over the river of death: This phrase may also be translated from passing [i.e., dying] by the sword. Both translations fit the context (cp. Job 36.12).
angels of death wait for them: Cp. Exo 12.23; 2Sa 24.16; 1Co 10.10.
An angel from heaven would intercede, taking the role of the mediator Job longed for (see Job 5.1; Job 9.33–34; Job 16.18–21).
The ransom is ultimately found in Christ (Mat 20.28; Rom 3.24–25; 1Ti 2.6; 1Pe 1.18–19).
God will receive him with joy: Cp. Num 6.24–26; Psa 67.1; Act 2.28; Jud 1.24.
For Elihu to say that he was anxious to see Job justified sounds ironic; he had entered the discussion in the first place “because Job refused to admit that he had sinned” (Job 32.1–5).
ear tests . . . mouth distinguishes: Elihu echoed Job’s earlier complaint about the other counselors’ weak argument that “wisdom belongs to the aged” (Job 12.11–12; see Job 6.30; Heb 5.14).
Job had claimed to be innocent: See Job 9.20–21; Job 13.18; Job 27.6.

Eliphaz had accused Job of being a liar (Job 15.5), fulfilling Job’s earlier worry (Job 6.28–29). • My suffering (literally My arrow): For the link with the Lord’s arrows, see Job 6.4; Job 16.13; Jer 10.19; Jer 15.18; Jer 30.12, Jer 30.15; Lam 3.12; Mic 1.9; Nah 3.19.

Elihu later repeated this accusation (Job 35.3; cp. Psa 73.13; Zep 1.12; Mal 3.14), but he misrepresented Job’s words (Job 9.22–23; Job 21.15). Job had actually condemned those who held this view (Job 21.14–16).

The passage attaches three ideas to the truth that God can do no wrong (Job 34.10, Job 34.12): (1) God pays back all people according to their behavior (Job 34.11); (2) as the Creator, God is not answerable to anyone (Job 34.13); and (3) every living being depends upon God for its existence, and God can withdraw that gift without doing anything wrong (Job 34.14–15; cp. Rom 9.19–29).

according to their deeds: Cp. Psa 62.12; Pro 24.12; Jer 32.19; Eze 33.20; Mat 16.27; Rom 2.6; Gal 6.7–8; 1Pe 1.17. The ultimate harvest will take place at the end of time (2Co 5.10; Rev 2.23; Rev 22.12).

The implied answer was that God could not govern if he hated justice (cp. Rom 3.4–7; Rom 7.7, Rom 7.13; Rom 9.14; Gal 2.17; Gal 6.14). • Later, God also asked if Job was going to condemn the almighty judge (Job 40.8).
doesn’t care how great a person may be: Impartiality flows from God’s justice (Act 10.34; Rom 2.11; Gal 2.6; Eph 6.9; Col 3.25; 1Pe 1.17).
The wicked might try to hide in darkness (Jer 23.24), but they will fail (Psa 139.11–12; cp. Amo 9.2–3). God brings everything to light (1Co 4.5).
We don’t set the time: Elihu rejected Job’s wish for a quick (Job 21.19), published time of judgment (Job 24.1).
God knows everything without asking anyone (Job 34.25). • sets up others in their place: Dan 2.21; Dan 5.28–30.
When God renders justice openly, it leads to proper fear among the wicked (Deu 21.21; 1Ti 5.20) and to public rejoicing among the righteous (cp. Exo 14.30–31).
Why don’t people say? Elihu was indirectly asking, “Job, why won’t you admit it?”
deserve the maximum penalty: Zophar had also said that Job was being punished less than he deserved (Job 11.6).

Elihu attempted to answer his own question (Job 35.2), but his answer did not add to what Zophar (Job 11.8–9), Eliphaz (Job 22.12), Bildad (Job 25.5–6), and Job (Job 9.8–10) had already said. Elihu failed to recognize that all sin wrongs God (Gen 39.9; Mat 25.41–46; cp. Pro 19.17).
Elihu echoed and then rejected Job’s words (Job 9.24; Job 12.6–10; Job 21.7–15, Job 21.17).
Elihu echoed his earlier accusation (Job 34.35); later, God would agree (Job 38.2).
I am a man of great knowledge (literally one who is perfect in knowledge is with you): Elihu was probably claiming to be completely sincere or saying that his logic was flawless.
The biblical principle that God never takes his eyes off the innocent (2Ch 16.9; Psa 33.18; Psa 34.15; 1Pe 3.12) answered Job’s frustration about divine surveillance (Job 7.17–21).
If they listen and obey God, they will be blessed: This is a valid biblical principle of repentance (see Job 11.13–19; Job 22.21–25; Deu 4.30; Jer 7.23; Jer 26.13).
dying from lack of understanding: See also Job 4.21; Pro 5.23; Pro 10.21.

The Hebrew yadin can mean he governs or he nourishes, which parallels food in abundance (Job 38.26; Psa 65.9–13; Psa 104.13–15, Psa 104.27–28). The more common meaning for yadin is “judge,” which would mean that God does all things to bless his people and judge his enemies (Job 37.11–13; Job 38.22–23; see Gen 6.17; Gen 19.24; Exo 9.23–25; Jos 10.11–14; 1Sa 12.18).
The Old Testament often associates thunder with God’s voice (Job 36.29, Job 36.33; Job 37.5; Job 38.1; Exo 19.16–19; Psa 104.7).
everyone stops working . . . watch his power: The ending of the agricultural work season gave people time to meditate on God’s providential control.
The same act by God can serve more than one function, such as storms that both destroy enemies and give God’s people victory (Jos 10.1–43; Jdg 4.1–24; 1Sa 7.10–11; Psa 18.7–15; Psa 105.32–33).
The hot south wind caused the sweltering conditions.
speak when they are confused? Or speak without being swallowed up? Punishment as severe as death might result from contesting God’s judgment (cp. Job 13.14).

the mountain of God (Hebrew from Zaphon): In the literature of the ancient city of Ugarit, Zaphon was the northern mountainous abode of Baal; here it figuratively refers to God’s lofty home in the heavens (see Isa 14.13–14).
cannot imagine the power of the Almighty: Cp. Job 11.7; Job 26.14; Rom 11.33; 1Ti 6.16. • he is just and righteous: Cp. Job 9.4, Job 9.19; Job 12.13; Psa 62.11; Psa 66.3; Psa 93.1; Psa 99.4.
Finally, the LORD answered Job. In this final section, the Lord challenges Job’s overreaching self-defense with a display of his works that remind Job of God’s transcendent greatness.

God challenges Job, who acknowledges his inability to judge the moral world by demonstrating his ignorance of the natural world’s cosmic (Job 38.4–21) and meteorological elements (Job 38.22–38), animals, and birds (Job 38.39–Job 39.30).

God challenged Job from out of the whirlwind. The Old Testament commonly associates storms with God’s presence (2Ki 2.1, 2Ki 2.11; Eze 1.4; Nah 1.3). Job finally had an audience with God (Job 13.22–23).
Theme: Understanding Job
questions my wisdom: God’s accusation sounds like a charge made by Eliphaz (Job 15.2) and Elihu (Job 34.35; Job 35.16) to which Job eventually admitted guilt (Job 42.3).
The morning stars are personified in parallel construction with the angels (Job 1.6; Job 2.1).
locked it behind barred gates: The sea is depicted as a dangerous creature kept under control.
it is robed in brilliant colors: The rising sun brings out the colors, shapes, and textures of things.
you were born before it was all created: Cp. Pro 8.25. This sarcasm resembles that of Eliphaz (Job 15.7).

Snow and hail are kept in divine storehouses such as those for the deep seas and winds (Psa 33.7; Psa 135.7; Jer 10.13; Jer 51.16). God uses these elements as weapons (Job 36.32; Isa 30.30; Eze 13.11–13; Rev 16.21) in the storms he sends on the day of battle and war (e.g., Jos 10.11; Jdg 5.20–21; 1Sa 7.10).

The east wind blows off the desert to scorch crops (Gen 41.6, Gen 41.23, Gen 41.27; Jer 4.11; Jon 4.8) and dry up seas (Exo 14.21; Isa 11.15). It is an arid contrast to the torrents of rain that cause flooding. • Beneficial rain to satisfy the parched ground (Psa 104.10–11; Psa 107.35; Isa 35.7; Isa 58.11) stands in contrast to both scorching winds (Job 38.24) and flooding rains (Job 38.25).

heart . . . mind: These words can also be translated ibis . . . rooster. The Egyptians thought the ibis was wise about the flooding of the Nile, the most important seasonal event in Egypt; and Israel’s rabbis thought the rooster could forecast rain or that its crow distinguished day from night. The idea would then be Who taught the ibis and the rooster? See also Psa 51.6; Pro 2.6; Jam 1.5, Jam 1.17.

wild donkey . . . hates (literally scorns) the noise of the city: This is the first in a series of animals that scorn others who are their inferiors in some way (cp. Job 39.18, Job 39.22; Job 41.29). These images illustrate how God scorns the opposition of a man like Job (see Psa 2.4).

Now extinct and already rare by Moses’ time, the wild ox was the most powerful land animal in early Canaan. This Old Testament symbol of strength (Num 23.22; Num 24.8; Deu 33.17; Psa 29.6; Psa 92.10) was never tamed (cp. Gen 1.28; Gen 9.2; Psa 8.5–6).
In the ancient Near East, the ostrich had a reputation as a bird that God had deprived of wisdom.

The ostrich is a symbol of neglect for her young (Lam 4.3) because she (1) lays her eggs on top of the earth; (2) appears to leave her eggs to die when a predator approaches them (although she is probably attempting to lure the predator away from the nest); and (3) lays her eggs with several other hens in one nest, so most of the eggs are not her own.
passes (literally scorns) the swiftest horse with its rider: See Job 39.7, Job 39.22; Job 41.29.
The ram’s horn was sounded in combat to call for the charge (Jos 6.4–6).
Where there’s a carcass, there you’ll find it—feeding on the remains (Eze 39.17–19; Mat 24.28; Luk 17.37).
The Greek Old Testament omits this conclusion to God’s first speech.

The Book of Psalms

Purpose

To offer praise and prayer to God, to supply God’s people with texts for worship, and to provide reflection on the sovereignty of God and some of life’s toughest questions

Author

Various; nearly half are linked with David

Date

Written over the course of many centuries; the process of collecting and editing was likely completed after the Babylonian exile

Setting

Varied, but a postexilic setting accounts for much of the editorial activity and grouping of the psalms

Jesus and the apostles loved the book of Psalms—they quoted from it and lived out of it. These ancient prayers and praises of Israel provide a bridge between the Old Testament and the New Testament; the themes introduced in the psalms find further development in the New Testament. Where David’s dynasty failed, Jesus gives hope. Yet, certain expectations that emerge in the book of Psalms still remain for the future, namely that God’s people will completely fulfill his purposes and that all nations will submit to the Messiah.

Summary

The psalms, like all Scripture, are inspired and given by God (see 2Ti 3.16). Yet each psalm originated with a human author as a prayer or praise to the Lord. The psalms are diverse: The Psalter includes laments, praise psalms, wisdom, thanksgiving, reflections on God’s actions, celebrations of God’s revelation, and worship.

The first two psalms serve as an introduction to the entire Psalter (the book of Psalms). Psa 1.1–6 describes a godly person who delights in God, lives by divine instruction, and is not influenced by evildoers. Psa 1.1–6 points to three questions: (1) Is there forgiveness for sins? (2) Why do the godly suffer? and (3) Why do the wicked prosper? The rest of the Psalter meditates on these questions.

Psa 2.1–12 speaks of how the nations and the wicked are in rebellion against God’s rule. God judges the rebellious and protects the godly. Psa 2.1–12 suggests two questions: (1) Why do the rebellious nations and the wicked prosper? and (2) Why were the kings of David’s line not victorious?

The psalmists largely wrestle with these questions. Some quietly accept their problems, while others question God or become exasperated. Meanwhile, new questions and issues develop out of their dialogues with God.

The Composition of the Psalms

For a thousand years, poets wrote these poems while people recited and collected them. The Temple liturgy encouraged both the writing and the collection of psalms. Gradually, editors incorporated smaller collections into larger collections, shaping five collections into the one book of Psalms. The process of editing the Psalter into one book took place over time and was completed following the exile to Babylon. There are several markers of this editorial activity:

1. The editors placed Psa 1.1–6 and Psa 2.1–12 as an introduction to the whole book of Psalms. Both psalms give idealized portraits: Psa 1.1–6 portrays the ideal godly person who lives by God’s instruction. Psa 2.1–12 portrays the Messiah, the ideal king of Israel. The rest of the Psalter develops and deepens these portraits, while at the same time exploring how neither the people of God nor their king were able to fulfill God’s ideals and bring about the happiness and peace of God’s kingdom.

2. Individual psalms were collected in groups. The editors arranged these groupings of psalms into five collections: Book One (Psa 1.1–41, with a doxology in Psa 41.13), Book Two (Psa 42.1–72, with a doxology in Psa 72.19), Book Three (Psa 73.1–89, with a doxology in Psa 89.52), Book Four (Psa 90.1–106, with a doxology in Psa 106.48), and Book Five (Psa 107.1–150, without a doxology).

3. Books One (Psa 1.1–41) and Two (Psa 42.1–72) form the first stage of the collection. The shift from David in Book One (Psa 3.1–32; Psa 34.1–41) to collections of psalms by various authors in Book Two (the descendants of Korah, Psa 42.1–49; Asaph, Psa 50.1–23; David, Psa 51.1–65; Psa 68.1–70; Solomon, Psa 72.1–20) reveals a thematic transition from David as the sole model and teacher to other perspectives. At the end of Book Two, the editor comments, “This ends the prayers of David son of Jesse” (Psa 72.20). This comment remained in place even when Books Three, Four, and Five (with additional psalms of David) were added to the collection.

4. Book Three (Psa 73.1–89) shares with Book Two its preference of the name Elohim for God (Psa 42.1–83) and its diversity of authors (Asaph, Psa 73.1–83; the descendants of Korah, Psa 84.1–85; Psa 87.1–88; David, Psa 86.1–17). Psa 73.1–28, which opens Book Three, questions God’s justice and power, thus calling into doubt the magnificent vision of the messianic kingdom outlined in the final psalm of Book Two (Psa 72.1–20). This questioning returns in Psa 89.1–52, at the close of Book Three.

5. The psalms of Book Four (Psa 90.1–106) wrestle with questions raised at the time of the Exile, when it seemed that God’s covenant with David had been dissolved (see Psa 89.1–52). In response to this crisis, several psalms encourage individual growth in character and godliness (see Psa 91.1–92). Most psalms in this collection present God as the true and faithful king whose kingdom extends to every part of creation (Psa 93.1–100). He still loves his people, the flock of his pasture (Psa 100.1–5), but they have to listen to him (Psa 95.1–11; Psa 100.1–5). God is the source of forgiveness, and his compassion assures his exiled people that he still cares for them. The review of redemption history from creation to the Exile (Psa 104.1–106) underscores both God’s wisdom and Israel’s folly as a framework for understanding the Exile.

6. The benediction of Psa 106.48 is also included in 1Ch 16.36 and might indicate that Book Four was completed in the postexilic era (when Chronicles was compiled).

7. Book Five (Psa 107.1–150) includes a number of smaller collections: the Egyptian Hallel (Psa 113.1–118); the Torah Psalm (Psa 119.1–176); the Great Hallel (Psa 120.1–136), which includes the Songs of Ascents (Psa 120.1–134); eight psalms of David (Psa 138.1–145); and five concluding hymns of praise (Psa 146.1–150). Book Five sets out the thematic progression of affliction, lament, God’s rescue, and praise. The opening psalm (Psa 107.1–43) begins this pattern, and its final verse (Psa 107.43) points to the importance of wisdom in discerning God’s ways. Psa 119.1–176, the longest psalm, celebrates the wisdom of God and the word of God. The psalms recounting the Lord’s historic care for Israel in the wilderness (Psa 114.1–118; Psa 135.1–136) prepare exilic and postexilic Israel to read David’s final prayers (Psa 138.1–145) in a new light: David looked forward to God’s kingdom (Psa 145.1–21). The psalms of praise affirm this hope (Psa 146.1–150).

8. Additions appear to have been made to already-existing psalms. This may explain the prayer for the restoration of Zion (Psa 51.18–19) and for God’s blessing on Jerusalem (Psa 69.34–36). Changes in circumstances may have occasioned the addition of new stanzas.

9. The available manuscripts reveal some flexibility in the organization and titles of the psalms. Both the Hebrew and Greek editions of the Psalter contain 150 psalms, but with differing divisions and numbering as well as differences regarding which psalms have titles. The Greek text combines both Psa 9.1–20 and Psa 10.1–18 and Psa 114.1–8 and Psa 115.1–18 into one psalm each, but it splits both Psa 116.1–19 and Psa 147.1–20 into two. Differences between the Hebrew and English numbering are indicated in the notes.

By the time of Jesus, the collected Psalter was well known (see Luk 20.42; Act 1.20). It was part of the third section of the Hebrew canon, called the Writings (see Luk 24.44).

Authorship

Many of the psalms are associated with David, but not all; in fact, less than half are explicitly connected with him. Others are connected with Asaph (Psa 50.1–23; Psa 73.1–83), the descendants of Korah (Psa 42.1–49; Psa 84.1–85; Psa 87.1–7), Solomon (Psa 72.1–20; Psa 127.1–5), Heman (Psa 88.1–18), Ethan (Psa 89.1–52), and Moses (Psa 90.1–17).

Of the 116 psalms with a title, most identify a person who is linked to that psalm. The person named may be the author, but not necessarily. The Hebrew preposition le before the name (often translated “of”) can also mean “for,” “dedicated to,” “concerning,” “to,” or “by.” So, ledawid (often translated “of David”) could be interpreted as “for David,” “dedicated to David,” “concerning David,” or “by David.” While many psalms “of David” may have been written by him, there are several reasons for caution. The titles occasionally have two names, such as David and Jeduthun or Asaph (Psa 39.1–13, Psa 62.1–12, Psa 77.1–20). It is possible that the other individual was the actual author of the psalm. Furthermore, the psalms whose titles connect them with an episode of David’s life (Psa 3.1–8, Psa 7.1–17, Psa 18.1–50, Psa 34.1–22, Psa 51.1–19, Psa 52.1–9, Psa 54.1–7, Psa 56.1–13, Psa 57.1–11, Psa 59.1–17, Psa 60.1–12, Psa 63.1–11, Psa 142.1–7) provide little or no specific connection with those episodes. For example, the title in Psa 51.1–19 connects the psalm with David’s sin and Nathan’s rebuke. The psalm speaks of sin, forgiveness, and a broken spirit, but any specifics of the situation are notoriously absent. In addition, several psalms “of David” seem to assume the existence of the Temple, which was not constructed until after David’s death (see Psa 5.7; Psa 122.1; Psa 138.2). Similarly, the title of Psa 30.1–12 connects David with the dedication of the Temple, and Psa 69.1–36 does not seem to fit with what is known of David’s life. Finally, some textual traditions vary in the mention of David in the heading (e.g., Psa 122.1–9, Psa 124.1–8). It is possible, therefore, that ledawid should be understood in many cases as meaning “for/dedicated to/concerning David” rather than “by David.” Such psalms evoke his persona as the chief representative of the dynasty without implying that he himself was the author. Still, there are many psalms that could have been authored by David.

Literary Issues

The title Psalms comes from the Greek word psalmos (“song”; see Luk 20.42; Luk 24.44), which translates the Hebrew mizmor, a word frequently found in the titles of individual psalms (e.g., see Psa 3.1, translated “psalm”). The word mizmor is related to a verb meaning “to play a stringed instrument.” The psalms were originally accompanied by instruments and were part of the oral tradition of Israel before they were collected. The Hebrew title of the Psalter is tehillim (“praises”), a word that is related to hallelujah (“praise Yahweh”).

Psalm Titles. The psalm titles, or short superscriptions accompanying most of the psalms, give information such as the author, the type of psalm (e.g., song, prayer), a musical notation, the use of the psalm, a historical context, or a dedication. Much of the information is not well understood, so many scholars do not emphasize the psalm titles in the interpretation of the psalms.

In Hebrew editions, the psalm titles are typically numbered as verse 1. As a result, the verse numbers for many entire psalms differ by one from most English translations.

Interlude (Hebrew Selah). This word is found throughout the book of Psalms. The meaning of the word is uncertain, though it is probably a musical or literary term. In the NLT it is consistently rendered Interlude.

Groupings of the Psalms. The psalms can be grouped in a number of ways:

• By the names they use for God: Yahweh (“the LORD,” Psa 1.1–41) and Elohim (“God,” Psa 42.1–72).

• By the names in the titles: David (Psa 3.1–32; Psa 34.1–Psa 41.13, etc.), the descendants of Korah (Psa 42.1–49; Psa 84.1–Psa 85.13; Psa 87.1–Psa 88.18), and Asaph (Psa 50.1–23, Psa 73.1–83).

• By genre (see below).

• By the collections of which they are already a part: e.g., the Songs of Ascents (Psa 120.1–134). Other collections were recognized in Jewish tradition, such as the Egyptian Hallel (Psa 113.1–118) and the hallelujah hymns (Psa 146.1–150).

• By thematic connections: e.g., God’s kingship (Psa 93.1–100), or the storyline from creation to the Exile (Psa 104.1–106).

Genres of the Psalms. The psalm titles often designate the genre of a psalm. The most frequent genre designation in the titles is the Hebrew term mizmor, referring to a song originally accompanied by stringed instruments. Less frequent are the words maskil (meaning “psalm” or “chant”: Psa 32.1–11; Psa 42.1–11; Psa 44.1–45; Psa 52.1–55; Psa 74.1–23; Psa 88.1–89), miktam (“psalm” or “chant”: Psa 16.1–11; Psa 56.1–60), shir (“song”: Psa 45.1–17; Psa 120.1–135), shiggayon (“psalm,” a generic or musical term: Psa 7.1–17), tepillah (“prayer”: Psa 17.1–15; Psa 86.1–17; Psa 90.1–17), tehillah (“psalm of praise”: Psa 145.1–21), higgayon (“meditation,” meaning unknown: Psa 9.16), and todah (“psalm of thanksgiving”: Psa 100.1–5).

In addition to the genre identifications that are found in the Hebrew text, the psalms may be divided into three main categories:

1. Wisdom or instructional psalms (Psa 1.1–6, Psa 15.1–5, Psa 24.1–10, Psa 33.1–22, Psa 34.1–22, Psa 37.1–40, Psa 73.1–28, Psa 90.1–17, Psa 107.1–43)

2. Psalms of lament (most psalms in books 1—3), which can be subdivided into individual laments and community laments

3. Hymns of praise or thanksgiving (Psa 8.1–9, Psa 19.1–14, Psa 29.1–11, Psa 65.1–13, Psa 67.1–7, Psa 114.1–8), which can similarly be divided into individual and community hymns

The psalms of praise include several subgenres, including “royal” psalms about the king (Psa 2.1–12, Psa 45.1–17, Psa 72.1–20, Psa 89.1–52, Psa 110.1–7); psalms ascribing kingship to the Lord (Psa 93.1–5, Psa 95.1–99); hymns about creation (Psa 19.1–14, Psa 29.1–11, Psa 104.1–35); and hymns about Zion (Psa 46.1–11, Psa 48.1–14, Psa 84.1–12, Psa 87.1–7).

Another way of reading the psalms is based on the movement in many psalms from instruction to a problem and from a problem to a renewal in commitment and character. The Psalter as a collection of five books is largely instructional in nature. It is “instruction” (torah; see Psa 1.2) and has the purpose of teaching God’s people how to live.

The Psalms in Israel’s Worship

The book of Psalms contains much information on music making in ancient Israel. The majority of psalms are songs of praise, thanksgiving, prayer, and repentance. Some of the psalms were used on specific occasions, such as at Passover (Psa 113.1–118, or when journeying to Jerusalem for the annual festivals (Psa 120.1–134. There are also historic odes that relate great national events (for example, Psa 30.1–12, “a song for the dedication of the Temple,” and Psa 137.1–9, which portrays the sufferings of the Jews in captivity). Such psalms played a role in the life of the community; however, the exact nature of that role is uncertain.

Meaning and Message

The psalms provide windows into the souls of the ancient saints who wrote them. Their theological reflections are not easy or simple-minded, but the psalmists’ faith, when tried, is purified.

The psalms model depth of character, wisdom, honesty, and authenticity. But the prayers in the Psalter are more than models to be imitated. They are God’s instructions for righteous living, part of his torah (“instruction”; see Psa 1.1–6; Psa 19.1–14; Psa 119.1–176). God teaches who he is, what he has done, and what he expects from his people. The psalms are God-centered, instructing his people to discern error in themselves, to receive his correction, and to be like him. They also encourage God’s people to worship him vibrantly and to bear witness about him to the world.

The psalmists reflected on the transitory nature of life, on suffering, and on the many kinds of adversity that human beings experience. As the psalmists faced alienation and pain, they longed for God’s presence, provision, and protection (e.g., Psa 23.1–6), and for a lasting glory. Even the psalms connected with David often reveal a humble rather than a victorious David—humiliated rather than glorious. The psalmists experienced alienation and shame, and they longed for redemption, trusting in the Lord to vindicate them.

The Psalter illustrates the failures of Israel and of David’s dynasty. The best of the godly Israelites and kings were unable to bring the happiness and peace that Psa 1.1–6 and Psa 2.1–11 speak of (see also Psa 72.1–20). The psalms are thus God’s exhortation to each person to cultivate wisdom, to trust in him, to live by grace, and to have hope in the one who can bring blessings to a needy world.

The psalms prepare God’s people for the coming of Jesus Christ as the perfect human and ideal king, the descendant of David who has absolute integrity. Jesus and the apostles understood Jesus’ life and ministry in light of the psalms (see Mat 13.34–35; Mat 21.16, Mat 21.42; Mat 23.39; Joh 2.17; Joh 15.25; Joh 19.24, Joh 19.28, Joh 19.36; Act 2.22–35; Act 4.11; Act 13.32–38; Rom 15.3; 1Co 15.25–27; Eph 4.7–10; 1Pe 2.7). Jesus entered the world of humans and lived out the patterns found in the psalms, including humiliation, suffering, death, vindication, and glory. He is the only human being who has completely pleased God (Psa 1.1–6). He is the Messiah and King (Psa 2.1–12) who has become our means of redemption, happiness, and peace.

Psa 1.1–6 and Psa 8.1–9 form an inclusio (set of literary bookends) that describes what God expects of the ideal person (cp. Psa 19.1–14; Psa 33.1–22; Psa 104.1–35; Psa 145.1–21), contrasts the godly person with the wicked, and extols the godly person’s dignity. Jesus the Messiah (Psa 2.1–12)—the sovereign Lord (Heb 2.6–8; see 1Co 15.27) and perfection of humanity—embodies this ideal.

The first two psalms are an introduction to the entire Psalter. Psa 1.1–6 introduces the Lord’s instruction in wisdom, while Psa 2.1–12 introduces God’s rule over a rebellious, sinful world. Together, these psalms invite people to leave the way of folly that leads to destruction and to enter the way of God that leads to wisdom and salvation. The New Testament affirms that God will rule the nations through Jesus Christ, his appointed agent (Heb 1.5; Rev 12.5; Rev 19.15).

This wisdom psalm sets the tone for the whole Psalter. The psalmist strongly contrasts the happiness of the godly with the condemnation of the wicked; in the end, the way of wisdom will triumph. This idealization of the godly person (as in Psa 8.1–9) highlights the Lord’s expectations of his people and especially of the coming Messiah (Psa 2.1–12). The people of Israel did not live up to this ideal, and neither did the kings of David’s dynasty. Not even the best of them could bring in the triumph of righteousness described in Psa 1.1–6, Psa 2.1–12, Psa 72.1–20. In the New Testament, the apostles’ use of the Psalter to describe the life and ministry of Jesus the Messiah confirms that Jesus alone fulfills the ideal of the godly person presented in the psalms. Only Jesus could please God and secure redemption, happiness, and peace. Psa 1.1–6 introduces the hopeful anticipation of the final hallelujah (Psa 150.1–6), when the Lord will remove all evil from his creation and prosper his children.
The Lord gives true happiness to all who reject evil and delight in him.

The law (Hebrew torah) of the LORD is the full revelation of God’s instructions (see study note on Deut Deu 4.44). • Meditating is a process of inner reflection that can be positive (Psa 1.2; Psa 63.6; Psa 77.12; Psa 143.5) or negative (see Psa 2.1; Psa 38.12). The Lord’s word is the object of godly meditation (Psa 119.48). • Day and night includes all times, whether one is walking, standing, sitting, or sleeping (see Deu 6.7).
The future belongs to the godly.
Well-watered trees endure and bear abundant fruit (cp. Jer 17.8).
The coming time of judgment (Psa 1.5) will carry off the wicked and their deeds (Psa 35.5; Psa 83.13; Isa 17.13; see study note on Jer Jer 13.24).
The wicked cannot abide the scrutiny of the Lord’s judgment; they are already condemned (see Psa 5.5; Psa 7.6; Psa 101.7).

The Lord’s care for the righteous and the demise of the wicked both demonstrate the Lord’s principle of retribution (see Gal 6.7–10). The brief and futile lives of the wicked will end, whereas the Lord and his saints will triumph (see Psa 9.5, Psa 9.6, Psa 9.18; Psa 10.16; Psa 37.20; Psa 73.27; Psa 92.9; cp. Psa 142.4; Isa 57.1). • The godly (see Psa 5.12; Psa 14.5) are joyful (Psa 1.1) because the LORD protects and cares for them, hears them when they cry out for justice, and secures their future (see Psa 121.3–4). • A person’s path is their life and character.

This royal psalm pertains to the Lord’s appointment of a king descended from David. It celebrates the mission of all the kings in David’s line, and it introduces the hope of an ideal ruler who will accomplish the Lord’s goal of bringing all nations into submission (Psa 2.11) or to destruction (Psa 2.9). The New Testament identifies Jesus as this descendant (see Act 13.33; 1Co 15.25–27; Heb 1.5; Heb 5.5; Rev 19.15).
Their futile paths lead to death (Psa 1.4, Psa 1.6), but fallen human beings unite in opposing the true God and his Messiah.
plans: The Hebrew verb rendered “meditate” in Psa 1.2 here suggests an attitude of opposing the Lord in speech (Isa 59.13) or in thought (Psa 38.12; Pro 24.2).
Theme: Royal Psalms

The kings hate the Lord’s established order in the world, so they desire to be independent of him (see Psa 36.4). They scheme about dominating the Lord’s people (Psa 31.13; see Psa 83.1–4). Their goal is to subvert the Lord’s rule in the world by overthrowing his anointed one (or his messiah); the Lord chose the kings of David’s dynasty to establish his kingdom throughout the earth. The New Testament confirms that Jesus, the appointed and anointed Son of God (Act 4.26; Act 13.33; Heb 1.5; Heb 5.5), fulfills the role in which these earlier kings failed.
break their chains: These kings believe that acknowledging the true God and his chosen ruler will result in their enslavement (Isa 28.22; Isa 52.2; cp. Lam 3.7; Rom 1.1; 1Co 7.22; Tit 1.1).

The Lord finds the human threat insignificant. He provided a solution long before their rebellion. He will end their agitation through the appointment of a human agent, a descendant of David’s line who will rule the nations.
rules in heaven: The Lord’s place in the universe is so certain that he scoffs at humans who boast that they can rebel against his power and authority (see Psa 37.13; Psa 59.8).
Theme: God’s Anger
my chosen king: The Lord establishes his anointed ruler.
The Lord adopted the king of David’s dynasty to conquer rebellious nations by force (see Psa 89.26–27).

Today I have become your Father: People in the ancient Near East commonly accepted a father-son relationship between gods and kings. In Israel, the Lord adopted kings as his sons. God set David apart as his most excellent and exalted son (Psa 89.27). All descendants of David were the Lord’s representatives or agents. As an eternal member of the Godhead (Joh 1.1) and a descendant of David (Act 13.33; Heb 1.5; Heb 5.5), Jesus is the true Son of God.

In an example of the suzerain-vassal relationship between the Lord and Israel’s king (see Deuteronomy Book Introduction, “Literary Form”), the Lord invites the king to ask for favors (see Psa 21.2, Psa 21.4). • All nations will be subject to David’s descendant, the Messiah.
The Lord gives his anointed ruler the power to conquer the nations as his inheritance (Isa 11.4; Rev 2.27; Rev 12.5; Rev 19.15), breaking their rebellion, resistance, and independence.
It pleases the Lord when his people submit to him and seek his protection. The wise accept the Lord’s rebuke and desire to repent.

rejoice: Rulers must welcome the Son as their true and only King. • Submit to God’s royal son (or Submit to God’s royal Son, or kiss the son): Kissing was an expression of submission (Hos 13.2). • The Lord gives joy to all who fear him (Psa 1.1–2) and trust him (Psa 18.30; Psa 34.22; Psa 119.1–3).

This group of psalms moves readers from the orderly world of Psa 1.1–2 to a disoriented one. The Lord’s anointed cries out while facing enemies, ferocious opposition, evil schemes, and the Lord’s apparent distance.

This psalm laments that the expectations raised by Psa 1.1–2 have not been met. But even when beset by enemies, godly people need not question the Lord’s just dealings. Rather, they can confidently trust his goodness and expect God to rescue them.

Psa 3.1 This sad episode in David’s life (see 2Sa 15.1–18) helps readers keep the promises of Psa 2.1–12 in perspective. The Lord granted victory to his anointed king (Psa 2.1–12), but the manner and timing of this victory remained in God’s hands.

The psalmist’s many enemies speak brashly (Psa 4.6; Psa 12.4; Psa 40.15) and question the Lord’s ability to rescue (Psa 10.11; Psa 22.7–8; Psa 71.10). Their words haunt him because it seems that the Lord will not answer his prayer. • These enemies wield great power (cp. Psa 2.1–3); unlike Psa 2.1–12, this psalm does not resolve the crisis.
The psalmist’s eyes turn from his enemies to the Lord.
The psalmist contrasts the contention of his enemies (Psa 3.2) with the Lord’s provision. The Lord is a shield for his people; he turns their defeat and shame into victory and glory.

By refocusing on the Lord (Psa 3.3–4) in the midst of his crisis, the psalmist can rest, confident of his safety (see study note on Psa 4.8). The Lord cares for his servant; he protects him and keeps his mind and heart from fear (Psa 37.17; Psa 54.4; Psa 119.116; Psa 145.14).

The psalmist’s peaceful confidence in the Lord’s protection and care shields him from evil and gives him a new sense of reality (Psa 23.4; Psa 27.1, Psa 27.3; Psa 46.1; Psa 56.4, Psa 56.11; Psa 91.5–6; Psa 118.6).
The psalmist does not seek revenge; instead, he waits for the Lord’s vengeance. • Arise: The psalmist calls upon the Lord to take action now.
Theme: Prayers for Vengeance
This individual lament includes a prayer for rescue (Psa 4.1), a rebuke of the adversary (Psa 4.2–3), an exhortation to the godly (Psa 4.4–5), and an expression of confidence (Psa 4.6–8).
Waiting for the Lord’s answer allows for growth in patience and for the refinement of living faith (Psa 38.15).
The opponents of the godly place their hope in delusions, treachery, and idolatry. • my reputation (or my glory): The honor of the psalmist, or possibly of the Lord, is at stake.

Angry feelings are not sinful, but letting anger control you leads to sin (see Psa 37.7–8; cp. Eph 4.26–27, Eph 4.31–32). • Instead of acting on their emotions, the godly think about their circumstances overnight. They might be disturbed as they sleep, but silence opens their hearts to trust in the Lord (Psa 4.5).
Offer sacrifices in the right spirit: Redirecting emotions toward the Lord prevents a godly individual from doing too much self-reflection (Psa 40.6–8; Psa 51.17).

your face (or the light of your face): The psalmist seeks God’s favor and peace (Num 6.25–26), which can transform darkness into light (see Psa 27.1). Confident trust in the Lord is an antidote to anger, resentment, jealousy, and materialism.
Peace comes from God’s blessing and protection (Psa 4.6; see Psa 37.11).

This morning prayer (Psa 5.3) expresses unwavering confidence in the Lord’s help and protection. The psalmist asks for and awaits God’s response (Psa 5.1–3). He describes the schemes of the wicked in detail but does not get lost in his circumstances. The psalmist also knows that the wicked cannot coexist with God (Psa 5.4–6, Psa 5.9; see Psa 1.5). He keeps returning to the Lord (Psa 5.7–8, Psa 5.10; see Psa 5.1–3), and then he prays for the godly community (Psa 5.10–12; see Psa 3.8).

The request hear me appears in several prayers as a call for God’s attention during a time of trouble (Psa 39.12; Psa 84.8; Psa 143.1), as does pay attention (Psa 17.1; Psa 54.2; Psa 130.2). The needy ask their God, “Are you listening?”

The psalmist begins and ends each day with prayer, awaiting new expressions of God’s fidelity and goodness (Psa 143.8). • wait expectantly: The psalmist does not demand God’s grace but places hope in it (see Mic 7.7; Hab 2.1).

the proud: Mockers (see study note on Psa 1.1), the wicked (Psa 73.3; Psa 75.4), and the arrogant (Psa 10.2) use their mouths to twist truth and challenge the faith of the godly. • The Lord allows only the godly into his presence (see Psa 1.5). His holiness and justice do not tolerate oppression or those who do evil. • you hate: The Lord rejects proud sinners (see also Psa 11.5).

God promises his unfailing love—his covenant goodness and faithfulness—to his people (see Psa 25.6; Psa 69.16; Lam 3.32). • your house: The godly long to come into God’s presence with reverence and awe (see Heb 12.28).

God guides those who are obedient, submissive, and patient in waiting for him to lead, provide, and protect them (Psa 27.11; Psa 43.3; Psa 143.10), not those who expect God simply to endorse their own decisions. • Following the right path of wisdom leads to the Lord (Psa 27.11; Psa 61.2; Psa 139.24).
The psalmist again describes the vile acts of the wicked, who cannot stand in God’s presence.

The psalmist prays for the justice and retribution that God promised against the wicked (Psa 1.6)—those who have rebelled against the Lord. • The wicked lay traps to kill (Psa 38.12) or deceive (Psa 140.4–5).

A blessing rests on all who take refuge in God (see Psa 18.30). • Joy and praise make good companions. The godly rejoice when they see evidence of God’s rescue. They sing joyful praises as a new song (see Psa 33.3). When the Lord restores peace to this world, puts down evil, and rewards the righteous, they will have lasting joy (Psa 9.2–4; Psa 53.6; Psa 90.14–15; Psa 118.24). • The children of God, who find refuge in him, love his name. To love his name is to love his very character.
The psalmist extends his concern beyond himself to all the godly. • A shield, here an image of God’s protection, deflects spears and arrows from its bearer.
The occasion for this lament might have been sickness or a mental or spiritual depression from which the psalmist sought healing.
The psalmist asks for God’s favor and restoration at a difficult time.
don’t rebuke me . . . or discipline me: The psalmist does not explicitly connect God’s discipline with sin here (cp. Psa 39.8–11), but it might be implied.

In his longing for God’s response to his prayer, the psalmist grew physically weak (Psa 6.6; see Psa 77.3; Psa 119.81; Psa 142.1–3; see also Psa 101.1–8). Fasting might have played a part in his agony, but this is not mentioned.
The experience was so painful that the psalmist might as well have been dead, or perhaps he feared for his life.
from the grave? Hebrew from Sheol? In the Old Testament, Sheol is the abode of the dead. It is not necessarily associated with punishment.

The psalmist is exhausted to the depths of his being from the anguish of his spiritual distance from the Lord (Psa 22.1; Psa 31.9–10; Psa 102.5). • When eyes dim, the body is failing (see Psa 13.3; Psa 31.9; Psa 38.10; Mat 6.22).
In a closing note of triumph, the psalmist reasserts his confidence in the Lord.

This psalm consists of a lament (Psa 7.1–2), an oath of innocence (Psa 7.3–5), an appeal to God’s justice (Psa 7.6–9), an affirmation of God’s just kingship (Psa 7.10–16), and a concluding hymn of praise (Psa 7.17).
Psa 7.1 Cush, an unknown person of the tribe of Benjamin, remained hostile to David.
Persecutors (a common term for “enemies”) intentionally seek out people in order to destroy them (Psa 31.15; Psa 56.1–2; Psa 71.11; Psa 143.3).
Like a lion, a wicked enemy relentlessly and violently pursues its prey (Psa 10.9; Psa 17.12; Psa 22.13, Psa 22.21; Psa 35.17; Psa 57.4), but God promises victory (Psa 91.13).
The psalmist swears to his innocence, making himself vulnerable to scrutiny (Psa 7.9.
The psalmist does not claim to be without sin, but he knows that he does not deserve the brutal attacks of his opponents (see Psa 35.7).
trample: Cp. Psa 44.5; Psa 60.12; Psa 91.13; Psa 108.13. • into the ground . . . in the dust: Disgrace and shame can lead to death and the grave (Psa 143.3; see Psa 13.3–4).
With this appeal to God for justice in the world, the psalmist also submits to God’s examination.
God’s judgment brings justice, despite the chaos created by adversaries (see Psa 7.11).

The judgment is against the defendants (the nations) and in favor of the righteous plaintiff (the psalmist; see Psa 43.1). • Although not innocent of all sin, the psalmist is a person of authentic integrity (see Psa 15.2; Psa 25.21; Psa 41.12; Psa 78.72; cp. Job 1.1, Job 1.8; Job 9.20, Job 9.22).
God examines the mind and heart of each person (see Psa 11.3–4; Psa 26.2; Psa 139.1, Psa 139.23).

The psalmist moves from his own situation (Psa 7.1–9) to speak for all the godly who long for redemption (Psa 7.10–16). He depicts God as the righteous King who vindicates his subjects when they cry out for rescue.
The honest Lord cannot be bought or bribed, nor does he abuse his power (Psa 9.4; cp. Psa 82.1–8).
sword . . . bow . . . deadly weapons . . . flaming arrows: As the Divine Warrior, God goes on the offensive on behalf of himself and his people.
Evil begins with small words or steps, and gives birth to increasingly worse deeds as time goes on (see Isa 59.4–5).

I will thank . . . sing praise: The laments in Psa 3.1–7 usually move from lament to praise, as does the Psalter as a whole. • Most High: This is an ancient designation for God (see Gen 14.19). • God is just and reliable, so his order prevails in this world.

Psa 8.1–9 opens the second segment of Book One (Psa 8.1–14). The psalmist celebrates God’s creation and the dignity of the ideal human being (see Psa 1.1–6). Instead of the world of enemies, wicked people, and distorted justice that is presented in Psa 3.1–7, this psalm promotes an image of the world as God originally created it. A weary person can envision a place of dignity in God’s world.

The LORD (Hebrew Yahweh), the covenant God of Israel (Exo 3.15), also holds the title of Lord (Hebrew ’adonay), the king of the earth. • The word translated majestic (sometimes translated “mighty”) can describe kings (Psa 136.18), heroes (Psa 16.3), mountains (Psa 76.4), or waves breaking on the seashore (Psa 93.4). While all are awe-inspiring and mighty, the created order pales in comparison with the Lord. • A person’s name embodies their reputation. • The earth and the heavens reveal the Lord’s splendor. All creation worships and praises the Lord (Psa 66.4; Psa 113.3; Psa 145.21).

silencing: The loud noise of the oppressors contrasts with the praise of God. In the end, the praise of God will overwhelm the sound of evil (Psa 31.18; Psa 63.11; Psa 101.5; Psa 143.12). • Those who oppose God seethe with vindictive anger (Psa 2.1–3; Psa 44.16; cp. Psa 149.6–7).
In light of God’s awesome glory, it might seem that people would be insignificant to him. However, he has crowned them with glory and honor and placed them over all creation.

The nations around Israel worshiped heavenly objects as deities. The sun, moon, and stars are indeed immense and glorious, but they are merely the work of your fingers, a reason to praise the Almighty.

human beings (literally son of Adam): The Hebrew idiom son of man (or son of Adam) means a human being. Through the influence of Dan 7.13–14, it became a title with divine overtones in the New Testament. See Heb 2.6–8, where this passage is quoted.

Yet you made them only a little lower than God: Humans bear God’s image; the Lord has endowed humans with dignity and charged them to rule (Gen 1.26–27). Heb 2.6–8 applies these words to Jesus Christ, the ideal human who fully realized God’s purposes.

gave them charge of everything: The psalmist is still referring to humans in general. Paul applies these words to Jesus as the perfect man who has made the created order—even death (1Co 15.25–27)—subject to God and his glory. The New Testament connects these themes of creation and salvation with Jesus Christ (Joh 1.1–2, Joh 1.14; Col 1.16).

Wild animals, including birds and fish, remind readers of God’s creation of the animal world in Gen 1.1–31. Contrary to beliefs among Israel’s neighbors in the ancient Near East, animals are not sacred.

This hymn celebrates the Lord’s kingship and victory over evil. It might also serve as a response to the laments of Psa 3.1–7. Some believe that Psa 9.1–20 and Psa 10.1–18 should be read together as one psalm in two parts because Psa 9.1–20 includes a title and Psa 10.1–18 does not, and although several letters are missing or inverted, the two psalms connect as an acrostic of the Hebrew alphabet (other such alphabetic acrostics are Psa 25.1–22, Psa 34.1–22, Psa 37.1–40, Psa 111.1–112, Psa 119.1–176, Psa 145.1–21). The ancient Greek and Latin translations treat 9 and 10 as one.

Psa 9.1 This psalm was originally sung to the tune “Death of the Son,” but that tune is no longer known. So also with the tunes mentioned in Psa 22.1–31, Psa 45.1–17, Psa 56.1–60, Psa 69.1–36, Psa 75.1–10, Psa 80.1–19.

The verb translated praise is translated “thank” in Psa 7.17, suggesting a close connection between Psa 7.1–17 and Psa 9.1–20 (see Psa 7.17; Psa 8.1–2). With all my heart expresses the psalmist’s deep devotion and commitment (Psa 86.12; Psa 111.1; Psa 119.10; Psa 138.1). • I will tell: These stories educate the next generation (Psa 78.4; Psa 145.4); when they are not remembered, a generation might easily depart from the Lord (Psa 78.11, Psa 78.32). • The marvelous things include the Lord’s judgments on the enemies of his people (Psa 9.4) and his care for the oppressed (Psa 9.9). The wonders in creation, in redemption, and in revelation reveal his character and show his power (Psa 89.5; Psa 111.4; Psa 119.18, Psa 119.27). His powerful manifestations evoke public praise (Psa 9.1; Psa 26.7; Psa 75.1).
Theme: Praise Psalms
filled with joy . . . sing praises: The psalmist often connects joy with praises, as one leads to the other (Psa 5.11–12; Psa 32.11; Psa 67.4; Psa 90.14; Psa 92.4).
The psalmist celebrates God’s judgment of the wicked, which is a testimony to the Lord’s reliable promise to establish his kingdom on earth (Psa 1.6; Psa 2.1–12).
retreated . . . staggered: The Lord overpowers even powerful enemies (see Psa 27.2). Israel also experienced judgment when it resisted the Lord (Psa 107.12).
The throne represents the Lord’s royal authority.

God created the heavens and the earth with a word (Gen 1.1–31), and he can bring nations to an end with a word (see Psa 2.5). Evil and those who do evil will come to an absolute end (Psa 69.28; Psa 109.13; Rev 21.4).
The godly do not put their hope in corruptible human government but in God’s everlasting rule of justice and fairness (see Psa 96.1–100).

The Lord provides shelter in dangerous circumstances and refuge from powerful and oppressive people. The Psalter includes many similar images of the Lord, such as fortress (Psa 18.2; Psa 31.2), rock (Psa 18.2; Psa 42.9), strength (Psa 18.1), and strong tower (Psa 144.2). These images occur frequently in the royal prayers (see Psa 9.9; Psa 18.30). • Even oppressed, afflicted, and marginalized people (Psa 10.17; Psa 74.21) can enjoy divine protection. • The times of trouble (Psa 10.1; Psa 20.1) stand in contrast with appointed times when the Lord openly bestows his favor upon the afflicted (Psa 69.13; Psa 102.13; see Psa 107.6).

Alienation from the Lord might be part of an individual’s experience (Psa 22.1; Psa 42.9; Psa 119.8), yet the psalms affirm that the Lord will not abandon his people (Psa 16.10; Psa 37.25, Psa 37.28).

Recognition that the Lord’s judgment falls on some of the wicked (Psa 9.3–6) and that God promises to judge all evil (Psa 9.7–10) motivates praise. The psalmist calls on the godly community to join him.

The psalm writers often connect the idea that God reigns (or sits, or is enthroned) with a place, such as heaven (Psa 2.4; see Psa 47.9), Jerusalem, “between the cherubim” (Psa 80.1; Psa 99.1), “on high” (Psa 113.5), or “at my right hand” (Psa 110.1). Since the Lord rules the world, all people must know of his unforgettable deeds of salvation (see Psa 9.1; Psa 64.9; Psa 66.16; Psa 105.1).

The Lord avenges and saves his servants (Psa 18.46) by righteously judging his enemies on earth (Psa 58.11). The godly do not seek revenge; they wait for the Lord to vindicate them (Psa 94.1–2; Deu 32.35; Rom 12.19).

The psalmist returns from a vision of the glorious future to the reality of facing his enemies (Psa 9.3). • The jaws (literally gates) are a vivid image of the powerful grip of death (see Psa 13.3–4). • Jerusalem’s gates provide an intentional contrast to the “gates” of death.
Hope requires waiting for the Lord’s rescue or justice (Psa 25.3, Psa 25.5, Psa 25.21). The godly find hope, rest, and quietness as they await the Lord (see Psa 1.6; Psa 27.14).

The psalmist ends his lament with a prayer for the Lord’s intervention and divine vengeance. • mere mortals . . . merely human: Humans who have received authority and glory sometimes become oppressive and assume glory for themselves (see Psa 8.4; Psa 10.18).

The lament of Psa 9.13–20 continues in Psa 10.1–18 (see study note on Psa 9–10 Psa 9.1–Psa 10.18), but the mood changes from confident assertion to anguished questioning. The psalmist prays for rescue, believing that the Lord, as a just king, takes care of the needy.
The opening questions set the mood. The Lord does not seem to hear the prayers of his people (Psa 22.1, Psa 22.19; see 2Ki 4.27; Isa 1.15).
Theme: The Poor and Needy in the Psalms
Wicked and oppressive people might prosper, leaving ugly consequences. Evil can be as dramatic as the psalmist portrays it here, or it could be more subtle.

The wicked brazenly defy God with their acts and speech (Psa 17.10; Psa 31.18; Psa 59.12; Psa 73.8; Psa 123.4). Although the Lord will deal with them (Psa 31.23), they disturb the righteous (see Psa 5.4–6) prior to their condemnation and judgment.
Unlike those who have evil desires, the godly wait for justice (Psa 10.17).
God is dead: See Psa 10.11; Psa 14.1.
Despite their evil ways (Psa 5.9; Psa 28.3; Rom 3.14), the wicked expect a future free of trouble such as the righteous will enjoy.
The wicked rely on outright violence (Psa 11.5; Psa 37.32) and deception (Pro 12.6; Pro 23.27–28).
With confidence that the wicked will be held responsible for their deeds and that the Lord will care for the helpless, the psalmist prays intensely for rescue from evil.
Because the Lord cares for the afflicted, he will take note and punish evildoers (see Psa 72.14; Psa 116.15).
The psalmist strongly invokes a curse as he prays (see “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note). • Arms represent an ability to wage war (Psa 18.34; Psa 44.3).
As the true and just king, God will bring the wicked to an end, as he promises (Psa 1.6).
The psalmist expresses his confidence in the Lord.
Mere people misuse their power and enslave the very people God wants them to serve (see Psa 9.19–20; Luk 22.25–26).

The psalmist affirms his faith in the righteous God. Even though the world appears hopelessly chaotic, both the godly and the wicked can count on God’s justice. The godly can depend on him as a refuge and shelter.
God provides protection (or refuge; see Psa 5.11; Psa 9.9; Psa 25.20) when the foundations of justice collapse. • The mountains provide another place of refuge (see Psa 121.1).
In the inevitable battle between the evil and the godly, the wicked cannot tolerate the righteous, so they victimize them. This seems to leave the godly with nothing but questions.
The wicked live in the shadows and create gloom for the godly (Psa 82.5; Psa 139.11; Psa 143.3; Pro 4.19).
The wicked create a world of darkness (see Psa 82.5).
The righteous King rules from heaven, where his throne is untouched by human corruption (see Psa 2.4). He examines everyone and sees everything that happens on earth (see Psa 14.2–3).
hates: See Psa 5.4–6; Pro 6.16–18. • Wicked deeds result in destruction and violence (Psa 58.2; Psa 73.6; Psa 74.20).
God rained blazing coals and burning sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19.1–38) as symbols of judgment (Psa 18.8; Psa 120.4; Psa 140.10).
The godly are assured of the Lord’s favorable presence when they see his face (see Psa 23.6).
This community lament seeks the Lord’s help against the prevalence of evil. Because of the Lord’s answer, the godly can face the future knowing that God protects them.
Evil becomes so pervasive that the godly pray for rescue (Isa 57.1; Mic 7.2; cp. Psa 1.6; Psa 37.20; Psa 58.7; Psa 104.35).
The words they say reveal the character of the wicked. They deceive and overpower the godly and arrogantly question the Lord’s purposes.
The godly can rely on the LORD’s promises, but not on the lies of the wicked (Psa 12.2–4). • Seven times means totally or completely.
The godly know that the Lord cares, even though the wicked continue to oppress them. The Lord sees the corrupt and foolish people who praise evildoers (see Psa 9.19–20; Psa 14.2–6).
The psalmist’s piercing cry for help becomes a confident song of hope.
How long? The fourfold repetition expresses agitation and deep anguish (Psa 79.5).

A sense of anguish and sorrow closes off any perspective of hope (Psa 6.3). Unless the Lord answers the psalmist’s prayers (Psa 22.1), death seems inescapable, torturous, and slow (Psa 6.6; Psa 32.3; Psa 55.4; Psa 61.2; Psa 102.5; Psa 116.3). The psalmist hardly knows how to pray; he longs for God’s redemption (Psa 25.17–18; Psa 31.10; Psa 38.8; Psa 39.2).
Only the Lord can bring enlightenment and relief. The psalmist longs for the Lord’s vindication so that his foes will not rejoice.
The psalmist’s affliction feels like death (Psa 22.15; Psa 55.4; Psa 88.15; Psa 94.17; Psa 116.3).
The psalmist no longer hears the ridicule of his foes. Instead, because of his trust in the Lord, he is full of joy.

This wisdom psalm contains some characteristics of lament and prophetic speech. The ideals of Psa 8.1–9 have run aground on the reality of foolish human attitudes and sinful actions. With the exception of vv Psa 5.1–6, this psalm parallels Psa 53.1–6.
Paul uses phrases from the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the depravity of all people (Rom 3.10–12).

Also known as fools, the wicked speak to themselves, think, scheme (Psa 10.4, Psa 10.6, Psa 10.11), and make claims; however, because they do not heed God’s revelation, they possess no understanding (Psa 14.1; Psa 39.8; Psa 53.1; Psa 74.18, Psa 74.22).

From heaven (Psa 33.13; Psa 80.14; Psa 102.19), the Lord sees the wicked, who stand out as vile sinners (Psa 11.3–5). The entire human race lacks wisdom and fails to live up to the glory originally given to them (Psa 10.4–11; see Rom 1.1–3).
The evil live at the expense of others (Psa 27.2; Psa 44.11; Psa 53.4; see Isa 5.8) and have no reverence or knowledge of God (Psa 79.6).
Though the wicked perish (Psa 1.5–6), God is with the godly.
The psalmist prays for the renewal of God’s relationship with his people. • Jacob is a synonym for Israel (see Gen 35.9–10).

The psalms in this section affirm integrity and purity (Psa 17.15; Psa 18.20–26; Psa 19.13–14). They refer to people as dwelling in God’s presence (Psa 16.9–11; Psa 17.15) and as not being shaken (Psa 15.5; Psa 16.8).

In this wisdom poem, the psalmist contrasts the lifestyle of the godly with the actions of fools (Psa 14.1–7). The questions in this psalm invite readers to examine themselves and to look away from problems with the wicked. The question of who dwells in God’s presence leads into a description of godly character qualities (cp. Psa 24.3–6; Isa 33.14–16).

Only the godly may reside in the Lord’s presence (Psa 5.4). As his guests, they experience his hospitality and protection. • sanctuary (or tent): In David’s time, God’s sanctuary was a tent (the Tabernacle; see 1Sa 21.6; 2Sa 6.17; 2Sa 7.6; 2Sa 12.20; 1Ch 6.32).
The godly speak truthfully and act faithfully in their relationships. Unlike the wicked, they are open and transparent (Psa 12.2–4).

The Lord prohibited Israel from charging interest to people in need (Exo 22.25–27). • The assurance of God’s presence keeps the godly from destruction (Psa 16.8; Psa 46.5; Psa 125.1). Their circumstances might shake them temporarily, but they ultimately stand firm (Psa 30.6; Psa 94.18; Psa 112.6).

In this psalm of confidence, the poet moves quickly from a short petition (Psa 16.1), to expressions of passionate commitment to God and his people (Psa 16.2–6), to a conclusion of confident praise (Psa 16.7–11).
The psalmist feels safe because the Lord alone offers security (Psa 16.5–6), guidance (Psa 16.7–8), and the joy of his presence (Psa 16.9–11).
I said to the LORD: The various writers of the psalms pray, lament, and praise the Lord throughout the Psalter, and the Lord answers them (see Psa 12.5–6).
The psalmist dissociates himself from ungodly worship, rituals, and words (see Psa 15.3–5).
The cup of blessing represents God’s provision for all the psalmist’s needs (Psa 23.5; see Psa 116.13; cp. Psa 75.8; Isa 51.17).
The land is God’s gift for his people (Deu 18.8).

God’s instruction brings life (Psa 16.11; see Psa 5.8; Psa 23.1–3; Psa 32.8; Psa 73.24). • The psalmist so deeply depends on the Lord for strength and joy that he senses that God is right beside him (Psa 16.11; see Psa 73.23; Psa 109.31; Psa 110.1, Psa 110.5; Psa 121.5). • Peter quoted Psa 16.8–11 in his sermon on the day of Pentecost (Act 2.25–28).
Knowing that not even death can separate him from the Lord strengthens the psalmist’s confidence. He fears a separation (see Psa 13.3–4), but he remains confident of seeing the Lord (see Psa 11.7).
The psalmist expresses his confidence that life continues beyond death. The apostles applied this text to the resurrection of Jesus (Act 2.25–33; Act 13.35).
with you: See Psa 16.7–8; Psa 110.1.
The psalmist pleads for God’s protection and vindication, affirms his own integrity, and prays that the Lord will prevail against his fierce enemies.

comes from honest lips: Deception characterizes the wicked. The godly reject such deceit as a failure of character and pray for rescue from such people (Psa 5.6; Psa 43.1; Psa 120.2). They love honesty, truth, and integrity (Psa 15.2–3; Psa 24.4; Psa 101.7).
The psalmist declares his innocence (Psa 17.1) and commits himself to integrity by being open to God’s examination.
Though he is not perfect, the psalmist commits himself to the Lord. He does not want to sin through deception, flattery, or gossip (see Psa 10.7; Psa 15.2–3; Psa 17.1).
This prayer for God’s care returns to the petition begun in Psa 17.1–2 for redemption from evil.

as you would guard your own eyes (literally as the pupil of your eye): This metaphor expresses God’s care and affection for the psalmist (see Deu 32.10). • The shadow of God’s wings is a place of his protection from enemies and adversity (Psa 36.7; Psa 57.1; Psa 61.4; Psa 63.7; Psa 91.4).

The psalmist confidently prays for the Lord’s victory, knowing that God possesses more power than the evildoers. The psalmist finds his joy in the Lord’s inheritance (Psa 16.5), whereas the wicked search for joy in this world.
see you face to face: The psalmist does not allow temporary concerns raised by adversaries to stand in the way of his experiencing a real and lasting relationship with the Lord.

This royal drama of divine rescue (also found with minor variations in 2Sa 22.1–51) encourages readers who are following the laments and requests for rescue in Psa 16.1–11 and Psa 17.1–15. The psalmist describes the dramatic nature of God’s rescue in three different ways (Psa 18.7–15, Psa 18.16–19, Psa 18.30–36). The psalm also extends hope that a future Son of David will be totally victorious over evil (Psa 18.43–50; cp. Psa 2.1–12).

Psa 18.1 David was a faithful servant of the LORD, charged with the responsibility of establishing God’s kingdom on earth (see Psa 78.70; Psa 132.10; Psa 144.10). • The Lord rescued David from all his enemies when he enabled David to conquer them (see 2Sa 8.1–14).
Theme: Salvation in the Psalms

A shield is an image of protection, salvation, and victory (Psa 7.10; Psa 18.2, Psa 18.30, Psa 18.35; Psa 84.11; Psa 91.4; Psa 115.9, Psa 115.10, Psa 115.11; Psa 119.114; Psa 144.2). It evokes a response of trust, waiting, and godly confidence.
God deserves praise for his greatness and faithfulness (Psa 48.1; Psa 96.4; Psa 145.3).
God dwells in his sanctuary, the heavenly temple (Psa 102.19; see Psa 14.2–3). He knows everything, sees everyone, and will vindicate the godly (see Psa 11.3–7).

The psalmist depicts the Lord’s descent from heaven to earth with phenomena such as earthquakes, flames, smoke, darkness, and rain. Creation shudders at God’s marvelous coming as the Divine Warrior (see Psa 97.2–5) and Judge (see Psa 50.1–6).
The destabilization of the whole earth will be a means of God’s judgment (Psa 77.17–18; Psa 96.9; Psa 97.4; Psa 99.1; Psa 104.32; Isa 29.6; Mic 1.3–4; Nah 1.2–6; Hag 2.7, Hag 2.21).

his nostrils . . . his mouth: The psalmist likens God to an angry person or a fierce creature (see Job 41.12–22). • The terrifying images of smoke, flames, and glowing coals express God’s wrath against sin.
The Lord’s sovereignty extends over all of nature (see Psa 104.2–4; Psa 148.5–6).
a mighty angelic being (Hebrew a cherub): See study notes on 1 Chr 1Ch 28.18; 2 Chr 2Ch 3.10–13.
Because God loves and delights in the psalmist (see Psa 18.1), he will save him (Psa 37.23; Psa 41.11; Psa 91.14–16).

The psalmist affirms that loyalty is rewarded. He puts his trust in the Lord (see Psa 16.1) and commits himself to living with integrity (see Psa 1.1–6, Psa 15.1–5, Psa 24.1–10; see also Psa 19.12–14).

kept the ways of the LORD: The psalmist faithfully obeys God’s instructions (see Psa 25.8–10). • not turned . . . to follow evil: The psalmist rejects the way of folly (see Psa 1.1–6 and Psa 14.1–7) and chooses the way of wisdom (see Psa 1.1–6 and Psa 15.1–5).
The faithful God remains true to his character. He loves faithfulness, blamelessness, and purity, and he hates the perverse (see Psa 1.6).
