The pure have clean hands (see Psa 18.20–24). • to the crooked you show yourself shrewd: The Lord knows each person’s character, and he justly responds to them in kind.
proud: The Lord hates pride (Psa 101.5; Psa 131.1; see Pro 6.16–17; Pro 21.4; Pro 30.13).
light a lamp: The Lord renews the psalmist’s life, helping him overcome the darkness of adversity (see Psa 112.4; Psa 119.105).
scale any wall: God helps his servants fight their battles.
The psalmist experiences God’s rescue and provision of victory.

perfect: God’s character has integrity (see Psa 18.26). • God promises to protect his people, and he does so. • Seeking God’s protection entails trust and faith. Regardless of his feelings or external circumstances, the psalmist makes a deep commitment to the Lord. He experiences joy (Psa 5.11; Psa 64.10) as he awaits the Lord’s rescue (Psa 57.1).
The psalmist’s victories come from the Lord. He completely depends on God.
A wide path represents freedom and safety (see Psa 4.8; Psa 119.35).
With help from the Divine Warrior, the psalmist experienced victory over his enemies.
Placing a foot on the necks of the enemy represents total victory (see Jos 10.23–26).
With God’s victorious help, the psalmist achieved military and political success, thus fulfilling the history of David’s dynasty (Psa 2.1–12). The previous laments find some resolution in this psalm.
The psalmist again reflects on the Lord’s victories. God’s marvelous rescue and the king’s victory are cause for celebration.
God vindicates his servant and so fulfills his mission (Psa 2.1–12; see Psa 47.3; Psa 144.2).
The psalmist’s vision of praise . . . among the nations motivated Paul in his mission to the Gentiles (Rom 15.9).
God appointed David, his anointed ruler, to bring order into God’s world (see Psa 2.1–12). Both David and his descendants received this responsibility.

God’s wisdom is manifest in heaven (Psa 19.1–4), in nature (Psa 19.4–6), in his instruction (Psa 19.7–11), and in the life of the psalmist (Psa 19.12–14). Like Psa 8.1–9, this hymn uses creation to motivate reflection—it is a peaceful oasis after the drama of the lament and victory psalms. The psalm begins with creation as a source of wisdom, then moves to God’s word as the perfect source of wisdom, and ends with the human need for redemption.

The created order is an arena of God’s wisdom, and the heavens are the place of God’s dwelling (Psa 2.4; see Psa 8.1; Psa 57.5; Psa 89.6; Psa 115.3). From heaven, God observes humanity (Psa 11.4; Psa 14.2; Psa 33.13; Psa 53.2; Psa 80.14; Psa 102.19) and comes to the rescue of his servants (Psa 18.6–8, Psa 18.13; Psa 20.6; Psa 57.3; Psa 76.8; Psa 144.5). The heavens remain unaffected by human failures and rebellions (see Psa 2.1–4). They display God’s qualities of fidelity, righteousness (Psa 36.5; Psa 50.6; Psa 57.10; Psa 85.11; Psa 89.2, Psa 89.5; Psa 97.6; Psa 108.4), and wisdom (Psa 136.5; see Psa 119.89–90). The heavens reveal the Lord’s glory (see Psa 19.1) and give evidence of his presence and handiwork.
The glory of God refers to the splendor or manifest presence of the Creator (Psa 113.4). • God (Hebrew ’el): El is an ancient designation for God that signifies his creative power.

God’s wisdom does not need to be spoken. Through creation, it is seen, felt, and experienced. Paul applied this text to condemn Israel for its lack of receptivity to Jesus Christ (Rom 10.18). • The sun is part of God’s creation, but it is not a deity, as people of other nations in the ancient Near East commonly believed.

God’s instructions to humans reveal his character and wisdom. God’s instruction is precious and pleasant (Psa 119.103). It nourishes the person (Pro 16.24; Pro 24.14) and is of more value than objects of human worth (Psa 81.13–16).
The psalmist knows his faults, so he prays to remain faithful and commits himself to the Lord.
An individual who commits deliberate sins does so with an insolent (Psa 86.14) or arrogant (Psa 119.21, Psa 119.69) attitude. • The great sin is rebellion (see Psa 32.1).
words of my mouth . . . meditation of my heart: The psalmist desires to please God in everything he says and thinks (see Luk 6.45; Rom 12.1–2).

This sequence of psalms expresses the experience of moving from confidence and commitment (Psa 20.1–21), through anguish and abandonment (Psa 22.1–31), and finally to comfort, insight, and hope (Psa 23.1–24).
This royal prayer for God’s victory (Psa 20.1–5) leads to confidence in God’s rescue (Psa 20.6–8) and a communal request for God’s response (Psa 20.9).
The community prays for the king’s protection and victory.

The title God of Jacob affectionately expresses God’s ancient relationship with his people (see Psa 46.7, Psa 46.11; Psa 75.9; Psa 76.6; Psa 81.1, Psa 81.4; Psa 84.8; Psa 94.7; Psa 114.7; Psa 146.5). • keep you safe from all harm: See Psa 59.1–2.
Gifts and burnt offerings express submission to the Lord (cp. Psa 40.6).
make all your plans succeed . . . answer all your prayers: These requests could be those stated in Psa 21.3–6 (cp. Psa 27.4).
Troops carried a victory banner to battle, under which they gathered and roused one another to action (see Isa 11.10, Isa 11.12).
An individual member of the community (Psa 20.1–5) responds with a word of assurance and confidence in God’s help.
God chose his anointed king to be ruler (see Psa 2.7).
chariots and horses: These were instruments of war (see Psa 33.16–17; Psa 76.6; Psa 147.10; Isa 30.16; Isa 31.1–3).
God’s people thank him for giving victory to the king.
The king has experienced his heart’s desire—God’s protection and blessing (see Psa 20.5; see also Psa 2.8).
The king returned victorious from battle and received honor from the people. His greatest honor came from God, who gave him blessings, life, and his presence.
success and prosperity: See Pro 10.6.

God offers a rich quality of life (Psa 61.6–7; Psa 91.14–16; Psa 128.4–6) characterized by his presence (Psa 16.11; Psa 23.6; Psa 27.4; Psa 36.9), joy (Psa 16.11), goodness (Psa 23.6; Psa 34.14–15), and protection (Psa 41.2; Psa 61.7).
God’s eternal blessings also bring fullness of life in the present (see Psa 133.1–3).
The king enjoyed victory not because of his strength or intrinsic goodness but because God honored his faith.
As long as even a single enemy opposed the king’s authority, God’s kingdom was not fully present. This prayer requests victory over all evil in the world.

The flaming furnace and fire portray the severity of God’s judgment on the wicked. In the Old Testament, this image often refers to hell (Psa 11.6; Psa 18.8; Psa 50.3; Psa 68.2; Psa 78.21; Psa 79.5; Psa 80.16; Psa 89.46; Psa 97.3; Psa 104.4; Psa 140.10; see Isa 66.24).
children . . . descendants: Evil will end when God destroys all opposition to himself (Psa 109.13; cp. Psa 18.50; Psa 22.30–31; Psa 25.13; Psa 102.28).
Rise up (or be exalted, as in Psa 57.5, Psa 57.11; Psa 108.5) expresses communal praise and joy in God’s greatness and power.

All previous laments pale in comparison with this outcry against the enemy and God’s abandonment. The psalm contains two main sections: the lament (Psa 22.1–21) and praise for redemption (Psa 22.22–31), which leads naturally to Psa 23.1–6. The apostles saw in this psalm an expression of the sufferings of Jesus Christ, who ultimately fulfilled the purpose of David’s humiliation, rejection by people, and divine abandonment (Mat 27.35, Mat 27.39, Mat 27.43, Mat 27.46; Mar 15.34; Joh 19.23–24, Joh 19.28; Heb 2.12).
The psalmist alternates between reflections on his present dire circumstances and memories of the Lord’s past faithfulness; he ends with a prayer for rescue.
A deep sense of alienation from God overwhelms the psalmist (see Psa 10.1).
Theme: Psalms of Suffering
God, the holy King, is set apart from all his creation, but he chooses to reveal himself to Israel. • God greatly desires that his people offer praises to him.
Both the Lord and people reject the psalmist. He vividly describes his anguish (Psa 22.1–2); he lives like a lowly animal.
Everyone mocks the psalmist’s confidence in the Lord (see Psa 3.2; Mat 27.43), which shames him (Psa 44.13–14; Psa 74.10; Psa 89.50; Psa 109.25).
The psalmist reflects on his past relationship with God (see Psa 22.3–5). The Lord has been his very life.
The Lord took care of the psalmist before he could do anything for himself (see Psa 71.6; Psa 139.13).
The psalmist returns to expressing his anguish and suffering (see Psa 22.1–2, Psa 22.6–8). His trouble comes from human beings who act like beasts.
Bashan, a region known for its herds and vegetation, produced strong bulls (Psa 68.30).
The psalmist’s sense of being poured out like water expresses a meaningless, transitory existence that leaves him depleted.
Facing adversity is as horrible as dying of thirst (see Psa 137.6). • Jesus may have had this verse in mind when he said, “I am thirsty” (Joh 19.28).
The wild pack of dogs represents fierce and unscrupulous people.

I can count all my bones: The psalmist’s enemies have utterly shamed him by taking his garments. Jesus also suffered this disgrace (see Mat 27.35). • stare at me and gloat: Enemies make the psalmist the object of their scorn (see Psa 35.24, Psa 35.26; Psa 38.16; Psa 55.3; cp. Psa 59.10). • throw dice: Literally cast lots. The casting of lots was sometimes a way for godly people to find God’s direction (Lev 16.8; Num 27.21; Act 1.24–26). Here, the lots are thrown simply as a game of chance. The soldiers threw dice for Jesus’ clothing after the crucifixion (Mat 27.35; Mar 15.24; Luk 23.34; Joh 19.24).
The psalmist faces his troubles by praying for God’s rescue. Only the Lord has the strength to ward off dogs, lions, and oxen.
The sword makes evident the lethal intent of the enemy.
The psalmist praises the Lord and calls for the godly to join him. He tells of God’s goodness to the needy, including himself.

I will proclaim your name: The writer to the Hebrews ascribes these words to Jesus (Heb 2.12). • my brothers and sisters: Literally my brothers. In the New Testament quotation, the Greek translation picks up the broader meaning as “my brothers and sisters.”
The godly respond with awe (see Psa 22.25).
Unlike his response to the wicked (see Psa 21.8–12), God cares about the needy and hears their prayers (Psa 51.17; Psa 69.33; Psa 102.17).
The psalmist vows to praise the Lord, the great King of the earth (Psa 22.27–28) who cares for the needy. God alone deserves praise.
The great assembly might include all nations (Psa 22.27; Psa 26.12; Psa 35.18).
God knows his people’s needs and addresses them (Psa 63.5; Psa 81.16; Psa 103.5; Psa 107.9; Psa 132.15; Psa 145.16; Psa 147.14).
families of the nations: All clans and tribes of humanity (see Gen 12.3; Rev 5.9–10) will live in submission to the Lord (Psa 96.1–3; see Psa 2.1–12, Psa 72.1–20; Isa 2.2–4; 1Co 15.25–27).
The universal kingdom belongs to God alone (Oba 1.21).
The Lord invites all people, rich and poor (Psa 22.26), to the banquet as long as they worship him.
Future generations will join those from the past who praised the Lord (Psa 22.3–5). The descendants of the godly will receive blessings (Psa 22.30–31), unlike the offspring of the wicked (Psa 21.10).

The Lord’s acts of redemption (Psa 40.9; Psa 50.6; Psa 71.15, Psa 71.16, Psa 71.24; Psa 97.6) demonstrate that he is righteous (see Psa 4.1). His righteousness provides the character required for rule, judicial decisions, and relationships. This virtue leads to harmony and order (see Psa 50.6).

These psalms develop the importance of integrity (Psa 25.4–7, Psa 25.12–14, Psa 25.21; Psa 26.6, Psa 26.11; Psa 27.7–12), God’s shepherding care (Psa 23.1; Psa 28.9), God’s guidance (Psa 23.2–3; Psa 25.5; Psa 27.11), God’s goodness (Psa 23.6; Psa 25.7–8; Psa 27.13), and living in his house (Psa 23.6; Psa 26.8; Psa 27.4, Psa 27.8).

This psalm of trust and confidence in the Lord has been a favorite of God’s people for generations. It expresses assurance of God’s presence in the midst of adversity. It evokes images of the Good Shepherd (Psa 23.1–3; see Eze 34.12; Joh 10.11) and of the messianic banquet (Psa 23.5–6; see Isa 25.6; Rev 19.9).
People in the ancient Near East commonly viewed their rulers as shepherds.
The Lord promises to take care of his children (Psa 34.9–10; Isa 51.14). He demonstrated this ability to Israel in the wilderness (Deu 2.7) and in the Promised Land (Deu 8.9).
Theme: The Shepherd

Sheep rest after they have eaten their fill (Zep 3.13; see Isa 11.7; cp. Isa 13.20; Isa 27.10). • The Lord leads the sheep for their own benefit (see Psa 5.8). • Sheep only drink from still water, so the shepherd seeks out peaceful streams for his flock.

Cp. Psa 19.7; the Lord’s word renews my strength. • The Lord guides by rescuing his people from evil (Psa 23.4–5; see Psa 31.3), bringing them back to himself (Psa 5.8; Psa 61.2), caring (Psa 48.14; Psa 139.10), ruling (Psa 67.4), counseling (Psa 73.24), protecting (Psa 78.53; Psa 107.30; Psa 143.11), and instructing them in wisdom (Psa 27.11; see Pro 4.11). • The Lord’s name guarantees the relationship; he guards his reputation against any accusation of his abandoning his people or allowing them to sin (see Psa 25.11; Psa 31.3; Psa 106.8; Psa 143.11).
The shepherd used his rod and staff to fend off danger.

A feast demonstrates the Lord’s care and mercy toward his people (see Psa 22.26, Psa 22.29). Although enemies can watch, they cannot trouble the guests. • The ritual of anointing the head with oil showed guests honor (Psa 92.9–11), hospitality, and refreshment (Psa 104.15; Psa 133.2).

The Lord expresses his unfailing love through the goodness of his presence and other benefits that he alone provides (Psa 69.16; Psa 86.17; Psa 109.21; see Psa 18.6; Psa 61.4). He actively bestows care that is greater than the temporary trials imposed by enemies (Psa 7.1).
The shepherd of Psa 23.1–6, who is also the King of the whole world, takes possession of Zion.
The kingdom belongs to the Creator, the Great King (cp. Psa 22.27).
The Lord created and now rules the earth and everything in it (see 1Co 10.25–26). He sees all its people (Psa 33.14), regardless of their status (Psa 49.1–2).
God created everything in an orderly and stable manner (see Psa 89.11; Psa 102.25; Psa 104.5).
The citizens of the King’s realm include all who seek him. The Lord invites them to enter his presence.

These questions invite readers to look away from their problems with the wicked and to examine themselves (see Psa 15.1). • God’s holy place is the holy mountain, a reference both to Jerusalem and to heaven.
Theme: God’s Presence in the Psalms

Those with pure hands have not shed blood or injured relationships between people (see Psa 9.12; Psa 15.2–5). • Those with pure hearts commit themselves fully to the Lord, as evidenced in strength of character, transparency, and selflessness (Psa 51.10; Psa 73.1; see Mat 5.8).
The LORD of Heaven’s Armies reigns from his home, the Temple in Jerusalem (Psa 84.3–5). He excludes sin and sinners (Psa 24.3–6) but protects all who dwell in Zion.

This individual lament includes instruction in wisdom and a community lament; it begins and ends with an affirmation of trust in the Lord (Psa 25.1–3, Psa 25.15–22). The psalmist prays for guidance (Psa 25.4–7) and encourages the godly to practice a lifestyle of wisdom (Psa 25.12–14). In addition to the enemies who trouble him, the psalmist confesses his sins (Psa 25.7, Psa 25.11, Psa 25.18) as part of his anguish. Trust develops with understanding God’s character: He is compassionate, faithful, and good (Psa 25.8–10).
The psalmist expresses confidence that the godly will be vindicated and his enemies will not succeed (see Psa 25.15–22).
The psalmist commits himself to the Lord instead of to idols (see Psa 24.3–4).
Enemies would rejoice by singing a victory song.

In this prayer for guidance, compassion, and forgiveness, the psalmist turns to the Lord for instruction in wisdom. He confesses his past failures and acknowledges that his hope lies with his merciful Savior.
The right path, the path of wisdom (see Psa 5.8), means being open to instruction that leads to life (Psa 27.11; Psa 43.3; Psa 73.24; Psa 119.12).
Biblical hope does not mean wishing for an event to turn out favorably. Hope trusts the Lord’s will and gives the courage to face disappointments (Psa 33.22; Psa 130.5).
compassion: See also Psa 51.1; Psa 57.1; Psa 103.8.
The Lord keeps his people close to himself.

The psalmist again asks forgiveness for his many sins (Psa 25.7; Psa 32.1–5). The sins of Israel’s kings demonstrated the weaknesses inherent in David’s dynasty and the reasons for its failure in Old Testament Israel (see Psa 89.1–52).
Those who fear the Lord will receive further instruction and experience God’s presence (Psa 25.14) and blessing (Psa 25.13).

prosperity: See Psa 23.6. • inherit the land: Unlike the wicked, who will perish (Psa 1.6), the godly have a secure future. In the end, God will bless them, and their blessings will endure (see Psa 37.9, Psa 37.11, Psa 37.22, Psa 37.29, Psa 37.34; Isa 57.13; Mat 5.5).
The psalmist expresses confidence in the Lord, commits to a life of integrity, and prays for rescue.
the traps of my enemies: See Psa 5.9–10; Psa 31.4; Psa 140.5; Pro 3.26.

The psalmist can find no relief (see Psa 4.1; Psa 13.1–2) as his problems go from bad to worse. He associates his anguish with sin, but he does not elaborate on the nature of his sin (see Psa 25.7, Psa 25.11).
Knowing that the Lord hates violent people (see Psa 11.5), the psalmist pleads with God to deal with these enemies.
Just as it opened, the psalm closes with a commitment of trust and hope (see Psa 9.18; Psa 25.5).
In this individual lament, the psalmist prays for redemption on the basis of his own innocence and the Lord’s justice.
The psalmist opens himself to divine examination of his life, especially in the areas of his character and devotion.
For God’s truth to become part of one’s character requires a habitual commitment.
Because of his devotion to the Lord (Psa 26.1–3), the psalmist dissociates himself from evil people (see Psa 1.1).
The psalmist demonstrates his loyalty to the Lord through pious rituals, praise, and acknowledgment of the Lord’s presence in the Temple.
Ritual purity required the worshiper to wash their hands, symbolic of separation from evil and evildoers (see Psa 73.13). • The altar symbolizes God’s presence (Psa 43.4).
The sanctuary symbolized the manifest presence of the Lord (see Psa 18.6).
Don’t let me suffer: The end of the godly cannot be the same as that of the wicked.
The psalmist’s footing on solid ground represents salvation (cp. Psa 143.10). • publicly: Or in the great assembly at the Temple (Psa 26.6–8; Psa 22.25).

This psalm mixes two genres—a psalm of confidence (Psa 27.1–6) and an individual lament (Psa 27.7–14)—held together by the theme of longing for the Lord’s presence. The psalmist focuses on the Lord; his circumstances are secondary. The strength of the psalmist’s faith is expressed in his openness to the Lord’s instruction, timing, and priorities.

The psalmist acknowledges the Lord at the center of his life (Psa 27.1). Because of God’s presence, he engages his adversaries with confidence. They cannot intimidate him or penetrate his inner security.
Light expresses the Lord’s goodness (Psa 27.13; see Psa 4.6; Psa 23.6; Psa 31.19; Psa 38.10; Psa 43.3; Psa 56.13).
The psalmist’s enemies seek to devour him by living at his expense (see study note on Psa 14.4).
remain confident: See Psa 25.2; Psa 26.1.

Searching for and enjoying the Lord’s presence provides the psalmist’s foundation for confidence and security. He lives in the assurance of God’s protection and looks forward to offering sacrifices of thanksgiving and praise (see Psa 18.6).
sanctuary (or tabernacle): This early shrine was the Israelites’ place of worship before the Temple was constructed.
hold my head high: A sign of victory. • The granting of the request of Psa 27.4 prompts sacrifices with shouts of joy.
The psalmist requests the Lord’s mercy, presence, and instruction. God is the psalmist’s greatest good; enemies and other circumstances are peripheral.

Unlike the wicked (Psa 10.4), who only want a temporary advantage (Psa 78.34–36), the godly search for the Lord as a thirsty person searches for water in the desert (Psa 63.1; Psa 105.4; Psa 119.2, Psa 119.10; Mat 6.33). They act wisely (Psa 34.10, Psa 34.14) while waiting for the Lord to resolve their crisis (Psa 34.4; Psa 69.6; Psa 77.2; Psa 119.58).

The psalmist expresses confidence and hope in the Lord’s presence. To live in faith means to wait patiently in recognition of the Lord’s goodness. Such a life is not always pleasant for the godly (Psa 42.2–3; Psa 43.5), but their future is secure (Psa 37.9; Psa 130.7; see Psa 9.18).
In this individual lament, the psalmist pleads for justice and mercy. He expresses confidence in the Lord’s strength and faithfulness, and he intercedes for the Lord’s people.
The psalmist urges the Lord to listen; his urgency flows out of the tension between his deep relationship with the Lord and the adversity he faces.
if you are silent: The psalmist appeals to the Lord to take action (Psa 35.22; Psa 50.3; Psa 83.1; Psa 109.1).
It was common to lift up one’s hands in a gesture of devoted prayer (Psa 63.4; Psa 134.2).
The psalmist curses his enemies, asking God for retribution and vindication.
The wicked do not acknowledge the difference between the sacred and the common, so they have no respect for the Lord’s creation, redemption, or revelation.
The psalmist anticipates rescue because of his confidence in the Lord’s justice.
my strength and shield: The Lord protects the psalmist (see Psa 59.9, Psa 59.17).
The poem closes with intercession for the Lord’s people. • Bless Israel, your special possession: See Psa 29.11; Psa 133.3.
This nature hymn in praise of the Creator declares that the Lord holds all power over nature. God uses the same unsurpassed strength to care for his people.

The psalmist issues a call to honor the Lord for his power (cp. Psa 96.7–8). • you heavenly beings: Angels or deities who, some believed, held special powers. The psalmist did not believe in other deities but called on people who thought they were real to look to the Lord as the only God.

The word translated voice (Hebrew qol) can also mean “noise” (1Ki 1.45) or “thunder” (Joe 3.16). The Lord’s voice is awe-inspiring, and it dominates whatever rumblings people might attribute to other deities.
The cedars of Lebanon were known for their size and quality (see Isa 2.13).
Lebanon’s mountains and Hermon are high mountains to the north of Israel. • The Lord can cause even immense mountains to shake at his command (see Psa 114.4).
The wilderness of Kadesh was located south of Judah. God’s voice can be heard throughout the land, from the north (Psa 29.6) to the south.
The image of powerful floodwaters connects with the Genesis flood (Gen 6.17). The Lord reigns as king over the whole created order; no one contests his kingdom.
The ruler of nature blesses his people with peace (see Psa 28.8–9; Psa 37.11; Psa 133.3).

This individual thanksgiving psalm opens in praise to the Lord for his salvation (Psa 30.1–3), then contrasts God’s favor with his anger (Psa 30.4–7), and ends with a transformation from mourning to dancing (Psa 30.8–12).
Psa 30.1 Perhaps David wrote this psalm in advance for the dedication of the Temple, making his own experience representative of the nation’s.
The psalmist praises God for his triumph over adversity, which he likens to salvation from the grave.

I will exalt you is a call to lift up the Lord’s name in praise and thanksgiving (Psa 34.3; Psa 81.1; Psa 99.5, Psa 99.9; Psa 107.32; Psa 118.28; Psa 145.1; see Exo 15.1; Isa 25.1). • you rescued me: God pulled the psalmist from death (Psa 30.3). • In his justice and care, God refused to let the psalmist’s enemies triumph (see Psa 26.9; Psa 27.12; Psa 28.3; Psa 31.8).
The godly should celebrate the Lord’s acts of rescue with song and praise (Psa 33.21; Psa 97.12; Psa 103.1; Psa 105.3; Psa 145.21).

Nothing can stop me now! The psalmist confesses his presumptuous attitude (cp. Psa 32.3–4). • secure as a mountain: In the psalms, this phrase creates a powerful image of stability and of God’s control (see Psa 11.1; Psa 18.7; Psa 36.6; Psa 46.2; Psa 72.3; Psa 76.4; Psa 83.14; Psa 97.5; Psa 114.4, Psa 114.6; Psa 125.2). • I was shattered: The absence of God’s favor destroys the security of the proud (cp. Psa 104.27–30).

The psalmist faced death (also in Psa 30.1–3)—perhaps literally, perhaps figuratively. But when he turned to the Lord, the Lord rescued him and turned his mourning into joyful dancing. Only God’s favor can permanently and powerfully overcome human failure and the depths of despair.

The psalmist encourages the godly to find refuge in the Lord and wait for his salvation. Despite having had a death-like experience, he testifies to the Lord’s faithfulness. This psalm foreshadows the suffering of Jesus (Luk 23.46).
The Lord offers refuge to anyone who comes to him for protection. The psalmist trusts in and submits to the Lord. See also Psa 71.1–3.
The psalmist issues an urgent call for the Lord to pay attention to his desperate situation (Psa 71.2; Psa 88.2; Psa 102.2).
I entrust my spirit into your hand: Whether he lives or dies, the psalmist will trust his Lord. Jesus uttered these words on the cross just before he died (Luk 23.46).
Trust in the Lord requires confidence that he has our best interests at heart.
A safe place literally means a broad place, in contrast to a “narrow” or constricted place of distress (see Psa 18.19).
In this prayer for mercy, the psalmist wedges a description of the intensity of suffering and the pain of rejection between two affirmations of trust (Psa 31.6, Psa 31.14).
wasting away from within: This is a powerful description of how despair takes a toll on our physical well-being.
Hope does not confide in frail and changeable human beings but only in the Lord. The sufferer entrusts himself to God while waiting for the Lord’s justice.
My future is in your hands: To relinquish control of timing is one way to express submission.
The psalmist, who did not deserve to be disgraced, invokes the principle of retribution (see study note on Psa 1.6; see also “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note).
The psalmist thanks the Lord for answering his prayer (Psa 31.1–18) and rescuing him.
Since the godly are under the Lord’s protection and shelter, evil has no power over them.
Praise the LORD: The psalmist expresses his joy at the experience of God’s goodness and love. Throughout his ordeal, the Lord has cared for him.

Out of his own pain and renewed awareness of the Lord’s goodness, the psalmist turns to others who suffer. He holds out the promise of God’s loving care for those who persevere in hoping for the Lord.

This wisdom psalm of confession and thanksgiving encourages and exhorts the godly to learn from the psalmist’s experience of sin, denial, confession, and forgiveness. This psalm was one of the seven psalms of penitence used in the early church (also Psa 6.1–10, Psa 38.1–22, Psa 51.1–19, Psa 102.1–28, Psa 130.1–8, Psa 143.1–12).
The Lord’s forgiveness restores people to fellowship with him, clears them of guilt, and gives them great joy. Paul quoted this text when explaining justification by faith alone (Rom 4.4–8).
The psalmist acknowledges his own sin (see Psa 19.12–13; Psa 25.7, Psa 25.11, Psa 25.15–22) and his resistance to confessing sin. The Lord pressed him hard until he confessed his guilt.
The psalmist attributes his suffering directly to the Lord’s hand of discipline (cp. Psa 38.2; Psa 39.10).
God has forgiven the guilt and rebellion of Psa 32.1. The Lord’s nature is to reconcile and forgive (Psa 78.38; Psa 85.2; Psa 130.4), but he requires confession and repentance.
The godly will learn from the psalmist’s experience to pray for forgiveness before it is too late.
The Lord promises to be his people’s hiding place (Psa 31.20). Instead of being overwhelmed by terror (Psa 31.13), the psalmist is surrounded by songs of victory.
God interrupts the psalmist’s teaching with a message that invites the godly to receive the Lord’s wisdom (see Psa 5.8; Psa 23.3; Psa 25.4–6).
The senseless person is not wise. Rejecting the Lord’s counsel ruins life and makes one like an animal (see Isa 1.3; Jam 3.3).
Difficulties common to all of life will ensnare the wicked, whereas the Lord promises to protect the godly with his care.

This hymn of creation (see also Psa 8.1–9, Psa 19.1–14, Psa 104.1–35, Psa 145.1–21) might be a continuation of Psa 32.1–11. It exhorts readers to praise God (Psa 33.1–3), to recognize the power of his word in creation (Psa 33.4–7), and to fear the Creator (Psa 33.8–11). It offers hope to forgiven sinners (Psa 32.1–11) that they can live a new life in the fear of the Lord and under divine protection.
The psalmist exhorts the godly to praise the Lord with melodies, with a new song, and with skillfully-played music.
God’s word displays his character and his power.
The nations surrounding Israel thought that the sea had divine power, but it is under God’s control, within boundaries that he set (see Psa 104.8–10).
Fear of the Lord begins with awe for God and for his powerful word. His word created everything and continues to order and sustain creation. He frustrates the plans of people who oppose his will.
The power of the Lord extends to all the nations (see 2; Psa 96.1–3).
The plans and schemes of the mighty will not prevail, except by God’s will (see Isa 8.9–10).
God’s word still orders creation and will do so forever. • God’s intentions are marvelous (Psa 40.5; Psa 92.5).
People who fear God are chosen as his inheritance (see Psa 33.13–19); this excludes rebellious people (Psa 78.62).
From the heavens, the Lord searches out and cares for anyone who fears him (see Psa 14.2–3).
army . . . great strength . . . warhorse: Even military might is under God’s control (see Psa 33.10–11; Ecc 9.11).
God watches over all who live by his counsel (Psa 32.8). He protects, rescues, and remains close to them (Psa 34.15–22).
The godly respond to this magnificent vision of God’s power in creation and in the affairs of the world with an affirmation of trust, commitment, joy, and hope as they pray and wait for God’s rescue.
Using a play on words, the psalmist contrasts his people’s sure hope (Hebrew yakhal) in the Lord with the supposed strength (Psa 33.17; Hebrew khayil) of the horses of the wicked.

This wisdom psalm includes a thanksgiving hymn (Psa 34.1–7) that celebrates the Lord’s care for and protection of godly sufferers. It also includes an invitation to wisdom (Psa 34.8–14) and an exposition of wisdom concerning the Lord’s care for the needy and the suffering of the wicked (Psa 34.15–22).
Psa 34.1 Abimelech is another name for Achish (see 1Sa 21.10–15). The body of the psalm makes no explicit connection to this event.
The psalmist exhorts the helpless to join him in praise.
The psalmist narrates his experiences of answered prayer.
The angel of the LORD represented the Lord’s presence during the wilderness journey. He protected Israel from the forces of Egypt (Exo 14.19–20), and he will guard all the godly (Psa 91.11).
The godly encourage everyone to seek wisdom, to fear the Lord, and to place themselves under the protection of the Lord’s angel.
Fear of the Lord includes reverence and respect, and it motivates a life of wisdom (see Pro 1.7; Pro 9.10).
Wisdom contains three components: fearing the Lord (Psa 34.11), doing good (Psa 34.14), and rejecting evil (Psa 34.13).
Anyone who listens, even children, can become wise followers of God.
Peter quotes this passage in his instructions for peaceful living (1Pe 3.10–12).
Godly people control their words; speaking evil and telling lies are foolish (see Psa 10.7; cp. Psa 17.1).
The way of peace leads to harmony and order, whereas evil destroys them (see Psa 37.11).
The Lord distinguishes between wise and foolish people; he shows his concern for the wise by rescuing them from trouble (Psa 34.15, Psa 34.17–20), but he destroys the foolish (Psa 34.16, Psa 34.21).

Those who are brokenhearted possess a spirit of deep contrition and dependence on the Lord. God accepts this spirit as a proper sacrifice (Psa 51.17). The wicked hate the brokenhearted (Psa 109.16), but the Lord heals them (Psa 147.3; see Isa 57.15; Isa 61.1).
The godly might suffer, but the Lord will reward them in the end. Similarly, the wicked might prosper for a time, but ultimately they will perish (Psa 1.6; Psa 34.15–16).
Bones represent a person’s entire being (see Psa 6.2). • not one of them is broken: John applied this statement to Jesus at the crucifixion (Joh 19.36).
In this lament, the Lord’s troubled servant calls for God to see his circumstances and vindicate him.
The psalmist longs for the Lord’s salvation. The language seems vindictive, but it arises from a desire for justice and for the Lord to care for the needy and oppressed.

A path that is dark and slippery suggests instability and untimely doom under the Lord’s judgment (see Psa 69.23; Psa 73.18; Psa 82.5; Psa 107.10; Psa 143.3). • The angel of the LORD is an agent of judgment as well as salvation.
Nothing in the universe can compare with the Lord (see Psa 86.8; Psa 89.6, Psa 89.8; Isa 40.18, Isa 40.25).
The psalmist presents the Lord with the reasons for his suffering. Evil has many faces. He is tired and worn out, and he knows that only the Lord can help him.
Malicious witnesses want nothing but violence (see Psa 11.4–6; Psa 54.3).
The psalmist’s attackers snarl to express their bitter envy.

In this prayer for vindication, the psalmist’s crisis looms so large that a resolution must be found in the Lord. The psalmist has taken the high road, believing that vengeance belongs to the Lord. God’s patience hardens the hearts of the wicked and gives them reasons to justify their evil lifestyle.
John applied this claim of innocence (see also Psa 69.4) to Jesus (Joh 15.25).
Aha! . . . Look: Both words translate the same expression of glee (Hebrew he’akh).
The psalmist calls on the Lord to judge the wicked and to rescue the godly and bring them joy.

This lament contrasts the world of folly devised by the wicked with the world of wisdom created and sustained by the Lord. The wicked care only about themselves, whereas the Lord cares for all of creation. He will intervene to bring about justice in his world. The righteous will enjoy his protection, but the wicked will perish.
Fools despise what is wise and good as they pursue evil.
no fear of God: Paul includes this phrase in his description of the depravity of all people (Rom 3.18).
As the source of wisdom, the Lord is reliable and incomparable. His faithful care extends to all parts of the created order.
God’s all-encompassing goodness surpasses that of the created order. God graciously meets his people’s practical needs.
All creatures live by God’s grace (1Ti 4.10).
God invites all humanity to the banquet in his house (cp. Pro 9.1–6).
Light represents salvation and celebration (Psa 18.25–29; Psa 27.1; cp. Psa 35.6).
Since God’s wisdom extends to all of creation, it protects the godly.
The psalmist remains confident that the disorder caused by the wicked (Psa 36.1–4) will end when they meet their demise.

This psalm elaborates on the problems posed in Psa 36.1–12: How should the godly respond to the reality of evil? When will the Lord bring justice? Why does he permit the wicked to destroy his created order? Psa 37.1–40 offers clear responses that reduce the tensions of life (Psa 37.1–9, Psa 37.34) and promise that the meek will have a future (Psa 37.10–11, Psa 37.39–40). The alternating contrast between the godly and the wicked emphasizes the futility of folly (Psa 37.12–24, Psa 37.27–33). The personal observations of the psalmist add a human touch (Psa 37.25–26, Psa 37.35–38). He encourages viewing the inheritance of the land from a long-range perspective: The earth belongs to the Lord, who will give it to those he blesses—the lowly and godly who trust in him, put their hope in him, and follow him (see Psa 37.9, Psa 37.11, Psa 37.22, Psa 37.29, Psa 37.34; see also Isa 57.13; Mat 5.5).

The wise respond to evil by trusting in the Lord. Trust includes five dimensions: (1) renouncing irritability and envy (Psa 37.1–2); (2) delighting in the Lord (Psa 37.3–4); (3) submitting to the Lord (Psa 37.5–6); (4) practicing patience in hope (Psa 37.7); and (5) avoiding anger (Psa 37.8–9).
envy: The jealous desire to have what others enjoy leads to further sin (Psa 73.3; Pro 3.31; Jam 1.14–15; Jam 4.1–2).
Theme: Wisdom Psalms
Finite existence is part of the human condition (see Psa 90.5–6; Psa 92.7; Psa 102.4, Psa 102.11; Psa 103.15; Psa 129.6; Isa 40.7–8).
The antidote to irritability and envy (Psa 37.1) is trust in the Lord.
To do good means cultivating a devotion to wisdom (see Psa 34.14; Pro 3.5–7).
To take delight in the LORD means aligning with the Lord’s way in order to enjoy him.
Justice occurs when the Lord’s will triumphs and the godly experience his rescue (Isa 45.8; Isa 51.5–6; Isa 58.8, Isa 58.10–11).
Be still: We should let the Lord be God rather than taking matters into our own hands.
Irritability and anger quickly corrode character.
The wicked will not possess the land; those who trust in the LORD will. The Lord promises an inheritance because he is committed to caring for his people.
The Lord is the author of peace (Psa 85.10)—he brings peace to a chaotic world (Psa 29.11; Psa 37.11; Psa 85.8; Psa 147.14). His wisdom guides the lowly into the way of peace (Psa 119.165; Mat 5.5).
The wicked seek to destroy the Lord’s order, but he defeats them.
The wicked snarl to express their bitter envy. They plot to bring an end to the godly, but the Lord derides them because they cannot succeed (Psa 2.4).
The weapons of the wicked will turn against them (cp. Psa 7.12–13).
Being wise with modest means is better than having prosperity and power and being wicked (Pro 15.16; Pro 16.8, Pro 16.19; Pro 17.1; Pro 28.6).
The Lord cares for the blameless in this life and for eternity, but the wicked will perish.
Smoke depicts the temporary nature of life (Psa 68.2; Psa 102.3).
To borrow and never repay is a behavior of a crooked lifestyle. • Generous givers freely share what they freely receive from the Lord (see Psa 111.5; Psa 112.5).
The rectitude and strength of a godly person’s life comes from the Lord (see Pro 4.12; Pro 14.15; Pro 16.9; Pro 20.24).
The Lord does not abandon his children or their descendants.

The godly are wise; they do good and reject evil. The Lord cares for them, protecting them and ensuring that they receive their rightful portion of the land as their inheritance. The wicked might try to ambush the godly, but they will not succeed.
The godly base their counsel on the Lord’s wisdom.
They have made God’s law their own: The godly internalize God’s wisdom and instructions (see Psa 119.11; Jer 24.7; Jer 31.31–34).
The wicked might appear to be flourishing like a tree (cp. Psa 52.8; Psa 92.12–13), but they eventually die and are forgotten (Psa 37.2).
The Lord provides strength for his people.
This psalm is a lament and prayer for healing. The psalmist’s suffering is associated with his unconfessed sin. He confesses his sin and entrusts his case to the Lord.
Psa 38.1 asking God to remember him: The meaning of this phrase is uncertain (also in Psa 70.1).
These verses form a prelude to the psalmist’s confession (Psa 38.18) and describe his woeful condition.
The psalmist’s sins had triggered the Lord’s anger and rage, resulting in the arrows and blows of discipline and rebuke; as a result, his whole body is sick.

Sin can lead to sickness and even death (1Co 11.30). Whether the psalmist actually felt physically ill or his sickness was a metaphor for emotional turmoil, he knew that it came from God and threatened his life (see Psa 32.3; Psa 39.10).
The psalmist’s burden results from sin (see Psa 40.12; Psa 41.4; cp. Gen 4.13).
The severity of God’s punishment brings anguish that affects every part of the psalmist’s being.
The psalmist longs for a restored relationship with God, but he feels alienated. He finds himself lost and alone as his friends disappear.
The psalmist suffers quietly before his opponents (see Isa 53.7).
The Lord alone will resolve the conflict (Psa 9.18; Psa 27.14; Psa 37.9, Psa 37.34).
No longer able to endure his suffering and teetering on the verge of collapse (cp. Psa 15.5), the psalmist confesses his sin (see Psa 32.5).
That the psalmist’s enemies hate him without reason compounds his pain.

Asking the Lord to act quickly in times of great need is common in the Psalter (Psa 22.19; Psa 31.2; Psa 40.13; Psa 69.17; Psa 70.1; Psa 71.12; Psa 79.8; Psa 102.2; Psa 141.1; Psa 143.7). However, wisdom and experience teach that God’s people must often wait for him to act (Psa 27.14; Psa 37.7; Isa 8.17; Isa 40.31).
This prayer for rescue reflects the psalmist’s discouragement, which comes from having a limited perspective on his situation.
Psa 39.1 Jeduthun was a levitical singer appointed by David along with Asaph (1Ch 9.16; 1Ch 16.38; 1Ch 25.1).
Suffering in silence only intensifies the psalmist’s anguish, pain, and inner turmoil.

Because of his suffering and sin, the psalmist concludes that life is meaningless and fleeting (see Job 7.7–10; Isa 40.6–8). He had expected a wicked life to have those qualities (see Psa 37.2, Psa 37.20; Psa 103.15–16), but now whether a person is godly or not seems to be irrelevant.

how fleeting my life is: This perspective comes out of suffering (see Psa 78.39; Psa 89.47–48; Psa 90.3–10). The human lifetime is but a moment to God (Psa 90.4), as temporary as a breath (see Psa 39.11; Psa 144.4).
The idea that rebellion brings on suffering is a common thread in Psa 32.1–11, Psa 38.1–41.
The psalmist links suffering with God’s discipline, assuming that it is punishment for his sin.
The Lord uses discipline to correct his children (Psa 38.1, Psa 38.3, Psa 38.7; Psa 40.12; see Pro 3.11–12; Heb 12.5–6).
A guest (or foreigner) had no rights of land ownership (see Lev 25.23). The patriarchs had lived as guests in Canaan (Psa 105.23).
Unlike the psalmist’s earlier request that God stay close to him (Psa 38.21–22), his present desire for God to leave him alone echoes Job’s disposition (Job 7.17–19).

This psalm includes a thanksgiving song (Psa 40.1–10) followed by a lament (Psa 40.11–17). The thanksgiving song includes the reason for the thanksgiving (Psa 40.1–5), an affirmation of commitment (Psa 40.6–8), and a public testimony of God’s character (Psa 40.7–10). The lament concerns the psalmist’s troubles because of his sins (Psa 40.11–12) and is followed by two prayers for vindication (Psa 40.13–15, Psa 40.17).
The psalmist thanks the Lord for his rescue and testifies that God can be trusted.

The Lord delights in the attitude and character of the person making an offering more than in the offering itself. • Now that you have made me listen, I finally understand: Greek text reads You have given me a body. In Heb 10.5–7, the writer quotes from the Greek version of Psa 40.6–8. He casts the words as something Jesus said as he left heaven and came into the world.
As is written about me in the Scriptures: Moses had recorded God’s requirements for Israel’s kings in Deu 17.14–15.
The psalmist prays that the Lord will be true to his character when answering this plea for mercy.
The psalmist is troubled by both his adversities and his own sins and prays for rescue. • This passage is repeated almost verbatim as Psa 70.1–5.
In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist prays for healing (Psa 41.4, Psa 41.10), laments his distress (Psa 41.5–9), and expresses confidence in the Lord’s blessing (Psa 41.1–3, Psa 41.11–12).

The poor who suffer hardship have special protection under God’s law (Lev 14.21; Lev 19.10); they receive God’s justice and godly rule (Psa 72.13; Psa 82.3–4). The word translated poor is often a synonym for the godly (Psa 113.7; see Zep 3.12).
when they are sick: This illness might be physical or spiritual (see Psa 6.2; Psa 38.1–22).

The psalmist applies the blessing to himself (Psa 41.12). Apparently he has taken care of the poor (Psa 41.1), but he has sinned against the Lord in other ways. Out of his pain, he cries for healing while confessing his sin. The Lord alone can grant the restoration that brings true joy (Psa 30.2; Psa 107.20–21).
The psalmist’s enemies disguise themselves as friends, while his friends openly become his enemies.
How soon will he die? The psalmist’s opponents regard his suffering as a divine judgment (cp. Psa 1.6).

the one who shared my food: Eating together was a sign of unity (Act 2.42). Refusing to eat with someone indicated hostility (1Co 5.11). Jesus experienced the same kind of betrayal (Joh 13.1, Joh 13.18).
The psalmist knows that the Lord has forgiven him and will bless him.
This doxology closes Book One (Psa 1.1–41). Cp. Psa 106.48.

These psalms, like Psa 9.1–20 and Psa 10.1–18, form a unit comprising a lament with a bittersweet refrain of hope (Psa 42.5, Psa 42.11; Psa 43.5). In many Hebrew manuscripts these two psalms are combined as one. The historical context is uncertain; these psalms might be the voice of God’s people in exile, confessing their loyalty to God as he punishes them for their prevailing apostasy. The psalmist longs for fellowship with God such as he enjoyed in Jerusalem (Psa 42.4); his memories only make him more discouraged. As the psalmist cries out to God, he recalls God’s love and faithfulness (Psa 42.8), which moves him to plead for vindication (Psa 43.1–4).

Psa 42.1 The descendants of Korah were members of a Levitical choir appointed by David to serve as Temple singers (see 1Ch 6.22–38; 1Ch 9.19–34; 2Ch 20.19). Their ancestor Korah was the apostate who had rebelled against Moses and whom the earth swallowed up (Exo 6.24; Num 16.1–50).

The psalmist’s longing for God comes from being geographically distant from the Temple as he remembers the past. • The verb translated longs is found only here and in Joe 1.20 (“cry out”); in both cases it refers to extreme thirst in a waterless desert (see Psa 63.1; Psa 143.6; see also Psa 84.2).
Theme: Questions and Doubt
Having tears for food speaks of great grief (Psa 80.5; Psa 102.9; see Psa 6.6; Psa 56.8; Psa 119.136; Psa 126.5). • The wicked try to hold God to their timetable and deny his power to intervene.
The psalmist recalls leading a great procession as a member of the Levitical choir, possibly during the high holy days.
The psalmist encourages himself with questions and answers.
The psalmist feels depressed, but it does not incapacitate him. He remembers that the living God is his Savior. This verse is repeated in Psa 42.11 and Psa 43.5.
Mount Hermon is a high mountain range northeast of Israel. The source of the Jordan is by Dan at the foot of Mount Hermon. • Mount Mizar might be a peak in the Mount Hermon range.
The raging seas, waves, and surging tides conjure images of God’s wrath (see Psa 88.7).
The psalmist sees rays of hope. A life oriented to God includes songs of joy and praying for justice and vindication (Psa 42.9–10; Psa 43.1–4).
The psalmist brings his many doubts, discouragements, and questions directly to God.
The psalmist turns to the Lord for rescue from his troubles, for guidance, for restoration, and for vindication.
tossed me aside: Other psalms similarly ask whether God has rejected his people (Psa 44.9, Psa 44.23; Psa 60.1, Psa 60.10; Psa 74.1; Psa 77.7; Psa 88.14; Psa 89.38; Psa 108.11).

In this prayer for God’s redemption, light and truth are viewed as guides (see Psa 18.25–29; Psa 27.1; Psa 85.10–13; Psa 89.14–18; see also Psa 119.105; Joh 3.19; Eph 5.8; 1Th 5.5–7). • The Temple on the mountain in Jerusalem symbolized God’s holy presence among his people (Psa 15.1; Psa 43.3; Psa 99.5, Psa 99.9; Psa 132.7).
This verse is repeated in Psa 42.5, Psa 42.11.

This national lament after defeat in battle continues the tone of the previous two psalms, including reflecting on an unspecified moment in Israel’s history and calling on God for salvation. The people recite God’s past acts of rescue (Psa 44.1–3), acknowledge God’s power to save (Psa 44.4–8), describe their humiliation in exile (Psa 44.9–16), claim their innocence and lament the injustice of their current situation (Psa 44.17–22), and cry for vindication (Psa 44.23–26).
we have heard . . . of all you did: The story of redemption encompasses the story of God’s favor and power in his past acts of rescue (see Psa 78.1–4; see also Psa 105.1–106).
God drove out the pagan nations during the conquests recorded in Joshua.
Though the Israelites used swords and other weapons (Psa 44.6), they would have lost their battles without the light of the Lord’s favor (see Psa 18.25–29; Psa 27.1; Psa 89.15).
God’s people feel confident about his mighty acts; he was with them in the past, and he is their king in the present.
The people have experienced defeat (Psa 44.9–12), so they understand suffering and disgrace (Psa 44.13–16).
scattered us among the nations: This probably refers to the Exile (see Psa 51.18–19; Psa 89.38–51; Psa 106.40–47; Psa 137.1–9).
Paul quotes this verse as a parenthetical aside in his list of things that cannot separate us from Christ’s love (Rom 8.36).
In the end, God’s people can turn to the Lord and trust him for rescue. Their petition for God to remedy their situation is as strong as their lament about God’s rejection.
Wake up: Biblical authors often call for God’s attention in a crisis (Psa 35.23; Psa 44.23; Psa 73.20; Psa 80.2; Mar 4.38).

This psalm celebrates a royal wedding; it might have been sung on many occasions and not just at one wedding. As God’s representative, the king carried the responsibility of dispensing justice and maintaining order in God’s world (see Psa 2.1–12).
Psa 45.1 The tune “Lilies” is no longer known (see also Psa 69.1–36).

This general description of the king’s symbolic status anticipates his permanent legacy (Psa 45.16). That the Lord has blessed him and charged him to bear God’s attributes is symbolized by his handsome appearance and gracious words.
The psalmist expounds on the royal splendor the king showed when fighting his enemies.
Glory and majesty belong to the Lord (Psa 96.6; Psa 111.3).
As God’s agent of truth, humility, and justice (see Psa 72.1–2, Psa 72.4, Psa 72.7), the king can carry out awe-inspiring deeds (Psa 65.5; Psa 96.4).

The king is like a god among humans; he is anointed by God, he has received a mighty throne, and he dispenses justice as he rules forever. • The writer to the Hebrews applies Psa 45.6–7 to Jesus as he argues that the Son is greater than the angels (Heb 1.8–9).
Justice characterizes God’s rule, as it should characterize the king’s administration.
Fine spices mixed with oil create distinctive perfumes. • The king’s palaces were wood paneled with ivory inlays (cp. Psa 6.4; Amo 3.15).
Marriages often sealed diplomatic connections between kings; the women became part of the harem (see 1Ki 11.1–3).

The bride is a representative of the king. Powerful people and nations try to gain her favor in order to get close to the king. This is a great honor, and she is encouraged to give herself fully to her new position.
The princess of Tyre: Israel traded with Tyre, a powerful city-state. The noblest woman of the city bears a wedding gift to her counterpart, the new queen, who represents an honored kingdom.

This psalm of Zion celebrates God’s special presence in Jerusalem (see also Psa 48.1–14, Psa 76.1–12, Psa 87.1–7, Psa 122.1–9), inviting confidence in the Lord because the citizens of Zion enjoy his protection.
Psa 46.1 sung by soprano voices: Hebrew according to alamoth (“maidens”; see also study note on 1 Chr 1Ch 15.20). In worship, a choir or a group of instrumentalists performed this hymn.
Even when faced with natural disasters, the citizens of Zion express no fear.
The strong city where God dwells protects its inhabitants. They enjoy the river flowing inside the city. This river contrasts with the turbulent waters (the powers of the nations) outside the city.
Like the streams flowing through Eden, this river brings the water of life, restoration, and healing (Psa 36.8–9; see Gen 2.10; Eze 47.1–23; Rev 22.2).
From the very break of day: In the ancient Near East, enemies attacked cities during the day; even during the most dangerous times, the Lord will protect the place where his name dwells.

People and nations live in chaos, characterized by opportunism (Psa 83.2), busyness (Psa 39.6), and noise. These people shake, totter, and crumble, unlike the city of God (cp. Psa 15.5). In contrast, when the godly feel disturbed, they cry out for God’s help (Psa 42.5, Psa 42.11; Psa 43.5; Psa 55.17).
This refrain reminds readers of the identity of the God of Zion. • among us: Hebrew ‘immanu, part of the name Immanuel, “God with us” (Isa 7.14; Isa 8.8; Mat 1.23).
This invitation to trust in the Lord offers a perspective on God’s interactions with human powers.
Israel saw the Lord’s glorious works in the wilderness (Psa 107.24; Psa 111.2), but the wicked, who have no concern for them (Psa 28.5), are left desolate (Psa 73.19).

A message directly from the Lord confirms the authenticity of the psalmist’s vision (see also Psa 12.5–6; Psa 32.8). • know that I am God: The Lord will do what he promises (Isa 45.3; Isa 49.23; Isa 60.16). • God will be exalted (Psa 47.1–9; Isa 6.1); he will judge the nations and rescue his people (see Psa 57.11; Psa 89.13; Psa 108.5–6; Psa 118.16).

This psalm celebrates God’s kingship over all the earth; it tells of God’s victory in dealing with Israel and the nations. Both Israel (Psa 47.3–4) and the nations (Psa 47.9) participate in God’s kingdom.
As the sovereign king over the nations, God requires praise.
People clap their hands in praise and recognition of marvelous deeds (Psa 47.3–4; see Psa 98.8; Isa 55.12; cp. Nah 3.19).
The Lord made Israel victorious, especially under David (see Psa 18.40–50). God’s mighty deeds of redemption manifest his love for Israel.

Jacob’s descendants: Jacob was the father of all Israelites (Gen 32.28); the name Jacob often represents the nation of Israel. • God loves and commits himself to Jacob (see Psa 78.68; Psa 127.2; see Rom 11.28).
The psalmist portrays the Lord as returning to heaven, having accomplished his victories. For a portrayal of his descent, see Psa 18.9–16.
trumpets: Or rams’ horns (see Psa 81.3). At times, rams’ horns were sounded in celebration (Psa 98.5–6; 2Ki 11.14; 1Ch 15.28).
People from all the earth (see Psa 96.1–3) will worship God.

This song of Zion (see also Psa 46.1–11, Psa 76.1–12, Psa 87.1–7, Psa 122.1–9) explicitly views Jerusalem (Zion) as the city of the Great King where the godly find protection (Psa 48.1–3). God rules from Zion in faithfulness, righteousness, and justice, and he inspires his subjects with confidence and joy (Psa 48.9–11). They commit themselves to seeing the glory of Zion for themselves so that they can tell the next generation about it (Psa 48.8, Psa 48.12–14).
God dwells in Zion to protect it from all enemies (see Psa 46.5).
The ships of Tarshish, built for long voyages, represent human accomplishment (see also 2Ch 9.21; Isa 2.16). Their destruction might be the event mentioned in 1Ki 22.48.
The psalmist joyfully celebrates the Lord’s presence in the midst of the community, reflecting on the faithfulness, righteousness, and justice of God’s rule.
towers . . . fortified walls . . . citadels: These structures provide a visual tour of Zion’s strength.

No one is like God (Psa 35.10; Psa 71.19; Psa 86.8; Psa 89.6, Psa 89.8; Psa 113.5; see Isa 40.18, Isa 40.25). He is the shepherd King (Psa 95.7) who will guide (see Psa 5.8; Psa 23.2) the sheep of his flock (Psa 77.20).

In this wisdom psalm, a wise teacher warns against enemies, whom he portrays as living a rich lifestyle and caring only for themselves (Psa 49.5–9). They cannot keep anyone alive, least of all themselves, even in their memories (Psa 49.10–12). Like fattened animals, they are led to slaughter (Psa 49.14–20).
The wisdom teacher invites everyone to the hall of wisdom; he promises to instruct with a proverb and a riddle.
Anyone who will listen can gain wisdom (Pro 1.5, Pro 1.8, Pro 1.33).
The teacher used both proverbs and riddles for instruction in wisdom (see Pro 1.5–6).
If enemies who live for material rewards cannot sustain themselves, how can they give life to others?
The teacher brings wisdom through irony. Everyone dies, and even those with estates named after them will be forgotten.
The teachers of false wisdom cannot rescue themselves from death. Only God has that power.
The wicked might have rich, luxurious lives, but they forget that they cannot avoid death.
God appears as judge to remind the godly and the ungodly in turn that outward performance of sacrificial rituals and recitation of the law are worthless without thankfulness, repentance, and justice.
The whole universe must pay attention when God approaches to bring justice into the world.

The Lord is coming to bring righteousness. This hope encourages his faithful people, but those who have been unfaithful will not experience blessing when the heavens above and earth below testify against them (cp. Deu 30.19; Deu 31.28; Deu 32.1; Isa 1.2). The Lord comes to restore order to the world (Psa 5.8; Psa 22.31; Psa 33.5; Psa 40.9; Psa 50.6; Psa 71.16; Psa 97.6).
The psalmist delivers a message against those who regard the sacrificial rituals as more important than having a proper heart attitude.
Unlike pagan gods, God does not need food; instead, he wants his people to serve him with a right heart (Psa 50.14–15).
I own the cattle on a thousand hills: God has no needs; he possesses everything.

Thankfulness means looking beyond self-interest to express gratitude for God’s blessings (see Psa 51.15–17; Psa 54.6). • True sacrifice requires offering one’s self to the glory of God (Psa 50.23; Rom 12.1–2).
God’s response to his people’s cry is to rescue them.
This message is against the wicked, who only pretend to listen to God.
my discipline . . . my words: The wicked may observe rituals, but they reject more important matters such as justice, mercy, and faithfulness (cp. Mat 23.23–24).
Because he is patient, God remained silent.
The wicked will experience God’s justice, while the godly will see God’s everlasting salvation.
God will tear the wicked apart like a lion tearing its prey (Isa 5.29; Isa 31.4; Eze 19.3; cp. Psa 7.2; Psa 22.13).

These psalms of David share a common thread in their reflection on the experience of evil. In Psa 51.1–19, the psalmist confesses the evil he has done and asks God’s forgiveness. Psa 52.1–64 lament specific evils that David experienced. A song of praise (Psa 65.1–13) brings David’s laments to an end.

This moving prayer for restoration asks for God’s favor, mercy, forgiveness, and cleansing. Out of a broken spirit, the psalmist confesses and accepts responsibility for his sin (Psa 51.3–6), then petitions God to remove his guilt and renew him inwardly (Psa 51.7–12). The psalmist then recommits himself to a lifestyle of wisdom and joy in the service of God and others (Psa 51.13–17).
Psa 51.1 regarding the time Nathan . . . Bathsheba: See 2Sa 11.1–27. The text of the psalm contains no explicit reference to this event.
The repentant offender has nothing to offer God. He needs God’s favor, mercy, forgiveness, and blessing before he can experience renewal and restoration.

A prayer for God’s mercy and kindness is part of the genre of lament. Sometimes the plea comes from the psalmist’s acknowledgment of his weakness and sin, as here (see also Psa 6.2; Psa 9.13; Psa 25.16; Psa 31.9; Psa 41.4, Psa 41.10). At other times, it arises from the psalmist’s commitment to the Lord (see Psa 26.11; Psa 27.7; Psa 119.29, Psa 119.58, Psa 119.132). In each case, God’s mercy brings an inner renewal.
Wash me . . . Purify me: The psalmist prays for cleansing and release from the guilt of his sin (Psa 51.7; see Psa 26.6; Isa 1.16, Isa 1.18; Isa 4.4).
The psalmist accepts the consequences of his sin against God. He knows that there is nothing good in him unless God renews his life.

Against . . . you alone: This is hyperbole—the psalmist knows he also sinned against human beings (2Sa 11.2–4, 2Sa 11.15–17), but his offense against God is more important. He expects God to rebuke him and will accept whatever verdict God renders (see Rom 3.4).
I was born a sinner: The psalmist is not making excuses but is acknowledging the depth of his sinfulness. From the time we are conceived, we all share in the human condition of sinfulness.
Purify me from my sins (literally Purify me with the hyssop branch; see Exo 12.22; Lev 14.4; Joh 19.29; Heb 9.19): The psalmist depends on God to purify and renew him (see Isa 1.18).
Regaining joy is a gracious gift from God. • you have broken me: The psalmist’s whole being feels broken (Psa 6.2; cp. Psa 34.20).
God’s Spirit renews and recreates the human spirit.
A loyal spirit yields the inner qualities of constancy and perseverance.
your Holy Spirit: Only the power of the Holy Spirit can change the human will to make it “loyal” (Psa 51.10) and “willing to obey” (Psa 51.12).
As he learns from his sin and its consequences, the psalmist wants to teach others.
shedding blood: This idiom includes any injustice, not just homicide (Psa 9.12; Psa 58.10; see 2Sa 11.14–26; cp. Isa 1.15–17).

rebuild the walls of Jerusalem: These verses were probably added as a prayer for national restoration after the Exile (see Psa 42.1–43); the entire community in exile identified with the spirit of the psalm.
Sacrifices offered in the right spirit come from a heart that is right with God and with others (see Psa 15.2–5; Psa 24.3–6; Psa 50.14; Mat 5.23–24).

Wicked people use words to destroy relationships and communities. They foolishly think that they can be heroes by their words (Psa 52.1–4), but their fate suddenly overtakes them (Psa 52.5–7). In contrast, the godly renew their commitment to the Lord (Psa 52.8–9) and find their future secure in him.
Psa 52.1 This psalm refers to an incident in 1Sa 21.1–10; 1Sa 22.9–10. The accuser, Doeg the Edomite, is a paradigm of evil.

Liars foolishly deceive themselves by thinking that they can be heroes by their words. They believe themselves innocent of any charges of evildoing, though they love evil and cause destruction. Those who speak curses, sarcasm, bitterness, arrogant boasting, and deceptions (Psa 31.18; Psa 34.13; Psa 59.7, Psa 59.12; Psa 120.2–3; Psa 140.3, Psa 140.9) bring about chaos, alienation, and destruction (Jam 3.5). Their sharp words cut like swords and daggers (Psa 55.21; Psa 57.4; Psa 64.3), the fangs of a snake (Psa 140.3), or a razor.
Deceptive speech changes one’s character.
God’s judgment on the wicked will come suddenly and forcibly. The godly rejoice in God’s justice, not in the misfortunes of the wicked.
God will strike the wicked down like a pagan altar, idol, or unclean vessel (Exo 34.13; Lev 11.35; 2Ki 10.27).
In Hebrew, the verbs here translated see and be amazed sound almost alike.

The psalmist commits himself to a life of trust in the Lord. • An olive tree lives a long time when cared for (Psa 1.3; Psa 128.3). The psalmist desires to be close to the Lord, his Savior and the source of his blessing (Psa 18.6; Psa 23.6).
This psalm parallels Psa 14.1–7, differing only in verse 5.
Paul uses the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the depravity of all people (Rom 3.10–12).
scatter the bones: Israel’s enemies would suffer shameful defeat and lack the peaceful rest of a decent burial (cp. Psa 141.7; 2Ki 9.10; Jer 8.1–2; Eze 6.5).

In this individual lament, occasioned by violent and godless people (Psa 54.3), the psalmist turns to God in prayer and maintains his focus on God’s help (Psa 54.4). He prays for God to save him from evil and to judge his enemies (Psa 54.5, Psa 54.7).
Psa 54.1 This psalm refers to the account of 1Sa 23.19–20, when the Ziphites were bent on violence.

The strangers were alienated from the covenant community (see Psa 109.11; Pro 5.10). • Proud and violent people hold no regard for God or for other people (see Psa 35.11, Psa 35.25; Psa 86.14; Pro 11.16).
In anticipation of God’s response, the mood of the psalm changes from gloom to thanksgiving.
A voluntary offering is a sacrifice of praise. Sacrifices of praise are the kind of offering God most desires (see Psa 50.14–15, Psa 50.23).

The psalmist is faced with adversaries whose leader is a former friend (Psa 55.12–14), and he is overwhelmed with anguish. He turns to the Lord in prayer and commits himself to the Lord for redress (Psa 55.22–23). Jesus experienced similar suffering when his friend (Judas) betrayed him. He also experienced the answer to the psalmist’s prayer: (1) by taking the place of the wicked and receiving their judgment (Isa 53.7–9), and (2) by committing himself to the Father, who rescued (Luk 23.46) and rewarded him (Isa 53.10–12).
The occasion for this prayer is an attack by an enemy.
In the experience of deep anguish, the psalmist confesses that his adversity has become unbearable and he seeks an escape.
The psalmist’s enemy was once a friend; memories of that close relationship bring him pain (see Psa 31.11).
God is good and faithful, but the psalmist’s enemies and so-called friend are deceitful and wicked.
The psalmist commits all his cares to the LORD.
To die young means that one fails to experience God’s full blessing (cp. Pro 3.2, Pro 3.16).
This individual lament moves from petition to confidence two times (Psa 56.1–4, Psa 56.5–13).
Psa 56.1 David was seized by Philistines concerned about his loyalties and brought before King Achish (1Sa 21.10–15).
mere mortals: Or mere flesh, in contrast to the immortal and infinitely more powerful God (see Isa 2.22).
The psalmist specifies his charge against his attackers as he prays for their evil to cease.
The psalmist makes a play on the Hebrew words translated sorrows (Hebrew nod) and bottle (Hebrew no’d).
mere mortals (Hebrew ’adam): The psalm also uses two other words for man: ’enosh (“people,” Psa 56.1) and basar (“mere mortals,” Psa 56.4). All express the ideas of mortality and finitude.
The light of God’s goodness and salvation will replace the darkness of death (see Psa 18.25–29; Psa 27.1).

The psalmist’s cry for mercy and protection quickly turns into an affirmation of trust and confidence in the Lord (Psa 57.1–4). When the wicked fall into their own traps (Psa 57.6), the psalmist will praise the Lord (Psa 57.7–10).
Psa 57.1 David . . . fled from Saul and went into the cave: See 1Sa 22.1 or Psa 24.1–8.
shadow of your wings: As a bird protects its young, God protects the one who trusts in him (see Psa 17.8).

God Most High (Hebrew Elohim-Elyon) is a generic title for God, who is more powerful than all real or imagined supernatural beings (see Psa 91.1; Psa 97.9; Gen 14.18–22). • who will fulfill his purpose: Or who will end my [trouble], or who deals kindly with me.

These verses are a prayer for rescue from powerful enemies. The metaphor of fierce lions describes human enemies; the psalmist feels unable to escape them without God’s intervention (see also Psa 35.11–21; Psa 124.6).
This verse is repeated in Psa 57.11 and Psa 108.5. • God’s glory—his manifest presence that excludes all evil (Psa 8.1; Psa 19.1–4; Psa 24.7)—will fill the whole created order (Isa 6.3).
This section is repeated with a few modifications in Psa 108.1–5.
The psalmist is confident that God will end the night of evil (cp. Psa 56.13).
God’s glory extends to the whole universe, as will praise for his unfailing love and faithfulness.

The administration of justice is a mark of good government. God expects nothing less from his people. The psalmist condemns Israel’s leaders for abusing their power, and he calls on the Lord to rain down his curses upon the wicked. The demonstration of divine justice will reassure the godly that God is just.
The administrators of justice were furthering their own interests rather than those of the needy. The absence of justice gradually resulted in a violent society.

rulers (or gods): This designation was used for high officials and administrators of justice (Psa 82.1, Psa 82.6). Elsewhere, it might refer to angelic creatures (Psa 89.7) or to the gods of the nations (Psa 82.1; Dan 11.36).
All human beings are born sinners (see Psa 51.5); however, whereas the wicked indulge their sinful nature, the godly fight against it (Rom 7.19–23; Jam 4.1–10).
Venom here means poisonous speech (see Psa 140.3).
The psalmist calls on God to break the destructive power of the wicked.
When moving over dry ground, snails dry up.
God’s judgment will come suddenly. The certainty of vindication brings joy to the godly.
Vindication is the reward of those who live for God.
The psalmist laments the power of enemies who conspire with other nations.
Psa 59.1 the time Saul sent soldiers to watch David’s house: See 1Sa 19.11–18.
Protect me (or place me on high): When surrounded by evil, the godly pray for God to set them apart for himself and protect them.
The psalmist asks God to show the treacherous, deceptive, and wicked traitors no mercy (see Psa 25.2).
The wicked threaten like vicious dogs, but the Lord responds with scorn.
The psalmist prays that the wicked will be forced to endure the same agonizing pain they have caused.
The wicked will go unsatisfied, but the psalmist will praise the Lord’s power and unfailing love.
The psalmist laments a national defeat and cries out to God for rescue.

Psa 60.1 useful for teaching: This psalm was taught to young people as part of their education. • regarding the time: See 2Sa 8.13–14. • Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah refer to the Arameans of northwest Mesopotamia and Syria (see study note on Gen Gen 24.10). • The tune “Lily of the Testimony” is unknown today.
When God’s people experience his discipline, they affirm their loyalty and await God’s answer.

wine (Hebrew yayin) that sent us reeling: Yayin, the generic Hebrew term meaning “wine,” is often associated with drunkenness (2Sa 13.28; Isa 5.11; Isa 28.7–8; cp. Psa 104.15; Deu 14.26; Isa 55.1); it symbolized God’s judgment of the wicked (Psa 75.8; Jer 51.7).

God raised a banner over his people to serve as a rallying point and as a source of pride and confidence. • The fear of God that leads to wisdom (Psa 111.10) is not weakness; it provides the perspective and strength required to do what is right.
This section is repeated verbatim in Psa 108.6–13.
The psalmist prays for rescue based on the special relationship between God and his people.
The Lord responds with a message of promise. He shares his land with his people as spoils of war.
Shechem and Succoth represent Israel’s heartland.

Destroying a defeated invader’s capital (the fortified city) would help to ensure that they would not attack again. The capital of Edom was Bozrah, located to the southeast of Israel. Only God could grant victory.
In these royal prayers, the psalmist longs for God’s presence. All three psalms concern themselves with the king’s security.
The lamenting psalmist petitions God to protect him and lead him into his presence (Psa 61.4–5). He prays for God to extend and protect the king’s rule and makes vows to praise God.
the ends of the earth: This expression has the connotation of a cry that comes from a place far away from God. • The psalmist’s heart is overwhelmed with deep anguish.

The poet longs for God’s presence and seeks entrance into God’s home on earth for divine protection and care. To be received into God’s sanctuary (literally tent) is the greatest good (see Psa 15.1; Psa 23.6; Psa 24.3–6). The Hebrew word translated sanctuary recalls the Tabernacle and the tent that David built for the Ark (1Ch 15.1). See also study note on John Joh 1.14. • The shelter of your wings symbolizes God’s protection and care (see Psa 9.9; Psa 17.8).

you have heard my vows: The psalmist’s vows might also be a part of ceremonial sacrifices (Psa 66.13–15; Psa 76.11; Psa 116.14, Psa 116.18). He praises and thanks God for his rescue. • The inheritance refers to the promise of the land (see Psa 60.1–12), the sacredness of the Temple, the joy of God’s presence (Psa 119.111), or any similar reward (Psa 16.6; Psa 37.9, Psa 37.11, Psa 37.18, Psa 37.22, Psa 37.29, Psa 37.34; Psa 127.3).

This psalm expresses confidence in the king and offers prayer for him. The king rests in God despite his difficulties. Although his deceptive and powerful adversaries push hard against him, he remains undaunted. He encourages himself and his people to trust in God and to see their human adversaries from God’s perspective, where they appear frail, fleeting, and deceptive (Psa 62.9).
Psa 62.1 Jeduthun: See 1Ch 25.1; also in Psa 39.1–13 and Psa 77.1–20.
Theme: Trusting God in the Psalms
The enemies desire to topple the king with lies and cunning.
My high position refers to the royal throne.
The psalmist encourages himself and others to place their hope in God.
Unlike God, humans are transient beings. Even when they thrive, their prosperity is fleeting.
not what they appear to be: People often try to look stronger and better than they are.
The crime of extortion means using intimidation and threats to make others give up what is theirs, while stealing is taking what belongs to others.
Strength and unfailing love remain in balance only in God. He cares for his people by ridding the world of evildoers (see Psa 1.6).

The king longs for God’s presence so vividly that he eats, drinks, and sees God’s goodness. Though worn out and harassed by the wicked, the king sees God, and this animates him with praise. God becomes his life (Psa 63.3), while the wicked perish (Psa 63.9).

Together, soul and whole body refer to a person’s entire being. • parched and weary land: When David was living in the desert, he also found himself in a spiritual wasteland, separated from God’s people and the sanctuary.
The psalmist remembers that he had found God to be present in his sanctuary (see Psa 18.6; Psa 61.4; Psa 62.5, Psa 62.11–12).
better than life itself: The highest quality of life is found in relationship with God (see Psa 4.7; Psa 63.5; Pro 16.8).

The psalmist reflects and meditates on God’s presence through the night. In the absence of light, God is the light. The quietness of the night and the longing for dawn provide time to focus on the true significance of life with the Lord.
Meditating on God requires focused awareness, concentration, thought, and reflection (see Psa 1.2).
The wicked were plotting to destroy the psalmist’s life through deception and lies, but they would meet their end. • The depths of the earth refers to the place of the dead.

Wild jackals are associated with desolation and abandonment (Isa 13.20–22; Isa 34.10–15; Jer 9.11; Jer 49.33; Jer 51.37; Lam 5.18; Mal 1.3). The wicked will not receive honor in death; their bodies will be left to scavenging animals (Ecc 6.3; Jer 22.18–19; Jer 36.29–30).

This lament decries the destructive plots and arrogant attitude of the wicked (Psa 64.1–6). The psalmist turns to God in prayer and takes heart in God’s justice because whatever the wicked do will be undone by the righteous judge. The godly will rejoice and grow in wisdom as they reflect on God’s mighty acts.
These verses form a prayer for rescue from bold and powerful liars.
their tongues . . . bitter words: Liars use their speech to kill. This description might also refer to practicing magic.
The enemies create a perfect plan to harm the innocent without getting caught. • Human beings will sink to unthinkable depths with evil words, acts, or plans (Psa 83.3; see Jer 17.9).
What God does is righteous. God undoes what is wicked and pays the wicked back with what they planned for others.
This psalm recounts the reasons why all people should praise and revere God for his almighty power and merciful care for his universe.
Praise is the appropriate response to God’s majestic deeds in redemption (Psa 65.3–5) and in nature (Psa 65.5–13).
God alone deserves praise and is worthy to have vows made to him.
All of us means all humans.
you forgive: God graciously removes the guilt of sin (see Psa 32.5).

those you choose to bring near: This includes people from Israel and from other nations. • Only those whom God sees as blameless live in his holy courts (Psa 15.1–5 and Psa 24.1–10). • At the Temple, God’s earthly palace, all nations can gather to experience God’s holy presence. No structure can separate humans from God (see Rev 21.22).

God brought order to the mountains, the raging oceans, and the pounding waves (see Psa 95.4–5; Psa 104.6–9). • The psalmist compares the chaotic forces of nature with the rebellion of the nations (see Psa 2.1–12; Psa 33.6–11; Psa 46.6).
All over the world (Job 38.13; see Psa 50.1–3), people should stand in awe of the Lord.
The created order provides clear evidence of God’s power (Psa 65.6–8). He shows his love by maintaining nature. Everything praises the Lord as all the parts fit together harmoniously.

The river of God and all rivers demonstrate God’s victorious power and goodness through the order in nature and the regularity of the harvests (see Psa 1.3; Psa 36.8; Psa 46.4; Eze 47.6–12; Zec 14.8; Rev 22.1).
Nature bursts out in praise of the Creator (see Psa 79.13; Psa 96.11–13; Psa 148.3–5, Psa 148.7–12; Isa 55.12–13).
This anonymous psalm includes two hymns (Psa 66.1–12, Psa 66.13–20) that praise God for his redemption.
The psalmist exhorts nature to join in a mighty chorus to praise God’s glory, name, and power.
The glory of his name represents the perfection of God’s character.
God conquers his enemies (see Psa 18.44; Psa 59.11; Psa 81.15).
The story of the Exodus and God’s victory over the sea evokes responses of astonishment (Psa 66.5) and worship (Psa 66.6). God works miracles . . . for people in order to redeem them for himself.
God’s power brings redemption. The same word occurs in Psa 65.6 for God’s power in creation (see also Psa 80.2).
The orderly lives of the redeemed reflect the order of God’s world. The Lord protects them from evil and purifies them.
God guides his people into wisdom and away from folly (Psa 17.5; Psa 37.31; Psa 121.3).
You have tested us, O God: As the silversmith heats silver to remove the dross, God’s discipline removes sin from his people (see Psa 12.6).
God decrees and permits the many trying circumstances his people experience.
Then you put a leader over us: Or You made people ride over our heads. This expression possibly refers to a foreign ruler who kept the Israelites in submission.
Vows often included sacrifices of thanksgiving, including burnt offerings (see Psa 20.3; Psa 40.6; Psa 50.8; Psa 51.19).
The private testimony in the conclusion of the psalm parallels the public praise of its opening (Psa 66.1–4).
Confession leads to restoration (see Psa 32.5).

In this anonymous prayer for God’s blessing, the psalmist addresses the knowledge and worship of God among the nations (cp. Psa 64.9; Psa 65.8). The prayer requests that God’s name be kept holy and that his kingdom come (cp. Mat 6.9–13).
This prayer is based on the priestly blessing found in Num 6.24–26. God’s goodness to Israel affects his reputation among the nations (see Psa 96.1–3).

God’s international reputation leads to his praise among the nations (see Psa 138.4), whose turmoil and rebelliousness will cease when they join Israel in praise of God. • One God rules over all, and the nations will give thanks for God’s just rule (see Psa 67.4).
God brings the ultimate justice that human beings desire (Psa 96.10; Psa 98.9).
