Bountiful harvests are evidence of God’s blessing (Gen 26.12; Isa 30.23). • all over the world: See Psa 2.8; Psa 96.1–3. • All will fear him, joining with Israel to acknowledge the God of Israel.

This prayer for God’s victorious rule traces God’s march from Sinai to Zion (Psa 68.7, Psa 68.16–18, Psa 68.24). He rescued the nation of Israel from Egypt, guided it through the wilderness, brought it into the Promised Land, and established his kingdom. He is a caring and victorious God, whose nature is unchanging. Therefore, the godly hope and rejoice in the prospect of God’s universal dominion.
These verses form a prayer for God to rise up and scatter his enemies, as he did when Israel entered the Promised Land (cp. Num 10.35–36; Jos 6.1–12).
Both smoke and wax represent a transitory existence (Psa 22.12–18; Psa 37.20; Psa 102.3).
The lot of the godly contrasts with that of the wicked (see Psa 1.6).
The psalmist praises God’s powerful and compassionate reign.

him who rides the clouds: This is an ancient description of Baal, a Canaanite deity. The psalmist applies it to the LORD as the true “Rider of the Clouds” (see Psa 68.33; Psa 104.3). God wields power over the clouds and the rain.

God, the Father of all marginalized and needy people, shows them compassion and protects their rights (see Psa 10.14, Psa 10.18; Psa 69.33; Psa 82.3). • Like his dwelling, the Lord is holy. The supreme example of the holy God coming down to rescue humanity is Jesus Christ.
God released Israel from slavery in Egypt (Exo 20.2; see Psa 69.33), and he still sets the prisoners free. • The sun-scorched desert represents alienation from God and separation from blessing.
The earth trembled as in an earthquake (see Exo 19.18). • the heavens poured down rain: Wells in the desert and rain showers in Canaan supplied an abundance of water.
a great army (or a host of women) brings: The Hebrew suggests women singers caroling the good news of victory (see Psa 68.25; Exo 15.20).
The seminomadic pastoral people who lived among the sheepfolds were surprised to receive silver and gold carvings from the battle.
The Almighty (Hebrew Shaddai) is an ancient designation for God (see Psa 91.1; Gen 17.1). • The identification of Mount Zalmon is uncertain; it was possibly a mountain in Bashan (see Psa 68.15).

Bashan is a plateau northeast of Jerusalem and east of the Sea of Galilee that was known for its woods and pastureland (see Psa 22.12; Isa 2.13). The mountains might have included Mount Hermon to the north of the plateau or Mount Zalmon, which might be Jebel ed-Druze on the east.

Why do you look with envy? Bashan is physically much more impressive than the mountains around Jerusalem, but it was not the home of the Lord. Only Mount Zion enjoyed the privilege of providing God’s dwelling place.
Chariots, the ultimate weapon of the armed forces in the psalmist’s day, are an image of the Lord’s power to grant victory (Psa 20.7; Psa 44.3).

When you ascended to the heights: The Most High established his reign victoriously in Zion. • a crowd of captives . . . gifts: This is an image of a victorious ruler leading the victory march after battle. Paul applied this image to Jesus Christ (Eph 4.8–13).
The Divine Warrior cares for his people like a shepherd; the people praise him.
Like a caring father or a shepherd, God carries his people in his arms (see Psa 55.22; Psa 68.5–6).
God will smash the heads of his enemies: Cp. Gen 3.15.
God will deal with all enemies, whether from high places (represented by Bashan) or low (the depths of the sea).
A great company joins together in the pilgrimage to Zion.
The people pray for God’s success and for victory over the enemy nations (Psa 68.1–3).
The conquered kings will bring gifts to the Lord.
Hostile and rebellious people delight in warfare and insurrection (see Psa 2.1–3).
The psalmist calls for the people to praise God, who is victorious over his enemies.
The term kingdoms of the earth includes all nations and power structures.
When the Lord demonstrates his power, majesty, and strength against the nations, he strengthens his people (see Psa 96.4–6).

These last four psalms of Book Two contrast with the psalms describing God’s mighty acts in creation and in redemption, capped by God’s march to Zion (Psa 65.1–68). Psa 69.1–71 portray the king’s anguish, and Psa 72.1–20 responds with a prayer for God to bless the king.
In this individual lament, the poet expresses his vulnerability, humiliation, and overwhelming pain, asking God to vindicate him for the sake of the righteous.
Psa 69.1 to the tune “Lilies”: Psa 45.1–17 also notes this tune, but Psa 45.1–17 celebrates the glory of kingship, whereas Psa 69.1–36 is the cry of a tired king who feels abandoned by the Lord.
The psalmist sees himself as almost drowning but still surviving chaotic forces and alienation from God (see Psa 42.7; Psa 69.14, Psa 69.15; Isa 8.8).
John applied this lament to Jesus (Joh 15.25).
The psalmist confesses his sins and prays that God’s response to him will encourage others in similar conditions to place their hope in the Lord.
Mistreated and abandoned by family, friends, and community, the psalmist turns to the Lord for comfort, relief (Psa 69.13–18), and redress (Psa 69.22–28).

Though the psalmist concerns himself with God and all that is holy, insults have been his earthly reward. This verse was later applied to Jesus’ anger at the Temple’s money changers (Joh 2.17) and to his undeserved suffering (Rom 15.3).
When the psalmist denies himself normal comforts to seek God in prayer, the wicked ridicule him.
The psalmist’s only recourse is to pray for rescue and relief from his enemies.
Alone and misunderstood, the psalmist confesses that he cannot bear his doubts. His heart has been broken by his problems.
sour wine for my thirst: This description applies to Jesus’ suffering (Mat 27.34, Mat 27.48; Luk 23.36; Joh 19.28–29).
The psalmist wants God to transfer his suffering (Psa 69.3) to his enemies. Paul applied these words to the unbelieving Jews of his day (Rom 11.9–10).
Peter quoted this verse after the death of Judas Iscariot (Act 1.20).
Erase their names from the Book of Life: Cp. Psa 1.5–6; Psa 9.5; Rev 3.5; Rev 20.15; Rev 21.22–27.
The psalmist prays that his pain will turn to praise.
Making a vow often included a sacrifice (Psa 20.3; Psa 51.19; cp. Psa 50.13–14; Psa 51.16).
despise: See Psa 22.24; cp. Mat 25.36; Heb 13.3.
The psalmist prays for Zion, offering a new petition from a new circumstance. He applies the prayer (Psa 69.1–33) to the desperate condition of Judah (see Psa 51.18–19).
God’s people will inherit the land because the wicked will perish (see Psa 37.8–9).
This psalm, nearly identical to Psa 40.13–17, contains an urgency (Psa 70.1, Psa 70.5) that fits with the surrounding psalms (cp. Psa 69.17; Psa 71.12).
Psa 70.1 asking God to remember him: The meaning of this phrase is unknown (also found in Psa 38.1).

This untitled lament by an aging believer is more of a confession of confidence and hope than the cry of someone abandoned by God. The psalmist experienced God’s power and protection in his youth (Psa 71.5–8) and now prays for rescue from the adversaries who stalk him in his old age (Psa 71.9–13). Even in the midst of his peril, he continues to tell of God’s past faithfulness and looks forward with hope to a time when he can testify to the next generation that God is faithful and righteous.
The poet has learned to acknowledge God as the reliable rock who will do what is right toward him and his oppressors. See also Psa 31.1–3.
The psalmist has trusted God throughout his life (see Psa 22.9).

The aging believer turns to the Lord for hope. As questions from his adversaries get under his skin and his own strength fails, he asks God to answer his prayers. He does not seek answers to prayer for himself but so that he can tell the story to the next generation.
The poet prays for continued fellowship with God (see Psa 9.10; Psa 51.11). In his weakness, he needs the Lord’s strength even more (see Psa 143.7).
In their plotting, the psalmist’s enemies take counsel and scheme together (Psa 2.2; Psa 21.11; Psa 31.13; Psa 35.4; Psa 63.9–10).
The psalmist contrasts his own goodness with his enemies’ evil; he centers his life in the Lord, even during hard times (see Psa 9.17–18; Psa 27.13–14).
God’s righteous character provides encouragement and strength in the midst of suffering. The wounded psalmist confesses faith in God’s ability to transform his misery and weakness into abundant life.
lift me up from the depths: The psalmist hopes for the renewal of an abundant earthly life. This later became grounds for belief in the resurrection of the dead.

Being assured of God’s comfort also assures the poet of God’s presence, care, and goodness (Psa 23.4, Psa 23.6; Psa 86.17). God’s comfort enhances the psalmist’s sense of being alive (see Psa 119.50).
As he awaits God’s rescue, the psalmist prepares himself to declare with instruments and voice that God is faithful and righteous.
Theme: Music in Ancient Israel

This royal psalm closes Book Two, with Psa 72.18–20 functioning as an epilogue to all of Book Two. The psalmist reflects on the prospects of David’s royal line and on Zion (see Psa 46.1–11, Psa 48.1–14). He prays that Israel’s kings will be good and prosperous, extending the Lord’s blessing on his people throughout the whole earth. The surpassing righteousness and dominion sought in this prayer foreshadow the coming of Jesus, the Son of David.
The blessings of justice create a balance in nature, resulting in harmony, prosperity, and fertility.
love of justice . . . righteousness: Kings in the ancient Near East were expected to represent justice; the standard for Israel’s kings was much higher because the Lord was their model.
The administration of justice transforms the earth into fruitfulness, abundance, harmony, and goodness (see Isa 32.16–17).
A just ruler will defend the poor against injustice, rescue them from violence, and bring their oppressors to account for their wrongdoing.

May they fear you: In Hebrew, this clause seems to be a response to the enforcement of justice. The Greek version reads May they endure, which makes this a prayer for longevity (Psa 21.4; Psa 72.15, Psa 72.17).
The administration of justice is refreshing like spring rain, enabling the godly to flourish (see Isa 45.8) like flowers. • until the moon is no more: This phrase means forever (see Psa 89.36–37).

The anointed king will rule over the whole world. Even hostile nations will submit to him. In the ancient Near East, bearing gifts to the king acknowledged his success and his reputation (see 1Ki 10.1–29).

from sea to sea: This phrase represents the whole world. • Solomon’s kingdom extended from the Euphrates River in the east to the Philistine territory in the west (1Ki 4.21; see Psa 80.8–11; Psa 89.19–25), where the Mediterranean Sea appeared to be at the ends of the earth (see Psa 2.8). Everyone will bow before this king, including the desert nomads (Psa 72.9), his enemies, and all the kings of the world (see Mic 7.17).

The western kings of Tarshish came from a major colony in the western basin of the Mediterranean. The eastern kings of Sheba came from an area in southern Arabia, home of the queen of Sheba (1Ki 10.1–29). • Seba was probably located somewhere south of Egypt, perhaps on the western shore of the Red Sea across from Sheba. • The gifts offered to the king represented a tribute and a token of submission.

All kings and all nations must submit to the messianic king. The hope expressed in Psa 2.10–11 will be realized (see Psa 96.1–3; 1Co 15.25) when other leaders and peoples bow before and serve this king.
The anointed king will rescue the needy. He is not only the judge but also a father to the poor (Psa 10.14, Psa 10.17; Psa 68.5).
To rescue the poor means to bring an end to the rule of their oppressors.
Like a father, the king feels pity for those in need (see Mal 3.17).
The just kingdom will be long-lasting and universal. The summary combines the themes of abundance of crops, longevity, tribute of the nations, and the prayer of the nations.
The people will bless him, fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham (Gen 12.3; see Psa 133.3).
the trees of Lebanon: Lebanon was renowned for its lumber (see study note on 2 Chr 2Ch 2.8).
This doxology concludes Book Two of the Psalter.

This parenthetical note ends Book Two, which consists mostly of prayers of David. Books Three to Five were probably compiled after Book Two; they include additional psalms of David (Psa 86.1–17, Psa 101.1–8, Psa 103.1–22, Psa 108.1–110, Psa 122.1–9, Psa 124.1–8, Psa 131.1–3, Psa 133.1–3, Psa 138.1–145).

The apparent prosperity of the wicked (Psa 73.1–28) and God’s apparent rejection of his people (Psa 74.1–23) raise questions about his justice. God is sovereign over the whole world, and he determines the time for judgment (Psa 75.1–10).

This wisdom psalm examines the injustice of the prosperity of the wicked. The psalmist affirms that God is good to the godly but his own experience differs (Psa 73.2–12). Nearly overcome by his doubts (Psa 73.13–16), the psalmist meets the Lord in the sanctuary and gains a perspective that stretches beyond his life and renews his confidence in God (Psa 73.17–26). His disturbing doubts stir a greater passion for truth. He knows that he can trust God and that God will rescue him (Psa 73.27–28).

Psa 73.1 Asaph was a Levitical singer appointed by David (1Ch 6.39); his descendants were singers and instrumentalists (1Ch 15.16–17). Many of the psalms of Asaph (Psa 50.1–23, Psa 73.1–83) were probably written by Asaph’s descendants at a later time in Israel’s history (e.g., Psa 74.1–23).
People whose hearts are pure are renewed by God’s Spirit (Psa 51.10), commit themselves to lives of godliness, keep away from anything that is sinful, and enjoy God’s presence (see Psa 24.3–4).

The poet sees the prosperity of the wicked as unfair (see Psa 72.7) and resents it. • The psalmist’s feet were slipping from the way of wisdom and godliness (see Psa 17.5; Psa 37.31), but God kept him from falling off the trail entirely (Psa 38.16; Psa 66.9; Psa 94.18; Psa 121.3). • when I saw them prosper: Cp. Psa 72.3, Psa 72.7.
The psalmist presents a caricature of the bliss of the wicked (cp. Psa 1.1–6).
The proud adorn themselves with pride and cruelty rather than wisdom (Pro 1.9).
The proud boast, claiming that they own everything and are not subject to anyone (see Psa 2.1–3).
Recognizing the ramifications of his discouragement and doubt, the psalmist turns to the Lord and receives special insight.

These rhetorical questions expect a discouraging “yes” for an answer. The psalmist wonders if godliness has become a meaningless ritual (see Mal 3.14–15). • My heart refers to his whole being. • The psalmist’s pain comes from discipline and rebuke (Psa 39.11; Pro 1.23, Pro 1.25; Pro 12.1).

If the psalmist had verbalized his suspicions about the futility of godly living, he would have discouraged God’s people and given God’s enemies an opportunity to blaspheme (cp. Joh 13.20). Instead, the psalmist internalizes the problem and reflects on it.

At this time, God’s sanctuary was the Temple in Jerusalem. There, in God’s presence, the psalmist receives special insight (cp. Psa 18.6). • God deals with the wicked over the long term. He waits patiently and gives them time to repent (Eze 33.11; 2Pe 3.9); those who do not repent will get what they deserve.
The psalmist’s feelings about the prosperity of the wicked had given him a bitter spirit.
The Lord leads the godly through their troubles and changes their misery into splendor.
Nothing in heaven or on earth is better than being near God.
The psalmist laments the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem (586 BC) with vivid imagery, questions, fresh memories, and a direct appeal for the Lord to act (Psa 74.19–23).
In the aftermath of Jerusalem’s fall, it seemed that God had forgotten his special covenant relationship with his people.
God rejected his people because their sin aroused his anger (Psa 106.34–46). • Like a tender shepherd, God cares for his people, the sheep of his pasture (Psa 23.1–6; Psa 100.3).
The Lord chose and redeemed Israel from Egypt in the Exodus (cp. Exo 15.13). • your own special possession: This is another expression for “your people” (Psa 28.9; Psa 78.62; Psa 94.14; Psa 106.40).
Like a guide, the psalmist points out to the Lord what took place during the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
my king from ages past: The psalmist acknowledges God’s power and his historical bond with Israel (Psa 5.2; Psa 44.4; Psa 84.3).
Leviathan: See Psa 104.26; Job 3.8; Job 41.1, Job 41.12, Job 41.22, Job 41.31; Isa 27.1. Here, the creature’s multiple heads suggest a mythical monster.
springs and streams to gush forth: God provided water in the desert for his people (see Psa 68.8–9; Exo 17.6); he dried up the Red Sea (Exo 14.21) and the Jordan River (Jos 3.17).
The poet urges God to act.

This hymn of thanksgiving includes two direct messages from God that provide assurance of his justice (Psa 75.2–3, Psa 75.10). The Lord rebukes arrogant people who defy him, promising to forcibly humble them (Psa 75.4–8). Together, the community and the psalmist respond with thanksgiving for God’s character (Psa 75.1, Psa 75.9).
The Lord will bring justice in his own time.
The wicked arrogantly defy the heavens—the dwelling place of God. Through their boasting they insist that they are wiser than God.
No creature has the right to rebel against its Creator.
The Lord alone is the Judge, with the power to exalt and humble (see 1Sa 2.7; Luk 1.52).

This psalm appears to celebrate a victory. The victory might have been recent, such as over the Assyrians (see note on Psa 76.1; see also Isa 37.1–38); or the psalm might be recalling God’s great acts of rescue in the past.
Psa 76.1 to be accompanied by stringed instruments: The Greek version reads for the Assyrian.
God’s victory over Zion’s enemies foreshadows his worldwide victory over all his enemies.
God brings an end to the attacks of his enemies (see Psa 46.9).
The psalmist praises God for his achievement and for his glorious majesty.
The victorious king’s splendor, glory, and majesty are greater than anything in the created order (Psa 8.1; Psa 29.4; Psa 111.3).
The needy await their victorious God, while the wicked stand in fear of him.
The word translated feared (Hebrew nora’) is a wordplay on the word translated “glorious” in Psa 76.4 (Hebrew na’or).

The psalmist laments that God has turned away from him, even though he feels innocent. He reflects on his situation (Psa 77.3, Psa 77.6, Psa 77.12) and finds hope (see Psa 25.5) in remembering God’s past deeds (Psa 77.11).
The night provides a special opportunity for prayer and meditation (Psa 77.6, Psa 77.11; see Psa 6.6; Psa 16.7; Psa 17.3; Psa 30.5; Psa 63.6; Psa 119.55, Psa 119.62, Psa 119.148).

I think of God: God’s people inevitably face difficult times, but recalling his mighty acts at the beginning of their relationship assures them of God’s commitment. • Feeling overwhelmed, the psalmist is unable to deal with the crisis (Psa 142.3; Psa 143.4).
As the psalmist meditates at night, he feels so disturbed that he cannot sleep or speak. He has pleasant memories of the past, but he cannot look beyond the present moment into the future.
The psalmist questions his status before God.
Feeling rejected (see Psa 43.2), the psalmist asks if the situation is permanent.
The memories of God’s mighty works in the past fill the psalmist’s mind.
The psalmist fears that God’s hand of protection (Psa 44.3; Psa 77.15; Exo 6.6) and favor (Psa 16.7–8; Psa 110.1) is now against him for no apparent reason.
This central section of the poem reflects on God as the holy and powerful redeemer.
the Red Sea: The Canaanites attributed divine power to the sea, but God is the one who made the sea and uses it for his own purposes.
This wisdom psalm exhorts the people to learn wisdom and faithfully pass it on.
The prologue is an invitation to learn wisdom.
The psalmist recites Israel’s story (Psa 78.5–72) in a parable in order to teach wisdom and insight. • Jesus quoted this verse to explain why he taught in parables (Mat 13.35).
This story of what God has done should be told from generation to generation (see Deu 6.20–25; Pro 4.1–4).
The telling of the story should motivate God’s people to obey what he commanded (Deu 6.4–9).

God holds each generation responsible for its own response, which should be to maintain faith and hope (see Psa 9.18; Psa 27.14) and avoid being stubborn, rebellious, and unfaithful (see Deu 9.6–7; Deu 10.16; Deu 30.6; Deu 31.27).

Ephraim, the second son of Joseph, received a special blessing from Jacob (Gen 48.15–20; Gen 49.22–26; Deu 33.13–17). The land that his descendants received included fertile valleys and strategic roads (Jdg 8.2). However, the people of Ephraim did not live in obedience to God’s gracious covenant.
The focus shifts from Ephraim (Psa 78.9–11) to Israel as a whole as the psalmist reflects on God’s power in Egypt (see Psa 81.4–7) and in the wilderness.
The miracles are the ten plagues against Egypt that God performed during Israel’s captivity (Exo 7.1–12).
God divided the sea when Israel crossed through the Red Sea (see Exo 14.1–15).
God used a cloud and a pillar of fire to guide and protect Israel in the wilderness (Exo 13.21–22).
Israel rebelled in the wilderness despite God’s abundant provision.
Abundance comes through the doors of heaven (Gen 8.2; 2Ki 7.2; Mal 3.10). • Israel ate manna for forty years in the wilderness (Exo 16.31–36; Joh 6.31).
God powerfully satisfied the people’s desires, but they did not respond with gratitude or faith. Therefore, God exercised his justice.
Israel’s rebellion resulted in God’s judgment, but even their short-lived and insincere repentance motivated God to exercise forbearance.
An entire generation died in the wilderness (Num 14.22–23, Num 14.28–35).
Israel’s continued existence, in spite of the people’s rebellion and unbelief (Psa 78.7–8), was due to God’s compassion.
They repented: This demonstration of zeal was not sincere.
The Israelites remembered the right doctrine (Psa 9.9; Psa 91.1), but they did not allow God to change their hearts (Lev 26.41).
The Israelites rebelled even though the Lord had rescued them from powerful plagues.
Israel’s rebellion desecrated the Promised Land. The people built shrines to false gods and worshiped idols (Psa 78.58) during the period of the judges (e.g., Jdg 2.11; Jdg 3.7, Jdg 3.17–18).
God abandoned his dwelling at Shiloh because of the people’s idol worship (1Sa 4.11; Jer 7.12).
The tribe of Ephraim was not completely rejected, but God favored Judah (Psa 78.68).
In the choice of Mount Zion instead of Shiloh as God’s sanctuary on earth, God moved from the north to the south (see Psa 69.1–36).
The God who had turned against his own people (Psa 78.62) chose David, a shepherd (Gen 46.34; 1Sa 16.10–11), to become their shepherd (Psa 78.52; cp. Psa 23.1).

This lament describes the occasion of Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC. The early history of Israel’s rebellions described in Psa 78.1–72 provoked God’s wrath, resulting in the desolation of Zion described here as the defilement of the Temple and the disgraced bodies that littered the landscape. The psalmist then prays for forgiveness and rescue (Psa 79.8–9), as well as for God to pay back the nation’s enemies (Psa 79.12–13). Other psalms lamenting the Exile include Psa 42.1–44, Psa 102.1–28, Psa 107.1–43, Psa 126.1–6, Psa 137.1–9.
The poet laments the desecration of the Temple and the success of the enemy.
your special possession: This phrase might refer to the land, the Temple (see Psa 61.5), or the people (see Psa 79.2; Psa 78.71).
The intensity of God’s judgment surprises the people; they cry out in despair for compassion, forgiveness, and relief. Verses Psa 6.1–7 are repeated almost verbatim in Jer 10.25.
The repentant among God’s people ask him to vent his anger not on them but on their wicked and unrepentant enemies.
The people’s accumulation of past sins contributed to the Exile (2Ki 17.7–23; 2Ki 24.3–4); however, the people perished because of their own sins (Jer 31.30; Eze 18.20).
The people ask God to rescue them. Although Israel’s sins caused the tragedy, the pagan nations must also be held responsible for the bloodshed.

The Exile resulted in national suffering and in individual searching for the Lord. • pay back: See Psa 1.6; Psa 94.2; Jer 32.18. • The expression seven times signifies something complete. • Israel’s neighbors included Edom, Moab, and Ammon (see Psa 137.7; 2Ki 24.2; Oba 1.1–21).

This psalm of lament might originate with the remnant of the northern kingdom after its fall in 722 BC. The people call on God as their Shepherd and as the God of Heaven’s Armies in the hope that he will return to them and restore them. They remember the Exodus and their special relationship with the Lord and conclude with an expression of renewed commitment to him (Psa 80.18).
Psa 80.1 The tune “Lilies of the Covenant” is unknown today.
The psalmist urgently calls upon the Lord to act.
God is the Shepherd of Israel: See also Psa 23.1; Psa 28.9; Psa 78.52–53. • radiant glory . . . power: These expressions (Psa 145.11) refer to God’s manifest presence.
This verse is repeated (with an increasing crescendo) in Psa 80.7, Psa 80.19.
The people cry out for rescue from the shame of their recent defeat. The enemy’s victory is less devastating, however, than the knowledge that they themselves are objects of God’s wrath.
Israel has a glorious past, beginning with its redemption from Egypt.

Israel had been a prosperous grapevine (Gen 1.28; Gal 5.22–23) that God transplanted into the land of Canaan at the time of the conquest. However, the people forgot the source of their prosperity and chose to do evil (Isa 5.1–7; Hos 10.1).
Solomon’s kingdom had extended west to the Mediterranean Sea and east to the Euphrates River (see Psa 72.8–9; Psa 89.25; 1Ki 4.21).
broken down our walls: God no longer defended Israel (Isa 5.5).
The surrounding nations were ceremonially unclean, like a wild boar or vicious wild animals.
Israel was the son that God had brought out of Egypt (see Hos 11.1) and planted in the Holy Land.
The community prays for God to change their desperate situation and restore them. They are still the Lord’s chosen people.
The son of your choice was probably the northern kingdom of Israel, although it might allude to the king of David’s dynasty (Psa 110.1).
This warning message invites Israel to worship only the Lord and to enjoy the fullness of his blessing.
As a prelude to the message of warning, the psalmist invites Israel to contemplate their God in song and dance.

An Israelite tambourine was a hand drum—a round frame covered with a skin, used as a percussion instrument during festivities, often to accompany dancing (Psa 68.25; Psa 149.3; Psa 150.4). • The sweet lyre and the harp, both stringed instruments, are the instruments most frequently mentioned in the psalms (e.g., Psa 33.2; Psa 57.8; Psa 71.22; Psa 150.3).
The ram’s horn mustered armies and announced special holy days (Psa 47.5; Psa 98.6). • new moon: The first day of the lunar month marked a festival.
The festival, a time to celebrate and listen to the Lord, took place at God’s appointed time.
for Israel: Literally for Joseph. The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (the sons of Joseph) are used here to refer to the entire nation of Israel.
The Lord heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and rescued them from oppressive slavery.
God pleads with his people to remember the covenant and the Ten Commandments.
God emphasizes that he and no one else rescued Israel. • The nation should open its mouth wide to take in God’s word (cp. Deu 8.3; Eze 3.1).
The Lord helps Israel to understand that their failure was not because of his weakness.

God wants to give his children his goodness, but only if they listen (Isa 1.18–19; Isa 28.12; Isa 48.18–19; see Deu 6.3). • God promises to subdue the enemies (Deu 9.3) of those who walk the paths of obedience and loyalty. He will also richly feed his people (Isa 1.19).
God condemns those who mistreat the helpless.
God presides and stands ready to render judgment (see Isa 3.13). • heaven’s court: See Job 1.6.
Since justice marks God’s reign (Psa 89.4), he opposes favoring the wicked. So the psalmist is perplexed and cries out to God for justice (Psa 82.3–4, Psa 82.8).
The unjust oppressors cannot bring or restore order. They wander about in darkness, unmoved by circumstances even when the whole world order falls apart around them (cp. Psa 11.3).
The gods (see study notes on Psa 29.1–2; Psa 58.1), like mere mortals, cannot escape the judgment common to human rulers. Jesus quoted from this passage in Joh 10.34.
The nations belong to God; he will take over the realms formerly ruled by local deities and give them to his people, just as he did with the Promised Land.

This community lament asks God for rescue and victory. The terse poetry suggests difficult times. A powerful coalition desires to destroy Israel (Psa 83.1–4) and allies itself against God (Psa 83.5–8). Recalling the fate of others who came against Israel (Psa 83.9–12), the psalmist prays that the same will happen to these enemies (Psa 83.13–16) so that God will receive honor among them (Psa 83.17–18). It is unclear whether this psalm arose out of a specific historical instance of opposition by these nations, or if it is a poetic collage of nations representing Israel’s enemies.
The enemy has successfully intimidated God’s people, so the poet prays that the Lord will hear and act.
signed a treaty: The allies agreed to fight against God and his people. The nations that are named in the alliance were situated around Israel and Judah.

The Edomites, descendants of Esau, were located to the southeast of Judah (see Gen 25.30; Gen 32.3; Gen 36.1–8). • Ishmaelites were desert-dwelling descendants of Hagar. • Moabites and Ammonites descended from Lot; both were located to the east of Israel and Judah. • The Hagrites were possibly located north of the Ammonites (1Ch 5.10).

The Gebalites probably came from Gebal/Byblos on the coast of Lebanon. • The Amalekites were located south of Israel in the Negev. • Philistia was southwest of Judah, by the Mediterranean Sea. • Tyre was a port city on the Mediterranean, northwest of Israel.
Assyria was northeast of Israel and north of the Persian Gulf. • The descendants of Lot were the Moabites and the Ammonites (Psa 83.6–7).
The psalmist prays that God will miraculously destroy the new coalition as he did three other enemies; doing so would bring him glory.
The Midianites, ruled by Zebah and Zalmunna and led by Oreb and Zeeb, were Israel’s enemy in the days of Gideon (Jdg 7.1–Psa 8.5). Barak’s coalition defeated Sisera and Jabin (Jdg 4.1–24).
The coalition’s motivation for wiping out Israel was to acquire the land (see Jer 3.19).
tumbleweed . . . chaff: This dry plant material easily blows away (see Isa 17.13).
fire . . . fierce storm . . . tempest: These are images of God’s manifestation in judgment (see Isa 29.6).

The psalmist expresses his deep spiritual longing for God’s presence. He faints with longing as he reflects on the Temple and on pilgrims making the journey to Jerusalem (Psa 84.1–7). He prays for himself and for the community (Psa 84.8–9). The conclusion of the psalm (Psa 84.10–12) clarifies that the Temple represents God—the psalmist truly longs for God’s presence. He knows that God’s goodness is greater than life and that only God can give his people favor and honor (Psa 84.10–11).
The psalmist is far from the Temple. He turns toward it in hopeful reflection.
The poet envies the birds that have nesting places in and around the Temple.
The priests and Temple personnel lived in the Temple.
The pilgrimage to Jerusalem reenacted the Exodus, when God marvelously provided for his people (see Psa 78.15–16; Psa 105.41). The psalmist imagines the pains of travel turning to the joy of arrival.
Travelers needed strength to meet the challenges of pilgrimage by foot along unpaved paths, in all kinds of weather and with the possibility of assaults.

The Valley of Weeping probably refers to the anguish that lonely pilgrims endured (see Psa 23.4), rather than to an actual location. • refreshing springs . . . autumn rains: Even when pilgrims feel totally exhausted, the prospect of drawing near to the Lord renews their spirits (cp. Isa 35.6–10; Isa 41.18–20; Isa 43.17–20; Isa 49.10).
Both kings and priests were anointed to dedicate them for service (see Psa 132.17; Exo 28.41; 1Sa 9.16; 1Sa 16.1–13; cp. Isa 61.1; Act 10.38).
The psalmist viewed being in God’s presence as much better than being anywhere else.
Some people worshiped the sun as a god, but the true God provides all that anyone needs.

The psalmist leads the postexilic community in lament and prayer for full redemption. He ponders God’s past rescue of Israel from exile (Psa 85.1–3), longs for greater evidence of God’s goodness, and leads the community in prayer for full restoration (Psa 85.4–7). God responds with a message of peace (Psa 85.8–9), and the psalm concludes with a lyrical outburst at the grandeur of God’s salvation (Psa 85.10–13).
Though the psalmist gratefully acknowledges God’s goodness, he also asks God whether his wrath will last forever.
God restored the fortunes of Israel by bringing the nation back from exile (see Psa 14.7; Psa 126.1).
When God forgave the guilt of their sins, he gave the people the possibility of fellowship with him (see Psa 32.5).
This prayer for renewal is based on God’s unfailing love for his people.

When God the LORD speaks, his faithful people listen. He promises them peace, meaning wholeness and well-being (see Psa 37.11). They fear the Lord and know that he and his salvation are near to them. • The Lord does not tolerate foolish ways, such as those that resulted in the Exile.

In the glorious world of renewal and salvation, all the qualities of God’s care—love, truth, righteousness, and peace—come together and transform the created order into something new (see Isa 32.15–20).
Righteousness is like a messenger preparing the world for God’s coming in response to the prayers of his people (Psa 85.4–7; Psa 89.14).

The psalmist invokes God’s help and praises his character in a lament prompted by the presence of evil (Psa 86.14, Psa 86.17). All people will worship the gracious and almighty God (Psa 86.8–10). To this end, the poet commits himself to a lifestyle of ethical integrity (Psa 86.11) and praising the Lord (Psa 86.12–13). The last stanza contrasts the qualities of evil people with those of the Lord (Psa 86.14–17).
Psa 86.1 This is the only psalm connected with David in Book Three.
God’s devoted servant prays for mercy. The psalmist sees himself as a member of the covenant community and as a citizen of the world.
The psalmist appeals to God to remain true to his character, which is the basis for hope.
The psalmist recounts the catalog of divine perfections (Exo 34.6–7), especially God’s willingness to forgive sin (see Psa 32.5; Psa 85.2; Psa 145.7–10).
All the nations must submit themselves to the Lord and worship him (Psa 45.17; Psa 117.1; Psa 148.7–11).
The poet responds to the Lord by seeking faithful instruction in the truth. • An individual with purity of heart has integrity and wholeness (see Psa 73.1).
In anticipation of God’s rescue, the psalmist praises him and trusts in his goodness.
The arrogant exist both inside and outside the community. The psalmist asks for a vision of God’s character; God is so great that just a glimpse of his goodness will shut the mouths of the wicked.

God has mercy on his people (Psa 51.1); he is gracious (Psa 25.6), slow to get angry (Psa 103.8; Psa 145.8), and filled with unfailing love and faithfulness (Hebrew khesed and ’emeth; Psa 143.1). This verse repeats a theme first expressed in Exo 34.7; Num 14.18 (cp. Psa 103.8; Psa 145.8; Neh 9.17; Joe 2.13; Jon 4.2).
This psalm envisions Jerusalem as the city of God where all the nations are citizens.
Jerusalem was Israel’s capital and the location of the Temple, God’s earthly palace (see Psa 84.1–12).

As great as Zion is, it will be even greater when it becomes an international city where believers from all the nations have citizenship. • God keeps a record of all who confess him as their Lord (Dan 7.10; Rev 13.8).
Jerusalem becomes the international city where all God’s children are citizens.

In this lament, the psalmist sees himself as cast out from God’s presence. At first, he calls on the Lord. When he finds no relief from his suffering, he presents three charges against God (Psa 88.6–7, Psa 88.8–12, Psa 88.13–17).

Psa 88.1 Heman the Ezrahite might be a sage from Solomon’s time (1Ki 4.31), a descendant of Judah (1Ch 2.6), or a member of the Levitical family charged with singing at the Temple (1Ch 15.17; 2Ch 5.12).
The psalmist calls on the LORD for salvation.

In his first charge, the psalmist blames the Lord for his demise. God’s overpowering anger did not make sense. • The phrase the darkest depths implies the place of the dead (Psa 143.3; see Lam 3.6) or the depths of the sea (Psa 68.22; Psa 69.1–2).

In his second charge, the psalmist claims that God has isolated him and caused his loneliness (cp. Psa 31.11; Psa 38.11). Loneliness was a curse in a culture where relationships were more important than personal achievement.
In his third charge, the psalmist accuses the Lord of rejecting him. The force and apparent cruelty of the psalmist’s suffering overwhelm him.
The psalmist restates his second and first charges.

Book Three (Psa 73.1–89) begins and ends with weighty questions. Though Psa 89.1–52 begins with a praise-filled account of how the Lord exalted the throne of David (Psa 89.1–37), the psalmist protests the Lord’s apparent rejection of his covenant with David (Psa 89.38–51; see 2Sa 7.8–16).
Psa 89.1 Ethan the Ezrahite was a wise man (1Ki 4.31; cp. Psa 88.1).
God’s unfailing love gives reason to celebrate forever.
Theme: Making Sense of the Exile
The psalmist restates God’s covenant with David (see also Psa 89.19–37).
The Lord has sworn by his own holiness (Psa 89.35; see Psa 110.4).
God is the absolute standard of faithfulness, commitment, and order. The angelic beings and the heavens testify to his constancy.
Praise for God’s greatness (see Psa 8.1) comes from the inhabitants of heaven who witness his faithfulness.
mightiest angel: Literally son of God (see study note on Psa 29.1–2).
In this hymn, the psalmist celebrates God’s comprehensive and powerful sovereignty over nature.

The Lord rules over all parts of the created order, including evil. • You scattered your enemies: The Lord will crush (Luk 1.51) evil powers that oppose him (Psa 2.1–3). • with your mighty arm: This phrase represents God’s strength (Psa 89.13).
Mount Tabor was in northern Israel. Mount Hermon formed the extreme northern border of the nation.
God rules wisely over creation. The qualities of righteousness, justice, and faithfulness fit the profile of a wise ruler. The happy people who live under his rule enjoy his protection.
Those who are wise worship God, walk in his light, rejoice in their relationship with him, and exult in his character.
The Lord protects his people with the same power by which he established the created order.
The Lord chose David as his son and as king of Israel (see Psa 2.4–6; 2Sa 7.8–16) to provide protection for his people.
I have anointed him: This is the verb from which anointed one (Hebrew mashiakh, “messiah”) is derived.
The Lord adopted David as his son, appointed him as his commander over the nations, and promised to support him forever. Verse 26 recalls a verse from David’s song of praise (2Sa 22.47).
David would be the most eminent of earthly kings. The Hebrew word translated mightiest is the same as the designation for God as “Most High” (‘elyon).
The Lord writes his faithfulness in heaven, on the canvas of his universe (see Psa 89.2). He records his commitment to the dynasty of David in the same way.

The Lord disciplines but does not reject his erring children. He foresees violation of trust and subsequent punishment, but he commits himself to uphold the covenant. His fidelity to David corresponds to his faithfulness to the created order.

holiness: The Lord is wholly distinct from the created order (Psa 22.3); his character is totally pure. He does as he pleases (Psa 115.3), and he chooses to be faithful (Psa 89.1; Psa 115.1); therefore, he cannot lie.
You are angry: The harshness of God’s wrath perplexes the psalmist.
broken down the walls: The Lord’s people are completely vulnerable.
Although the Lord promised to strengthen David, he secretly strengthened David’s enemies.
The psalmist wonders if he will live to see the end of the Lord’s anger. Our lifetimes are short, like a day in the Lord’s sight (Psa 90.4, Psa 90.10).
The phrase your servants refers to the community loyal to the Lord.

This doxology concludes all of Book Three (Psa 73.1–89); it is not intended to be read as part of Psa 89.1–52. It stands in stark contrast to the anguish and questioning of Psa 89.1–52. Cp. Psa 41.13; Psa 106.48.

Although the Lord’s people have made their home in him for generations, their sin widens the gap between them and their infinite Lord. The Lord’s wrath against a person’s sin might last a lifetime and yet be only a taste of his displeasure with sin. This lamentable situation calls the community to seek the Lord’s light. Taking the first step means seeking restoration with the Lord on the basis of his compassion and love (Psa 90.13–14). He alone makes his servants glad and blesses their future generations (Psa 90.16–17).

Psa 90.1 Moses led God’s people from slavery in Egypt to Mount Sinai, where he received the law and established God’s covenant with Israel. • the man of God: Moses enjoyed a special relationship with God (Deu 33.1).

The Lord becomes the home of the godly; he has provided shelter for countless generations. The word translated home is not used frequently in the Psalter. It describes a place of safety where the Lord meets his needy people and cares for them (Psa 68.5; Psa 71.3).
The Lord is the eternal God. • The Lord gave birth to the earth by creating it.
Unlike God, humans are mortal and transitory.
Sinners cannot escape God’s wrath because the Lord sees their sins. Their fleeting lives are filled with afflictions.
A groan of sorrow (Eze 2.10) sums up a life spent in facing the consequences of sin. • Humans cause trouble (see Psa 10.6) and receive pain in return.

In the search for wisdom, no one can comprehend the Lord (see Isa 40.13). The appropriate human response to the Lord is godly fear (see Psa 60.4). The Lord alone can teach humans to follow the path of wisdom (Psa 25.4–6).
The psalmist prays for the Lord’s favor and restoration.
The phrase your servants refers to the community of those loyal to the Lord.
The psalmist calls upon the Lord to give the people gladness to replace their mourning (see Psa 92.4–5).
The children represent future generations in contrast to the generations past (Psa 90.1).
Humans waste their efforts unless the Lord makes them successful (Psa 44.3).

This wisdom psalm expresses confidence in the Almighty God, who provides a shelter for those who take refuge in him. They receive redemption, life, and glory from the Lord, who loves and cares for those who seek him.
The Lord is an ancient shelter (see Psa 90.1), open to those who seek refuge in him.
The Most High is an ancient title that expresses the Lord’s exalted status as the ruler and protector of the godly (see Gen 14.19).
The psalmist invites the godly to trust in the Lord and find protection in him.
God protects the godly from deadly disease and even a destructive word.
The armor might refer to a body shield, while protection refers to a small shield worn on the arm.
The godly should not be afraid, because the Lord watches over them. These promises do not guarantee an escape from trouble, but they create an expectation of the Lord’s goodness.
The reference to disease represents any kind of affliction.
The poet again invites the godly to seek refuge in the Lord and enjoy the benefits of divine protection.

he will order his angels: Satan cited these words when he tempted Jesus (Mat 4.6; Luk 4.10–11), but God makes this promise for those who obey him (Psa 91.14), not for those who arrogantly test him (Mat 4.4, Mat 4.7).
The godly can trust the Lord’s protection and provision.
Those who love the Lord will obey him (Deu 30.20; 1Jo 5.3) and seek his protection (Psa 91.1; Psa 145.18).

The Lord promises to answer the prayers of his people. • The Psalter often speaks of people honoring the Lord (Psa 50.15); here, God promises to honor the godly who risk everything for his sake (Psa 62.7; Psa 71.21; Psa 84.11).
A long life on earth represents just a small part of the Lord’s goodness and eternal friendship (Psa 23.6).

Thanksgiving and praise open this psalm. The Lord—the Most High—is faithful and just in discerning between the godly and the wicked. The godly will enjoy a glorious, vigorous future, while the wicked will perish. The wise see and understand the Lord’s works as they reveal his justice (Psa 92.6–7, Psa 92.11, Psa 92.15). The wicked, like grass, are quickly destroyed (Psa 92.7–10).

Psa 92.1 on the Sabbath Day: Jewish tradition assigned one psalm to each day of the week: Sunday (Psa 24.1–10), Monday (Psa 48.1–14), Tuesday (Psa 82.1–8), Wednesday (Psa 94.1–23), Thursday (Psa 81.1–16), Friday (Psa 93.1–5), and the Sabbath (Psa 92.1–15). This is the only psalm that indicates this use in its title.
The psalmist offers praise and thanksgiving for God’s unfailing love and faithfulness.
Fools perish because they do not understand the Lord’s marvelous works and eternal plans.
The Lord acts and the psalmist responds in praise (Psa 92.4). God’s actions spring from his thoughts (Psa 92.5).
The Lord’s thoughts do not make sense to the simpleton or the fool, the immoral person who desires no wisdom (Pro 1.22; Pro 10.23).
Even when the ungodly seem to grow luxuriantly (Psa 73.3–5), they have no future (Psa 92.9; see Psa 1.6; Psa 90.5–6; Isa 40.6–8).
The glory of the Lord provides the reason for the poet’s renewed strength and glory, and for the imminent defeat of the enemy.

The transcendent Lord stays above the world of human experience. From this exalted place, he rules and judges (Psa 7.7), celebrates his victories (Psa 68.18; see Psa 47.1–9), comes to rescue the needy (Psa 102.19), brings an end to the wicked (Psa 92.7–8), and receives praise (Psa 148.1).
as strong as a wild ox: The Lord allows the psalmist to share his exaltation (Psa 92.8), thus ensuring victory.
The psalmist understands the Lord’s mighty acts. He shares in the glory of the wise of heart.

Carvings of palm trees (1Ki 6.29, 1Ki 6.32, 1Ki 6.35; 1Ki 7.36) adorned the Temple, and builders made rich use of cedars (1Ki 5.6). The trees represent the godly, who are planted in the very courts of the Temple.
The Temple area consisted of the LORD’s own house and the courts that surrounded it.
There is no evil in him! The Lord is consistently just; he rightly judges everyone (see Zep 3.5).

These psalms challenge the doubts created by the Exile (see Psa 89.1–52) and answer the questions asked in Psa 90.11, Psa 90.13. The Lord has established a kingdom (Psa 93.1–5) that is characterized by the punishment of the wicked (Psa 94.1–23), reverent obedience among his people (Psa 95.1–11), justice for the poor (Psa 96.1–13), celebration in Zion (Psa 97.1–12), salvation for Israel (Psa 98.1–9), holiness (Psa 99.1–9), and praise (Psa 100.1–5).
The everlasting Lord gloriously establishes his kingship (cp. Psa 47.1–9, Psa 99.1–100).
robed in majesty: The Lord stands victorious both before and after battle (see Psa 45.3).
Theme: The Creator-King
God’s victory over natural chaos gives the psalmist confidence that the Lord will also defeat his present enemies (cp. Jer 46.8; Jer 47.2).
Through his stable rule and royal laws, the Lord orders the world. • Your reign (literally your house): The house from which God reigns might be the Lord’s heavenly palace or the earthly Temple.

This plea for the Lord’s justice includes both communal and individual expressions of lament (Psa 94.1–7, Psa 94.16–23). The psalmist gives voice to the pain and suffering caused by the wicked, but he also depicts the comfort and stability of the Lord’s protection. He calls on the Lord to avenge the needy against the arrogant and foolish, he rebukes such people for their folly (Psa 94.8–11), and he pronounces a blessing on the wise (Psa 94.12–15).
After the community falls victim to the wicked (Psa 94.5–7), they pray that the Lord will render justice (see Psa 7.11; Psa 9.12).
Just as the Lord’s enemies rise up against him and his people (Psa 3.7; Psa 93.3), he must arise and make retribution against the enemy (see Psa 79.12; Isa 65.6).
widows . . . foreigners . . . orphans: The Lord’s law protects needy people (Deu 24.17; Deu 27.19), but they remain vulnerable in society.
The wicked think that they can get away with their vile acts and speech, foolishly assuming that God isn’t looking or doesn’t care.
The psalmist rebukes human folly.
It is preposterous that those with ears and eyes would imagine their Creator to be deaf and blind.

punishes: This word also carries the idea of “warns” (Psa 2.10), “disciplines” (Psa 6.1; Psa 94.12), or “instructs” (Psa 16.7). The Lord disciplines his people to purify their character (Pro 3.11–12; Heb 12.6–11). He punishes his enemies by giving them what they deserve (Psa 1.6; Rom 6.23).
While the Lord’s thoughts are deep, people’s thoughts are worthless (cp. Psa 92.5; 1Co 3.20).
True to his nature, the Lord rewards those who live by his wise instruction and makes them happy according to his promises.
God’s relief includes his comfort and rescue.
Even when it seems that he has, the LORD will not reject his people.
The psalmist’s prayer resumes (see Psa 94.1–7) with a desperate cry for the Lord’s justice; it concludes with the hopeful expectation that evil will end.
Only God has the power to stand up to the wicked (see Psa 2.2).
The psalmist’s experience of slipping contrasts with God’s promise to stand with him (Psa 94.12–13; see Psa 15.5; Psa 93.1).

This call to worship urges the people to respond to the Lord, the Shepherd, and to follow him faithfully. The previous generation, who refused to obey, did not receive the blessings of the Promised Land.
The Lord is the great King over the whole universe.
above all gods: The psalmist refutes idolatry and paganism (Psa 96.4–6; Psa 135.15–18; see also Isa 46.5–7).
The whole created order owes its existence to the sovereign Lord alone—not to various gods.
The great King cares for his people as a shepherd cares for his flock (Isa 40.11). • The LORD our maker, the Creator of heaven and earth, also made a people for himself (Isa 45.9–12; Isa 51.12–16).
If people want to enter into the Lord’s rest, they need to respond immediately (see Heb 3.7–Psa 4.11).
To harden your hearts means to be stubborn and resist the Lord’s grace (see Num 20.2–13; see also Mat 13.3–23; Joh 12.37–43; Eph 4.17–32; Heb 3.6–19; Heb 4.6–11).
Israel’s ancestors . . . saw the wonders of the Lord, but they foolishly did not try to grasp their significance (see Psa 92.5–6).

The generation of Israel that wandered in the wilderness for forty years failed to enter the place of rest that Israel enjoyed after the conquest of the land (1Ki 8.56; see Deu 12.9). The Lord promised them the land and gave it to them (Isa 28.12), but they did not obey him (Isa 28.1). The warning reminds every generation of the need to obey in faith. • The rest that God provides includes peace, provision, and protection (Psa 132.14–18). The author of Hebrews challenged a new generation to enter the rest provided by Jesus Christ (Heb 3.7–Psa 4.13).

This psalm establishes the Lord’s universal kingship (see Psa 93.1–5) and prepares for the coming of the Lord to bring justice and righteousness into the world. The psalmist invites everyone to worship the Lord (Psa 96.1–3), the glorious Creator of all the earth (Psa 96.4–6), because worship is due to him alone (Psa 96.7–9). The universe joins in praise as the righteous Judge establishes a new order (Psa 96.10–13). • This psalm (along with Psa 105.1–15; Psa 106.1, Psa 106.47–48) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1Ch 16.1–43.
Three psalms open with the exhortation to sing a new song (Psa 96.1–13, Psa 98.1–9, Psa 149.1–9); the song celebrates the Lord’s universal kingship (see Psa 33.3).
The gods of the nations are as nothing before the glorious and majestic Creator of the earth.

Great is the LORD! . . . most worthy of praise: With this refrain, the poet exalts the Lord over all the gods (Psa 95.3) and nations (Psa 99.2). He inspires awe more than anyone or anything else (Psa 76.7, Psa 76.12; Psa 89.7; Psa 99.3; Psa 111.9). He is beyond human possession or comprehension. The story of what he does to redeem his people causes them to praise him.
The LORD made the heavens, an even greater task than creating the earth. The idols, made by human hands (Psa 115.4), created nothing.
Honor and majesty: The Lord is glorious (Psa 96.6; Psa 104.1; Psa 148.13), and so are his works in nature (Psa 8.1) and in redemption (Psa 111.3; Psa 145.5).

nations of the world (literally families of the nations): Families and clans represent subdivisions of the nations (see Gen 12.3). • The nations must respond to the Lord’s glory (Psa 8.1; Psa 19.1–4; Psa 24.7).

The courts of God’s sanctuary were usually off-limits to non-Jewish people. In this psalm the nations of the world—the non-Jews—are invited in (Psa 65.4; Psa 84.2, Psa 84.10; Psa 100.4; Psa 116.19; Psa 135.2; Isa 1.12).
Worshipers should tremble in awe (Psa 96.4; see Psa 18.7–15; Psa 97.4) at the splendor of the Lord’s majesty and holiness (Heb 12.25).

The Lord’s coming means the end of injustice. He rules fairly (Psa 9.8; Psa 96.13; Psa 98.9) and inaugurates an era of harmony and order not experienced since Eden. • The Lord’s reign over the world is founded on the strong pillars of “righteousness and justice” (Psa 89.14), so it cannot be shaken (cp. Psa 11.3).
The psalmist exhorts the created order to respond with joy to the news of the Lord’s coming. Cp. a similar theme in Psa 98.7–9.
All of nature will experience renewal in God’s presence (Psa 65.13; Psa 72.6, Psa 72.16; Isa 44.23; Isa 55.12; Rom 8.21–22).

God is greatly exalted over the gods and over all the earth. Awe-inspiring phenomena accompany his coming. Even the created order is visibly affected and the wicked perish, but the people of Zion love his coming and rejoice.
The farthest coastlands represent the most remote parts of the world.
Dark clouds . . . Fire . . . lightning: This language shows that the Lord is coming in judgment.
Theme: Darkness and Light
The created order stirs at the coming of its King. He alone deserves worship.

As the Lord enters the world, the testimony of his righteousness resounds from above (Psa 50.6). • Every nation will view the open display of the Lord’s glory (see Psa 8.1; Psa 19.1–4; Psa 24.7; Isa 40.5).
At the Lord’s coming, when every god must bow to him, those who worship other gods will face their own folly (see Psa 95.3–5).
Jerusalem rejoices at the news of the Lord’s coming, for he brings justice and rescues the upright of heart.

The godly people of integrity (see Pro 2.7, Pro 2.21; Pro 3.32; Pro 11.6, Pro 11.11; Pro 14.2), whose hearts are right, maintain a relationship with the Lord and with others (Psa 94.15; Psa 125.4). The wicked plan the downfall of the godly (Psa 11.2), but the Lord rescues them (Psa 11.1; Psa 36.10). Then the sorrows of the godly turn to joy and praise (Psa 32.11; Psa 64.10; Psa 111.1; Psa 119.7).

This psalm celebrates the Lord’s kingship. The Lord is Israel’s true King, its champion and savior. His people sing a new song celebrating his victorious power and faithfulness to them. The Lord displays his righteous rule to all the nations throughout the earth, which will culminate in a worldwide kingdom of justice (Psa 98.2, Psa 98.9). Consequently, all the earth must worship and rejoice together because the Lord is coming (Psa 98.4–6).
The Lord makes known his righteousness and faithfulness (see also Isa 52.10).
The psalmist invites the whole earth to worship the King (see Psa 96.1).
The Temple musicians used trumpets to call people together for meetings (cp. Psa 81.3).
The created order is personified as rejoicing at the coming of the righteous Judge (see Psa 93.3–4; Psa 96.11–13).
The psalmist calls the nations to worship the Lord, the king of the earth who rules from Zion.

The Lord is the holy and righteous King (Isa 6.1–5). Mount Zion, the location of the Lord’s Temple, metaphorically stands as the highest point on earth (Psa 113.4; Isa 2.2; Isa 6.1). From this summit, the Great King (Psa 47.2) can see, rule over, and receive praise from all nations and peoples.
It is fitting to tremble and quake in response to the Lord’s holiness (see Psa 96.9). • The throne between the cherubim refers to the cover of the Ark of the Covenant (Exo 25.17–22).
The qualities of the Lord’s rule include strength, justice, love, fairness, and righteousness (see Psa 93.4; Psa 97.2, Psa 97.6–7, Psa 97.12; Psa 98.2–3, Psa 98.9; Psa 138.6).
God showed favor by responding to his people in the past, while holding sinners accountable.
Moses and Samuel were great models and leaders who had prayed on behalf of the Lord’s people (Exo 32.31–32; 1Sa 12.23).
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron from the pillar of cloud (Exo 33.9; Num 12.5–6), and for a time, the people responded to the revelation.
This psalm calls all nations to come to Jerusalem to worship the Lord and acknowledge his goodness to Israel.
The LORD is the one who determines who his people are. • the sheep of his pasture: God will guide and protect his people (Psa 23.1, Psa 23.4).
Gates and courts were part of the Temple in Jerusalem.
This hymn expresses a commitment to live with integrity and to avoid evil. Jesus meets this ideal.

in my own home (literally in my house): This commitment to integrity might refer to private life at home. Some interpreters view my house as referring to the king’s palace; the commitment would then refer to the policies of his administration. • Leading a life of integrity means choosing a wise lifestyle.
The psalmist hates what the Lord hates (Pro 6.16–19; see Psa 5.5; Psa 11.4–5). • Perverse ideas come from corrupt human hearts (cp. Psa 18.26).
The psalmist surrounds himself with people who are also committed to integrity (Psa 101.2).
The psalmist commits himself to ridding his house and the city of the LORD—representing the entire kingdom—of all evil.
A frail and afflicted human being prays for the Lord’s compassion on Jerusalem and for his presence with its inhabitants.
The psalmist appeals to the Lord not to turn away (or hide your face). Israel experienced his turning his face away during their exile.
Smoke is an image of transitory life (Psa 37.20; Psa 68.2). • The psalmist’s bones represent his whole being (see Psa 6.2; Psa 34.19–22).
Like dried grass, the psalmist senses his life ebbing away.
skin and bones: The psalmist has wasted away because of his anguish (see Psa 102.9; Psa 109.24).
The owl was associated with ruin and desolation (Isa 34.11, Isa 34.15).
The psalmist cannot sleep (see Psa 63.6–8). Like a bird on the roof, he feels isolated from both friends (see Psa 88.8) and enemies.
The psalmist blames the Lord for his troubles.
The psalmist’s existence seems empty and transitory (Psa 102.4; Psa 109.23; Psa 144.4).
The topic changes from the psalmist’s miseries to the Lord’s glory. A vision of the Lord’s compassionate kingship gives him confidence in Zion’s future.
forever . . . to every generation: The frailty of humans (Psa 102.3–11) contrasts with the permanence of the Lord.
Now is the time for the Lord to restore Jerusalem from exile (see Psa 75.2; Jer 29.10; Dan 9.1–19).

When the Lord arises (Psa 102.13), the nations will tremble with fear because they will see his glory (see Psa 8.1; Psa 19.1–4; Psa 24.7). The rebuilding of Zion and the Temple portray God’s glory and fulfill this promise. An even greater fulfillment will come with the New Jerusalem (Rev 21.1–27).
The people of Israel were destitute (or naked) during the Exile.
The Lord will have mercy; Jews and Gentiles alike will worship him.
Let this be recorded: The written record stands as a memorial to the Lord’s goodness.
The heavenly sanctuary refers to God’s holy place on high (see Psa 92.8–10).
The multitudes—both Jews and Gentiles—will join in the worship of the Lord (see Psa 96.7, Psa 96.9; Psa 106.48; Isa 2.2–4; Isa 43.10–13; Isa 57.15; Isa 60.3–7).
Although the psalmist suffers in the present, he bases his hope for the future on the Lord’s past faithfulness.
The psalmist draws a contrast between his days (Psa 102.23) and God’s years (cp. Psa 90.4).

In contrast with the permanence of the Creator, the created order will wear out like a piece of clothing (see Isa 40.28). • The writer to the Hebrews describes this passage as having been addressed to Jesus, the Son (Heb 1.10–12).
The Lord’s presence provides the basis for the security and happiness of his people (Psa 23.6).
This psalm celebrates the Lord’s perfection, compassion, forgiveness, and goodness.
The psalmist offers praise for the Lord’s goodness.
Let all that I am praise the LORD: Psa 103.1–22 and Psa 104.1–35 each open and close with this commitment (Psa 103.1–2, Psa 103.22; Psa 104.1, Psa 104.35; see also Psa 146.1).
The Lord revealed himself to Moses in distinctive ways that ensured his relationship with his people (see Exo 34.6–7; Num 14.18).
If the Lord were to constantly accuse or remain angry forever, no one would be left (see Isa 54.7–8; Isa 57.16).
The Lord’s love and forgiveness are infinite and complete.

The LORD is like a father to his children: This analogy forms the basis for Jesus’ teaching about God’s fatherhood (see Mat 5.43–48; Mat 6.1; Mat 10.19–20; Mat 12.50; Luk 6.36; Luk 12.29–32; Joh 8.31–59; Joh 15.1–8; see also 2Sa 7.14; Jer 3.19; Jer 31.9; Mal 1.6; 2Co 6.16–18).
The Lord compassionately cares for frail humans (see Psa 37.2; Psa 90.5; Psa 92.7; Psa 102.4; Isa 40.6–8).
the love of the LORD remains forever: The Lord’s kingdom is everlasting, so he commits himself to his people across many generations.
To obey God means to be faithful and loyal to him.
The psalmist exhorts the Lord’s angels, his servants and messengers, to praise the Lord.
God’s kingdom extends over all things, so all things are called to praise the Lord. • The concluding phrase takes us back to Psa 103.1–2.

This creation hymn (see also Psa 8.1–9, Psa 33.1–22, Psa 145.1–21) exalts God’s goodness and majesty. The psalmist reflects on the present world, the original creation, and a future new creation. He sees both creations as marvelously and wisely made (cp. Psa 139.14), as the work of the Lord’s Spirit (Psa 104.30; Gen 1.2; 2Co 3.6).

Let all that I am praise the LORD: Psa 103.1–22 and Psa 104.1–35 each open and close with this commitment to praise (Psa 103.1–2, Psa 103.22; Psa 104.1, Psa 104.35). • how great you are! This acclamation expresses praise for rescue (see also Psa 35.27; Psa 40.16; Psa 70.4).
The psalmist interacts with two of the days of creation (see Gen 1.1–8), when God created the heavens and light.
This poetic portrayal envisions the clouds as beams that support heaven.

Wind and lightning are seen as divine messengers. The Lord uses weather phenomena as he desires (Psa 77.17–18; Psa 78.26; Psa 135.7; Psa 148.5–6). • The psalmist interacts with day three of creation (Gen 1.9–13). The Lord is master of water and earth.
At first, water covered the earth.
The Lord created dry ground on day three of creation (Gen 1.9–13).
The earth originates in God’s will.

The Lord reigns over all bodies of water, including those on land. He replaced chaotic waters with order and abundance, and the earth became a splendid place for animals and humans, with water refreshing the ground, the birds, and the animals.

The Lord set a firm boundary for the seas to protect the land. God’s sovereignty over sea and land was an argument against the existence of Baal, whom the Canaanites celebrated as victorious over the waters (see Psa 29.1–11).
The psalmist celebrates animal, plant, and human life, as well as the Lord’s abundant provision for all of it (Gen 1.9–30).
people to use: People are the managers of the created order, and they receive nourishment from the work of their hands.
While both can be misused (cp. Pro 21.17), the Lord provides wine and olive oil as gifts to enhance life. Life is sustained by basic food, represented by bread.
The storks migrated from northern Europe and resided in Palestine during the winter. • hyraxes: These animals are about the size of a rabbit and live in rocky places.
The psalmist rejoices in the order of night and day, marking day four of creation (Gen 1.14–19). This cycle gives all creatures an opportunity to live.

the moon to mark the seasons: Ancient Israel based its calendar on the cycles of the moon. • the sun knows when to set: This is a poetic description from the perspective of normal observation. The sun goes down at a regular time every evening.
Cycles of darkness and dawn mark the days on earth.
The Lord’s works testify to his wisdom. All parts fit together—land and sea, night and day, land creatures and sea creatures. The Lord’s wisdom makes life orderly and wonderful.
The ocean, . . . teeming with life of every kind (see Gen 1.20–21), exemplifies the Lord’s creative activities.

ships sailing: Commercial vessels engaged in sea trade were one of the wonders of the ancient Near East (see Isa 2.16; Isa 23.1, Isa 23.3). • Leviathan: The psalmist says that this feared creature is nothing but the Lord’s pet.
All life depends on the gracious sustenance of the Lord of life and death (cp. Mat 6.11).

When you give them your breath: Life on earth is only possible as the Lord’s gift, symbolized by his breath (Hebrew ruakh, “breath, wind, spirit”). The Lord’s Spirit is the agent of renewal (Isa 32.15–20).
The psalmist moves from describing the known creation to anticipating the new creation, when the Lord will renew the created order into a world without sinners.
The Lord reveals his presence in the created order (see Psa 8.1; Psa 19.1–4; Psa 24.7) and takes pleasure in his new creation (see Isa 65.19).
The trembling earth and the smoking mountains represent the Lord’s coming in judgment against sinners and salvation for his faithful people (see Psa 18.7–15).
The Lord will remove all forms of evil that defile his creation. • The concluding phrase takes us back to Psa 104.1 (see also Psa 103.1–2, Psa 103.22; Psa 146.1).

This hymn praises the Lord’s faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants in all their journeys—from Ur to Canaan (Psa 105.12), to Egypt (Psa 105.17, Psa 105.23), through the wilderness (Psa 105.37, Psa 105.41), and back to Canaan (Psa 105.44). All of this fulfilled the Lord’s promise to Abraham (Psa 105.9, Psa 105.42), which was the basis for Israel’s very existence. Joseph, whose suffering was changed into glory, is a paradigm of encouragement for Israel (Psa 105.16–25). • Psa 105.1–15 (along with 96; Psa 106.1, Psa 106.47–48) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1Ch 16.1–43.

The poet begins with the exhortation Give thanks (see also Psa 106.1; Psa 107.1; Psa 118.1; Psa 136.1). The other psalms continue with the refrain “for he is good!” The rest of Psa 105.1–45 tells of God’s goodness.

The story of Israel is based on the Lord’s commitment to Abraham. Even when a question arises about the future of God’s covenant with David (Psa 89.1–52), God’s covenant with Abraham stands, as does the spiritual bond between God and Israel, Abraham’s descendants.
The covenant is the Lord’s irrevocable oath to be the Father of Abraham and his descendants (see Gen 12.1–9; Gen 15.1–21).
God promised the land of Canaan to Abraham’s descendants as their special possession, where they could live as God’s people (Psa 105.44–45; Gen 12.7; Gen 15.7–21).
The Lord protected Israel’s patriarchs.
Abraham was one of the nation’s prophets (Gen 20.7).
These verses tell the story of Joseph (see Gen 37.1–41).
tested Joseph’s character: See Gen 39.6–12.
These verses tell the story of Israel’s affliction in Egypt (see Exo 1.1–14).
Egypt (Hebrew mitsrayim) is called the land of Ham.
The psalmist recounts the story of Moses and the plagues in Egypt (Exo 7.20–Psa 12.30).

The Exodus and the conquest of Canaan fulfilled God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Psa 105.9–10). Unlike Psa 78.1–72, the poet recites the Lord’s goodness without commenting on Israel’s history of rebellion (cp. Psa 106.1–48).
not one . . . stumbled: The Lord protected all of his people (cp. Psa 9.3).
The Lord’s presence was as evident to all as a fire in the darkness (Exo 13.22).
The story of redemption is also the story of the Lord’s faithfulness.
Canaan was a land of pagan nations (see Psa 111.6). The psalmist might also be reflecting on God’s promise to Abraham (Gen 24.60) regarding the lands given to Isaac (Gen 26.3).
The Lord planned for Israel to testify about him by obeying him; Israel was to be his model people.

The Israelite community in exile confessed the Lord’s goodness and justice and their own historic sinfulness. From the humble state of exile, they pleaded for redemption and restoration, asking to be gathered back from all the places the Lord had scattered them in his wrath. The psalm does not end in despair but with the memory of the Lord’s former mercy and the hope that his mercy will be renewed (Psa 106.44–48). Israel failed, but the Lord is constant. • Verses 1, Psa 47.1–48 (along with Psa 96.1–13; Psa 105.1–15) are included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1Ch 16.1–43.
Praise the LORD! This refrain (Hebrew haleluyah) characterizes four small subgroups in the psalms: Psa 104.1–106, Psa 111.1–113, Psa 115.1–117, Psa 146.1–150.
Wise people who practice justice and righteousness receive encouragement to proclaim the Lord’s great acts.
The poet prays individually for the Lord’s favor before leading the community confession that follows.
The community joins together to confess their sins and their ancestors’ many acts of unbelief.

The story of Israel’s redemption encompasses their sinful response from the days of the ancestors to the present (Psa 106.43). The themes of sin and divine wrath both open and close Book Four (Psa 90.1–9; Psa 106.6, Psa 106.23, Psa 106.43).
Red Sea: See Exo 14.15–31.
They wouldn’t wait: God’s impatient people did not trust him to work according to his will (e.g., see Exo 15.24; Exo 16.2–3; Exo 17.1–3; Num 14.26–45; Num 21.4–9).
he sent a plague: See Exo 32.35; Num 11.33.
The people became jealous because they presumed to have the same privileges as God’s appointed priests (see Num 16.1–35). • the earth opened up: See Num 16.28–33.
they bowed before an image: The people forgot their Savior and committed the sin of idolatry (see Exo 32.1–6).
The land of Ham here means Egypt (Psa 106.21).
The people disobeyed God’s command when they refused to enter the pleasant land (the Promised Land; see Jer 3.19). • they wouldn’t believe his promise: See Num 13.25–Psa 14.12.

God’s judgment when Israel refused to obey was death and exile (Num 14.26–30). The occasion for these severe judgments seems to have been disobeying God’s word (Psa 106.24–25) and provoking the Lord’s wrath (Psa 106.28–46).
Israel’s idolatry outside of the land came with them into the land. Their nature did not change; they continued to provoke the Lord to anger by their actions.
the worship of Baal at Peor: See Num 25.3; Deu 4.3.
Phinehas, who executed a flagrantly apostate Israelite man (Num 25.3–8), is an even better model of a righteous man than Moses, who failed at Meribah (Num 20.11–13).
Israel continued to disobey the word of the Lord while living in the Promised Land. Rather than destroying the nations, Israel accepted them and their ways (see Jdg 2.1–3, Jdg 2.11–15; Jdg 3.5–6).
Pagan gods were demons (see Deu 32.17).
Idolatry, like adultery, defiles God’s people (see Lev 18.24; Hos 5.3).
The psalmist returns to the Babylonian exile (Psa 106.26–27). The Lord judged Israel severely, but he also restrained his wrath, remembering the covenant he had made with Abraham.
God abhorred Israel’s sin, as he does all sin.
When Israel was finally destroyed, the destruction was not complete. The Lord pitied them, so he left a remnant.
He remembered . . . and relented: Unlike Israel, the Lord is faithful to his covenant (Psa 105.8).
As harsh as the Exile was, the Lord still protected his people (see 2Ki 25.27–29).
Gather us back: The community prays for restoration from exile (see Psa 102.19–22; Psa 107.3; see also Isa 11.12; Isa 40.11; Isa 43.5; Isa 54.7; Isa 56.8; Isa 66.18).

This doxology concludes Book Four (cp. Psa 41.13; Psa 89.52). • from everlasting to everlasting! The reference to God’s eternal nature links to the opening of Book Four (Psa 90.1–2). • Let all the people say, “Amen!”: The Hebrew word ’amen means “It is true.” The godly accept the Lord’s will in exile and his promise to be their God.

This psalm is a hymn of praise to God the Redeemer. After an introduction exhorting the redeemed to praise God for his goodness (Psa 107.1–3), the psalmist brings together four case studies of people whom the Lord redeemed from adversity (Psa 107.4–32). He then sums up the Lord’s sovereignty (Psa 107.33–42) and concludes with an invitation to discern God’s unfailing love in all areas of life (Psa 107.43).
The redeemed might be all who came out of exile.
exiles: People came from all nations where the people of Israel and Judah had been scattered.
Those who were lost in the wilderness thank God for his rescue. The wilderness might be a metaphor for leaving the path of wisdom (Psa 1.1; Pro 4.10–15).
The psalmist does not specify the occasion of his trouble and distress. The generic nature of the adversity permits readers in a variety of circumstances to identify with the laments.
God led them like a shepherd (see Psa 23.1). • Verse 8 is a refrain that is repeated in Psa 107.15, Psa 107.21, Psa 107.31.
The psalmist calls for thanksgiving and praise from people in despair over the consequences of their rebellion.
God’s counsel includes his instruction and will.
Exhausted by their hard labor (Lam 5.13), the people fell. While this might be expected of the wicked (Psa 9.3; Psa 27.2), it was unlike the Israelites’ flight from Egypt (Psa 105.37).
Fools who received what they deserved but were rescued from death offer thanksgiving to the Lord.
The Lord creates (Gen 1.3) and sustains the universe (Heb 1.3) simply by speaking (Psa 147.18); when he speaks, people are also healed (Mat 8.8).
Sailors give thanks to the Lord when he saves them from the chaos and peril of the sea.
The same God who speaks and brings about the sailors’ distress can also calm the storm with just a word (cp. Jon 1.4; Mat 8.26).
This call for public praise expands the refrains in Psa 107.21–22 and Psa 107.31.
These two sections (Psa 107.33–38, Psa 107.39–42) expand the theme of the Lord’s sovereignty over things that humans cannot control.
The Lord can choose to make the earth fertile or barren (Psa 74.15; Isa 35.6–7).
God’s presence can be seen in the abundance of his people’s families and herds (Psa 127.3; Psa 133.3; cp. Psa 109.8).
People often become impoverished when their rulers practice oppression.
In his contempt for human rulers, the Lord rectifies their corruption on earth.
The large families of the poor are evidence of God’s blessing.
Justice prevails in God’s world (Psa 1.6), and Israel’s history demonstrates God’s faithful love.
This psalm combines two excerpts from David’s other psalms (cp. Psa 57.5, Psa 57.7–11; Psa 60.5–12).

The psalmist begins this lament with a general charge against his accusers: They do evil in return for good (Psa 109.1–5). At the end of the psalm, he turns to the Lord in prayer, asking for his protection (Psa 109.21–25) and vengeance (Psa 109.26–31).
The psalmist sees no evidence that God cares (see Psa 28.1).
The psalmist’s acts of kindness and godliness (see Psa 35.12–14) have only met with stubborn opposition and expressions of hatred.
The NLT translates these verses as the words of the psalmist’s accusers; Hebrew lacks They say, which makes it unclear who is speaking.
Family members of those guilty of capital crimes often died with the perpetrator (Num 16.1–33; Jos 7.1–25) or had their property confiscated (1Ki 21.13–16).
The wicked person apparently held a position of leadership. Peter referred to this psalm in regard to Judas Iscariot (Act 1.20–26).
If one’s family name was blotted out, it meant there was no offspring to carry on the family name or remember its history (see Pro 10.7).

Children inherit the sinful nature of their parents (Psa 51.5; Exo 20.5; Eph 2.3). The speaker wants the Lord to punish the perpetrator for the guilt of family members who went before him (cp. Mat 23.35–36).
The defendant committed capital crimes and did not exercise even basic decency.
Cursing is the accused person’s whole way of life.
The psalmist appeals to the principle of retribution (see Psa 94.23).
Vulnerable and miserable, the psalmist appeals to his Lord for help. The accusations have killed his inner spirit and even his physical stamina.
The Lord’s reputation is at stake. If the wicked triumph, others could think that the Lord is also wicked and be drawn to that wickedness (Psa 1.1).
A shadow at dusk suggests a transitory, empty existence (Psa 102.11; Psa 144.4); a single locust could easily be brushed off one’s clothing.
These verses form a prayer for God’s presence and for vindication. The psalmist wants everyone to see that he is vindicated by the Lord, not by any human agent.
The Lord’s servant demonstrates loyalty and obedience.
The psalmist had been accused of being clothed with curses (Psa 109.18); now he asks that his accusers be clothed with disgrace and humiliation.

Jesus and the apostles cite this psalm to explain Jesus’ unique ministry and status as the Messiah (Mat 22.43–45; Act 2.32–36). It reaffirms God’s covenant with David and gives hope for the future (see 2Sa 7.8–16).

The king of Israel had the great privilege of being the Lord’s adopted son (Psa 2.1–12; 1Ch 22.10), but he fell (Psa 89.1–52). This decree restores and heightens his position. • The LORD: Hebrew Yahweh, the name of God (see Exo 3.6–14; Exo 6.2–8; Exo 20.2). • my Lord (Hebrew ’adoni) means “my master” or “my superior.” The psalmist viewed God’s messianic ruler as his superior. The New Testament frequently cites this psalm to validate Jesus’ claim to be the Messiah (Mat 22.44–45; Mar 12.36–37; Luk 20.42–44; Act 2.34–35; Heb 1.13). • The Lord’s right hand represents his authority, strength, presence, and benefits. The Lord chose the descendant of David and raised him up to be close to him (Psa 80.17). Jesus claimed this position for himself (Mat 26.64; Mar 14.62; Mar 16.19; Luk 22.69), and the apostles announced that Jesus, having ascended to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father (Act 2.33; Act 5.31; Act 7.55–56; Rom 8.34; Eph 1.20; Col 3.1; Heb 1.3; Heb 8.1; Heb 10.12; Heb 12.2). • Ancient Near Eastern kings were sometimes portrayed as placing their feet on the backs of their conquered enemies as on a footstool (see Heb 10.12–13).
The kingdom will expand and increase, beginning from Jerusalem, until all enemies are conquered.
