The Lord had made an unbreakable oath and covenant, so his apparent rejection of David’s dynasty (Psa 89.38) in the Exile had led to a crisis. The placement of Psa 110.1–7 in Book Five reaffirms the future of the dynasty: David’s descendant must conform to God’s standard of integrity (Psa 101.1–8). His ministry will be transformed as he serves under God’s kingship (Psa 93.1–100). • You are a priest forever: The role of God’s messianic ruler changes. The priestly kingship of David and his descendants extended to serving as patrons of the Temple. David had the Ark brought to Jerusalem (2Sa 6.15) and arranged for the Temple service (1Ch 6.31–48; 1Ch 15.11–26; 1Ch 16.4–42; 1Ch 23.4–32; 1Ch 25.1). Solomon supervised the Temple construction (1Ki 5.1–Psa 7.51). Even so, Israel’s kingship was separate from its priesthood. In the messianic kingdom, the king would also minister as priest, as Melchizedek, king of Salem (Gen 14.18), had done. The New Testament develops the ministry of Jesus Christ as a fulfillment of this new order (see Heb 5.6–10; Heb 6.20–Psa 7.25).
The new priestly role of David’s descendant does not rescind his old role as conquering ruler. He must still bring the nations under his rule (Psa 110.2–3; see Psa 2.1–12).

at your right hand: This position brings help and protection (see Psa 16.7–8; Psa 108.13). • The Lord will strike down rebellious kings. Rebellion against the Lord is a capital offense (Psa 2.1–12; Rom 6.23).
God’s messianic ruler obtains victory as a vigorous person, as if he had received nourishment from brooks along the way (Psa 110.3).
The refrain Praise the LORD! (Hebrew haleluyah) characterizes this group of psalms.

This wisdom psalm contains many references to the works of the Lord that reveal his character. God is righteous, gracious, compassionate, faithful, just, trustworthy, upright, holy, and awe-inspiring (Psa 111.3, Psa 111.4, Psa 111.7, Psa 111.8, Psa 111.9). God’s character gives hope in the covenant relationship (Psa 111.5). He rescued Israel from Egypt (Psa 111.9), gave them the land (Psa 111.6), and provides for his people (Psa 111.5). However, God demands that the beneficiaries of this relationship also be people of righteousness and integrity.

The godly praise God and delight themselves in his great works. His mighty acts reflect his righteousness, grace, and compassion (see Psa 116.5–7). All who submit themselves to him experience his glory.
God takes care of his people’s needs, even providing food. He remembers his covenant with Abraham (see Psa 105.8–11).

Giving Israel the lands of other nations was just and good because the Lord was executing his justice on those he dispossessed and showing grace to the Israelites. However, if the Israelites do not live faithfully and with integrity, they will also be dispossessed. The Lord’s people must reflect his character.
The people of the Exodus generation went free because of God’s grace.
True wisdom is the source of life (Pro 3.18; Pro 9.11; Ecc 7.12); it begins with the fear of the LORD (Pro 9.10).
This psalm reiterates the themes of wisdom and the fear of the Lord (Psa 111.1–10). The wise have reason to be happy (Psa 112.1–5) and vigorous (Psa 112.6–10).
The fear of the Lord leads to a life of wisdom that honors God and blesses the family and community. The godly joyfully imitate God; their obedience is not slavish.
successful: All will know the children of godly people (see Psa 127.4) because the godly leave a legacy for their children (see Psa 1.3; cp. Mat 6.20).
The godly imitate God by being generous, compassionate, and righteous (Psa 51.1; Psa 111.1–10; 2Co 9.9). They lend money to the poor without charging interest (Psa 15.5; Psa 112.9; Exo 22.25).
The honesty and compassion of the wise keeps them from stumbling (Psa 15.5; Psa 37.23–24), ensuring that they will be long remembered (Pro 10.7).
Because the godly joyfully expect God to prevail and rescue them, they face their foes triumphantly (Psa 59.10; Psa 112.4; Psa 118.7).
Paul quotes this verse in his instructions about generous giving (2Co 9.9).

The wicked . . . grind their teeth in anger out of their bitter envy (Psa 35.16; Psa 37.12). The vigor and reputation of the godly cause conflict with those who want them dead. • The wicked will slink away out of fear and shame.

These psalms form what is known as the “Egyptian Hallel” (hallel means “praise”) because Jews use the collection in the celebration of Passover, which was instituted at the beginning of the exodus from Egypt. Psa 113.1–114 are recited before the Passover meal and Psa 115.1–118 afterward.

This hymn of praise exalts the greatness of the Lord’s name and glory. God is greatly exalted and glorious in heaven (Psa 113.4); he also stoops down to take care of the lowly and needy on earth (Psa 113.5–9).
The name of the LORD (Hebrew Yahweh; see Exo 3.15) reveals his being, character, and reputation. He is exalted in time (now and forever) and in space (from east to west).
The Lord’s glory reaches to the heavens (Psa 57.5, Psa 57.11; Psa 99.2; Psa 108.5; Psa 138.6; Isa 6.1; Isa 57.15) and throughout the world of human relationships.
The incomparable Lord intimately involves himself in caring for people on earth.
The Lord stoops to the world’s level to be directly involved with his people (see Psa 138.6; Phi 2.6–8).
These phrases are a quotation from Hannah’s prayer of praise (1Sa 2.8–9).

A childless woman was customarily treated with disdain (Gen 16.4); the Lord has the power to make her a happy mother, as he made Sarah (Gen 21.2), Rebekah (Gen 25.21), Rachel (Gen 30.23), and Hannah (1Sa 1.20). • God’s greatness and goodness provide ample reason to praise him.

This lyrical celebration of the Lord’s power in nature recalls Israel’s beginning as a nation at the Exodus (Psa 114.1–2) and upon their entry to the Promised Land (Psa 114.3–6). It promotes reverence for the God of Jacob (Psa 114.7–8).

At the time of Israel’s exodus from Egypt and their entrance into the Promised Land, Israel was one holy kingdom (Exo 19.5–6). • The separate references to the land of Judah and Israel indicate that the psalm was composed after the kingdom was divided (1Ki 12.16–17; cp. 1Sa 11.8; 1Ki 1.35), and probably after the Exile. The land of Judah became God’s sanctuary because the people worshiped God; his Tabernacle and later his Temple were located there.

hurried out of their way! The waters divided for Israel to escape Egypt (Psa 77.17–18; Exo 14.1–31). • The Jordan River turned away when Israel arrived to cross over (see Jos 3.1–17). • skipped like rams: God’s presence caused the mountains to quake (Exo 19.16–20).
The Lord miraculously provided for his people in hard times after the Exile, just as he had done in the wilderness after the Exodus.

In this hymn of thanksgiving for God’s blessings, the community ascribes all glory to the name of the Lord, who is the true source of hope and blessing. Meanwhile, those who trust in idols are greatly disappointed. The blessing of the Creator of heaven and earth extends to future generations (Psa 115.14), and especially to the priesthood (Psa 115.12).
The community confesses their faith that God will rescue them for the glory of his name.

Where is their God? People deny God’s presence or power when he does not act as they think he should (cp. Psa 14.1; Psa 42.3, Psa 42.10). However, God is in the heavens—he has all power, authority, and knowledge. He does as he wishes, not what people think he should do. He works out his plans in accord with his will (Eph 1.11) and acts in his own time and in ways he chooses.
This entire section is repeated in Psa 135.15–20. • Unlike the Lord (Psa 95.3–5), idols cannot do anything; they are good for nothing.
Worshiping idols leads one astray and corrupts those who trust in them (Isa 44.20).

Israel . . . priests . . . you who fear the LORD: The psalmist calls on all those in the God-fearing community to commit their ways to the living God. The threefold address assures them that the Lord is their true helper and shield (cp. Psa 118.2–4).
The groups named in Psa 115.9–11 receive assurance of the Lord’s blessing, regardless of their social status (see Psa 113.8).

The psalmist blesses (Psa 107.37–38, Psa 107.41) all who trust in and fear the Lord. The Creator will care for the families of those who fear him. • who made heaven and earth: This statement speaks of the Lord’s all-encompassing power in creation.

The heavens belong to the LORD:’s: God’s exaltation begins in heaven (Psa 113.4), far above the gods of the nations. Of course, the earth also belongs to him (Psa 47.9; Psa 95.4). • The dead cannot participate in God’s blessings. The living praise God in thanksgiving for his blessings (Psa 79.13).

This hymn of thanksgiving rejoices in God’s character and in rescue from death (Psa 116.1–11). It gives an assurance of God’s protection in life and reminds the godly that the Lord watches over them even at death. The psalmist commits to living as God’s servant and resolves to honor him publicly (Psa 116.12–19).
The psalmist praises the Lord for answering his prayers and rescuing him from death.
I love the LORD: This unique opening expresses affection for and commitment to the Lord (see Psa 18.1; Deu 6.5) on the basis of what the Lord has done.
Because the Lord responds to the cry of his people (Psa 107.41; Psa 113.6–8), the psalmist now strongly believes in prayer.
It isn’t clear if the psalmist’s crisis was a literal near-death experience or if he was using the term figuratively.
This is the first of three times that the psalmist calls on the Lord’s name (i.e., reputation).
The gracious, righteous, and compassionate Lord (see Psa 111.1–5) rescued and gave rest to the psalmist.
People with childlike faith readily receive his wisdom and instruction (Psa 19.7–11; Mat 18.3–4).
The psalmist’s near-death crisis made him more aware of life and of walking before the Lord. Though he had been in anguish, the Lord was faithful. However, people are all liars.
I walk in the LORD’s presence: The psalmist already lived with integrity, but since his experience of deep distress, he now enjoys open fellowship with the Lord (see Psa 56.13; cp. Job 42.5).
I believed in you: Paul quotes this phrase in 2Co 4.13.

The Lord’s gracious gifts are so great that the psalmist can do nothing to repay his debt. Keeping his promises publicly demonstrates his gratitude. • All he has done for the psalmist includes answers to prayer, rescue, and life. • The cup of salvation overflows with God’s blessings (Psa 23.5), unlike the cup of judgment (Psa 75.8). • The psalmist makes promises (“vows,” Psa 116.18) to praise the Lord publicly (Psa 116.17–18).
No one lives or dies outside of God’s will. Having been given a second chance at life, the poet readily commits himself to the Lord with renewed acts of public devotion.
This psalm, the shortest in the Psalter, invites all . . . people of the earth to praise the LORD because of his unfailing love and enduring faithfulness.
Paul quotes this verse to show that Gentiles would eventually praise the God of Israel (Rom 15.11).

With an exultant testimony, the psalmist gives thanks for the Lord’s goodness and encourages others to trust in his faithful love (Psa 118.1–4, Psa 118.29). This poem is the last of the Egyptian Hallel (Psa 113.1–118).
Israel . . . Aaron’s descendants . . . all who fear the LORD: These three groups represent the whole of the covenant community (cp. Psa 115.9–11; Psa 135.19–20).
The Lord alone is the psalmist’s helper.
The LORD is for me: Cp. Rom 8.31; Heb 13.6. • God’s presence cancels out the need to fear mere people (Psa 56.11). The psalmist joyfully expects God’s rescue (Psa 59.10; Psa 112.8).
Trusting in the Lord is better than placing confidence in even the most powerful human leaders (Psa 118.6; Psa 146.3).

Strength comes in the name of the Lord, declared by the threefold mention of the attackers, the Lord’s name, and victory. • Even when hostile people blazed . . . like a crackling fire, the Lord caused them to subside like burning thorns (see Isa 9.18; Isa 10.17).
The psalmist celebrates the victory of the Lord’s strong right arm, which kept him from death.
God has restored the psalmist from death to life, so he praises the Lord publicly (cp. Psa 116.6, Psa 116.12–19).
The psalmist sees his own salvation as the beginning of a new day in which the Lord will do great things.

The cornerstone (or keystone) of a building or an arch gives the structure its shape and foundation. It is the most important of all the stones. The Lord chooses and places this stone for his sanctuary (Isa 28.16). Jesus referred to himself as this cornerstone (Mat 21.42; Mar 12.10–11; Luk 20.17; see Act 4.11; Eph 2.20; 1Pe 2.6–7).
This is the day the LORD has made: The day of the Lord’s victory has already arrived, although its completion awaits another day (Psa 118.25).
The psalmist concludes with prayer and thanksgiving, anticipating an even greater revelation of God’s victory and rescue.

The one who comes in the name of the LORD brings the Lord’s complete victory (see Psa 118.10–12). • During Jesus’ triumphant entry into Jerusalem, the crowds called out various blessings, including phrases taken from this verse (Mat 21.9; Mar 11.9; Luk 19.38; Joh 12.13). Jesus himself quoted this passage as he wept over Jerusalem (Mat 23.39; Luk 13.35).

This psalm combines elements of wisdom, lament, praise, thanksgiving, and confession. Eight Hebrew words are used frequently, translated as “instructions,” “laws,” “words,” “regulations,” “statutes,” “commands,” “decrees,” “commandments,” and “promises.” Together, these words encourage love for and obedience to God’s instructions, as found in the Scriptures (see 2Ti 3.14–17). The expression of deep commitment to these instructions unifies the psalm.
Aleph (א): God, the author of these instructions, commands that his followers live by them. The psalmist prays to be given the grace to live by that revelation.

The wise are happy. They are people of integrity (see Psa 84.11) who follow the path of divine instruction. They obey God’s revelation and search for it with all their hearts (see Psa 27.7; Psa 119.10, Psa 119.45, Psa 119.94, Psa 119.155), and they reject all forms of evil. Cp. Psa 1.1–2.
To keep God’s commandments means to guard them by obeying them.
Beth (ב): The psalmist is determined to pursue purity and encourages the cultivation of wisdom through God’s principles (Psa 119.9) and instructions (Psa 119.10–16).

A young person tends toward foolishness (Pro 22.15) and can easily make mistakes that destroy his life (Pro 7.6–23). Youth is also the best time to develop personal discipline and pursue wisdom (see Psa 34.11; Pro 1.4). • To stay pure means to remain uncorrupted by wickedness and sin and to develop the integrity of life defined in Psa 15.1–5.
The student asks God the teacher to discipline him so that he will not wander.
God’s wisdom is far greater than any riches humans seek (Psa 119.72, Psa 119.127; Pro 3.14–15).
The way of wisdom includes meditating on God’s ways (see Psa 119.1, Psa 119.3). The wise reflect on the implications of God’s word.
Gimel (ג): Like a foreigner in hostile territory, God’s servant needs God’s guidance.

The psalmist seeks to please the Lord with a full and obedient life of praise (Psa 118.17; Psa 119.25, Psa 119.77, Psa 119.116, Psa 119.144, Psa 119.175). Only the Lord can remove his adversaries and enable him to see the wonderful truths found in God’s instructions.
The arrogant are probably those who mock the psalmist (Psa 119.22–23).
Those who meditate on God’s instructions receive wise advice from them.

Daleth (ד): Though the poet feels anguish and sorrow, he entreats the Lord to revive him because he wants to obey the Lord. Suffering and death may result from the Lord’s chastening (Psa 118.17–18; Psa 119.67, Psa 119.71, Psa 119.75), but his instruction revives the weary soul (see Psa 119.12).
lying to myself: Self-deception is a fruit of sinful human nature (Jer 17.9); it leads to folly. • Access to God’s word is a privilege, not a right.
He (ה): As a student, the poet asks his teacher, God, to renew life and to transform disgrace into righteousness.
The love for money can lead to sin (cp. Exo 18.21; 1Ti 3.1–5; 1Ti 6.10).
Waw (ו): The psalmist prays that God’s word would continue to be the source of his love and salvation.
The psalmist asks to be saved from enemies who speak harshly (see Psa 42.10; Psa 44.16; Psa 89.50–51; Psa 102.8).
The psalmist is determined to obey the Lord.
The psalmist finds delight in God’s word in spite of pain (Psa 119.92, Psa 119.143).
Zayin (ז): The psalmist asks God to remember his word as the psalmist also remembers God’s word and his name. Remembrance expresses devotion.
The age-old regulations are the Torah (God’s “instructions” or “law”), a term that refers to the books of Genesis—Deuteronomy.
Heth (ח): The psalmist seeks God’s favor and unfailing love. Although surrounded by evildoers, he remains a loyal servant of the Lord.
Evil people try to drag him into sin, but the psalmist’s memory of God’s word keeps him standing firm (see Psa 119.16).
God’s goodness fills the earth; the whole created order provides evidence of his goodness (see Isa 6.3; Isa 11.9).
Teth (ט): The psalmist describes himself as a penitent sinner who gratefully accepts the Lord’s discipline.

Good judgment and knowledge come from wisdom (Psa 111.10). • The psalmist admits that he used to wander off like a stray sheep (Psa 119.176). • you disciplined me: See Psa 119.25–29. • You are good and do only good: God’s character is perfect (Psa 97.2; Jam 1.17; 1Jo 1.5).

Yodh (י): In this prayer for comfort and compassion, the psalmist commits himself to his Creator, who has afflicted him. He wants God to pay back his enemies for the wrongs they have done. He also prays to receive the gift of life. He not only prays for himself but also considers the whole community of the godly, asking that God’s answers to prayer would encourage them.
As God’s child, the psalmist asks for divine wisdom.
Kaph (כ): The psalmist is worn out from waiting for the Lord, but his hope is in God’s future rescue.
God’s word is trustworthy, in contrast to the deceptions of the enemies who hunt the psalmist down without cause (see Psa 119.78).
Lamedh (ל): The stability of God’s wisdom gives understanding. God’s word provides order and a framework for living, even when under pressure from adversaries.
The wicked intended to kill the psalmist, but destruction (Psa 1.6) was their own fate.
Even perfection has its limits: Humans cannot fully understand God’s ways (see Ecc 3.11).
Mem (מ): The instruction and wisdom of God through his word are far superior to the best that human teachers can offer.
make me wiser: God’s word provides wisdom and perspective. God is the true source of wisdom.

Wisdom is preferable to even the finest food (Psa 19.10; Psa 81.16). • The psalmist had already rejected the delusion offered by the way of folly (see Psa 119.18, Psa 119.78, Psa 119.86, Psa 119.163).
Nun (נ): The psalmist’s devotion to God’s word comes from within his being (Psa 119.112) and guides his external life.
The Lord’s word is a lamp that provides perspective, hope, and guidance in darkness (Psa 18.25–29; Psa 119.130). Even more, this light gives life (Pro 6.23).
offering of praise: This Hebrew expression is unique in the Old Testament (cp. Psa 50.23). • The psalmist is vulnerable to his opponents because of his commitment to a wise life.
Samekh (ס): The psalmist declares his hatred of evil and his love for God and his ways.
The godly hate the wicked and their deeds (Psa 5.4–6; cp. Eze 33.11).
Ayin (ע): The servant of the Lord strains to endure the evil around him. He boldly petitions the Lord to rescue him immediately!
Simply possessing God’s law does not provide any benefits. The psalmist knows that only as the Lord gives discernment will he understand it.
Pe (פ): The psalmist prays earnestly for God to speak to him as he suffers from his adversities.
Tsadhe (צ): God is righteous, and his word is right and just, especially in contrast to the deceptions of the wicked.
The psalmist’s indignation (cp. Psa 69.9) comes from seeing the wicked disregard God’s word.
The psalmist is greatly troubled by his oppressors (see Psa 119.143; cp. Isa 53.1–12).
Qoph (ק): The psalmist prays to the Lord at night. Although God appears to be distant, he is nearby.
I pray and I cry out translate the same Hebrew verb. • I rise early and I stay awake translate the same Hebrew verb.
Coming to attack me (or are coming near to me) is a Hebrew wordplay on but you are near. The wicked remain far from God’s instructions, whereas the psalmist stays near, so he does not need to fear.
Resh (ר): This petition for life can be found throughout Psa 119.1–176, but it is concentrated in this stanza.
Shin (ש): The psalmist looks beyond his adversaries to the peace of God. This perspective allows him to praise God throughout the day.
my heart trembles . . . I rejoice: Fear, trembling, and joy mark the psalmist’s devotion to God. • God’s word is a treasure. • In the Old Testament, seven signifies wholeness.
Taw (ת): God’s servant petitions the Lord one final time; he still feels like a lost sheep.
God, the Great Shepherd, seeks out his lost sheep (Psa 23.1; Luk 15.4–6).

These short, appealing songs were sung during pilgrims’ journeys to Jerusalem for the national festivals three times per year (Deu 16.16). The title of these psalms includes the Hebrew word for stairs, which some take to mean “ascending to Jerusalem.” These psalms (sometimes called the Songs of Ascents) take the reader on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to praise God for his goodness to Israel throughout history.

This short, individual lament expresses the psalmist’s trust that the Lord will deal with deceptive evildoers. It also laments living as a stranger among hateful liars. The psalmist’s picture of his life in a foreign land might have been a reality as he set out for Jerusalem, or it might depict his feelings and concerns as he begins his pilgrimage. Overwhelmed with injustice, he trusts God and looks forward to arriving in the Lord’s presence.
The psalmist is surrounded by liars, so he makes his lament to the LORD, the only one who can help him.

The psalmist dialogues with the liars who surround him. He feels reassured that the Lord will judge them. • The Divine Warrior (see Psa 7.12–13; Psa 11.4–6) will throw sharp arrows and glowing coals on the liars.
The psalmist feels the anguish of alienation, isolation, and perpetual conflict.

Meshech was a Japhethite territory far to the north of Canaan. Kedar was an Ishmaelite territory in Arabia. Violent people lived in both locations. Meshech was the home of a famous slave trade (Eze 27.13; cp. Exo 21.16) and Kedar of renowned warriors (Isa 21.16–17). These places can be understood as representative of the apostate, violent land where the psalmist suffered.
The leader of the group of pilgrims uses word pictures to assure the group of the Lord’s presence during the journey.

The mountains were known for their idolatrous worship (Deu 12.2), and Israel was enticed to the hilltop shrines (Hos 4.13). This verse can be understood as a rhetorical question expecting a negative answer: The gods of the hilltop shrines cannot rescue anyone. Others understand the mountains to be a symbol of the Lord’s strength (Psa 95.4). In that case, the question would be interpreted literally (Where does my help come from?), with the answer given in the next verse

The Creator (Psa 121.2) is the guardian of Israel. • God stands beside Israel, supporting and caring for the godly (see Psa 16.7–8). • Both the sun and the moon were regarded as deities in the ancient Near East, but the Creator limits their power. They, too, praise the Lord (Psa 148.3).
God watches over his own, even and especially when they face many troubles (Psa 12.5, Psa 12.7; Psa 69.29; Psa 91.14; Psa 146.9).

Jerusalem is here idealized as the city of God, the city of David, and the city of faith. A group of people on a pilgrimage joyfully arrive in the city (Psa 122.1–2). The psalmist sings an ode to Jerusalem (Psa 122.3–5) and prays for the city’s peace (Psa 122.6–9).
The central sanctuary was the house of the LORD. This phrase originally referred to the Tabernacle (Exo 23.19; Exo 34.26).
Several psalms celebrate or look forward to being inside the gates of the city (Psa 9.14; Psa 87.2; Psa 100.4; Psa 118.19).
Jerusalem is a metaphor for God’s heavenly dwelling. David was the archetype for God’s chosen rulers.
In the time of David and Solomon, Jerusalem was renowned as a place of security (1Ki 10.6–7).

Each of the people of Israel belonged to one of the tribes, and all of the tribes belonged to the Lord. • To give thanks is to present an offering acceptable to the Lord (Psa 50.14, Psa 50.23; Psa 100.4; Psa 118.19). • as the law requires of Israel: See Exo 23.17; Deu 16.16.
the thrones where judgment is given: In the eras of David and Solomon (1Ki 3.28), Jerusalem was the home of wisdom and justice; it would be so again (Isa 9.7).
Prayers for the peace of Jerusalem are motivated by love of family and God’s sanctuary.

This lament on the psalmist’s lowly position expresses vivid trust in the Lord (Psa 123.1–2). The psalmist prays for God’s favor on the community, as the reality of evil surrounds them (Psa 123.3–4). The poet looks beyond Jerusalem (Psa 122.1–9) to God’s throne in heaven.
This thanksgiving song describes what might happen if the Lord were not present with his people.
The negative rhetorical questions emphasize the positive idea that the LORD was indeed on their side.
the raging waters of their fury: The enemies could have overwhelmed the Israelites and wiped them out if the Lord had not been with his people (cp. Psa 69.15; Jer 46.8).
The enemies of God’s people, like lions or bears who tear their prey with their teeth (see Psa 57.4; Pro 28.15), had their mouths shut by the Lord (Dan 6.22).
The psalmist expresses the community’s confidence in the Lord’s protection (Psa 125.1–2) and prays for peace (Psa 125.3–5).
surrounds: God guards and protects like a wall of fire (Zec 2.5).
The godly might be tempted through peer pressure and cultural domination.
People who reject the straight path of the upright are fools (Pro 2.12–15). God pours out his goodness on the godly (see Psa 122.6–9).
This hymn celebrates Israel’s return from exile (Psa 126.1–3). The psalmist prays for full restoration (Psa 126.4–6).

The Lord brought about Israel’s restoration from exile, just as he had brought Israel out of Egypt (Psa 114.1). The restoration transformed the weeping of the Lord’s people into laughter and showed the Lord’s character to the nations (Psa 9.11; Psa 64.9; Isa 12.4).

The prophets had spoken of the restoration as a time when the wilderness would change into the Garden of Eden (Isa 51.3; Eze 47.1–23); the reality fell far short of paradise. Here the restoration community prays for full redemption (see Hag 2.19). • as streams renew the desert: The seasonal rains filled the dry river beds (wadis), and the land turned green again. The prayer looks for a similar transformation of Israel’s fortunes, a fulfillment of the imagery of the “Second Exodus” in Isaiah (see “The Promise of a Second Exodus” Theme Note). • The harvest represents God’s full restoration.
Blessing and protection come from God. Without his presence, there is no success (Psa 127.1–2). This is particularly true for children, who are God’s gift (Psa 127.3–5).

Unless: These conditional sentences emphasize the positive idea that the Lord will protect the city (cp. Psa 124.1–2). • Human effort is futile unless the Lord blesses it (see Psa 44.3). • from early morning until late at night: This depicts an aggressive and competitive lifestyle. • God’s loved ones enjoy a quiet night’s sleep (Psa 3.5; Psa 4.8).
Children are one of God’s blessings. The words translated “children” (Hebrew banim) and “builders” (bonim, Psa 127.1) form a wordplay. Having children builds a family.
like arrows: God uses children to protect the reputation of his people against the wicked (cp. Psa 120.4; Psa 7.12–13).

The godly, who fear the Lord, will know true happiness (Psa 128.1–2). The Lord is with them (see Psa 127.1–2), building their home life (Psa 128.3–4) and blessing them across the generations (Psa 128.5–6).
Enjoying the fruit of one’s labor means gaining benefit from whatever work one does.
Like vigorous young olive trees, children are saplings filled with potential. Olive oil symbolizes God’s blessing (Psa 104.15; Num 18.12; Jer 31.12; Hag 2.19).

God will continually bless all who fear him (Psa 133.3) from his dwelling in Zion (Psa 20.2; Psa 50.2; Psa 110.2), no matter where they live. • grandchildren: God’s blessings extend from generation to generation for the faithful (Psa 79.12–13; Psa 89.1; Psa 100.4–5; Psa 103.17–19).
The psalmist briefly reviews Israel’s history of trouble (Psa 129.1–2) and redemption (Psa 129.3–4). He concludes with curses against the enemies and blessings on the godly (Psa 129.5–6).
Israel’s earliest youth as a nation was during its sojourn in Egypt.
the LORD is good: He rescued Israel from Egypt, from many enemy attacks, and from the Babylonian exile.
Grass on a rooftop had shallow roots and would scorch easily. A crop was ignored by the harvester when the yield was low. The enemies who had sown hurt among God’s people would gain little.

Beginning with himself as a representative of the community, the psalmist cries for God’s mercy (Psa 130.1–3) out of deep distress. A cry from the depths is from a place of deep distress (cp. Psa 69.2, Psa 69.14; Isa 51.10; Eze 27.34). Out of the frailty of his being, the psalmist prays for divine favor.
The psalmist knows that his sins make him guilty and deserving of God’s judgment.
The good news comes in God’s readiness to forgive sinners. His grace encourages people to fear him and hope in him.
God’s word imparts hope (Psa 119.42–43, Psa 119.49; Psa 147.11).

The heart represents the whole being (see Psa 27.8). • God hates arrogance, which is a foolish way of life (Pro 6.16–19). • The psalmist does not trouble himself with matters that properly belong to the Lord.

The psalmist recounts the early history of Israel’s redemption.
The psalmist relates the recent history of Israel’s redemption, although the circumstances are not specified.
The Lord provides for all of his creatures.

The phrase God of heaven is an exilic and postexilic designation for the Lord; it is found in Ezra (Ezr 1.2; Ezr 5.11, Ezr 5.12; Ezr 6.9, Ezr 6.10; Ezr 7.12; etc.), Nehemiah (Neh 1.5; Neh 2.4, Neh 2.20; etc.), and Daniel (Dan 2.18, Dan 2.19, Dan 2.37, Dan 2.44).

In response to the pain of exile (Psa 137.1–4), the psalmist resolves to remember Jerusalem even though the memories cause him pain (Psa 137.4–6). He also writes an astounding imprecation, or prayer for vengeance (Psa 137.7–9).

Because the music of Jerusalem was tied to the joys of life in the Promised Land, the Exile removed any occasion for singing joyous songs. The Babylonians wanted the Judeans to sing and dance for them, but the exiles’ grief made doing so either distasteful or impossible. The songs celebrating the Lord speak of his power and goodness, but his people were filled with doubts and questions. They hung their harps in trees, perhaps signifying the death of their joy under God’s curse (Deu 21.23).

The poet witnessed the betrayal of God’s people from Judah by the Edomites, so he curses Edom. The long rivalry between Edom and Judah came to a head during Judah’s last days, when the Edomites handed the Judeans over to the Babylonians (Oba 1.10–11) and rejoiced in Jerusalem’s fall. • This prayer for vengeance is shocking.
In this final collection of psalms of David, praise and wisdom psalms (Psa 138.1–139, Psa 145.1–21) form a frame around five poems of lament (Psa 140.1–144).

God’s holiness and excellence are great, beyond the scope of humanity (see Psa 99.2; Psa 113.4; Isa 6.1; Isa 57.15).
The psalmist expresses confidence in the Lord’s plans, which are perfect, and prays for God’s continued involvement. The psalmist sees himself as part of God’s plans (see Psa 9.10; Psa 139.14).

In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist opens every aspect of his being, character, behavior, and speech to God’s examination. As hard as life is, he wants to ensure his own growth in wisdom so that he does not come under God’s judgment of the wicked (Psa 141.5; Psa 142.3; Psa 143.8, Psa 143.10; Psa 144.3–4). Further, the poet recognizes that he cannot escape from the Lord. His sense of stress disappears when he considers the Lord’s loving care for him, even before birth (Psa 139.13–18). He then invites the Lord to continue examining him as he walks in the path of wisdom (Psa 139.23–24).
The Lord knows the psalmist well; God has examined him thoroughly, in an inescapable examination that is painful at times (Job 7.17–19).
