The phrase sit down or stand up refers to daily activities (cp. Deu 6.6–9).
The Lord’s omniscience and omnipotence provide comfort to the godly, but they imprison the hearts of the wicked (Psa 2.3).
The Lord’s wonderful understanding lies beyond the psalmist’s ability to comprehend (see Jdg 13.18).
The psalmist expresses his awe at the Lord’s omnipresence.
down to the grave: God has total access to his entire creation—even the most hard-to-reach places.

ride the wings of the morning: This poetic expression describes traveling eastward, as far as the sunrise, if that were possible. • the farthest oceans: This expression takes the traveler in the opposite direction, far to the west.
The delicate, inner parts of the body include a person’s very being. • Even when hidden in his mother’s womb, the psalmist was guided by the Lord.
How precious are your thoughts about me: God’s investigation reveals loving care. Fellowship with the Lord provides riches beyond description.

The psalmist’s sense of awe leads him to consider the wicked and to reflect on himself. The Lord, as the examiner of all people, judges the wicked for their destructive acts and speech; thus, the psalmist prays that he will not be among them.
I hate: Rejection of evil is a mark of wisdom (see Psa 1.1; Psa 5.4–6).
The psalmist’s prayer against the wicked leads him also to reflect on himself; he does not presume that he is righteous. This prayer has been repeated by believers over the centuries.
The path of wisdom leads to everlasting life (see Psa 1.6; Pro 4.18; Pro 6.23).

In this individual lament, the psalmist artistically sketches God’s enemies with all their evil intents. He prays for the Lord’s protection and rescue with confidence in God’s strength and justice. He foresees the evil as being judged by fire (Psa 140.9–11) and himself as being vindicated and dwelling in the Lord’s presence (Psa 140.13).
The psalmist prays for the Lord to rescue him from wicked people.
sting like a snake . . . a viper: These creatures depict the wicked as very corrupt people (see Pro 23.32; Isa 14.29; Rom 3.13).
The psalmist asks for divine protection (see Psa 121.1–8), praying that the Lord will keep him safe from the many schemes of the wicked.
The expression Sovereign LORD comes from combining the name Yahweh with the title Adonai (Master). See also Psa 68.20; Psa 69.6; Psa 71.16; Psa 73.28; Psa 109.21; Psa 141.8.
The psalmist prays for God’s judgment on the wicked.

The psalmist wants fire to descend on his enemies, and he wants them thrown into pits so they can never attack again. The language foreshadows the New Testament teaching on hell (Mat 5.22, Mat 5.29–30; Mat 10.28; Mat 18.9; Mar 9.43–47; Luk 12.5; Jam 3.6; 2Pe 2.4).
The psalmist prays for rescue and wisdom, and he envisions the end of evil. The principle of retribution (Psa 141.10) unifies the psalm.

The psalmist prays urgently for rescue. He does not have at hand either incense or an evening offering (Exo 29.38–39), but his prayers and devotion are the reality that those elements represent (cp. Isa 1.13; Rev 5.8). • Upraised hands are a posture of prayer (Psa 28.2; Psa 88.9; Psa 143.6; Exo 9.29; 1Ti 2.8).

Wisdom sometimes requires protection from oneself. One could say or think things that lead to the evil path (Pro 13.3; Pro 21.23). • Wisdom opens itself to correction from godly people (see Pro 3.11; Pro 9.8; Pro 15.31; Pro 19.25).
The psalmist faces severe persecution, so he cries to the Lord, and the Lord will rescue him.
regarding his experience in the cave: Cp. Psa 57.1.
Though overwhelmed by his persecutors (Psa 142.6), the psalmist looks to the Lord for wisdom.

The psalmist reaches a point of despair (see Psa 77.3), and the Lord cares for him in his distress. The psalmist commits himself to the Lord’s wisdom (see Psa 139.1–24) but laments his entrapment by the wicked (Psa 5.9–10; Psa 140.5; Psa 141.9; Psa 142.3).
Though he is alone, the psalmist’s trust remains in the Lord, who is his life (see Psa 9.9; Psa 16.5; Psa 27.13).
Though overwhelmed by loneliness and trouble, the psalmist focuses on the Lord’s goodness and protection. He knows that the Lord alone is his Redeemer, so he offers his praise.
His experience of confinement and duress is like being in prison (see Psa 107.10).

In this lament, the psalmist feels overwhelmed by constant harassment from his foes, so he turns to the Lord’s love, righteousness, and faithfulness. He remembers God’s acts in the past and yearns for the renewal of the Lord’s love. He opens himself to God’s wisdom because he knows that instruction will lead to life.
The psalmist prays for God’s love and mercy.
All people are guilty before God (Rom 3.20–24).
I am losing all hope: The psalmist confesses his desperation as his life slips away under oppressive and ruthless foes.
Remembering God’s acts from the past reassures the psalmist of God’s faithfulness (Psa 42.4; Psa 63.6; Psa 77.3, Psa 77.6; Psa 119.55).
The psalmist’s thirst is a deep longing for God’s redemption (see Psa 42.1–2).
The psalmist petitions the Lord for a renewal of his love.

The psalmist experiences depression. He feels that he is dying from anguish (Psa 31.10; Psa 119.87), exhausted (Psa 39.10; Psa 71.9; Psa 119.81), fainting with longing (Psa 84.2), and overwhelmed by the weariness of life (Psa 90.7, Psa 90.9).
The psalmist prays for wisdom (see Psa 5.8; Psa 25.4–6; Psa 138.1–8; Psa 143.10). • your gracious Spirit: The Spirit brings God’s goodness (see Psa 23.6).
To preserve means in this case to restore from despair (Psa 80.19; Psa 85.6; Psa 138.7).
A prayer for vindication and renewal of life concludes the psalm.

This lament begins with an exclamation of love for the Lord. The community then reflects on the transitory nature of life (Psa 144.3–4). The psalmist prays for divine intervention and anticipates victory (Psa 144.5–11). A new song (Psa 144.9–10) and a prayer for rescue (Psa 144.11) open up the theme of the Lord’s blessing through his provisions and protection (Psa 144.12–15).
The psalmist’s descriptive names for the Lord reveal his deep love for him.

what are human beings? The same question in Psa 8.4–6 elicits the answer that humans are mere mortals but are also glorious rulers. The psalmist depicts humans as having a transitory, empty existence (see Psa 90.3, Psa 90.7–10; Psa 102.11; Psa 109.23; Psa 146.4).
The psalmist prays for God’s intervention against his enemies (cp. Psa 18.7–19).

This prayer for the Lord’s blessing brings the laments of Psa 140.1–144 to a close. It offers a vision of God’s provision and protection (see Psa 127.1–5), not only for the psalmist, but for his descendants and those of all the godly.
The psalmist compares sons and daughters to plants and pillars, which are images of strength and beauty.
no enemy . . . no cries of alarm: These images depict peace and security.

This hymn of praise is the last in this collection of the psalms of David (Psa 138.1–145). Praise continues in the last five psalms (Psa 146.1–150). This psalm celebrates the Lord as King of all (Psa 145.1–3, Psa 145.10–13). God’s actions reveal his royal qualities (Psa 145.4–7). He cares for all creatures (Psa 145.14–17) and for those who fear him (Psa 145.18–20).
The psalmist praises God, the Great King who reigns over all other rulers (see Psa 47.2).
This litany praises God’s character and mighty deeds. Each generation will continue to testify to God’s power (Psa 22.30).
God consistently demonstrates his character toward all his creation (see Psa 136.25).
These verses form a description of the Lord’s kingdom.
The Lord cares for his creatures.

The Lord cares for those who love him and fear him. God-fearers love the Lord and find refuge in him (Psa 5.11); they seek him as their only true Savior (Psa 40.16; Psa 70.4). They will experience a grand future (Psa 69.36), as well as God’s peace (Psa 119.165).
The Psalter ends with five hallelujah psalms, so named because each begins and ends with Praise the LORD! (Hebrew haleluyah).
The call to praise (Psa 146.1–2) leads into a warning against folly and false confidence (Psa 146.3–4). The psalm concludes with a blessing for all who place their hope in the Lord (Psa 146.5–7).
This verse is reminiscent of Psa 103.1, Psa 103.2, Psa 103.22; Psa 104.1, Psa 104.35.
The fourfold repetition of the name of the LORD emphasizes that only he heals, unburdens, loves, and protects.
The psalmist calls for the Lord to be praised for restoring and blessing Zion, caring for the poor, displaying his power over nature, and revealing himself to his people.
This verse is a call to worship.
The psalmist recalls the restoration of Jerusalem and the Lord’s afflicted exiles.
The Lord created the heavens. • He counts the stars: God’s people can feel secure in knowing that the Lord attends to every detail of his creation; he knows all that belongs to him.
God measures out his justice on the poor and on the wicked (Psa 55.22; Psa 140.12; Psa 145.14; Psa 146.7).
Human achievements fail to impress the God who commands nature; rather, he takes pleasure in those who fear him.
God holds sovereign power over the weather (Psa 77.17–18; Psa 78.26; Psa 104.4; Psa 148.5–6).
human might: Any physical or intellectual achievement is a gift from the Lord, just like the strength of a horse. These gifts are a reason to praise the Lord, not to boast (Jer 9.23–24).
The bars of the city gates symbolize defenses against enemies. • God blessed his people by empowering them with safety, prosperity, peace, and provisions (see Psa 133.3).
Simply by speaking his command, the Lord can change the season from unbearable winter to refreshing spring (see Psa 147.8; Psa 148.5–6).
words . . . decrees . . . regulations: The Lord gave powerful words to Israel so that they might obey him (Psa 105.45).
This psalm calls for the whole created order to praise the Lord because he has honored his faithful people.
During Jesus’ triumphant entry into Jerusalem, the crowds called out various blessings, including a phrase taken from this verse (Mat 21.9; Mar 11.10; Luk 19.38).
The created order is stable because of the Lord’s word (see Psa 33.9).

In the ancient Near East, people viewed different gods as having control over separate aspects of nature. The Lord, however, reigns sovereign over all natural phenomena; all the parts of creation are his servants, bringing praise to him through their obedience (Psa 77.17–18; Psa 104.4; Psa 135.7; Psa 147.8, Psa 147.15–18; Num 11.31).
The psalmist calls all humans to offer praise to God, regardless of status, age, or gender.

Universal praise of the Lord is fitting because he is glorious, and he has blessed his people (see Psa 147.13; Isa 46.13; Eph 3.10). • His faithful ones are his trusting and devoted servants (Psa 86.2).
This hymn of praise celebrates the Lord’s victory. He is the Maker of Israel (Psa 149.1–2) and the victorious King who shares his glory with his faithful ones (Psa 149.3–9).
God’s people, whom the world ignores and despises, will be vindicated (Mat 19.30). The humble will experience victory over their oppressors and persecutors (see Isa 61.3).
Vengeance is the Lord’s business (see Psa 2.3; Psa 94.1; Psa 102.20; Psa 142.7; Psa 146.7).
Everything that breathes is commanded to praise the Lord as he deserves. The whole Psalter describes the greatness of the Lord, so this psalm is a fitting conclusion.
The phrase mighty heaven alludes to Gen 1.1–31 and to God’s glorious work in filling the emptiness.

The psalmist calls all people to praise God with instruments and dancing. flutes: These wind instruments are not mentioned as being used in Temple worship. • clanging cymbals: Temple musicians clapped two bronze bowls together as percussion instruments.
Praise the LORD: This refrain is a fitting conclusion to the entire book of Psalms.

The Book of Proverbs

Purpose

To offer practical wisdom for making decisions and ordering life

Author

Various; many are attributed to Solomon

Date

Written and compiled over the course of several centuries, beginning during Solomon’s reign (971–931 BC) and continuing until at least the reign of Hezekiah (728–686 BC)

Setting

Part is directed to a young man; other parts hint at diverse settings

Each day, life confronts us with many decisions. The book of Proverbs is a compass that helps us navigate the murky waters of life. It provides wisdom, instructions for living, and guidance for achieving strong character. Proverbs tells us how to succeed in any situation by remaining calm-headed in a crisis, patient when pressed, gentle when challenged, and firm when confronted with temptation. Above all, Proverbs shows us that the source of all wisdom is a right relationship with God.

Setting

Proverbs is a collection of sayings from various times and social contexts. Many individual proverbs find their primary setting in the royal court, addressing matters such as how to act in front of a king. Some proverbs have a family setting and best fit an agricultural context. Others pertain to the world of commerce, trade, and business. Much of Proverbs is directed toward a young man who seems to be at the age of beginning a profession. Proverbs offers wisdom and guidance for success in all the spheres of life that a person in ancient Israel might face. Yet it is also timeless, with significant application to readers today.

Summary

Proverbs is ancient Israel’s anthology of wise sayings, advice, instructions, and warnings. The book has two major sections: It begins with talks that a father gives to his son (Pro 1.1–9). These are followed by collections of wise sayings (Pro 10.1–31) from a variety of authors on a wide range of topics; most frequently mentioned are wealth and poverty, planning, laziness, prostitutes, hard work, relationships, pride, and humility.

Genre and Style

Wise Sayings. In the ancient Near East, wise sayings were collected into anthologies for people to consult for guidance on a correct course of action. In Israel, as in neighboring nations, the purpose of these collections was to educate the young and give them direction for living well. Evidence suggests that Babylonian and Egyptian wisdom collections were incorporated in the curriculum of schools.

A proverb expresses an insight, observation, or piece of advice that has been popularly accepted as general truth. Often, uttering the right proverb at the appropriate time is all it takes to resolve a discussion.

Hebrew Poetry. Proverbs is also poetry. Its compact language holds a lot of content in few words. It is literature that rewards reflective time and meditation on its rich nuances. Many proverbs teach through poetic imagery. For example, laziness is discouraged through the use of a comparison with common irritants:

Lazy people irritate their employers,

like vinegar to the teeth or smoke in the eyes (Pro 10.26).

One important characteristic of Hebrew poetry is parallelism. Many proverbs use synonymous parallelism—the second part continues and sharpens the thought of the first part:

The king is pleased with words from righteous lips;

he loves those who speak honestly (Pro 16.13).

Other proverbs are antithetical, meaning that the first and second parts are opposites:

A wise woman builds her home,

but a foolish woman tears it down with her own hands (Pro 14.1).

Still other proverbs make comparisons:

Better to have little, with fear for the LORD,

than to have great treasure and inner turmoil (Pro 15.16).

Awareness of these elements of Hebrew poetry enhances one’s ability to understand and interpret the proverbs.

Authorship

Proverbs was begun by Solomon (Pro 1.1), a wise king (1Ki 3.5–15) who collected wise sayings and composed his own (1Ki 4.29–32). Material written or edited by later teachers was then added. For example, two hundred years after Solomon, “the advisers of King Hezekiah of Judah” collected additional proverbs of Solomon and added them to the anthology (Pro 25.1). Other composers or editors mentioned in Proverbs include Agur (Pro 30.1), Lemuel (Pro 31.1), and “the wise” (Pro 22.17; Pro 24.23).

Some of the sayings are influenced by neighboring nations, such as the “thirty sayings” of the wise (Pro 22.17–Pro 24.22), which appear to have borrowed heavily from an Egyptian writing called The Instruction of Amenemope (around 1100 BC). Proverbs was edited to its final form several hundred years after Solomon’s time.

Readers

Pro 1.8–Pro 9.18 contains a series of discourses from a father to a son. There is some debate as to whether this was a biological son or an apprentice since the recipient of the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope was an apprentice. However, the presence of the “mother” in Proverbs (e.g., Pro 1.8) suggests a biological son.

Much of the material is more appropriate for young males than for women (such as warnings to avoid immoral women), yet Proverbs has a much broader audience than just young men. Its purpose is to teach wisdom to people (Pro 1.2), both to the simple (Pro 1.4) and to the wise (Pro 1.5). Proverbs is addressed to everyone—but not everyone will receive it (Pro 1.7).

Meaning and Message

Proverbs is a book of practical wisdom for life. It often takes the form of a father teaching his son. As the son walks the path of life, he will come to crossroads where he must make decisions about which way to go.

The book of Proverbs helps us to make right choices today. It teaches that there are rewards for wise behavior and punishments for foolish behavior. But while these rewards motivate us to heed instruction, they are not universal promises. Proverbs offers principles that are generally true, but these principles do not always guarantee a favorable outcome. For example, a person who works hard and has integrity is likely to have more material resources than a lazy and shiftless person. However, a lazy person might inherit wealth, and a hard worker might lose wealth when exploited by a corrupt government official. (This disjunction between righteousness and material reward is a major theme of Job and Ecclesiastes.)

The advice of Proverbs sometimes seems to contradict itself, but wisdom and careful reading reveal the circumstances to which each piece of advice applies. Should we answer a fool’s arguments? Or should we be silent when we realize that we are arguing with a fool (Pro 26.4–5)? It depends. We find the same thing with English aphorisms. On some occasions “Look before you leap” applies; other times we are reminded that “He who hesitates is lost.” Contradictory sayings might both be true in different situations. The truly wise person knows when to apply a particular proverb and when not to.

The wisdom of Proverbs is practical, but the sayings contain much more than good advice. Real wisdom is based on a reverent, faith-filled relationship with God, who is the true source of all wisdom. This message is expressed in Pro 1.7: “Fear of the LORD is the foundation of true knowledge.” Proverbs invokes a fundamental spiritual choice, because there is no true wisdom apart from a living relationship with God.

Solomon is the foremost authority on Israelite wisdom (see 1Ki 3.1–28; 1Ki 4.32). Many proverbs are ascribed to Solomon, but he did not write all of them (see Pro 22.17; Pro 24.23; Pro 25.1; Pro 30.1; Pro 31.1).
Theme: Wisdom
This prologue explains the purpose of the book and identifies the different readers to whom it is addressed.

Wisdom is practical knowledge that involves ethical choices. Words such as right, just, and fair are associated with biblical wisdom. Gaining wisdom involves discipline, an active, intentional training of energy toward wisdom and away from folly. The book of Proverbs encourages us to resist our natural sinful tendencies toward wrong behavior.
The simple are like empty containers. Wisdom and folly compete to fill their minds and hearts (see Pro 9.1–18).
Proverbs help the wise person to understand riddles. Here the Hebrew word (khidoth) indicates enigmas or paradoxes—difficult sayings that require interpretation (cp. Jdg 14.14).

Fear of the LORD recognizes total dependence on God for everything, including knowledge and wisdom (Pro 9.10). It is not just a mental attitude but involves service, love, and obeying God’s laws (see Deu 10.12–13). Fear of the Lord is the basis of all knowledge. How can we understand life without knowing the most fundamental truth about it—that it is God’s creation?
Theme: Fear of the Lord

My child (Literally My son): Like other wisdom literature of the ancient Near East, much of chs Pro 1.1–9 is a father’s (and occasionally, a mother’s) instruction to a son. Because the son is being trained to follow in his father’s profession, much of the teaching concerns the son’s occupation. The NLT usually translates the term as child, since the lessons are applicable to both sons and daughters.
There are two paths (Pro 1.15) in the book of Proverbs: a wise, just way and a foolish, evil way. The parents represent the wise way and encourage their child to follow it.
crown you . . . chain of honor: Ornaments often represent wisdom and its rewards (see also Pro 3.22; Pro 4.9). This imagery inspires readers to pursue wisdom with diligence.

The father warns his child not to join a gang of sinners in their plan to pounce on the innocent, for their evil actions will rebound on themselves (see Pro 28.10; Psa 9.15; Psa 35.8). The evil way is a path of violence and robbery.
like the grave: Hebrew like Sheol. In the Old Testament, Sheol is the abode of the dead. It is not necessarily associated with punishment.

Birds will not go into an obvious trap, but greedy people will. By resorting to violence and robbery, they will be violently robbed of life. They might be killed in the attempt or executed when caught. Even if sinners prosper until the end of their lives, they will find judgment in death, while the righteous will be in God’s presence (see Psa 1.1–6).
The author personifies wisdom as a woman (the Hebrew noun translated wisdom, khokmah, is grammatically feminine) and encourages his son to embrace her (see Pro 3.18; Pro 8.1–Pro 9.6).

Three main words in Proverbs describe those who lack God’s wisdom. Simpletons (Hebrew pethim) have not hardened themselves against God’s wisdom and are most open to correction (see Pro 1.4). Fools (Hebrew kesilim) have heard God’s wisdom but resist it. Mockers (Hebrew latsonim) not only resist wisdom but even ridicule it.

Wisdom invites all three groups (Pro 1.22) to come so she can make them wise. An intimate relationship with Wisdom means entering an intimate relationship with God, the foundation of true knowledge (Pro 1.7; see Job 28.1–28).
You ignored my advice—i.e., the call of God himself (see Psa 14.1–7). God calls to us through creation (Psa 8.1–9; Rom 1.18–20) and Scripture (2Ti 3.16–17; 2Pe 1.20–21).
I will not answer: If a person has not sought wisdom before calamity strikes, it is often too late to learn.
they hated knowledge: There is no middle ground in the language of Proverbs. One either loves and embraces Wisdom or hates and rejects her.
Evil people suffer the consequences of their own actions (see Pro 1.15–19); God will ensure that sinners receive their proper punishment (see Mat 25.44–46; Heb 10.29; 2Pe 2.9).
Truly wise people are untroubled by fear. They know that God is in control, and wisdom guides them in dealing with every situation.
The father urges his son to seek wisdom. It will protect him from evil men and from the dangers of promiscuous women. The son must seek wisdom, while understanding that it is a gift from God.
To treasure my commands means to give attention to them and obey them; they allow us to live to the fullest.
wisdom . . . insight . . . understanding: All three words point toward skills needed to navigate life’s difficulties.
Searching for silver or hidden treasures would be undertaken with urgency, excitement, and anticipation of reward (cp. Mat 13.44; Luk 15.8–10).
The quest for true wisdom leads to God. Wisdom is impossible without fear of the Lord (Pro 1.7).
The LORD grants wisdom to those who learn it from the Scriptures, which come from his mouth (2Ti 3.16; 2Pe 1.20–21). It is impossible to become wise through empirical observation alone.
Here, common sense is intuitive understanding built through listening to God’s words and observing his world. God is a shield who guards and protects those who live in relationship with him.

Wisdom will enter your heart, becoming an integral part of life. Rather than occasionally doing wise things, the wise person consistently makes wise choices. • Knowledge brings joy because it helps people live successfully.

Wisdom discerns when words are twisted to represent what is wrong as being right. The right way leads to life, the wrong way to death (Pro 1.10–19; Pro 2.18–19; Pro 5.5–6; Pro 9.1–6, Pro 9.13–18). • dark paths: In the New Testament, darkness represents the realm of evil, while light represents the realm of God’s goodness (Mat 4.16; Mat 5.14–16; Joh 1.14; Rom 2.19).

Wisdom keeps a young man from an immoral woman, helping him to resist her flattering, seductive words. Wisdom includes emotional maturity, restraint, and the ability to assess the purpose of someone’s speech.
Theme: Marriage and Sexuality
By pursuing another man, an immoral woman has abandoned her husband. Her marriage covenant . . . before God included vows of faithfulness (cp. Mal 2.14–16).
leads . . . to the grave: Adultery betrays a fundamental covenant with one’s spouse and with God (see also Gen 39.2–9; Mal 2.14).

Those who make wise choices will live in the land; those who do not will be evicted. God gave the land of Israel to his people, but they could only stay in it if they followed God’s commands (Deu 28.9–11, Deu 28.64–68). Because they broke his law, they were expelled (in 586 BC; see 2Ki 25.1–30; 2Ch 36.15–21).
The Lord blesses those who trust him and seek his will. His correction benefits those who follow him.
To store God’s commands in your heart means not just memorizing them but making them an integral part of life and acting on them.

Those who obey God’s laws are more likely to live many years; wickedness generally has negative physical and psychological consequences. However, evil people sometimes outlive righteous people (Ecc 7.15–18).
Loyalty and kindness reflect the intimate and wholehearted commitment of God’s covenant relationship with his people (see Deu 6.8–9). • Write them: For a parallel command, see Pro 7.3.
On the path of wisdom, God himself guides us by the wisdom embodied in his word.
Healing and strength mean enjoying physical vitality as God’s reward for following wisdom’s way.

God receives honor and blesses his people when they recognize him as the source of all they have and when they give him the best part of everything they produce (Gen 4.3–5; Gen 18.6; Num 18.12, Num 18.29).
The LORD’s discipline can take the form of hardships, disappointments, and frustrations (see Heb 12.4–6). Like a good father, God’s purpose is to make us wise, good, and happy.
Wisdom and understanding provide skill for living and handling life’s problems.
Wisdom is worth more than precious metals and jewels. It leads to relationship with God, the ultimate joy-giver (see Pro 2.1–8).
The tree of life alludes to the original tree in the Garden of Eden (Gen 2.9).
God’s wisdom created harmony in the universe. Having wisdom means living in conformity with principles embedded in creation.
This passage enumerates the benefits of common sense and discernment, which are fruits of wisdom.
A wise person is a kind and helpful neighbor. Proverbs strongly emphasizes helping the financially needy (Pro 11.24; Pro 28.27; Pro 29.7, Pro 29.14).
Because we have frequent contact with those who live nearby, we must not take advantage of them.
While it is impossible to avoid all conflict, we are not to pick a fight.

The violent will ultimately be punished for their ways (Pro 1.18–32), even if they seem to have an enviable position in the world (Pro 11.16). The wise will not envy them, because they are detestable to the LORD. God’s friendship is of far greater benefit than anything the violent achieve.

Discourses in chs Pro 1.1–9 often begin with the call to listen (cp. Pro 1.8, Pro 1.23; Pro 2.1; Pro 4.20–21; Pro 5.1–2; Pro 6.20–23; Pro 7.1–3). • when your father corrects you: The children have reason to listen, because they have made mistakes.
Wise people navigate life’s difficulties successfully because they have heeded good guidance.
my father’s son . . . my mother’s only child: In Proverbs, both parents give instruction in wisdom. This involvement of both parents is unique among the traditions of the ancient Near East.

my commands: The words that describe the father’s teaching are used elsewhere in Scripture for God’s law. Fathers represent God to their children; the instruction of wise fathers conforms to God’s law.
In the Old Testament, to forget means more than not to remember; it is failure to obey.
she: In Proverbs, wisdom is sometimes personified as a woman (see Pro 1.20–33; Pro 8.1–Pro 9.6).
Wisdom often, though not always, brings relational and material prosperity.
A lovely wreath and a beautiful crown represent wisdom’s rewards (see also Pro 1.9 and Pro 3.22).
The father again lays two paths before his children, encouraging them to avoid evil with its horrible consequences and to embrace good with its promise of blessing.
Not every wise person lives longer than every evil person, but obedience and wise living make a long, good life much more likely (see also Pro 5.1–14, Pro 5.21–23; Pro 23.29–35; cp. Ecc 2.12–17).
Wisdom’s . . . paths are straight (nondeceptive), while those of a fool are crooked (Pro 2.15). • When you walk . . . run: The wise reach their goals more quickly and efficiently.
The wicked stay up at night to plan evil (Psa 36.4; Mic 2.1).

To eat . . . wickedness and drink . . . violence means that those attributes are at the very center of someone’s life. Just as we eat and drink to stay alive, evil people sustain themselves by committing evil acts.

Light stands for wisdom and righteousness, and darkness stands for foolishness and wickedness (see Ecc 2.12–14). Light brings actions into the open; darkness hides them. Righteous people have nothing to hide, while the wicked try to hide what they do and end up stumbling over obstacles in the dark (see Mat 4.16; Mat 5.14–16; Joh 1.14; Rom 2.19).
The wise walk the path of life with eyes straight ahead.

pay attention: See also Pro 1.8, Pro 1.23; Pro 2.1; Pro 5.1–2; Pro 7.1–3; Pro 8.1. The child is to let these teachings transform his personality, represented by his heart. A lifelong commitment to follow wisdom requires a change of heart.
Life and healing are rewards for following the wise instructions of the father (see Pro 4.10).

In the Old Testament, the heart represents the center of emotions, thinking, and reasoning (e.g., Gen 6.5; Deu 4.29; Psa 131.1). The heart is crucial in the battle between wisdom and foolishness, between righteousness and evil (see Mat 5.8; Mat 13.15; Joh 12.40; Rom 6.17).

Because a person’s words originate in the heart, Proverbs teaches extensively about speech. One of the most basic lessons is to avoid perverse or corrupt speech, later defined as lies, slander, gossip, and rumor (Pro 6.12; Pro 17.4; Pro 18.8).

These instructions on embracing one’s wife and avoiding immoral women were originally addressed to young men just beginning their professional careers (see also Pro 2.16–22; Pro 7.1–27). This topic is also popular in ancient Egyptian wisdom writing.
Paying attention to instruction results in discernment—the ability to tell a right action from a wrong one. These instructions are vitally important when dealing with an immoral woman.
The lips of the immoral woman seem sweet and enticing but are actually bitter and deadly. Sexual activity often begins with a kiss, and flattering words can entice.
A relationship with an immoral woman leads to death, as does a relationship with the woman named Folly (see Pro 9.13–18).

An illicit relationship can be tempting, but it eventually brings shame. If the woman is a prostitute, the young man will have to pay her and thus lose income. If the woman is another man’s wife, he might have to pay her husband (see Lev 20.10).

Some sexually transmitted diseases were well known in the ancient Near East. Lev 15.1–15 describes what is probably gonorrhea; other texts from Mesopotamia describe “the disease of intercourse” and the “disease of Ishtar” (goddess of love) with the physical symptoms of venereal diseases.

To drink from one’s own well (see also Sol 4.12, Sol 4.15) is to enjoy sexual relations within marriage. Rather than expend sexual energy on immoral women, a man should cultivate a healthy sexual relationship with his wife. Sex is not to be shared with strangers. This honors marriage (Gen 2.22–25) and keeps the seventh commandment (Exo 20.14 and Deu 5.18).
deer: cp. Sol 4.5.
Even if a man keeps an illicit relationship secret from his family and society, nothing is hidden from the LORD. Adultery is a sin against God (Gen 39.8–9).
Habitual sins are like ropes that catch and hold people.
He will die: Young men must exercise self-control because death can result from acting on sexual desire for what is forbidden.

To secure the debt of another person is to guarantee it with one’s own possessions. Whether to earn a friend’s goodwill or to turn a profit from a stranger (cp. Exo 22.25; Lev 25.36–37; Deu 23.19–20), the risk is too great to take; it could lead to financial ruin. This message is repeated in Pro 11.15; Pro 17.18; Pro 20.16; Pro 22.26; Pro 27.13.
save yourself: The danger of ruin is so great that escaping the situation is almost a matter of life and death, as highlighted by the images of animals caught in a trap.

Lazy people sleep rather than make necessary provisions (see also Pro 24.33–34). They are the opposite of self-motivated and industrious ants. • Extra sleep . . . more slumber sarcastically expresses a lazy person’s ambition.
// The result of laziness is poverty. It will come suddenly and ruthlessly, like a bandit or an armed robber.
eye . . . foot . . . fingers . . . hearts: The different parts of a worthless person’s body describe overall character, not just an occasional foolish act.
wink . . . nudge . . . wiggle: These behaviors were signals used while trying to deceive the innocent.
Even if wicked people seem to prosper, they will suddenly be punished.

The first line gives a number followed by a second line that increases that number by one. This device (called number parallelism) introduces a list of items and often, as here, draws attention to the climactic final item (see also Pro 30.15–23).
A false witness perverts the truth in court or in everyday conversation.
This passage emphasizes the life-threatening risk of sleeping with another man’s wife (see also Pro 1.8, Pro 1.23; Pro 2.16–22; Pro 5.1–23; Pro 7.1–27).
The immoral woman uses smooth talk and physical beauty to appeal to the vanity of young men.
Sleeping with a prostitute has consequences, and sleeping with another man’s wife can cost you your life. Her husband will seek revenge (Pro 6.34–35), and God is watching in judgment.
walk on hot coals: Of course his feet will blister. The consequences are horrible.
Seven times is probably a way of saying a great amount since the law never stipulated such high repayment (see Exo 22.1, Exo 22.4, Exo 22.9).

A thief might be punished severely even if he had a reason for his actions, but his punishment is nothing compared to an adulterer’s, who has no excuse for his crime. A jealous husband will seek the full punishment provided by law, which is death (Deu 22.22).
This is the last of four sections in chs Pro 1.1–9 that warn against the dangers of promiscuous women (see also Pro 2.16–22; Pro 5.1–23; Pro 6.20–35).
as you guard your own eyes: That is, with great care.

The Old Testament uses the phrase tie . . . on your fingers as a reminder for something that needs to be remembered, most notably God’s commands (Deu 6.8; Deu 11.18). • The NLT’s write them deep within your heart reflects the Hebrew idiom write them on the tablet of your heart (see also Pro 3.3). Only obedience that comes from the heart will last.
In Hebrew, sister is a term of endearment that expresses intimacy (see Sol 4.9–10).
Loving wisdom will leave no room for a promiscuous woman, whose arsenal includes flattery that appeals to a young man’s vanity.
The young man’s father tells a story to illustrate his teaching about immoral women.
Naive young men, not yet set in their ways, are still open to correction. With each foolish act, they move closer to becoming fools.
Foolish actions are often associated with darkness (see Pro 4.18–19; Ecc 2.13–14).
The woman, seductively dressed, looks good on the outside but inside is full of trouble.
Prostitutes commonly solicited business in public areas such as markets and at every corner of busy streets (e.g., Gen 38.13–16).
The immoral woman’s observance of religious ritual makes her look good on the surface, but her immoral behavior reveals a corrupt heart.
Her emphasis on her bed and exotic perfumes (myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon) is explicitly sexual (cp. Sol 4.13–14).
let’s drink our fill of love: cp. Sol 5.1.
The naive young man’s foolish actions might cost him his life (see Pro 5.11; Pro 6.32–35).
The father reasserts the point of his lesson: While an adulteress might look good and a relationship with her is enticing, harm or even death will result.

The first part of Proverbs climaxes when the son encounters two women. Both invite the young man, and the reader with him, into an intimate relationship. The young man and the reader must decide between the woman named Wisdom, personifying the true wisdom of God (Pro 8.1–Pro 9.6), and the woman named Folly (Pro 9.13–18), representing the wisdom of the world (1Co 1.18–Pro 2.16). Both women’s houses are on “the heights overlooking the city” (Pro 9.3, Pro 9.14), suggesting ancient temples; the choice is thus between the true God and false gods.
Wisdom calls out openly and publicly, appealing to all and offering them her gift of wisdom. Like a prophet, she wants all to respond to her words.
Theme: Speaking
The hilltop and crossroads provide maximum public access to all who pass by.

In ancient Near Eastern cities, the city gates had built-in chambers for conducting legal proceedings and business transactions. It was an appropriate place for Wisdom to make her appeal to the most people.
Wisdom is associated with truth, understanding, and knowledge, which are right, wholesome, plain, and clear. Wisdom detests deception, which is devious and crooked (cp. Pro 1.2–7; Pro 6.16–19).
Choose: An ethical choice must be made between seeking money or valuables and seeking wisdom, which is far more valuable.
Good judgment, knowledge, and discernment are only available to those who have Wisdom.
Those who choose wisdom, i.e., those who fear the LORD (see Pro 1.7; Pro 9.10), will not speak in ways that harm others or bend the truth.
The best rulers choose wisdom to guide them (e.g., 1Ki 3.16–28).

formed me from the beginning . . . I was appointed in ages past: God’s wisdom has always existed. His wisdom is here personified, but wisdom itself is not a person. Wisdom does not exist outside of God; wisdom is an expression of his character and nature. Unlike pagan gods, God needs no outside counselor to give him instructions (see Isa 40.13–14). Jesus is the apex of God’s wisdom (see Col 1.15–17; Col 2.3).
God used his wisdom to establish the created order, so wisdom can tell us how the world works and testifies to God’s greatness.
architect: God’s wisdom guided the shaping of creation, bringing order out of chaos.
Wisdom offers great rewards to those who listen to and follow wisdom.
Life is the ultimate reward for the wise, while rejecting wisdom results in death. These verses point to eternal life and death (see Luk 23.43; 1Co 15.1–58).
The invitation to join Wisdom for a lavish meal is met by a competing invitation in Pro 9.13–18.
The number seven can denote grandeur or fullness, so the seven columns represent the grandeur of Wisdom’s house, the place where it dwells.

In the ancient Near East, a great banquet would accompany a marriage, a military victory, or the making of a treaty. Wisdom’s celebration marks the beginning of a committed relationship with the hearer.
Throughout the ancient Near East, temples were built on the heights overlooking the city. A commitment to wisdom involves a commitment to the Lord (contrast Pro 9.14).

Wisdom makes her appeal especially to the simple and those who lack good judgment because they have not yet decided between wisdom and folly. See Pro 9.16, where Folly mimics and then perverts Wisdom’s words.
Wisdom gives people the ability to navigate life successfully.

These verses seem to create an awkward break between the invitations of Wisdom and Folly, but perhaps the purpose is to caution that, in contrast with inviting the simple (Pro 9.4), inviting mockers and the wicked is futile at best. Such people have already chosen their path and respond to Wisdom’s advice with violence. By contrast, the wise appreciate corrective advice; they welcome it and benefit from it.
Fear of the LORD: See study note on Pro 1.7.
The woman named Folly also invites the simple and those who lack good judgment to join her for the banquet she has prepared. Her invitation and advice are antithetical to Wisdom’s (Pro 9.1–6).
The woman named Folly is brash: Fools talk boldly and without shame but have nothing intelligent to say.

On the heights overlooking the city was the traditional location for a temple. Folly personifies false gods and goddesses that compete for the affection and loyalty of God’s people (contrast Pro 9.2–3).
Like Wisdom, Folly has prepared a banquet for her guests (cp. Pro 9.2–5). However, this meal is dishonest and perverse.
Folly’s dinner guests end up in the depths of the grave, in contrast to the reward for Wisdom’s guests (see Pro 9.6).

This long section is called The proverbs of Solomon. It consists mostly of brief bits of advice and observation. These sayings make heavy use of antithetical parallelism to contrast wisdom and righteousness with folly and wickedness. The arrangement of these proverbs appears to be essentially random, as in Egyptian and Mesopotamian wisdom literature. Some proverbs are repeated (see Pro 6.10–11 and Pro 24.33–34; Pro 14.12 and Pro 16.25; Pro 18.8 and Pro 26.22; Pro 19.24 and Pro 26.15; Pro 20.16 and Pro 27.13; Pro 21.9 and Pro 25.24; Pro 22.3 and Pro 27.12). Sometimes a group of proverbs shares a similar theme (e.g., Pro 16.1–11).
The joy or grief of godly parents reflects the degree of their child’s obedience to principles of wisdom.
Tainted wealth . . . right living: The book of Proverbs promotes good behavior over having money (see also Pro 11.18; Pro 13.11, Pro 13.22).

This proverb can be misused if outward results are regarded as a barometer of godliness. Job’s three friends, for example, wrongly reasoned that Job must have sinned to earn his suffering (see Job 22.6–11).
Lazy people are foolish, while hard workers are wise (see also Pro 10.26; Pro 26.13–16).
the name of a wicked person rots away: In ancient Israel, as is still true today in the Middle East, honor and shame were powerful motivators.
Paths are a metaphor for life (see Pro 1.15).

To wink at wrong suggests approving of bad behavior rather than confronting it. • but a bold reproof promotes peace: The NLT translators assume that the original text is reflected in the Greek version. The second line in the Hebrew text may have been copied by mistake from Pro 10.8.

As a fountain provides water that sustains life, the words of the godly give life to those who hear them. In contrast, the violent intentions concealed in the words of the wicked bring death (see also Pro 10.6; Jam 3.1–12).
beaten with a rod: People lacking sense will bring harm upon themselves through what they say. Concerning physical discipline, see Pro 23.13–14.
Although wealth can be a fortress against trouble, money can also create trouble (Pro 13.8) and can provide false security (Pro 18.10–11).
Wise people are not afraid to have their thinking or behavior corrected—they accept discipline as an opportunity to grow in wisdom.
Those who talk too much show their ignorance and get in trouble (see also Pro 10.17; Pro 13.3; Pro 17.28).
Words are an expression of the heart.
The wicked might enjoy the material blessings of life, but only temporarily, in contrast with the godly. Jesus also expressed this reality (Mat 7.24–27).
This proverb connects with God’s covenant promises to Israel (see Deu 28.1–14, Deu 28.63–68). Such connections are rare in the book of Proverbs.

Here, honest practices are applied to the business world (see also Pro 16.11; Pro 20.10, Pro 20.23; Lev 19.35–37; Deu 25.13–15; Eze 45.10; Hos 12.7–8; Mic 6.11). • Scales were often made of two metal bowls suspended from a crossbar. The unit of currency, the shekel, comes from the verb meaning “to weigh” (see Amo 8.5–6).
Pride is dishonest self-promotion, whereas humility is an honest assessment of one’s strengths and weaknesses.
Right living, which flows from wisdom, is more important than riches. Nothing is wrong with riches (Pro 10.15, Pro 10.22; Pro 14.24) that are gained properly (cp. Pro 13.11; Pro 21.6; Pro 22.16).
Our actions, whether godly or wicked, affect the whole city (cp. Ecc 8.9–13).
This perspective on a gossip is repeated in Pro 20.19.
The future of an entire nation depends on wisdom.
This message is repeated in Pro 6.1–5; Pro 17.18; Pro 20.16; Pro 22.26; Pro 27.13.
Respect is the great and lasting reward of being gracious, while wealth is the lesser and temporary prize of being ruthless (see also Pro 10.2; Pro 11.18).
Godly behavior has positive consequences for the next generation.
Discretion is the ability to tell right from wrong, the beautiful from the ugly, and good taste from bad taste.
The wicked might prosper and the godly might suffer in the short term, but the future will right this imbalance.
Generous people who give freely to others will prosper, but those who hoard their money will lose it (see Pro 28.27; 2Co 9.6–9).
Money can be a blessing from God, but it is uncertain. The godly trust in God and flourish (see Psa 1.1–6).
The implied answer is that wicked sinners will be punished on earth.
Elsewhere in Proverbs a crown symbolizes wealth (Pro 14.24), long life (Pro 16.31), and grandchildren (Pro 17.6). • cancer (literally rot): A disgraceful wife is a deep and life-threatening problem.
The wicked might prosper momentarily, but they do not last. The family of the godly stands firm for generations.
To be sensible means to act only after reflecting on the consequences. A warped mind acts on impulse.
Reality is more important than appearance.
This proverb is repeated but with a different conclusion in Pro 28.19.
The instability of thieves can produce violent behavior at any moment. By contrast, the godly are well rooted: Their relationships are stable even under duress.
Fools fail to realize what the wise know—that listening is the way to learn.
Keeping a level head allows a wise person to think clearly and avoid reactions that could cause a fight.
The message of this proverb is repeated in Pro 14.5.
A wise child accepts a parent’s discipline: Gaining wisdom requires discipline and correction.
Having control of the tongue demonstrates wisdom (see Jam 3.1–12).
Appearances do not always reflect reality.
Money can be a blessing or a curse (see Pro 3.9–10; Pro 21.6).
snuffed out: Cp. Pro 20.20; Pro 24.20.
Oral messages were the primary form of communication, so an unreliable messenger delivering the wrong message could incite all kinds of trouble.
We are influenced by those we associate with.
Hard work does not always bring prosperity (cp. Pro 10.4–6; Pro 12.11; Pro 13.4) because injustice occurs in the world.

Punishment is sometimes necessary to motivate instruction. Discipline is a product of love, whereas refusal to discipline one’s child is a sign of laziness (see also Pro 19.18; Pro 23.13–14; Pro 29.17).
Building or tearing down the home is a metaphor for strengthening or weakening one’s family.
The path is a metaphor for life and conduct (see Pro 2.13, Pro 2.20; Pro 3.6; Pro 4.11; Pro 6.23). • fear the LORD: See Pro 1.7.
A fool’s word can be used against him.
It’s easy to keep a stable . . . clean if it is empty, but a farmer without an ox has no harvest.
Honest speech and lies both flow from deep within a person’s character. Cp. Pro 12.17.
The godly acknowledge their mistakes and sins, leading to change and reconciliation. Fools defend themselves by making fun of guilt.

No one can fully understand the emotions of another (cp. Psa 103.14; Isa 63.9; Nah 1.7; Rom 8.27). Bitterness and joy are at opposite ends of the emotional spectrum; this poetic device of referring to polar opposites (merism) covers the whole range in between.
Although a house is typically more stable than a tent, wickedness destroys and tears down, while godliness builds up (Pro 14.1).
// The right choice is not always the one that seems right on the surface (see Mat 7.13–14).
A person’s outward demeanor might not reflect what is in the heart.
Backsliders foolishly act against what they know to be good and right and wise.
Short-tempered people do not anticipate consequences before expressing anger. Schemers reflect, but they, too, are hated because of the evil that they do.
are clothed with foolishness: One’s true nature and heart attitude will eventually show in one’s demeanor.
This proverb might commend moderation, having neither too little nor too much (Pro 30.7–9).
blessed are those who help the poor: See also Pro 3.27–28; Pro 11.24; Pro 28.27; Pro 29.7, Pro 29.14.
This proverb states a general principle, even though fools sometimes have wealth (Pro 10.2; Pro 11.18), and poverty is not always the result of foolishness (cp. Pro 13.23; Pro 16.8).
The well-being and growth of the people, not wealth or military victory, are the true signs of a king’s success.
Wise people can control their emotions and express them appropriately.
Theme: Anger
A peaceful heart has resolved its inner tensions. Freedom from jealousy is beneficial to physical health.
Wise people help the poor (cp. Pro 11.24–26; Pro 28.27; see Lev 19.9–10; Deu 15.11; Deu 24.10–15; Isa 3.14–15; Jer 2.34; see also Jam 2.1–13). • insult their Maker: See also Pro 17.5.
Proverbs infrequently hints at life after death. Some scholars think this verse refers to God’s granting courage to face death with dignity and serenity.
A great nation is not defined by wealth, power, or military victories (Pro 14.28) but by godliness.
Moderating emotions and suiting them to the context helps others listen to what we say without reacting.
A wise teacher presents lessons in an attractive way. Crude belching describes the ugly teaching of a fool.
Knowing that thethe eyes of the LORD is watching everywhere is motivation for wise behavior.
Wisdom requires learning from correction.

God blesses the godly with wealth (Pro 10.22; cp. Pro 10.15 and Pro 14.24). The wicked may also gain wealth, but it will bring trouble rather than blessing (Pro 11.4, Pro 11.18; Pro 13.11; Pro 21.6; Pro 22.16).
God looks beyond the outward actions of sacrifice and prayers to see if they reflect the heart’s attitude (see also Pro 21.27; Psa 40.6–8; Mic 6.6–8).

Death and Destruction (Hebrew Sheol and Abaddon) personify the destiny of the dead. Sheol is the abode of the dead; Abaddon is a synonym for Sheol that has an added implication of punishment. • God knows all secrets (see Psa 139.1–12).
Mockers cannot become wise because they keep criticism at a distance (cp. Pro 10.17; Pro 13.1, Pro 13.10).
What people feel affects how they present themselves (cp. Pro 15.30).
Whether we enjoy knowledge or trash reveals whether we are on the path of wisdom or of folly.
Personality affects our outlook on life.
A healthy fear for the LORD counteracts inner turmoil and brings inner peace. • Better to have little: See also Pro 16.8.
This better than proverb shows the relative value of wealth. A substantial meal (steak) is good, but love is better.
Controlling one’s anger is a sign of wisdom (see also Jam 1.19–20).
A lazy person can find all kinds of obstacles (e.g., a path blocked with briers) to avoid work (see Pro 10.4, Pro 10.26; Pro 12.11, Pro 12.14; Pro 13.4; Pro 14.4).
An individual might not think of all the angles of a problem; a wise person invites advice from many advisers.
A wise person avoids death by choosing the path of life.
The proud think that they are self-sufficient. Widows in the ancient Near East were just the opposite—completely vulnerable and without means of support or protection.
The heart behind prayers determines whether God hears them.
Just as how we feel affects our demeanor (see Pro 15.13), what we experience (such as another person’s cheerful look or good news) can affect how we feel.
Fear of the LORD fosters humility because proper regard for God counteracts our delusions of self-sufficiency.
Our own plans will come to fruition only if God allows (see also Pro 16.9, Pro 16.33; Jam 4.13–16).
God’s moral evaluation is what counts (see Gen 8.21; 1Sa 13.14; 1Sa 16.6–7; Luk 16.15). This proverb is repeated almost verbatim in Pro 21.2.
God must affirm our plans (Pro 16.1), so it makes sense to ask his help in accomplishing our goals (see Jam 4.13–16).
The wicked will have trouble in this life and in death. Nothing is outside of God’s control (see also Rom 9.10–24; 2Pe 2.9).
God detests the proud, who refuse to commit their ways to the Lord (Pro 16.3) and mistakenly believe that they can accomplish their plans on their own (Pro 16.1).
God’s unfailing love and faithfulness are foundational in his covenant relationship with Israel (see Exo 15.13; Exo 34.6–7; Num 14.18–19; Deu 7.9–11).
Better to have little: See also Pro 15.16.
Theme: Wealth and Poverty in the Wisdom Literature
This series of sayings reflects on the king, who represents God’s power on earth.
Divine wisdom refers to divinely inspired guidance that helps the king make judgments (e.g., 1Ki 3.28; see also Psa 72.2).
The message of this proverb is stated four times in the collection (cp. Pro 11.1; Pro 20.10, Pro 20.23).
These proverbs presuppose a wise, godly king (see Isa 9.6–7). Many of Israel’s kings loved wrongdoing and hated truth (e.g., Ahab in 1Ki 21.1–29).
The king is powerful, so people are wise to avoid his anger and gain his favor.
Wisdom and good judgment may lead to wealth, but wealth cannot buy wisdom.
The pride of those who resist God and stubbornly rely on their own strength (Pro 16.5) is self-destructive and foolish because, apart from God’s help, no one has the resources required for life.
This proverb repeats Pro 14.12.
Scoundrels, a troublemaker, and violent people all disrupt relationships, creating trouble with their harmful actions.
Godly people grow in wisdom as they grow older, so their gray hair is a crown (cp. Pro 4.9; Pro 12.4; Pro 17.6).
Patience and self-control are far more valuable than brute force.
We may throw the dice: These dice were not for gambling but were a means commissioned by God to determine his will (Exo 28.30; see also Jos 14.2; 1Sa 10.17–27; 1Sa 14.40–43).
Wisdom is so much more important than privilege that if children act like fools, a wise servant will rise to prominence over the household.
The Lord’s refining fire (see Psa 66.10; Jer 9.7; Mal 3.2–3) separates what is precious from the impurities in a person’s heart (cp. Pro 16.2; Pro 21.2; Pro 27.21).
Lies (Pro 6.16–19; Pro 14.5, Pro 14.25; Pro 25.18), gossip (Pro 11.13; Pro 18.8), and slander (Pro 10.18) distort reality for malicious purposes.
To make fun of what God created is to mock God.

Only those who have been blessed with a long life live to become grandparents, and the continuation of the family line is a sign of God’s blessing (see Gen 12.1–3). • parents: Literally fathers. This proverb applies to both fathers and mothers.
Theme: Bribes
Maintaining a good relationship with another person means forgiving rather than dwelling on faults.
The wise will listen to a mild rebuke and act on good advice. Even harsh correction (a hundred lashes) will not change a fool.
Rebellion flows from the inner character of evil people who defy the punishment that will follow.
This saying cautions those who try to teach fools. A fool caught in foolishness will react with anger and violence.
opening a floodgate: Once a quarrel starts, it is very difficult to stop it; a dispute should be avoided if at all possible (see Pro 10.12; Pro 15.18; Pro 16.28; Pro 20.3; Pro 22.10; Pro 26.21).
The essence of this message is repeated in Pro 6.1–5; Pro 11.15; Pro 20.16; Pro 22.26; Pro 27.13.
high walls: Foolish confidence in the ability to win a fight emboldens people to engage in disastrous arguments.
Wisdom is not a natural quality but must be pursued. Sensible people persistently cultivate wisdom, but a fool’s eyes cannot stay focused.
Foolish children: This proverb is equally true of sons and daughters.
Words flow from one’s character as water bubbles up from the earth (see also Pro 10.20; Pro 12.23; Pro 16.23; cp. Jam 3.10–12).
// Rumors may be delicious to hear and repeat, but they are deadly.
In a troubled world, only the LORD can save. The rich might believe their wealth is a strong defense, but the power of money is limited (Pro 11.4; Pro 13.8).
Haughtiness cultivates pride. It leads to failure because it does not allow for change in the face of criticism. Humility learns from others and leads to the honor of success.
A spiritual or emotional problem (a crushed spirit) can be more trying than a physical one (sick body).
See “Bribes” Theme Note.
It is important to hear both sides of a dispute. Only fools jump to conclusions and rush to judgment; the wise take time to discern.
Flipping a coin (literally Casting lots): Casting lots was a valid way of seeking God’s will (Num 27.21; Jos 18.6–10). The Lord determined how the lots would fall (Pro 16.33).
Life and death: The wise speak thoughtfully (Pro 10.19; Pro 11.12; Pro 12.23) because they know that what we say has consequences (Pro 13.3; Pro 14.3).
God will punish the powerful who disparage the poor; wise people care for the needy (Pro 11.24; Pro 28.27; Pro 29.7, Pro 29.14).
Some people who present themselves as “friends” are not. The wise see beyond pretense, discerning a real friend from false friends by how they act in adverse circumstances.

It is better to be . . . honest, though poor, because wealth gained by dishonest means is short-lived (Pro 10.2) and will not preserve one from harm (Pro 11.4; see also Pro 15.16–17; Pro 16.8, Pro 16.16; Pro 17.1; Pro 22.1; Pro 28.6).
Rushing into things without understanding is dangerous.
Rather than acknowledge wrong choices and actions, fools blame the LORD.
God will make sure that liars are punished (see Pro 12.17, Pro 12.19; Pro 14.5, Pro 14.25; Pro 19.9).
It is in our self-interest to acquire wisdom because understanding helps us prosper.
The reference to a false witness (see also Pro 19.5) reminds us of the ninth commandment (Exo 20.16).
A lion’s roar is a frightening prelude to life-threatening violence (cp. Pro 20.2). Dew on the grass is soothing and contributes to growth (see Pro 16.14–15).

No choice for a son is more important than a good wife (cp. Pro 31.10–31); a poor choice brings agony (see Pro 10.1; Pro 11.22; Pro 12.4; Pro 21.9, Pro 21.19; Pro 25.24; Pro 27.15–17). The wise man will look to the LORD to give an understanding wife.
Keeping God’s commandments (i.e., the law of Moses) protects one’s life (see Deu 28.15–68).

Growing in wisdom requires discipline for everyone, including children (see Pro 10.17; Pro 13.1, Pro 13.10; Pro 15.31–32; Pro 17.10). The temporary grief that accompanies discipline is worth the protection from ruin.
// This proverb is a humorous comment on the foolishness of being lazy (see also Pro 10.4–6, Pro 10.26; Pro 12.11, Pro 12.27; Pro 13.4; Pro 15.19; Pro 18.9).
A mocker is beyond help (see study notes on Pro 1.22; Pro 21.11). A leader should still punish him because the simpleminded will learn a lesson.

Too much alcohol clouds a person’s judgment. The Old Testament is not against drinking wine in moderation (Pro 3.10; Pro 9.5; Psa 104.14–15), but it adamantly opposes excessive drinking (Pro 21.17; Pro 23.29–35; Pro 31.4–5).
Queen Esther was willing to rouse the king’s anger and risk her life (Est 7.1–10).
True friends are reliable even in difficulties.
The king should be the epitome of wisdom and justice.
Wise people recognize their own weaknesses. Pride prohibits people from seeing their faults (Pro 6.17–18; Pro 11.2; Pro 13.10; Pro 15.33; Pro 16.18; Pro 18.12; see also 1Jo 1.8–10).
False weights and unequal measures: Merchants, for example, should not cheat their customers by using false weights to weigh out grain (cp. Pro 11.1; Pro 16.11; Pro 20.23).
The ability to observe and learn from experience is a divine gift.
Laziness generally leads to poverty (see Pro 10.4–6, Pro 10.26; Pro 12.11; Pro 13.4; Pro 14.4; Pro 15.19; Pro 18.9; Pro 19.15, Pro 19.24; Pro 20.4).
Sellers must see past a buyer’s words to avoid being cheated.

// A wise lender gets security or a deposit on a loan. A stranger was an Israelite unknown to a lender, who required security. Proverbs warns the wise to avoid borrowing altogether (see Pro 6.1–2). • The message of this proverb is repeated in Pro 6.1–5; Pro 11.15; Pro 17.18; Pro 22.26.
This perspective on the gossip is repeated in Pro 11.13.
An inheritance gained early in life is likely to be spent long before death, leaving nothing to live on.
See also Rom 12.17–21.
The message of this proverb is presented in three other proverbs (cp. Pro 11.1; Pro 16.11; Pro 20.10).
God’s role in guiding our steps is clear (see Pro 16.1, Pro 16.9, Pro 16.33). We do not need to understand why things happen, but we should not lose hope, for God is in control.
Counting the cost is particularly important when making a promise to God (see Jdg 11.29–40; Ecc 5.4–6).
A king represents God on earth, so he should support the godly and punish the wicked.
The LORD’s light penetrates the human spirit: God sees deep into people’s hearts (see Pro 16.2).
God’s unfailing love and faithfulness are closely connected to his covenant with his people (see Exo 34.5–7; Deu 7.7–9). The king represents God on earth, so God will protect him (see 2Sa 7.1–29).
Physical punishment cleanses away evil: See Pro 13.24; Pro 22.15; Pro 23.13–14.
A king was the most powerful individual in an ancient nation, and it seemed that he could do as he pleased. However, God directs the heart of the king.
This proverb is repeated almost verbatim in Pro 16.2.
God is not pleased with worship unless godly actions flow from a godly heart (see Psa 40.6–8; Mic 6.6–8).
Demeanor (eyes), character (heart), and actions are all significant. God hates pride (see Pro 6.17–18; Pro 11.2; Pro 13.10; Pro 15.33; Pro 16.18; Pro 18.12).
The crooked path of foolishness ends with death; the straight road of wisdom leads to life.
// A marriage that looks good on the outside (in a lovely home) is unrewarding if it is filled with quarrels (see also Pro 21.19; Pro 25.24; Pro 27.15–17; cp. Pro 11.22; Pro 12.4).
Evil people do not just act evil; they are evil. No appeal will persuade them to act otherwise.
The simpleminded learn by seeing a mocker punished (see Pro 1.22; Pro 19.25). The wise do not need the threat of punishment because they already desire wisdom.

The Righteous One: God sees what the wicked do in the privacy of their homes and will punish them for their sins. Alternatively, the Righteous One might refer to the insight of any righteous individual.
God is just, so he will reward the innocent and punish the wicked. No wonder the godly love justice while the wicked fear it.
Those who have common sense can avoid life’s dangers.
The expenses of wine and luxury prevent people from amassing their resources—they spend rather than save.
The wicked will fall prey to the traps they set for others (Pro 26.27; see also Pro 11.8).
It’s better to live alone: Cp. Pro 21.9; Pro 25.24.

Righteousness and unfailing love are character traits associated with Israel’s covenant with God (see Exo 34.5–7; Deu 7.9–11). The covenant promised life and honor to those who obeyed God’s law (Deu 28.1–14).
A wise military strategist can devise ways to defeat stronger forces. This makes wisdom superior to raw power (cp. Ecc 7.12; Ecc 9.13–18).
Mockers: See Pro 1.25–27; Pro 9.7–9. Also see study note on Pro 1.22.
Generosity is a trait of the godly, while stinginess is characteristic of fools (Pro 29.7, Pro 29.14). Paradoxically, the more you give, the more you get (Pro 11.24).
Human wisdom is impotent if it stands against the LORD (see Pro 16.1, Pro 16.3, Pro 16.9, Pro 16.33). Similarly, military power (represented by the horse) is impotent without the Lord’s blessing.
A wise person will never compromise his reputation in pursuit of money.
Remembering that the LORD made them both helps prevent the exploitation of the poor.
// The theme of taking precautions is found in several proverbs (Pro 14.8, Pro 14.15; Pro 21.29).

Fear of the LORD (see Pro 1.7; Pro 9.10) goes hand in hand with humility. A humble person knows that he is not the center of the universe. Humility is more valuable than wealth (Pro 16.19; see also Pro 11.2; Pro 15.33; Pro 18.12).
Living by deceit is dangerous; corrupt people never know when their treachery will be discovered or backfire.
Theme: Children and Parents
This is a warning against being a borrower; other proverbs warn against guaranteeing others’ debts (Pro 6.1–2; Pro 20.16).
Even a wicked ruler wants advisers who have a pure heart—i.e., who are completely loyal—and who can communicate with gracious speech.
This proverb reminds the wise (those with knowledge) that the LORD is in control.

Of the many proverbs on laziness (Pro 10.4–6, Pro 10.26; Pro 12.11; Pro 13.4; Pro 14.4; Pro 15.19; Pro 18.9; Pro 19.15, Pro 19.24; Pro 20.4, Pro 20.13; Pro 21.25; Pro 26.13), this is among the funniest. Lazy people will come up with any outlandish excuse for not working.
An immoral woman, using flattery and seduction, tries to trap a young man to commit sin.
Wisdom is learned, not inherited or innate. It takes discipline to change foolishness into wisdom.
A person . . . gets ahead by hard work, not by exploiting the poor or bribing the rich (cp. Pro 22.29).

This section is ascribed to a group called the wise. Who they were is unknown. There is a reference to thirty sayings (Pro 22.20), and the wisdom sayings that follow can be divided into thirty sections that are similar to an Egyptian composition called the Instruction of Amenemope, which is also divided into thirty chapters.

As with the prologue that opens the book of Proverbs (Pro 1.2–7) and the introductions to the individual discourses (see Pro 1.8–9; Pro 2.1–11), this section begins with an encouragement to listen. This wisdom is more than good practical advice—its purpose is to inspire trust in the LORD.

thirty sayings: Early scribes noticed that the Hebrew word for thirty has been written in an unusual form (shlshwm) rather than the usual form (shlyshym). All the early translations of the Old Testament (e.g., Greek Septuagint, Latin Vulgate, Syriac Peshitta) read it as thirty. Nonetheless, some prefer to translate the word as excellent sayings.
Saying 1: God defends the weak, including the poor. Those who are well off are responsible to be generous to the poor (Pro 11.24–26; Pro 21.13; Pro 22.9, Pro 22.16; Pro 28.27).
Saying 2: An angry . . . hot-tempered person is unable to control his emotions and expresses his anger at inappropriate times.
Saying 3: The message of this proverb is repeated in Pro 6.1–5; Pro 11.15; Pro 17.18; Pro 20.16; Pro 27.13.
Saying 4: Property was marked by stones set up as boundary markers; it was a great offense to move these ancient markers of real estate (see also Pro 23.10; Deu 19.14).
Saying 5: Those who hone their skills and work hard will have the best jobs and work for the best people.
Saying 6: Many proverbs address young men in government service. A ruler’s rich fare might tempt a novice to overindulge through lack of self-control. But he will be vulnerable when sated.
Saying 7: Riches can be God’s blessing (Pro 3.9–10, Pro 3.15–16; Pro 10.22), but there are other things in life that are more important.
Saying 8: Proverbs puts a high premium on generosity (Pro 11.24–26; Pro 21.13; Pro 22.9).
Saying 9: Fools ignore advice (cp. Pro 9.7–12; Pro 10.18), so the wise do not waste their breath (see Mat 7.6).

Saying 10: The wise avoid unfair business practices and illegitimate gains (see Pro 22.28), knowing that the Lord will judge wrongdoing. • Redeemer: The NLT is probably correct in capitalizing the word Redeemer and identifying him with God, although a human redeemer might be intended.
Saying 11: listen carefully: Learning is the way to improve (see Pro 10.17; Pro 13.1, Pro 13.10; Pro 15.24, Pro 15.31–32; Pro 17.10; Pro 19.24).
Saying 12: See Pro 19.18; Pro 29.17.
Saying 13: A wise parent will rejoice in a wise child (see Pro 10.1).
Saying 14: Sometimes sinners prosper, but the wise will see that to fear the LORD is what ultimately rewards (see Pro 1.7).

Saying 15: Discipline is necessary for living a wise and balanced life. Overindulgence in drink (drunkards, see also Pro 23.29–35), food (gluttons, see also Pro 23.1–3), or sleep (see also Pro 10.5; Pro 19.15) results in poverty.

Saying 16: This saying is an exhortation to pursue the wisdom that a godly father and mother provide. Unlike other ancient Near East wisdom texts, Proverbs attributes wisdom to both father and mother (Pro 1.8; Pro 6.20).

Saying 17: Falling for a promiscuous woman is a trap, not a source of benefit. Proverbs repeatedly emphasizes avoiding sexual relations outside of marriage (see ch Pro 5.1–23; Pro 6.20–35; Pro 7.1–27).
Saying 18: This extended saying portrays the foolishness of the person who overindulges in alcohol (see Pro 20.1).
Saying 19: See Pro 1.8–19.
Saying 20: See Pro 14.11.
Saying 21: See Pro 21.22.
Saying 22: Rulers should be wise (see Pro 8.5–6).
Saying 23: Fools are alienated from the community because of their evil actions.
Saying 24: A wise person has self-control and strength under pressure (e.g., Dan 1.8–16; Dan 3.1–18).
Saying 25: The wise do what they can to prevent injustice and suffering (e.g., Job 29.12–17).
Saying 26: Both honey and wisdom are sweet. Wisdom improves the soul, enhancing opportunities for the future.
Saying 27: Those who are godly will not allow a setback to keep them down. • Seven times is symbolic for “many times.”
Saying 28: This saying leads to Jesus’ call to love our enemies (Mat 5.43–48).
Saying 29: Don’t envy the apparent prosperity of the wicked (see Pro 24.1–2), because their success is fleeting. • snuffed out: Cp. Pro 13.9; Pro 20.20.
Saying 30: The king is associated with the LORD, reflecting his power and sovereignty on the earth (see 1Sa 12.1–25; Psa 2.1–12).
This addendum to the thirty sayings of the wise (Pro 22.17–Pro 24.22) includes five further sayings.
Saying 1: Truthfulness in rendering judgment is a hallmark of wisdom (see Pro 6.19; Pro 12.17; Pro 19.28; Pro 24.28–29; Pro 25.18).
Saying 2: A true friend does not cover up problems but honestly points out areas for improvement. A wise person welcomes the correction of a friend.
Saying 3: A wise person establishes a source of income before spending money on himself.
Saying 4: The truth should not be bent, not even for revenge (see Pro 6.19; Pro 12.17; Pro 14.25; Pro 19.28; Pro 24.23–24; Pro 25.18).
Saying 5: Laziness and love for sleep lead to poverty (see Pro 10.4–5, Pro 10.26; Pro 12.11; Pro 13.4; Pro 15.19; Pro 18.9; Pro 19.15, Pro 19.24; Pro 20.4, Pro 20.13).
Theme: Laziness and Hard Work
This proverb repeats Pro 6.10–11.
During the reign of King Hezekiah (728–686 BC), wise men (advisers) collected these proverbs of Solomon and added them to the collection.
This warning reminds young men entering royal service that some things cannot be understood, including the king’s sometimes mysterious reasoning (e.g., 2Sa 11.14–25; 2Sa 24.3).
As silver is ready for use once it is refined of impurities, the king’s court can do justice when wicked people are removed. A little bit of evil can spoil much good (Ecc 10.1).
To gain an audience with the king, a wise person will practice humility instead of pride (cp. Mat 20.20–28).
Rash actions often result in shame.

Timely advice and valid criticism are precious, beautiful, and rare (see also Pro 15.23; Pro 26.7, Pro 26.9), and should be welcomed (see Pro 10.17; Pro 13.1, Pro 13.10; Pro 15.24, Pro 15.31–32; Pro 17.10).
Snow would be a welcome relief in Israel’s hot, dry summers (cp. Pro 26.1); trustworthy messengers refresh their employer by enabling him or her to plan for the future.

In Israel, rain is rare. When rain does not follow the appearance of storm clouds, it is like the disappointment caused by someone who gives empty promises. Cp. Jude’s description of false teachers (Jud 1.12).

Honey in moderation is tasty and healthy (Pro 24.13–14); too much will cause vomiting. This principle can be applied to other areas of life; for example, it is good to visit your neighbors, but not too often.
Lying can have deadly consequences (see Pro 6.16–19; Pro 14.5, Pro 14.25).
Contrary to expectation, compassion toward an enemy is more effective than anger (see Rom 12.20).
This proverb repeats Pro 21.9.
A spring or fountain that yields fresh water gives life. When godly people allow the wicked to dominate them, what was life-giving becomes deadly.
The wise have self-control and cannot easily be dominated.
It is not fitting to give honor to fools.
Curses and blessings can have real effect (see Gen 27.1–41; Gen 48.8–9, Gen 48.15–20; Num 6.23–27), but an undeserved curse has no effect.
A fool is like a dumb animal that can only be guided by brute force (see Pro 10.13; Pro 14.3).
Proverbs are often context sensitive. Whether or not to answer the foolish arguments of fools depends on what kind of fool and what kind of situation.
A fool might know a proverb but not be able to use it correctly. Cp. Pro 26.9.
A proverb misapplied by a fool might actually cause harm. Cp. Pro 26.7.
A fool or a bystander might easily be lazy (see Pro 10.4–6) or incompetent (see Pro 26.6–7). An employer should beware!
Even when foolishness brings terrible consequences, a fool persists in it (Pro 17.10; see also 2Pe 2.22).
Fools have hope because they might recognize their folly and seek advice. However, those who think they are wise will remain ignorant.
The lazy person: See Pro 6.6–11; Pro 10.4–5; Pro 15.19; Pro 22.13.
This proverb repeats Pro 19.24.
The wise avoid getting involved in other people’s arguments (cp. Pro 26.21).

Lies are extremely dangerous because they lead people to act on false information. Liars cannot cover up later by claiming that they were only joking (see Pro 6.16–19; Pro 14.5, Pro 14.25; Pro 25.18).
A gossip and a quarrelsome person are both like fuel to the fire of trouble and discord.
This proverb repeats Pro 18.8.
People sometimes hide evil attitudes and wicked intentions through flattery. In the end, the true hatred of smooth talkers will be exposed.
People usually receive the bad consequences they intend for others (see Pro 1.17–19).
We should plan (Pro 24.27), but our plans succeed only when God so wills (Pro 16.1, Pro 16.3, Pro 16.33; Jam 4.13–16). Only fools think that they control the future.
The Hebrew word translated praise comes from the same root as “brag” in Pro 27.1. Bragging (self-praise) is foolish.
Fools cause heavy . . . resentment by their foolish words and actions.
Anger can be dangerous but can be countered with a gentle answer (Pro 15.1). Jealousy is harder to resolve (Pro 6.34–35).
A rebuke improves life by correcting harmful behavior (Pro 13.1; Pro 14.6). Hidden, unexpressed love has no value.
Wounds from a . . . friend are from a loving rebuke (Pro 27.5). They are better than flattery (many kisses) from an enemy who intends to harm rather than help.
Even the best teaching (honey) will be refused if offered at the wrong time. The key to real learning is the receptivity of the student.
A person who forsakes his family and strays from home will more likely find trouble than whatever he was seeking (e.g., Luk 15.11–16).
Nothing is more encouraging than heartfelt counsel from an intimate friend (see also Pro 27.6).
In a crisis, one might need immediate assistance, so it is important to have friends close by and neighbors who can help.
Fairly or not, parents are evaluated by their children’s public behavior.
This proverb repeats Pro 22.3.
This proverb repeats Pro 20.16.
It is important to speak appropriately for the circumstances (cp. Pro 15.23).
A quarrelsome wife: Cp. Pro 19.13; Pro 21.9, Pro 21.19; Pro 25.24.
iron sharpens iron: Wisdom comes from interaction, often critical, with a good friend (see Pro 27.6, Pro 27.9).

An employer values loyal workers who protect their employer’s interests. Wise employers give their workers incentives to be loyal, such as allowing them to eat the fruit (see Deu 25.4; 1Co 9.7–10; 1Ti 5.17–18).
Death and Destruction: See study note on Pro 15.11. • Human desire is never satisfied by money, power, or pleasure.
A person who avoids conceit in response to praise demonstrates purity of character (cp. Pro 17.3).
Foolishness is deeply ingrained in the character of a fool.
Agricultural property can provide food and clothing from generation to generation; these resources require continuous labor and attention or, like riches, they disappear.
The wicked experience God’s curse for breaking his covenant (see Lev 26.14–17, Lev 26.36–37).
Wise . . . leaders rule justly and effectively (Pro 8.15–16).
Without law, chaos results and the wicked flourish.
Evil people seek gain by breaking the law. Justice ensures that they are punished and the righteous are rewarded.
Virtue is more valuable than material wealth. This proverb is repeated with a slightly different conclusion in Pro 19.1.
their parents: This proverb applies to both fathers and mothers.

The law prohibited charging needy Israelites interest on loans (Exo 22.25; Lev 25.36; Deu 23.19). The rich were instructed to lend generously to the poor (Pro 3.27–28; Pro 11.24; Pro 28.27; Pro 29.7, Pro 29.14).
A person who ignores the law shows no fear of the Lord (Pro 1.7), the lawgiver. That person’s prayers are hypocritical—why should God listen to them?
When the wicked take charge: See also Pro 28.28.
The wise admit their mistakes and sins and pursue correction (see Psa 32.1–5).
A wicked ruler will not help the poor because his rule is not just. Like a roaring lion or an attacking bear, he destroys their lives.
tormented conscience: See 1Sa 25.31; Rom 2.15; Rom 13.5; cp. Heb 10.22. • Don’t protect him! Murder is such a serious offense that a fine could not replace the death penalty (see Num 35.32).
This proverb is repeated but with a different conclusion in Pro 12.11.
quick riches: Wealth must be earned ethically, or it will cause harm and will not last (see Pro 13.11, cp. Pro 10.2; Pro 11.18; Pro 13.22; Pro 21.6).
Rendering a wrong verdict based on a bribe is evil (Pro 17.23; Pro 22.16).
The wise desire honest criticism of their faults so they can improve (Pro 10.17; Pro 13.1, Pro 13.10; Pro 15.24, Pro 15.31–32).
