The similar sequence of the verbs in Isa 7.14 and Isa 8.3 (conceive . . . give birth . . . call) and the link between Immanuel and Maher-shalal-hash-baz in Isa 8.5–10 suggest that Immanuel and Maher-shalal-hash-baz were the same person. • The name Immanuel (which means ‘God is with us’) symbolized God’s presence and protection. God was with Judah during the attack by the alliance of Syria and Israel (734 BC), in the Assyrian crisis (701 BC), and throughout their prolonged existence until their fall in 586 BC. The kingdom of Israel fell during the time of Isaiah (722 BC). The assurance “I am with you” remained significant even in the exilic and postexilic periods (Isa 41.10; Isa 43.2, Isa 43.5). The greatest assurance ultimately came in Jesus Christ, the incarnate Son of God (Mat 1.23; see also Rev 12.5).

By the time this child is old enough: The crisis involving the alliance of Syria and Israel against Judah was in 734 BC; by 732 BC Damascus, capital of Syria, was destroyed, and the northern kingdom, Israel, was defeated. • choose what is right and reject what is wrong: This was to happen by the age of 12, when a child was held responsible as an adult. In 722 BC, Israel went into exile. • he will be eating yogurt and honey: The land would be so depopulated that these delicacies would be available to all.

Israel broke away from Judah in 931 BC (see 1Ki 12.19–20). • will bring the king of Assyria upon you: Ahaz called Assyria in to help (2Ki 16.8–9), but Assyria turned against him and made Judah a vassal state.

The repetition of in that day referred to the yet future day of the Lord. Judah would experience the judgment already announced by Isaiah as a foretaste of an even greater judgment to come: exile in Babylon (586–538 BC).
Locations such as desolate valleys, caves, and thorny places were places of refuge for the desperate (see Isa 2.10). However, Judah’s enemies would find them there.

shave off everything: your land, your crops, and your people: In the ancient Near East, forced shaving was an act of disgrace (see 2Sa 10.4–5). Here it was a metaphor for the despoiling of the country.
Farmers faced near total disaster. Fertile agricultural fields (lush vineyards) would revert to wild grazing lands dominated by worthless plants (briers and thorns; see Isa 5.6).

The meaning of the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz (“Swift to plunder and quick to carry away”) applies both to Judah’s enemies (Isa 8.4) and to Judah itself (Isa 8.7–8). They had trusted Assyria in place of God, and now Assyria would turn on them and all but destroy them. God was with them (Immanuel; see Isa 7.14), but his presence would be destructive if they refused to trust in him (see Isa 8.14).

my wife: Literally the prophetess. • Like the name Immanuel (Isa 7.14), Maher-shalal-hash-baz is symbolic. It is possible that this child was the partial fulfillment of the Immanuel prophecy as well (see study note on Isa 7.14). The ultimate fulfillment of the Immanuel prophecy occurred with the birth of Jesus (Mat 1.22–23).
before this child is old enough: See also Isa 7.16. • Damascus and Samaria were ruined and destroyed in 732 BC, fulfilling this verse along with Isa 7.8, Isa 7.19–20.
This prophecy connects the sign of Maher-shalal-hash-baz with the sign of Immanuel (Isa 8.8, Isa 8.10).

The gently flowing waters of Shiloah supplied Jerusalem with water. Here they represent God’s loving presence and provision (see Psa 46.4). • Ahaz rejected the sign and the promise of God’s protection. He was not a man of faith (Isa 7.9), and now the people were following in his footsteps by placing their hope in Assyria to save them from King Rezin and King Pekah (cp. Isa 7.7–9, Isa 7.16).

The mighty flood from the Euphrates River represents the invading Assyrian army (see Jer 47.2). The river would overflow all its channels when the Assyrians marched deep into Judah. This stood as a frightening contrast with the gently flowing waters of Shiloah (Isa 8.6).

chin deep: Judah barely survived the Assyrian assaults in 701 BC (see chs Isa 36.1–37). • submerging your land from one end to the other: From north to south, Judah was nearly devastated, except for the city of Jerusalem (see Isa 1.8–9; chs Isa 36.1–37). • Immanuel: Despite their failure to trust him and the disaster it brought, God was still with his people (see Isa 7.14).
God’s plan to rescue his stubborn people would ultimately be fulfilled. God planned to destroy Assyria, just as he does every other proud nation that rejects him or boasts in its own power.
Theme: Trusting God in Isaiah
God is with us: See Isa 7.14; Isa 8.8.

This text reveals the heart of Isaiah’s message. The issue was fear of the Lord versus fear of people (see Isa 7.9; Isa 8.6). When an individual fears people, the Lord becomes a trap and destruction is certain (cp. Pro 29.25; see “Fearing People” Theme Note). For those who fear the Lord, he becomes a sanctuary; their salvation is assured.

People regarded Isaiah’s message of non-involvement with Assyria as treasonous, part of a conspiracy. But Isaiah was not trying to play political games; rather, he proclaimed God’s message. • What frightens them was the alliance of Syria and Israel attacking Judah (see Isa 7.1, Isa 7.4).

To make the LORD . . . holy meant giving him first place in life and acknowledging that nothing is greater than he is. • Fear of God means reverencing him as God (Pro 1.7). The people of Judah were not to fear Israel and Syria or the Assyrians (Isa 7.9; Isa 10.24).

He will keep you safe (literally he will be a sanctuary): God is a place of refuge. • stone . . . stumble . . . rock . . . fall: By trusting Assyria rather than God, the people of Jerusalem would find themselves in a trap and a snare as the Assyrians turned against them. For those who trust in the Lord, however, he is faithful and strong (Isa 28.16; see Psa 118.22–23; Luk 2.34; Rom 9.32–33; 1Pe 2.6–8).

The command to preserve Isaiah’s teaching suggests that it was harshly received by his contemporaries, who might have wanted to snuff it out. Faithful disciples safely preserved the prophet’s messages.
instructions (Hebrew torah): The Torah defined Israel’s covenant relationship with God, but the people were quick to forget (see also Isa 1.10).

I will wait for the LORD . . . I will put my hope in him: Isaiah’s message against Syria, Israel, and Assyria would be proven true in the historical events that followed. The fulfillment would further encourage the godly to await the final downfall of all ungodly power structures (see Isa 8.9–10). Waiting for the Lord requires submission, prayer, hope, and faith (see Isa 25.9; Isa 26.8; Isa 33.2), resulting in a quiet spirit and a renewal of inner strength (Isa 40.31). The book of Hebrews applies these words to Jesus Christ (Heb 2.13). • God had turned away; the people of Israel and Judah were alienated from the Lord because of their sin.

I and the children the LORD has given me (see the application to Jesus Christ in Heb 2.13): The names of the prophet Isaiah and his children carried significance as signs and warnings. Shear-jashub (a remnant will return; Isa 7.3) was a sign of God’s faithfulness to Judah. Maher-shalal-hash-baz (swift to plunder and quick to carry away) signified the destruction of Damascus and Samaria (Isa 8.1–4) and the desolation of faithless Judah (Isa 8.5–8). The name of Isaiah (Yahweh is salvation) itself signifies that salvation is from the Lord alone. These three names also represent major themes in the book: the remnant, the desolation of Judah, and salvation. Immanuel (God is with us) embodies all of these themes, along with the idea that Judah would be protected if only it would trust in the Lord.

Isaiah contrasts his counsel with that of his ungodly contemporaries. Isaiah’s message gives light, whereas the message of the spiritists led to darkness and death. • Mediums used various means of divination, including summoning the dead, in the attempt to determine the future (see Isa 19.3). God had banned these useless activities (Isa 47.9; Deu 18.9–11).
God gave instructions and teachings through the law and through his prophets, such as Isaiah (see Isa 8.16).

Beyond destruction there is hope. In the Messiah’s kingdom, the darkness would give way to great light, which was to dawn in Galilee and reach the whole nation, and then the whole world. The Messiah’s rule would be marked by the vindication of the oppressed and the end of all oppression. He would bring justice and righteousness forever in a kingdom of peace.

Zebulun and Naphtali were northern tribes in Israel (Jdg 6.35). They were humbled by the Assyrian invaders under Tiglath-pileser III in 734 and 732 BC. In Jesus’ lifetime, this prophecy was connected with his coming out of Galilee (Mat 4.14–16). • Galilee of the Gentiles was the region of Israel between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean Sea. It was heavily influenced—culturally, religiously, and politically—by the surrounding Gentile nations.

The people experienced the rule of other nations as a yoke of . . . slavery and a heavy burden (Jer 30.8). • oppressor’s rod: In Isa 10.5, the Assyrians are called “the rod of [the Lord’s] anger.” Just as God’s anger will cease, so will Assyria’s oppression of Judah (Isa 14.5). • The Lord had destroyed the army of Midian through Gideon (see Jdg 6.35; Jdg 7.22–25).
Burning the boots and uniforms marked the end of the need for instruments of war.

a child is born to us, a son is given to us: This child, the Messiah, would be David’s descendant (Isa 11.1). • he will be called: These names can be read as four throne names, signifying the nature of the child’s rule: (1) The Wonderful Counselor conforms to God’s wisdom (Isa 11.1; Isa 25.1; Isa 28.29; Isa 40.13), unlike the counselors of Judah (Isa 1.26; Isa 3.3). (2) Mighty God is an affirmation of the Messiah’s divine nature. (3) He cares for his children as the Everlasting Father, the father whose care continues forever (cp. Isa 22.21; Isa 63.16). (4) The Prince of Peace is a leader who brings peace. • Alternatively, the four names could be collapsed into two: (1) “A Wonderful Counselor [is] the Mighty God”; and (2) “the Everlasting Father [is] a Prince of Peace” (on his nature, see Isa 11.1–9). • Jesus Christ, the Son of David (Mat 1.1; Luk 1.32; see also Isa 7.14; Isa 8.3, Isa 8.18), will bring in the kingdom of his peace (Rev 19.1–21).

Like Ahaz, this ruler will be a descendant of David. Unlike Ahaz and the rulers of Jerusalem (Isa 1.21–23), he would trust God and rule with justice and righteousness (Isa 11.1–3). Jesus the Messiah reigns for all eternity (Luk 1.32–33).

This prophecy of judgment was against the northern kingdom of Israel. Despite God’s message that the Assyrians would crush them (chs Isa 7.1–8), the people of Samaria were foolishly confident that they could withstand the siege.
In their proud confidence, Israel thought it would replace whatever was lost with more expensive items (see Isa 2.13–16; Amo 5.11).
Rezin’s enemies were the Assyrians (Isa 7.4, Isa 7.17; Isa 8.4). Rezin was king of Syria (see ch Isa 7.1–25).
God’s punishment was intended to bring repentance, not destruction; but Israel was apostate and refused to repent or seek the Lord.
Even widows and orphans, ordinarily objects of God’s compassion (Isa 1.17, Isa 1.23; Isa 10.2), became objects of his wrath when they were unrepentant.
Following the decimation of leadership, civil war would destroy the nation like an out-of-control brushfire.

Manasseh and Ephraim represent the northern kingdom as its largest tribes. The two largest tribes of Israel and Judah fought amongst themselves. This is probably a reference to the war between Judah and the alliance of Syria and Israel, which is commonly called the Syro-Ephraimite War (Isa 7.1–12). In that conflict, brothers savagely fought against brothers (2Ch 28.1–27).
This prophecy was directed against Judah’s leaders, who used their positions to enrich themselves at the people’s expense.
What sorrow introduces a threat of divine judgment.
The implied answer to Isaiah’s rhetorical questions was that there would be no one to turn to when God punished Judah. • Disaster came first from the distant land of Assyria and later from Babylon.

The primacy of the Lord’s moral law was established in Isa 9.8–Isa 10.4; this passage works out the implications of the law: (1) Assyria was only a tool in God’s hands and was therefore as liable to judgment by God as any other nation (Isa 10.5–19, Isa 10.28–34); (2) those among God’s people who trusted in him and obeyed his covenant would be rescued (Isa 10.20–27); and (3) God would establish his kingdom on earth (ch Isa 11.1–16).

This judgment was pronounced on Assyria because of their ruthless destruction of nations (Isa 10.7), blasphemous boasting (Isa 10.12), oppression (Isa 10.13–14), and self-perceived autonomy (Isa 10.15).
The Assyrians were God’s instrument (rod . . . club) in judging Syria, Israel, and Judah, but they would not go unpunished for their own wickedness.

Despite their privileged calling as God’s covenant people, Judah had become a godless nation, making them the object of God’s anger (Isa 10.4). • The word plunder translates both the Hebrew words shalal and baz, recalling the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz (see Isa 5.19; Isa 8.1, Isa 8.3, Isa 8.5–10).

will not understand: The Assyrians did not realize they were following God’s intended purpose to punish Israel and Judah. Because they went about savagely killing and looting other nations of their own accord, God would also hold them guilty.

We destroyed: By 717 BC, the regions to the north of Judah were firmly in Assyrian hands. Calno, in northern Syria (referred to as Calneh in Amo 6.2), fell to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III in 738 BC. Carchemish, on the Euphrates River, was taken by King Sargon II in 717 BC. Hamath, on the Orontes River, was subjugated in 738 and 720 BC. Arpad was located south of Calno. Damascus and Samaria, the capitals of Syria and Israel, were taken in 732 and 722 BC, respectively (Isa 7.8; Isa 8.4).
whose gods were greater than those in Jerusalem and Samaria: Assyria would make this argument while threatening Jerusalem (Isa 36.19–20; Isa 37.12).

Assyria destroyed Samaria under Shalmaneser V and Sargon II in 722 BC (2Ki 17.3–6). If Samaria and Judah worshiped the same God, and Assyria had already defeated Samaria, the king of Assyria could expect to defeat Judah also.
Any royal power that exalts itself against the Lord, the Great King, is proud and arrogant (see Isa 2.11–12) and will be crushed.
my own powerful arm . . . my own shrewd wisdom (cp. Isa 10.5): God alone is all-powerful and wise. He plans the future, and he determines which nations will rise to power and which will be defeated.

ax . . . saw . . . rod . . . wooden cane: Such instruments are only as good as the person who uses them. Assyria considered itself independent of the hand of God, but their conquests were made possible only by his permission and to serve his purposes (Isa 10.5).
The fulfillment of this prophecy was in 701 BC, when 185,000 Assyrian troops were killed by plague and flaming fire (see Isa 37.36).
In the midst of Assyrian oppression, there was hope for the remnant. This passage develops more fully the meaning of Shear-jashub, a remnant will return (Isa 10.21; see Isa 7.3; Isa 8.18).

left . . . the survivors: A remnant from Jerusalem barely survived, but their safety was secure because God promised to preserve them (see Isa 1.8–9; Isa 4.2; Isa 6.13; Isa 37.31–32). • All these wars would teach the Israelite remnant to no longer depend on allies such as Assyria. Instead, they would faithfully trust in the Lord (see Isa 8.13; Isa 17.7).

God had similarly promised descendants as numerous as the sand of the seashore to Abraham (Gen 22.17). • rightly decided to destroy: God’s decision was a just response to the people’s persistent wickedness.
God assured his people of his presence and purpose.
as the Egyptians did long ago: See Exo 1.8–Isa 2.25.
Gideon triumphed over the Midianites: See Jdg 7.25.
Israel’s bondage ended in 539 BC with a new exodus from exile.

Look, the Assyrians are now at Aiath: The march described in Isa 10.29–32 is a poetic account of Assyria’s defeat. The places follow a route from the north down to Jerusalem. Upon arriving at Jerusalem, the Assyrians were forced to retreat. God was with Jerusalem, and eventually Assyria would be utterly destroyed. This passage might foretell Sennacherib’s invasion in 701 BC (see chs Isa 36.1–37), but it could just as well describe an earlier or later invasion.

The kingdom of the Messiah, first introduced in Isa 9.1–7, is now considered in more detail. Isaiah challenged the Israelites about why they would trust in any of the nations when God had far better plans in mind.

stump . . . shoot . . . new Branch . . . from the old root: This new growth refers to the continuity of David’s royal family line despite its virtual cessation during the Exile (see also Isa 6.13; Isa 39.7; Rev 22.16). The new growth from the old roots would not be like the former frail and unjust descendants of David (see Isa 4.2). Jesus, the Messiah, is the final fulfillment.

The Spirit of the LORD will rest on the Messiah. The succession of David’s line is guaranteed by the Spirit. The Messiah’s coming would bring justice and righteousness (Isa 11.4), peace (Isa 11.8), and the extension of the Kingdom to the nations (Isa 11.10; see also Isa 32.15–16). • The promised Messiah would have great wisdom and understanding, like Solomon, as well as knowledge and the fear of the LORD (1Ki 3.28; 1Ki 4.29; Pro 1.1–7; Pro 2.6–7). • The Spirit of counsel and might alludes to Isa 9.6. The Messiah will be full of wisdom and will have the power to execute his righteous rule.
obeying the LORD: Literally the fear of the LORD, as in Isa 11.2 (see Pro 1.7).

The poor and . . . the exploited would receive the justice due to them, which the wicked leaders of Judah had previously withheld. • the force of his word: Literally the scepter of his mouth (see Psa 2.9; Rev 19.15).
By virtue of the righteous character of the Messiah, his reign will be characterized by justice, righteousness, and truth, in contrast to the conditions of Jerusalem described in Isa 1.21.

In that day means in the coming age of the Messiah. The prophecy that follows received partial fulfillment in Isaiah’s day or shortly thereafter. The final fulfillment is found in the coming of the Messiah to inaugurate and then fully establish the age to come.
Nothing will hurt or destroy: There will be no evildoers, corruption, or sin on God’s holy mountain (Zion).

the heir to David’s throne: Literally the root of Jesse (Isa 11.1; Rev 5.5; Rev 22.16). • The Messiah will bring salvation to all the world (Isa 2.1–5). Members of other nations will even serve as priests and Levites (Isa 66.20–21), but only if they repent and believe in the true God.
Theme: The Remnant

The first time the Lord reached out his hand was at the Exodus; the second time will occur in the future when the Messiah gathers Gentiles (Isa 11.10) and his own people who live among the Gentile nations (Isa 11.11). The Exodus remained the paradigm of hope for those in exile (see Isa 11.16; Isa 35.8; Isa 40.3; Isa 43.19–20; Isa 48.21). • The remnant of his people included Israelites who survived the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions and were sent into exile.

jealousy between Israel and Judah: The two kingdoms had become enemies during Judah’s war with the alliance of Syria and Israel (see Isa 7.1–12). In the future, they would cooperate in joint military expeditions.
Philistia to the west: The Philistines were Israel’s historic enemy. • The nations to the east included the Edomites, Moabites, and Ammonites. All foes would be vanquished.

Using imagery from Israel’s past exodus, Isaiah encouraged his listeners by promising that God would bring his people out of Assyria the way he brought them out of Egypt (Exo 14.29–Isa 15.18; see also Rev 16.12).

The prophet’s personal song of praise for God’s salvation closes the meditations on trust in chs Isa 7.1–12. God will prove himself trustworthy in his promises to rescue his people even though they initially refused to trust him. The song anticipates chs Isa 40.1–66 with its themes of salvation, forgiveness, praise, joy, and the nations.
God’s comfort is the main subject of chs Isa 40.1–66.

God’s promise to save includes reconciliation (Isa 1.18), participation (Isa 11.10), cleansing and protection (Isa 4.3–6), peace and confidence (Isa 32.16–17), and restoration (Isa 11.6–9). • LORD GOD (Hebrew Yah Yahweh): The first word is an abbreviation of the second. • The LORD GOD is my strength and my song: See Exo 15.2; Psa 118.14.
God’s salvation is like a deep and unending source of water that provides life (see also Isa 41.18; Psa 87.7).
Tell the nations what he has done: The story of salvation must be told, even beyond the community of Israel (Psa 67.2; Psa 70.4; Psa 98.2).

This section contains prophecies of judgment against the nations. By including a prophecy against Judah and Jerusalem (Isa 22.1–25) in the midst of prophecies against the pagan nations, Isaiah emphasized that Israel’s identity as God’s people would not protect them from God’s punishment when they sinned as the other nations do.

At the time of this prophecy, Assyria was the major power. Isaiah anticipated the rise of Babylon as an even crueler kingdom that would destroy Judah and Jerusalem (Isa 39.6–7; chs Isa 46.1–47). The universal language of Isa 13.1–Isa 14.23 suggests that in this context, Babylon represents all wicked and arrogant nations in the same way that “Babylon the Great” does in the book of Revelation (Rev 18.1–24). Therefore, while this description of Babylon’s fall applies to the fall of historic Babylon in 539 BC, it also applies until the final judgment against the ultimate kingdom of evil (Rev 19.1–21).

A signal flag or banner that could be seen clearly from a great distance was often placed on a bare hilltop as a call to battle. • God stands against Babylon as the symbolic representative of all evil kingdoms.
Theme: The Day of the Lord

Just as Assyria was the rod of his anger (Isa 9.4; Isa 10.5, Isa 10.15), other nations serve as the LORD’s weapons and carry out his will. The Medes and Persians conquered Babylon in 539 BC. • God’s wrath is an expression of his justice as well as his intent to restore order to the world by obliterating evildoers (Isa 10.25–26; see Lam 2.22; Eze 7.19).

When pronouncing judgment that is still in the future, the prophets sometimes spoke as though it had already arrived. This emphasized the urgency of turning back to God (Eze 30.3; Joe 1.15; Joe 3.14; Oba 1.15; Zep 1.7).
Pangs . . . like those of a woman in labor: The day of the Lord brings sudden and overpowering pain and fear for the wicked (see also Jer 30.6; Hos 13.13; Mic 4.9, Mic 4.10; Mic 5.3).

Cosmic upheaval and darkness are common images for the day of the Lord, a time of God’s judgment (see also Eze 32.7–8; Joe 2.10, Joe 2.31; Joe 3.15; Mat 24.29; Mar 13.24; Rev 6.12–13; Rev 8.12; cp. Isa 30.26).
punish the world: See Rev 20.11.
Solomon’s imported gold came from Ophir (1Ki 9.28).

God will shake the heavens. The earth will move: Cosmic upheaval will accompany God’s coming in judgment (see study note on Isa 5.25; see also Hag 2.7, Hag 2.21; Heb 12.26–27; Rev 16.17–18; Rev 18.21–22).
These terrible acts of war would be perpetrated against Babylon, itself a cruel conquering power (see also Psa 137.8–9; Jer 6.11–12; Nah 3.10).
The Lord is sovereign and controls history. He can stir up kingdoms to execute his will. • The Medes from northwestern Iran joined Persian King Cyrus in fighting against Babylon in 539 BC.
This picture of Babylon as a perpetually haunted ruin contrasts with its magnificence at its peak (see Dan 4.29–30).
Babylon will never be inhabited again: Babylon, often a symbol of idolatry, immorality, imperialism, and oppression in Scripture, will one day come completely to an end (see Rev 18.2; Rev 19.2).
This message for Israel separates two prophecies of judgment against Babylon (ch Isa 13.1–22; Isa 14.3–23).

The Hebrew word here translated mercy draws from the imagery of a woman’s maternal care for her child to illustrate God’s merciful love for his people (see also Isa 49.15; Isa 66.13). • God had initially chosen Israel as his special people when he called Abraham (see Isa 41.8; Gen 12.1–3). Although their status did not change during the Exile, they faced God’s wrath like any other wicked nation because they had rejected him. • settle once again in their own land: This promise began to be fulfilled in 538 BC (see Ezr 1.1–11). • People from many different nations would join Israel as the people of God (see also Isa 2.3–4; Isa 11.11–12; Isa 19.18–25; Isa 60.1–14).

Just as Israel was subject to the Lord, so the nations of the world would submit themselves to the Lord through Israel (Isa 45.14; Isa 49.7, Isa 49.23; Isa 60.12, Isa 60.14; Isa 66.23). • The oppressed nation of Israel will rule over its enemies, assuming a position of power and favor with God.
This taunting song for the king of Babylon is in the form of a funeral dirge (cp. Rev 18.1–24).
God gives . . . rest (i.e., relief; Isa 28.12; see Deu 25.19; 2Sa 7.11) from the sorrow and fear, . . . slavery and chains Israel experienced under foreign oppressors (see Isa 9.4).
A taunt is a mocking comparison in song form. In this instance, the king of Babylon is compared to a dead man entering the world of the dead.

The land and people will be at rest and quiet because the oppression has ended and the king of Babylon has died. • The whole creation will join in praise, able to sing again (see also Isa 42.11; Isa 44.23; cp. Rom 8.22).

The Babylonians saw the place of the dead (Hebrew Sheol) as a place of no return. • stand up (literally get up from their thrones): The thrones reflect the Babylonian concept of the life hereafter as a continuation of the same mode of existence as the present life. It appears that the other kings are honoring the great king of Babylon, but the next verses tell a different story.
weak as we are: The Babylonian king had no power over anyone after death and was unable to leave Sheol. The Israelites will mock this great king who on earth appeared to have no weaknesses.
Babylon’s might and power and the sound of the harp were ended, and its magnificence was destroyed (see also Rev 18.22). • Maggots and worms symbolized death and decomposition (Isa 66.24).

fallen from heaven, O shining star: These words allude to the Canaanite story of the god Helel’s rebellion against the god El (chief deity of the Canaanite pantheon) and his fall from heaven. Some see the fall of the king of Babylon here as symbolizing the fall of Satan (see Eze 28.1–26; Luk 10.18; Rev 12.9). However, there is little to suggest that Isaiah understood it in that way. He was thinking of the historical king of Babylon. • son of the morning: The battle took place under the early morning sun. The Latin Vulgate translates the term as Lucifer (morning star), a name for Satan in Christian tradition, but the Hebrew text makes no apparent reference here to Satan.

This verse alludes to the Canaanite belief that the chief god El and the other gods were enthroned on Mount Zaphon, a northern mountain (see Psa 48.2; for a New Testament application, see Mat 11.23; Luk 10.15).
Most High: See Gen 14.19–22.

This is a restatement of Isa 14.9–11. The dead spirits inhabiting the place of the dead will be startled and amazed that the Babylonian king, who ruled the world with his merciless might, has absolutely no power in death.
The absence of a proper burial was a sign of great shame and dishonor. Unlike other kings, the king of Babylon would be disgraced in judgment.

As another sign of disgrace, the king of Babylon would have no children to provide a future legacy. • because of their father’s sins: God looks at individuals in relationship to their families and their people. Here, the Babylonian king’s children had joint responsibility for their father’s actions (see also Deu 5.9–10).
Isaiah summarized the previous taunt (Isa 14.3–21) with this prophecy, spoken in the first person. God decrees the destruction and desolation of Babylon.
This prophecy resumes declaring judgment on Assyria (see ch Isa 10.1–34). The placement of this prophecy after the judgment against Babylon suggests close connections between Assyria and Babylon.

I have planned . . . I have decided: No nation can either diminish or resist God’s plans to bring judgment against Assyria or his plans in general. The prophets understood and communicated God’s plan so that his people could respond appropriately.
This prophecy told what would happen when Sennacherib attacked Hezekiah some years later in 701 BC (see chs Isa 36.1–37).
The Lord’s power over Assyria is just one example of his sovereignty over the whole earth.

The king who attacked Philistia was probably Ahaz (Isa 14.28). • a more poisonous snake: This probably refers to one of the later Assyrian kings, either Sennacherib (701 BC), Esarhaddon (680 BC), or Ashurbanipal (668 BC).
The advancing army, probably Assyria, would stir up clouds of dust like smoke that were ominously visible in the north.

The LORD has built Jerusalem: God was fully willing and capable of defending Judah, and he did not want the kingdom to make alliances with nations such as the Philistines to protect themselves from the invading Assyrians.
This message of judgment and lament concerned Moab’s fall. The extensive references to Moabite place names indicate that Isaiah was thoroughly familiar with Moab.
Moab was Judah’s enemy, situated on the eastern side of the Dead Sea. • In one night: Destruction would be sudden and decisive.
In the ancient Near East, actions such as shaving or cutting off their beards revealed deep sorrow (see Jer 48.37).
Heshbon was the former capital of Sihon (Num 21.23–26). • Elealeh was located close to Heshbon. • Jahaz was between Heshbon and the Arnon River (see Jer 48.34).
My heart weeps for Moab: The prophet joined in the lament to express the greatness of Moab’s pain. • Zoar was in the southeastern area of the Dead Sea (Gen 14.2; Gen 19.23).

Identification of the waters of Nimrim is uncertain (see also Jer 48.34). • dried up . . . scorched . . . tender plants: For the theme of natural resources drying up as a form of judgment, see study note on Isa Isa 24.4.
The precise locations of the Ravine of Willows and of Eglaim and Beer-elim are uncertain.
Dibon: The Masoretic Text reads Dimon, which is a play on the word translated blood (Hebrew dam). • blood: Apparently many people from Moab had already been killed, but their judgment had only begun.
A request for asylum.

Moab was known for its sheep (see 2Ki 3.4). The lambs were sent as tribute to Judah in recognition of Judah’s sovereignty over Moab. • Sela (the cliff), an unknown remote site, was apparently where the Moabites escaped through the desert.
Do not betray us . . . Hide them: Moab’s situation would become so dire that they would beg for asylum in other lands.
This prophecy of salvation spoke of the future of David’s dynasty. • Activities such as oppression and destruction would cease with the end of Moabite hostilities (see 2Ki 13.20).
God would establish one of David’s descendants as king (see also Isa 9.7; Isa 11.1–5, Isa 11.10–12).
The response to Moab’s request for asylum (Isa 16.1–4).
The Moabites’ hardened state of pride and arrogance and rage and boasting prevented them from humbling themselves before God.

The vineyards at Sibmah were located by the Moabite city of Heshbon. • Moab was like a luxuriant vine that extends far and wide, but Israel’s beautiful vine reached to the ends of the earth (Isa 27.6). • The location of Jazer is unknown.
The hilltops were sites for pagan shrines (see Isa 15.2). • No one will be able to save them, including the idols the Moabites called on for protection (see Isa 40.18–19; Isa 44.18–19).

Within three years, counting each day (literally Within three years, as a servant bound by contract would count them; see also Isa 21.16): A man who had sold himself into servitude for a period of time would calculate how much time remained right down to the final day. This verse refers to events that are unknown. • The glory of Moab will be ended, probably because of the Assyrian conquest of Moab (late 700s BC). • only a feeble few will be left alive: Though decimated by war, the Moabites still existed during Nehemiah’s time (Neh 13.23).

This section contains prophecies of judgment against Damascus, Israel, Ethiopia, and Egypt. The scene moves from the crisis of 734 BC (the alliance of Syria and Israel—see study note on Isa 7.1–25) to the Assyrian crisis in 701 BC (see chs Isa 36.1–37).
Damascus, the ringleader in the alliance of Syria and Israel against Judah, fell when the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III invaded in 732 BC.
The towns of Aroer were east of the Dead Sea (see 2Ki 10.32–33). • Flocks will graze in the streets: The city would be useless for any other purpose.
The strategic fortified towns of Israel were the pride of Israel, but they could not resist God’s purposes.
The vision shifts from Damascus (Isa 17.1–3) to the northern kingdom of Israel; Damascus and Israel were allies in the war against Judah, and both were later destroyed by Assyria.
Israel’s glory will grow dim: God will judge all human pride. • Israel’s robust body will waste away like a person who is ill.
The valley of Rephaim was a fertile valley in Judah; however, it looked bare after each harvest.
Although the God of Israel judged the wickedness of Israel, he was still its God.
The people referred to here are either Israelites or humanity at large. • look . . . turn their eyes: They will again put their trust in the Lord.
Canaanites and then Israelites worshiped the fertility goddess Asherah in wooded areas or, in the absence of wooded areas, using Asherah poles (see Isa 27.9; Isa 65.3; Mic 5.14).
The Hivites and Amorites were members of the original population of Canaan; they were to be destroyed when the Israelites conquered the land (see Deu 20.17).

The Israelites had mixed faith in the Lord with elements of Baal worship. They turned from the Lord, who alone is God and will not be held alongside an idol in people’s hearts. • The term Rock refers to the Lord’s ability to provide refuge (see Isa 26.4; Isa 30.29; Psa 18.2, Psa 18.46).
God was present with Judah during the crisis.
At times, the sea represents opposition to God (see Job 7.12; Job 26.12; Psa 46.3; Psa 93.3).
God will silence them: The Lord is sovereign over the nations, as he is over the sea (Psa 65.7).
In the evening . . . by dawn: Despite frightening circumstances, Israel can have confidence in the Lord’s ability to save quickly (see Isa 37.36–38).
Ethiopia was at the southern extremity of the kingdom of Egypt. At the time, Egypt was ruled by the dynasty of the Ethiopian Piankhi.
Both the battle flag and ram’s horn were used to marshal and send signals to armies in battle (see Jdg 3.27; Jdg 6.34; 2Sa 2.28).
The Lord is untroubled by human activities; he watches quietly from his dwelling place and acts in his own time (see Psa 2.1–4).
your plans are ripening: Ethiopia had made every effort to form alliances to protect itself against Assyria, but its alliance with Judah would not help.

Conquered or weaker nations were often forced to pay tribute to a dominant king in the region (see Isa 16.1; 2Ki 3.4–5). The Ethiopians would come bringing gifts to honor the Lord for his defeat of the Assyrians (see also 2Ch 32.23).
Egypt was vulnerable, depending on the Nile for food, fish, and industry. When the Lord struck the Nile, Egypt would be in dire straits, and their gods would not be able to help.

Riding on a swift cloud shows God’s sovereignty and power over creation (Psa 104.3). He is coming in judgment against Judah’s enemies (see Deu 33.26; Psa 18.9–10; Psa 68.4; Psa 97.2–3). • The idols of Egypt tremble because they are weak and impotent, unable to help (see Isa 40.18; Isa 45.16; Isa 46.1).
Egypt had a history of civil wars that ravaged the country. Egypt’s fragile unity was breaking apart.
Idols . . . spirits, mediums, and those who consult the spirits of the dead were called upon in an attempt to ward off impending destruction (see Isa 8.19–22; Isa 47.12–13).
hard, cruel master: In 671 BC, the Assyrian king Esarhaddon invaded Egypt and destroyed the royal city of Memphis. In 663 BC, Ashurbanipal attacked and destroyed Thebes (see Nah 3.8–10).

The waters of the Nile were Egypt’s lifeline. Any disturbance in the regular pattern of flooding affected the whole nation. In ancient Egypt, the Nile was considered to be a god. However, the true God could easily dry it up.
There was no flax or thread: The drought crippled the linen industry.
The prophet taunted the leaders and wise men of Egypt, who were helpless to avert tragedy.

Zoan was the capital of Egypt, located in the Nile delta (see Num 13.22). • officials . . . best counsel: The king depended on the strategies and counsel of wise men (Isa 19.12; see Gen 41.39–40). • The officials of Zoan were known for all their wise ancestors, and Egypt liked to brag about them.
Where are your wise counselors: Cp. 1Co 1.20.
Memphis was an ancient capital in Egypt located south of the Nile delta. It was destroyed by Esarhaddon in 671 BC.

There is nothing Egypt can do: No leader, idol, or conventional wisdom can stand against God’s judgment. • The head and the tail represented all of Egypt’s leaders from the greatest to the least important (see Isa 9.14–15).
An upraised fist (literally waving the hand) was a threatening motion.

five of Egypt’s cities: This is probably just a way of saying “a number of cities” (see also Isa 17.6; Isa 30.17). • Jews living in Egypt after the destruction of Jerusalem spoke Hebrew, here called the language of Canaan. • Heliopolis was devoted to Re, the sun god. At a time when Judah was resisting the Lord, Isaiah envisioned the Egyptians following the Lord.
The new Egypt would receive a place in God’s purposes together with Assyria and Israel.

This altar or monument refers either to the temple that was built by Jews at Elephantine in Egypt (500 BC), to some other Jewish place of worship, or perhaps to a memorial the Egyptians constructed in devotion to the Lord.

The altar (Isa 19.19) would be a sign and a witness of the Egyptians’ religious connection with Israel (see Isa 19.24–25). • God answers the prayers of those who cry to the LORD for help. • The Lord is a savior; he would protect the Egyptians even as he protected Jerusalem from the Assyrians.

strike Egypt: The Hebrew verb used here is the same as the one used for the tenth plague (Exo 12.13, Exo 12.23, Exo 12.27), bringing up associations of what God did during the Exodus. • The Lord, who brings a plague, can also bring healing. • he will listen to their pleas and heal them: This expresses a covenantal relationship between the Lord and Egypt (see Isa 65.24).

Traditionally, Egypt and Assyria were enemies of one another and of Israel. They were idolatrous to the core, but they would leave behind their enmity and their idols to worship the true God. • In the rugged terrain of the ancient Near East, a highway provided a means for safe, easy travel and trade (see Isa 11.16; Isa 35.8; Isa 40.3; Isa 62.10).
Israel will be . . . a blessing in fulfillment of God’s promise to Abraham (Gen 12.3).

Two designations usually reserved for Israel, my people and the land I have made (see Isa 29.22; Isa 32.18), are applied here to foreign nations. The Lord promised to regard those from the nations who turn to him as his special possession (Isa 63.17).
Ashdod’s reliance on Egypt and Ethiopia was useless. As a complement to his words, Isaiah walked about exposed and barefoot, a symbolic action for what God would do.
Sargon of Assyria is Sargon II (721–705 BC). • Ashdod was one of the five Philistine cities that rebelled against Assyria in 713 BC.

Prophets characteristically wore burlap or other rough clothing as a sign of mourning over the sins of the people (see 2Ki 1.8; Mar 1.6). • naked: That is, exposed in some way, possibly even completely nude.
This symbolic event took place some three years before the fall of Ashdod (see Isa 20.2). Through it, Isaiah became an object lesson for the people (see Isa 8.18).
Philistia’s downfall was a warning to the people of Judah, who also relied on Egypt and other alliances rather than on God.

concerning Babylon—the desert by the sea: This description of Babylon was perhaps an ironic way to say that the land was physically lush but spiritually desolate. • Disaster . . . from the desert: Literally from the desert, from the terrifying land (cp. Deu 8.15).

I see: The prophet personalized Babylon’s experience, which intensifies his poetry, as does the terse language and the repetition of similar sounds, such as the betrayer betraying (Hebrew habboged boged) and the destroyer destroying (Hebrew hashoded shoded; also in Isa 33.1). • The Elamites lived to the northeast of Babylon. Along with the Medes, they were archrivals of the Babylonians. • I will make an end to all the groaning Babylon caused: Babylon had caused groaning by attacking and enslaving many nations. It is likely that the Elamites and Medes played a part in the overthrow of Babylon in 539 BC (Isa 21.9).
I grow faint . . . I am too afraid: Through his vision, Isaiah experienced the terror of the Babylonian people (see also Dan 8.27; Dan 10.16–17).
The riders were messengers who reported what had taken place on the battlefield.

Babylon is fallen, fallen: Assyrian king Sennacherib destroyed the city of Babylon in 689 BC. The final fall of Babylon was in 539 BC. In Scripture, Babylon represents all the ungodly power structures of this world, including nations and kingdoms that do not submit to God and his word. The apostle John gave hope with his prophecy that all Babylons will fall (Rev 14.8; Rev 18.2). • All the idols of Babylon lie broken: False gods could not save the Babylonians (see Isa 46.1–2).

O my people: The focus shifted back to the people of Judah. • Judah would be oppressed (threshed and winnowed) by the Babylonians but Babylon, too, would fall. • I have told you everything: The prophet had been faithful in his duty to report what the Lord revealed to him.

These two prophecies pertain to Edom and Arabia, located in the territory between Babylon and Israel. These outlying regions suffered under Assyrian domination, and like Judah, they would not be able to rest under Babylon’s oppressive regime.

Edom: Hebrew Seir, which was the mountainous area of Edom. • how much longer until morning: Edom’s suffering would be a long ordeal. The Assyrians were dominant in the ancient Near East during the 700s and 600s BC.
Morning is coming, but it would mark the beginning of another oppressive era. Because the Babylonians were on the horizon, night will soon return.

Dedan was a tribe in Arabia (see Eze 27.20; Eze 38.13). • Caravans would hide in the deserts of Arabia from attacks by the Assyrians and Babylonians, both of whom harassed the Arabian tribes (see Isa 21.1–10; Jer 49.28–29).
Tema was an oasis in Arabia on a main trade route from Babylon.
Assyrian weapons of war such as the drawn sword and the bent bow were highly advanced compared to the primitive weapons used by desert peoples.
Kedar was an Arabian tribe that had great wealth and possessions (see Isa 60.7; Eze 27.21).
Only a few . . . will survive: Cp. Isa 10.22; Isa 14.30; Isa 16.14; Isa 24.6, Isa 24.13; Isa 37.32.
This message addresses the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC (see chs Isa 36.1–37; 2Ki 18.17–Isa 19.37) and perhaps the people’s preparation for the subsequent Babylonian siege in 588–586 BC.

The prophet rebukes the people for their excitement over the Assyrian retreat (701 BC). They did not foresee that the Babylonian army would later (in 586 BC) complete what the Assyrians failed to do, namely, the destruction of Jerusalem.

concerning Jerusalem—the Valley of Vision: The meaning of the Hebrew phrase is uncertain. Assuming that it refers to Jerusalem (see Isa 22.5), it is ironic: Jerusalem sits atop a hill, and visions were not typically thought to originate in a valley. Similarly, Jerusalem was proud of its self-perceived religious vision, but its inhabitants were spiritually blind (see Isa 6.10; Isa 42.18).

The reveling city was full of feasting and drinking (Isa 22.13; see Isa 23.7; Isa 32.13), probably in response to the Assyrian retreat. Now a new threat approaches—the Babylonian siege (586 BC). • The people died not in battle but by famine and disease. Siege warfare left the inhabitants of the city cut off from needed agricultural resources and in a terrible sanitation and health crisis.
Leaders might try to flee, but they would not escape (see 2Ki 25.4–6).
Leave me alone to weep: Isaiah mourned the victims and the decimation of his people (see Isa 6.13).
The defeat of Judah would be a manifestation of the yet-future day of the Lord (see study note on Isa 2.5–22). Jerusalem would be impotent in the day of disaster.
Jerusalem’s walls were broken by the invading Babylonians, who breached them with battering rams (2Ki 25.4).
Elamites: Elam was to the east of Babylon and would later play a role in Babylon’s defeat (see Isa 21.2; also Jer 49.34–39). • The actual location of Kir is unknown (see also Amo 1.5).
The Kidron and Hinnom valleys were located to the east and south of Jerusalem.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem planned for war by counting weapons, checking walls, and preparing a water supply. However, the people did not consider God’s plans (see Isa 13.1–Isa 14.23). Although Hezekiah was very prominent in these efforts, the second person verbs are plural. Isaiah was apparently not singling out Hezekiah, as he did Hezekiah’s father Ahaz (Isa 7.1–4).
to the armory: This magnificent building was both an armory and a storage place for valuables (see Isa 39.2; 1Ki 7.2–6).

Jerusalem (literally the city of David): Calling Jerusalem “the city of David” evokes memories of Israel’s greatest king and God’s blessing upon him and the nation (see also Isa 60.14). • You store up water in the lower pool: Hezekiah expended great energy in ensuring a constant supply of water (see Isa 22.11; 2Ki 20.20).
Judah’s feasting and disobedience resulted in a prophecy of judgment.

you will never be forgiven for this sin: The people of Judah added sin upon sin to the point that God would justly condemn them. This foreshadowed the Exile; although it took place in 586 BC, Isaiah was already anticipating it in 701 BC.

Shebna and Eliakim were two royal officials in King Hezekiah’s court (see 2Ki 18.18; 2Ki 19.2). Apparently assuming that death at the hands of the Assyrians was inevitable, Shebna planned for an ostentatious burial place (Isa 22.16). Although the rebuke of Shebna preceded Assyria’s siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC (see Isa 22.19–21; Isa 36.3), it connects well with the admonitions of Isa 22.1–13 regarding the ensuing Babylonian siege.

The actions of Shebna represent among the populace a lack of confidence in God’s ability to rescue Jerusalem from the Assyrian attack. • A palace administrator held the highest possible position in the royal court (see Isa 22.21–22).
Shebna was building a beautiful tomb . . . a monument. This lavish burial place was intended to last for centuries.
toss you away into a distant, barren land: Shebna would not find a resting place or have a memorial (cp. Isa 14.11–20). • your glorious chariots: In his high position, Shebna had lived in luxury.

drive you out of office: Shebna (Isa 22.15) was demoted to court secretary by the time of Jerusalem’s siege, when Eliakim (Isa 22.20) was the palace administrator (Isa 36.3). Eliakim was a true servant of the Lord.
A leader is like a father to the people when he truly cares for them and addresses their needs. In contrast, Shebna was concerned only for himself.

The key to the house of David represents a high position of honor in the royal court (see also Rev 3.7). • When he opens doors . . . when he closes doors: The officer with the highest position has sole authority in giving access to the king (cp. Mat 16.19).
I will pull out the nail: Even godly Eliakim would not be able to save Judah or David’s dynasty from God’s judgment. The people of Judah would go into exile more than a century later (Isa 39.6–7).

Tyre was a prosperous seaport northwest of Israel. The relationship between Judah and Tyre went back to the time of David and Solomon (1Ki 5.8–9). Tyre, with its proximity to plentiful forests and to the Mediterranean Sea, was one of the commercial centers of the ancient Near East. Its fleets were renowned, and its colonies brought it great prestige and riches. The city came under repeated attack by the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Macedonians, and it fell to Alexander the Great in 332 BC. Isaiah not only prophesied the end of Tyre but by implication warned all whose wealth and earthly securities lead to pride instead of dependence on God (see Isa 2.12–16; Mat 11.21).

The ships of Tarshish plied the sea between the Phoenician coast and the port of Tarshish in Spain (see Isa 2.16; Isa 23.6). • rumors you heard in Cyprus: Cyprus was the last port of call for sailors coming home from Spain before the final leg of their journey to Tyre.
Sidon was a Phoenician port to the north of Tyre. • Tyre’s commercial network of traders was extensive.

Fish, agricultural produce, flax, and linen were all harvests from along the Nile (see ch Isa 19.1–25). • Tyre was known as the marketplace of the world, comparable to modern cities like New York, Hong Kong, or London.

Part of the great port city of Tyre was on an island. The island city was a fortress of the sea, but it fell in 332 BC. • I am childless; I have no sons or daughters: This metaphor was a judgment on Tyre’s colonial ports around the Mediterranean Sea. In the ancient world, to reach old age without having children was considered a terrible fate (see Isa 49.21; Isa 54.1).
Egypt depended on the ships from Tyre for the export of its products (see Isa 23.3).
The Lord had brought this disaster on Tyre (Isa 23.9). • Through commercial links, Tyre had created wealth for itself and its trading partners; in this sense, Tyre was a great creator of kingdoms.

Sweep over the land like the flooding Nile: This difficult phrase means either (1) that the sailors who had returned from Tarshish were being invited to loot ruined Tyre; or (2) that the people of Tarshish were forced to move back to their agricultural fields to make their living (instead of trading) now that Tyre had been destroyed.
Phoenicia was the region north of Israel. Tyre and Sidon were its main cities.
Babylonia was stripped and looted by the Assyrians under Sennacherib (689 BC); eventually it rose to be a mighty empire once again.
There was hope for Tyre.
Metaphorically, Tyre was a prostitute because of its indifferent willingness to sell anything to anyone (cp. Rev 17.2; Rev 18.3, Rev 18.12–13).

Even though Tyre’s earnings came from unrighteous commerce, the profits will be given to the LORD rather than being squandered. • There will be good food and fine clothing for the LORD’s priests. The theme of the wealth of the nations being brought to the Lord in Jerusalem is more fully developed in Isa 60.5–11; Isa 61.6.

This section is often referred to as the “Little Apocalypse” because of its similarities to the book of Revelation. In these chapters Isaiah takes readers out of the present into a vision of the future world. The universal imagery of the Little Apocalypse makes it difficult to assign the events described to any precise historical situation. That means that these chapters cannot be used to outline a sequence of events or create a historical blueprint for the future. Instead, the imagery is intended to create an impressionistic drama of an unfolding world that is both like and unlike the present. The combination of aspects of the old era with aspects of the new era (for instance, people of Zion will all be righteous [new], but still long for their redemption [old]) is consistent with the New Testament concept of the future age breaking into and overlapping with the present evil age (2Co 4.4; Gal 1.4). Peter, for example, wrote of believers as living in the last days (1Pe 1.12; 2Pe 3.3) even though the last day remains yet future (2Pe 3.10).
Here the judgments described in chs Isa 13.1–23 are extended to the creation at large.

destroy the earth and make it a vast wasteland: There is a play here on the Hebrew words baqaq (destroy) and balaq (make a wasteland). The devastation will begin with Judah and be extended to the whole world (see 1Pe 4.17). • All the earth will be destroyed, the people as well as national political structures.
All humanity is guilty (Rom 3.23) and under condemnation (see Isa 59.1–15). Judgment is likened to a failed grape harvest that brings drinking and feasting to a halt.
earth . . . dries up . . . land wastes away and withers: The prophets often used the imagery of a drought to get the attention of people who live off the land (see also Jer 23.10; Joe 1.12; Amo 1.2).

Isaiah was probably referring to the everlasting covenant that God made with all humanity through Noah (Gen 9.8–17). The prophet saw a parallel with the wickedness in his day and the wickedness of the pre-flood world.
The effect of sin is so great that no earthly thing or action can adequately atone for it. Hope ultimately lies in God himself. God has reconciled the world to himself in Christ (Col 1.19–20).
Merrymakers will sigh and mourn because they are dependent on wine for pleasure.
Tambourines and melodious chords of the harp represent good times (see Isa 5.12; Rev 18.22).
city writhes in chaos: With normal levels of urban disarray being raised to chaotic and dangerous disorder, people will be forced to seek refuge in locked homes.
Gladness has been banished from the land, not by edict, but because there is no reason to celebrate.

stray olives left on the tree: The remnant will include godly people both from Israel (see Isa 17.6) and from other nations. • The theme of the remnant is common in Isaiah (see “The Remnant” Theme Note; see also Isa 10.22; Isa 14.30; Isa 16.14; Isa 24.6; Isa 37.32).

In spite of wailing and ruin, the sound of praise is heard from all directions. Even while still experiencing the pain of the devastation of the old world, the godly will respond with joyous expectation for the new world.

But my heart is heavy with grief: The prophets were well acquainted with the emotional pain brought on by the sin of their people and its consequences (see Isa 15.5; Isa 21.4; Jer 15.10; Mic 1.8). • Although aspects of the new world are present, the deceit of the old world still prevails for a time.

No one can escape the day of the Lord (see study note on Isa 2.5–22). • Destruction falls like rain from the heavens (literally the floodgates of heaven are opened): The imagery is like the flood in Noah’s time (see study note on Gen Gen 7.11–12). • the foundations of the earth shake: An earthquake is characteristic of a theophany, a physical manifestation of God’s presence (see also Isa 6.4; Isa 13.13; Isa 19.1).

The phrase translated gods (Hebrew tseba’ hammarom, “armed host of the heavens”) might refer to pagan gods represented by the stars. It might also refer to the angels or even demons (Rev 12.4, Rev 12.9). Judgment will extend to all parts of creation (Isa 13.13; Isa 34.5; see Eph 6.11–12).
put in prison . . . punished: See also 2Pe 2.4; Rev 9.2, Rev 9.11; Rev 17.8.
The second part of the Little Apocalypse (see study note on Isa 24.1–Isa 27.13) describes praise for God’s judgment (Isa 25.1–5, Isa 25.11–12) and salvation (Isa 25.6–9).
Isaiah here praises God for protecting the needy (see Isa 12.1–6).
Assyria and Egypt were strong . . . ruthless nations, but in the future they will exalt God rather than their own power.
The banquet is a symbol of God’s providing richly for all those who will receive his gracious invitation (Rev 3.20–21; Rev 19.9).

In Jerusalem: Literally On this mountain—that is, the mountain of the Lord (see Isa 2.2; Isa 24.23): This does not refer to a geographical city but to Zion, the eternal city of God (see Isa 1.8, Isa 1.27).

He will swallow up death forever: Isaiah’s hope was God’s power over sin and sin’s devastating results. In the New Testament this promise is realized in Jesus Christ (1Co 15.54). • The Lord’s presence will be a source of eternal comfort; he will wipe away all tears (see Rev 21.4).
The new community of God’s people will respond in joy and faith. When the enemy is defeated, God’s people will be free forever.

on Jerusalem: Literally on this mountain. • Moab (see Isa 15.1–Isa 16.14) here represents the nations under judgment, those who trust only themselves (see Isa 34.5–17). • like straw trampled down: The people would be helpless and dying in the most degrading circumstances.
Isaiah used the image of a swimmer forcibly kept under water to illustrate that Moab’s people are hopelessly doomed and their human pride will be conquered.
This section of the Little Apocalypse (see study note on Isa 24.1–Isa 27.13) is a song of praise and a prayer for redemption.
The new community of God’s people is likened to the citizens of a city, securely held together by the Lord. They are righteous, faithful, peaceful, and trusting.

Our city refers to Zion, the eternal city of God, where the Lord is present to protect and bless his people (see Isa 1.8, Isa 1.27; see also Psa 46.1–11). Zion stands in direct contrast to the “mighty cities” of the nations (Isa 25.2; Isa 26.5), which are helpless and are brought down to “ruins.” • The walls of God’s salvation protectively enclose his people; no one can hurt them again.
Open access is given to all who, like God and his Messiah, are righteous and faithful. The citizens of true Zion are committed to the Lord.
A perfect peace, marked by harmony, quietness, and confidence, is a benefit of the new creation.
The proud and arrogant are often characterized as exalting themselves (see Isa 2.11–12), whereas God humbles them.
Justice finally occurs when the needy walk all over the ruins of the city where the proud have perished.

The godly pray for the end of oppression and the full establishment of God’s kingdom. Isaiah encouraged the godly to persevere as they wait for their final vindication and the resurrection of the body.
God will do what is right for those who walk in his way, even if they have to suffer a while longer (see Isa 24.16). One day, they will experience harmony and integrity (see Pro 2.8–9; Pro 15.19).

we show our trust (see Isa 26.3–4; literally we wait for you): Waiting involves trust in the Lord and longing for his redemption. • People express their commitment to God by obeying his laws; mere lip service is not sufficient.
I search . . . I earnestly seek: Cp. Psa 63.1.
God has shown kindness to the wicked. Although they deserve judgment (see also Rom 2.4; 2Pe 3.9), he has been patient and forbearing and has blessed them. However, time will run out one day.
An upraised fist expresses anger and the threat of judgment (see also Isa 19.16). • Fire was often an image for God’s judgment.

This verse is a confident expression of thanks for God’s blessings. In Isaiah’s time, during King Hezekiah’s prosperous reign, the borders of the nation of Israel were extended, and people gave glory to God for his great deeds.

While waiting for God’s salvation (Isa 26.1), the godly were in distress and longed for their vindication. They prayed beneath the burden of God’s discipline. In Hezekiah’s time, Judah was in distress when Sennacherib attacked and destroyed the whole nation except for Jerusalem.
The imagery of a pregnant woman in childbirth describes the nation’s pain when Assyrian king Sennacherib attacked it in 701 BC (see Isa 37.3).
Only God can give salvation and bring life (see Isa 59.9–15).

those who die . . . will live: There is hope for the remnant. Some hold the minimal interpretation that this means the people would be restored to the land after the Exile (see Eze 37.11–12) or that the Lord would preserve Jerusalem (see Isa 29.4, Isa 29.6–8). More likely it refers to the resurrection of the body from the grave (see Isa 25.7–8). The Old Testament has little to say about the resurrection, but this text anticipates fuller development in the New Testament (see 1Co 15.12–58).
God will punish the wicked, so the godly should go home and stay out of the way.
The wicked retain power now, but their oppressive rule will end in the day of the Lord’s wrath, when he will punish them for their sins.

Israel adapted the imagery of Leviathan to refer to evil powers that oppose God. Leviathan’s death symbolizes the end of evil, Satan, the demonic, and the dominion of forces hostile to God (see Isa 51.9; Psa 74.14; Psa 104.7–9, Psa 104.26; see also the serpent in Gen 3.1–24; Rev 12.1–18; Rev 13.1–18; Rev 16.13; Rev 20.2, Rev 20.10).
The Song of the Fruitful Vineyard, in which the vineyard represents God’s people (cp. Isa 5.1–7).

God identifies himself as the LORD of the covenant to assure his people that what he says and does is reliable (see Exo 6.2–3). The phrase is used many times throughout Isaiah. • watch . . . watering . . . watch: The Lord will provide even greater care and protection for his ultimate vineyard than he did for Israel, his first vineyard (see Isa 5.1–2).
God expects all his people to turn to him and to trust him for help. • Let them make peace with me is God’s offer of reconciliation for his people.

Jacob’s descendants will take root and the remnant will increase (Isa 37.31; cp. Isa 5.24; Isa 14.30; for application to the Messiah, see Isa 11.1, Isa 11.10). • fill the whole earth: The fulfillment of this prophecy extends beyond the restoration of Israel from exile to the second coming of the Lord Jesus. It includes all the righteous children of God—Jews and Gentiles—who suffer but remain obedient as they wait for the fullness of redemption (see Isa 26.18; Joh 15.1–8).
Isaiah reminded readers of the reasons for the Exile and judgment: Israel’s sinfulness, God’s righteous judgment, and the absence of divine compassion.
Despite being God’s covenant people, Israel was struck and punished like any other wicked nation. However, Israel was not completely destroyed; a remnant remained.

The Assyrians exiled large numbers of citizens from the northern kingdom of Israel when Samaria fell in 722 BC. The Babylonians exiled many from Judah from 605 to 586 BC. • Storms from the east were known for their destructive effects (see Job 27.21; Job 38.24; Jer 4.11).

God’s justice requires him to punish sin. That punishment is designed to correct behavior and to purify. Being conquered and exiled wasThe Exile occurred so that to purge Israel’s wickedness and to take away all her sin (see Rom 11.27). • This was to be the end of all the pagan worship in Israel, including the incense altars and the poles that were used in worshiping the goddess Asherah.
Places previously associated with human power and accomplishment would be ruined to the extent that animals would graze in them.
The people were outside of God’s covenantal care; they foolishly turned away from him.

Yet: God’s withholding of mercy from Israel (Isa 27.11) will be temporary. • from the Euphrates River . . . to the Brook of Egypt: God’s remnant will return from Assyria and Egypt to the territory that God promised to Abraham (Gen 15.18; see 1Ki 4.21).
The great trumpet was used to gather the people (see Mat 24.31).

This section is connected by a series of six threats of judgment or woes (cp. Isa 5.8–23). Apart from the initial address to Samaria in Isa 28.1–13, the remainder of the section is addressed to Judah, especially because of their inclination to trust Egypt to rescue them from Assyria (Isa 30.2).
The glory of Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, is here contrasted with the glory of the Lord. This section represents the first of the six woes (What sorrow . . .).
The drunks of Israel epitomized pride, spiritual complacency, and scorn for God and his commands. • Unlike Jerusalem, Samaria was in a fertile valley.

the Lord will send: The covenant God will act against his own people, whose behavior had effectively disqualified them as God’s people (see Hos 1.9). • The mighty army is that of the Assyrians, who destroyed Samaria in 722 BC.

In the future, after God’s judgment has purged his people, he will restore a righteous remnant, transforming the desires and character of his people. Samaria will no longer be the source of Israel’s pride; instead, they will glory in the Lord, their true crown.
The focus returns to the lamentable present situation in Israel (and Judah). The leaders and people will be ensnared by their own schemes.
The priests and prophets led the people astray. • Intoxicating beverages such as wine and alcohol were prohibited for priests while fulfilling their duties (Lev 10.9).
The people had become hardened to God’s revelation (1Co 14.21).

God will have to speak through circumstances such as hardship, exile, and death in order to get through to his hardened people. • a strange language: In the New Testament, Paul applied this text to the spiritual gift of tongues as a sign of judgment to unbelievers (see 1Co 14.21–22).
Had his people listened, God’s revelation would have led them to rest (see Isa 48.18–19). But they would not listen because of their hard hearts (Isa 65.12).

one line at a time, one line at a time, a little here, and a little there: The Hebrew here is difficult to understand. The words might be intentional nonsense to illustrate the point that the people were so spiritually blind that God’s clearest revelation was nonsense to them (see Isa 6.9–10).
After having pronounced judgment on Samaria (Isa 28.1–13), Isaiah now pronounces judgment on Jerusalem. The leaders of Judah are accused of being as blind as those in the northern kingdom of Israel.

cheat death (literally have made a covenant with death) . . . dodge the grave: There are two interpretive possibilities: (1) The people had sold themselves to the Canaanite god of death, Mot, in return for his supposed protection. (2) The prophet was being sarcastic; the people thought their various political and economic moves guaranteed their personal security, but they had actually destroyed themselves. • lies and deception: The leaders did not think of themselves as deceptive, but they were.

The Lord himself is the reliable foundation stone in Jerusalem, a precious cornerstone of the true city of God. There would be real hope in Jerusalem if the leaders and the people would only turn to him. If they would trust in God, they would be secure in the most terrible storm or the most devastating earthquake (see Isa 8.14; Psa 118.22; Mat 7.24–27; Mat 21.42; see the application to Jesus Christ, Rom 9.33; Rom 10.11; 1Co 3.11; Eph 2.20; 1Pe 2.4–7).
The Lord judges people on their works, which reveal the presence or absence of living faith (for justice and righteousness, see Isa 1.21–23).
The bed. . . . The blankets: The leaders were ill-prepared for God’s coming in judgment.
as he did . . . at Mount Perazim: See 2Sa 5.20. • God had rescued Israel through a hailstorm at Gibeon (Jos 10.10–12), but now he would turn against them.
Listen to me: The analogy that follows was written as a wisdom poem, with Isaiah calling on his audience to pay careful attention and to discern what is right.
A farmer knows that there are right and wrong ways to do things, but the leaders of Judah were not that intelligent.
The Lord has a variety of means (a heavy sledge . . . a light stick) for accomplishing his purposes. There are degrees of judgment.
he doesn’t keep on pounding it: This process would end; after judgment would come redemption.
wonderful teacher (or counselor; see Isa 9.6): God’s people should learn wisdom about God’s ways, as the farmer has done.
This is the second of the six woes (What sorrow . . .).
In the Assyrian siege, the Lord would be fighting against Jerusalem, but he would force the Assyrians to abandon Jerusalem in his own time.
Ariel was another name for Mount Zion (Isa 29.8); it probably means altar of God.
The Lord himself would come against Jerusalem, surrounding and attacking it.
God’s goal was to destroy the sinful pride of the people of Jerusalem. Their voice would rise as if from the grave. Through the Assyrians, God would humble his people, but he would not abandon them.

will act for you (literally you will be visited): God would bring rescue for his people. • thunder and earthquake . . . storm and consuming fire: These phenomena indicate a theophany (see study note on Isa 5.25).
The Assyrians’ sudden lifting of the siege came like a dream . . . like a vision in the night. God would save Judah and judge Assyria.
Jerusalem’s blindness kept its people from understanding God’s plan.
Like a hungry or thirsty person, the Assyrians could taste the victory over Jerusalem. Yet they never became victorious.

a spirit of deep sleep: The people’s folly was reinforced by God’s judgment on them (cp. Rom 1.24–32; Rom 11.8); they had no perception of reality. • Prophets were also sometimes called visionaries. Neither the people nor their prophets would understand what God was doing (Isa 6.9–10).

These people used pious-sounding language in their prayers and talk (see Mat 15.8; Mar 7.6–7), but they did not truly honor God. • In their hearts, they were not committed to the Lord at all. • In their worship, they followed man-made rules and regulations rather than God’s word.
Human wisdom . . . intelligence . . . will disappear (see 1Co 1.19). The prophet had already spoken of the failure of Egypt’s wise men (Isa 19.11–12); even Judah’s wise men would blunder.

This threat of coming judgment is the third of the six woes (see study note on Isa 28.1–Isa 33.24). It begins with judgment but moves to a vision of creation being renewed and of the wicked coming to an end.

Their plans might refer to the advice that royal counselors were giving Hezekiah, who at first attempted to free himself from Assyria by making alliances with Egypt (715 or 701 BC). • The people were conspiring to commit evil deeds in secret, but God saw everything.

Potter . . . clay: The Lord’s sovereignty is beyond challenge. Scripture does not discourage asking God hard questions, but there is no place for resistance to God’s will (see Isa 10.15; Isa 45.9; Isa 64.8; Rom 9.20). • He didn’t make me: Such claims against God demonstrate a total unwillingness to recognize God’s intimate involvement with every aspect of a person’s life.
The forests of Lebanon are usually an image of luxuriant growth (see Isa 2.13; Isa 14.8), but here they represent desolation.
Theme: The Holy One of Israel
The people were deaf and blind in heart and spirit (see Isa 6.10; Isa 42.18; Isa 43.8). Yet humanity and all of creation would be renewed (see Isa 35.1–5).

The false testimony that led to the oppression of the poor through trickery in the courts of Isaiah’s era would end. Because of God’s work in their hearts, the people would turn from their sinful behavior of the past.
The prophecy of woe, which began at Isa 29.15, now ends with a prophecy of salvation.

Abraham was the father of all Israel (see Gen 12.1–3; see also Gal 3.29). • Rescued from human abuse and God’s judgment, the people would no longer be ashamed; their disgrace resulted from the apparent failure of what they had trusted (see Psa 71.1; 1Pe 2.6).

After threatening Judah with judgment because of their stubbornness and their reliance on Egypt (Isa 30.1–17), God again committed himself to deal compassionately with his people and to break the power of their enemies.
This prophecy was against Judah’s dependence on Egypt. It is the fourth of the six woes (see study note on Isa 28.1–Isa 33.24).

The wisdom of the people of Judah was not directed by God’s Spirit (cp. Isa 11.2); instead, they had formed alliances that God did not approve of. Although the Assyrian attack on Jerusalem was overwhelming, making an alliance with Egypt demonstrated that the leaders of Judah depended on human resources for their protection rather than on God. Fortunately, Hezekiah later had a change of heart (see chs Isa 36.1–37).
Zoan: See Isa 19.11. The location of Hanes is uncertain.
This taunt was against those who were busy trying to please the Egyptians in order to get Egypt’s military support.

Caravans moved from Judah through the Negev and the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt to avoid the main coast road that was under Assyrian control. It was a dangerous region, filled with lions and poisonous snakes. People would risk their lives to make a worthless alliance. • Being weighed down with riches might refer to money being sent to Egypt to buy that nation’s help.

Harmless Dragon: In ancient mythology, Rahab was the enemy of the good gods and was depicted in fearsome terms, somewhat like a giant crocodile (see Isa 27.1; Isa 51.9; Job 41.1–34). By saying that Egypt was harmless, the prophet meant that it would be of no help to Judah.

God instructed the prophet to write down the vision for future generations. The present generation was rebellious; they rejected God’s word in favor of the false prophets’ fantasies (see Isa 8.16–17).
Stop telling us: The people of Judah did not want to be confronted about sin or judgment.
Judgment would suddenly overtake the people of Judah because they were content with their fantasy world, and they refused God’s path to rest and quietness.

The whole society accepted oppression and lies. People reinforced each other’s delusions, so it was considered acceptable to trust that Egypt would protect them from Assyria, even though that was a lie. It was also considered legal and legitimate to oppress the poor by taking their land.

The people of Judah needed to repent of their sinful ways (Isa 30.12–14), returning to the Lord, in order to be rescued. • Trust in the Lord would bring quietness and confidence, unlike their frantic negotiations with Egypt.
Judah’s reliance on Egypt to supply swift horses (see Psa 33.17) amounted to a rejection of God’s help and threatened to bring about its fall.

One . . . Five: This curse is the opposite of God’s blessing for obedience (Lev 26.8; Deu 32.30). • The Assyrians had dominated the rest of the land of Judah, leaving Jerusalem isolated like a lonely flagpole on a hill.
This prophecy of salvation includes promises that directed Israel’s attention away from their present adversity to the glorious future awaiting the children of God.

A faithful God would restore righteous order to the world by punishing the wicked and rescuing his people from them (see Isa 1.27; Psa 96.10–12). • God blesses those who wait; faithful people do not rush ahead of him to solve their own problems but instead rely on his power and goodness.

This was probably a challenge and promise to Hezekiah during the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem (see chs Isa 36.1–37). If he would just trust in God, his people would weep no more. • The Lord cares for the needs of his people; when they ask for something, he will surely respond.

adversity for food and suffering for drink: A city under enemy siege for a long time would eventually be overcome by starvation and disease. God did not intend that this disaster should destroy the people of Jerusalem, rather that it would be a tool to teach them.
The people’s own ears will hear and follow God’s instructions (see Isa 6.9–10; Isa 29.18; Isa 35.5).
One aspect of Hezekiah’s reforms was to remove silver idols and other idolatry of Ahaz’s era and to call the people back to the worship of the God of Israel (2Ki 18.4–5; 2Ch 29.1–36).
The people of Judah would again enjoy covenant blessings rather than curses (see Lev 26.4).
The Lord who struck his people would also heal them and cure the wounds he gave them.
In this prophecy of judgment against the nations, Isaiah foretold that Assyria’s power would be broken by God’s strong arm, not by the Egyptians.
like a flood up to the neck: Assyria’s destruction would be as devastating as their invasion of Judah (see Isa 8.8).

His mighty arm presents an image of strength that echoes God’s victory over the Egyptians in the Exodus (Isa 63.12; see Exo 15.6). • devouring flames . . . huge hailstones: Such phenomena are associated with God’s appearance in a theophany (see study note on Isa Isa 5.25).
royal scepter: The Lord, the true King, would be victorious over the threatening Assyrian king.

tambourines and harps: Instruments formerly silenced in judgment (Isa 24.8) would again be used by God’s people; this time, the people would celebrate the Lord’s goodness rather than becoming spiritually complacent (see Isa 5.12).
Topheth was a pagan altar in the valley of Ben-Hinnom outside Jerusalem where child sacrifices were offered to the Ammonite god Molech by burning (2Ki 23.9–10).

Isaiah delivered another vision regarding Judah’s negotiations with Egypt, which probably took place in 705–701 BC. During that time, the conquering Assyrians were on the move, threatening Judah. At first, Hezekiah tried political and military means to avert being totally conquered (see 2Ki 18.13–16).
What sorrow: This is the fifth of the six woes (see study note on Isa 28.1–Isa 33.24). • Looking to the LORD implies seeking his guidance with a worshipful attitude (see Deu 4.29; Psa 105.3–4).
This prophecy concerned God’s protection of Jerusalem and its rescue from the Assyrians.
princes will flee: This was fulfilled when Sennacherib fled to Nineveh after God destroyed 185,000 troops (see Isa 37.36–37). • God himself was the fire or flame that would devour Assyria.
a righteous king: The Messiah (Isa 11.1); the emphasis now is on righteous and wise leadership (Pro 8.20). • In Isaiah’s day, honest princes were few and far between (see Isa 3.1–6; Isa 28.7–19).

like a shelter . . . a refuge: The same words were also used to describe God’s protection (Isa 25.4) and his provision of life-giving water (Isa 41.18; Isa 43.19–20). The leaders would serve as God’s agents in blessing his people.
Only foolish people value fools and scoundrels as heroes (see also Isa 19.11, Isa 19.13; Isa 32.6–8).
Because they do not care about God’s standards of justice and righteousness, fools have no regard for those who are hungry or thirsty (see Isa 1.17; Isa 58.7, Isa 58.10).
smooth tricks . . . crooked schemes: See Pro 6.12, Pro 6.18; Pro 16.27; Pro 24.8–9.
This prophecy of judgment was against the complacent women of Jerusalem. God’s promises regarding the future did not justify continuing in sin.
The women of Jerusalem lie around in ease. Complacent in their high standard of life and low standard of morality, they put their trust in wealth and status to maintain their way of life.
In a short time: Assyria’s siege of Jerusalem (701 BC) was looming.

Burlap was worn to show . . . grief, especially when mourning (see Psa 30.11). The Assyrian conquest of the farmlands of Judah and most of its cities (except Jerusalem) would cause rich people in the large cities to mourn.
Jerusalem was eventually destroyed, but by the Babylonians, not the Assyrians (for a prediction of this, see Isa 39.1–8).

The Spirit would transform the nation into a godly community and bring in an era of justice and righteousness (see also Joe 2.28–32). The Spirit is connected to the Messiah (Isa 11.1) and the servant (Isa 42.1; Isa 61.1). • wilderness . . . bountiful crops: When the people are transformed, nature will be too.
Theme: God’s Justice
