Being right with God and humans will bring peace (Hebrew shalom; see Isa 26.3; Isa 48.18; Isa 52.7; cp. Jam 3.18). Peace is more than the absence of conflict. It includes personal wholeness and does not depend on outside circumstances (see also Rom 5.1).
Living in safety and feeling at rest were blessings of Israel’s covenant with the Lord (see Lev 26.5–6), but the people’s sin had previously brought curses rather than blessings (cp. Isa 32.9–11).
the forest . . . the city: The godly would remain secure even with evidence of God’s judgment all around them.

This was the sixth threat of woe (see study note on Isa 28.1–Isa 33.24). • Although the Hebrew text does not specifically name Assyria as the object of the prophecy in this chapter, Isaiah undoubtedly had Assyria in mind; they were the destroyer most immediately at hand when the prophecy was written. The prophecy applies, however, to any who seek to destroy God’s people; this included, but was not limited to, the Babylonians (see chs Isa 13.1–14). • When you are done betraying: Wicked nations often break political agreements with other nations when these contracts are no longer to their own advantage.
The godly community prayed for God to be merciful in response to the promise of Isa 30.18.
Sharon, Bashan, and Carmel were all fertile areas. Their desolation represents the destruction Assyria had inflicted on Israel.

In most passages, the Assyrians were turning other nations into worthless dry grass and stubble (see Isa 17.13; Isa 29.5; Isa 40.24; Isa 41.2). Here, ironically, they get a taste of their own medicine.

The godless were people who lived without regard for God and his law. • The image of a devouring fire came from God’s judgment of offenders during the wilderness journey (Exo 24.17; Deu 4.24). God still expects people to worship him with reverence and awe (Heb 12.29).
A godly life provides evidence that an individual truly knows God (see Col 3.5–17; Jam 2.14–18; 1Pe 1.14–16; 1Jo 1.5–6).
This vision is about God’s reign in Zion.

The king is the human representative (Isa 32.1) of the Great King, God himself (Isa 33.22). • The land belonging to God’s people would appear to be without borders because the foreign enemies had been judged (Isa 54.3).
Assyrian officers brought great terror to Judah when the Assyrians defeated various cities around Jerusalem (2Ki 18.13).
The strange, unknown language was the tongue of Assyria and later of Babylon (see Isa 28.11).
The people of Israel were the people of Zion (cp. Isa 33.20). • sick . . . the LORD will forgive their sins: See Isa 43.25.
This prophecy of judgment was against the nations at the terrifying day of the Lord (see study note on Isa 2.5–22; see also Isa 63.1–6).
completely destroy: See Lev 27.28–29.
It was a disgrace for a corpse to remain unburied.
Edom here represents what all the nations would experience, just as Moab was singled out in ch Isa 25.1–12.
Bozrah was a city in Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea.

The LORD’s revenge refers to God’s wrathful but righteous vengeance against his enemies and the oppressors of his people on the day of the Lord. • Edom will be paid back: There will be retribution for Edom’s crimes against Judah (see also Psa 137.7; Lam 4.21; Obad; Mal 1.3–5). Edom, with its history of treachery, would come to an end.
Edom’s judgment was similar to the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19.24; see also Jer 49.17–18).
See also Rev 14.11; Rev 19.3.
Wild animals, night birds, and hostile plants with thorns and nettles created an eerie environment.
The identification of some of these birds is uncertain, but they inhabited wild and deserted places and many were considered unclean (Deu 14.11–18).

Search the book of the LORD: Isaiah’s prophecy was God’s witness to the truthfulness of his word. • The power of the Spirit enacts the Lord’s decrees, assuring that all prophecy comes together to be fulfilled as God promised.
God will come to vindicate and transform his people. Instead of being deaf, blind, and lame (see Isa 6.10), the people will be pure, holy, and redeemed.
God’s land would become like a wasteland, spiritually desolate and physically depleted. However, God would turn the desert into a garden (see also Isa 32.15), taking his people from exile to glory.
Lebanon . . . Mount Carmel . . . Sharon: There will be a reversal of earlier judgments (see Isa 2.13; Isa 10.34; Isa 29.17; Isa 33.9). • glory . . . splendor of our God: See also Isa 6.3; Isa 40.5.
Tired hands and weak knees express discouragement and anxiety (see Heb 12.12).

do not fear: The Lord here assures his people of his presence and purpose (see also Isa 7.4; Isa 10.24; Isa 40.9; Isa 43.1; Isa 44.2; Isa 54.4). • The essence of the good news is that God is coming to save his people (see also Isa 40.9; Isa 52.7; Isa 62.11). God’s coming brings spiritual transformation as well as rescue from enemies.
eyes . . . ears: There will be a transformation from spiritual blindness and deafness to understanding and knowing God (Isa 6.10; Isa 29.18; Isa 32.3; Isa 42.7; see also Luk 7.22; Act 26.18).
The lame . . . those who cannot speak: All disabilities will be removed (see Mat 11.5; Mat 12.22; Mar 7.37; Act 3.7–8).

The imagery of the great road recalls Israel’s crossing through the Red Sea (Isa 51.10). • Only holy and undefiled people will share the Highway of Holiness. God’s goal in salvation is that humans will share in his character and act as he does (see Eph 5.1–2; 1Pe 2.21).

Jerusalem: The prophecy extends beyond the return of Israel from exile to the final establishment of God’s kingdom on earth. It will be characterized by joy and gladness and the absence of sorrow and mourning (see also Isa 25.7; Isa 51.11; Rev 21.4).

Jerusalem’s rescue from King Sennacherib of Assyria is a focal point of chs Isa 1.1–39. The Lord promised to rescue his people by remaining present with Jerusalem (see Isa 7.14) and by maintaining a remnant (see study note on Isa 10.20). Even though much of the country was desolate and the population decimated because of their foolish alliance with Assyria (chs Isa 7.1–8), the Lord preserved his people from total conquest through Hezekiah, a godly king. Hezekiah faced the same test that Ahaz did, a test of trust (note the recurrence of words for trust in the Assyrian officer’s challenge in ch Isa 36.1–22). But Hezekiah has learned the lessons taught in chs Isa 13.1–35 and, at least initially, he passed the test. This narrative is duplicated in 2Ki 18.13–Isa 20.19.

King Sennacherib of Assyria ruled from 705–681 BC. Hezekiah, like many other kings under Assyrian vassalage, had reasserted his independence when Sennacherib came to the throne in troubled circumstances. By 701 BC, the Assyrian king was ready to punish Hezekiah. Sennacherib recorded having conquered forty-six fortified cities and many villages, and having taken 200,146 captives. Hezekiah responded by attempting to appease Sennacherib (see 2Ki 18.14–16), but it was too late.

Lachish was a city overlooking the low-lying hills to the west of Jerusalem. It had to be taken before the final attack on Jerusalem could be launched. • the aqueduct that feeds water into the upper pool: This was a pool on the north side of Jerusalem, not the Gihon Spring in the Kidron valley. • Isaiah had met Ahaz on this same road leading to the field where cloth is washed some thirty-three years earlier (see Isa 7.3). At that time he had challenged Ahaz to trust God. However, Ahaz trusted Assyria instead, and this desperate situation was a result. Now the challenge to trust God came from mocking, foreign lips (see Isa 28.11–13).
Eliakim eventually advanced in rank, while Shebna was demoted (see Isa 22.15–24).

The Assyrian chief of staff attempted to use intimidation to negotiate a settlement without bloodshed. In his first speech (Isa 36.4–10), he rightly argued against Egypt’s ability to rescue but wrongly charged Hezekiah with misplaced trust in the Lord. Strikingly, the Assyrian did not see the contest as being between the gods of Assyria and the Lord but rather between Sennacherib—the great king—and the Lord.
Great king is a title similar to emperor.
Who are you counting on: Judah had asked Egypt to help them (see Isa 30.1–5).

Egypt . . . is completely unreliable: Isaiah argued the same case, pointing to the Lord as the only reliable source of help (Isa 31.1–3, Isa 31.7; Isa 39.7). • A kind of reed that breaks easily grows near the Nile (see Eze 29.6–7).

We are trusting in the LORD our God: Ironically, the Assyrian chief of staff knew about and played on Isaiah’s message (Isa 26.4; Isa 36.15; Isa 37.10). • Hezekiah showed his zeal for the Lord by tearing down the pagan shrines and altars (2Ki 18.4), but the Assyrians mistakenly thought Hezekiah had angered God in the process.
At this time, cavalry mounted on horses was the newest military technology. The Assyrian chief of staff was mocking the Judeans because he knew that Judah had no trained men who knew how to ride.
The LORD himself told us: It was common for a king to claim the approval of a deity in destroying other kingdoms. This claim was consistent with Isaiah’s prophecy in Isa 10.5–6.
Aramaic was the lingua franca used throughout the Assyrian Empire, understood by the elite but not by the common people of Judah.

In the Assyrian chief of staff’s second speech, he claimed that his nation’s gods were more powerful than the God of Judah (cp. Isa 10.9–10). God’s ability to rescue his people was at stake. In the ensuing drama, the Lord shocked the Assyrian with his power (Isa 37.36–37).
Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you: This public accusation against Hezekiah was intended to undermine the people’s confidence in him.
Hezekiah demonstrated a strong faith in the LORD, unlike Ahaz (ch Isa 7.1–25). Hezekiah’s faith would bring rescue, whereas Ahaz’s lack of faith brought him trouble (see Isa 7.9).

The Assyrian was tempting the people of Jerusalem with provisions that the Lord had promised to provide his obedient people (see Isa 1.19; Isa 37.30–35; Deu 8.7–9). It was a tempting offer, but a counterfeit. And it covered up the reality of exile that would have followed (Isa 36.17).

The populations of Hamath and Arpad had been relocated to Samaria, where the new local deities were the gods of Sepharvaim (2Ki 17.24). The logic of the argument made sense to an Assyrian. If the Assyrian gods defeated all the gods of the other nations and the God of the Israelite nation of Samaria, would they not also defeat the God of Judah?
Hezekiah responded to the threats by seeking the Lord’s favor. • The king tore his clothes and put on burlap as a sign of mourning and prayer.

perhaps . . . God has heard the Assyrian chief of staff . . . defy the living God: Hezekiah’s hope was not based on Judah’s or his own goodness, or the presence of the Temple in Jerusalem; instead, it was based on God responding to Assyria’s blasphemy.
God answered that he would deal with the Assyrians and rescue the remnant of his people from their distress (see Isa 63.9).
Libnah was a city on the Philistine plain near Lachish. Sennacherib was preparing to fight both Egypt and Jerusalem when he sent word to Hezekiah.
King Tirhakah of Ethiopia was then the ruler of Egypt.

The argument was that Judah’s god, like the gods of other nations already conquered by Assyria, would be unable to save Judah (see also Isa 36.18–20). • Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, . . . Eden, and Tel-assar were cities in Mesopotamia.
When he received Sennacherib’s boastful threat, Hezekiah returned to the Temple and prayed for rescue. His prayer stands in contrast to Ahaz’s response to danger decades earlier (see ch Isa 7.1–25).

God of Israel: Hezekiah was not taken in by the false claims of Sennacherib that the Lord was powerless. In his prayer, Hezekiah acknowledged that, because the Lord is the Creator, he is God of all the kingdoms of the earth. The Lord is sovereign over all kingdoms. • The mighty cherubim were located in the Temple atop the Ark of the Covenant, which was God’s throne in his Temple (see study note on Lev Lev 16.2; see also Psa 80.1; Psa 99.1).

you alone, O LORD, are God: Hezekiah was concerned for the Lord’s reputation, which Sennacherib had impugned. Hezekiah recognized that if the Lord defeated the Assyrians and their gods, his holy name would be glorified among all the nations of the world (cp. Exo 9.16; Exo 14.4, Exo 14.17–18; Jos 2.9–11; 1Sa 4.7–8).
Because you prayed: Prayer is powerful; it moved God’s heart and was part of the reason why the Lord answered with this message of hope.
The virgin daughter of Zion: Jerusalem is personified as a young woman who mocks the Assyrian king (see also Isa 3.26).
Whom . . . Against whom: Sennacherib’s speech was not so much an insult against Judah as it was against the Lord.

Isaiah seems to be familiar with the typical royal Assyrian boasts, including that they possessed the highest mountains. These words sound very much like those found in the annals of the Assyrian kings inscribed on the walls of their temples.

I have dug wells . . . I stopped up all the rivers of Egypt: Sennacherib’s boasts demonstrate his attitude of independence. However, the Lord alone is sovereign over nature (Isa 42.15; Isa 43.19; Isa 44.27).

I planned for you to crush . . . into heaps of rubble: Assyria was God’s agent of destruction, but the Assyrians did not realize that they were only a tool in God’s hand (see ch Isa 10.1–34), fulfilling what God had planned long before (Isa 14.24–27).
you have raged against me: Assyria was utterly hostile to the Lord, which brought them even greater condemnation.
my hook . . . my bit: The Assyrians would be led away like animals, just as they had led so many of their captives away.

In this prophecy of salvation, Isaiah assured Hezekiah that Jerusalem would be spared and that the remnant was under God’s protection. The names of Isaiah and his sons anticipated God’s rescue (see Isa 7.1–Isa 11.16). The book’s record of God’s presence and rescue provided assurance that the Lord would always have a remnant that he will protect and rescue.

This year . . . next year . . . the third year: Because of the Assyrian siege and its destruction of agriculture, the people of Judah would not be able to plant and harvest as usual. The promise that life would resume after the siege assured them that God was with them and would provide as they carried out their everyday activities. They needed to develop their trust in God over a period of three calendar years in the confident expectation that God’s word would be true (cp. Isa 30.15, Isa 30.18). Perhaps the point was that after rescue from the Assyrians, it would be too late in the present year for fall planting. They would have to wait until fall in the second year to plant again, and they would reap their first crop in the spring and summer of the third year.
The passionate commitment of God includes his energetic zeal to keep his promise, the best guarantee his people could ever have (see also Isa 9.7).
armies . . . arrow . . . shields . . . banks of earth: Despite their advanced military technology and great power, the Assyrians would not succeed against Jerusalem.
for the sake of my servant David: God had promised David a perpetual dynasty (see Isa 9.6–7; 2Sa 7.8–17).

The angel of the LORD was a special heavenly agent through whom God worked on earth. Often his role was to communicate special messages (see Gen 16.7–14), but sometimes he brought judgment (see 2Sa 24.16). • killed 185,000 Assyrian soldiers: The Lord began to fulfill what he had repeatedly promised—rescue of Jerusalem and judgment of Assyria (see Isa 10.16, Isa 10.33–34; Isa 30.31; Isa 31.8).

One day: Sennacherib was probably killed in 681 BC, about twenty years after his withdrawal from Jerusalem. • Esarhaddon was king of Assyria from 680–669 BC. It is ironic that Sennacherib, who mocked the Lord, was killed by his sons in the temple of his god.

The story of Hezekiah’s healing connects Hezekiah’s extension of life with Jerusalem’s relief from the Assyrians. The events of this story took place before Jerusalem’s rescue from the Assyrians but were placed in a thematic rather than chronological order. One theme is the importance of prayer (see Isa 37.14–20; Isa 38.2–3). The Lord does listen! Hezekiah had learned the lesson of trust that his father, Ahaz, refused. As a result, Judah and Jerusalem were spared total destruction by the Assyrians. Yet Hezekiah was not the Messiah, the Son of David promised in Isa 7.14; Isa 9.1–7; Isa 11.1–16; Isa 16.5; Isa 32.1, Isa 33.17–22. Thus, these accounts of his failure and mortality (chs Isa 38.1–39) prepare the reader for the revelation of the true Messiah that follows (chs Isa 40.1–66).

About that time (literally in those days): This is a very general time statement. Hezekiah’s illness and subsequent healing probably preceded Jerusalem’s rescue (chs Isa 36.1–37), even though Isaiah places it afterward. Merodach-baladan’s reign in Babylon (Isa 39.1) ended before Sennacherib’s invasion in 701 BC. The order in the text indicates a connection between these two events (see Isa 38.6).

I have always been faithful to you: Hezekiah’s heart was right with the Lord for most of his reign (2Ki 18.1–5), although his dependence on Egypt was a time of weakness when he did not act faithfully (Isa 31.1–9).
the God of your ancestor David: Hezekiah faithfully walked in David’s footsteps (see Isa 37.35; Isa 38.1–22).

I will rescue you . . . I will defend this city: This promise refers to the rescue of Jerusalem (chs Isa 36.1–37); it also provides a greater context for understanding Hezekiah’s sickness and healing. Just as Hezekiah received another fifteen years, Jerusalem also received a temporary reprieve (see ch Isa 39.1–8).
Hezekiah’s poem contains both lament (Isa 38.9–14) and praise (Isa 38.15–20), although the praise is distinctly muted until the final verse.

enter the place of the dead? (literally enter the gates of Sheol?): This image comes from an ancient idea that people enter death through gates (see Isa 14.9). Old Testament believers did not understand the afterlife as the New Testament reveals it. It was a shadowy place where all the dead were together and where no praise of God existed (see Isa 38.18; Psa 88.10; Psa 115.17).
Hezekiah lamented that if he died, he would not enjoy fellowship with God, his family, and his friends.
These images depicted the brevity of life (cp. 2Co 5.1).
I will walk humbly: Hezekiah might have previously taken his life and good health for granted. Now he recognized that these gifts from the Lord can be withdrawn at any time.
God’s restoration of Hezekiah’s health also symbolized the restoration from exile that Judah would experience in the future.

Hezekiah received a sign, reminiscent of another sign the prophet had offered Ahaz (Isa 7.11). Ahaz and Hezekiah were two bookends to a long story. Ahaz represented the ungodly king and Hezekiah the godly king. The former brought disaster on his people, while the latter rescued his people (but see ch Isa 39.1–8).
Hezekiah could not go to the Temple with an infection (see Lev 13.1–59), so going to the Temple signifies restored health.
Hezekiah was exemplary in godliness, prayer, and care for the people of Jerusalem. But he failed the Lord by parading his financial and military strength before the envoys from Babylon.

Merodach-baladan, the king of Babylon (722–710 and 704–703 BC), planned to rebel against Assyria and sought help from Hezekiah. His envoys visited after Hezekiah had been very sick and had recovered but before Sennacherib’s final attack in 701 BC.
silver . . . aromatic oils . . . his armory: Showing these treasures demonstrated to Babylon’s envoys that Hezekiah had the resources to be a worthy ally.

carried off to Babylon: This prophecy was given before the prophecy of the rescue of Jerusalem (Isa 37.35). Although this pronouncement of judgment and exile comes as a surprise ending to the story of Hezekiah, the exile of both Israel and Judah had been in the background from the beginning (Isa 10.3–4, Isa 10.20–23). The Lord had promised that he would spare Judah and Jerusalem when the Assyrians attacked in 701 BC, but he had clearly revealed to Isaiah that worse things would come if they did not change their ways. God had demonstrated the truth of his sovereignty and trustworthiness in his defeat of the Assyrians, but that did not mean the people had changed. The only way the promises of Isa 2.1–5 and Isa 4.2–6 were going to be realized was through the fires of judgment (Isa 4.4). Until the burning coal of exile was applied to the nation’s unclean lips (Isa 6.5–7), their mission to the nations would fail.

The rest of Isaiah provides a message of comfort and a revelation of God’s character and his purposes for Israel. As Isa 39.6–7 predicted, Judah would experience judgment and exile after the time of Isaiah. Throughout chs Isa 40.1–66, Isaiah prophesied from the vantage point of the Exile having already become a reality. Therefore, the Babylonian exile provides the background for understanding these chapters.

This section announces the good news of God’s coming salvation. The Lord is coming to vindicate his own and to judge his enemies. Salvation would be accomplished through the arrival, suffering, and exaltation of the Lord’s servant—the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

This chapter introduces chs Isa 40.1–66. In this section, comfort refers to the result of God’s merciful way of dealing with people in the age to come. It includes encouragement, strength, and acceptance. God wants to rescue his people (Isa 40.1–11) and is more than able to do so (Isa 40.12–26). The exiles needed to believe God’s promises and wait on him for their rescue (Isa 40.27–31; see also Isa 30.15–18).

Speak tenderly: The prophet’s message was to encourage Jerusalem with the good news of God’s forgiveness, reconciliation, and restoration. • From the prophetic perspective, Israel’s sad days are gone because the Exile is over. • punished her twice over for all her sins: Israel experienced the full brunt of God’s wrath (Isa 51.19–23; cp. Isa 61.7).

There is now a shift from the general announcement of the good news to the specific expectation of God’s coming. The good news (Isa 40.1–2) is grounded in God himself. Isaiah portrayed the Lord as coming on a highway through the desert (see ch Isa 35.1–10), although the imagery is here reversed: In ch Isa 35.1–10, the people were traveling to Zion, toward the Lord. Here, the Lord is coming toward his people (see also Isa 52.8, where the two images are brought together).

the voice of someone shouting: In Mal 3.1 this person (possibly the Elijah of Mal 4.5) was God’s messenger who prepared the way for God’s coming. In the Gospels, this announcer was identified with John the Baptist (Mat 3.3; Mar 1.3; Luk 3.4; Joh 1.23). • Clear the way . . . Make a straight highway: The announcer’s message would expedite God’s coming (see Isa 35.8). As God made a way for Israel through the Red Sea (Isa 43.16), so a way would be opened up for the Lord (see Isa 52.11–12).

The future revelation of God’s glory would include the return of Judah from exile but would also go beyond it. The New Testament confirmed that the revelation of God’s glory came in Jesus Christ (Joh 1.14; Heb 1.3). • The LORD has spoken: The coming salvation and judgment would certainly occur because the Lord, who keeps his word, had declared it (see Isa 1.20; Isa 58.14).
All humanity is mortal and fleeting. By contrast, God persists in his plans and succeeds. Time does not limit him from carrying out his will (see Isa 14.24).
Shout: So that all can hear. • People are not worthy of the revelation of God’s glory because they are mortal.
The breath of the LORD refers to God’s spoken words of judgment (see Isa 4.4).

the word of our God stands forever: All of God’s words (his plans as well as the written word) will succeed. God might frustrate human expectations, but everything will happen according to his wise plan (see Isa 14.24; Isa 55.8–11; see also Mat 25.34).
God is the good news. Although he comes like a warrior to rescue his people with power, he also holds them tenderly as a shepherd.
God is coming to save and restore human beings (see also Isa 35.4; Rev 22.12).

The Lord’s rule is not like that of the unjust and powerless rulers whom he will judge. It is compassionate, just, righteous, and powerful. • with a powerful arm: God manifested his power in events such as the defeat of the Egyptians (Isa 63.12), the judgment of his enemies (Isa 30.30; Isa 48.14; Isa 51.9), and the rescue of his people (Isa 59.16).
Isaiah used the familiar biblical metaphor of a shepherd to speak of God’s care for his people (see also Isa 49.10; Psa 23.1; Jer 3.15; Jer 23.4; Eze 34.11–17; Mat 2.6; Joh 10.1–18).
Against the backdrop of Israel’s questions (spoken by the prophet), the Lord affirmed that he is the incomparable God, a wise and sovereign creator who rules over the nations.
These rhetorical questions evoke the answer “No one!” God alone created all that exists. He will judge creation (Isa 24.17), and he alone can and will restore creation through his salvation.

God is sovereign over all the nations of the world and over their human power structures. In comparison to God, they are almost nothing. This included the Babylonian Empire, which was merely a tool in God’s hand. • whole earth: Literally coastlands or islands.
Lebanon was prized for its abundance of wood and its wildlife (see Isa 2.13–16; Psa 104.16–17).
The nations, including their leaders (Isa 40.23), pagan structures (Isa 41.24, Isa 41.29; Isa 44.9–11), and all enemies of God’s people (Isa 41.11–12), are worth nothing apart from God.

To whom . . . What image: Earlier in the book, idolatry was shown to be ridiculous (Isa 16.12; Isa 37.16–19). Chapters Isa 40.1–48 open up a much more extensive argument against idolatry. Idols are symbolic representations of gods and, at times, other religious concepts. Those who worship them don’t recognize the implication that they are man-made trinkets. Idols are powerless (Isa 41.7, Isa 41.22–24; Isa 48.14), give a false sense of security (Isa 42.17), delude people (Isa 44.20), and lead to severe disappointment (Isa 42.17; Isa 45.16, Isa 45.20). They cannot help those who care for them. In fact, they are so weak that they fall down (Isa 40.20; Isa 41.7). In the end, idols compete for God’s glory (Isa 42.8) and take away human dignity (Isa 44.9; see also Isa 41.21–29). • The Lord, the true God, is incomparable (see Isa 40.25; Isa 46.5; Psa 86.8; Psa 89.6); no one could resemble him.
image that won’t fall down: This is a sarcastic remark; it would be embarrassing if the idol did not even have the power to remain standing (see Isa 40.18; Isa 41.7; 1Sa 5.4).

Idolaters fail to discern who God is or to respond wisely to him. The godly in Israel would understand and see the hand of God in the unfolding story of redemption, which includes both exile and restoration (Isa 41.20).

God sits enthroned as King over all the earth (see Isa 6.1; Psa 2.4; Psa 80.1; Psa 99.1; Psa 102.12; Psa 113.5). God is so immense and awesome that humans are like grasshoppers in comparison. • Belief in God as creator of the heavens and earth contradicts the popular Babylonian and Egyptian belief that the sun, moon, and stars represent gods. • like a curtain . . . his tent: See also Psa 104.2.
great people: God is unimpressed by human power and fame.
The Holy One is a shortened form of “the Holy One of Israel,” a common designation for God in Isaiah (see also Isa 10.17; Isa 43.15; Psa 22.3).

Look up into the heavens: Just as God directed Abraham to look into the sky (Gen 15.5), he also directed Israel to look to the stars for encouragement (see also Isa 51.2–3). The cosmos bears witness to God’s great power and incomparable strength. The Strong One is able to strengthen the weak (Isa 40.27–31; see Psa 147.5).

does not see your troubles . . . ignores your rights: The coming exile, a period when God’s powerful presence and rescue would not be seen, would prompt questions (see also Isa 49.14; Isa 54.7; Lam 5.20–22).

heard . . . understood: Cp. Isa 40.21. • the everlasting God, the Creator of all the earth: Creation reveals God’s power and wisdom. He is also the Creator of the age to come, a world of righteousness, justice, and peace (Isa 45.8; Isa 48.6–7; Isa 65.17–18). • He never grows weak or weary: God is not susceptible to human limitations.
The weak in this context are those who face persecution or oppression (such as the Babylonian exile); the Lord is their only recourse (see Isa 49.4–5; Isa 50.4; Psa 68.9; Psa 119.28).
trust in the LORD: See Isa 33.2; Isa 49.23; Isa 51.5. • like eagles: This powerful image of rescue reminded readers of the Exodus event of long ago (Exo 19.4; Deu 32.10–12; see also Psa 103.5).

The Lord here invited the nations to a trial where he would prove that he alone is God. They were defenseless as he declared that a king from the east (Isa 41.2) would crush Babylon, opening the way for Israel to return.

The nations coming together for a trial have to listen in silence to the presentation of God’s arguments. • Bring your strongest arguments: Literally let them find new strength, a play on Isa 40.31. • God invited the nations to come . . . and speak, challenging them to refute his case.

This king from the east was Cyrus, the Persian king who conquered Babylon in 539 BC and permitted the Jews to return to their land and rebuild Jerusalem (538 BC; Ezr 1.1–4). Isaiah’s prophecies about Cyrus (see Isa 44.28–Isa 45.13; Isa 48.14–15) encouraged Israel to look to the Lord as sovereign over all of human history, including the actions of great kings. • Who gives this man victory over many nations? As victorious as the conquering Cyrus was, he was still subject to the Lord.

each new generation from the beginning of time: God is sovereign over all things. From the beginning he has unfolded each stage of history according to his plan. • In the book of Revelation, Jesus identifies himself as the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End (Rev 1.8, Rev 1.17; Rev 2.8; Rev 21.6; Rev 22.13). • I alone am he: The Lord alone is God (see also Isa 43.10, Isa 43.13; Isa 46.4; Isa 48.12; Deu 32.39). Jesus used similar expressions for himself (see Joh 6.35; Joh 8.12, Joh 8.24; Joh 9.5; Joh 10.7, Joh 10.9, Joh 10.11, Joh 10.14; Joh 11.25; Joh 14.6; Joh 15.1, Joh 15.5).
This taunt against idolatry was a response to God’s raising up of Cyrus; the nations hope to find protection in their idols.
Be strong! The nations put their hope in things that have no strength, objects made by human craftsmen.
These two prophecies of salvation for God’s servant Israel (Isa 41.8–13, Isa 41.14–16) prepare for the first of the suffering servant songs (see study note on Isa 42.1–4).

The servant—here the nation of Israel—was God’s chosen one, whose calling was grounded in God’s purposes. • Abraham my friend: The phrase in Hebrew could mean Abraham who loves me or Abraham whom I love. See also Jam 2.23.

I have chosen you restates Isa 41.8 to emphasize God’s commitment and faithfulness to his people Israel, who had not been faithful to him. • not throw you away: Because of the Exile, the people felt that God had rejected them (see Isa 49.21; Isa 54.6). However, God had good purposes for them.

I am with you: The promise of God’s presence (see Isa 7.14) is central to the Bible. Because God is present, his people do not need to fear (see also Isa 43.1–2, Isa 43.5). • I am your God: The Lord used the language of the covenant to affirm that he is their God and that they are his people (see also Jer 7.23; Jer 31.1, Jer 31.33; Eze 14.11; Eze 36.28; Eze 37.27; Zec 8.8). • hold you . . . my victorious right hand: The Lord used language reminiscent of the Exodus (cp. Exo 15.6) to encourage Israel (see also Isa 41.13; Isa 63.12).

In exile, Israel was in a lowly state. • God is the Redeemer. He works mightily to rescue and restore people from sin and its consequences (for Israel, the Exile; for application to Jesus, see Luk 2.38; Luk 21.28; Rom 3.24; 1Co 1.30; Gal 4.5; Eph 1.1–14; Tit 2.14; Heb 9.12).
When the grain is thrown into the wind, the chaff is blown away. Likewise, Israel’s enemies appeared to be strong but would easily be driven off.

rivers . . . fountains . . . pools of water . . . springs: These images would strike a responsive chord in an agrarian culture. They also suggest that rescue from the Exile would be a second exodus (cp. Exo 15.27; Exo 17.6).

This trial scene develops the Lord’s case against idolatry. Idols are nothing but a human creation, whereas God is the Creator of all things. Idols cannot speak, act, accomplish anything, or save their worshipers.
the King of Israel: See Isa 6.5; Isa 43.15; Isa 44.6.

I have stirred up a leader: The God who had planned the Exile through Babylon had already planned for Israel’s restoration from exile through Cyrus (see Isa 41.2; see also Isa 13.17). • Although Persia is located to the east, rough terrain required those traveling to Israel and Judah to enter from the north. • I will give him victory . . . He will trample them: As Babylon was sent to trample Assyria, so Persia would trample Babylon.
Idols and false gods could not predict the future.
The messenger with good news told of God’s coming to rescue his people (see Isa 40.9).

The servant here is not the people Israel (as in Isa 41.8–28 and elsewhere in chs Isa 41.1–48; see Isa 49.5–6) but is a royal figure who accomplishes his mission with care for people, especially for those who are hurting. The passage is the first of four songs about this servant (Isa 42.1–4; Isa 49.1–13; Isa 50.4–11; Isa 52.13–Isa 53.12). He brings in an era of universal justice. For the connection of the servant with Jesus Christ, see Mat 12.18–21.

who pleases me: God used similar language at Jesus’ baptism (Mat 3.17). • I have put my Spirit upon him: Any leader might be called a servant, but the presence of the Spirit suggests a king of David’s line or a prophet like Moses (see Num 11.17, Num 11.24–29). • Establishing justice is the responsibility of a king (see Isa 9.6–7; Psa 72.1). • This king’s mission will be a greater mission to the nations than simply governing the small nation of Judah.
shout or raise his voice: The royal servant will have calm confidence in his message and calling from God (see also Isa 11.1–5).
The royal servant will be gentle with the oppressed and discouraged (see Isa 3.15; Isa 41.17).

distant lands: The nations long for justice and for instruction on bringing it about. In this regard the servant is like Moses, to whom the law was given. However, the servant is greater in that he extends justice beyond Israel to all the nations.

my people, Israel . . . my covenant with them (literally a covenant for the people): It is also possible that “the people” referred to all the peoples/nations of the earth (see Isa 49.6). • light to guide the nations: See also Isa 51.4; Act 13.47.

The servant will open the eyes of the spiritually blind (see Isa 6.10; Isa 29.18) and free the spiritual captives from the prison of sin, in addition to those who were captive in the Babylonian exile (see Isa 61.1 with Luk 4.18).
I am the LORD: As Creator of the world, and as the only one who can bring about the things he predicts, the Lord alone is glorious and worthy of praise.

The various geographical regions represent the extremes of human habitation. The whole earth is called to praise God for his commitment to redeem humanity. • Kedar and Sela (Isa 42.11; see also Isa 16.1; Isa 21.16–17) were representative desert sites.

a mighty hero . . . a warrior: The background of this theme is God’s victory at the Red Sea during the Exodus (Exo 15.3). • God will be victorious over all his enemies in order to rescue his people (Isa 51.9; Isa 63.1–6; see also Psa 54.7; Psa 108.9; Psa 112.8).

I have long been silent . . . restrained myself: Israel had experienced God’s absence in the Exile, which came about because of their idolatrous ways (Isa 57.11–13; 2Ki 17.6–24). The godly will pray for God’s presence and renewed involvement in their situation (Isa 64.12), and the Lord will answer their prayers because of his commitment to their redemption (Isa 62.1, Isa 62.6).

The Israelites who refused to listen to what God said and to understand what they saw God doing in history were rendered spiritually blind and deaf (see Isa 6.9–10). They had knowledge of the truth through God’s word and the prophets, but their closed minds refused to act upon it.
exalted his glorious law: God’s word is a witness to his righteous rule (see Isa 1.10).

Throughout its history, Israel’s sin (Isa 42.24) made Israel fair game for foreign oppressors. Many nations, Assyria and Babylon in particular, became instruments God used to pour out his fury (Isa 42.25) on his rebellious people.
Generation after generation of Israelites did not learn their lesson, even when God disciplined them through military defeat.
In this promise of salvation, the Lord addressed his plundered people in the first person.

the LORD who created you: The language of creation (see study note on Isa 40.28) was now applied to God’s formation of the nation Israel. • I have ransomed you: At the Exodus, when God brought his people out of bondage. Similarly, God planned to bring his people out of exile and back into their land. Ultimately, Jesus gave his life as a ransom for all humanity (Mat 20.28; 1Ti 2.6; Heb 9.15) • I have called you by name; you are mine: Despite having faced his wrath, the people of Israel are still God’s chosen people.

Conquering forces could be compared to flooding rivers (see Isa 8.8). • I will be with you: God is committed to being with his people to protect and care for them (see Isa 7.14; Isa 41.10; Isa 43.5; Isa 45.14). • Israel experienced God’s judgment as the fire of oppression during the Exile.
One of God’s purposes in restoring his people was to display his glory to the watching world.

The Lord here called on Israel, his blind servant, to be his star witness in a mock trial against idols and false gods. Israel knew that the Lord alone is God, and the people had experienced his salvation.

you are my witnesses: By their very presence in exile, Israel was evidence that God is truly God. He predicted the Exile long beforehand, and now it had come to pass. God alone is the true God because he speaks and acts and controls all of history. Idols and false gods could do none of these things. Israel would later become even greater evidence because God had also predicted their redemption (Isa 43.11–12).
The Lord assured Israel of its coming redemption from Babylon; the redemption would be modeled on Israel’s past redemption from Egypt and would be greater in some ways (Isa 43.18).
God did not want the Israelites to forget the exodus from Egypt. However, they needed to look forward in faith to the spectacular event that was about to occur rather than dwelling on the past.
One purpose of redemption is to honor God through the praises of the redeemed (see 1Pe 2.9).

Israel’s history of rebellion had led them into crisis after crisis, yet their rebellion was so great that they stubbornly refused to ask God for help. When they did pray, their wickedness often caused their prayers not to be heard (Isa 1.15).
God alone can and does blot out . . . sins, no matter how many or how great (see also Isa 44.22).
leaders: God held Israel’s and Judah’s kings especially responsible for leading the nation into sin (see 2Ki 21.1–26).

The promise of salvation extended the usefulness of sinful Israel to another generation (Isa 44.3). The past was bleak (see Isa 43.22–28), but the future would be a glorious new era transformed by the Spirit.

The restoration theme is connected with God’s promise to pour out the Spirit (see also Isa 32.15–17; Joe 2.28–32; Act 2.16–18). • on your descendants . . . children: The next generation of Israelites offered hope.
This passage uses the form of a trial speech to press God’s argument that disgrace comes to all who trust in idols and false gods.

he uses part of the wood to make a fire . . . he takes the rest of it and makes himself a god to worship: This description of the process of making an idol drips with sarcasm and ridicule at the stupidity of the foolish idol worshipers (see also Isa 44.19).
Their minds are shut: Idol worshipers cannot see the irony in using one part of a log to warm themselves and another part of the same log to be their god.
The Lord promised to forgive Israel’s sins.
All creation is called to celebrate God’s redemption of Israel (cp. Isa 1.2).
The Lord alone is sovereign over history. He raised up Cyrus of Persia to execute judgment on Babylon and restore Israel to the Holy Land.
False prophets and fortune-tellers used forbidden forms of divination to try to predict the future. Eventually God would expose them as deluded liars (see Isa 3.2; Isa 9.15; Isa 47.13; Deu 18.10–11).

The sudden depletion of natural resources at times indicates a divine judgment (see Isa 42.15; cp. Isa 43.20). Here, however, God’s ability to dry up streams with just a word illustrates his power to do what he said he would do through Cyrus of Persia.

He is my shepherd: Cyrus went beyond simply permitting the Jews to return to their homeland. He facilitated a major restoration project to rebuild Jerusalem and restore the Temple (see Isa 45.13; Ezr 1.2–4; Ezr 6.3–5).

anointed one: This designation, commonly reserved for David or the Messiah, is here applied to Cyrus. Cyrus was anointed in the sense that he was selected to fulfill a special mission. This title was never used of any other foreign ruler (cp. 1Sa 10.1; Rom 13.1). • whose right hand he will empower: The Lord would give Cyrus victory over Babylon (see Isa 43.14).
so you may know: Cyrus’s victories provided factual proof that the Lord has the power to fulfill his plans, whereas idols and false gods do not (see Isa 41.21–29).

I call you by name: Cyrus did not know the Lord, but the Lord knew him. Isaiah predicted the rescuer Cyrus by name 150 years in advance. This prophecy would prove to the exiles that the Lord is indeed God and that he knows the future.
light . . . darkness . . . good times and bad times: Everything is under God’s control.

The Lord confronts those who question his right to use a pagan king to achieve his purposes. He, the Creator, is free and sovereign in his activities. He promised to bring his people back to their land, and he would use anyone he chose to accomplish that purpose.
pot . . . its maker . . . baby . . . its father: It is ridiculous for a creature to question the wisdom of its creator.

Egyptians . . . Ethiopians . . . Sabeans: Israel’s restoration would bring them a new sovereignty. Foreign nations would honor God, and because they recognized God’s special blessing on his people, they would also want to honor his people.
Israel would never again be humiliated and disgraced, oppressed, harassed, or abused. The finality of these declarations suggests that this promise will be fulfilled at the end of time.

Salvation is from the Lord alone. He is the creator, the revealer, and the executor of his will in human history. He promised to establish a new era of salvation and righteousness (see Isa 45.8). Every human being will submit to God, either willingly or unwillingly (Isa 45.23–24).
Ancient pagan people viewed the world as a place of empty chaos. However, God’s purposes are good, and he made the world from the beginning as a place to be lived in with him in harmony.

Let all the world look to me: All humanity needs to seek the Lord, the true God who created all things, while he may be found (Isa 55.6). • In God there is salvation, the only hope for all of humanity (Isa 45.8).

God’s words are always true. God’s swearing by his own name reinforces the certainty that he will never go back on his word (see also Isa 14.24; Isa 54.9; Isa 62.8; Heb 6.13). • Every knee . . . every tongue: At the end of time all nations will submit to his authority, whether willingly or unwillingly (see Rom 14.11; 1Co 15.25–27; Phi 2.10–11).
In this context, the people are all who turn to the Lord for salvation, even those from foreign nations (Isa 45.22).
justified: Literally righteous (see also Isa 45.8, Isa 45.24).
This taunt was against the self-contradiction of Babylonian religion.

Marduk-bel was the most important god in the Babylonian pantheon. Bel (similar to “Baal”) designated lordship. • Nebo (Nabu, Nebu), the patron deity of Babylonian scribes, was thought to be the son of Marduk-bel. • Instead of being paraded in glory at a Babylonian festival, these gods would be hauled away on ox carts and disposed of, rejected by the Babylonian people.

Those who remain in Israel refers to the remnant that would be left alive after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. • The Lord, the Creator of humanity, cares for and carries his people (contrast the Babylonian idols that must be carried instead). • since you were born . . . before you were born: The Lord chose Israel even before they were a nation (see also Isa 49.5).
Many of the exiles would be completely discouraged and not believe the prediction of God’s rescue. God challenged this unbelief.
God knows the future before it even happens; he has comprehensive control over all events, and all his acts match his words (Isa 41.4, Isa 41.26). He is the First and the Last (Isa 44.6; Isa 48.12).
The swift bird of prey from the east refers to Cyrus, the Persian king (see study note on Isa 41.2).
Formerly, Israel cared little for doing right (literally righteousness; see also Isa 58.2; Isa 59.9).

The good news for Israel was that God was coming to set things right (literally I will bring my righteousness near; see Isa 40.9; Isa 51.5). • show my glory to Israel: Unlike a craftsman who bestows material splendor on an idol (Isa 44.13), the Lord bestows true dignity on his people.

Two conclusions can be drawn from the preceding evidence that the Lord alone is God: (1) Babylon’s great pride is foolishness (Isa 47.1–15); (2) Israel needs to pay attention to the word of the Lord (Isa 48.1–22).
In this taunt against Babylon, the queen of nations is humiliated, forced to work as a servant girl.
To sit in the dust was a way of expressing humiliation.
God’s vengeance against those who oppose him and those who oppress his people (see Isa 34.8) will bring justice to the world by purging it of wickedness.
Babylon’s confidence and arrogance were well known (see Isa 14.13–17; Dan 4.30). All of this nation’s charms, magic, and wisdom were useless against the disaster decreed for it.
The people of Israel had provoked God’s wrath, prompting him to use Babylon to punish them. Now wicked Babylon itself would be punished.

I am the only one, and there is no other: This was a claim to divinity (cp. Isa 45.5; Isa 47.10). Only the Lord can make such a claim. For any created thing, including a nation, to utter this is the height of hubris. • To be a widow or to lose one’s children was a disgrace.
Witchcraft and magic were commonly used in an attempt to ward off evil and to secure a happy future.

In this context, ‘wisdom’ and ‘knowledge’ probably refer sarcastically to the pseudo-knowledge gained through occult practices, which actually led Babylon away from the truth and into disaster (Isa 47.11).
In the face of calamity, Babylon would turn to occult practices for help, but it would not find help.
Babylon was advanced in astronomy, which the astrologers and stargazers used as a form of divination (see Dan 2.2, Dan 2.10; Dan 5.7).
The Lord here calls on Israel to forsake her historic rebelliousness and listen to what he says. The Hebrew word translated listening is often synonymous with obeying or acting upon what is heard.
This prophecy is a disputation, a speech in which the prophet argues a set of points against his audience.
Israel was religious but not truly committed to the Lord.
Jacob . . . Judah: Although Isaiah’s normal focus was on Judah, here he addressed all the tribes of Israel.
The Lord had forewarned Israel of what was going to happen in the Exile.

Even though Israel had repeatedly failed to believe God’s past predictions, here he revealed new things that were not yet heard. Specifically, God revealed that Babylon would fall and Israel would be restored.
The Exile was a furnace of suffering (cp. Deu 4.20) through which God refined Israel.

I will not let my reputation be tarnished: Israel’s exile raised questions among the nations about the Lord’s character and reputation. The nations would not have perceived that Israel’s wicked character led to the Exile. Instead they would have viewed it as a failure of Israel’s God to protect his people and their land (see Isa 36.19–20; Isa 37.12; Eze 36.19–26).
This final trial speech reviews the arguments of chs Isa 40.1–48 and announces the final conclusion.
chosen Cyrus (literally him) as his ally: See Isa 44.28; Isa 45.1–2.
I will send him and will help him succeed: Cyrus would humiliate Babylon and liberate Israel (Isa 45.1–4).

I have told you plainly: God’s promises are clear, though not always specific as to manner and time. • now the Sovereign LORD and his Spirit have sent me with this message: The identity of the one who is sent is unclear. Isaiah might be referring to himself as a Spirit-inspired prophet who spoke the very words of God to Israel. The connection with the Spirit suggests that it refers to the promised servant, the Messiah. • The presence of the Spirit assures the servant’s success.

Peace and righteousness will be established when the Kingdom of God comes in its fullness (see Isa 66.12). • like a gentle river . . . like waves: An abundance of comforting peace and overflowing resources of righteousness (cp. Amo 5.24) could have been Israel’s if its people had only listened to God.
Your descendants . . . like the sands: This would fulfill God’s covenant to Abraham (Gen 22.17); by contrast, the Israelites were nearly wiped out in the Exile (see Isa 44.26).
Leave Babylon: See also Isa 52.11–12; Isa 55.12.
not thirsty . . . rock . . . water gushed: These reminders of God’s provision in the Exodus provide a fitting summary of what he would do to rescue Israel from captivity in Babylon (see Num 20.11).
This refrain, no peace for the wicked (also Isa 57.21), continues the sharp divide between the godly and the wicked (see Isa 66.24). Peace speaks of God’s kingdom, from which the wicked are excluded.

God intended to rescue the Israelites from exile. However, the question remained: How could sinful Israel again become the servant of the Holy One? God would make a way for Israel’s sin to be atoned for and their fellowship with him to be restored. That way would be the promised servant, who would come for Israel and for all peoples. This servant was introduced in Isa 42.1–9, but in this passage he becomes the central focus.

This has traditionally been regarded as the second of four suffering servant songs (see study note on Isa 42.1–4). The suffering role of the promised servant becomes increasingly clear (see also Isa 50.4–9; Isa 52.13–Isa 53.12).

distant lands: The servant’s ministry would extend beyond Israel (see Isa 42.4, Isa 42.10, Isa 42.12; Isa 51.5; Isa 60.9; Isa 66.19). • called me before my birth . . . from within the womb . . . by name: The promised servant’s prophetic call was similar to the call of Jeremiah (see Jer 1.5; see also Gal 1.15). It was not a general call but a very specific, personal one (see also Isa 43.1; Isa 45.3–4).
Theme: God’s Servant
my words of judgment: The servant’s mission would be prophetic (see Isa 11.4; Eph 6.17; Heb 4.12; Rev 1.16; Rev 2.12, Rev 2.16; Rev 19.15).

The suffering servant would come out of Israel (see Isa 41.8) and would himself be the true Israel. He would serve as both king (Isa 42.1) and prophet (Isa 49.1), anointed with the Spirit of God (Isa 61.1) and commissioned (Isa 48.16) as a faithful witness to God’s purposes (Isa 43.12; Isa 48.20). In his mission toward both Israel and the other nations (Isa 49.6), he would suffer rejection and disgrace while being faithful, unlike the nation of Israel (see Isa 50.4–9). His suffering would be on behalf of God’s chosen people. Jesus became the ultimate fulfillment of the suffering servant (see study note on Isa 52.13–Isa 53.12).

my work seems so useless . . . to no purpose: Even though people stubbornly refuse his message, the servant would reach out to them. • I will trust God: Despite discouragement and suffering, the servant would continue to discharge his duty faithfully, trusting God for the outcome. God promised to reward the servant’s faithfulness (see also Isa 40.10; Isa 50.8).

a light to the Gentiles: As the Messiah, the servant’s mission would have a worldwide reach (see Isa 11.10, Isa 11.12; Isa 42.6). The apostle Paul explained his apostolic mission to the Gentiles on the basis of this prophecy (Act 13.47; Act 26.23).

The promised servant would be despised and rejected by the nations (see Isa 52.14–Isa 53.5) as well as by his own people (see also Isa 50.6–7; Isa 53.8–9). • Kings and princes will also bow low to express respect and humility before the servant (see also Isa 52.15), whom God will exalt after he has suffered. God is faithful to his servant.

God acts at just the right time to accomplish his purposes (Act 1.7; 2Co 6.2). Israel returned to reestablish the land of Israel after the Exile. The land was restored and the city rebuilt beginning with Cyrus’s edict (Isa 44.26–28).

Like a shepherd, the Lord in his mercy will lead the returning exiles beside cool waters; he promised to comfort them and tend to their needs (see also Isa 40.11; Psa 23.1). • level paths . . . highways: The Lord would open up the way of salvation.
The remnant would come from the north (i.e., from Babylon and Persia), from the west by sea, and from as far south as Egypt.
This hymn of praise is in response to the salvation that the servant would make possible.

Although the prophet announced cause for rejoicing (Isa 49.8–13), the exiles continued to ponder the calamity that came upon them when Babylon invaded the land, destroyed Jerusalem, and carried the people of Judah into exile where they felt deserted and forgotten.
like jewels or bridal ornaments: As a wedding calls for festivity and public display, so God’s restoration of Israel would be an open act for all to see (see also Isa 61.10).

The population explosion would reach beyond Israel to include the members of foreign nations who turn to the Lord (see Isa 56.6–8; Rev 7.9). • more room: The expanded population would require space far beyond the traditional boundaries of the land of Israel (see also Zec 2.4).

carry your little sons . . . your daughters: The mighty rulers of the nations, some of whom had previously killed children in Israel, would aid in their return to Zion (see also Isa 60.3–9). Elsewhere Isaiah envisioned people of foreign nations streaming to Zion to worship the Lord (see Isa 2.2–4).

you will know that I am the LORD: The stunning role-reversal—kings and queens serving the lowly exiles upon their return—would reveal God’s power to do the unimaginable (see also Isa 60.16). • The godly would experience temporary disgrace in the Exile but would not ultimately be put to shame, as the idolaters and ungodly were.
Who can snatch . . . Who can demand: The people considered it nearly impossible that they would be rescued from their oppressors.
The Lord is like a warrior who will fight to protect his children, as promised to Abraham (Gen 12.3; see also Isa 54.15).
This disputation shows that God was not forced to give Israel up, and therefore he could take the nation back as his people if he desired.

God was not at fault for the people’s problems; it was their sin that brought about their exile (see also Isa 59.1–15). • Jerusalem—the mother city of Judah (Psa 87.5–6)—was destroyed, and the people of Judah were taken into exile in 586 BC.

Why didn’t anyone answer: The people had not responded to God’s repeated call to trust in him and repent of their sins. They were deaf and stubborn (see Isa 6.9–10; Isa 29.18; Isa 35.5; Isa 42.18–19). • The Lord came and called the people through the prophets (see also Isa 65.1–3). • Is it because I have no power to rescue? God was fully able to rescue Israel and Judah from the Assyrians and Babylonians, but he first had to deal justly with his people’s sinfulness (see Isa 59.1). • speak to the sea and make it dry: This was an allusion to the parting of the Red Sea during the exodus from Egypt (Exo 14.21–22).

Phenomena such as darkness and the wearing of clothes of mourning were associated with the day of the Lord (Isa 13.10; see study note on Isa 2.5–22). The mention of darkness might allude to the plague of darkness in Egypt (Exo 10.21).
This is the third of four servant songs (see study note on Isa 42.1–4). The faithful and suffering servant portrays an ideal Israel; the image was realized in Jesus Christ.
The Lord, who never grows weary (Isa 40.28), sends the servant with good news (see Isa 40.28–31) to comfort those who are weary (see study note on Isa 40.1–31).

beat me . . . pulled out my beard . . . mockery and spitting: These connections with the experience of Jesus at his crucifixion are too close to be coincidental—Jesus is the true suffering servant (see Mat 27.27–31).

Externally, the servant would be disgraced and put to shame, but within himself he would calmly await God’s vindication (see Isa 29.22; Isa 54.4; Isa 61.7). • set my face like a stone: The servant would be determined to do God’s will (see Luk 9.51).

He who gives me justice is near: God vindicates those who suffer for doing his will. Vindication is an act of God by which he exalts those who have been wrongly disgraced and strikes down the wicked, self-exalted, and arrogant (see also 2Th 1.6–9). • bring charges . . . my accusers: Confidence in God’s vindication removes fear and bolsters faith (see Rom 8.31–34).
Who will declare me guilty? The implied answer to this rhetorical question is, “No one!” This answer foreshadows the New Testament understanding of justification (see Rom 8.31–35).
This is a call for response to the servant’s ministry.

The test of whether or not an individual fears the LORD is how he or she responds to God’s righteous servant. The same idea is present in Jesus’ claim that no one can come to the Father except through him (Joh 14.6). • Those who trust in the LORD have great hope for the future (see Isa 12.2).
warm yourselves by your own fires: Spiritually complacent people are unresponsive toward God. Though they have comfort and security now, they will soon fall down in great torment (see Isa 66.24).
This prophecy calls for trust in the Lord. Each of its three units begins with the phrase, Listen to me (Isa 51.1, Isa 51.4, Isa 51.7).
The rock and the quarry represent Abraham and Sarah (Isa 51.2).
Abraham . . . became a great nation: The exiled community had decreased in number. They needed to have faith that God could restore them again to a healthy and thriving population.
Eden . . . the garden of the LORD: God’s salvation will one day reestablish conditions like those in which human beings first lived (see Gen 2.1–3).

my law . . . my justice: The work of the servant will prosper because justice will be the rule in God’s kingdom on earth (see Isa 42.1–4). • a light to the nations: The nations will receive the Lord and his revelation (see also Isa 42.6; Isa 49.6; Isa 60.1–3; Isa 66.19–23; Mat 4.15–16; Luk 2.32; Joh 1.4–9; Joh 12.35–50; Act 13.47).
God is strong enough to crush his enemies and rescue his people, such as when he rescued Israel in the Exodus (see Isa 51.9; Exo 6.6; Exo 15.16).
die like flies: The wicked will die in great multitudes on the day of God’s judgment.

cherish my law in your hearts: Beyond simply knowing God’s word, the Lord desires for his people to internalize, treasure, and obey it (see also Psa 37.31; Jer 31.33). • Those who obey the Lord often endure scorn and insults (see also Mat 5.10–12).

Wake up, wake up: God does not sleep; this prayer is for God to act immediately to save his people (see Isa 52.1; see especially God’s military garb in Isa 59.17). • in the days of old: The exodus from Egypt was an act of redemption that displayed God’s power as he made a path of escape (Isa 51.10) for his people (see also Isa 11.15).
you have forgotten the LORD: The Lord will never forget Israel (see Isa 44.21; Isa 49.15), so they should not forget him. • The Creator of the world also created the nation Israel.
The Exile brought such brutal conditions as imprisonment, starvation, and death.
I am the LORD: The Lord uses this formula to identify himself as the covenant God and to assure his people of the truth of his word and the reliability of his actions (see Isa 27.3–4).
my words in your mouth: The focus shifted back to the servant. • You are my people: Israel was the covenant community.
The prophet called the people of Israel to be done with their past and to anticipate God’s future for them.

Wake up, wake up: Israel used these words in a prayer to the Lord (Isa 51.9). Israel’s problems were not the result of God’s slowness to act; rather, the people were slow to believe God’s promises. • the cup of the LORD’s fury: The Lord will appropriately measure out his judgment; those who fall under his judgment must figuratively drink from his wrath (see also Mat 26.39).
children have fainted: A sad commentary on Jerusalem’s desolation is provided in Lam 1.13, Lam 1.22; Lam 2.11–12, Lam 2.19.
God would be the Defender of Israel as he was when Assyria besieged Jerusalem (Isa 38.6).
The tormentors were the Babylonians who brought about destruction, war, and famine (Isa 51.19).

This second call to wake up (see Isa 51.17) was in preparation for a glorious future. • holy city: The new city would be holy because its citizens would be holy (see Isa 4.3). • enter your gates no longer: Things that are unclean will not be permitted to enter the holy city (see Rev 21.27).

I sold you into exile . . . Now I can redeem you: The Lord was fully in control when he gave his people into the hands of their enemies. Likewise, he remained fully in control and could redeem them if he chose to do so.
in Egypt . . . oppressed by Assyria: The exodus from exile would be like Israel’s past exodus from Egypt.

The oppressors would shout in exultation because they believed they had conquered not only Israel but also its God. • My name is blasphemed all day long: The condition of God’s people affects God’s reputation in the eyes of the watching world (see Isa 37.6, Isa 37.23; Isa 48.11).
Just as God did to Moses before the Exodus (Exo 3.15), he will reveal himself in the coming rescue from exile.

This is a poetic description of God’s promise to rescue his people from the alienation their sin created. The imagery is of a besieged city waiting for word that its hero has defeated the enemy armies. Paul applies these words to the proclamation of the Good News of the Lord Jesus (Rom 10.15).

How beautiful on the mountains: See Nah 1.15; Rom 10.15. • The good news goes beyond proclaiming an end to the Exile; it also points to the peace and salvation of the age to come (Isa 54.13–14; see Isa 40.9–10; Isa 41.27).
The watchmen were those looking for the news of Zion’s redemption. • the LORD returning to Jerusalem: The sin of the city’s inhabitants had driven God away.

victory of our God: The rescue of God’s people from disgrace foreshadows an even greater victory when God will reign victoriously to the ends of the earth (note the many similarities with Psa 98.1–3).
This is an exhortation to leave the captivity of sin (see Isa 48.20 on leaving physical captivity in Babylon). See also 2Co 6.17; 2Ti 2.19.
Here the imagery of leaving the unclean enemy city encourages the people to purify themselves by turning away from all known sin. Those who carry home the sacred objects of the LORD need to be pure.
Theme: The Promise of a Second Exodus

not leave in a hurry: At the time of the Exodus the people had to leave quickly (see Exo 12.11, Exo 12.31–36). Isaiah drew this contrast to emphasize the newness of God’s plan. • protect you from behind: See Exo 13.21; Exo 14.19–20.

This is the fourth of four passages that speak about the promised servant (see study note on Isa 42.1–4). The Hebrew poem is carefully constructed in five three-line stanzas. It begins with the servant’s exaltation (Isa 52.13), proceeds to his humiliation (Isa 52.14–Isa 53.9), and ends with his exaltation (Isa 53.10–12). The faithful servant’s suffering would bring reconciliation between God and humans. The Lord Jesus perfectly fulfilled this prophecy (see ch Isa 40.1–31; Mat 8.17; Act 8.30–35; Rom 10.15–17; Rom 15.21; 1Pe 2.24–25).
prosper . . . be highly exalted: The servant would be wise and successful, set apart with the great and noble. Similar terms describe God in Isa 6.1 and Isa 57.15.
Despite the servant’s greatness, the actual way he would appear on earth would shock people.
were amazed: No one expected that the rescuer would suffer and die.

startle many nations: They would be amazed that a rescuer would appear so weak and helpless and would stand speechless. • What they will see and what they will understand will be in complete contrast to anything they had previously imagined.

our message: The identity of the speaker has been debated—the main possibilities are (1) a faithful remnant of Israel, and (2) Isaiah himself. Most likely, Isaiah the prophet was speaking for and with Israel. • powerful arm: God’s strength, so dramatically described in the previous chapters (see Isa 50.2; Isa 51.5, Isa 51.9; Isa 52.10), would actually manifest itself in weakness and apparent helplessness through the servant’s humiliation and exaltation (see 1Co 1.27–30).

a tender green shoot . . . in dry ground: Such a plant is vulnerable to extinction (cp. Isa 37.27). It can hardly stay alive for itself, let alone provide anything for anyone else. • nothing beautiful or majestic: The servant appeared to have no greatness or self-evident royal splendor (see Isa 52.13–15). • nothing to attract us to him: People like their leaders to be physically attractive and personally charismatic. The servant would be neither.

a man of sorrows, acquainted with deepest grief (or a man of pains, acquainted with illness): The servant would fully experience the effects of sin and the Fall. • we did not care: Because people would fail to see how such a weak, insignificant person could do anything beneficial for them, they would be unconcerned about his suffering.

The callous world would assume that the servant somehow brought his suffering on himself, never realizing that he was suffering for them. • troubles . . . punishment: These descriptions of the servant’s humiliation contrast with the descriptions of his exaltation.

he was pierced: See also Zec 12.10. • crushed . . . beaten . . . whipped: These were typically punishments for crimes. Sin is a crime against God. • be whole: Hebrew shalom, usually translated “peace.” Shalom means to experience wholeness in body, in mind, and in relationships with others. The servant would be injured so that humanity can be whole and healthy in all aspects of life (see also Isa 57.18). We do not need to suffer divine condemnation for our sins because the servant has already done so (see Gal 1.4).
strayed away . . . left God’s paths: These are metaphors for sin (see also Rom 3.10–18).
The Ethiopian eunuch was reading this passage when Philip met him (Act 8.32–33).
See 1Pe 2.21–25 for the fulfillment of this prophecy in Jesus Christ.
Unjustly condemned: The servant will be given no legal protection or proper defense. • cut short in midstream: To die in midlife was understood to be God’s judgment.

no wrong . . . never deceived anyone: See 1Pe 2.21–25. • in a rich man’s grave: Literally he was with the rich in his death (see Mat 27.57–61). Although the Bible often considers riches as a blessing from God, it regularly condemns the rich as crooked and oppressive. The point here might be ironic: This good man would be buried with oppressors.
The final stanza of the poem first explains why the servant suffered and was treated unjustly in the place of others; it then explains what the result of that obedience would be.

The servant’s grief would accomplish a greater good; the forgiveness and reconciliation of sinful humanity. Note also God’s good plan to prosper and exalt the servant. • when his life is made an offering for sin: The suffering of the servant provided a substitute for others, just as the animal sacrifices in the Temple did. • Having many descendants and enjoying a long life are rewards for godly and wise living (see Pro 3.2; Pro 17.6; Pro 20.7). Because the servant left his fate in his God’s hands, he would receive eternal rewards from the God who vindicates the righteous (see Phi 2.9–11).

his experience (literally his knowledge): This clearly does not refer to intellectual knowledge but to all that the servant would experience in his obedience, suffering, and intimate relationship with God. • The servant’s righteous obedience enables people to be put right with God (see Gen 15.6; Rom 5.18–19), for he will bear all their sins.

the honors: See Phi 2.9–11. • He was counted among the rebels: Rebels (Hebrew poshe‘im) is a stronger word than sinners and is a key word in Isaiah. It refers to those who are in willful defiance of a lawful authority, in this case, God. • interceded for rebels: The servant would pray for sinners in the midst of his suffering (see Exo 32.30; Luk 23.34).
This is an invitation to participate in the restoration to God’s favor made possible through the ministry of the promised servant.

Salvation flows from the vindication of the suffering servant. The promises mentioned here go beyond the return from Babylonian exile and apply to the coming of Jesus Christ, the extension of the kingdom to the church, the benefits of the second coming of Jesus Christ as the bridegroom of the church, and the new Jerusalem.
The prophet encourages Jerusalem, likened to a barren woman, to rejoice because its fate was rapidly changing. She would have so many children that she would outgrow her home (see Gal 4.27).

In the ancient world, a woman who had never given birth after being married for a time would be ashamed. Isaiah compares Jerusalem to a barren woman who rejoices at the long-awaited blessing of children (see Gal 4.27).

Israel’s descendants (cp. Isa 53.10) would occupy other nations in fulfillment of God’s promise to Abraham (Gen 22.17) and to Jacob (Gen 28.14). • As desolation took place (Isa 6.11; Isa 14.21), the people of God would inherit the earth and resettle the ruined cities (Isa 51.6; Isa 52.10; Isa 65.17; see also Mat 5.5; Rom 4.13).

Creator . . . husband: The Lord committed himself to the abandoned woman (his people in exile) as her maker (Isa 44.24) and husband (see also Isa 62.4–5; Hos 2.19–20). • The Redeemer transforms misery into freedom and fulfillment (see also Isa 41.14).

The pain of separation would be brief compared to the depth of the renewal of love and compassion. • The Lord abandoned Israel in exile for a little while because of the people’s sins. • everlasting love: The Lord is eternally committed to his people, making the seventy-year punishment of exile seem short indeed (see Isa 25.1; Hos 2.1).

The Exile was similar in both drama and trauma to the flood in the time of Noah. In both instances, people sinned grievously against the Lord, but the Lord renewed his commitment to creation (after Noah’s flood) and to his people (after the Exile).

God’s faithful love for his people endures despite their unfaithfulness. • God’s covenant of blessing was the assurance of his presence, resulting in wholeness, blessing, and protection. It replaces the shame and disgrace of the Exile (see Eze 34.25; Eze 37.26).

This is a vision of the renewed Jerusalem as a city under God’s protection, a place of peace and righteousness (see Isa 59.21–Isa 60.22). This section forms the background of John’s vision of the new Jerusalem (Rev 21.10–21).
The Lord himself would rebuild the city (see Heb 11.10). • Lapis lazuli is a semi-precious stone.
I will teach: Jesus alluded to this verse in Joh 6.45. • They will enjoy great peace, the benefits of God’s presence and protection (Isa 53.5; see Isa 48.17–18; Isa 54.10).
Jerusalem would again be a righteous city, secure under a government that is just and fair (see Isa 1.26).
God gives assurance that no nation can defeat his people . The Lord has promised to protect them, just as he had promised Abraham (Gen 12.3; see Isa 49.25).

no weapon . . . will succeed . . . accuse you . . . vindication: God will protect his people in war and in the courtroom. • These benefits are enjoyed by the servants of the LORD: Only the true children of God—people who come out of Israel and the nations—will enjoy the promised blessings of the age to come that God establishes.
This final chapter of the prophecies of comfort (chs Isa 40.1–55) summarizes the section’s prominent themes: blessing, covenant, witness, word, nations, glory, forgiveness, and joy.

thirsty . . . wine or milk: The invitation to eat and drink is similar to Wisdom’s call in Pro 9.5. The image promises the slaking of thirst not only by water but also by more costly items such as wine and milk. John applied a similar theme to Jesus Christ (Joh 4.14; Joh 6.27, Joh 6.35; Joh 7.37; Rev 21.6; Rev 22.17). • it’s all free: Reconciliation with God is for anyone and has no cost.
Listen to me . . . eat what is good: Responding positively to God satisfies one’s spiritual, social, and physical being (see Isa 1.19; Isa 58.13–14; Pro 4.10).

Come to me. . . . Listen . . . find life: Those who respond obediently to God’s word find eternal life (see also Isa 55.11). • an everlasting covenant . . . I promised to David: King David received a special covenant from God, a promise to preserve his kingly line (see 2Sa 7.15–16). David’s dynasty was eternally confirmed in the kingship of the Messiah, Jesus Christ (see Isa 9.6–7; Isa 11.1–16; Act 2.22–36; Act 13.34).
The prophet calls for a response while the time is right.

while you can find him: When God graciously extends an invitation to salvation, people must respond (Isa 65.1; Jer 29.13–14; Hos 5.6; Hos 10.12). Those who do not seek him at such times risk never having the opportunity again.

Let the wicked change . . . turn to the LORD: True conversion demands a change of how we live in favor of God’s requirements (see Isa 1.16–17; Isa 30.15; Isa 59.20). • have mercy on them: God’s compassion reaches out to the needy and finds them where they are. • he will forgive generously: Forgiveness of sin is foundational to the good news of redemption (see Eph 1.7; Col 1.14; see also Psa 32.1; Psa 86.5; Psa 99.8; Psa 103.2–5).

My thoughts are nothing like your thoughts: God’s plans are marvelous (Psa 92.5; cp. Psa 94.11). God’s creatures, including humans, can never fully understand the Creator’s thoughts, but his revelation through his messengers gives great insight and knowledge of some of the things he will do.

The Creator not only sends rain and snow but also his word (Hebrew dabar). In this context, dabar means his will or plan (see Isa 14.24; Isa 40.8). God’s written word, as an expression of God’s plan, accomplishes his purposes. God is effective in whatever he does (see Isa 14.26–27; Isa 46.10).
The prophet encourages his people to forget the past, to leave Babylon, and to accept the perspective of the coming age.

Joy is found in being redeemed from bondage. • Godly people experience an inner peace not known to the wicked (Isa 48.22). • mountains and hills . . . trees of the field: Creation participates in the freedom of the children of God (Isa 44.23; Isa 49.11, Isa 49.13; see Rom 8.19–23).

Redemption is like the transformation from desert to forest (see also Isa 35.1; Isa 41.19; Isa 60.13). • great honor to the LORD’s name: God’s glory will be more and more visible to humanity as his redemption takes effect.

This last major division of the book of Isaiah brings together themes from chs Isa 1.1–39 (sin, justice and righteousness, responsibility, vengeance and vindication) and chs Isa 40.1–55 (salvation, the age to come).
This section summarizes chs Isa 1.1–55 with an invitation to the outcasts to participate in God’s redemption.

Be just and fair: A key aspect of the message of chs Isa 1.1–39 is the call for justice in relationship with others and God. True godliness comes only through having character that is shaped by the character of God, which only happens by understanding and consistently applying God’s word. • I am coming soon: This statement summarizes the message of chs Isa 40.1–55, that the Lord is creating a world of harmony, peace, restoration, vindication, and the removal of enemies (Isa 46.13).

Blessed: Cp. Isa 30.18; Isa 32.20; see also Psa 1.1; Psa 119.1; Mat 5.3. • The Sabbath, as a sign of the covenant (Exo 31.13–17), is God’s gift to his people; it belongs to this age as well as to the age to come (Isa 56.4, Isa 56.6; Isa 58.13–14; see Heb 4.1–13).
The blessing (Isa 56.2) would extend to eunuchs and to the Gentiles.

Foreigners who commit themselves to the LORD would become full participants in the covenant community. Previously, their participation had been carefully regulated (Deu 23.3, Deu 23.7–8). • eunuchs: In the past, an emasculated person was excluded from the community (Deu 23.1). Both eunuchs and foreigners had no share in Israel’s holiness and were considered marginal to God’s kingdom. In the age to come, God would bring to the center those who had previously been marginalized (cp. Mat 20.16).
The Sabbath is a sign of the covenant (Exo 31.13–17).

within the walls of my house: Those previously excluded would have a place in God’s presence. • a memorial and a name: Everlasting existence in God’s presence is better than the blessing of physical descendants.
The essential ingredient for covenant fellowship is love for God (Deu 6.5; Deu 30.20; Mat 22.34–38). • Keeping the Sabbath is a sign of keeping the covenant itself (see Exo 31.13–17).

burnt offerings and sacrifices: God had previously rejected sinful Israel’s expressions of piety (Isa 1.11–13) but would welcome offerings from righteous Gentiles or foreigners. Nationality is worth little without true piety. • a house of prayer for all nations: The Lord would open the doors of the Temple to all nations (see Isa 2.2–4). Jesus rebuked the people for desecrating the Temple and for preventing it from functioning as the house of prayer (Mat 21.13; Mar 11.17).
The outcasts of Israel were those dispersed among the nations as the result of the Exile (see also Isa 11.12). • The others would be eunuchs and Gentiles (Isa 56.3–7; see also Isa 57.19; Joh 10.16).
This is a reflection on the prevalence of evil among God’s people; they were greedy (Isa 56.9–12), hostile to the righteous (Isa 57.1–2), and idolatrous (Isa 57.3–13).
Wild animals are here a metaphor for the hostile nations surrounding Judah.
The leaders of Israel failed to guide and protect God’s people from the sins that led to the Exile. • sleeping and dreaming: See Isa 29.10.

ignorant shepherds: Israel’s leaders did not know how to rule in a godly way (see also Eze 34.1–6). By contrast, the Lord is the faithful Shepherd of his people (Isa 40.11). • all following their own path: They had no concern for God or his standards of godly leadership (see also Isa 53.6). • personal gain: Cp. Isa 33.15.
This is a lament for the righteous who suffer in a wicked society.
