Those controlled by Satan immediately recognized Jesus’ true identity as the Son of God (see Mar 1.24) and answered the question asked by Jesus’ disciples when he had calmed the storm (Mat 8.27). Elsewhere, Jesus’ true nature and identity are acknowledged by the Father (Mat 3.17; Mat 17.5), Satan (Mat 4.3, Mat 4.6), humans (Mat 14.33; Mat 16.16; Mat 27.54), and Christ himself (Mat 11.27; Mat 24.36; Mat 28.19). • God’s appointed time is the final, eternal damnation of all who oppose God (see Jud 1.6; Rev 20.10).
The demons were no match for Jesus’ authority; they desperately begged to avoid imminent doom.
Jesus’ word had sufficient authority to expel demons. • drowned: Jesus had begun to defeat the enemy (Mat 12.28; Luk 10.17–20; Rom 16.20; Col 2.15).
The tragedy of the incident is that those who witnessed the Son of God’s power to give salvation feared having their world upset, so they rejected him.
Controversy ensued among Jesus’ opponents, the teachers of religious law and Pharisees (Mat 9.1–13), and among the disciples of John the Baptist (Mat 9.14–17).
His own town was Capernaum (Mar 2.1), where he apparently relocated from Nazareth after being rejected there (Mat 4.13; Luk 4.16–31).

Does he think he’s God? God alone could forgive sins (Psa 103.3; Isa 43.25; Jer 50.20). The teachers of religious law failed to comprehend Jesus’ mission as God’s incarnate Son (Mat 3.17; Mat 11.25–27). As God’s Messiah (Mat 1.1; Mat 11.2–6), he was saving mankind (Mat 8.17; Mat 26.26–28).

It is easier for Jesus to pronounce forgiveness, since that might have no verifiable effects; it is harder to enable a paralytic to walk. The miracle, visible to all, corroborates Jesus’ authority to forgive sins and forces all who witness it to decide about Jesus.
So I will prove: Jesus performed the miracle to reveal his authority and identity as God’s Messiah (see Mat 11.2–6; Mat 12.28).
The mixture of fear and praise in the crowd’s response corresponds to the awesome truth they perceived about Jesus. He is indeed the Son of God who has authority on earth to forgive sins (Mat 9.6).
Jesus, as Lord and Messiah, tore down the barriers that prevented righteous Jews from intermingling with those who were unclean or sinful.
Matthew was also called Levi (Mar 2.14). Matthew might have had two names, or he might have been given a new name by Jesus.
Profile: Matthew (Levi)

The Jewish people despised Jewish tax collectors (Mat 5.46–47; Mat 18.15–20), who cooperated with Roman oppressors and were considered betrayers of the Israelite nation. Many also considered them unclean because of their frequent contact with Gentiles and because of the idolatrous images on Roman coins. Tax-collection was a private enterprise. In each district, Rome granted the right to collect taxes to the highest bidder (cp. Luk 19.1–10). Anything collected above the bid was profit for the collectors, who, driven by greed, often used extortion.
Theme: Eating Together

I want you to show mercy, not offer sacrifices: God’s desire is applied to the question of table fellowship with sinners; Jesus’ mercy in eating with sinners contrasts with the Pharisees’ separation from sinners (symbolized as sacrifices). • Jesus revealed the true spiritual condition of the Pharisees, who think they are righteous; they failed to recognize that they were in fact unrighteous and in need of the Messiah’s salvation. See Mat 7.1–5; Mat 8.11–12; Mat 19.30; Mat 20.16; Mat 21.43.

fast: Fasting expressed personal humility and repentance (2Sa 12.16–23; Dan 9.3). It called attention to the national need for repentance (Lev 16.29–31; Neh 9.1) and probably sought to hasten the arrival of the Messiah through purification. The fact that Jesus and his disciples did not fast (Mat 11.18–19) subtly proclaimed that the Messiah had already arrived (see also Mat 6.16).

wedding guests . . . groom: John the Baptist had also described the Messiah and his disciples in this way (Joh 3.29), drawing on Old Testament imagery to reveal Jesus’ status (see Mat 25.1–13; Isa 54.5–6). • taken away: This is Jesus’ first prediction of his violent death (see Mat 16.21; Mat 17.12, Mat 17.22–23; Mat 20.18–19; Mat 26.2, Mat 26.26–35; Isa 53.8). • then they will fast: Jesus may be referring to the disciples’ sorrow immediately after his crucifixion, or to the disciples’ lifestyle after his death and resurrection (see Act 9.9; Act 13.2–3; Act 14.23; Act 27.9, Act 27.33).

These riddle-like parables contrast the new covenant that Jesus has established (Mat 26.26–29) with the old covenant, especially in relation to such rituals as fasting. Jesus consummates, but does not abolish, the law (Mat 5.17–20; see Gal 2.21; Gal 5.4). Yet the new covenant requires new practices.
Jesus is the Messiah whose power knows no boundaries. He calls people to have faith in him.

lay your hand on her: The laying-on of hands is a visible symbol of prayer for God’s power to flow into someone, often resulting in new life or ministries (Mat 19.13; Num 27.18–23; Deu 34.9). • The man believed that Jesus had the power to raise the dead (cp. 1Ki 17.8–24; 2Ki 4.18–37).

The woman’s constant bleeding rendered her always ceremonially unclean and made whoever she touched unclean as well (Lev 15.25–30). But instead of rendering Jesus unclean, her touching him made her clean, a stunning reversal that illustrates Jesus’ power to redeem and sanctify (see Mat 14.36; Mar 3.10). • fringe: The tassels at the bottom of a tunic (Mat 23.5; Num 15.37–41) reminded Jews to live in accord with God’s law.
Your faith has made you well (literally has saved you): Physical healing demonstrated her spiritual salvation (see Mat 8.17).

noisy crowd . . . funeral music: Sorrow over the death of a family member was publicly expressed, with musical accompaniment and dirges by professional mourners. “Even the poorest in Israel should hire not less than two flutes and one wailing woman” (Mishnah Ketubbot Mat 4.4).
Though she was physically dead, from Jesus’ perspective the girl was just asleep—she would soon be raised back to life (see Isa 26.19; Joh 11.11–14, Joh 11.25; 1Th 4.14).

Eye diseases were common in the ancient world. Blindness was often considered to be divine punishment (see Exo 4.11; Deu 28.28; 2Ki 6.18; Joh 9.2–3). The Old Testament predicts that the Messiah’s coming would bring restoration of sight for the blind (Mat 11.4–5; Isa 29.18–19; Isa 35.5–6). • Son of David is a messianic title particularly associated with miraculous healings (see Mat 1.1; Mat 12.23; Mat 15.22; Mat 20.30–31; 2Sa 7.12–16).
Jesus intended his question to elicit confessions of faith from the two men.
The Messiah’s acts invoke faith, astonishment, and derisive rejection.
Enabling the deaf to hear and the mute to speak is a sign of the Kingdom of God (Mat 11.4–5; Isa 35.5–6).

Jesus here extends his ministry (shown in Mat 4.23–Mat 9.34) to others within Israel through his disciples (Mat 10.5–6). Jesus’ instructions to his disciples (Mat 10.5–42) focus on missionary activity and its consequent opposition and hardship.

This verse connects with the section begun at Mat 4.23. Matthew has presented Jesus to his readers as the Messiah who teaches, preaches, heals, casts out demons, and calls for a decisive response of faith.
Theme: Compassionate Healer

like sheep without a shepherd: Jesus lamented the Pharisees’ pastoral negligence (see Mat 12.11–12; Mat 18.12). Their attacks against Jesus were a clear indication of their hard-hearted rejection of God. The crowds languished due to pastoral neglect and mistreatment (Mat 10.5–6; Mat 15.12–14; Mat 23.4; Zec 11.16).

Harvest refers to the multitudes (see also Mat 13.24–30, Mat 13.36–43; Mar 4.26–29; Joh 4.35–38; Rev 14.15–20). • the Lord who is in charge of the harvest: All ministries are ultimately under God’s call (see Mat 23.8–10, Mat 23.13), so Jesus urges his disciples to pray for God himself to call more workers.

Jesus called his twelve disciples as workers in the harvest (Mat 9.37–38). The choice of twelve is not accidental—it recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus was appointing new leaders for the new people of God under his reign as Messiah (Mat 16.18–19; Mat 18.18; Mat 19.28; Mat 21.43). • gave them authority (Mat 9.6–8; Mat 28.18): Jesus enabled the Twelve to perform ministries that the Jewish leaders could not accomplish (Mat 9.32–34; Mat 10.5–8). The authority to cast out evil spirits (Mat 8.28) and to heal are ascribed to Jesus (Mat 4.23; Mat 8.1–Mat 9.35) in similar terms.

The four lists of the apostles (see also Mar 3.16–19; Luk 6.14–16; Act 1.13) are all different, although the differences are minimal. The order within each list varies slightly, but only the names Thaddaeus (Mat 10.3; Mar 3.18) and Judas son of James (Luk 6.16; Act 1.13) differ. They might be two names for the same man.

The apostles are ambassadors or messengers, authorized and sent by an authority to represent and accomplish prescribed tasks (see Mat 10.1–8, Mat 10.40; Mat 28.16–20). The term is also used for Paul (Gal 1.1). • first, Simon (also called Peter): Peter had priority in time (Mat 4.18–22; Mat 16.17–19) and position as the representative leader of the apostles (see Mat 19.27; Mat 26.33; Act 2.14).
Matthew (the tax collector) (see Mat 9.9) is also called Levi (Mar 2.14).

the zealot: Zealots were militant Jews who thought violence and war were capable of accomplishing the will of God. As a Jewish nationalist, Simon was probably zealous for the law (Act 22.3–5; Gal 1.14; Phi 3.6). Josephus blamed the Zealot party for the great war with Rome in AD 66–70. • Iscariot might refer to someone from Kerioth in southern Judea (Jos 15.25) or from Kerioth in Perea (Jer 48.24).

Don’t go to the Gentiles: Jesus’ mission was limited to Jews at this stage (Mat 15.24). Through the Jews, God would reach the Gentiles (Isa 2.2–4; Isa 42.6–7; Isa 49.6; Isa 60.3). • Jews regarded Samaritans as impure Jews (Luk 17.18) because of their intermarriage with Gentiles during and after the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles (2Ki 17.24–41). Tension was provoked in 128 BC when the Jewish leader John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (Josephus, Antiquities 13.9.1).
Being lost is the result of neglect by their shepherds (Mat 9.36; Mat 15.24).
By doing these things in the name and authority of Jesus, the apostles demonstrated Jesus’ status as Messiah (see Mat 11.2–6).
Give as freely as you have received! While remuneration is not improper (1Co 9.3–19; Gal 6.6; 1Ti 5.17), Jesus urged the apostles to avoid accusations of greed (see Act 8.20; Act 20.33).

Jesus’ disciples were to trust in God’s provision (Mat 6.11, Mat 6.25–34; Mat 7.7–11), to avoid greed that would give others the opportunity to defame the Lord’s name, and to encourage the newly formed communities to provide for their leaders’ needs (see 1Co 9.3–19).
give it your blessing: Greetings were more significant than a simple hello. Often, a greeting would convey a blessing for those who received it (cp. Rut 2.4).

A worthy home would embrace the message about Jesus and the Kingdom (Mat 10.37–38; Mat 22.8). • The disciples’ blessing was an offer of salvation; to take back the blessing was a sign of judgment as the offer was withdrawn.

shake its dust from your feet: This prophet-like gesture is explained by the Israelite custom of expressing displeasure with ungodliness by shaking off Gentile dust whenever crossing the border into Israel. The gesture signifies the disciples’ rejection of those who oppose God’s work (see Act 18.6). Pronouncing judgment on those who reject the message is part of proclaiming the Good News about the Kingdom (see Mat 11.20–24; Mat 13.10–15; Mat 23.37–39; Mat 24.1–36).

God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah for their wickedness (Gen 18.16–Mat 19.29). Now, with a more complete revelation in Jesus Christ, a town that rejected the disciples’ preaching would receive a more complete judgment. • such a town: An entire village or city is culpable when a significant majority rejects the message (see Act 13.45–47, Act 13.50–51; Act 14.1–7). However, individuals who respond in faith are saved (e.g., Lot; see Gen 19.1–29; 2Pe 2.6–9).

False leaders who prey upon people’s spiritual vulnerability rather than exercise appropriate pastoral care are often called wolves (Eze 22.27; Zep 3.3; cp. Pro 28.15). • be as shrewd as snakes and harmless as doves: The proverb calls for being astute but not deceitful.
As God gave Moses a spokesman in Aaron (Exo 4.10–17), so God would give Jesus’ disciples the right words at the right time through the Spirit (Joh 14.26; Act 4.8).

Jews regularly associated family strife with the last times (see Mat 24.9–10). Jesus experienced such conflicts as well (Mat 12.46–50). • Everyone who endures to the end refers to those who remain faithful to Jesus, to the point of death or until his return (Mat 10.23). • will be saved: Though some have taken this phrase to mean temporal deliverance from persecution (such as release from prison), the idea here is eternal salvation for those who remain faithful.

will return: Scholars are divided as to whether this refers to the second coming of Christ for his church or an earlier coming in judgment—namely, the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (see Mat 16.28). • before you have reached: Jesus meant either “before you have fled through all the towns” or “before you have evangelized all the towns.” The focus on persecution in the context (see Mat 10.17–39) favors the former, suggesting that the towns were like cities of refuge (Num 35.9–32). The emphasis is on how widespread the rejection of the message will be—i.e., “not until the whole nation has run you out of town.”

In Jesus’ day, Satan was often called prince of demons. The Greek term is Beelzeboul, from the name of an Old Testament pagan deity, Baal-zebul (“lord, the prince”). The Latin version reads Beelzebub, which is a transliteration of a Hebrew phrase meaning “lord of flies,” which was most likely a Jewish insult of Baal-zebul (see 2Ki 1.2).
Jesus’ disciples are to fear only God by obeying him and testifying of him; in contrast to human authorities, God’s authority and judgment are unlimited. • hell: See study note on Mat 5.29.
Because God cares about every sparrow, and because Jesus’ disciples are much more valuable, certainly the disciples need not fear—God will providentially care for them.

God accepts the one who acknowledges Jesus publicly in the context of trial and persecution (Mat 10.16–25). These verses pertain to a person’s pattern of life (see Mat 7.13–27) and not to a single confession or a single denial. For example, Judas acknowledged Jesus in individual instances yet was damned (Mat 26.23–24), whereas Peter denied Jesus (see Mat 26.69–75) yet was saved.
Allegiance to Jesus has priority over allegiance to family.

Jesus did bring peace (Joh 14.27), but not of a social and political kind. Instead, Jesus calls humans to make a decision about him, which brings a sword—i.e., division (see Mat 8.21–22; Mat 12.46–50; Luk 12.51).

The cross was a Roman instrument of torture and execution (Mat 27.27–55). To take up your cross and follow Jesus involves loving him above all other things and being willing to follow him regardless of the physical or social consequences.

The same reward as a prophet (literally A prophet’s reward) means either the same reward a prophet would receive or the benefit of the prophet’s ministry. • Righteous people are those who conform their behavior to God’s law as taught by both John the Baptist (Mat 21.32) and Jesus (see Mat 3.15), and therefore are approved by God (Mat 13.43, Mat 13.49; Mat 25.37–46).
The least of my followers probably refers to the low social standing of most of Jesus’ followers (cp. Mat 5.3; Mat 18.1–5 and Mat 6.5; Mat 23.5–12).

This section highlights the two primary responses to Jesus: acceptance and rejection. The first section (Mat 11.2–Mat 12.50) features the rejection of Jesus by Jewish leaders while his disciples were learning to understand and accept him.

This section begins with John the Baptist’s doubt, but it ends by exalting his faith and ministry (Mat 11.7–19). The people’s rejection of John (Mat 11.16–19) foreshadows their later rejection of Jesus.

John was arrested (Mat 4.12) by Herod Antipas because he had denounced Herod’s immoral relationship with Herodias, his half-brother’s wife (Mat 14.1–12). • the things the Messiah was doing: These actions demonstrated that he is the Messiah (Mat 8.1–Mat 9.34).
Jesus’ miracles of compassion inaugurated the Kingdom of God (Mat 12.28; see Isa 29.18–19; Isa 35.5–6; Isa 61.1). Jesus expected John to understand that he was fulfilling Old Testament expectations.

who do not fall away because of me: The works listed in Mat 11.5 were intended to drive John and his disciples to a decision regarding Jesus. Jesus was aware, however, that certain unexpected elements of his ministry would cause some to reject him.
a weak reed, swayed by every breath of wind: An unstable person. The implied answer to Jesus’ rhetorical question is no.
John the Baptist was the greatest person ever to have lived. Yet the least of Jesus’ followers are greater than John because they live in the new covenant of salvation through Christ (see Mat 4.17).

the Kingdom of Heaven has been forcefully advancing: Or the Kingdom of Heaven has suffered from violence. These alternatives reflect either a positive or negative nuance of the Greek verb. In Luk 16.16, a different verb (“preached”) makes it a clearly positive statement. • violent people are attacking it: This phrase may also have a positive or negative sense. If negative, it might refer to those who imprisoned John (see Mat 11.2; Mat 14.1–12), and attacking might mean either that they were trying to attack the Kingdom but were unable to thwart God’s sovereign plans, or that they were attacking it by persecuting its members. In Luk 16.16 this statement has the positive sense that they were “eager to get in” and were forcefully laying claim to the Kingdom through radical trust and obedience.
Elijah, the one the prophets said would come: John is the fulfillment of Old Testament expectations of Elijah’s return (Mat 17.10–13; see Mal 4.5).

John’s prophetic message is represented by funeral songs—he didn’t drink wine and he often fasted (Mat 11.18; see Mat 3.4). Jesus’ message is seen in wedding songs and in feasts and drinks (see Mat 9.9–17). In both cases, this generation responds to God’s messenger with indifference and rejection.

Here Jesus describes the specific ways in which John and Jesus offended the present generation. John, who stayed in the wilderness and ate locusts and honey (Mat 3.1, Mat 3.4), was accused of being possessed by a demon; while Jesus, who ate and drank freely, was accused of being a rebellious son (see Deu 21.18–21).

The miracles Jesus performed confirmed him as Messiah (Mat 11.5–6) and demanded repentance (Mat 11.20). Rejecting the Messiah would result in terrible judgment because the evidence of Jesus’ identity was clear.

As Jesus moved through the villages of Galilee—from Korazin to Bethsaida to Capernaum—he gave the people a greater revelation of himself, with a correspondingly more severe judgment when they refused to listen. The severity is indicated by comparison with the pagan cities of Tyre (Isa 23.1–18; Eze 26.1–Mat 28.19), Sidon (Eze 28.20–23), and Sodom (Gen 18.22–Mat 19.29).
the place of the dead: Greek Hades, which corresponds to the Hebrew term Sheol (see study note on Ps Psa 6.5).
This passage focuses on the remnant who, despite the present generation’s overall rejection of the Messiah, willingly embrace him and follow his teachings.

those who think themselves wise and clever: The Pharisees and teachers of religious law thought their access to God was guaranteed through their knowledge and practice of the law. Jesus’ disciples were more childlike (see Mat 21.15–16).
Jesus was revealing his intimate relationship to the Father. Everything he said and did was rooted in this Father–Son unity (see Joh 10.14–15; Joh 14.6–7; Joh 15.23–24; Joh 16.15; Joh 17.25–26).

The heavy burdens were likely caused by the legal requirements of the teachers of religious law and Pharisees (see Mat 23.4). • rest: Spiritual refreshment in either a present or a future sense (cp. Mat 1.21; Heb 4.8–11).

A yoke, which forms a harness between two animals, is a metaphor for the demands of discipleship. In contrast to the “yoke” of the religious leaders, Jesus’ yoke is easy and light, not because it is less demanding (see Mat 7.13–14), but because the power of the Messiah (by the Holy Spirit) makes it possible (see Act 15.10; 1Jo 5.3). The religious demands of Israel’s spiritual leaders (Mat 23.4; Act 15.10) included 613 Old Testament commands and their expansion through tradition. Jesus urged those who were suffering from the burdens of the Pharisees’ stipulations to come to him (Mat 11.28) in order to find the salvation their hearts desired. It is a call to salvation involving a life of obedience to Jesus’ new teachings. People are invited to enter a relationship with a humble and gentle teacher.

Matthew places Jesus’ offer of rest (Mat 11.28–30) in close connection with a discussion of the Sabbath. Jesus’ rest liberates people from human traditions concerning the Sabbath (cp. Heb 4.1–11). The Pharisees rejected Jesus because of their commitment to tradition.
This exchange highlights the Pharisees’ lack of compassion as they imposed a burdensome yoke (Mat 11.29–30).
The Sabbath, the seventh day of the week, was to be a day of complete rest according to Old Testament laws (Gen 2.2–3; Exo 20.8–11). The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (cp. Heb 4.1–11).
The Pharisees did not understand that the Sabbath was designed to benefit people. Their view of the Sabbath placed onerous burdens on people.
Ritual laws were at times rightly suspended for particular people or circumstances (1Sa 21.1–6).

Priests worked on the Sabbath (Lev 24.8–9; Num 28.9–10), and this was not offensive to Pharisees. If the priests’ work for the Temple on the Sabbath is allowed, then certainly Jesus can do the same because he is greater than the Temple (see Mat 4.23; Mat 9.35; Mat 11.2–6, Mat 11.20–30).
The Pharisees’ view of the Sabbath was unscriptural since it broke the deeper principle of mercy.
Jesus is superior to David, the priests, and the Temple. He reigns even over the Sabbath.
This second Sabbath controversy castigates the Pharisees for elevating regulations over human needs (see Mat 12.7, Mat 12.11–12).
their synagogue: A disunion was developing between Jesus and Judaism (also Mat 4.23).
Does the law permit: Rabbinic tradition permitted healing on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. Since life was not in jeopardy, the Pharisees thought healing was not permitted.
Their practice of rescuing animals but neglecting fellow humans was inconsistent.
This summary of Jesus’ ministry clarifies Jesus’ nature as the Messiah, the Servant of God who will bring salvation to the nations (see Isa 42.1–4).
This quotation parallels Jesus’ baptism (Mat 3.13–17). • Justice (or judgment) can have positive or negative implications; the context here favors a positive meaning (Mat 12.20; cp. Mat 23.23).
Instead of increasing people’s spiritual burden, Jesus offers compassionate forgiveness and sustenance (see Mat 11.28–30; Mat 12.1–14).
The Messiah was rejected by the Pharisees, the teachers of religious law, and his own generation.

Amazement was a common response to Jesus’ miracles (Mar 2.12; Mar 6.51; Luk 2.47; Luk 8.56; Luk 24.22). • Could it be: The question expected a negative answer: Jesus did not fit their expectations for the Messiah, but his miracles did prompt the question.
Satan: Greek Beelzeboul; see study note on Mat 10.25.
Jesus argued, in essence, “If I cast out demons under the influence of Satan, then Satan is dividing his camp, which obviously would be a foolish thing for Satan to do.”

what about your own exorcists (literally your sons): Jesus forced them to think consistently. If demons are cast out under Satan’s influence, then their disciples were equally guilty (see Act 19.13–16).

The Pharisees were being confronted with and were rejecting the Kingdom of God itself (see Luk 17.20–21; 1Jo 3.8). Jesus’ miracles brought the power of the Kingdom into the present reality; its ultimate consummation awaits Christ’s second coming.

This parable forced the Pharisees to answer a simple question: Can anyone cast out demons without first binding Satan’s powers and thus opposing him (see Isa 49.24–26; Isa 53.12)? • tie him up: Jesus overcame Satan first at his temptation (Mat 4.1–11), then throughout his ministry (see Luk 10.17–20), and ultimately on the cross (see Col 2.14–15).

In the face of the Pharisees’ accusations of Satanic influence, Jesus had just argued that he, the Messiah, cast out demons through the power of the Holy Spirit. In this context, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit can only mean attributing the ministry and exorcisms of Jesus to Satan’s power.

One may stumble over Jesus’ mysterious revelation of himself as Son of Man and be forgiven, but one cannot be forgiven for attributing the work of the Spirit to Satan. The present-day analogy is the outright rejection of the conviction of the Holy Spirit concerning Christ—that is, the ultimate rejection of the Good News by an unbeliever (cp. Heb 6.4–6; 1Jo 5.16–21).
Jesus got to the heart of the matter: The Pharisees did not accept him or the divine origin of his ministry because they were wicked (see Mat 7.15–27).
The idle word, in this context, was the accusation that Jesus had demonic inspiration. • What one says will acquit or condemn; one’s words reflect the true condition of the heart.

a miraculous sign to prove: A popular expectation of the Messiah, probably fueled by biblical accounts about Moses (Exo 4.1–9; see also Isa 7.11, Isa 7.14; Isa 38.7–8), was that the Messiah would display spectacular miracles on command (see Mat 16.1–4; Luk 23.8; Joh 2.18; Joh 4.48; Joh 6.30; Joh 7.31; Joh 9.16; Joh 11.47; 1Co 1.22).

To demand a sign demonstrates a lack of faith. • The sign of the prophet Jonah consisted of Jonah’s “resurrection” from the large fish after three days and three nights as well as his preaching (Mat 12.41; Luk 11.32); it was analogous to Jesus’ burial and resurrection and his preaching. Jesus was drawing a parallel between Jonah’s experience and what he himself would experience. He was not predicting an exact chronology of his death and resurrection. • Heart of the earth is a euphemism for the grave.

someone greater: Jesus is greater than the Temple (Mat 12.6), a prophet (Jonah), and a king (Solomon); therefore, rejection of him entails greater judgment on this “evil, adulterous generation” (Mat 12.39).
The queen of Sheba: See 1Ki 10.1–13.

The Messiah came in victory over demonic powers, but instead of repenting, the nation as a whole rejected the Messiah. Just as an exorcised demon will return if the house is not properly prepared against it, so judgment would come to this evil generation for rejecting the Messiah.
Demons were thought to prefer the arid desert (see Rev 18.2; cp. Isa 13.21; Isa 34.14).

Those who are true members in Jesus’ family do the will of the Father, as expressed in the commands of Jesus (see Mat 7.21). Obedience does not earn entrance into this family, but one cannot be considered a member if he or she is not obedient (see Mat 3.15; Mat 5.17–48; Mat 6.10, Mat 6.12; Mat 7.13–27; Mat 21.31).

In the third major discourse recorded by Matthew (see study note on Matt Mat 5.1–Mat 7.29), Jesus here recognized the separation of his followers from others (Mat 13.14, Mat 13.16) and began to reveal the secrets of the Kingdom privately to them through parables.

This parable (interpreted in Mat 13.18–23) addresses the mostly negative responses of the Jewish nation to Jesus and his message. • Parables (Greek parabolē) are stories that usually express an analogy between a common aspect of life and a spiritual truth. To understand a parable, it is necessary to locate the central analogy and understand it in its historical context and in the context of the Gospel text; then the central message can be understood. Speculative allegorical meanings that were not intended should not be found in every element of a parable.

From this point on, Jesus rarely taught the general public. Instead, he focused on teaching those who had committed themselves to him (Mat 13.1–Mat 20.34), though he would once again confront Israel (Mat 21.1–Mat 23.39). • The people were the unbelieving opponents mentioned again in Mat 13.11 (“others”) and Mat 13.12 (“those who are not listening”).
Jesus’ answer to the disciples’ question (Mat 13.10) was essentially that the people’s stubborn unbelief and rejection of Jesus had brought God’s condemnation.

You are permitted to understand: God had enabled the disciples to comprehend Jesus’ significance and to respond to his message of the Kingdom in faith and obedience (see Mat 13.19, Mat 13.23). • the secrets of the Kingdom of Heaven: Namely, that salvation is available to them in Jesus as the fulfillment of Old Testament promises.

Jesus told parables, and those who believed understood while those who had rejected Jesus found that his parables intensified their unbelief. • they don’t really see . . . listen or understand: They lacked the faith that perceives the truth (Mat 13.19, Mat 13.23) and acts upon it (Mar 8.18; Joh 12.40; see also Jer 5.21).
Like that of Isaiah, Jesus’ message has a dual effect: It judges people for unbelief and disobedience, and it creates a remnant of faithful ones who accomplish the Lord’s will (Mat 21.43).
Jesus brought into reality what the prophets and Old Testament saints desired to see and hear, that is, the fulfillment of Old Testament promises (see Isa 52.15; Joh 8.56; 1Pe 1.10).
don’t understand it: Responding to the message of the Kingdom is directly related to discerning its significance.
Theme: Jesus and Satan
don’t have deep roots . . . don’t last long: The problem is a lack of persevering faith and obedience (see Mat 7.13–27; Mat 10.22), particularly when persecution arises.

Jesus spoke of competing demands in life, (see also Mat 8.18–22). The worries of this life can become so great that they divert one from the path of faithful obedience (see Mat 6.19–34). The lure of wealth, particularly in its ability to deceive, appears often in Matthew (e.g., Mat 4.8–10; Mat 6.24; Mat 13.44–45). God does not desire that his people have wealth as much as that they have faith, obey him, and willingly help those in need (e.g., Mat 19.21; Mat 25.31–46).
produce a harvest: Probably a general reference to faithful obedience to Jesus’ commands (e.g., Mat 5.1–Mat 7.27; Mat 28.20).
This story is explained in Mat 13.36–43.

Weeds (or tares, bearded darnel) are almost indistinguishable from wheat and so were left until growth revealed their true nature. Malevolent contamination of crops in this manner was punishable by law.

Just as Jesus rebuked the sons of Zebedee for wanting to destroy unbelieving villages (Luk 9.54–55), he prohibited his followers from retaliating against enemies. Judgment is God’s work (see Mat 7.1–5). Jesus urges his followers to wait patiently for God’s righteous judgment (the harvest; see Luk 13.6–9).

Jesus used surprising, evocative imagery in these parables, either to emphasize the inevitable growth of the Kingdom through proclamation of the gospel or, more probably, to emphasize the contrast between insignificant beginnings and glorious consummation, and to exhort the disciples to patience (see also Mat 16.24–Mat 17.13).
Normally yeast refers to the influence of evil (e.g., Mat 16.6; 1Co 5.6; Gal 5.9); here, however, it is positive, speaking of the all-pervasive influence of the Kingdom.

Even Jesus’ manner of teaching fulfilled Old Testament predictions. Psa 78.2–3 speaks of passing down the history of God’s revelation to children of the next generation. Jesus’ revelation is the climax of that history (Mat 13.10–17; 1Co 2.7).

These verses are the interpretation of the parable told in Mat 13.24–30. The people of the Kingdom (wheat) coexist with nonmembers (weeds) in the world (field) until the end of history. The mystery of the Kingdom is that it is present in the world without weeding out the wicked in judgment; Jesus’ disciples must learn patience.

They went into the house (see Mat 13.1). Jesus taught in parables publicly, but the interpretations were reserved for his disciples in private. • Please explain: Though the disciples were privileged to know the mysteries of the Kingdom (Mat 13.11–17), they did not understand the parables until Jesus explained them.
The field is the world: The Kingdom includes all nations (Mat 28.16–20). • The people of the Kingdom are those who follow Jesus (Mat 13.11–17, Mat 13.23; Mat 21.43).
The harvest of judgment, which began with the first coming of the Son of Man (Mat 3.12), will be completed when he returns (Rev 14.14–16).
his Kingdom: Not until the “end of the world” (Mat 13.40) will the rule of the Son of Man be visible over all things.
The righteous do the will of God as revealed by Jesus, in contrast to those “who do evil” (Mat 13.41).
Another mystery of the Kingdom (Mat 13.11) is that its value exceeds all other treasures, and so everything should be forfeited to acquire it (see Mat 19.21, Mat 19.29; Phi 3.7).

treasure . . . hidden in a field: Treasures were buried for protection against thieves and military enemies (Mat 25.25). • In his excitement: Those who discover the Kingdom find greater joy in it than can be found in any temporal pleasure (see 1Pe 1.8).

This parable refers to God’s judgment at the last day (Mat 25.31–46), which will eternally separate the wicked from the righteous. This note of warning reinforces the urgency of the previous two calls to decision.
The wicked are those who do not do the will of God as revealed in Jesus, and the righteous are those who do (see Mat 5.21–48; Mat 6.1, Mat 6.33; Mat 7.13–27; Mat 12.33–37; Mat 16.27).
The ability to understand the mysteries of the Kingdom is a gift from God (Mat 13.10–17, Mat 13.23).

A teacher of religious law who becomes a disciple in the Kingdom has had his allegiance radically altered toward Jesus as the way of salvation. • new gems of truth as well as old: The sequence reflects the preeminence of the new covenant inaugurated in Jesus (Mat 5.17–20; Mat 19.16–22) over the old covenant administered under Abraham and Moses.
That Jesus was rejected at home is part of the ongoing theme of the Messiah’s rejection by his own people (see ch Mat 12.1–50; Mat 15.1–20; Mat 16.1–12).
carpenter’s son: A carpenter (literally craftsman) worked with his hands, whether in wood, metal, or stone.
They were deeply offended. Dwelling on Jesus’ all-too-common heritage (Joh 6.42), they could not see his uncommon significance.
Faith is required both to understand Jesus’ message (Mat 13.10–17) and to experience his miracles.

Herod Antipas’s official title was tetrarch (ruler of a fourth part of a kingdom) of Galilee and Perea (4 BC—AD 39; see Mat 2.19–22). Jesus referred to Antipas as “that fox” (Luk 13.32), and John the Baptist justly condemned him for adultery (Mat 14.3–12; Luk 3.19–20).
There was a rumor that John had been resurrected (see Mat 16.14).

The popular appeal of John’s message posed a political threat (see Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.2). Years after John’s execution, the Jews viewed Herod’s military defeat at the hands of Aretas (AD 36) as a just recompense for putting an innocent man to death.
John had continually warned Herod of his sin (see Lev 18.6; Lev 20.21).
Herodias’s daughter was probably Salome, a daughter from Herodias’s previous marriage to Philip. Sexually provocative dances such as this were a regular occurrence for depraved royalty.
Such an extravagant, foolish oath was consistent with Herod Antipas’s character.
The practice of bringing a head . . . on a tray was not unknown in the ancient world (see Josephus, Antiquities 13.4.8; 14.15.13; 18.5.1; 20.5.1).

Jesus’ actions consistently fulfilled Old Testament promises regarding the Kingdom and the Messiah (Mat 11.5–6; Mat 12.28). Here Jesus evoked the memory of God’s provision of manna for the Israelites (Exo 16.1–36; see Joh 6.32), demonstrating that he is the promised end-time prophet (see Deu 18.15–16).
5,000 men . . . in addition to all the women and children: The count was of families, denoted by heads of households, rather than individuals.
Jesus’ power over nature presented the disciples with the opportunity to trust in him as the Son of God (Mat 14.33; see also Mat 8.23–27; Psa 8.6; Heb 2.8–9).
After the miraculous feeding, the crowds sought to make Jesus king (Joh 6.15), prompting his withdrawal because it was not the appropriate time.
Jesus often sought solitude in order to pray, particularly in conjunction with important events in his life and ministry (Mat 26.36–46; Mar 1.35; Luk 5.16; Luk 6.12; Luk 9.28).

About three o’clock in the morning: Literally In the fourth watch of the night. This was approximately Mat 3.00–6:00 am by Roman reckoning. • The fact that Jesus came . . . walking on the water demonstrates God’s sovereign reign over the stormy waters (see Job 9.8; Psa 77.19; Isa 43.16).
I am here: Literally I am. This declaration is associated with the appearance of God himself (see also Joh 8.24; Joh 18.5–6; cp. Exo 3.14).
On the purpose of Jesus’ miracles, see study notes on Matt Mat 11.5; Mat 12.28.
Jesus indicted the Pharisees for disobeying God’s law in their zeal to preserve traditions.
Jerusalem was the location of the Temple and thus the seat of authority in Judaism; this gave the ambassadors greater leverage in their arguments with Jesus.

The Jewish teachers’ age-old tradition sought to apply the written Torah to common circumstances in the ordinary course of life. This tradition was memorized and passed on orally from teacher to student (cp. 1Co 11.23; 1Co 15.1–5). • To ignore the tradition of . . . hand washing (see Mar 7.2–4; Luk 11.38) was considered disobedient to the Torah and unfaithful to God’s will for Israel (cp. Mat 23.25–26).
vowed to give to God: Such a gift was likely donated at the Temple (see Mar 7.11; see also Pro 28.24) but functioned as a way to dodge financial responsibility for one’s parents.
cancel: Because of a greater commitment to their traditions, the Pharisees in effect rendered God’s law nonbinding, turning their piety into sinful disregard for the word of God.
You hypocrites! See study note on Matt Mat 23.13.

what goes into your mouth: Jesus was speaking here either of foods that were not permitted (e.g., pork or shellfish) or of food contaminated by unclean hands (Mat 15.20). • That which defiles makes a person unfit for communion with God. Jesus pressed the matter beyond ceremonial purity to true inner purity (see Mat 15.18–19; Mat 23.25–26; Act 10.1–48; Rom 14.14). • One’s words are a measure of one’s character (see Mat 15.18–20; Jam 3.1–12).

not planted by my heavenly Father: These Pharisees did not belong to the true people of God (see Mat 3.9–12; Isa 5.1–7; Jer 45.4). They will be uprooted at the final judgment (see Mat 3.10; Mat 8.12).
This encounter highlights another controversial issue: Gentile participation in the Kingdom of the Messiah (see Mat 8.11).

Gentile woman: Literally Canaanite woman. Matthew uses this archaic Old Testament expression to describe the woman as a pagan. • Lord, Son of David: The woman apparently perceived that Jesus was the Messiah (see Mat 1.1; Mat 9.27; Mat 17.15; Mat 20.30).
no reply: Jesus’ silence was a test of the woman’s faith (Mat 15.28; cp. Mat 8.24; Mat 14.16).

Jews often referred to pagans as dogs, which are ceremonially unclean (Lev 11.27). Jesus was speaking to the woman of her spiritual condition as a Gentile—as unclean and separated from God (cp. Mat 7.6).

Jesus returned to a predominantly Gentile area and performed many miracles. Though Jesus was sent primarily for Israel’s sake (Mat 15.21–28), the new era that he inaugurated is also the beginning of Gentile salvation (Mat 1.3, Mat 1.5–6; Mat 2.1–12; Mat 4.12–16; Mat 8.5–13; Mat 15.21–28; Mat 28.16–20). • Such healings are signs that the Kingdom has broken into history through Jesus’ ministry (Mat 8.1–Mat 9.34; Mat 11.5–6; Mat 12.28). • the God of Israel: This phrase suggests that the crowd (Mat 15.30) was predominantly Gentile.

The previous feeding miracle (see Mat 14.13–21) was for Jews, whereas this one extended to Gentiles; it thus develops the theme of Mat 15.27. Through this miracle Jesus demonstrated that he is the true bread of life (see Mat 16.5–12; Joh 6.1–71).
Magadan is an unknown site, perhaps Magdala (as in some Greek manuscripts; see also Mar 8.10).
Having been warmly received in the Gentile world, Jesus returned to his fellow countrymen only to encounter further rejection.
Profile: The Sadducees

Jesus made a deliberate play on their words when they sought a “sign from heaven” (Mat 16.1). They were able to read the weather in the sky (Greek ouranos, the same word translated “heaven”), but they failed to discern the Messiah despite the many signs already given (see Mat 11.1–6).
The signs of the times were Jesus himself (Mat 16.4) and the various miracles that he performed (cp. Mat 11.2–6; Mat 12.28).

Jesus had demonstrated to his disciples that he is the true bread of life (Mat 15.32–39; Joh 6.35, Joh 6.48), whereas the Jewish leaders, particularly in their teachings, were like yeast in permeating everything they touched with their sinfulness (see study note on Matt Mat 16.11–12).
Yeast is often a symbol of sin and evil (see Exo 12.8, Exo 12.15; Lev 6.16–17; Gal 5.9); here it indicates the permeating nature of the deceptive teaching.
Caesarea Philippi, located approximately twenty-five miles north of Capernaum, hosted many shrines to the Roman god of nature, Pan.
Theme: The Messiah

Some, such as Herod Antipas (Mat 14.1–2), thought Jesus was John the Baptist resurrected. • Elijah was expected as a forerunner to the Messiah (Mat 11.14; Mat 17.10–12; Mal 3.1; Mal 4.5–6). • Jeremiah or one of the other prophets: Some Jews expected Jeremiah to be raised (see 2 Maccabees Mat 15.13–16). Jesus’ strong stand on sensitive matters (Mat 5.17; Mat 15.1–20) may have led some to think Jesus was Jeremiah. Jesus was not yet understood as God’s Messiah.
Peter’s acknowledgment of Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God (Mat 3.17) shows that his eyes had been opened by faith (see Mat 11.25–27; Mat 14.33; Mat 27.54).
God revealed to Peter his plan of salvation in Jesus, the Messiah. This moment of revelation was a high point in the unfolding of God’s will for humanity (cp. Gal 1.16; Gal 3.23; Eph 3.5).

The phrase upon this rock is a pun on Peter’s name. Peter was the foundational rock in that he was the first confessor and leader of the apostles—he was the “founding member” of the church (see Eph 2.20–22; Rev 21.14). Some scholars have suggested that Jesus was referring to himself when he said this rock, but it seems clear that Jesus was referring either to Peter or to his confession. However, it is clearly Jesus’ church (my church), not Peter’s, and Jesus himself will build it. So it is not necessary to conclude that later church leaders must derive their authority from Peter. • Matthew is the only Gospel writer who uses the term church (also Mat 18.17). The idea here is more the community of God’s people than an ecclesiastical institution. • will not conquer it: The church will not be defeated by the attacks of Satan (see Mat 11.12; Mat 13.24–30, Mat 13.36–43).

Keys are an image for access to privileged knowledge that gives one authority (see Mat 13.16–17; Mat 23.13; Isa 22.22; Rev 3.7). • forbid . . . permit: Jesus granted to Peter (and later to the rest of the Twelve, Mat 18.18) the authority to teach the will of God as revealed in Jesus Christ (Mat 13.52; Mat 18.15–20; Mat 23.2–12; Mat 28.16–20). • will be: This could be translated will have been, emphasizing that God’s sovereign decision comes first.

Jesus, now officially recognized by his disciples as the Messiah, begins to reveal a startling aspect of his mission: He must suffer before entering his glory (Mat 16.21–23), and those who follow him will meet a similar fate (Mat 16.24–28).

This is the first of three predictions of Jesus’ passion—his suffering through betrayal, crucifixion, and death (see also Mat 17.22–23; Mat 20.18–19). Each prediction gives a lesson on the cost of discipleship (Mat 16.24–27; Mat 20.20–28). • That he would suffer was God’s sovereign and necessary purpose for the Messiah (see Mat 17.12).
began to reprimand him: Though Peter accurately perceived Jesus’ identity as God’s Messiah, he did not understand that the Messiah must suffer.

As when Satan tempted Jesus to assume royal privileges without first enduring the cross (see Mat 4.8–10), so now Jesus perceived Peter’s suggestion as incited by satanic forces. • dangerous trap: Literally stumbling block.

give . . . take . . . follow: These three imperatives use different images to speak of the same radical commitment of confessing one’s sinfulness before God in humility, surrendering one’s personal ambition to God, and living according to his will (see also Mat 5.20; Mat 10.34–39; Mat 18.1–5; Mat 20.20–28). • Take up your cross is a metaphor for devotion (see Luk 9.23) rather than a call to martyrdom, although martyrdom is an ever-present possibility for Jesus’ disciples (Mat 5.10–12; Mat 10.21). • In Matthew, follow is used both literally (Mat 9.19; Mat 26.58) and metaphorically. Metaphorically, it indicates interest in a teacher (Mat 4.25; Mat 8.1, Mat 8.10; Mat 12.15; Mat 14.13; Mat 19.2; Mat 20.29; Mat 21.9) or personal allegiance to Jesus involving a call, a commitment, and great ongoing costs (Mat 4.20, Mat 4.22; Mat 8.19, Mat 8.22–23; Mat 9.9; Mat 10.38; Mat 16.24; Mat 19.21, Mat 19.27).

Jesus’ disciples must relinquish control of their lives, even to the point of being willing to suffer and die for Christ. Jesus promised that those who follow him with such radical abandon, though they may suffer now, will be vindicated at the final judgment (see 1Pe 2.23).
your own soul? “Soul” and “life” (Mat 16.25) both translate the same Greek term (psuchē) and refer to the essence of a person—the self.

The exhortation to deny oneself and follow Jesus is rooted in the fact that Jesus will return to judge all people according to their deeds (see Mat 19.28; Mat 24.29–31; Mat 25.31; Psa 62.12; Pro 24.12).

This saying has been taken to refer either to (1) the transfiguration that follows (Mat 17.1–13); (2) the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ (Mat 27.50–53; Mat 28.1–10); (3) Pentecost (Act 2.1–47); (4) the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (Mat 24.1–31); (5) the second coming of Christ in the future (Mat 24.29–31); or (6) an unfolding revelation of God’s Kingdom in various ways, including the evangelism of the world. In the fourth view, coming would mean “coming in judgment” upon sinful Israel. • The expression Son of Man (Mat 16.27–28) forms an inclusio (bracketing expression) with Mat 16.13, unifying Mat 16.13–28 around the theme of the identity of the Son of Man. He is the Messiah who would suffer and then be exalted by God and return as Judge.

Peter . . . James and John later accompanied Jesus at Gethsemane (Mat 26.37; 2Pe 1.16–19). • It is impossible to determine the exact location of this high mountain. The traditional site, Mount Tabor, is only about 1,900 feet (580 meters) high and is out of the way for a trip from Caesarea Philippi (Mat 16.13) to Capernaum (Mat 17.24). Mount Hermon, another possibility, is about 9,200 feet (2,800 meters) high and located in Syria, forty miles north of Capernaum. It is unlikely, however, that “teachers of religious law” (Mar 9.14) would have congregated at the foot of a mountain in Gentile territory. A strong candidate is Mount Meron, about 4,000 feet (1,220 meters) high and situated between Caesarea Philippi and Capernaum.

Jesus’ appearance was transformed: Jesus’ inner, divine nature, previously veiled, was now disclosed so that the three caught a glimpse of his glory (see Exo 34.29–35; Psa 104.2; 2Co 3.12–18; Rev 1.16). Jesus’ followers will one day share in this glory (Mat 13.43).

Moses symbolizes the law and Elijah the prophets. They appeared as witnesses to Christ, to demonstrate that Jesus, God’s Son, is the fulfillment of everything written in the Law and the Prophets (see Mat 5.17–20; Mat 11.2–6; Mat 12.28).
three shelters as memorials: Peter probably thought that the Kingdom was about to be ushered in with full glory (cp. Act 1.6), and he desired to memorialize the moment.

a bright cloud overshadowed them: Such an occurrence accompanied God’s presence among the ancient Israelites during Moses’ ministry (see Exo 24.15–18; Exo 25.8; Exo 29.45–46; Exo 40.34–38). • my dearly loved Son: The Father was confirming what Peter had previously affirmed (Mat 16.16–17). • They should listen to him because Jesus is God’s Son, who, as a prophet, reveals God’s will (Mat 11.27; see Deu 18.15, Deu 18.18; Act 3.22–23; Act 7.37).
Such a response is typical for encounters with God’s glory (e.g., Isa 6.5; Dan 8.17; Dan 10.9, Dan 10.15–19; Rev 1.17).
Jesus could not be fully understood until all of his work was accomplished, particularly his death and resurrection.

Elijah’s presence at the transfiguration prompted a question about the view that Elijah must return before the Messiah comes (see Mal 4.5–6). In pointing to John the Baptist, Jesus reinforced the unexpected idea that the Messiah must suffer, even as his precursor had suffered (Mat 14.3–12).

faithless and corrupt people: The expression is often used for moral depravity (see Deu 32.5, Deu 32.19–22). Normally, this exclamation of Jesus was directed at the unbelieving Jewish crowds or leaders who refuse to acknowledge God’s presence in him (see Mat 12.39). Here, however, it was a sharp criticism of his disciples’ failure to trust Jesus and his saving, healing power.

Here, the expression don’t have enough faith is virtually synonymous with no faith. • faith even as small as a mustard seed: This could mean that if the disciples had even very little faith they would be able to accomplish great things (Mat 21.21; cp. 1Co 13.2). It could also mean that if they would allow their faith to grow (see Mat 13.31–32), they could act with courageous belief. • Moving mountains is an adage for overcoming obstacles and fulfilling God’s purposes (Isa 40.4; Isa 49.11; Isa 54.10; 1Co 13.2).
betrayed: See Mat 20.18; Mat 26.14–16, Mat 26.45–49 for the fulfillment of this prediction.

Every adult citizen of Israel was required to pay the Temple tax of one-half shekel. In Jesus’ day, priests and some rabbis did not pay the tax. • Peter was the spokesman for the Twelve (see Mat 10.2).

As an obedient Jew, Jesus would have paid the tax annually, and he did pay it. Jesus’ point was that as God’s Son, he is greater than the Temple (Mat 12.5–6), and he makes a decisive break with it (see Mat 16.18–19; Mat 21.33–46).

This fourth major discourse in Matthew (see study note on Matt Mat 5.1–Mat 7.29) focuses on responses to the Messiah—acceptance by the disciples and rejection by the Jewish leaders and most of the populace. In light of this growing polarization, Jesus began to instruct his followers on the nature of community life. For a community to live according to Jesus’ standards, it must live with humility (Mat 18.1–5), sensitivity (Mat 18.6–9), compassion (Mat 18.10–14), discipline (Mat 18.15–18), and forgiveness (Mat 18.21–35). As with the other discourses, a concluding formula (Mat 19.1–2) bridges to the next section.

About that time: Matthew connects the disciples’ questions with the previous discussion concerning the Temple. The disciples began to assume that their new freedom in relation to Jewish authority entitled them to authority of their own. In addition, talk of special revelations (Mat 11.25–27; Mat 13.11–17) and roles of leadership (Mat 10.2–4; Mat 19.28) probably gave rise to jealous comparisons and petty desires for power among the disciples, perhaps revolving around the apparent privilege of Peter (Mat 17.25) or Peter, James, and John (Mat 17.1–3).
Like little children means to be humble (Mat 18.4). The disciples had been intent on status and ambition.
Jesus moved the discussion toward solidarity within the community; to welcome a humble follower of Jesus is to welcome Jesus himself (see Mat 10.40–42).

To cause one . . . to fall into sin is to lead believing children (or possibly believing adults who become “like children”; see Mat 18.3) to reject Christ and abandon the faith. • The designation little ones emphasizes their humility (Mat 5.3–12; Mat 18.4; Mat 19.13–15). • Though the thought of being drowned with a large millstone around the neck is frightful, Jesus warned that causing another to fall away will bring far greater misery (Mat 18.7; Mat 26.24; Rev 18.21; see Mat 22.13).
Concern shifts to the individual: Get rid of whatever causes you to sin (see Mat 5.29–30; Col 3.5–17).
Don’t look down on them, either by refusing to receive them (Mat 18.5–6) or by refusing to give pastoral care when needed (Mat 18.12–14; see Mat 19.13–15). • their angels: See Mat 4.5–7; Heb 1.14.
Just as a shepherd will work to recover a lost sheep, the “little ones” (Mat 18.6) must not be despised or neglected.
The shepherd’s joy is also the joy of the Father; the purpose of pastoral care is so God will not lose any of his sheep.

The believing community must not be fractured into rival parties and unreconciled relationships. Its members are to pursue reconciliation (Mat 18.15–20) and forgive willingly (Mat 18.21–35). At times, however, stern discipline may be necessary (Mat 18.17).
Restoration begins privately and should be made public only as a last resort.
If another believer sins, love requires us to go privately and point out the offense (Lev 19.17; Luk 17.3; Gal 6.1; 1Ti 5.20; Tit 3.10).
By requiring the presence of one or two others, Jesus prevented slanderous, unsubstantiated accusations from being presented to the congregation (see Joh 8.17; 2Co 13.1; 1Ti 5.19; Heb 10.28).

The church is the local Christian community. • The unrepentant person is to be considered a pagan or a corrupt tax collector, a wicked transgressor of the law. Church discipline by exclusion (excommunication; see Act 5.1–6; Rom 16.17; 1Co 5.1–13; 2Co 6.14–18; Gal 5.7–12; 2Th 3.14–15) is rooted in the conviction that God’s people are to be holy and that sin corrupts fellowship, both between people and between the people and God. The goal is neither vindictive retribution nor a public display of power, but restoration of the wayward to holiness and fellowship (Mat 18.10–15; Gal 6.1; Jam 5.19–20).
These sayings provide the basis for a process of discipline and restoration in the community of disciples.

forbid . . . permit: The privilege and authority granted to Peter (Mat 16.19) are here granted to the church (or possibly to the twelve apostles, Mat 18.1). The decisions of the community, when in accord with God’s will, are eternally binding.
anything you ask: In the context of church discipline (Mat 18.15–17), this suggests that discipline must be done in prayer.
Christ is present in the process of discipline, so the process is a ratification of God’s decision.

Peter’s suggestion of seven times was generous, so Jesus’ answer was startling. The disciple’s willingness to forgive should be like God’s forgiving grace, limitless and free (see Mat 18.10–14). Those who do not forgive in this way cannot themselves have experienced God’s forgiveness (Mat 18.35; see Mat 6.12).
seventy times seven: Or seventy-seven times; either way, Jesus prescribes limitless readiness to forgive from the heart (Mat 18.35; cp. Gen 4.23–24).

millions of dollars (Greek 10,000 talents): The talent was the highest unit of currency, but its value fluctuated. The debt was clearly impossible to pay—this amount exceeded the tax revenue of all Galilee.
I will pay it all: The exaggerated debt and the slave’s promise amplify the greatness of the king’s mercy and the slave’s unforgiving attitude (Mat 18.29–30).
a few thousand dollars: The first servant’s debt was about one million times greater than this sum owed to him.
This is how God responds (Mat 18.35) to anyone unwilling to forgive. • until he had paid his entire debt: I.e., permanently, because he could never repay.
That’s what my heavenly Father will do to you: Prison and torture (Mat 18.34) is thus a metaphor for hell (see Mat 5.22).
Jesus was now on the move toward Jerusalem (Mat 19.1; Mat 20.29; Mat 21.1), with a further opportunity for instructing the disciples on various aspects of discipleship.

There were two divergent views on when one was allowed to divorce one’s wife. One group of Pharisees, following Rabbi Shammai, argued that divorce was allowed only in the case of adultery or other grave sin, while the other group, following Rabbi Hillel, contended that a man could divorce his wife for any reason, such as if she burned his dinner.
The Pharisees were not considering all of God’s word. The Creator had made marriage as a permanent union (see Gen 2.18–25; see also 1Co 7.10–16).
Since God made marriage a union, humans do not have the right to break that union. Jesus affirmed the indissolubility of marriage.

why did Moses say (literally command): The Pharisees thought Jesus had contradicted a command of the law (see Deu 24.1–4), but Moses permitted divorce only as a concession to their hard hearts. Jesus introduced the revolutionary principle that God’s permission is not necessarily his desire (see 1Co 6.12). Divorce is never God’s desire (Mal 2.14–16); it is an expression of human sin.

Jesus permits only one legitimate reason for a man to divorce: if his wife has been unfaithful (see Mat 5.32). In the face of those who thought divorce could be taken lightly, Jesus affirms God’s created order: Marriage was designed to be permanent (see Mar 10.11–12). • commits adultery: This speaks only of the man who divorces his wife unlawfully. In such a case, his remarriage is adulterous. Jesus’ motivation is to reestablish the permanency of marriage.
This statement refers to the disciples’ comment (Mat 19.10).

Eunuchs are males castrated either by a birth defect or by a surgical operation. Jesus also uses the term metaphorically for those who choose not to marry (see Luk 14.26; Luk 18.29; 1Co 7.7–8). • for the sake of the Kingdom: Jesus was not denigrating marriage; he was simply indicating that the unmarried often have greater potential for ministry (see 1Co 7.25–35).

Jesus would lay his hands on others to bless them (see Luk 4.40; Luk 13.13; see also Gen 48.14–15; Act 19.6). • The disciples, motivated to protect Jesus, scolded the parents, demonstrating a wrong attitude toward children (see Mat 18.5–6, Mat 18.10).

Why ask me? The man, as a Jew, should have known that God’s standard of goodness is clearly reflected in his commandments. The man’s questions (also Mat 19.20) show that he was not trusting in the adequacy of God’s revealed will. • only One . . . is good: The man may have believed he could act with perfect goodness on his own, whereas only God is truly good and thus the source of all goodness. • keep the commandments: Jesus has in mind either leading the man to see his sinfulness by asking him to do the impossible, or more probably, restating that good works are a telling gauge of the truthfulness of a person’s faith (see Mat 7.13–27).

By calling the man to go and sell and come, follow me, Jesus revealed that the man had not in fact kept the first of the ten commandments (Exo 20.3). His possessions—his wealth and security—had become his god (see Mat 6.20, Mat 6.24; Mat 13.44–46).

Jesus draws a lesson for discipleship from the rich man’s tragic denial. It is hard for the rich to humble themselves, admit their need, and trust in God (see Mat 5.3; Luk 6.24; 1Ti 6.9–10). • Kingdom of Heaven is equivalent here to eternal life (Mat 19.16–17, Mat 19.29) or to salvation as the result of God’s regenerating work (Mat 19.25–26).

easier for a camel: This analogy reinforces the difficulty that wealthy people face in entering the Kingdom. A few manuscripts have a Greek word meaning rope (Greek kamilos) instead of camel (Greek kamēlos), a difference of only one letter. • to go through the eye of a needle: The image makes the wealthy entering the Kingdom an impossibility. The situation is not utterly hopeless, however (Mat 19.26–27). See study note on Mark Mar 10.25.
God’s regenerating grace is absolutely essential before the wealthy are able to repent from their idolatry, abandon their possessions if called to do so, and follow Jesus (Mat 19.21).

you . . . will also sit on twelve thrones: The disciples’ part in judging is a reversal—those who are wealthy and powerful now will be judged by those who are humble and poor (see Mat 19.30). • Judging can mean both ruling and condemning (see Rev 20.4).
This parable is similar to the parable of the Lost Son (Luk 15.11–32). In both, God’s grace is shown to two parties while one grumbles about unjust treatment.
Payment followed the day’s work (Deu 24.14–15).

Each prediction of Jesus’ suffering in Matthew is connected to instruction on the nature of discipleship in light of that suffering (see Mat 16.24–28; Mat 17.24–Mat 18.5). This teaching called the Messiah’s disciples to follow his example of service and sacrifice.
This mother’s question appears to have been inspired by her sons, since Jesus responded to the sons rather than to the mother (cp. Mar 10.35–37).

The promise of sitting in positions of authority in God’s Kingdom had already been given (Mat 19.28); the brothers’ request seems to have been motivated out of selfish desire for prominence, with no regard for the suffering the Messiah would soon undergo (see Mat 23.6; Luk 14.7–11).
The cup refers to Jesus’ duty, calling, and destiny (see Mat 26.39; Joh 18.11; see also Psa 75.8; Isa 51.17, Isa 51.22; Rev 16.19).
You will indeed: James was eventually martyred (Act 12.2), and John suffered significant persecution (Act 4.3; Act 5.40; Rev 1.9).
The other disciples . . . were indignant: Selfish ambition was apparently not unique to James and John (see also Mat 21.15; Mat 26.8; Luk 13.14).
The desire for power is characteristic of pagan rulers in this world. It ought not to be a trait of those who follow the Son of Man (Mat 18.1–5; Mat 19.13–15; Mat 23.1–12).

The word slave is a common metaphor for the submissive relationship of a disciple to his master (Mat 8.9; Mat 10.24–25; Mat 24.45–51; Mat 25.14–30). Jesus’ disciples serve others, following Jesus’ example (e.g., Joh 13.1–17).

This expression, the Son of Man came, suggests Jesus’ preexistence (see Dan 7.13–14). • Jesus was describing his voluntary offering of himself as a ransom for many, to pay the debt all people owe (see Mat 26.26–29; Isa 53.10–12; Rom 3.24), thereby buying them out of slavery (see Gal 5.1).
The blind men’s expression of faith in the Son of David was an acknowledgment of Jesus as the Messiah (see Mat 21.9; Mat 22.42; 2Sa 7.12–16).
Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem initiates Matthew’s account of how the Messiah’s suffering and resurrection establish salvation.
Bethphage (a Hebrew name meaning house of figs) was probably located on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives between Bethany and Jerusalem proper.
Jesus was revealing himself as the Lord who, as king of Israel, ascends to Mount Zion on a donkey (Mat 21.5; see Zec 9.9).
The Old Testament fulfillment here emphasizes the Messiah’s non-violent, humble, and saving work (see Mat 11.28–30; Isa 62.11; Zec 9.9–10).
The crowds with Jesus understood him to be a prophet, empowered by God to teach and to perform miracles. • The description from Nazareth in Galilee highlights Jesus’ humble origins (see Mat 2.23).

The close association of the Temple cleansing (see Joh 2.13–16) with the cursing of the fig tree (Mat 21.18–19) reveals Jesus as the Messiah who confronted Israel and warned that God judges those who reject the Messiah and his message.

Buying and selling took place within the Temple complex, in the Court of the Gentiles. • Money changers profited from the exchange of money from other currencies into official Jewish currency. Jesus criticized the commercialism that profaned the holiness of the Temple (see Mar 11.11–18).
Jesus’ actions were justified, because God’s glory was being desecrated through financial exploitation.
The Jewish leaders’ stubborn refusal to believe is contrasted with the exuberant faith and praise of little children (see Mat 18.1–14; Mat 19.13–15).

Haven’t you ever read the Scriptures? Jesus put this penetrating question to opponents who did not perceive the fulfillment of messianic promises in his ministry. See also Mat 12.3, Mat 12.5; Mat 19.4; Mat 21.42; Mat 22.31.

there were only leaves: Mark observes that “it was too early in the season for fruit” (see Mar 11.13). It was spring (just before Passover); figs form in the spring but ripen in the fall. • immediately the fig tree withered: Matthew has apparently compressed the story (cp. Mat 21.18–22; Mar 11.13–14, Mar 11.20–23). The cursing of the fig tree is a symbolic gesture depicting God’s judgment on Israel for rejecting the Messiah (see Mat 3.9; Mat 8.11–12). Like a fig tree that shows promise but no fruit, the Israelites (especially the hypocritical leaders) did not bear the fruit of receiving the Messiah (see Mat 21.33–46).
Jesus was exhorting the disciples to trust in God and to pray accordingly. He was not offering God’s unconditional endorsement of all that they might desire (1Jo 5.14–15).

This section focuses on the Jewish leaders’ attack on Jesus’ authority. In each case, Jesus’ wisdom revealed the leaders’ spiritual blindness. These debates also revealed Jesus’ status as Messiah and the consequences of rejecting him. Tragically, the leaders grew more resistant with each encounter and plotted to eliminate Jesus (Mat 21.23, Mat 21.46; Mat 22.15–17, Mat 22.23, Mat 22.34, Mat 22.41).
Elders (literally elders of the people) were family heads from each tribe who were members of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem (cp. Ezr 5.5; Ezr 6.14; Ezr 10.8).

Jesus propounded a riddle, the solution to which answered the leaders’ question and forced them into a dilemma that revealed their hearts (Mat 21.25–26). Answering by counter-question was typical for such debates.

John’s ministry, like Jesus’ (see Mat 3.1, Mat 3.5–6), was controversial, especially after John’s public denouncement of the sins of Herod Antipas (see Mat 14.4). The leaders did not want to acknowledge that John’s ministry was from God, since they had refused to believe John by repenting of their sins (Mat 3.2) and accepting Jesus as the Messiah (Joh 1.29–34).
The leaders lacked integrity and courage to confess what they believed about John. So Jesus’ refusal to answer their original question was fair.
Three parables expose the guilt of those who had rejected the Messiah and forfeited their privilege as God’s chosen people. The new people of God are only those who embrace the Messiah.
This parable continues the point about John’s significance.
I won’t go: This response must have offended Jews who were taught to show outward respect for the authority of a father (see Mat 8.21–22).
The right way to live is in conformity to God’s will (Mat 3.15; Mat 5.20; see also Pro 8.20; Pro 12.28).

In this story Jesus draws on Isa 5.1–7. The people of Israel who rejected God’s Messiah forfeited the privilege of being God’s people. The Christian community, comprised of both Jews and Gentiles, has now been called to be the people of God (cp. Rom 9.4–8; Rom 11.1–12).
sent his servants: The prophets had spoken God’s word to Israel. The tenant farmers represented the leaders of Israel, whom Jesus held responsible for the deaths of God’s prophets (Mat 23.29–37).
Finally: God’s revelation climaxed in Jesus (see Mat 13.16–17; Heb 1.1–2).
When the owner of the vineyard returns refers to the Lord’s coming in judgment (see Mat 16.27; Mat 24.1–36).
The Jewish religious leaders pronounced their own condemnation.

The cornerstone was either the first stone of the foundation or the capstone (as of an arch), the last to be laid. The very stone that the builders rejected as unworthy of use was, in fact, the most important. Jesus was referring to his own role in the Kingdom of God (Mat 21.43) and to the religious leaders’ rejection of him.
Theme: The Stone the Builders Rejected

taken away from you: Either the privilege of being God’s chosen nation no longer belonged to the Jews, or the religious leaders had lost the privilege of being leaders of God’s people (see Rom 9.1–11). • The Christian community is a nation that will produce the proper fruit—that is, a life of trust and obedience that demonstrates the inauguration of the Kingdom (see Mat 3.8; Mat 7.15–20; Mat 12.33; Mat 13.8, Mat 13.26).

Though in a short while the Messiah’s opponents would gain a brief victory, they would ultimately be broken and the stone would crush them because the cross became the gateway to Jesus’ vindication and triumph (see also Dan 2.34–35, Dan 2.44–45).
This explanation fits with Matthew’s theme of God’s judgment on the Jewish leaders who misled the people of Israel (see Mat 23.13–15).

In this parable, Israel, having repeatedly rejected God’s word in the past, rejects the Messiah and is judged as a result. In Israel’s place, God raised up the church (Mat 16.17–19; Mat 21.43), of which righteousness is also expected (Rom 11.11–24).
The king represents God, whose son is Jesus (Gal 4.4; Heb 1.1–2). • The feast represents the Kingdom of the Messiah.
Those who were invited refers to the nation of Israel, who ignored God’s servants, the prophets (see study note on Matt Mat 21.33–46).
Jesus was alluding to the coming destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (see Mat 23.37–39; Mat 24.2).
Those who reject God’s invitation aren’t worthy to enter his Kingdom (cp. Mat 3.8; Mat 10.13, Mat 10.37–38).
everyone you see: God’s invitation is no longer restricted to the nation of Israel (see Mat 28.16–20; cp. Mat 10.5–6; Mat 15.21–28).
good and bad alike: See Mat 13.24–50.
The proper clothes correspond to spiritual fruit that demonstrates real faith (see Mat 7.13–27).

Weeping and gnashing of teeth express the intense pain and sorrow that result from condemnation for sin and unbelief (see Mat 8.12; Mat 13.42, Mat 13.50; Mat 24.51; Mat 25.30). • Outer darkness is a metaphor for eternal punishment.
While many people are called—they hear the invitation to the Kingdom—few are actually chosen by God and respond in faithful obedience to Jesus.
Roman taxation was a controversial issue in first-century Palestine (see also Mat 17.24–27).
The Pharisees, strict nationalists who resented Roman rule, were normally at odds with the supporters of Herod. Here, the unlikely alliance arose from a mutual hatred of Jesus.

Is it right . . . or not? The question was designed to trap Jesus. If he answered no, he could be arrested for rebellion against Rome. If he answered yes, he could be accused of supporting Roman oppression.
You hypocrites! See study note on Mat 23.13.

The poll tax had to be paid using the denarius coin, which bore the picture and title of Caesar. Old Testament prohibitions against images (Exo 20.4; Lev 26.1; Deu 4.15–24) made the use of this coin controversial among Jews (see Josephus, War 2.9.2-3). Some Roman procurators apparently produced coins without images for use in Palestine in order not to offend the Jewish conscience.

Jesus outwitted his opponents by affirming the honor due to Caesar, while clearly differentiating it from the supreme honor and allegiance due to God. Loyalty to God does not necessarily entail disloyalty to the governing authorities. Jesus was acknowledging two dominions, Caesar’s and God’s, the latter having priority (Act 4.19).
The resurrection was an important issue of Jesus’ day, but the question was raised only to trap Jesus.
The Sadducees (see Mat 3.7) described a situation involving levirate marriage (see Gen 38.6–11; Deu 25.5–6), which they considered proof that resurrection from the dead is not possible.
The power of God most likely refers to God’s ability to raise the dead.

like the angels in heaven: Jesus was not teaching genderlessness (i.e., androgyny) nor disparaging the divine order of marriage and sexuality; rather, he was affirming that people will be transformed into a glorious new existence (see 1Co 15.35–49; 2Co 5.1–5) in which aspects of the present order, such as marriage, will not be present.
Since God spoke of being the God of Abraham in the present tense, this proves that Abraham still lives and thus that there is a resurrection.
Since many strict Jews saw all commandments as equally binding, a careless response to this question could lead to the accusation of undermining the law of God.
Jesus answers from the Shema (Deu 6.4–9), one of the core statements of God’s covenant with Israel (The first Hebrew word of Deu 6.4–9 is shema‘, “hear”).
Love your neighbor as yourself: Lev 19.18; see also Rom 13.9; Gal 5.6, Gal 5.14; Jam 2.8.
are based on: Jesus’ statement affirmed the unity and coherence of God’s will, as recorded in Scripture.

Having successfully defended himself against his opponents’ traps (Mat 21.23–Mat 22.40), Jesus questioned them as to how the Messiah can be called both the son of David and, at the same time, the Lord of David (Psa 110.1).
the son of David: See study note on Matt Mat 9.27; see also 2Sa 7.12–14; Psa 2.7–9; Psa 110.1–7; Isa 11.1, Isa 11.10; Jer 23.5–6.
The quotation is from Psa 110.1, which is frequently cited by New Testament authors to describe Jesus (see Act 2.34–35; 1Co 15.25; Heb 1.13; Heb 2.8; Heb 10.12–13; Rev 3.21).
how can the Messiah be his son? The answer is that Jesus is more than the son of David: He is the Son of God (Mat 14.33).
No one could answer him because they had never thought the Messiah would be God as a human being in the flesh (see Joh 1.1–14).
This final extended discourse (see study note on Matt Mat 5.1–Mat 7.29) centers on judgment for rejecting the Messiah.

The religious leaders had sought a reason to accuse Jesus publicly (Mat 21.23–Mat 22.46) but found none. Jesus now turned to the crowds and to his disciples to openly indict the religious leaders for their numerous failures to conform to God’s righteous standards.

the Pharisees are the official interpreters of the law of Moses: They transmitted the oral traditions that were associated with the law and thought to be from Moses, and they judged religious and social matters on the basis of these traditions (see Mat 15.2).

practice and obey: This was not a blanket endorsement of all that the Pharisees teach (see Mat 15.1–20; Mat 16.5–12; Mat 23.13–39). It might refer only to what was in accord with the law of Moses, or it might be bitter irony or sarcasm. Jesus might also have been counseling conformity to the Pharisees’ teachings to avoid giving offense (Mat 17.24–27).

unbearable religious demands: There were 613 legal prohibitions and commands, according to the rabbis (see Mat 11.28–30; Act 15.10, Act 15.28). • never lift a finger: The religious leaders were unwilling to consider relaxing traditional legal statutes.

prayer boxes: Pious Jews wore, on the head and upper left arm, a small pouch or box (phylactery) containing written copies of important Old Testament commands (see Deu 6.6–9; Deu 11.18–19). • Wearing tassels was another custom associated with piety (see Mat 9.20; see also Num 15.38–41). Lengthening the tassels called attention to their wearer’s pious practices.
The seats of honor in the synagogues were near the scrolls of the Torah and facing the congregation.
Rabbi was a title of authority and respect.

Jesus does not prohibit the use of titles (especially for one’s own father), but rather the assumption of undue honor by those who transmit knowledge about God. The community of Jesus is a group of equals, each of whom knows God (see Mat 12.46–50; Mat 18.15–20). The terms Rabbi, Father, and Teacher are roughly equivalent.

Rabbi: These men functioned in Judaism as mediators for dispensing knowledge about God (see Mat 23.7). The new covenant, by contrast, has only one teacher, Jesus himself as Messiah (see Jer 31.31–34).

Writings from later Judaism provide ample evidence of revering the teachers by calling them Father (see, e.g., Mishnah Eduyyoth Mat 1.4). • God . . . is your Father: See Mat 6.9; Mal 2.10; cp. 1Co 4.15.
Teacher: This title denotes the function and office of leading others into knowledge about God. Jesus, not the scribes and Pharisees, is the teacher of God’s will (Mat 5.17).
Jesus’ disciples should lead by serving, in stark contrast to Israel’s religious leaders (who are described in Mat 23.5–7).

Matthew collected seven statements of what sorrow awaits you (literally woe to you), drawing upon similar Old Testament listings (Isa 5.8–23; Hab 2.6–20), and he arranged them to climax in the murder of the prophets.

What sorrow awaits you: A stark warning of judgment from God. • Hypocrites! In English, hypocrisy describes a contradiction between reality and appearance. But in biblical usage, hypocrisy is misperceiving God’s will, leading people astray, and thus incurring God’s judgment. Coupled with this is often a desire for prestige and power (Mat 23.5–12), abuse of teaching authority, false teachings on doctrine or practice (Mat 23.13–22), and preoccupation with ethical minutiae (Mat 23.23–28). An accurate English term for this combination of factors is heresy. The Pharisees and teachers of religious law displayed all of these characteristics. As the Christian church began to grow, these characteristics continued to appear (e.g., 1Ti 4.1–3; 2Pe 2.1–22), so God’s children always need to guard against them (Jam 4.7–10; 1Pe 2.1–3). • shut the door of the Kingdom: By their false teaching and opposition to Jesus (see Mat 9.32–34; Mat 12.22–37; Mat 15.12–14; Mat 21.15; Joh 9.13–34), the teachers of religious law and Pharisees prevented others from hearing and believing the truth about the Messiah.

A convert (proselyte) made a full conversion to Judaism, performing such observances as baptism, sacrifice, and circumcision (see Act 13.43). A convert was thus distinct from a “God-fearer,” who adopted certain Jewish beliefs, most notably monotheism, without fully converting to Judaism (see Luk 7.4–5; Act 10.2). It is likely that to make one convert means to persuade God-fearers to become full converts to Judaism by undergoing circumcision (cp. Gal 2.3, Gal 2.14; Mat 5.2–12; Mat 6.12–13). • of hell: Greek of Gehenna; see study note on Mat 5.29.
The religious leaders declared certain oaths less binding in order to commit fraud. Jesus calls for honest fulfillment of commitments (see Mat 5.33–37).

The teachers of religious law and Pharisees thought that meticulous tithing demonstrated their zeal for the law. Without denying the validity of the tithe, Jesus revealed how they had utterly failed to attend to the more important aspects of the law (Isa 1.16–17; Jer 22.3; Hos 6.6; Mic 6.8; Zec 7.9).
gnat . . . camel: These words form a pun in Aramaic (qalma . . . gamla), the language Jesus probably spoke.
Internal purity will result in external righteousness, but the reverse is not true (Mat 6.19–34; Mat 12.33–37; Mat 15.15–20).

It was a Jewish custom to coat limestone tombs (perhaps funerary urns or ossuaries) with a mixture of marble and lime to fill their porous surfaces, giving them a more pleasing appearance and helping visitors to Jerusalem to notice the graves and avoid touching them so as not to contaminate themselves.
