Jesus is not criticizing the adorning of tombs; rather, he points to the similarity between these whitewashed tombs and the teachers of religious law and Pharisees. Both may have looked good on the outside, but both were contaminated and impure within.

By building and decorating the tombs for the prophets, the teachers of religious law and Pharisees showed outward solidarity with the prophets, while inwardly they were of the same sinful character as their ancestors who had murdered the prophets.
finish what your ancestors started: By killing God’s Messiah, they would bring to completion Israel’s history of killing God’s messengers (see 1Th 2.14–16).

The span from Abel (Gen 4.8–11) to Zechariah (2Ch 24.15–22) follows the order of the Hebrew Bible, in which 2 Chronicles is the last book. The implication is that this generation will be guilty of every murder of the righteous in the Old Testament (cp. Mat 27.25).

Despite the severe judgment Jesus had just leveled against Israel (Mat 23.29–36), he truly longed for them to repent and receive God’s grace. • as a hen: An image of protective care (see also Deu 32.11; Rut 2.12; Psa 17.8; Psa 36.7; Psa 57.1; Psa 61.4; Psa 91.4).
your house is abandoned and desolate: God would withdraw his presence from the Temple (Eze 10.18–19; Eze 11.22–23; cp. Mat 1.23), and both the Temple and Jerusalem would be destroyed.
Blessings on the one who comes in the name of the LORD: This is possibly the prediction of an end-time conversion of the nation of Israel to the Messiah (see also Rom 11.12–32).

Some believe chapter Mat 24.1–51 pertains to the return of Christ at the end of history. Others view the chapter as a prediction of the events of AD 70, when Jerusalem and the Temple were destroyed by the Romans. Others believe it refers to both. See also study notes on Mark 13 Mar 13.1–37.
The architecture of the Temple was a source of pride among Jews—see study note on Mark Mar 13.1.

Not one stone: The destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple was a sign of God’s judgment (see 1Ki 9.7–9; Jer 7.8–15; Jer 9.10–12; Jer 26.6, Jer 26.18; Mic 3.12; see also Isa 64.11; Luk 19.44; Act 6.14).

The Greek term translated return is parousia, which can mean coming or appearing. • end of the world (or end of the age): This expression refers to the climax and end of an epoch in salvation history (see Mat 13.39–40, Mat 13.49; also Heb 9.26). Jesus’ second coming will bring normal history to a close with decisive judgment. The disciples assumed that the destruction of the Temple and the end of history were closely connected.

Jesus warned the disciples not to be deceived by impostors or overwhelmed by catastrophes in hope of a premature end to history. Time must run its predestined course. The signs predicted in Mat 24.4–8 are not necessarily at the end; rather, they are signs prior to the end.

claiming, ‘I am the Messiah’: A series of false prophets and miracle workers evoked messianic images and persuaded the masses to follow them in hope of deliverance during the period between AD 30 and 70 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.4.1; 20.5.1; 20.8.6; War 6.5.2). The earliest recorded instance of an outright claim to be the Messiah was Bar Kochba’s claim in AD 132. It is not clear whether Jesus is referring only to impostors in the period prior to the destruction of the Temple or to false messiahs throughout the church age or perhaps during a future tribulation.

these things must take place: Tumultuous times are part of God’s sovereign plan as he brings history to a close (see Mat 24.7, Mat 24.29–30; 2Th 2.8–12). • The end could refer to the close of an epoch (such as at AD 70) or the end of human history as we now know it (cp. Mat 24.13–14; see also Mat 10.22; Mat 13.39–40, Mat 13.49).
first of the birth pains: Intense anguish is expected just prior to Jesus’ second coming (see also Mat 24.29–31; Isa 13.8; Isa 26.17; Jer 4.31; Jer 6.24; Mic 4.9–10).

hated (see Act 28.22): At the end of the first century, the Roman historian Tacitus described Christians as “the hated ones of mankind” (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). The affliction of the righteous sometimes has the purpose of inciting repentance and obedience (see Exo 4.31; Deu 4.30; Jdg 10.6–16; Psa 34.19; Psa 37.39; Psa 50.15).
Persecution will lead some to abandon loyalty to Jesus (Mat 10.25; Mat 13.21; Mat 16.24–28; Mat 26.33).

the love of many will grow cold (see Rev 2.4): If the love within the community of Jesus’ disciples diminishes to the point of extinction, then the community ceases to be what God has designed it to be.
The one who endures maintains faithful allegiance to Jesus despite persecution. Here, the end may refer to the end of one’s own life, the judgment on Israel in AD 70, or the end of history.

throughout the whole world: This anticipates the expansive Gentile mission (see Mat 21.43; Mat 28.16–20). There will be a delay prior to the end, however short or long, during which the Good News will spread significantly throughout the nations. • The end will be signaled by a “sacrilegious object” (Mat 24.15), furious persecution (Mat 24.16–28), and finally the sign of the Son of Man (Mat 24.29–31).

Daniel . . . spoke about a profaning or desolating of the Temple (see Dan 8.13; Dan 9.27; Dan 11.31; Dan 12.11). • the sacrilegious object that causes desecration: Attempts to identify a specific fulfillment include: (1) a false priest assuming the priesthood (see Josephus, War 4.3.6-10); (2) the presence of unlawful images of God or humans, or certain humans themselves (such as Antiochus Epiphanes, Caligula, Vespasian, or Titus) who were not to be allowed within the Temple precincts (see Josephus, War 4.4.1–4.7.1); (3) the presence of the antichrist in the Temple (cp. 1 Maccabees Mat 1.54–64; 2 Maccabees Mat 8.17). • Reader, pay attention! This covert statement reflects a special bond between writer and reader, based on a shared understanding that the events being described fulfill the prophecies of Dan 9.1–27, Dan 11.1–45, and Dan 12.1–13.

Josephus records the winter swelling of the Jordan River, which made it more difficult to cross (see Josephus, War 4.7.5). Muddy roads also made travel difficult in winter. • Normally Jews did not travel on the Sabbath in order to rest as God had commanded (see Gen 2.1–3; Exo 20.8–11; Exo 23.12; Exo 31.12–17; Lev 23.3; Deu 5.12–15; Jer 17.19–27).
greater anguish: Similar language is found in Neh 9.37; Jer 11.16; Dan 12.1; Joe 2.1–17. The blatant savagery of the times has been documented by Josephus (see War 5.10.2-3).
God’s chosen ones endure (Mat 24.13) and remain faithful (Mat 24.37–Mat 25.46; see Isa 65.8–9; Rom 11.7).

false messiahs and false prophets (see Mat 7.15; Mat 24.4–8; also Act 13.6; 2Pe 2.1; 1Jo 2.18; 1Jo 4.1): Revelation describes a particular false prophet (see Rev 16.13). • signs and wonders: Not all miracles are proof of God’s approval (see Deu 13.1–4; Rev 13.13).
These verses are an expansion of Mat 24.23. The place and manner of the Messiah’s appearing was disputed among Jews. The Messiah’s glorious appearance and vindication will be unmistakable.

Some Jewish prophets persuaded the masses to follow them into the desert to see signs of deliverance (cp. Mat 24.4–8). • hiding here: This is perhaps a reference to secretive sects, such as those at Qumran, or to the small fellowship groups associated with the Pharisees.

Lightning may be an allusion to the astrological phenomena attending the Messiah’s coming (see Mat 24.29–31; 1Th 4.13–18). It is not the suddenness of lightning that is in view but rather the magnitude of its visibility. Very possibly, Jesus gave these sayings to ward off premature excitement regarding the end (1Th 4.13–Mat 5.10; 2Th 2.1–12).

These sayings form the climax of the discourse and answer the second of the disciples’ initial questions (see Mat 24.3). Some take Mat 24.29–31 to refer to God’s judgment on the Jewish people in AD 70, using apocalyptic images and metaphors to describe it. Others see a reference to the second coming of Christ at the end of history.

the sun will be darkened . . . will be shaken: This phenomenon can be taken literally, as befitting the climactic self-disclosure of God’s Son, or metaphorically, as for a cosmically significant event (see Act 2.17–21; Heb 12.26–27; 2Pe 3.10; Rev 6.12–13). Similar apocalyptic language is used frequently in the Old Testament for describing political disasters and the collapse of a government as cosmic judgments from God (e.g., Isa 13.9–16; Eze 32.1–10; Joe 2.1–17; Amo 8.7–10).

the sign that the Son of Man is coming (literally the sign of the Son of Man): The sign is probably the Son of Man himself (see Mat 12.38–42; Mat 16.4). His coming expresses his vindication (see Mat 26.64) and will bring deep mourning to those who experience God’s judgment. • All the peoples of the earth could be translated all the tribes of the land. The term used here is not the usual Greek term for Gentile nations (ethnoi), but a term used frequently of the tribes (phulai) of Israel (the land), suggesting that a national disaster in Israel might be in view (see Mat 21.43; Zec 12.10–14). • the Son of Man coming on the clouds: See Dan 7.13. Many believe that this means a descent of the Son of Man from God’s presence to reside on earth as Judge and Deliverer—i.e., the second coming of Christ. Others have argued that this describes the Son of Man coming in judgment, but not necessarily the second coming of Christ (see Mat 10.23; Mat 16.27; Mat 19.28; Mat 25.31; Mat 26.64; Mat 28.18).

Many believe that the rapture of God’s people through angels (Mat 13.41; Mat 16.27; Mat 25.31) is predicted here. Others believe that angels (Greek angeloi, “messengers”) here are human messengers (Mat 11.10; Luk 7.24; Luk 9.52; Jam 2.25) and that Jesus is describing the expansion of the Good News among Gentiles (see Mat 21.33–46; Mat 22.1–14; Deu 30.1–10; Isa 27.13; Zec 2.6–13).

all these things: This expression, used first in Mat 23.36 (“this judgment”), refers to the events associated with the destruction of the Temple (see Mat 24.2, Mat 24.8). • his return (literally he or it): It could mean Jesus’ return (see Jam 5.9; Rev 3.20), the destruction of the Temple, or the end of history (see Luk 21.31).

this generation: In Matthew, generation is used particularly for contemporary, unbelieving Jews, especially focusing on the leaders who have led people away from the Messiah (Mat 11.16; Mat 12.39, Mat 12.41–42, Mat 12.45; Mat 16.4; Mat 23.36).
Jesus’ words are as sure as God’s own (see Mat 5.18; Isa 40.8; Isa 55.11; Isa 59.21).

The day is the day of judgment. • or the Son: Jesus’ limited knowledge is suggested also in Act 1.7. Because the day is unknown, Jesus’ hearers should be vigilant and faithful (see Mat 24.37–Mat 25.46). This statement ought to deter those who attempt to calculate the date of our Lord’s return.
Jesus now applied his predictions (Mat 24.1–36) to his followers so they will be faithful and prepared for his second coming.
Jesus’ second coming, like the flood (Gen 7.1–24), will come upon people unawares. The only adequate preparation is a life of consistent vigilance and obedience (cp. Luk 17.26–27, Luk 17.34–35).

When the Son of Man returns: Jesus’ second coming (see Mat 24.3; cp. Luk 17.26). • in Noah’s day (see Gen 6.9–22; 2Pe 2.5; 2Pe 3.5–6): The comparison here does not concern the magnitude of sins, but a lack of discernment about what God is doing, accompanied by a preoccupation with life’s festivities (Mat 6.19–34).

The term taken most likely means taken in judgment, at AD 70 or at the end of history; left would then mean remaining to enter the new era of either the church (see Mat 21.43; Mat 22.1–14) or the Millennium.
To keep watch is to maintain active, energetic, single-minded obedience to the Lord (see Mat 25.13; Mat 26.38–41).
This parable and the three that follow (Mat 25.1–13, Mat 25.14–30, Mat 25.31–46) each dramatize the need for faithful obedience during the delay of Jesus’ second coming.

servant: It is possible that Jesus’ listeners would have thought of God’s special servants, the prophets and lawgivers; however, Jesus so frequently used servant figuratively that it is more likely a description of every disciple’s responsibility (see Mat 10.24–25; Mat 13.27–28; Mat 18.23–35; Mat 20.26).
This parable reinforces the need for individuals to be watchful and to prepare for the return of Christ (Mat 25.13; see also Luk 12.35–36).

To meet the bridegroom is an image for the coming of the Messiah (see Mar 2.19–20). • Details of wedding customs during the period are not known. Some think that the bride was led to the home of the bridegroom, who would stay away until the time appointed for the wedding feast. The bridesmaids, who had already escorted the bride to the groom’s home, would then wait for news of his arrival and escort him to the feast (Mat 25.10). Others think the groom may have come late in the night to the bride’s home, where he was announced. Then, after celebrating with the bride’s guests, the groom would take his bride under torches or lamps to his home.

While some have speculated that the oil symbolizes something specific (such as the Holy Spirit), it probably merely supports the point that proper preparation for the second coming of Christ is needed.
Both the prudent and the foolish bridesmaids sleep while waiting. The parable criticizes only the foolish bridesmaids’ failure to bring enough oil.

The arrival of the bridegroom at midnight while the bridesmaids slept further highlights the fact that the second coming of Jesus will come suddenly, at a time that no one can anticipate (Mat 24.42–51).

This parable teaches that the Lord expects his servants to be faithful to the task given to them while waiting for his return. The delay of Christ’s return will cause some to turn to evil deeds (Mat 24.48–49), some to inactivity (Mat 25.3), and some to fearful passivity (Mat 25.18).
After a long time: This highlights the long delay of Christ’s return (Mat 24.45–51).
See Mat 24.45–51; Luk 16.10. • Let’s celebrate together is a metaphor for the Father’s approval and perhaps for the messianic banquet (see Mat 6.1, Mat 6.4, Mat 6.6, Mat 6.18; Mat 9.9–17).
I knew you were . . . harsh: A false understanding of his master becomes this servant’s excuse for laziness.
God gives abundant grace to those who are faithful with what they have already been given (see Mat 13.12).
This is a description of the final judgment of which Jesus had been warning (see Mat 7.13–27; Mat 8.10–12; Mat 11.20–24; Mat 12.38–42; Mat 13.24–30, Mat 13.36–43; Mat 16.24–28; Mat 24.37–Mat 25.30).
To sit upon his glorious throne is here a posture of judgment (see Mat 19.28; Mat 22.44; Dan 7.13–14).
Theme: Faith and Good Deeds
The right hand is the place of honor (Gen 48.13–20; Psa 110.1).

prepared for you from the creation of the world: This might be a reference to God’s choosing individuals for salvation in eternity past (see Mat 13.10–17; Eph 1.4; Rev 17.8), or it might simply refer to the Kingdom itself as a place (cp. Mat 25.41).

The deeds described here, often called “deeds of mercy,” were acts of compassion shown to the helpless (see Isa 58.1–12; Eze 18.7; Jam 1.26–27). These good deeds are not attempts to merit God’s favor; rather, they arise from a love for Christ that results in compassion toward others (see Mat 6.1–4).
These righteous ones (see Mat 5.6, Mat 5.20) are those who do God’s will as taught by Jesus, expressed most clearly in deeds of love (Mat 7.12; Mat 9.9–13; Mat 22.34–40; Mat 25.35–40).

my brothers and sisters: This expresses either Jesus’ solidarity with his disciples (see Mat 10.42; Mat 18.1–14; Gal 6.10) or Jesus’ solidarity with humanity in general, irrespective of the faith of the one being helped (see Mat 6.1–4; Mat 25.43; Pro 19.17). The use of brothers and sisters points to the first interpretation (Mat 12.46–50; Mat 18.15–35; Mat 23.8; Mat 28.10) but does not invalidate social responsibility for other people in general (see Luk 10.30–37).

The Greek term translated eternal can mean either “lasting forever” or “lasting for an age,” in this case “the age to come” (Mat 13.39–40, Mat 13.49; Mat 24.3; Joh 17.3; 2Th 1.9; Phm 1.15; 1Jo 5.11, 1Jo 5.13). Some hold out hope that the punishment of the damned will, after “an age,” be ended by annihilation or forgiveness. The parallel between eternal life and eternal punishment suggests strongly that it means “lasting forever,” since eternal life does not end (see also Luk 16.19–31; Heb 6.2; Rev 20.10).

The irony is that the Son of Man, who is to judge the nations (Mat 25.31–46), must first be wrongly judged and condemned to death by evil people. Jesus’ death was the ultimate Passover sacrifice (see Joh 19.31–37; 1Co 5.7).

The residence of Caiaphas, the high priest, was near the Temple in Jerusalem’s Upper City. Since it was not the normal meeting place, this gathering was ad hoc, urgent, and probably secretive. The council chamber, the traditional meeting place for the Sanhedrin, was located either at the southern end of the Court of the Israelites in the Temple, or on the western edge of the Temple hill. • Joseph Caiaphas, son-in-law of Annas (see Joh 18.13), was high priest from AD 18 to 36 (Joh 11.49), the longest tenure of any high priest from the time of Herod’s rule until AD 70. His father-in-law, Annas, had been deposed but continued to be called high priest as well (see Luk 3.2; Joh 18.13, Joh 18.19–24).

Jerusalem was flooded with pilgrims at Passover, and the Jewish leaders worried about having their authority taken away if they caused or allowed anything that resembled revolt against Rome (see Mat 21.8–11, Mat 21.14–16).

A similar anointing took place earlier in Galilee (Luk 7.36–50). Matthew’s insertion of the episode at this point (cp. Joh 12.1–8) sets the Jewish leaders’ murderous plotting (Mat 26.3–5) and Judas’s betrayal (Mat 26.14–16) in sharp contrast to the woman’s praiseworthy actions.
Simon, a man who had previously had leprosy: Jesus’ presence in the man’s home exhibited the forgiving, healing love Jesus often showed toward outcasts (see Mat 8.7; Mat 9.10).

The jar of expensive perfume was a burial ointment (see Mar 16.1; Luk 23.56–Mat 24.1; Joh 12.1–7; Joh 19.38–42) made of nard, which was harvested in India. The value of this jar of perfume was nearly a year’s wages (Joh 12.5).
The disciples were indignant: Joh 12.4 indicates that Judas Iscariot incited this reaction.

to prepare my body for burial: It is not clear whether the woman fully understood the significance of her actions. In addition to preparation for burial, the anointing also speaks of Jesus as king (1Sa 10.1; 2Ki 9.6) and priest (Exo 29.7).

Judas sold himself to the authorities (see also Joh 11.57), concealed it (Mat 26.25), and then took them to Jesus at the appropriate time so they could carry out their plans (Mat 26.47–56; see Joh 18.2). Later, Judas was overcome by guilt and committed suicide (Mat 27.3–10; see Act 1.15–22). Judas was apparently known for his greed (Mat 26.14–15; Joh 12.4–6; Joh 13.29). It is also possible that he was motivated by disappointment over the nature of Jesus’ reign as Messiah, his own humiliation over the anointing of Jesus (see Joh 12.1–8), or resentment over the leadership of the Galilean apostles, Peter, James, and John. Whatever his motivation, Judas’s betrayal was a part of God’s sovereign plan (Act 1.16–17).
My time: The Messiah would now complete the work for which he was commissioned, to die for the sins of the world.

eaten from this bowl with me: It was the custom for everyone present to dip their food into a common bowl, which probably contained herbs and fruit puree. Sharing a meal was a sign of friendship and trust, making a betrayer’s presence all the more startling (Mat 26.21; but see Joh 13.26).

as the Scriptures declared: Jesus might have been referring to Isa 53.7–9 or to the broader Old Testament theme of a suffering Messiah. This verse combines God’s sovereign will with human responsibility.
Judas referred to Jesus as Rabbi, while the other disciples call him “Lord” (Mat 26.22). • “You have said it”: This enigmatic statement affirmed that Judas was the betrayer.

The Last Supper derives its significance in part from the Jewish Passover (see Exo 12.1–51). The phases of the Jewish liturgy for Passover are as follows: (1) Festal blessing; (2) first cup (see Luk 22.17–18); (3) eating bitter herbs (see Mat 26.23 and corresponding study note Mat 26.23); (4) eating unleavened bread (Mat 26.26; Mar 14.22); (5) second cup is mixed; (6) the Passover haggadah (reading) is given (Exo 12.1–51); (7) first part of the hallel (Psa 113.1–114; see study note on Psa 113–118 Psa 113.1–Mat 118.29); (8) second cup is taken; (9) blessing and eating of unleavened bread (Mat 26.26; Mar 14.22; Luk 22.19); (10) the Passover lamb is eaten; (11) third cup (Mat 26.27–28; Mar 14.23–24; Luk 22.20); (12) fourth cup (see Mat 26.29[?]; Mar 14.25[?]); (13) time of fellowship; (14) second part of the hallel (Psa 115.1–118; see Mat 26.30). None of the New Testament accounts of the Last Supper includes every aspect of a typical Jewish Passover. However, the most important aspects of the Passover that gave meaning to the early Christian celebration of the Lord’s Supper are included (see 1Co 11.23–25). Jesus, the Lamb of God, is the ultimate Passover lamb and the perfect sacrifice for sin. • this is my body . . . my blood: Ever since the Reformation, there have been three dominant interpretations of Jesus’ statements concerning the bread and the wine: (1) that the bread and wine change into the actual body and blood of Jesus Christ (transubstantiation); (2) that Christ is mysteriously present in the sacrament either spiritually (real presence) or “in, with, and under” the bread and wine (consubstantiation); (3) that the bread and wine symbolize the body and blood of Christ, benefiting the recipient through the Spirit by faith (symbolism).

The unleavened bread of the Passover (Exo 12.18) is also described as the “bread of suffering” (Deu 16.3), referring to hardships in Egypt. • The customary blessing over the bread in the Passover meal was “Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.”

He gave thanks. The traditional blessing for the Passover cup was “Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine.” An early Christian variant is, “We give thanks to you, our Father, for the Holy Vine of David, your child, whom you made known to us through Jesus your child; glory be to you forever” (Didache 9.2). • The four cups of the Passover meal correspond to the fourfold promise of Exo 6.6–7, with two for deliverance, one for redemption (see Mat 26.27–28), and one for fellowship (see Mat 26.29).

the covenant: Under God’s covenant with Israel, the blood of sheep or goats (Exo 12.5, Exo 12.13; Exo 24.8) was shed and placed on the two doorposts and on the lintel at Passover (Exo 12.7). The blood of Jesus, the sinless Lamb of God, establishes a new covenant (see Jer 31.31). The idea of the covenant is God’s unilateral commitment to establish salvation for mankind, fulfilling the promise to Abraham (see Gen 12.1–20; Gal 3.15–29; Gal 4.12–31). • to forgive the sins of many: Jesus shed his blood as a sacrifice for sin (see Jer 31.31–34; Mar 14.24). Some have understood many to refer only to God’s chosen people, while others have understood many to be an expression meaning “all” (cp. Mat 20.28).

until the day: Though the Kingdom had been inaugurated in Jesus’ ministry, it awaits final consummation (see 1Co 15.20–28; Rev 19.1–22). • until the day I drink it new: The final consummation of the Kingdom is pictured as a feast like the Passover, symbolizing an eternal fellowship of love and peace.
they sang a hymn: Some have suggested that the Great Hallel (Psa 136.1–26) was sung.

God will strike: In Zec 13.7–9, the Shepherd, God’s partner, is struck down (understood by Jesus as a prediction of his own death), and out of the scattered sheep emerge a purged, purified remnant of faithful ones (Zec 13.8–9). In the short term, the disciples would soon be scattered and deny association with Jesus (Mat 26.34, Mat 26.56, Mat 26.69–75).
Jesus foresaw a time of restoration for the disciples despite their imminent abandonment of him (see ch Mat 28.1–20; Joh 21.1–25).
While Peter’s denial receives the most attention, all the other disciples denied or avoided association with Christ as well (see Mat 26.56).

This scene reveals the depth of Jesus’ awareness of the suffering that awaited him on the cross, as well as his utter commitment to God’s will (see Mat 20.28). Expressions in Mat 26.41–42 echo the Lord’s Prayer (Mat 6.9–13).

Gethsemane is the name of an olive orchard approximately 250 yards east of Jerusalem’s Golden Gate, overlooking the Kidron Valley on the edge of the Mount of Olives. Jesus and his disciples apparently met there often (Luk 22.39–40; Joh 18.1–2).

He took Peter . . . James and John: These three, apparently the leaders of the apostles, received special revelation (Mat 17.1–13) and accompanied Jesus in this difficult hour. • Jesus became anguished and distressed from contemplating the Father’s plan for him, to absorb God’s wrath toward humans for their sin (see Mat 27.45–46).
crushed with grief: See Joh 12.27; cp. Psa 42.5–6, Psa 42.11; Psa 43.5.

If it is possible: Jesus’ heart’s desire was for uninterrupted communion with the Father instead of coming under God’s wrath. • Yet I want your will to be done: His resolution to do the Father’s will was firm (Mat 4.1–11; Mat 16.23; Joh 6.38).
Judas . . . gave him the kiss: Judas’s use of a sign of affection to betray Jesus amplifies the heinousness of his betrayal.
one of the men with Jesus: This was Peter (Joh 18.26).

thousands (literally twelve legions): Jesus used Roman military language (a legion consisted of approximately 6,000 soldiers) to describe the aid he could receive from God. Jesus was not a helpless victim; he permitted his own arrest.
For Jesus to have resisted would have impeded the fulfillment of God’s saving work (see Mat 16.21–23).
The leaders’ clandestine behavior was driven by fear of the masses who revered Jesus (see Mat 21.26, Mat 21.46; Mat 26.3–5).

It is not clear which of the Scriptures Jesus was alluding to—perhaps Isa 53.1–12, or perhaps the Old Testament theme of a suffering Messiah in general. • As Jesus had predicted earlier that evening, all the disciples deserted him (Mat 26.31–35).

The Gospels record Jesus as undergoing five hearings: (1) an informal hearing before Annas (Joh 18.13–24); (2) a night hearing before the Sanhedrin (Mat 26.59–66); (3) a morning hearing before the Sanhedrin (Mat 27.1–2); (4) a hearing before Herod Antipas (Luk 23.6–12); and (5) a two-stage trial before Pilate (Mat 27.11–31; see Luk 23.6–12). It all amounts to two trials, a Jewish trial and a Roman trial.

This hearing might have been little more than an unofficial preliminary hearing designed to establish consensus on the terms of the charges. The Jewish leaders were under considerable pressure to keep this incident secret, lest their actions cause a riot (see Mat 21.26, Mat 21.46; Mat 26.5, Mat 26.55; Joh 11.45–53).
Profile: The Jewish High Council
the high priest’s courtyard: This location suggests an ad hoc meeting of the Sanhedrin at the palace of the high priest (Mat 26.3).
were trying to find witnesses: The verb tense suggests an extended, perhaps desperate, attempt to find any testimony that could lead to a formal accusation (see Mar 14.55–56).

could not use anyone’s testimony: The evidence was too insubstantial or inconsistent to meet their goal of a death sentence until two men came forward (Deu 17.6; Deu 19.15) with testimonies that did not conflict.
The charge is either a misunderstanding or a deliberate distortion of Jesus’ prediction of his death and resurrection (see Joh 2.19–21).
if you are the Messiah: This question from the high priest was prompted by Zec 6.12, which had predicted that the Messiah would rebuild the Temple (cp. Mat 26.61).

You have said it: This purposefully enigmatic response is essentially an affirmative answer (see Mat 26.25; Mat 27.11); Mark has “I AM” (Mar 14.62). • you will see: By quoting Dan 7.13, Jesus affirmed that he was the Son of Man who would be vindicated and exalted by God. • seated in the place of power at God’s right hand: Literally seated at the right hand of the power; see Psa 110.1. Jews were reluctant to name God directly (see study note on Matt Mat 5.4). • The expression coming on the clouds of heaven could refer either to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 or to Jesus’ second coming at the end of history.
Blasphemy! Caiaphas evidently understood Jesus’ claim to be the exalted Son of Man as a blasphemy against God’s majesty. The Son of Man (Dan 7.13–14) was closely associated with this majesty.
Such abuse fulfills Isa 50.6; Isa 53.4–9 and Jesus’ own predictions (Mat 16.21; Mat 17.22–23; Mat 20.18–19; Mat 26.2; see also Mar 14.65).
Peter’s denials fulfill Jesus’ prediction (Mat 26.34).
your Galilean accent: Jews from Galilee had a distinctive accent, compared with those from Judea (cp. Mat 4.13 and corresponding study note Mat 4.13).
When the crowing of the rooster reminded Peter of Jesus’ prediction (Mat 26.34), he was struck with sorrow.
The Jewish leaders were ready to level charges against Jesus before Pilate so that he would order Jesus’ execution. Pilate, a Gentile, fulfills Jesus’ prediction (Mat 20.19).

The charge of blasphemy (Mat 26.65–66), though sufficient for the death penalty among Jews, would not convince a Roman judge. Hence, the leading priests and the elders conspired together to prepare a more political charge consistent with capital offenses in Roman law (see Mat 27.11–26; Luk 23.2).

Tiberius Caesar appointed Pilate to be the governor (or prefect) of Judea. Pilate ruled primarily from Caesarea, not Jerusalem, from AD 26 to AD 36. Though he had sovereign power in Judea, Pilate was ultimately responsible to the legate of Syria, the central authority in the eastern portion of the Roman Empire. Josephus records several instances where Pilate’s disregard for the sanctity of Jewish customs led to revolt.

There are two accounts of Judas’s death—this one and Act 1.18–19. There are differences between the two: (1) Matthew states that the priests bought the field (Mat 27.6–7), while Acts seems to suggest that Judas bought it (Act 1.18); (2) Matthew reports that Judas committed suicide by hanging himself (Mat 27.5), while Acts enigmatically refers to a fall and an abdominal rupture (Act 1.18); (3) Matthew implies that the field of blood was so named because it became a place of burial (Mat 27.7–8), while Acts suggests that it was because of Judas’s violent death there (Act 1.19). The two accounts are compatible if one takes the account in Acts as describing the effects of the actions described in Matthew.
Judas was filled with remorse (Greek metamelomai), but he did not repent (Greek metanoeō), which would have changed his heart and resulted in obedience and a relationship with God based on faith.
an innocent man: Jesus’ innocence is a dominant theme in the narrative of his suffering (see Mat 23.35; Mat 26.55–56, Mat 26.59–60; Mat 27.18–19, Mat 27.24; see also Luk 23.47).
hanged himself: Judas’s suicide resulted from a guilt-stricken, unrepentant conscience. His death satisfied Old Testament law regarding the punishment of a false witness (see Deu 19.16–21).

Foreigners were Gentiles who died in Jerusalem. An asset whose owner could not be traced was used for public charity. In this instance, unclean money was used to buy an unclean place for unclean people.
Field of Blood is a way of describing a cemetery (cp. Act 1.18–19).

the prophecy of Jeremiah: The citation is from Zec 11.12–13. Matthew might merely have been conforming to the Jewish custom of citing books by referring to the first book in the particular scroll—the first book in the scroll containing Zechariah would have been Jeremiah. Or, Matthew might have thought of similar passages in Jeremiah (Jer 19.1–13; Jer 18.2–6; Jer 32.6–15) along with Zec 11.12–13. • Matthew sees a striking resemblance between Zechariah’s actions and those of the leading priests. Both contexts deal with the rejection of God’s messenger who was to be king of God’s people.
The Roman trial included an initial hearing before Pilate (Mat 27.11–14), one before Herod Antipas (Luk 23.6–16), and a second hearing before Pilate (Mat 27.15–26).

king of the Jews: The Sanhedrin’s original charge of blasphemy (Mat 26.65–66; Mat 27.1) held no interest to the Romans, who saw it as a Jewish religious question (cp. Act 25.18–20). The charge was therefore changed to incriminate Jesus in Roman eyes as a political rebel (see Luk 23.2).

Pilate’s custom seems out of character; he was not known for wanting to please his Jewish subjects. However, if Pilate’s position with Caesar was precarious at this point (see study note on John Joh 19.12; see Philo, On the Embassy to Gaius 159–161), then this gesture may have been to keep the peace and thus avoid negative attention from Rome.

notorious prisoner . . . named Barabbas: Elsewhere he is called a “revolutionary” (Mar 15.7; Joh 18.40), a term that also denotes a robber or insurrectionist (see Luk 23.19). To the zealots, Barabbas was a hero.
through a terrible nightmare (cp. Mat 1.20): It is ironic that a pagan recognizes and takes a stand for Jesus’ innocence, while the Jewish crowd does not.
The responsibility is yours! The priests had said the same thing to Judas (Mat 27.4).

all the people (see Mat 21.43): This does not mean every living Jew. Instead, those urging Jesus’ condemnation are representative of all of unbelieving Israel, whose actions bring consequences for the nation as a whole (e.g., the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70). • We will take responsibility for his death—we and our children (see Mat 23.35; 2Sa 1.16; 2Sa 14.9; Jer 51.35; Act 5.28; Act 18.6; Act 20.26): Christians have at times misunderstood and misused this verse in persecution of Jews, but it is not an indictment against Jews in general.

When a man was flogged, he was beaten with whips that had leather thongs at the end, some with sharp bone, lead, or rock fragments stuck to the ends of the thongs (see also Deu 25.1–3; 1Ki 12.11, 1Ki 12.14; Act 16.22; Act 22.25; 2Co 11.24–25).
In the Jewish trial Jesus was mocked as a prophet (Mat 26.67–68); here he is mocked as a king.

The governor’s soldiers were auxiliary troops recruited from non-Jewish residents of Palestine. • Their headquarters was located at the official residence of the governor in Jerusalem (the Antonia Fortress on the northwest corner of the Temple compound).
The scarlet robe was probably the cloak of a soldier meant to emulate royal garb solely for the purpose of ridiculing Jesus. • Weaving thorn branches into a crown was a mockery of Jesus as king.
Ironically, the taunts and ridicule of the crowd express the truth about Jesus: He is the Son of God and King of Israel, the Messiah.

Normally, the victim carried his own cross. Only the crossbeam was carried; the vertical pole would be waiting at the crucifixion site. Simon might have been forced because Jesus was weak from the effects of scourging. The act of enlisting Simon might also have been a further mockery. Jesus was treated as one who deserved a servant even though he was being marched to his death.

Giving Jesus wine mixed with bitter gall was probably intended for ridicule (see Psa 69.21). It was also a sedative—Jesus probably rejected it in order to suffer fully for our sins (see Isa 53.10). • Gall, otherwise known as wormwood, is a bitter narcotic made from the oil of Artemisia (cp. Mar 15.23).

they . . . nailed him to the cross: Crucifixion, though not generally practiced by Jews, was a widespread Roman punishment for military and political offenders, particularly slaves, rebels, and insurrectionists. The sheer cruelty and the public spectacle of crucifixion worked as a powerful social deterrent. Victims were flogged and then crucified naked, adding to the humiliation. It was seen as the most painful of all possible deaths; it involved intense suffering, exposure to weather and insects, suffocation, and often a final violent thrust of a spear to end life. Further, since crucifixion was a curse from God (Deu 21.22–23), the act was particularly heinous to Jewish sensibilities. Paradoxically, what was so despicable among humans has become the instrument of our salvation. Jesus previously had instructed his disciples to take up their crosses and follow him (Mat 16.24).
The official charge was fastened to the cross above the criminal’s head; Jesus was crucified for political sedition.
Crucifying Jesus between two convicted revolutionaries added further humiliation and guilt by association.

if you are the Son of God: This taunt recalls Jesus’ temptation at the very beginning of his public ministry (Mat 4.1–11), in which the devil appealed to Jesus’ privileged status in order to tempt him to avoid suffering (see also Mat 16.21–23).
Darkness symbolizes the judgment of God or, more specifically, the arrival of the day of the Lord (see Amo 5.18, Amo 5.20; Amo 8.9–10; also Jer 4.27–28; Jer 13.16; Jer 15.9).

Eli, Eli: This cry means My God, my God, but the similarity in sound accounts for the people’s confusion (Mat 27.47). • My God, my God, why have you abandoned me? Jesus was experiencing God’s wrath for the sins of humanity.
It was widely believed that Elijah would return before the day of the Lord (Mat 11.14–15; Mat 17.10–13; Mal 4.5).

The sour wine was vinegar. The drink was probably designed to mock Jesus (cp. Psa 69.21 with Mat 27.34) by pretending to help assuage his thirst. Others have suggested that it was given as an act of genuine kindness.

Each of the four Gospels highlights different aspects of Jesus’ last moments. • released his spirit: This emphasizes the sovereignty of Jesus in that he released himself to death (see also Joh 19.30). • shouted out again (see Mat 27.46): This cry was Jesus’ final prayer (see Luk 23.46).

The significance of the splitting of the curtain in the Temple is that the wall dividing people from God has been torn down by the death of Jesus Christ (see also Eph 2.11–22; Heb 6.19; Heb 9.1–Mat 10.25). • The earth shook, rocks split apart: These are portents of the arrival of judgment (see Exo 19.18; Jdg 5.4; Psa 18.7; Joe 3.14–17; Amo 8.8–10). Josephus records the appearance about AD 30 of a star resembling a sword and a spontaneous opening of the gates of the Temple (Josephus, War 6.5.3-4).

tombs opened: Jesus’ climactic death inaugurated the Kingdom of God by breaking the powers of death and establishing the final resurrection (see Isa 26.19; Dan 12.2; 1Co 15.1–58; Col 1.18; Heb 2.14–15). • These godly ones either did not enter the city until after Jesus’ resurrection or they were not raised until then, with Jesus as the firstfruits (see 1Co 15.20, 1Co 15.23; Col 1.18). If that is the case, Matthew has included this episode to form a more powerful commentary on the impact of Jesus’ death.

The Roman officer and the other soldiers were Gentiles. • the Son of God: This may be an unqualified affirmation that Jesus is the unique Son of God (see Mat 14.33; Mat 16.16) or possibly a more general affirmation of Jesus’ innocence (see Luk 23.47). They are responding to the earthquake and all that had happened as evidence of divine interest in this occasion.
Profile: Women Named Mary

In Roman crucifixion, the bodies of criminals were often left to rot. Deu 21.22–23 prohibits a body from remaining on a cross or a gallows overnight. Joseph’s action was in accordance with Jewish law, while his motivation was probably his loyalty to Jesus. • Pilate issued an order: Pilate was accommodating, probably because he did not believe Jesus was guilty of insurrection (see Mat 27.24–26).

Burial customs were important in Judaism, especially in contrast to the Greeks and Romans, who cremated their dead. Leaving a corpse unburied was the severest form of judgment (Deu 21.22–23; 2Ki 9.37; Psa 79.3; Jer 16.4, Jer 16.6; Eze 29.5; Rev 11.9). Death was lamented and mourned (Mar 5.38–39); the body was washed (Act 9.37), anointed (Mat 26.6–13; Joh 12.3, Joh 12.7; Joh 19.39), and wrapped in burial cloths (Mat 27.59; see Gen 50.2–3). The body was placed in a tomb (see Mat 23.27) that had been tunneled into a rock or carved into the side of a cave wall. The entrance to a tomb was often closed with a huge stone and sealed to prevent ceremonial uncleanness or robbery. • clean linen . . . new tomb: Both reflect ceremonial purity. Joseph had purchased the tomb for his own family, but it had not yet been used.
This incident bolsters the truth of Jesus’ resurrection—it is inconceivable that Matthew would fabricate such a story since witnesses abounded who could have countered the claims.

The discovery of the empty tomb and the various resurrection appearances are presented with different emphases in each of the four Gospels. Matthew focuses on the reunion in Galilee, the attempt on the part of the Jewish leaders to discredit the resurrection, and the significance of the resurrection for the salvation of the world.

Mary Magdalene (see Mat 27.56): The mention of two women as witnesses lends credibility to the historicity of the account—an inventor of tales would not have used women as witnesses, since a woman’s testimony was considered less reliable than a man’s.
Theme: The Resurrection of Jesus
Such a bribe was contrary to the law (see Exo 20.16; Exo 23.8). • elders: See study note on Matt Mat 21.23.
stole his body: Tomb robbery was a common problem in the ancient world, so such an accusation would have been entirely believable.

still tell it today: Justin Martyr wrote to Jews of his day (about AD 165), “You have sent . . . men throughout all the world to proclaim, ‘A godless and lawless heresy has sprung from one Jesus, a Galilean deceiver, whom we crucified, but his disciples stole him by night from the tomb . . . and now [the disciples] deceive men by asserting that he has risen from the dead and ascended into heaven’” (Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 108). This misinformation probably became widespread after the disciples began to proclaim Jesus’ resurrection (see Act 2.22–36).

some of them doubted: This might be a veiled reference to Thomas (Joh 20.24–29), but all eleven might have experienced a mixture of both worship and doubt (see also Mat 14.31; Luk 24.10–11; Joh 20.24–29).
Jesus’ authority is power delegated from the Father (see Mat 7.29; Mat 9.6–8; Mat 21.23–27; Mat 26.64; Joh 3.35).

go and: Literally going, a participle that supports the main imperative, make disciples. Matthew probably intended go to be understood as a separate command (as it is translated) and not as a circumstantial modifier (i.e., while you go; cp. the same construction in Mat 9.6; Act 10.20). • make disciples: A disciple is one who repents of sin, trusts in Jesus for salvation, and obeys his teachings. • all the nations: The mission to the Gentile nations formally began here (see Mat 10.5–6; Mat 15.24; see also Mat 1.1; Mat 2.1–12; Mat 8.5–13; Mat 21.43; Mat 24.14; Mat 26.13). • Two aspects of making disciples are baptizing and teaching (Mat 28.20).. Baptism indicates public identification with, and surrender to, Jesus and the work he has done for salvation (see Mat 3.13–17; Mat 10.32–33; Mat 20.28; Mat 26.28; Act 2.38; Rom 6.1–11; 1Pe 3.21). • In the name of means entrance into a relationship and its benefits, which come to those who truly believe. • Father . . . Son . . . Holy Spirit: This is a formulaic expression for the nature of God as a trinity (see also 1Co 12.4–6; 2Co 13.14; Eph 4.4–6; 2Th 2.13–14; 1Pe 1.2; Rev 1.4–6).

Teach: The disciples’ curriculum is comprised of all the commands of Jesus (e.g., the Sermon on the Mount, chs Mat 5.1–7). The church is to be marked by its obedience to Jesus’ commands (Mat 5.17–20; Mat 7.13–27). Jesus’ authority and presence are the basis for the disciples’ mission (see also Mat 1.23; Mat 18.20).

The Gospel of Mark

Purpose

To relay the Good News about Jesus, who is the Messiah and Son of God

Author

John Mark, who according to early tradition put in writing the recollections of the apostle Peter

Date

Likely written sometime during the late 60s AD

Setting

Written at a time in which Christians in the Roman world were facing persecution—necessitating that the gospel traditions begin to be written down—and Jerusalem’s destruction was imminent

In his opening verse, Mark provides readers with the main key to understanding his Gospel: Although we can learn much about the disciples and other characters from reading Mark, it is most important to understand what he is teaching about Jesus: Jesus is “the Messiah, the Son of God” (Mar 1.1).

Setting

It is generally agreed that Mark was the first of the four canonical Gospels to be written. Before the writing of Mark, there were no Gospels as such. The gospel traditions were circulated or “delivered” orally under the supervision of the eyewitnesses and ministers of the word of God (Luk 1.2). As these eyewitnesses began to die, it became important to record the gospel traditions in writing. According to church tradition, after the martyrdom of Peter in the mid-60s AD, the church in Rome asked John Mark to put into writing the accounts of Jesus’ life and teachings that Peter had delivered to them orally. As a result, Mark became the first to compose what we call a “Gospel,” a written account of Jesus’ life and teachings, from the oral materials about Jesus.

Summary

The overall structure of Mark is geographical. The first nine chapters narrate events of Jesus’ ministry in Galilee and its environs. In Mar 10.1–52, Jesus and the disciples travel from Galilee to Jerusalem, and the last chapters of the book (Mar 11.1–Mar 16.20) take place in and around Jerusalem. (Matthew and Luke, in their use of Mark, followed this geographical outline, but John organized his Gospel in a different way.)

Within the geographical outline, Mark has arranged much of his material topically. Thus we have collections of miracle stories (Mar 1.21–45; Mar 4.35–Mar 5.43), controversy stories (Mar 2.1–Mar 3.6; Mar 12.13–37), parables (Mar 4.1–34), and teachings about the end (Mar 13.5–37). Some of the materials include indicators of chronological sequence: Jesus’ ministry began with his baptism (Mar 1.2–11; see Act 1.22; Act 10.37) and temptation (Mar 1.12–13); his suffering, death, and resurrection occurred at the end (Mar 11.1–Mar 16.8). A few individual accounts are tied together chronologically, such as Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi (Mar 8.27–33) and Jesus’ transfiguration (Mar 9.1–13; see also Mar 1.29, Mar 1.35).

The major turning point in Jesus’ ministry is highlighted in Mar 8.27–33, very near the center of the book. At Caesarea Philippi, the disciples confess for the first time their belief that Jesus is the Messiah (Mar 8.29). Upon this acknowledgment, Jesus “began to tell them” of his forthcoming death and resurrection (Mar 8.31; cp. Mat 16.21). Jesus’ death and resurrection are the dominant theme of Mar 8.31–Mar 16.8.

Author

The earliest known reference to the authorship of Mark comes from Papias at the beginning of the second century. The early church historian Eusebius quotes Papias as having said, “Mark became Peter’s interpreter and wrote accurately all that he remembered, not, indeed, in order, of the things said or done by the Lord. For he had not heard the Lord, nor had he followed him, but later on . . . followed Peter” (Eusebius, Church History 3.39.16).

The early church was unanimous in attributing this Gospel to John Mark. It is unlikely that Papias and others would have attributed this Gospel to a non-apostle with a tarnished reputation (see Act 13.13; Act 15.36–41) unless Mark were in fact the author.

The author of this Gospel was bilingual, as the Aramaic phrases in its Greek text suggest (e.g., Mar 5.41; Mar 7.34; Mar 15.34). He was also Jewish, in that he knew and explained various Jewish customs to his Gentile readers (e.g., Mar 7.3–4; Mar 14.12). John Mark was indeed a Jew who was raised in Jerusalem (Act 12.12). He thus knew Aramaic (the native language of the people of Judea) and was familiar with Jewish customs.

Some have objected that this Gospel does not clearly indicate a connection between Mark and Peter and that it looks more polished as a literary composition than one might expect from a direct record of Peter’s eyewitness testimony. But if this Gospel was written near or after Peter’s death (see “Date” below), Peter had been telling these stories for over thirty years. Through continual retelling, his gospel account would have been become well polished. There are also references to Peter in this Gospel that might be due to Mark’s personal connection with him (e.g., Mar 1.16–20; Mar 8.32–33; Mar 9.5–6; Mar 14.28–31, Mar 14.66–72). It fits the evidence well to consider this Gospel as having indeed been written by John Mark, Barnabas’s cousin, based on Peter’s gospel accounts.

Date

John Mark probably wrote down Peter’s teaching about Jesus around the time of Peter’s death. Peter died in Rome around AD 64 in the persecution that Nero waged against Christians. Mark probably wrote this Gospel in the late 60s, and a couple of considerations support this hypothesis. (1) The emphasis on faithfulness in time of persecution (Mar 4.17; Mar 8.34–38; Mar 10.30; Mar 13.9–13) suggests a time during or shortly after Nero’s persecution in the mid-60s. And (2) The discourse of Jesus recorded in chapter Mar 13.1–37 suggests that the destruction of Jerusalem was rapidly drawing near—the Jewish revolt (AD 66–73) had probably already begun.

Audience

The Gospel of Mark was written for the church in Rome, according to tradition. It is clear that the original readers were Greek-speaking and that they were Gentiles, because the author explains Jewish customs (e.g., Mar 7.3–4; Mar 14.12) and distinguishes his readers from “the Jews” (Mar 7.3).

The original readers were Christians. They were familiar with the gospel traditions, for the author does not explain various Old Testament references (Mar 2.25–26) or such things as who John the Baptist was (Mar 1.2–8), who Isaiah the prophet was (Mar 1.2), or who the Pharisees and teachers of religious law were (Mar 7.1).

It is also apparent that the readers were Romans, as indicated by the “Latinisms” in Mark. In Mar 6.27, he uses a Latin word meaning “soldier”; in Mar 12.42, he uses a Roman coin (the quadran) to explain the meaning of “two lepta” (Greek coins); and in Mar 15.39, Mar 15.44–45, he uses the Latin word “centurion” rather than the Greek word with the same meaning that Matthew and Luke use.

Literary Features

Mark’s own editorial work can be seen most clearly in his introductory statements (e.g., Mar 1.21–22; Mar 2.1; Mar 4.1; Mar 7.1), in his explanatory comments (e.g., Mar 1.16; Mar 2.15; Mar 5.8, Mar 5.28, Mar 5.42; Mar 6.14, Mar 6.17, Mar 6.20, Mar 6.52; Mar 7.3–4), and in his summaries (e.g., Mar 1.14–15, Mar 1.34, Mar 1.39; Mar 3.7–12; Mar 6.53–56).

Mark repeats various terms and expressions to show progress, such as “suddenly,” “at once,” and “immediately” (e.g., Mar 1.23; Mar 3.6; Mar 6.45). He uses the Greek present tense in the narrative, rather than a simple past tense, to give a sense of immediacy (e.g., Mar 1.12, Mar 1.21, Mar 1.38, Mar 1.40, Mar 1.44; Mar 2.3; Mar 3.13). Mark also often sandwiches one story within another (e.g., Mar 3.22–30 into Mar 3.20–21, Mar 3.31–35; Mar 5.25–34 into Mar 5.21–24, Mar 5.35–43; Mar 11.15–19 into Mar 11.12–14, Mar 11.20–26); in the last example, this sandwiching indicates that the middle part (Mar 11.15–19, the cleansing of the Temple) is to be understood in light of the story surrounding it (Mar 11.12–14, Mar 11.20–26, the cursing of the fig tree)—the cleansing of the Temple was a symbolic act of judgment (cp. Mar 13.3–37). Thus, Mark’s editorial work relates different events and shows meaningful connections.

Meaning and Message

The Person of Christ. Mark’s major theological emphasis is the identity of Jesus of Nazareth. This emphasis is stated in the opening verse of the Gospel: Mark wanted his readers to know that Jesus of Nazareth is “the Messiah, the Son of God.” The title “Son of God” occurs frequently in Mark, and there are diverse witnesses to Jesus’ status as God’s son: the demons (Mar 1.34; Mar 3.11; Mar 5.7; cp. Mar 1.24); God himself (Mar 1.11; Mar 9.7); Mark, the author (Mar 1.1); a Roman centurion (Mar 15.39); and Jesus himself (Mar 12.6; Mar 13.32; Mar 14.61–62). Other titles for Jesus occur in Mark’s Gospel, including Jesus’ own favorite, “Son of Man” (e.g., Mar 2.10). But in Mark’s Gospel all of these titles, as well as his actions (e.g., Mar 1.22; Mar 4.41), point to his identity as the Christ (or Messiah), the Son of God.

During his life, the Son of God needed to protect himself and his followers from the prevailing misconceptions in the minds of the people about what the term “Christ” (or “Messiah”) meant (see “The Secret of the Messiah” below). Jesus’ ultimate mission as the Son of God is explained through his death, in which he gave his life as a ransom for many. The call to Christian discipleship is a call to follow the Messiah, the Son of God, especially in his servanthood and sacrifice. Jesus’ ministry as Son of God during his life on earth also points forward to his return as the Son of God, ruling God’s Kingdom.

The Death of Jesus. The Gospel of Mark puts a lot of emphasis on the account of Jesus’ passion—his suffering, death, and resurrection. Throughout the Gospel we find numerous references to the death of Jesus (Mar 2.19–20; Mar 3.6; Mar 8.31; Mar 9.9, Mar 9.12, Mar 9.31; Mar 10.33–34, Mar 10.45; Mar 12.1–11; Mar 14.1–11, Mar 14.21, Mar 14.24–25, Mar 14.36, Mar 14.64–Mar 15.47). Mark emphasizes that Jesus’ death was part of God’s plan. His death was a divine necessity (Mar 8.31), for God had willed it (Mar 10.45; Mar 14.36). The Old Testament also teaches of the Messiah’s death (see Mar 9.12; Mar 14.21, Mar 14.27, Mar 14.49). Jesus came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mar 10.45) and to pour out his blood sacrificially in order to establish a new covenant (Mar 14.24).

Christian Discipleship. Mark emphasizes the importance of following Jesus by denying oneself and taking up one’s cross (see Mar 8.34). Christian discipleship does not permit a half-hearted response but requires leaving everything to follow Jesus (Mar 1.18, Mar 1.20; Mar 10.21, Mar 10.29). Christian discipleship might even bring persecution and martyrdom (Mar 13.9–13a), but Christians are promised that endurance in faith means salvation (Mar 13.13) and eternal life (Mar 10.30).

The “Secret of the Messiah.” Throughout Mark’s Gospel, Jesus tells others not to broadcast his true identity. This is likely because of the tendency for people to misunderstand who he is and what he has come to do. Yet the secret is not and cannot be kept (Mar 7.36). Jesus creates such wonder and amazement that he simply cannot remain hidden. But while the characters in the story struggle to grasp Jesus’ identity correctly, Mark’s readers have the privilege of understanding the full picture of Jesus’ identity in light of his death and resurrection.

The Coming of God’s Kingdom. The arrival of God’s Kingdom is central to Jesus’ message. People need to repent and believe the gospel because the Kingdom of God has arrived (Mar 1.14–15). Old Testament promises are being fulfilled. Life in the Kingdom is different from what it was during the time awaiting the Kingdom.

Mark opens with an introduction. This Gospel is about Jesus. With every account in Mark, one should ask, “What is Mark teaching about Jesus in this passage?” • Good News, a frequent term in Mark (see Mar 1.14–15; Mar 8.35; Mar 10.29; Mar 13.10; Mar 14.9), is frequently translated gospel. See study note on Mark Mar 1.15. • The Hebrew word mashiakh (Messiah) is equivalent to the Greek term christos (Christ). Both words mean “anointed.” In the Old Testament, priests (Exo 28.41; Lev 16.32; Lev 21.10), kings (2Sa 1.14, 2Sa 1.16; 2Sa 19.21; Psa 2.1–12), and prophets (1Ki 19.16) were anointed with oil to indicate the Lord’s presence, blessing, and authority for the tasks to which God called them. As time went on, Israelites increasingly looked forward to the coming of the Messiah, “the Anointed One,” a descendant of David who would be Israel’s king. The first-century political connotations of this title were such that Jesus avoided openly declaring that he was the Messiah (see Mar 3.11–12; Mar 8.27–30; Mar 14.61–63; Mar 15.2, Mar 15.26; Joh 4.25–26). • the Son of God: This title emphasizes Jesus’ unique relationship with God the Father (Mar 1.11; Mar 9.7; Mar 12.4–6; Mar 14.61–62).
This account is not primarily about John the Baptist, the messenger, but about the one he announces as “Jesus the Messiah, the Son of God” (Mar 1.1).

Mark includes Old Testament prophecies to support his account of the Good News about Jesus Christ. John the Baptist’s role as the prophetic messenger reveals that Jesus is the promised Lord—Christ, the Son of God. • Isaiah: Mark follows the Jewish practice of mentioning only the most prominent of the sources that make up the quotation (Mal 3.1; Isa 40.3).

John the Baptist was the voice shouting in the wilderness for people to prepare the way for the LORD’s coming. In Isaiah, this prophecy refers to the coming of the Lord, the God of Israel. Here it refers to the Lord Jesus (see Mar 12.35–37). The early church called itself “the Way,” probably in reference to this promise (see Act 9.2; Act 19.9, Act 19.23; Act 22.4; Act 24.14, Act 24.22; cp. Act 2.28; Act 18.25–26; Rom 2.20; 2Pe 2.2, 2Pe 2.21).

John’s mission as the Lord’s messenger was to prepare people for the Messiah’s coming (see Luk 1.76–77) by instructing them to confess their sins, turn to God for forgiveness, and be baptized. Those who did this were prepared to receive Jesus’ message (see Luk 7.29–30). • That John was in the wilderness, probably the desert area around the Jordan River north of the Dead Sea, shows that he was the “voice” of whom Isaiah had spoken (Mar 1.3). • be baptized: The exact origin of John’s baptism is unclear. The Qumran community had an initiatory “baptism” which was repeated regularly, but John’s baptism was once for all. Jewish proselyte baptism has also been seen as a possible source, but it is more likely that such baptisms were not practiced until after John’s ministry.

All of Judea: John the Baptist created a lot of interest. It was generally believed that there had been no prophet for over 400 years, so prophets were associated with Israel’s past and with the future reign of the Messiah. John preached repentance like the ancient prophets, and he dressed like the great prophet Elijah (Mar 1.6), who was predicted to return in the last days (Mal 4.5).
camel hair . . . leather belt: Cp. Elijah (2Ki 1.8). • For food John ate what was available in the wilderness; locusts were allowed as food (cp. Lev 11.20–24).
Someone is coming: John knew that he was preparing for the Messiah’s coming, but he did not yet know that Jesus was he (cp. Luk 7.18–23).

John’s baptism prepared people for God’s Kingdom by calling them to repentance. The baptism of Jesus brought the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom sinful people become God’s children (Rom 8.15–16; 1Co 12.13; Gal 4.6).

Jesus’ home at this time was in Nazareth, a small town in lower Galilee (Mat 2.19–23; Luk 2.39). Jesus soon left Nazareth for Capernaum, a city on the Sea of Galilee (Mat 4.13). • John baptized him: Jesus’ reason for receiving the baptism of repentance is explained in Mat 3.14–15.

The expression the heavens splitting apart indicates Jesus’ unique access to God the Father; in Mar 15.38, the same verb includes believers in that access through Jesus’ death. • All four Gospels refer to the Spirit descending on him like a dove. The Spirit, who was involved in the first creation, acted with Jesus in bringing the new creation (Gen 1.2; Rom 8.15–17; 1Co 6.11; Eph 1.13–14; 2Th 2.13).
You are my dearly loved Son: By age twelve, Jesus was aware of his unique relationship with God the Father (Luk 2.49).

The Spirit then compelled Jesus (cp. Mat 4.1; Luk 4.1): Jesus was victorious over Satan and temptation from the beginning of his ministry; the later exorcisms (Mar 1.21–34; Mar 3.11–12; Mar 5.1–20; Mar 9.14–27) are an outworking of that victory (see Mar 3.27). • Jesus was tempted in the wilderness of Judea. Satan and wild animals (Isa 13.19–22; Eze 34.25) give the wilderness an evil aura. The wild animals included dogs, wolves, leopards, jackals, and bears. • The period of forty days recalls Israel’s forty years of testing in the wilderness. Israel failed, but Jesus was victorious—he was tempted without sinning (Heb 2.18; Heb 4.15; cp. Jam 1.3, Jam 1.12; 1Pe 1.7; Rev 2.10).
This summary introduces Mar 1.14–Mar 3.6. Such summaries (see also Mar 3.7–12; Mar 6.6) help hearers understand what follows; most of Mark’s original audience would have heard the Gospel read aloud.

Jesus’ ministry is described as beginning after John was arrested. There was some overlap (Joh 3.22–24; Joh 4.1–2), but most of Jesus’ ministry occurred after John’s. John also belongs primarily to the old order (Mat 11.7–14), while Jesus belongs primarily to the new. Both men fulfilled God’s plan through being arrested and executed (Mar 6.14–29; Mar 9.31; Mar 10.33). Jesus began preaching in Galilee at this time, but Joh 2.13–Mar 4.43 suggests that Jesus had had an earlier ministry in Judea.
Theme: The Coming of God’s Kingdom

Jesus’ preaching is summarized by his announcement that the Kingdom of God had come, and that people needed to repent and believe the Good News about the Messiah (Mar 1.1). • The Kingdom of God is not tied to a territory; it dynamically began in Jesus’ person and extended to his followers. • In response to the arrival of God’s Kingdom, people are called to repent (to turn from sin and yield to God) and to have faith in God’s Good News. In Jesus’ time, the Good News was the arrival of God’s reign through the Messiah. For Mark’s later audience, it was the news of Jesus’ death, resurrection, ascension, and promised return (Mar 15.1–Mar 16.8). All people, Jews and Gentiles alike, need God’s forgiveness through repentance and faith in Jesus.
The call of the two pairs of brothers—Simon and Andrew, James and John—followed an earlier encounter with Jesus (Joh 1.35–42).

Mark uses Jesus’ invitation—Come, follow me (Mar 1.20; Mar 8.34)—and the expression “to follow him” (Mar 1.18; Mar 2.14–15; Mar 3.7; Mar 5.24) to indicate what it means to be a Christian (see “Following Jesus” Theme Note).
Zebedee’s sons . . . leaving their father: Jesus later taught that this is the kind of thing that his followers will do (Mar 8.34–35; Mat 10.37–39).

Jesus’ exorcisms reveal Jesus’ identity and his power over Satan (see study notes on Mark Mar 1.12–13 and Mar 3.27; see also Mar 1.34, Mar 1.39; Mar 3.11–12, Mar 3.22; Mar 5.1–20; Mar 6.13; Mar 7.24–30; Mar 9.14–29).

Mark introduces his first account of an exorcism with Jesus and his companions going into the synagogue in Capernaum. Jesus’ teaching in the synagogue suggests that he already had a reputation as a teacher and was therefore invited to speak (cp. Act 13.15).

The teachers of religious law were professional scribes—scholars who taught, copied, and interpreted Jewish law for the people. They were primarily associated with the Pharisees. The scribes’ authority was derived from quoting other scribes (cp. Mat 5.21–48). Jesus’ teaching caused amazement because he spoke and acted with real authority (see Mar 1.27; Mar 5.20; Mar 6.2; Mar 7.37; Mar 10.24–32; Mar 11.18; Mar 15.5).

The demon spoke through the man who was possessed by an evil spirit (Mar 1.24). Demons frequently cause disease (Mar 9.17, Mar 9.27; Mat 17.15) and self-destructive behavior (Mar 1.26; Mar 5.2–5; Mar 9.17–18, Mar 9.20–22). Demons know who Jesus is (Mar 1.34); they consistently testify that he is the Holy One of God (see Mar 3.11; Mar 5.7). • In saying us, the evil spirit spoke on behalf of all demons. It recognized Jesus’ complete authority and understood that he had come to interfere with and destroy evil.

Jesus did not need to shout or utter magic words. He simply spoke with the authority of the Son of God (Mar 1.1), and the evil spirit obeyed. • Be quiet! Jesus commanded the evil spirit not to make him known. This is an instance of the “messianic secret,” an expression for passages in Mark in which Jesus commands demons or people not to reveal his identity (Mar 1.25, Mar 1.34; Mar 3.11–12; Mar 8.30; Mar 9.9).
The screams and convulsions caused by the evil (literally unclean; also in Mar 1.27) spirit were its parting cries of defeat (Mar 5.13; Mar 9.26; cp. Mar 15.37).

The amazement caused by this exorcism quickly led to the spread of the news about Jesus. • What sort of new teaching is this? Jesus’ healings and exorcisms were understood holistically as being part of his teaching (Mar 1.21–22, Mar 1.27; cp. Mar 1.38–39; Mar 3.14–15; Mar 6.2, Mar 6.5, Mar 6.12–13, Mar 6.30).
Simon (Peter) was married (see 1Co 9.5).
Jesus healed Simon’s mother-in-law instantaneously (see also Mar 1.40–45; Mar 2.1–12; Mar 3.1–6; Mar 5.25–34; Mar 7.31–37; Mar 8.22–26; Mar 10.46–52).
These public healings took place after sunset following the Sabbath (Mar 1.21, Mar 1.29), and there were many witnesses (see also Mar 1.39; Mar 3.10–11; Mar 6.5, Mar 6.53–56).
Jesus’ popularity among the crowds was growing (also in Mar 1.37, Mar 1.39, Mar 1.45), as contrasted with the growing rejection by the leaders (Mar 2.1–Mar 3.6).
the demons knew who he was: See Mar 1.23–25.

Despite Jesus’ busy ministry, he sought time to pray (Mar 6.46; Mar 14.32–39). Mark emphasizes the importance of prayer in Jesus’ life (cp. Luk 3.21; Luk 6.12; Luk 9.18, Luk 9.28–29; Luk 11.1–4; Luk 18.1; Luk 22.32).

Prayer (Mar 1.35) equipped Jesus to preach, teach, heal, and cast out demons. • Jesus’ mission in Galilee centered on preaching in the synagogues, where he took the opportunity to speak (Mar 1.21; Luk 4.16–30). Paul later used this same opportunity (Act 13.5, Act 13.14–15; Act 14.1; Act 16.13; Act 17.1). • Jesus counted on Jewish hospitality when he traveled (cp. Mar 6.10; Gen 18.1–8; Gen 19.1–8; Luk 10.7; Heb 13.2; 3Jo 1.5–8). • The region of Galilee was roughly forty miles north to south and twenty-five miles east to west (sixty-five by forty kilometers). In Jesus’ day, Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas.

Leprosy refers to a number of skin diseases (or even mildew in a building). An infected person was considered unclean and was ostracized from family and society (Lev 13.45–46; Num 12.9–12; 2Ch 26.16–21; Luk 17.12).
Jesus’ willingness to touch a ceremonially unclean leper reflects the new order of the Kingdom of God (Mar 1.15; Mar 5.25–34; Luk 7.36–50; see Mat 10.8; Mat 11.5).

Jesus told the man to go to the priest to certify his healing and to make the appropriate sacrificial offering. This would be the public testimony of his healing. • Despite Jesus’ stern warning, . . . the man went and spread the word, so that Jesus was not able to go into town but had to preach in more secluded places. Jesus’ fame could not be confined as people from everywhere came to see him (Mar 3.7–8).
Five controversy stories (Mar 2.1–12, Mar 2.13–17, Mar 2.18–22, Mar 2.23–28; Mar 3.1–6), grouped by their common theme, reveal Jesus’ great authority and the leaders’ hostility toward him.
This controversy story is also a miracle story, which links it to the previous collection (Mar 1.21–45).
back home: See Mat 4.13. The crowd’s size shows Jesus’ popularity.
because of the crowd: See Mar 2.1. • The roof would have been flat, constructed of mud, thatch, and branches. They literally dug a hole to make an opening.
Jesus saw the faith of the paralytic and the four men who brought him. • your sins are forgiven: Those listening understood Jesus’ words as a claim to divine authority (Mar 2.6–10; Luk 7.48–49).
Only God can forgive sins, yet Jesus had authority to do so (Mar 2.10).

It is easier to say . . . your sins are forgiven because this claim cannot be directly proved or disproved, while the claim to heal can be. Jesus showed his ability to heal in order to show his authority to forgive.
We’ve never seen anything like this before! Mark consistently records Jesus creating amazement (Mar 1.22, Mar 1.27; Mar 4.41; Mar 6.50–51).
This controversy centers on Jesus’ befriending disreputable sinners such as tax collectors and eating with them.

Levi was also called Matthew (cp. Mat 9.9–10). Certain people are known by two names in the New Testament (e.g., Simon=Peter; Saul=Paul; Judas son of James=Thaddaeus, see study note on Mark Mar 3.18). • This kind of tax collector (Greek telōnēs) collected sales taxes, customs, and road tolls, in contrast with those who collected the poll tax (Mar 12.14). Local tax collectors like Levi were hated by other Jews because they often gouged the public (Luk 19.8), and as agents of the Romans, they were regarded as traitors. Jesus invited Levi, a tax collector, to follow him, joining Peter, Andrew, James, and John (Mar 1.16–20).

The teachers of religious law who were Pharisees understood Jesus’ act of eating with sinners as intentionally accepting them as friends (Luk 15.1–2; Luk 19.5, Luk 19.7; Act 11.2–18; Gal 2.11–12). Jesus indicated that these tax collectors and sinners were invited to share in the Kingdom of God. In Jesus’ ministry, even Gentiles were invited to share the Kingdom (Mar 5.1–20; Mar 7.24–30; cp. Mat 8.5–13; Luk 7.1–10; Joh 4.43–54).

Jesus answered his opponents with a well-known proverb, comparing himself to a doctor and sinners to sick people. Salvation is for those who know they are sinners, not those who think they are righteous (Luk 16.15; Luk 18.9; Rom 3.23).

This controversy deals with fasting, which Jesus did not practice with his disciples. The Pharisees regularly fasted two days a week, on Mondays and Thursdays (Luk 18.12), and Jews often fasted when mourning or specially seeking the Lord’s favor (Lev 16.29–31; 1Sa 31.13; 2Sa 1.12; 2Sa 12.21–23; Ezr 8.23; Est 4.3; Mat 6.16).

Jesus was like a groom at his wedding, so fasting was inappropriate. It was a time for celebration (Luk 15.23–25, Luk 15.32). The disciples would fast when Jesus was taken away by death (see Act 13.2–3; Act 14.23).

Old customs of the old covenant are incompatible with the new arrival of God’s Kingdom. Common experience shows that an unshrunken new patch sewn on old clothing will tear the old cloth as it shrinks. Similarly, brittle old wineskins will burst when new wine ferments in them. Jesus’ meaning was that the fasting of the old cannot mix with the feasting of the new.

In this controversy, Jesus and his disciples are accused of breaking the Sabbath (Exo 20.8–11). Picking grain by hand in another person’s field was lawful (Deu 23.25). The charge was that by rubbing the chaff from the kernels, the disciples were working on the Sabbath, which was forbidden (Exo 34.21).

Jesus countered with reference to an incident in the life of King David (1Sa 21.1–15). When David and his followers ate the sacred loaves—the twelve loaves in the Tabernacle that only priests were allowed to eat—they broke the law (see Lev 24.5–9). But deeper principles were at work (Mar 2.27–28).

Since Jesus is the Lord of humanity (1Co 15.25–28; Eph 1.20–22; Phi 2.9–11) and since the Sabbath was made to meet the needs of people, he is Lord . . . over the Sabbath. As with Jesus’ authority to forgive sins (Mar 2.7), this was a claim to divine authority.

This account concludes the collection of controversy stories (Mar 2.1–Mar 3.6). As in the preceding story, Jesus is in conflict with the Pharisees over the Sabbath; as with the first story, the controversy involves a healing (Mar 2.1–12).

The scene again involves a synagogue, probably in Capernaum (Mar 1.21, Mar 1.29). The presence of a crippled man on the Sabbath (Mar 3.1–2) created a situation that Jesus’ enemies wished to exploit if he healed the man’s hand, so they watched him closely.

Jesus challenged his enemies’ view that doing good deeds was forbidden on the Sabbath (cp. Luk 13.10–17). • To destroy . . . life may refer to an incident in which the Maccabees decided to fight if attacked on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees Mar 2.32–41). These great Jewish heroes were willing to kill on the Sabbath, yet the Pharisees would not allow good deeds on the Sabbath. Jesus’ question shamed them into silence but did not change their hearts (Mar 3.5).
Jesus’ opponents’ hard hearts would not listen to sound reason, so instead of having changed attitudes, they began to plot how to kill him (see also Mar 11.18; Mar 12.12; Mar 14.1–2, Mar 14.10–11).

Jesus’ departure to the lake (the Sea of Galilee) sets the scene for Mar 4.1–Mar 5.43. The multitude that came to see John the Baptist (Mar 1.7) was surpassed by the multitude that came to see Jesus. • Idumea was a region in southern Judea that had been occupied by the Edomites after the Exile. • Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities on the Mediterranean coast that Jesus later visited (Mar 7.24, Mar 7.31).
The boat probably belonged to Peter and Andrew or to James and John. The crowd’s desire to see Jesus was so great that he needed to escape the crush of people (Mar 4.1; Mar 5.24, Mar 5.31).
Jesus healed many people that day; perhaps he healed all the sick (cp. Mat 12.15).
The evil spirits knew who Jesus was (Mar 1.34; see also Mar 1.22; Mar 5.7), but Jesus did not want his identity revealed.
Theme: The Secret of the Messiah
The scene now changes to a mountain, and Mark tells how Jesus called his disciples, which is reminiscent of God’s call of Old Testament prophets (Exo 3.14–22; 1Sa 3.4–14; Jer 1.5–19).

Jesus appointed twelve to represent Israel’s twelve tribes and to proclaim that the Kingdom of God had arrived. He called them apostles (Greek apostoloi, “emissaries”). He chose them to accompany him and to be sent out (Greek apostellō) to preach and to cast out demons. They represented Jesus and were endowed with his authority.
Simon and Andrew were brothers, as were James and John (Mar 1.16–20). • Peter is the Greek equivalent of the Aramaic kepa’, meaning “rock.”
but Jesus nicknamed them “Sons of Thunder”: This nickname probably speaks of their character (cp. Luk 9.53–54).

Philip is fifth on all four lists of the twelve disciples (Mat 10.1–4; Luk 6.12–16; Act 1.13); James the son of Alphaeus (not the son of Zebedee and brother of John) is always ninth. Bartholomew might be Nathanael (Joh 1.43–51), and Matthew is probably Levi, the tax collector (Mar 2.14; Mat 9.9). Although Thomas is referred to as “the twin” (Joh 11.16; Joh 20.24; Joh 21.2), nothing else is said in the New Testament about this. Thaddaeus (Mat 10.3) is missing from Luke’s list; he might be Judas, the son of James (Luk 6.16; Act 1.13). That a government official (Matthew) and an anti-government activist (Simon . . . the zealot) were among the twelve apostles testifies to Jesus’ ability to change people’s hearts and overcome natural antagonism.

Identifying Judas as Iscariot suggests that Mark wanted to avoid confusing him with another Judas (Luk 6.16; Act 1.13). Iscariot probably comes from ’ish (“man of”) qeriyoth (“Kerioth,” a town in Judea). • who later betrayed him: See Mar 14.10–11, Mar 14.43–46.

This story about Jesus and his family (Mar 3.20–21 and Mar 3.31–35) brackets a controversy story about Jesus’ exorcisms (Mar 3.22–30); this arrangement identifies Jesus’ family with the religious leaders in opposing him.
That Jesus and the disciples can’t find time to eat emphasizes Jesus’ great popularity with the crowds (Mar 3.7–9).

He’s out of his mind: Mark does not explain whether the attempt by Jesus’ family to seize him was motivated by sincere but misguided concern, or by hostility. Jesus’ brothers and sisters were not among his followers until after his resurrection (Mar 3.31–35; Joh 7.3–5; 1Co 15.7 mentions James, the brother of Jesus, who became a leader of the Jerusalem church, Act 15.13–21).

The teachers of religious law (see study note on Mar 1.22) from Jerusalem attributed Jesus’ apparent madness to his being possessed by Satan (Greek Beelzeboul; see study note on Matt Mat 10.25). Jesus’ opponents credited his miracle-working ability to Satan (as in the rabbinic work, Sanhedrin Mar 3.43a, where miracle-working is ascribed to sorcery).
Jesus showed the absurdity of this charge by giving several analogies. Satan would not undo his own work.

Jesus provided a better explanation for his ability to cast out demons: Someone stronger than Satan had arrived (Mar 1.7) and was able to loot Satan’s house. Jesus, the Messiah, the Son of God (Mar 1.1), was introducing God’s Kingdom and rescuing people from Satan’s power.

The phrase I tell you the truth introduces many of Jesus’ sayings and gives emphasis to what follows (see also Mar 8.12; Mar 9.1, Mar 9.41; Mar 10.15, Mar 10.29; Mar 11.23; Mar 12.43; Mar 13.30; Mar 14.9, Mar 14.18, Mar 14.25, Mar 14.30). • All sin and blasphemy can be forgiven, but there is a sin with eternal consequences—blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. To blaspheme the Holy Spirit is to attribute the work of God to an evil spirit. Resisting and denouncing the work of God in this way prevents the convicting work of the Spirit that leads to repentance, saving faith in God, and pardon for sin (see study notes on Matt Mat 12.31; cp. Heb 6.4–6; 1Jo 5.16–17).

Mark resumes from Mar 3.20–21. • Your mother and your brothers: Jesus’ brothers are commonly understood to have been children born to Joseph and Mary after Jesus’ birth (see also Mar 6.3; Mat 1.25; Mat 12.46; Joh 19.26–27); some interpreters instead believe that they were either Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage or Jesus’ cousins, due to the Roman Catholic belief that Mary was perpetually a virgin.
In God’s Kingdom, one’s true relatives are determined not by blood but by a faith relationship (see also Mar 10.29–30).
Doing God’s will includes repentance from sin, faith in God, and following Jesus (Mar 1.15, Mar 1.18, Mar 1.20).
In this section Mark collects a number of Jesus’ teaching parables.
Jesus again uses a boat to avoid the press of the crowd when he is teaching (Mar 3.9; Luk 5.2–3).

Parables are often stories (Luk 15.11–32; Luk 18.1–8) but can also be proverbs (Mar 3.24–25; Luk 4.23), similes and metaphors (Mat 5.14; Mat 10.16), riddles (Mar 7.15; Mar 14.58), comparisons (Mat 13.33; Luk 15.3–7), examples (Luk 10.30–35; Luk 12.16–21), or allegories (Mar 4.3–9; Mar 12.1–12).
The collection begins with the longest parable and its interpretation (Mar 4.13–20), focusing on various types of soil as an analogy for various conditions of the human heart.

The scene changes from Jesus’ teaching a very large crowd from a boat to his being alone with the twelve disciples and . . . others. Their question concerns all the parables (Mar 4.33–34), not just this one.

Jesus’ real followers were permitted to understand the secret of the Kingdom of God—namely, that the Kingdom of God had come (Mar 1.14–15) and that Christ, the Son of God, was in their midst (Mar 1.1). For outsiders, it all seemed like riddles. • Jesus’ reply to the disciples’ question suggests that the parables were intended to prevent outsiders from understanding them, so that they would be unable to repent and be forgiven. The quotation from Isa 6.9–10 (Greek version) suggests that it was an intentional judgment on the hearers.
