As news of the miracle spread rapidly into the city of Jerusalem (Joh 12.9, Joh 12.17), public opinion was again divided (Joh 6.66–69; Joh 7.43; Joh 9.16; Joh 10.19; Joh 11.37). Jesus’ reputation as a healer and as one who could raise the dead was known in Galilee (see Mat 9.24–26; Mat 10.8; Mat 11.5). Now he had brought this power to Judea.

The council’s deliberations unveiled their fears that everyone would believe in him. If people believed that the Messiah had come, the political implications would be threatening. The Romans viewed Jewish messiahs with suspicion, and the movement surrounding Jesus might inspire them to invade and destroy Jerusalem and its Temple.
Caiaphas was the ruler of the high council from AD 18–36. He worked for ten years alongside Pontius Pilate, governor of Judea (AD 26–36; see Joh 18.29), keeping the peace with Rome.
Profile: Annas and Caiaphas

it’s better . . . that one man should die: Caiaphas’s words were ironic. He meant that it was better for a revolutionary to die than to have the Romans crush the entire Jewish nation. But Caiaphas was correct in a way that he could not perceive. The salvation that Judaism needed had little to do with Rome; it would come through the cross of Christ. John notes that Caiaphas’s inspiration was not his own but came from God.
Christ’s death was not for Israel only, but for all, including people of other cultures scattered around the world (Joh 10.16; Joh 12.32).

When the Jewish leaders began to plot Jesus’ death, Jesus made a judicious political move in response (Joh 11.54). • Ephraim was a village about twelve miles north of Jerusalem, where Jesus was safe from the Sanhedrin but close enough to walk to the upcoming Passover festival (Joh 11.55).

As crowds arrived in Jerusalem on pilgrimage for Passover (see Joh 2.13), the city was buzzing with talk about Jesus and his miracle of raising Lazarus from the dead. People wondered if Jesus would be obedient to the law and come to the city to celebrate or play it safe in the countryside. The priests and Pharisees knew that Jesus was faithful to the law and would attend the festival, so they tried to make the city a trap for him.

Two stories build simultaneously. A growing number of people are praising Jesus (this climaxes in Joh 12.12–13), and the authorities are increasingly determined to arrest him and put him to death. • John records three events that occurred just days prior to Passover (Joh 12.1–11, Joh 12.12–19, Joh 12.20–36). Then he explains why most of the people refused to believe and details Jesus’ final public appeal (Joh 12.37–50).
Pilgrims from throughout Israel began arriving in Jerusalem the week before the Passover. The festival was on Thursday that year; Jesus arrived late the preceding Friday, just before the Sabbath.
who ate: Or who reclined. The typical posture for eating was to recline at a low table.

Mary . . . anointed Jesus’ feet: Doing so was not awkward, because Jews reclined at formal meals, but it was certainly a dramatic gesture (cp. Mat 26.6–16; Mar 14.3–9). • Nard, a precious spice imported from North India, was sweet, red, and smelled like gladiola perfume. Twelve ounces of nard cost a year’s wages (Joh 12.5). According to Mark, Mary also anointed Jesus’ head (Mar 14.3), and the perfume ran down and scented his garments (Mar 14.8). • her hair: Women never unveiled their hair in public (see Luk 7.38). Mary was acting with extravagant abandon and devotion.
a year’s wages: Judas may have been exaggerating, but Mary’s sacrifice was certainly very costly.

Leave her alone: Jesus’ defense of Mary interpreted her deed. The nard was a burial spice for his death. Jesus was readied for burial as he moved toward the hour of glorification and death (see study note on Joh 12.23).
Jesus would never neglect the poor, but this opportunity to serve him was unparalleled.

The next day was Sunday (see Joh 12.1). • A large crowd of pilgrims (many from Galilee) camped in this region. As Jesus followed the road to Jerusalem, they cheered him. This triumphal entry appears in all four Gospels (Mat 21.1–11; Mar 11.1–11; Luk 19.29–38).

palm branches: The date palm was a celebratory symbol of Jewish nationalism. • meet him: The Greek word commonly describes crowds greeting a returning, triumphant king. • Blessings on the one: The crowd quoted Psa 118.25–26, with a greeting for those who came to Jerusalem. The phrase Hail to the King of Israel is not in the psalm (but see Zep 3.15). Although the people saw Jesus as a national political liberator, he rejected this role (Joh 6.15).

By choosing a young donkey rather than a warhorse, Jesus calmed the frenzied crowd that was passionate for his kingship. He also fulfilled Old Testament predictions regarding the Messiah (see Zec 9.9) and showed that his kingship was not that of a warrior. His gift is life, not conquest.

The crowds and even the disciples didn’t understand Jesus’ true significance. When the disciples received the Holy Spirit following Jesus’ glorification, they fully comprehended who Jesus was (see Joh 2.22).
This scene describes the apex of Jesus’ popularity.
everyone: Literally the world. The Pharisees’ words were more significant than they realized. Jesus came to reach the world (Joh 3.17), and the Pharisees said that Jesus had accomplished his task.

Among the people drawn to Jesus (Joh 12.19) were some Greeks, God-fearing Gentiles who had come to Passover to worship. Jesus’ mission was not simply to Israel but encompassed the entire world (Joh 10.16; Joh 11.52). Following Jesus’ resurrection, the church’s mission was to go beyond Judea to Samaria, and ultimately to the ends of the earth (Mat 28.19; Act 1.8).
The Greeks approached Philip because he had a Greek name and was no doubt Greek.

Jesus often said that the time (literally the hour) had not yet come (Joh 2.4; Joh 7.30; Joh 8.20), but now it had. The coming of the Greeks also marked the beginning of the key moment in Jesus’ ministry—the time of his glorification. This occurred when Jesus’ sacrificial work on the cross was completed (Joh 19.30), he rose from the dead (Joh 20.1–31), he gave the Spirit (Joh 20.22), and he returned to his place of glory in heaven (Joh 17.5, Joh 17.11). The connection with the Greeks who had come to Jerusalem (Joh 12.20) was significant: Jesus’ ministry among the Jews alone was finished and he now belonged to the wider world.
The central event of Jesus’ glorification (Joh 12.23) was the cross. As with a kernel . . . planted in the soil, Jesus’ death would bring abundant life.

For disciples, sacrifice and self-effacement are means of gaining the fullness of life provided by Jesus’ sacrifice. Those who renounce the world will join Jesus in eternity and be honored by God just as Jesus is.

my soul is deeply troubled: John used the same term (Greek tarassō) to describe Jesus’ strong emotion of agony before Lazarus’ tomb (Joh 11.33; also Joh 13.21). When Jesus stood before death, he could not be impassive. Jesus experienced genuine anguish, yet he remained strong in obedience to the Father’s will (Joh 5.19–23; Joh 6.37; Joh 8.29, Joh 8.38; Joh 14.31).

a voice spoke from heaven: Cp. Mat 3.17; Mat 17.5; Mar 1.11; Mar 9.7; Luk 3.22; Luk 9.35. • God had already brought glory to himself when Christ entered the world (Joh 1.14) and through Jesus’ work, which showed God’s power to the world. • I will do so again: The final display of glory would come at the cross (see Joh 12.23; Joh 17.1). In John, the cross is an event of glory as Christ was “lifted up” (Joh 12.32) and glorified there. Jesus was prepared for crucifixion like a king coming to his coronation; the cross was like a throne (see Joh 19.19–22), and he was buried like royalty. Jesus’ time of glorification included the entire sequence from arrest through resurrection.

It was impossible for people to comprehend what was happening with Jesus, and many of his signs led to confusion and division in the crowd. Only later did his disciples understand (Joh 2.22; Joh 12.16), when Jesus was glorified and the Spirit was given. Still, God’s voice symbolized his validation of his Son before the world.

The time for judging does not occur only on Judgment Day; it began when the light penetrated the darkness and unmasked it (Joh 3.19; Joh 5.24; Joh 9.39). • Satan, the ruler of this world, is the architect of darkness, corrupter of the world, and promoter of death. Although Satan’s final demise lies in the future, the work of Christ unraveled Satan’s domain (see Luk 10.17–18; Mar 3.27). Christ is now enthroned as ruler in heaven (Act 7.55–56; Eph 1.19–22).

when I am lifted up from the earth (see Joh 3.14; Joh 8.28): The crowd did not understand what Jesus meant. The Greek verb refers to being exalted (Mat 23.12) or honored (Luk 10.15). In John, the cross was not a place of shame and disgrace for Jesus, but the place where Jesus’ true glory was shown.

Popular Judaism believed that the Messiah would live forever and triumph over his foes. Jesus’ point of view seemed incomprehensible. • who is this Son of Man, anyway? The Jews did not understand what sort of Messiah planned to die.

Jesus was the light (Joh 1.4, Joh 1.7–9; Joh 3.19–21; Joh 8.12), and he urged the crowd to quickly make the choice to believe in him before it was too late. • They had the choice of becoming children of the light by rebirth through the power of God (Joh 1.12–13). • Jesus . . . was hidden from them: Jesus withdrew first from Judea (Joh 11.54) and then from this audience (Joh 12.36), and soon he would withdraw from the world (Joh 17.11).
Jesus’ work was finished, yet most of the people . . . did not believe in him. His sermons before the world were complete and the signs had been displayed, but he was rejected (Joh 1.11).

The people couldn’t believe: John quotes Isa 6.10 to explain Israel’s unbelief (see Mat 13.13–15; Mar 4.12; Luk 8.10; Act 28.26–27). When revelation comes, we must believe. If we refuse, the light disappears (Joh 12.35–36). When God’s light departs from the world, the darkness closes over unbelieving hearts.
Isaiah had glimpsed the Messiah’s glory and how the world would respond (see Isa 6.10).
Many people did believe in him, but they wouldn’t admit it. To follow Jesus involves telling others about him despite the social consequences (Joh 1.35–51; Joh 4.1–42).

Jesus makes a final appeal for belief. These verses summarize chs Joh 1.1–12. Jesus was sent by the Father, the sole source of his ministry. Jesus is the light shining in darkness to bring salvation and eternal life to all who believe in him.
The greatest error is for people to see the light and reject it, thinking it has no connection with the Father who sent the light.

This section focuses on the sign of the cross, the great climax of Jesus’ life, as well as the time Jesus spent preparing his disciples for it (chs Joh 13.1–17). Jesus is glorified through each event of these momentous days. Jesus’ arrest, trial, crucifixion, and resurrection all evoke responses of awe. On the cross, Jesus is elevated in glory before the world (Joh 12.32).

The setting is Jesus’ final Passover meal on Thursday evening, when Judas Iscariot betrays Jesus. John does not record the meal itself as the synoptic Gospels do (Mat 26.17–29; Mar 14.12–25; Luk 22.7–20; see also 1Co 11.23–26). John emphasizes other activities at the event, such as the foot washing (Joh 13.1–17), Judas’s betrayal (Joh 13.18–30), and the prediction of Peter’s denials (Joh 13.31–38).
Judas . . . Iscariot, who had refused to believe, was engulfed by darkness and had become Satan’s pawn (cp. study note on Joh 12.39–40).

Foot washing, common in the Hellenistic and Jewish cultures as a daily routine and as a gesture of hospitality (see Luk 7.36–50), was a lowly, menial task reserved for servants. When Jesus began to wash the disciples’ feet, he took the posture of a slave.

Based on the depth of his devotion to Jesus, it is understandable that Peter protested. But Jesus was not simply giving Peter a model of service; this was a symbolic pre-enactment of his greater act of sacrifice on the cross (Joh 13.7). Receiving Jesus’ spiritual cleansing is a condition for discipleship, so if Peter could not accept this act, he could not be Jesus’ disciple at all.

wash my hands and head as well: Peter misunderstood Jesus (cp. Joh 2.19–20; Joh 3.3–4). Peter thought that to have more water was to have more of Jesus. Only when Peter received the Spirit did everything become clear (e.g., see Act 2.14–36).
Jesus referred to an ultimate cleansing through his sacrifice which makes a person clean all over.

Jesus’ acts of service, such as washing feet and dying on the cross, provided an example of personal sacrifice to follow. • wash each other’s feet: Foot washing was so commonplace that Jesus might have intended a literal repetition of his act, or he might have seen it as symbolic. Either way, Jesus wants similar servanthood and sacrifice to characterize his followers.

slaves are not greater than their master: This proverb was popular and appears in many places (see also Joh 15.20; Mat 10.24; Luk 6.40). Here, Jesus meant that the sacrifice modeled by the master should be seen in the life of the servant.

I am not saying these things to all of you: The subject of Judas’s betrayal enters the story for the third time (Joh 13.2, Joh 13.11). The matter weighed heavily on Jesus (Joh 13.21). • I know the ones I have chosen: The statement does not imply that Jesus chose only the eleven and that Judas was an outcast. Jesus chose Judas and gave him every opportunity to believe. He realized that Judas had embraced the darkness rather than the light (Joh 6.70). • The one who eats my food has turned against me (literally has lifted his heel against me): Eating together was a cultural symbol of personal intimacy, which made Judas’s betrayal all the more treacherous.

Judas’s betrayal did not take Jesus unaware, and it should not shock his disciples when it happens. • that I AM the Messiah: Literally that I am. By using the phrase “I am,” Jesus clearly equated himself with the God of the Old Testament. See Exo 3.14.
For the third time in the Gospel of John, Jesus was deeply troubled (Greek tarassō; see Joh 11.33; Joh 12.27). The personal betrayal of Judas brought Jesus profound grief.

The disciple Jesus loved appears at the cross (Joh 19.26–27), at the tomb (Joh 20.2–9), and at the resurrection (Joh 21.1, Joh 21.20–23). He is the author of this Gospel (Joh 21.24–25). Some scholars believe that Lazarus was in fact the disciple whom Jesus loved (see Joh 11.3, Joh 11.5, Joh 11.36), but the person referred to here was among the twelve apostles and is usually identified as the apostle John. • was sitting next to Jesus at the table: Literally was reclining on Jesus’ bosom. They were probably reclining at a triclinium, a U-shaped table with couches. Guests reclined on the couches, while the center provided access to servers. The diners supported their bodies by their left elbows while using their right hands for eating. Feet were extended away from the table (cp. Luk 7.38).
Profile: John, Son of Zebedee
Peter told “the disciple Jesus loved” (Joh 13.23), who was sitting next to Jesus, to ask the betrayer’s identity. As he reclined next to Jesus, he leaned over to Jesus and spoke privately.

Meals included flat bread, which diners would dip into a common bowl. When Jesus gave a morsel to Judas (cp. Rut 2.14), the disciples might have thought Jesus was honoring him. They did not understand what was occurring. They even thought that Judas’s departure (Joh 13.29) fulfilled an official duty for the feast! But Jesus was signaling to Judas that he understood Judas’s plan and was not taken by surprise. Jesus’ knowledge is profound and complete (see Joh 1.48; Joh 2.25).

When Satan entered into Judas (see Luk 22.3), Judas became an example of what happens to those who are consumed by the darkness. Satan uses such people as pawns in a wider struggle against the light. • Hurry and do what you’re going to do: In issuing this command, Jesus once again showed that he was in control, not human beings or Satan (see study note on John Joh 7.30).

None of the others suspected that something odd was happening. Passover evening was one of the only nights when the city gates were left open. The night was spent in prayer and meditation, money was given to the poor, and provisions were always needed for this complex meal.

out into the night: Judas’s departure was emblematic: The darkness had swallowed him completely (see study note on Joh 13.2; cp. Joh 3.19). Jesus, the light of the world, is the antithesis of the night.

The Old Testament and later Jewish literature include numerous examples of farewells in which a dying person offers last words to intimate friends (see Gen 49.1–27; Deu 31.1–34; Jos 23.1–24; 1Sa 12.1–25; 1Ch 28.1–Joh 29.30). Such farewells used a standard form. The dying person, surrounded by his loved ones, comforted them and exhorted them to obey the law. He prayed and blessed them and often left behind some writings. In some cases, the departing person passed on his “spirit” to his followers or his successor (see Num 27.18; Deu 34.9; 2Ki 2.9–14). Each of these elements is present in Jesus’ farewell. • This section is often called the Upper Room Discourse, since the meal was taken in an “upstairs room” (Luk 22.39).

The time has come: Judas’s departure into the night marks a solemn divide in the plot of the Gospel. Jesus was left with his intimate friends as the hour of glory was dawning. This time was launched by Judas’s betrayal, and it culminated in the resurrection.
Jesus addressed the apostles as his children, marking the start of his farewell address.

That the disciples were to love one another was not a new commandment (see Lev 19.18). However, that they were to love each other with the sort of love modeled by Jesus was dramatic. Jesus’ love for God was expressed in perfect obedience (Joh 14.31); now this kind of love was his command—that disciples express their love for Jesus in committed obedience.

Peter claimed to be ready to die for Jesus, yet his denials are well known (Joh 18.15–18, Joh 18.25–27; see also Mat 26.32–34; Mar 14.27–30; Luk 22.31–34). Although Peter’s verve and devotion failed, he was restored (Joh 21.15–19).
Jesus provided answers to his disciples’ many spoken and unspoken concerns.

Jesus had himself been troubled (Greek tarassō) on three occasions (Joh 11.33; Joh 12.27; Joh 13.21). His confidence in God’s power made it possible for him to face these crises. Faced with the upsetting words of Joh 13.33, the disciples confronted similar feelings. • Trust (or believe, or have faith) in God: Only trusting God would help them through his hour of death.

There is more than enough room in my Father’s home: God’s house is the dwelling place where he resides (Rev 21.9–Joh 22.5). The word translated “room” is related to the Greek verb meaning “remain, abide, dwell.” Jesus promises that his followers will have a place to “dwell” alongside him, wherever he is. Later, this “dwelling” becomes a place of “indwelling” as Jesus makes his home in his followers’ hearts through the Spirit (Joh 14.23).

Some scholars believe that Jesus meant he would come and get his followers after the resurrection (Joh 14.18). Others think these words refer to Jesus’ second coming. For the disciples, the more important coming was Jesus’ return from the grave (ch Joh 16.1–33).

I am: See study note on Joh 6.35. Access to the Father’s presence is only through Jesus, who is the way, the truth, and the life. • The way to the Father is only through Jesus. Other religions and philosophies propose different avenues to God, but Jesus asserted that he is the one exclusive path to God. • Jesus is the truth because God is truth. • God is the source of eternal life. At Lazarus’s tomb, Jesus showed his divine power over life and death (Joh 11.25).
Theme: “I Am” Sayings of Jesus
Philip did not yet understand that in Jesus he was seeing the full embodiment of God (Joh 14.9).

Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father! Cp. Joh 1.1–2. Jesus Christ is God-in-the-flesh (Joh 1.14), which explains his capacity to accomplish divine works. Jesus did not simply teach about God; in him God can be found. Jesus’ remarkable statement echoed what he had said at Hanukkah: “The Father and I are one” (Joh 10.30). This claim is at the root of the world’s opposition to Christ (Joh 5.18).
Jesus’ claims were astonishing (Joh 10.30, Joh 10.37–38). Yet true faith recognizes Jesus’ union with God the Father.

Jesus promised that anyone who believes in him would perform great miracles and experience answers to their prayers (see 1Jo 5.14). These things would become possible when Jesus went to the Father, because he would send the Holy Spirit to empower the works (Joh 14.16). • The greater works will not outdo Jesus’ work, but regular people empowered by the Spirit will be doing them. God promised that in the era of the Spirit, he would bring his Kingdom and power into the world in a way not seen before.

If you love me: Because Jesus loves the Father, he is obedient to what God directs him to say and do (Joh 12.49). If we love him, we will obey him too (Joh 14.21, Joh 14.23; Joh 15.10, Joh 15.14; see 1Jo 2.3–4; 1Jo 5.2).
Theme: Our Advocate
another Advocate: The Spirit continues Jesus’ work by advising, defending, and protecting believers.

The Holy Spirit, who leads into all truth (literally the Spirit of truth; see also Joh 15.26; Joh 16.13), communicates the truth about God. The Spirit maintains Jesus’ presence in the world, duplicating and sustaining Jesus’ work.

Jesus had already assured his followers that they would not be spiritual orphans and that he would return to them (Joh 14.1–4). While he is away, they will be filled with the Spirit, who will sustain them with his presence (Joh 14.12–17).
Jesus’ resurrection (Joh 14.19) inaugurated his spiritual union with his disciples, which is parallel to the union he enjoys with the Father (see Joh 15.4–5; 1Jo 1.3).

Several men are named Judas in the New Testament. Judas, the brother of Jesus, (Mar 6.3) wrote the epistle of Jude. Judas, the son of James, whom John is referring to here, is listed as an apostle in Luk 6.16; he is elsewhere identified as Thaddaeus (Mat 10.3; Mar 3.18). • Lord, why? Judas posed an important question. If Jesus planned to return mightily from death, why not use the opportunity to reveal himself definitively to the world and validate his power and identity?

Jesus answered Judas’s question, explaining that his coming would be a profound spiritual revelation beyond the world’s grasp. • Jesus’ coming would occur in three experiences: his resurrection, the coming of the Spirit, and his second coming. When he comes in the Spirit, he and the Father will reside within believers, making a home with each of them (see study note on Joh 14.2).

Jesus promised to send the Holy Spirit (see also Joh 14.16; Joh 15.26; Joh 16.7, Joh 16.12–14). • The Spirit will teach . . . everything, recalling Jesus’ words and clarifying their meaning. John experienced this power as he wrote his Gospel (Joh 2.22); Christians experience this work of the Spirit as they read the Scriptures.

The Jewish greeting peace (Hebrew shalom) captured the spirit of Jesus’ work on earth to restore humanity’s relationship with God (Isa 9.6–7; Isa 52.7; Isa 57.19; Rom 5.1). The resurrection (Joh 14.28) and the Spirit were instrumental in achieving this work.
the Father, who is greater than I am: See also Joh 5.19–20. Jesus is submissive to the Father but is also one with the Father (Joh 10.30).

The events unfolding in Jerusalem that led to the cross were not controlled by the ruler of this world, meaning Satan. The cross was not an accident, and Jesus was not a helpless victim. Rather, Jesus was obedient to God’s plan.

Jesus prepared his disciples for his departure, instructing them to remain in close fellowship with him. The image of a grapevine illustrates both intimacy and fruitfulness. To sustain genuine spiritual life in the world, believers must remain intimately connected to Christ.

I am: See study note on Joh 6.35. The grapevine and the vineyard traditionally represented God’s people, planted and tended by him in Israel (Psa 80.8–18; Isa 5.1–7; Jer 2.21; Jer 12.10–11; Eze 15.1–5; Hos 10.1–2). When Jesus used this image, he made an important departure: He declared that he is the true grapevine and that a relationship with God requires attachment to him.
Theme: Remaining in Christ
Gardeners cut away dead branches and trim healthy branches so they will produce more fruit. Fruitfulness is the result of life-giving connection to the vine.

The term remain (Greek menō) is key to understanding Joh 15.4–10. A growing disciple, in whom the Father and the Son live through the Spirit, must be continuously connected to Christ (see Joh 14.16–25; Joh 15.26).

Anyone who does not remain in Christ is separated from the vine and its life. A living branch produces clusters of grapes (Joh 15.5). Connection with the vine allows the life of Jesus to flow fruitfully through the disciple. Those who claim to be attached to Christ but yield no fruit are useless and will be burned.
Those whose lives are in harmony with Jesus may ask for anything because their prayers are controlled by his word. Their prayers will be answered and bring glory to God (Joh 14.10–13).
True disciples will experience a transformed, fruit-bearing life because they live in a relationship of love with both Jesus and the Father (Joh 15.9–10).
Just as Jesus demonstrated his love for the Father by obeying his will (Joh 14.31), Jesus’ disciples exhibit their love through obedience to him (Joh 13.34–35; Joh 14.15; 1Jo 2.5; 1Jo 5.2–3).
This is my commandment: Love each other: See Joh 13.34. • Jesus demonstrated his love by sacrificing his life at the cross.

Both Abraham and Moses were called friends of God (Exo 33.11; 2Ch 20.7; Isa 41.8; Jam 2.23). This is the highest relationship possible between God and a person. Jesus chooses his friends (Joh 15.16), who demonstrate their friendship by obeying him.
The disciples of a rabbi were considered his servants or slaves. Jesus elevated his followers to a higher relationship as his friends.

Disciples must be like their master in every respect, both in showing love and obedience and in experiencing the antagonism of those who oppose their message (Joh 15.20–21; see Joh 9.1–41; Joh 11.16). If the darkness is opposed to the light (Joh 1.5), and if Jesus’ followers are bearers of that light in the world (1Jo 1.7; 1Jo 2.9), they should expect the world to hate them in the way it hated Jesus (see Joh 17.14). Jesus’ disciples share his separation from and conflict with the world.
A slave is not greater than the master: See study note on Joh 13.16. Jesus’ disciples should mirror him in every way, even in his experience of persecution and martyrdom.
But now they have no excuse: Jesus’ ministry provided both words (Joh 15.22) and works (Joh 15.24) as evidence that pointed to God. Once people have heard and seen him, they are accountable.
They hated me without cause: This Old Testament citation reveals the unwarranted anger of those who belong to the darkness.
But I will send you the Advocate—the Spirit of truth: Like a legal advocate, the Holy Spirit counsels and protects Jesus’ followers.
Disciples are not alone when they testify about Christ (Mat 28.20). The Spirit accompanies them, providing the words to say (Mat 10.19–20).

Jesus had outlined the coming conflicts (Joh 15.18–25) so that the disciples would not abandon their faith (literally be caused to stumble). The greatest obstacle his disciples would face was to stumble and renounce their faith before their opponents (see Mat 23.34; Luk 6.22), especially during the dark days ahead (see Joh 12.35; 1Jo 2.9–11).
the Advocate: The Spirit was a gift awaiting Jesus’ departure and glorification (Joh 7.37–39; Joh 14.16, Joh 14.26; Joh 15.26; Joh 16.12–14).

One of the Spirit’s roles is to convict the world. Convict is a legal term: The world had conducted its trial of Jesus, examining the evidence for his case (his signs and claims). Now the world would stand trial before the Spirit, and its guilt would be proven.

The Spirit unveils to the world the real nature of its sin, the truth about righteousness found only in God, and the coming judgment, which has already dawned on the world as light penetrating the darkness.
Judgment of sinners had already begun, for the ruler of this world, Satan, had already been judged (see Joh 12.31). The world thought it was judging Jesus, but the opposite occurred.

The Spirit of truth, who conveys truth from God, guides the judgment of the world. • The Spirit says only what he has heard from the Father. The Father, Son, and Spirit work in perfect unity (Joh 16.15). The disciples could expect the Spirit to reveal things they had not heard before about the present and the future (see Joh 14.26).
a little while: This refrain reassured the disciples that their separation from Jesus would be short-lived.

Jesus reassured the disciples that his departure (on the cross) would be short and his return (in the resurrection) would be soon. When they saw him again, the disciples would experience overwhelming joy and intimacy with him in the Spirit.

At the crucifixion, the world thought it had won a victory over the light. The shock of the cross would cause the disciples to weep and mourn, but their sorrow would change to joy when Jesus defeated the grave (Joh 20.20).
the pains of labor: This metaphor symbolizes anguish that is followed by God’s blessing and wonder (cp. Isa 21.2–3; Isa 26.16–21; Isa 66.7–10; Jer 13.21).

Ask . . . and you will receive: Two notable effects of the resurrection are the joy of understanding and the joy of successful prayer. The disciples would no longer experience the confusion described in Joh 16.16–18.
Jesus spoke using figures of speech, which could only be interpreted with God’s help (1Co 1.18–25). With the coming of the Spirit, the disciples would understand.
After Jesus’ resurrection, the Spirit brought intimacy, allowing individual disciples to ask the Father to meet their needs. (Joh 14.23).

But take heart, because I have overcome the world: “Such a saying as this is worthy to be carried from Rome to Jerusalem on one’s knees” (Martin Luther). Jesus’ final words did not chastise but brought comfort. Jesus promised peace (Joh 14.27) and joy (Joh 16.20, Joh 16.22). Now he added that his disciples can discover peace even when surrounded by threats; they can be tranquil despite those who are hostile to their faith.

This chapter records Jesus’ longest prayer, which is often called his “high priestly prayer.” It provides an intimate glimpse into his heart. In this prayer, which closes the farewell that began at Joh 13.31, Jesus expressed his own concerns to his Father (Joh 17.1–8) and then turned to concerns for the church and its future (Joh 17.9–26).

Jesus looked up to heaven, assuming the traditional Jewish posture for prayer (Joh 11.41; Psa 123.1). He probably also raised his hands (Exo 9.33; Exo 17.11; Psa 28.2). Prayers like this were said aloud so that followers could hear (Joh 11.41–42; Joh 12.27–30; also Mat 11.25–30; Luk 10.21–22). • Father was Jesus’ usual way to address God, which he did six times in this prayer (see also Joh 11.41; Joh 12.27). This title—unusual in Judaism—reflected Jesus’ intimacy with God. • This hour included Jesus’ betrayal, arrest, torture, death, and resurrection (see study note on Joh 12.23). • Glorify your Son: In the Gospel of John, the cross is a place of honor. Jesus’ oneness with the Father means that if the Son is glorified, the Father will also be glorified.
All authority has been placed in Jesus’ hands (Joh 3.35); he can give eternal life as only God can (Joh 3.15; Joh 5.21, Joh 5.25–26).

to know you: The Hebrew idea of knowing encompassed experience and intimacy, which for Christians means love for God and obedience to him. • sent to earth: Jesus originated in heaven and was returning there (Joh 17.5), so he exercises divine authority as the agent of God.
Jesus’ miracles displayed God’s glory for the world to see (Joh 1.14). This task was finished; Jesus’ life and obedience had glorified God.
Jesus prayed to return to the position he had with God before the world began (Joh 1.1).
Theme: The World

This verse summarizes Christ’s mission. He revealed the true person of God to the world, gathered up God’s people into his flock, and instructed them in obedience. The result of this work is the church.
Jesus revealed himself widely to the world. Those who embraced his message became children of God (Joh 1.12; Joh 11.52), and he revealed God’s word to them.
Jesus prayed for his disciples, who must carry on after his departure.

Just as the Son brings glory to the Father (Joh 17.1, Joh 17.4–5), the disciples bring the Son glory (Joh 17.22). The love and obedience that brought glory to God in Jesus’ life become features of his disciples’ lives.
Jesus’ first concern for his disciples was that they . . . be united with an intimacy similar to the oneness shared by Jesus and the Father.

Until now, Jesus had guarded his followers. Now he was concerned for their strength and survival in his absence, because the world would be hostile toward them (Joh 15.18–27) and their mission of challenging the world by heralding the truth (Joh 16.8–11). After Jesus’ departure, the Spirit would protect them (Joh 15.26) and bring them joy.

God’s word, which Jesus had given his disciples, also provides a defense against the world. The Spirit would preserve and recall God’s word in the church (Joh 14.26), equipping the church for its encounter with the world.

Being holy refers to purity gained by separation from the world, and living a life so aligned with God that it reflects his passions. Disciples are set apart by God, equipped by the Spirit, and readied by God’s word to enter the world without being victimized by its darkness.

I give myself as a holy sacrifice (literally I sanctify myself): Priests and prophets were similarly set apart for service to God (Lev 8.30; Jer 1.5). Jesus recommitted himself to his mission, acknowledging that he was set apart for the purpose of the cross. The disciples would benefit because his death would enable them to experience new holiness in a deep attachment to God.
Jesus was praying for other sheep who were not yet in his flock (Joh 10.16). These are the believers through the centuries who have come to faith through the witness of Jesus’ disciples.

For believers, becoming one with one another is an outgrowth of the union they enjoy with Jesus himself, a union modeled on the oneness of the Father and the Son. • may they be in us: Through the power of the Spirit, believers would experience a profound spiritual intimacy with the Father and the Son and be transformed (Joh 14.20, Joh 14.23; 1Jo 4.13). • Disciples of Jesus represent him, so their conduct and relationships with each other reflect the credibility of Christ in the world. When there is disunity, infighting, and intolerance, their testimony to the world is unconvincing. When people observe the community of believers, they know that it represents Jesus; a unified, loving community convinces the world to believe (Joh 13.35; 1Jo 3.11).
The community of believers should display the same glory that Jesus displayed from the Father.
that the world will know: If the church lives in the Spirit, reflects God’s glory and love, and shows unity sustained by a shared knowledge of God, then its testimony will astonish the world.

I want these . . . to be with me: Someday, Jesus’ followers will see Jesus’ true glory, the true love that has existed in heaven since the beginning of time (Joh 17.5). Jesus was returning to heaven, and he yearned to see his disciples there so that they might glimpse what no words on earth can describe.

All who accept the Son and embrace the Father will experience the kind of love known only between the Father and the Son. • I will be in them: Jesus loves his followers and wants to indwell them with glory and joy unmatched by anything in the world.

After completing his farewell in the upper room (Joh 13.31–Joh 17.26), Jesus left the city and entered a garden just east of Jerusalem to pray. Here he was arrested, taken under guard into the city, and interrogated by the Jewish leaders. The climactic “time” that Jesus referred to repeatedly throughout the Gospel (see Joh 2.4; see also study note on Joh 12.23) was now at hand.

Jesus crossed the Kidron Valley, a dry river valley (a wadi ) outside Jerusalem’s walls on the city’s east edge. • The Garden of Gethsemane (Mar 14.32) was a grove of olive trees that grew along the west shoulder of the Mount of Olives (gath shemaney means “olive press” in Aramaic). Jesus liked this place and frequently prayed there (see Joh 8.1; Luk 21.37; Luk 22.39).

John’s full description of the arresting party expands the picture from the other Gospels. The Temple authorities sent Roman soldiers and Temple guards; while the Temple guards made the arrest, the Roman detachment stood by to prevent a riot. The Roman detachment was large enough to warrant a commander (Joh 18.12) and came armed, anticipating a struggle (Joh 18.10). Numerous men had claimed to be the Messiah, and often they had made politically explosive attempts to expel the Romans.
I AM he (literally I am): Jesus identified himself by the divine name God had revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai (see Exo 3.14; see also Joh 4.26; Joh 8.24, Joh 8.58).

The soldiers and guards all drew back before the Lord (cp. Isa 6.5; Eze 1.28; Dan 10.9; Act 9.4; Rev 1.17). Even Roman soldiers, who were trained not to fall, fell to the ground before Christ. Although they took this posture of submission, they didn’t really understand what had occurred and proceeded with the arrest.
I AM: Jesus used God’s divine name for the second time (see study note on Joh 18.5).

I did not lose a single one: Jesus continued to be a good shepherd, offering his life for the sheep and protecting them from the wolves (Joh 10.11–15). From the beginning, however, Judas Iscariot had not been a true disciple of Jesus (Joh 17.12).

Simon Peter drew a short sword or a long knife that was generally worn with everyday garments. • The Hebrew name Malchus means “king,” a detail that John might have included for its wordplay on Jesus’ true identity (see Joh 18.36–37; Joh 19.19). • Put your sword back: Jesus’ mission was not to fight for his life, but to die for ours.

Jesus was bound by the soldiers and returned to Jerusalem. • First they took him to Annas, who had been the high priest and remained highly influential (five of his sons also became high priests). Caiaphas, his son-in-law, was the official high priest at that time (see Joh 18.24).

one man should die for the people: Caiaphas had previously made this political analysis (Joh 11.49–50). John points out the irony of this statement. Jesus’ death did not bring Israel political salvation—it brought spiritual salvation to all who believe.
That other disciple is unnamed but was probably the “disciple Jesus loved” (Joh 13.23)—John, the author of this Gospel.

During Jesus’ interrogation by Annas (Joh 18.12–14, Joh 18.19–24), the woman watching at the gate asked Peter if he was one of that man’s disciples. In contrast to Jesus, who stood up to his questioners and denied nothing, Peter quickly denied his link to Jesus three times (Joh 18.17, Joh 18.25, Joh 18.27).

The high priest began asking Jesus questions, but his inquiry was contrary to Jewish legal procedure. In Jewish court, the priest did not ask questions directly of the defendant but accumulated evidence from witnesses to establish guilt (see Num 35.30; Deu 17.6; Deu 19.15; cp. Mat 18.16). If Jesus said anything incriminating, Annas would later use it to testify against him at Jesus’ trial. He was attempting to follow Roman practice by making Jesus incriminate himself, rather than gathering evidence through witnesses as Jewish law demanded.
Jesus’ sharp answer, reminding Annas that everything was in the public record, unmasked the priest’s attempt to follow Roman practice.

When Jesus reminded Annas of correct judicial procedure, one of the Temple guards viewed it as insolence and slapped Jesus. However, Jesus knew the law and represented it truthfully. No witnesses were accusing him, and no evidence was being presented.
Annas was at an impasse—his probing had been unsuccessful. So he sent Jesus to Caiaphas to be prosecuted before the Sanhedrin, Jerusalem’s judicial high council (see Mar 14.53–Joh 15.1).
He denied it: Peter’s three denials were later echoed when Jesus invited him three times to reaffirm his love (Joh 21.15–17).

The trial before Caiaphas ended in the early hours of the morning. Since they did not have the power of capital punishment (Joh 18.31), the Sanhedrin needed to enlist Pilate, the Roman governor, to carry out an execution. • it would defile them: They did not want to become ritually unclean by contact with Gentiles in Pilate’s headquarters. So Pilate, probably fearing a riot, went outside to meet them. • The Passover meal itself had occurred the night before (see Joh 13.1; Mar 14.14–16). The following day, another meal began the weeklong Festival of Unleavened Bread (Lev 23.5–6).

Pilate, the fifth Roman governor of Judea, ruled the country from AD 26 to 36. He usually lived on the coast in Caesarea, but kept troops stationed in a fortress in Jerusalem where he appeared personally for major festivals. He was a brutal ruler whose atrocities against the Jews were legendary (e.g., Luk 13.1; Josephus, War 2.9.2-4).

Pilate found the charges unsatisfying and told the Sanhedrin, judge him by your own law. Pilate saw this as a Jewish squabble, which he refused to investigate. The Jewish leaders, however, insisted that an execution was necessary. • fulfilled Jesus’ prediction about the way he would die (see Joh 12.32–33): The Jews would have employed stoning; the Romans used crucifixion. If Pilate delivered Jesus’ sentence, he would be crucified.

Pilate was personally responsible for capital crimes in which the interests and security of the Roman Empire were at stake, so he began his formal legal inquiry. • Are you the king of the Jews? To get the governor’s attention, Caiaphas had charged that Jesus had urged people not to pay their taxes to the Roman government and had claimed to be a king (Luk 23.2). To Pilate, Jesus might have been just another Jewish terrorist–revolutionary (see Luk 23.18–19; Act 5.36–37) with a head full of messianic notions and a band of well-armed followers.

Jesus’ reply forced the governor to show the origin of his question. The Temple leadership was behind these charges. Pilate only wanted to know if Jesus was a rebel who might threaten Roman interests.

Jesus was willing to accept the title of king, but he made it clear that he did not govern an earthly kingdom that might rival Rome. Jesus’ kingship is not of this world. Rather than being a political ruler, he rules through the devotion and obedience of his followers.

What is truth? Truth was not a foreign idea to Pilate, but he did not wait for an answer to his question because he did not believe there was one. • Pilate returned to the council members waiting outside and delivered his verdict: not guilty. Although he referred to Jesus as “King of the Jews” (see also Joh 19.19), the title meant nothing more to Pilate than a mocking expression of contempt. Pilate’s offer of amnesty revealed his desire to let Jesus go.

Jesus was no threat to Rome, but Barabbas was a revolutionary, a violent man who took part in political uprisings (see Luk 23.19), with a proven capacity to challenge the Roman military occupation of Israel.

Jesus was also beaten after his sentencing (Mar 15.15), but here John records an earlier beating, which was likely Pilate’s attempt to show that Jesus had been punished and could be released (Joh 19.4). When this failed, Pilate passed his sentence and handed Jesus over to the Jewish leaders for crucifixion (Joh 19.16).

The crown of thorns might have come from a date palm (cp. Joh 12.13–14), the thorns of which can exceed twelve inches. There are Greek coin images showing such crowns, with the stems woven and the thorns radiating upward above the crown. • The purple robe was probably a soldier’s robe—dark red to complete the picture of mock royalty.

Pilate’s intention was to bring Jesus out to display the marks of his punishment to sway the crowd to let him go. After being flogged with a lead-tipped whip, Jesus was bleeding profusely. • Pilate announced his verdict of not guilty a second time, but he was met with a strident call for Jesus’ death (Joh 19.6).
Pilate knew that a riot could happen when a man popular with the masses was executed, so he shifted responsibility to crucify Jesus to the Temple leaders.

During the trial before Caiaphas, the charge of blasphemy—calling himself the Son of God—was determined to be Jesus’ true crime (see Mar 14.61–65). • The leaders had already tried pitting Jesus against Roman imperial interests (Joh 18.33), and would do so again (Joh 19.12). Now they challenged the governor on another level: Pilate must keep the peace by upholding local law, even when it was irrelevant to Rome. Claiming to be God’s son was not illegal, because Israel’s kings did this (Psa 2.7; Psa 89.22–27). However, Jesus claimed to have the divine authority of God himself (see Joh 5.18), which they saw as blasphemy.

Pilate . . . was more frightened than ever: He was superstitious, and the idea of gods appearing in the world was not uncommon (Act 14.11). He sensed that more than a political fight was going on, so he asked Jesus, Where are you from? He did not mean Jesus’ birthplace, but whether Jesus was a divine man who had descended from heaven. • Why Jesus gave no answer is unclear. Perhaps it was because Pilate would not have been able to understand the answer—that true power comes only from God, and God had empowered Jesus (cp. Joh 19.11).

You would have no power over me: Although Pilate had the power to . . . crucify Jesus, it was only because God had given him this temporary power so Jesus could advance toward the cross (see Joh 10.18).

Each time he had a conversation with Jesus, Pilate tried to release him: He kept trying, but his repeated efforts were fruitless. • “Friend of Caesar” was an official title given to individuals such as senators who showed exceptional loyalty and service to the emperor. The Jewish leaders were implying that they would ruin Pilate’s career by reporting that he was not working in Rome’s interests. They probably knew that Pilate was also having a personal crisis. His patron in Rome, Sejanus (the chief administrator of the empire under Tiberius Caesar), had fallen from favor and was executed in AD 31. Pilate had every reason to be afraid.

Pilate took the governor’s judgment seat (Greek bēma, cp. Act 25.6, “seat in court”) to render his verdict. • The Stone Pavement was the platform holding the judgment seat; from there Pilate now spoke with the authority of his office.

the day of preparation for the Passover (or the day of preparation during the Passover): Here, Passover does not refer to the Jewish Passover meal, which had taken place the night before, but to the whole Festival of Unleavened Bread. It was now Friday, the day of preparation for the Passover Sabbath, which would begin at sundown (cp. Mar 15.42; Luk 23.54).

The final words of the priests, “We have no king but Caesar,” stood in direct contradiction to the Old Testament understanding that God was Israel’s king (cp. Jdg 8.23; 1Sa 8.7; 1Sa 10.19). Jerusalem and its leaders were in the process of killing their true king (Joh 18.37) while paying homage to Caesar, the pagan king of Rome.

Pilate turned Jesus over to the Roman garrison, who prepared Jesus for crucifixion by a second flogging (Mar 15.15), which brought him near death. Bleeding profusely, his clothes soaked in blood, his thorn-laced crown now digging deeply into his head, and nearly in shock, Jesus was marched to a site outside the city.

The vertical beam (Latin staticulum) of the cross was generally kept at the crucifixion site, and the victim was forced to carry only the heavy crossbeam (Latin patibulum). • Crucifixions were public executions that took place near major roadways. They were designed to shock and warn the people. • Place of the Skull (Hebrew and Aramaic Golgotha; Latin calvariae, “Calvary”): Most archaeologists agree that Jesus’ crucifixion was at the site of the present-day Church of the Holy Sepulchre, located in the Christian Quarter of the old walled city of Jerusalem. An alternate site, Gordon’s Calvary (north of the Damascus Gate), provides a model of what the scene possibly looked like, but it holds only a tomb from the 500s BC and therefore is unlikely to be the authentic site of Jesus’ crucifixion and burial.
Theme: The Cross and Passover

None of the Gospel writers dwell on the details of being nailed . . . to the cross because they were well known and horrific. The soldiers used the cross as a means of torture; they wanted victims to survive for a while, in some cases for days. Because the Sabbath would begin at dusk (Joh 19.31), they expedited Jesus’ crucifixion. Jesus had been thoroughly beaten with stone- or metal-tipped whips, so his back was thoroughly lacerated, and he was bleeding profusely.

Pilate posted a sign on the cross: It was customary for the Roman soldiers to provide a written public notice of the criminal’s name and crimes. Perhaps as a final act of revenge against the Jewish high council, Pilate ordered that the sign should identify Jesus of Nazareth as the King of the Jews. Jesus’ kingship was posted in three languages for the whole world to understand.
As was their common practice, the Roman soldiers divided his clothes. The soldiers gambled for his valuable robe, which was seamless, rather than dividing it up.

This is the only reference to Jesus’ mother’s sister in the New Testament. She might have been the wife of Zebedee and the mother of James and John (cp. Mat 27.56), which would make Jesus and John cousins. If so, it would help explain why Jesus assigned the disciple he loved (John) to care for Mary (John’s aunt). • Mary (the wife of Clopas) is only mentioned here. She might be the same person as Mary the mother of James and Joseph (cp. Mat 27.56). • Jesus had healed Mary Magdalene, a woman from the village of Magdala (Mar 16.9; Luk 8.2). • Dear woman was a formal and polite form of address (see Joh 2.4).

Here is your mother: Jesus employed a Jewish family law that assigned the care of one person to another. The scene had an additional significance: The people who were present represented the new community of the church that was born at the cross. Jesus wanted them to care for each other in obedience to his command to love one another (Joh 13.34; Joh 15.12, Joh 15.17).

The hyssop bush had been used in Egypt to brush lamb’s blood on the doorposts and lintels during the first Passover (Exo 12.22). Jesus is God’s Passover lamb (Joh 1.29, Joh 1.36), and his blood likewise saves.
Jesus called out in triumph and exhaustion that he had finished the work he set out to do. On the cross he was not a victim, but a servant doing God’s bidding.

The Jewish authorities, eager to complete the crucifixion before Sabbath began at dusk, asked Pilate to break the legs of the men. Breaking the legs with a mallet was common: It promoted asphyxiation and hemorrhaging, because the victim could no longer push up to breathe.

To confirm that Jesus was dead, a Roman soldier pierced his side with a spear. • blood and water flowed out: This has several levels of meaning: (1) The spear probably punctured Jesus’ pericardium, the sac around the heart, releasing these fluids. (2) John might have been thinking of more Passover symbolism. The Passover lamb’s blood had to flow as it died. (3) The water flowing from Jesus’ side reminds readers of the language of living water that Jesus had used earlier (see Joh 4.10–14; Joh 7.37–39).

John was at the foot of the cross (Joh 19.26). He was not simply a collector of traditions about Jesus, but an eyewitness giving an accurate account of the events of Jesus’ life (cp. Joh 21.24). This same confidence can be seen in the opening of John’s first letter (1Jo 1.1–4).
“Not one of his bones will be broken”: The Passover lamb could have no broken bones (Exo 12.46; Num 9.12); Jesus was the perfect Passover lamb (cp. Psa 34.20; see also 1Co 5.7).
“They will look on the one they pierced”: Zec 12.10 describes how Israel would look on a prophet or the Messiah and lament their own fatal lack of faith.

According to Luke, Joseph of Arimathea was a courageous man who was waiting for the Kingdom of God (Luk 23.50–51). He was a wealthy (Mat 27.57) and influential leader in Jerusalem and a member of the high council (Mar 15.43) who disagreed with the decision to kill Jesus. He asked Pilate for the favor of burying Jesus in his personal tomb. • Joseph was a secret disciple (cp. Joh 12.42–43), but his bold deed brought out his public support of Jesus.

Nicodemus (see Joh 3.1; Joh 7.50), a member of the high council, understood that these bodies had to be buried before the upcoming Sabbath (Joh 19.31, Joh 19.42). His public support, as with Joseph of Arimathea, might indicate that he, too, was becoming a disciple (see study note on Joh 7.49–51). • Myrrh was a commonly used aromatic powder. • The aloes were fragrant powdered sandalwood often used as perfume. • seventy-five pounds: This enormous amount of spices was appropriate for royalty; Jesus, the king, was given a royal burial.
a new tomb: More than 900 first-century burial tombs have been discovered in Judea, carved into the limestone hills.

because it was the day of preparation for the Jewish Passover: See study note on Joh 19.14. The Sabbath was approaching, so Joseph and Nicodemus (Joh 19.38–39) would return to complete the burial process later.
As a devoted follower of Jesus (see Mat 27.55–56; Luk 8.1–3), Mary Magdalene arrived at the tomb to help complete Jesus’ burial (see Joh 19.42). • Many Judean tombs were sealed with a rolling stone.
Mary Magdalene ran and found Simon Peter. Her natural assumption was that someone had robbed the tomb and perhaps stolen the body—which was not an uncommon occurrence.

The other disciple was probably John, “the disciple Jesus loved” and author of this Gospel (see Joh 13.23). He and Peter validated Mary’s testimony by examining the tomb for themselves. John arrived first, but Peter entered first.

What Peter and John found in the tomb was remarkable. The linen wrappings (Joh 19.40) were on the burial bench. Jews also used a facial cloth for burials (cp. Joh 11.44), which was rolled, wrapped under the chin, and tied on the top of the head. The apostles found this face cloth folded up on the bench. John’s inclusion of these details counters any suggestion that grave robbers had taken Jesus’ body; such costly garments would have been stolen in a robbery.
he saw and believed: Despite not fully understanding, John knew that God had been at work, and he realized that Jesus was alive.
Although two . . . angels appeared inside the tomb, the riddle of Jesus’ disappearance remained unsolved (see Luk 24.4). • why are you crying? Sorrow was not the appropriate response in this moment.

Jesus, whom Mary mistook for the gardener, repeated the angel’s question and added, Who are you looking for? Jesus’ question was to provoke Mary’s thinking: At this point Mary was looking for the body of Jesus, but she was about to meet the living Christ.
When Jesus called Mary by name, she recognized him immediately (see Joh 10.3–4).

Mary thought that with the resurrection, Jesus would resume normal relations with his disciples. She was trying to cling to the joy she discovered in her resurrected Lord. But his fellowship with her would come in a new form (Joh 20.22). Jesus had not yet ascended to complete his return to the Father, but the process was underway. Before his final departure, he would give the Holy Spirit (Joh 20.22; see Joh 14.15–21, Joh 14.26; Joh 15.26–27; Joh 16.5–15).

Mary was the first eyewitness to see the Lord following his resurrection. She not only saw him, she heard him and touched him (see 1Jo 1.1–4). This great privilege was given to a woman whose broken life had experienced healing (Luk 8.2). In Jewish culture this was astounding; a woman could not even be a witness in court. No Jew in this period would make up such a story.

meeting behind locked doors: The disciples feared prosecution for following Jesus. • Peace be with you: This was a standard Jewish greeting (see also 3Jo 1.15), but Jesus was doing more than just greeting his disciples: he was offering the Messiah’s peace (see Isa 9.6; Isa 52.7) and delivering the gift of his Kingdom (see Joh 14.27; Joh 16.33).

The reality of Jesus’ resurrection was quite clear. Jesus showed them the wounds from the nails and the spear. He did not feign death but conquered it. He was no phantom but a real man with a real body. He had been dead but was now alive. Jesus was fully human both in life (Joh 1.14) and in his resurrection.

I am sending you: God had sent Jesus into the world to establish his Kingdom, and now Jesus was sending his disciples to carry on his mission. Christ’s emissaries carry the truth of Jesus’ words to the world (cp. Joh 17.18).

Jesus commissioned the disciples and then empowered them with the Holy Spirit. The Spirit had not been given previously because Jesus had not yet been glorified (Joh 7.39). The glorified Jesus, resplendent in his resurrected body, poured the Spirit on his followers. This gift fulfilled many promises that the Spirit would be sent (Joh 14.16, Joh 14.26; Joh 15.26; Joh 16.7, Joh 16.13). It foreshadows the arrival of the Spirit’s empowering presence at Pentecost (Act 1.4–5; Act 2.1–47).

If you forgive anyone’s sins: The ongoing work of Christ’s followers parallels the work of Christ. Christ’s followers do not distribute and withdraw God’s forgiveness on a whim, but they follow Jesus’ prompting through the Spirit (Joh 15.5), just as Jesus obeyed his Father (Joh 14.31).

Thomas: See also Joh 11.16; Joh 14.5). Thomas was absent when Jesus revealed himself. He remained skeptical despite the testimony of his friends, who had seen the Lord. Thomas demanded a concrete experience identical to theirs.

Eight days later was Sunday, one week after Jesus’ resurrection (it was customary to include the current day when counting forward). Jesus’ appearance on the following Sunday helps explain the disciples’ meeting on “the Lord’s Day” (see Rev 1.10). • Peace be with you: This scene was exactly like Jesus’ first appearance (Joh 20.19–20). Jesus had already heard Thomas’s complaint and now answered directly. • Believe! Jesus challenged Thomas to believe in the resurrection like the others.
“My Lord and my God!” This was not an astonished exclamation but a proclamation of heartfelt belief. It concludes John’s declaration of Jesus’ deity that has framed the whole book (see Joh 1.1–18).
Jesus points to the generations of Christians who, through the testimony of others, would believe without seeing.
Many scholars view these words as the conclusion of John’s Gospel, viewing ch Joh 21.1–25 as an appendix. John’s account is only a selection from Jesus’ many . . . miraculous signs.

that you may continue to believe: The present tense (found in some manuscripts) indicates that John wrote to encourage believers. Other manuscripts read that you may [come to] believe, suggesting that John wrote to stimulate new faith (cp. Joh 1.7).

This final chapter adds an account about the resurrected Jesus in Galilee (Joh 21.1–14) and records the exchange between Peter and Jesus concerning Peter’s love (Joh 21.15–23). The chapter ends by summarizing the authority and importance of John’s eyewitness report (Joh 21.24–25).
Theme: Fishing in Galilee

Several of the disciples returned to fishing in the Sea of Galilee. This was not a sign that their faith had weakened—even rabbis who regularly preached kept practicing their occupations (see Act 18.3; Act 20.34; 1Co 4.12). • The sons of Zebedee were James and John (see Mat 4.21).
Fishing was usually successful in the early hours of the morning. However, this trip was useless and they caught nothing all night.
Jesus was standing on the beach, but the men did not recognize him (cp. Joh 20.11–16; Luk 24.13–53).
“Throw out your net on the right-hand side”: Casting a net into the sea at random was futile. But when they did as the stranger said, the immense catch was immediate (Joh 21.11).

“It’s the Lord!” John recognized Jesus, probably remembering that a miracle like this had happened before (Luk 5.1–11). • Peter, who had stripped off his clothes while working, put on his tunic in order to meet the Lord.
Cooked fish and bread were the mainstays of the Galilean diet; Jesus provided the men with breakfast. The charcoal fire is reminiscent of the scene of Peter’s denials (Joh 18.18).
This miracle showed generous provision (as in Joh 2.1–12; Joh 6.1–15). No symbolism attaches to the number 153.
None of the disciples dared to ask him, “Who are you?” Jesus’ resurrected appearance was different. His offer of fish and bread removed all uncertainties (cp. Joh 6.11; Luk 24.30).
This scene on the beach was the third time Jesus had appeared (see Joh 20.11–23, Joh 20.26–29).

do you love me? The three questions and affirmations mirror Peter’s three denials (Joh 18.15–18, Joh 18.25–27). Jesus invited Peter to reaffirm everything he had denied. • The Greek term translated love in Jesus’ first two questions (agapaō) is different from the word in his third question (phileō). In each case, Peter answered with the second word (phileō). Most Greek scholars view the two words as synonyms in this situation. The focus of Jesus’ exchange with Peter was not the quality of Peter’s love, but Peter’s commission to take care of Jesus’ flock. Peter might be meditating on these events in 1Pe 5.2–4.

more than these? Or more than these others do? Jesus was reminding Peter of his insistence that he would be more faithful and courageous than the others (Joh 13.37; Mat 26.33; Mar 14.29). He was urging Peter to examine himself.

feed my sheep: Jesus, who knows all things (Joh 1.42; Joh 2.25; Joh 16.30), understood that despite Peter’s terrible failing, he still had faith and commitment to Jesus. These words called Peter to nurture and protect Christ’s followers.

you will stretch out your hands: Jesus was probably predicting crucifixion, which according to tradition is how Peter died. • others will dress you (literally bind you): Jesus alludes to captivity, bondage, and even crucifixion—victims were often tied to the cross.

The rest of Peter’s life was a ministry tending the flock of God, and his martyrdom was a kind of death that glorifies God. • Follow me: This might require suffering and death (see Joh 13.16; Joh 15.18–21).

“What about him, Lord?” Peter asked Jesus about the fate of John, wondering if he, too, would experience martyrdom. Jesus’ answer was abrupt: It was not Peter’s business to know how or when John would die. Peter’s only task was to follow Jesus, which John was already doing. This episode forms the core of John’s concept of discipleship: What matters most for the disciple of Jesus is to follow him and do his will, come what may.

Jesus’ words to Peter spread, causing some to conclude that John would not die until Jesus returned in his second coming. Jesus’ rebuke to Peter (Joh 21.22) is repeated to answer that rumor. Those among the community of believers who believed this rumor were thus instructed to abandon any speculation about John. According to tradition, John died peacefully in Ephesus at an old age, surrounded by fellow believers.

This disciple is the one who testifies . . . and has recorded: John’s Gospel is anchored in his personal experiences. It is not a story written from hearsay or speculation, but from the remembrance of a man who spent life-changing years with Jesus and recalled, with the help of the Holy Spirit (Joh 14.26), what Jesus said and did. • we know: This account of the life of Christ was not speculation or weak reminiscence. Rather, it was based on the confident knowledge of reliable eyewitness accounts.

the whole world could not contain the books: John ends his Gospel acknowledging that the story he has described is larger than anything he can imagine or fully communicate. Though it is glorious for us to read, John’s account pales in comparison to the glory of the person it describes.

The Book of Acts

Purpose

To describe the spread of the Good News of Jesus Christ and the birth of the church from Jerusalem throughout the Roman world

Author

Luke, a physician and occasional companion of the apostle Paul

Date

Likely between the early 60s AD and the mid-80s AD. The events recorded in Acts end in the early 60s, but a commonly held view suggests that it was written later, presuming that Luke’s Gospel used the Gospel of Mark—likely written in the late 60s—as a source

Setting

Written during a time when the Good News of Jesus had spread throughout the Mediterranean world and it had become evident that God’s salvation extended to both Jews and Gentiles

The book of Acts has a central role in the New Testament: It connects Jesus with the emerging Christian community, and the Gospels with the rest of the New Testament. It frames the proclamation of the Christian message in both Jewish and Gentile settings and underscores the key roles of Peter and Paul in the spread of the Good News throughout the Mediterranean. It is the story of a dynamic message with an outreach to all.

Setting

Luke wrote at a time when the Good News about Jesus Christ was spreading from Jerusalem throughout the Mediterranean world. Luke was probably a Gentile (non-Jew), and his material on Christian origins keeps the needs and outlook of the wider world in mind.

Luke began his presentation of the message of Christ with an account of Jesus’ life (the Gospel of Luke). In the book of Acts, Luke describes how the Christian faith was carried across the Mediterranean world.

It was important for Luke to show that God’s love and mercy reaches out to all people—“God shows no favoritism,” as Peter told Cornelius (Act 10.34). Christ is the only Savior (Act 4.12), and all can believe in him for salvation and new life (see Act 16.30–31). Despite the tendency of Jewish Christians to keep God’s grace to themselves, the church came to the united conclusion that Gentiles are fully included in God’s promises (see Act 15.1–31). The message of the forgiveness of sins and new life through Christ is for all nations.

Summary

The apostles and other followers of Christ were filled with the Spirit and empowered to carry out the great commission (Mat 28.18–20). Acts specifically highlights the ministries of Peter (Act 1.1–Act 12.25) and Paul (Act 13.1–Act 28.31).

Acts follows a geographical outline based on Act 1.8. The Christian message and community of believers spread in Jerusalem (Act 1.1–Act 8.3), in Palestine and Syria (Act 8.4–Act 12.25), and in the Gentile world throughout the Roman empire (Act 13.1–Act 28.31). The closing word in the Greek text of Acts (akōlutōs, “unhindered,” Act 28.31) recalls the unhindered spread of the gospel to Jews (Act 3.1–Act 5.42), Samaritans (Act 6.1–Act 8.40), “God-fearers” (Act 8.26–40; Act 9.32–Act 11.18), and Gentiles (Act 11.19–30; Act 13.1–Act 28.31).

Purposes of Acts

History. Acts describes people, places, and events involved in the early spread of the Good News.

Geography. Acts shows how the message was taken from Jerusalem to Rome (Act 1.8; Act 9.15).

Biography. Acts highlights the ministries of Peter and Paul, who, along with James, were the principal figures leading the early Christian movement. Other influential early Christians—including Stephen, Philip, and Barnabas—also play a significant role.

Evangelism. Acts gives clear examples of how Christian leaders proclaimed the Good News to different audiences (note the speeches of chs Act 2.1–5, Act 7.1–60, Act 10.1–48, Act 13.1–52, Act 22.1–30, Act 26.1–32). Acts shows that the gospel is open to all—not only to Jews but also to Gentiles (Act 2.8–11; Act 8.26–40; Act 10.1–Act 11.18), and not only to men but also to women (Act 5.14; Act 8.12; Act 16.13–15; Act 17.4, Act 17.12, Act 17.34; Act 18.26; Act 21.9).

Politics. Acts presents a strong defense of the Christian faith to Jews (Act 4.8–12; Act 7.2–53) and to Gentiles (Act 24.10–21; Act 26.1–23). Luke argued that Christianity was entitled to the same protection Judaism enjoyed as a religio licita (“permitted religion”) and that it presented no danger to the Roman state (Act 18.14–16; Act 19.37; Act 23.29; Act 25.25; Act 26.32).

Authorship

Luke was Paul’s traveling companion (see Act 16.10 and footnote there) and was with Paul during his later years (2Ti 4.11). Several passages in Acts appear in the first person (“we”; Act 16.10–18; Act 20.5–15; Act 21.1–18; Act 27.1–Act 28.16), which suggests that Luke was with Paul for those parts of his journeys. In Colossians, Luke is referred to as the “beloved doctor,” listed as one of several non-Jews who were working with Paul (Col 4.11–14; see also Phm 1.24). Paul was grateful for Luke’s love and support as a faithful coworker and friend.

Luke was also apparently the author of the Gospel that bears his name. The theological viewpoint is consistent throughout both works. Each book highlights the historical reality of God’s action in redemption, the role of the Holy Spirit, the central place of prayer, the importance of angels, and the fulfillment of Old Testament promises in the life of Jesus and in the Christian community. Luke saw God as governing the course of history for the outworking of the divine purpose.

As a responsible Hellenistic historian, Luke used good historical methods and described his procedures in detail, showing concern to write an accurate and orderly account of the truth of Christian origins (Luk 1.1–4). Where other sources can verify Luke’s writings, he proves to have been careful and accurate in handling historical details. Luke was also a literary artist, a gifted storyteller who perceived and clearly portrayed the hand of God in the development of the Christian mission and community. He is one of the most important historical writers between Polybius, “the last of the great Greek historians” (100s BC), and Eusebius, the first major church historian (AD 275–339).

Place and Date of Writing

The precise location from which Acts was written is unknown, but Rome is likely.

Acts is generally dated between the early 60s AD and the end of the expected life span of Paul’s coworkers and traveling companions (mid-80s AD). Many scholars have opted for a date after AD 70, arguing that Luke used Mark as one of his sources (presuming that Mark was written in the late 60s). However, Acts makes no mention of the outcome of Paul’s trial (around AD 62); the death of James, the Lord’s brother (early 60s AD); the persecution of Christians carried out by Nero following the fire of Rome in AD 64; the deaths of Peter and Paul (around AD 64–65) and Nero (AD 68); the Jewish revolt (AD 66); or the destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70). Acts ends with Paul under house arrest (AD 60–62). Thus, a valid case can be made that Luke wrote Acts before AD 64. Those who date Acts after AD 70 would answer that Luke omits these events because they were not pertinent to his purpose (see Act 1.8; Act 9.15; Act 28.31).

Recipients

The book of Acts is the second volume of a two-part work (see Luk 1.1–4; Act 1.1–2). The prime recipient of Luke’s Gospel and the book of Acts was Theophilus (Luk 1.3; Act 1.1), whose name means “one who loves God.” Theophilus is described by the title, “most honorable” (Luk 1.3), which is used elsewhere for Roman governors such as Felix and Festus (Act 23.26; Act 24.2–3; Act 26.25). Theophilus may have been Luke’s patron and benefactor. He was a Gentile who had received Christian instruction (Luk 1.4). Luke wanted him and others to have an accurate understanding of the Christian faith and of its spread into the Mediterranean world so they could be “certain of the truth” concerning Christianity (Luk 1.4).

Literary Characteristics

The material of Acts is presented carefully and precisely (e.g., Act 11.28; Act 18.2), and the accuracy of the information has often been affirmed by archaeology, geography, and related studies. Luke has combined historical accuracy and detail with a gift for vivid and dramatic descriptions (e.g., Act 5.17–32; Act 12.1–17; Act 14.8–20; Act 16.11–40; Act 27.1–44).

Acts is punctuated by the powerful speeches of Peter, Stephen, James, and Paul (Act 2.14–40; Act 7.2–53; Act 15.13–21; Act 22.3–21). The varied literary styles in Acts fit the cultural settings in a remarkable way. Peter’s sermon on the day of Pentecost has a strongly Jewish character (Act 2.14–40), while Paul’s preaching before the cultured Greek philosophers in Athens uses the forms of Greek oratory (Act 17.22–31). These characteristics all support the historical authenticity of the book, as well as the literary skill of its writer.

Meaning and Message

Acts shows that the Christian faith truly fulfills God’s promises in the Hebrew Scriptures (Act 2.16–36; Act 4.11–12; Act 10.42–43; Act 13.16–41; Act 17.30–31; see Luk 24.25–27, Luk 24.44–47). It also demonstrates that Christ brought salvation (Act 8.35; Act 10.36; Act 16.17, Act 16.30–31), prayer advances God’s Kingdom (Act 1.12–15; Act 2.1–4; Act 4.24–31; Act 12.5), and the Holy Spirit energizes and equips God’s people to carry out their mission (Act 1.8; Act 4.8, Act 4.31; Act 6.3, Act 6.5, Act 6.10; Act 7.55; Act 11.24; Act 13.9, Act 13.52).

Acts shows the importance of the individuals that God chose to carry his message and testify about Christ. At the beginning the apostles—especially Peter—testified about the life and ministry of Jesus (Act 1.22; Act 10.39–41; see Luk 1.2) and explained Jesus’ significance in God’s plan to redeem humanity (Act 2.40; Act 3.15; Act 4.33; Act 10.42). Later, other Christian leaders shared in the task of testifying for their Lord; Stephen and Philip are two outstanding examples of bold witnesses for the faith (Act 7.2–53; Act 8.4–40). Other Christians simply shared their faith as they had opportunity (e.g., Act 8.1–4; Act 11.19–21). Later, God called Paul to participate in this enterprise as his “chosen instrument to take [his] message to the Gentiles and to kings, as well as to the people of Israel” (Act 9.15; Act 22.1–21; Act 26.2–23). Paul, like Peter, occupies a central role in Acts as a major witness for Christ.

The apostles proclaimed that the death and resurrection of Jesus was God’s plan in fulfillment of Scripture (Act 2.22–36; Act 3.15; Act 4.27–28, Act 4.33; Act 7.52; Act 8.32–35; Act 10.38–43; Act 13.26–39). Jesus was the one appointed to redeem humankind, so the apostles’ message was, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved” (Act 16.31). God offers his grace and forgiveness to all, and “there is peace with God through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all” (Act 10.36).

Finally, the book of Acts demonstrates that no opposition can prevent the Good News of Jesus Christ from spreading. The messengers of this good news faced imprisonment, physical harm, and even death. Nonetheless, the message spread from a small group gathered in a room in Jerusalem (Act 1.12–14) to Jews and Gentiles spread across the Roman world. In fact, the book closes with Paul sharing the message freely at the epicenter of the known world (Act 28.30–31).

Chronology of the Apostolic Age

Events in the apostolic age are difficult to date because few precise statements are made about time. Many events, however, can be correlated with known dates in the Roman world.

Events from AD 30 to 50. We know from Roman sources that Herod Agrippa I died in AD 44 (Act 12.23), so his execution of the apostle James and imprisonment of Peter (Act 12.2–17) must have happened before that date.

The famine prophesied by Agabus befell Judea during the reign of Emperor Claudius (Act 11.28–29). When the church in Antioch sent famine relief to the church in Jerusalem, Barnabas and Paul were appointed to carry the money (Act 11.29–30). It was Paul’s second trip to Jerusalem after his conversion. The Jewish historian Josephus dates the famine between AD 46 and 48.

While Paul was in Corinth on his second missionary journey, Gallio was governor of Achaia (Act 18.12). An inscription discovered at nearby Delphi indicates that Gallio’s term was AD 51–52. The incident in Act 18.12–17 probably occurred at the beginning of Gallio’s term. Paul then left Corinth not long afterward, probably in the summer or autumn of AD 52. Paul had spent eighteen months in Corinth (Act 18.11), so he probably arrived in early AD 50. That arrival date is confirmed by Act 18.2. When Paul came to Corinth, Aquila and Priscilla had recently been exiled from Rome. Claudius expelled Jews from Rome in AD 49.

Events from AD 50 to 70. Festus replaced Felix as governor of Judea during Paul’s imprisonment in Caesarea (Act 24.27), probably in the summer of AD 59. This event helps us date events in the rest of the book of Acts. Paul’s arrest (Act 21.33) was about two years beforehand (AD 57). Earlier that spring, Paul had celebrated Passover in Philippi (Act 20.6; April AD 57). Paul had just spent three months in Greece (Act 20.3), probably the winter of AD 56–57 (see 1Co 16.6). Previously Paul had spent three years in Ephesus (Act 20.31; AD 53–56).

After Festus arrived in the summer of AD 59, Paul quickly stood trial and appealed to Caesar (Act 25.1–12). The voyage to Rome most likely began in the fall of AD 59 (Act 27.2) and ended early in AD 60 (Act 28.11–16). Paul stayed in Rome “for the next two years” (Act 28.30). The New Testament does not report the outcome of Paul’s trial, but he was probably released and then recaptured and martyred in Rome along with Peter and many others during Nero’s persecution (around AD 64–65).

In Jerusalem, James the brother of Jesus was stoned to death by the Jewish authorities in AD 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1). Not long afterward, the church in Jerusalem left that doomed city and settled in Pella, one of the cities of the Decapolis east of the Jordan. Thus, when war broke out between the Jews and the Romans in AD 66, the Christians largely escaped its fury. The war ended in AD 70, when Jerusalem and the Temple were destroyed.

Events from AD 70 to 100. The New Testament writers and other early Christians left few records of the period following the destruction of Jerusalem. It is possible that both Matthew and Luke wrote after AD 70, but they did not write about the developments that occurred after AD 70. Similarly, the apostle John probably wrote his Gospel and three letters close to AD 90, but we learn few specifics about the late first-century church from those writings. If Revelation was written in the early 90s AD, then it gives us a glimpse of what the churches in Asia Minor were facing during that time (see Revelation Book Introduction, “Date of Writing”).

As the apostolic age came to a close, the church around the Mediterranean grew and developed, as it would continue to do after the last of the apostles had died and the leadership of the church had passed on to the following generations.
