These scenes help to lift the spirits of persecuted Christians. John lays out his basic vision (Rev 21.1–8) and follows it with two expansions: (1) In Rev 21.9–27, he presents the new Jerusalem as the site of holy perfection; (2) in Rev 22.1–5, he describes the new Jerusalem as the ultimate Garden of Eden that Adam and Eve could have experienced had they not sinned.

The vision involves God’s creation of the new heaven and earth (cp. Gen 1.1 with Isa 65.17; Isa 66.22). The old creation has disappeared—it was subject to decay (see Rom 8.20–21; 2Pe 3.7, 2Pe 3.10). • the sea was also gone: The sea was associated with chaos or the abyss (see study note on Rev Rev 9.1–12) and was sometimes portrayed as a roaring monster (see Psa 46.3; Psa 74.14; see also Job 3.8; Job 41.1–34; Luk 21.25). The new creation will be free from all such evil.

coming down from God: The new creation is a gift from God. In the beginning, God created everything good, and in the end, God will create a new, unbroken world. • This picture of Jerusalem as a beautiful bride (see Isa 61.10) contrasts starkly with the vision of Babylon (or Rome) as the prostitute (Rev 17.4–5; Rev 18.2–3; see study note on Rev 21.9–Rev 22.9).

God’s home is now among his people! Old and New Testament expectations are fully and finally realized. Ever since humanity sinned (Gen 3.1–24), separation from God has been humanity’s greatest problem (Gen 3.23). God has repeatedly called his people to himself through the prophets, through Jesus his Son, and through the presence of the Spirit (see Gen 17.8; Exo 29.45–46; Psa 46.4–5; Psa 95.7; Jer 7.23; Jer 31.33; Eze 34.14; Eze 37.27; Zec 8.8; Joh 14.2–3; Joh 17.24). In the new heaven and new earth, God’s people will finally experience ultimate and everlasting fellowship with God.
no more death or sorrow or crying or pain: See Isa 25.8; 1Co 15.54. God’s people will know the creative wholeness and salvation that Christ brings (see 2Co 5.17; Gal 6.15).

God restates Jesus’ final words from the cross, It is finished! (Joh 19.30; cp. Rev 16.17), connecting Christ’s death with the assurance of eternal life. • I am the Alpha and the Omega: With the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, John portrays God as encompassing total reality and total truth. God was from the Beginning (see Gen 1.1; cp. Joh 1.1–2) and is also the End (see Rev 1.8; Rev 22.13). • Because Christ is supreme and in charge of all things (see Rom 9.5; 1Co 15.28; Eph 1.22–23; Eph 4.5–6), he dispenses the water of life to all who are thirsty for it (see study note on Rev Rev 7.16–17; see also Isa 55.1; Joh 4.10; Joh 7.37–38).

All who are victorious: God’s children who persevere in life will inherit his blessings. Adoption is a covenant relationship; the language of adoption certifies their privileges and responsibilities (cp. Gen 17.8; 2Sa 7.14–16; Jer 31.33; Eze 34.24).

This vice list summarizes sins described throughout Revelation. These sins characterize people who have not experienced adoption by God; their fate is the fiery lake (see Rom 1.29–32; Gal 5.19–21; 2Ti 3.2–5; cp. Exo 20.13–17; see also study note on Rev Rev 20.10). • all liars: John apparently viewed deception as the root of sin; elsewhere he describes Satan as the “father of lies” (Joh 8.44; 1Jo 2.4; see Rev 14.5; Rev 21.27; Rev 22.15; cp. Mat 12.34).

This symbolic vision of the new Jerusalem uses vivid word pictures to describe the bride, the wife of the Lamb—all those who respond to Christ’s message of salvation (see Rev 21.2; Rev 22.17; Eph 5.22–32).

a great, high mountain: In Scripture, experiences with God frequently take place on the mountains (cp. Eze 40.2; see also Exo 3.1; Exo 19.10–25; Deu 34.1–4; 1Ki 18.20–40; 1Ki 19.8–18; Mat 5.1; Mat 15.29; Mat 17.1; Mat 24.3; Mat 28.16). • the holy city . . . descending out of heaven from God: God’s presence and eternal life cannot be reached by human effort but are received as a gift (Eph 2.8–9; cp. 2Co 5.1).

Like the true people of God, the glory of the city reflects God’s glory (cp. Exo 34.29–35; 2Co 3.7–11). • Jasper (see also Rev 4.3; Rev 21.11, Rev 21.18) is opaque on earth; the heavenly jasper is clear as crystal, having a transparency that mirrors God’s purity and integrity.

In this vision, the twelve tribes of Israel represent the redeemed people of God (see Rev 7.4–8; see also Rom 9.6–7). The foundation for this community of God’s redeemed is the twelve apostles of the Lamb. In Jesus, God’s promise to bless all of the families of the earth through Abraham has been fully realized (Gen 12.3).
measure the city: Measuring defines accepted boundaries (contrast the unmeasured section of the Temple, Rev 11.2; see also Eze 40.3–Rev 42.20).
The city is described as a perfect cube. Each dimension is 1,400 miles (Greek 12,000 stadia); the number 12,000 symbolically represents the people of God (see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note).

In the ancient world, walls were important not only to the defense and boundary of a city, but also to its status. That these walls are 216 feet thick (Greek 144 cubits) indicates the strength of God’s redeemed people. The measurement of 144 cubits again uses a multiple of 12 to represent God’s people. A cubit was the length of a man’s forearm, with a standard length of about 18 inches.

The wall is built of jasper (see study note on Rev 21.11; cp. Rev 4.3). The city is fashioned in gold, which is not opaque like earthly gold; rather, like God’s transformed people, the heavenly gold is clear and pure.

The twelve precious stones adorning the foundation stones of the city’s wall are a reminder of the twelve stones on the high priests’ breastplate that represented the people of God (see Exo 28.17–20).
Things that are precious and luxurious on earth are common building materials in heaven.

I saw no temple: This apparent conflict with earlier visions (Rev 11.19; Rev 14.15–17) is resolved by understanding each visionary picture in Revelation as a separate symbolic representation of God’s presence. There is no longer any need for a temple in heaven because God is present with his people.

The vitality, energy, and life of the city are not in institutions or physical sources of power and light, but in the glory of God and the Lamb. The sun and moon were features of the first creation (Gen 1.14–19; see Isa 60.19–20). • the Lamb is its light: Jesus is the light of the world (see Joh 8.12; Joh 9.5; Joh 12.35–36).

The nations: God’s promise to Abraham is fulfilled (Gen 12.3; see Isa 2.3). • In Revelation, the kings of the world usually refer to God’s enemies (Rev 6.15; Rev 17.18; Rev 18.3, Rev 18.9). Now that the enemies have been destroyed (Rev 16.9, Rev 16.11; Rev 19.1–2, Rev 19.19–21), the picture is of God’s glory as reflected in those people who have repented (Rev 14.6–7; cp. Rev 11.13) and walk with God (Rev 5.9; Rev 15.4). • The gates that are never . . . closed contrast with the ancient scene in which closed gates protected cities from enemies, particularly at night. The people enjoy peace and security in God’s supremacy (see Isa 60.11). God’s enemies have been destroyed, and fear and failure have ended (see Zec 14.7; Joh 11.8–10; Joh 12.35–36).

evil (or ceremonially unclean): Spiritual impurity is a basic concern in Revelation (see Rev 21.8). Evil is here generalized as idolatry and dishonesty (see Rev 14.5; Rev 21.8; Rev 22.15). Those who fail to appear in the Book of Life are excluded from the city of God. Only those whose names are written in the Book of Life, the pure of heart (Mat 5.8), will see God.

This part of John’s vision of the city deals with God’s provision of water and food for his people (cp. Exo 16.4, Exo 16.22–24; Eze 47.1–12; Joh 4.10; Joh 6.32–35). Although God originally made a “garden of delight” (Eden) for Adam and Eve, they disobeyed him and lost it (Gen 2.1–3). Now Eden is refashioned and united to the celestial city as God’s marvelous gift for his faithful people.
the water of life: See Rev 7.17; Joh 4.10–15; cp. Exo 17.1–7; Isa 55.1; Eze 47.1–10; Zec 14.8.

Although humans were denied access to the tree of life after they sinned (see Gen 3.22–24), it is now freely available. The tree on each side of the river (cp. Eze 47.12) shows that there is no wrong side of the river in heaven. The tree produces a fresh crop of fruit each month, demonstrating God’s constant provision.

No longer . . . a curse: Ever since the first sin (Gen 3.14–19), humanity has been cursed because of their rebellion against God (see 1Co 16.22). Now rebellion, sin, and the curse are gone forever. • his servants will worship him: Revelation gives glimpses of authentic worship (see Rev 4.1–5; Rev 7.9–17).

The human fears of death and of seeing God (see Gen 16.13; Gen 32.30; Jdg 6.22; Isa 6.5) will be removed. God’s people will bear his name and will see his face with joy (see Mat 5.8; 2Co 3.18; 1Jo 3.2–3).
They will reign with God forever (see Rev 20.4; see also Rev 5.10) in his radiant light that banishes night and the need for lamps (see Isa 60.19–20).

This epilogue to Revelation contains utterances by an angel (Rev 22.6, Rev 22.8–11) and Christ (Rev 22.7, Rev 22.12–19) followed by a concluding plea for Christ’s return (Rev 22.20) and a closing benediction (Rev 22.21). The epilogue has a number of direct verbal connections with the introduction to the book (Rev 1.1–11), and it sums up important themes such as encouraging faithful perseverance, warning evildoers, affirming the authenticity of the prophetic message, and restating the nearness of Christ’s return.

Everything that John records in Revelation is trustworthy and true because God, who has all authority (cp. Mat 28.18), has sent the messenger. But it does not mean these visions are easy to understand.
Blessed: The sixth blessing of Revelation (see Rev 1.3; Rev 14.13; Rev 16.15; Rev 19.9; Rev 20.6; Rev 22.14) is for those who obey. Obedience is key to God’s blessing.

The earlier warning against false worship (see Rev 19.10) is reiterated when John again falls at the feet of the angel. Only God deserves our worship (cp. John the Baptist in relation to Jesus; Joh 1.6–8, Joh 1.26–27; Joh 3.27–35).

Do not seal up: The angel expands John’s initial instruction to “write in a book” (Rev 1.11) and warns against curtailing its communication. Although some things are sealed—God does not reveal everything (cp. Rev 10.4)—what has been written must be communicated so that people will understand the seriousness of the message and that the time is near (see Rev 1.1, Rev 1.3; Rev 22.6–7; cp. Dan 12.4).

Vile people who refuse to accept God’s forgiveness will continue to be vile (see Rev 16.9), yet John reminds the righteous to maintain their integrity. This verse is a warning to evildoers, and it calls the righteous to recognize the crucial significance of Christ’s return relative to their commitments and their actions.

Christ is coming soon . . . to repay all people, not just on the basis of their profession of faith, but according to their deeds (see Rev 2.23; Rev 11.18; Rev 14.13; Rev 20.12–13; see also Pro 24.12; Mat 16.27; 2Co 5.10). Not every statement of belief is genuine (Joh 2.23–25); faith will show itself in actions (Jam 2.14–26). We are indeed saved by the grace and power of God in Christ. Our works do not save us, but they do indicate the seriousness of our confession and provide a just basis for our ultimate reward or punishment.

Blessed are those: In response to the connection between actions and ultimate results (Rev 22.12), the seventh blessing of Revelation (see also Rev 1.3; Rev 14.13; Rev 16.15; Rev 19.9; Rev 20.6; Rev 22.7) promises acceptance for those who wash their robes—those who have been purified by trusting in Christ and following him faithfully (Rev 3.5; Rev 6.11; Rev 7.9–10, Rev 7.14; Rev 19.13; Eph 5.26; Heb 10.22). • enter through the gates of the city: See study note on Rev Rev 21.24–25.

This verse again lists those who are not admitted to contrast with those admitted in Rev 22.14 (see Rev 21.8, Rev 21.27; Rev 22.11). These unrepentant sinners remain outside the city; it is another warning to those who do not repent that they will not be allowed to enter the city of God (Rev 22.14). • The reference to sinners as dogs was a familiar Jewish designation for rejected outsiders (see Mat 7.6; Phi 3.2; also 2Sa 3.8; 2Ki 8.13); Jews used this term to refer to Gentiles (see Mar 7.26–28).

I am both the source of David and the heir to his throne: Jesus validates the message of Revelation (cp. Joh 21.24) by swearing that he is simultaneously the source of David (see Rev 5.5; Isa 11.10) and David’s heir (see Eze 37.23–24; Rom 1.3). • The morning star was a name for the Messiah (see Num 24.17; 2Pe 1.19; cp. Luk 1.78–79).

Come is a repeated invitation and a confession (see Rev 22.20). • the bride: The Lamb’s wife (see Rev 21.9) is the church, the people of God. • The thirsty can drink freely from God’s provision (see Rev 21.6; Rev 22.1; Psa 42.1; Isa 55.1; Joh 4.10–14).

I solemnly declare: John issues an oath to protect the integrity of the book of Revelation. He declares a curse upon anyone who alters the contents of the book or its message (cp. Deu 4.2; Deu 12.32). The curse contrasts with the statement of blessing on all who read aloud, listen to, and obey the prophecy (Rev 1.3). At the time Revelation was written, scribes would sometimes alter books to suit their own views. Early Christians quickly developed means of authenticating both messages and messengers (see Joh 21.24; 1Co 16.21; Gal 6.11; Col 4.18; 2Th 3.17; 1Jo 4.1–3). • Since the time of the early church, the scope and content of the New Testament has been established as the measure of the Christian proclamation. Yet the church continues to be plagued by those who would attempt to reconstruct the borders of Scripture by adding other works that they believe are of equal status with the Bible or by arguing that certain segments of the Bible are unreliable creations of human effort and perception. The genuine church has rejected and will continue to reject efforts to redefine the boundaries of the canon as human and even demonic attempts to alter the basis of the Christian faith.
I am coming soon! See Rev 3.11. • Come, Lord Jesus! Paul uttered the same response (1Co 16.22; see also Phi 4.5).

Revelation closes with a benediction similar to those in Paul’s letters (e.g., Rom 15.33; 1Co 16.23–24). • The fitting final sentence invokes the grace of the Lord Jesus, the foundation of our forgiveness and the basis of our eternal hope.
